10_1016_j_istruc_2025_108285.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Concrete dams, specifically gravity dams and arch dams. Two case studies are presented: a concrete gravity dam (113.0 m maximum height) and a concrete double-curvature arch dam (305.0 m height). The analysis focuses on mechanical parameter identification through displacement data inversion.

- **Material / Medium:** Concrete dam structures with granite foundations. Key material properties analyzed include elastic modulus (E) for dam body and deformation modulus for foundation. Specific properties mentioned: concrete (density 2400 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio 0.167), foundation (density 2790 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio 0.25). The arch dam model includes three concrete zones (A, B, C) with varying elastic moduli.

- **Application & Importance:** Ensuring dam safety and operational reliability through accurate mechanical parameter identification. Concrete dams (constituting ~56% of dams >200m in China) require precise deformation field understanding due to material aging, structural damage, and changing operating conditions. The analysis addresses limitations of conventional laboratory/in-situ testing methods by developing a faster, more efficient inversion approach.

- **Geometry / Domain:** Gravity dam model includes 21,924 nodes and 19,338 elements (primarily C3D8) with foundation extending upstream/downstream to ~twice dam height. Arch dam model contains 62,014 elements and 69,248 nodes with three concrete zones. Boundary conditions: normal constraints around perimeter with fixed constraints at base. The dam-foundation system is analyzed under water level variations (151.61-168.85 m for gravity dam; 1800-1880 m for arch dam), with displacement monitoring at multiple plumb line measurement points (e.g., P1-P3 for gravity dam, PL13-1 to PL13-5 for arch dam).
10_1016_j_istruc_2025_108285.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Normal constraints applied around perimeter; fixed constraints imposed at base; X direction points downstream; Y direction points toward right bank; Z direction points vertically upward; dam-foundation interface with homogeneous granite strata (no fissures); concrete fillet and concrete support cushion interfaces in arch dam model.

- **Loads / Excitations:** Upstream water pressure; reservoir water level variations (151.61 m to 168.85 m for gravity dam; 1800 m to 1880 m for arch dam); hydrostatic component defined as δH = ∑i=1n ai(Hi - H0i) where n=3 for gravity dams and n=4 for arch dams; temperature loads; time-dependent effects.

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Dam body divided into multiple concrete zones with varying mechanical properties (three zones for arch dam: Zone A, B, C); concrete foundation interface; plumb line measurement points distributed across dam structure (P1-P3 for gravity dam, PL13-1 to PL13-5 for arch dam); separation of displacement into hydrostatic, temperature, and time components using HST model.

- **Simulation Type:** 3D Finite Element Model using ABAQUS2022; gravity dam model comprises 21,924 nodes and 19,338 elements (primarily C3D8 with some C3D6); arch dam model contains 62,014 elements and 69,248 nodes; analysis focused on along-riverward horizontal displacement for gravity dam and radial displacement for arch dam; deterministic parameter inversion approach.
10_1016_j_istruc_2025_108285.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Mechanical deformation behavior of concrete dams under hydrostatic loading, specifically the elastic displacement response to water level variations. The hydrostatic component of displacement is isolated from measured data and used as the primary basis for parameter inversion.

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Elastic modulus values for dam body (E_C for gravity dam; E_A, E_B, E_C for arch dam zones)
  - Deformation modulus of foundation (E_R)
  - Hydrostatic displacement components at multiple measurement points (P1-P3 for gravity dam; PL13-1 to PL13-5 for arch dam)
  - Relative displacement differences between two water levels (Δδ)
  - Fitness function value representing error between measured and calculated hydrostatic components
  - Computational time for inversion process

- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize the error between measured hydrostatic displacement components and those calculated by the finite element model through the objective function J(Z) = ∑i=1m ‖ωi(Δδ_Hi^inverse - Δδ_Hi^measure)/Δδ_Hi^measure‖². The method specifically aims to achieve this with high accuracy while significantly reducing computational time compared to traditional FEM-based inversion (93.26% time reduction for gravity dam, 83.97% for arch dam cases).
10_1016_j_istruc_2025_108285.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** 
  - Gravity dam: Maximum height 113.0 m, crest elevation 179.0 m, normal storage level 173.0 m
  - Arch dam: Height 305.0 m, normal reservoir water level 1880 m, dead water level 1800 m
  - Foundation extends upstream/downstream with depth approximately twice dam height
  - Gravity dam analysis limited to 2# left bank water retaining section
  - Arch dam analysis restricted to crown cantilever section (Dam Section 13) with measurement points PL13-1 to PL13-5
  - Parameter search space for elastic modulus constrained to [10,50] GPa for gravity dam and [20,50] GPa for arch dam

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Analysis focuses exclusively on along-riverward horizontal displacement for gravity dam (cross-riverward displacement has larger measurement error)
  - Hydrostatic component must be isolated from measured displacement using HST model before inversion
  - For <5 measurement points, weighting factor ωi is set to 1; for more points, weights assigned based on displacement variation
  - Inversion limited to elastic displacement response (not applicable to plastic deformation)
  - The method assumes homogeneous granite foundation with no fissures in the analyzed sections
  - The study period for water level surge was constrained to May 24-June 22, 2017 (151.61 m to 168.85 m) for gravity dam and June 15-July 15, 2018 for arch dam

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Computational resources: 64-bit OS, 32 GB RAM, Intel i7-9750H CPU, NVIDIA RTX 1660Ti GPU
  - Population size (N) and maximum iterations (T) set to 30 and 100 respectively
  - Each scenario run independently 30 times with average value recorded
  - Surrogate model sample size constrained to range 20D-200D (D=number of inverted parameters; D=2 for gravity dam, D=4 for arch dam)
  - Training/testing sample ratio fixed at 4:1
  - Method requires parameter adjustment for complex environments (e.g., high-altitude regions need freeze-thaw/solar radiation considerations)
  - Not validated for dynamic response analysis or dams in plastic deformation state (stated as future research direction)

10_1016_s2095_7564_15_30273_7.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Tied-arch bridge (Canonica bridge), designed by Giulio Krall around 1950 to replace an iron bridge on the same span. Reinforced concrete tied-arch bridge with Nielsen structure configuration.
- **Material / Medium:** Concrete (unit weight 24.0 kN/m³, Poisson's ratio 0.20, Young's modulus 34 GPa); Steel (unit weight 78.0 kN/m³, Poisson's ratio 0.25, Young's modulus 210 GPa). Four-cell concrete box girder deck with inclined ties made of conventional reinforcement bars in cast-in-place grout.
- **Application & Importance:** Condition assessment of bridge structures to evaluate structural safety under dynamic loads (winds, traffic, earthquakes). Critical for aging infrastructure where initial FE models cannot predict exact structural response due to uncertainties.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Parabolic arch structure with rise/span ratio of 1/6; deck suspended over 75.50 m length; total deck width 12.69 m (two traffic lanes + two pedestrian walkways); girder depth 1.23 m; longitudinal deck slope 2.5%. Bridge spans Adda River with fixed arch footings and spring-supported ends (5E+8 N/m stiffness). FE model comprises 3096 nodes, 1856 beam elements, 36 truss elements, and 1896 shell elements.
10_1016_s2095_7564_15_30273_7.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Arch footings considered fixed; resultant stiffness of all springs at bridge ends is 5E+8 N/m; supports include three degrees of freedom each (two translations and one rotation); bridge divided into three regions with different material properties (regions 1, 2, and 3); ambient vibration testing conducted in frequency range of 0-9 Hz.
- **Loads / Excitations:** Ambient acceleration-time histories recorded for 3600 s at 0.005 s interval using 14 uniaxial piezoelectric accelerometers (WR model 731 A); natural frequency identification through Frequency Domain Decomposition method; operational modal analysis based on output-only time-histories.
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Rigid links between concrete slabs and grid of lateral stringers/transverse cross-beams; ties modeled as truss elements; four-node shell elements used for upper/lower concrete slabs of deck and lower parts of arches; two-node 3D beam elements for lateral box stringers and transverse cross-beams.
- **Simulation Type:** 3D finite element model containing 3096 nodes, 1856 beam elements, 36 truss elements, and 1896 shell elements; global mode analysis (bending and torsional modes); iterative FE model updating using Douglas-Reid method and Rosenbrock optimization algorithm; eigenvalue analysis for natural frequency determination.
10_1016_s2095_7564_15_30273_7.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Modal vibration analysis of a reinforced concrete tied-arch bridge; structural dynamics involving natural frequencies and mode shapes; experimental modal analysis using ambient vibration testing data.

10_1007_s00211_022_01273_4.key_1:
- Elastic wave scattering by rigid obstacles in two dimensions
- Homogeneous and isotropic elastic medium with unit mass density; Lamé constants λ, μ (μ > 0, λ + μ > 0); rigid obstacles; compressional waves (wavenumber κ₁ = ω/(λ + 2μ)¹/²), shear waves (wavenumber κ₂ = ω/μ¹/²)
- Applications in seismology and geophysics for detecting fractures in sedimentary rocks for underground gas and liquid production; relevant to radar, sonar, geophysical exploration, medical imaging, and nondestructive testing
- Two-dimensional domain R² with bounded obstacle D having Lipschitz continuous boundary ∂D; computational domain Ω = B_R\D where B_R is ball of radius R; inner boundary B_R̂ with R > R̂ > 0 such that D ⊂ B_R̂ ⊂ B_R; Example 1: disk obstacle D = B₀.₅ with Ω = B₁\B₀.₅ (R̂ = 0.5, R = 1); Example 2: U-shaped obstacle within {x ∈ R²: -2 < x < 2.2, -0.7 < y < 0.7} with R = 3, R̂ = 2.31
10_1007_s00211_022_01273_4.key_2:
- Rigid obstacle boundary condition: u = 0 on ∂D
- Transparent boundary condition on artificial boundary ∂B_R: Bu = T u + g, where Bv = μ∂rv + (λ + μ)∇·v e_r and T is Dirichlet-to-Neumann operator
- Kupradze-Sommerfeld radiation condition: lim r→∞ r^(1/2)(∂r u^s_p - iκ₁ u^s_p) = 0 and lim r→∞ r^(1/2)(∂r u^s_s - iκ₂ u^s_s) = 0
- Incident wave u^inc as either point source or plane wave (Example 1: u^inc(x) = -κ₁H'(0)(κ₁r)/r [x y]^T - κ₂H'(0)(κ₂r)/r [y -x]^T; Example 2: u^inc(x) = d e^(iκ₁x·d) with d = [1 0]^T)
- Angular frequency ω > 0 as parameter (tested values: ω = 1, π, 2π)
- Lamé constants satisfying μ > 0, λ + μ > 0 (used values: λ = 2, μ = 1)
- Compressional wavenumber κ₁ = ω/(λ + 2μ)^(1/2) and shear wavenumber κ₂ = ω/μ^(1/2) with κ₁ < κ₂
- Scattered field defined as u^s = u - u^inc
- 2D time-harmonic elastic wave scattering problem
- Linear elasticity regime
- Computational domain Ω = B_R\D with artificial boundary ∂B_R (Example 1: R = 1; Example 2: R = 3)
- Truncated DtN operator with parameter N chosen so that truncation error ε_N ≤ 10^-8

10_1016_j_energy_2023_129975.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Thick-walled cylindrical pressure components in steam boilers, specifically the drum-downcomer connection junction. The analysis focuses on optimizing cooling processes for boiler drums and similar pressure vessels.
- **Material / Medium:** 15NiCuMoNb5-6-4 (1.6368) ferritic steel for the pressure vessel; water/steam operating at saturation temperature as the fluid medium. Key steel properties: thermal conductivity λ(T)=37.931+0.0349T-0.0001T²+0.00000006T³ W/(m·K), specific heat capacity c(T)=456.958112+0.221079T-6.088849×10⁻⁵T² J/(kg·K), density ρ(T)=7859.852807-0.289101T-8.567824×10⁻⁵T² kg/m³, heat transfer coefficient h=3000 W/(m²·K), circumferential stress concentration factors αm=2.67 (pressure), αT=1.615 (thermal), allowable stress σal=613.84 MPa.
- **Application & Importance:** To determine optimum cooling rates that minimize shutdown time while preventing circumferential stress at hole edges from exceeding allowable limits. The analysis improves boiler flexibility, reduces greenhouse gas emissions, and enables safer emergency cooling of nuclear reactor vessels. The new method reduces cooling time by approximately 3× compared to the conservative European standard EN 12952-3.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Cylindrical pressure vessel with 1770 mm outer diameter and 85 mm wall thickness, connected to downcomers (159 mm outer diameter, 16 mm wall thickness). Analysis focuses on the drum-downcomer junction where stress concentration occurs at hole edges (points P1 and P2). The domain is modeled with 11-20 radial nodes for finite volume analysis, with critical stress evaluation at the hole edge where thermal and pressure stresses concentrate.
10_1016_j_energy_2023_129975.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Outer surface thermally insulated; inner surface with third-kind boundary condition; heat transfer coefficient h = 3000 W/(m²·K) at inner surface; initial uniform wall temperature T₀ = 346.85 °C; ambient temperature Tₐ = 20 °C; initial fluid temperature equals saturation temperature at p = 15.9 MPa; outer-to-inner radius ratio u = rₒᵤₜ/rᵢₙ; dimensionless radius R = r/rₒᵤₜ; wall thickness s = 85 mm; outer diameter dₒ = 1770 mm; downcomer outer diameter dᵢ = 159 mm; downcomer wall thickness sᵢ = 16 mm; 11-20 radial nodes used in FVM analysis; Fourier number Fo* = 1 threshold for quasi-steady state.

- **Loads / Excitations:** Saturated fluid operating condition (pressure dependent on temperature); pressure-temperature relationship p = A + B(T_f/20)^C where A=0.302310, B=8.344550×10⁻⁴, C=4.260781; allowable stress σ_al = 613.84 MPa; stress concentration factors α_m = 2.67 (pressure), α_T = 1.615 (thermal); material constant φ_m = 4.172 MPa/K; temperature-dependent material properties: λ(T)=37.931+0.0349T-0.0001T²+0.00000006T³ W/(m·K), c(T)=456.958112+0.221079T-6.088849×10⁻⁵T² J/(kg·K), ρ(T)=7859.852807-0.289101T-8.567824×10⁻⁵T² kg/m³.

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Fluid-structure interaction at inner surface; pressure-temperature dependency for saturated fluid; thermal and pressure stress superposition at hole edge (point P₁); circumferential stress at hole edge is sum of thermal stress (α_Tσ_Tφ) and pressure stress (α_mσ_ρφ); fluid temperature determined by third-kind boundary condition at inner surface.

- **Simulation Type:** Transient thermal-stress analysis; 1D radial heat conduction model solved by Finite Volume Method (FVM); 3D Finite Element Method (FEM) for stress analysis; nonlinear analysis due to temperature-dependent material properties; comparison between quasi-steady state (EN 12952-3) and non-quasi-steady state (proposed method); time steps including Δt = 0.5 s for Runge-Kutta method; cooling time comparison showing 450.7 s (proposed method) vs 1324 s (EN 12952-3).
10_1016_j_energy_2023_129975.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Transient thermal-stress analysis of thick-walled cylindrical pressure components; heat conduction in solid domain with temperature-dependent material properties; fluid-structure interaction at inner surface; superposition of thermal and pressure stresses at hole edges; time-dependent temperature distribution through wall thickness during cooling from saturated fluid conditions.

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Circumferential thermal stress (σ_Tφ); circumferential pressure stress (σ_ρφ); total circumferential stress at hole edge (α_mσ_ρφ + α_Tσ_Tφ); time variation of fluid temperature and pressure; temperature distribution across wall thickness at discrete time points; cooling time duration; stress concentration factors (α_m=2.67, α_T=1.615); allowable stress limit (σ_al=613.84 MPa); comparison of cooling times between proposed method (450.7 s) and EN 12952-3 standard (1324 s).

- **Optimization Goal:** Determine the minimum time required to cool the pressure component from initial temperature (346.85°C) to ambient temperature (20°C) while ensuring total circumferential stress at hole edge (point P₁) never exceeds allowable stress (613.84 MPa); achieve the fastest possible cooling rate by optimizing the fluid temperature profile without assuming quasi-steady state temperature distribution; reduce cooling time by approximately 3× compared to the conservative EN 12952-3 standard while maintaining structural integrity.
10_1016_j_energy_2023_129975.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Outer diameter of drum dₒ = 1770 mm; wall thickness s = 85 mm; downcomer outer diameter dᵢ = 159 mm; downcomer wall thickness sᵢ = 16 mm; radial discretization using N = 11-20 nodes for FVM analysis; dimensionless radius R = r/rₒᵤₜ; outer-to-inner radius ratio u = rₒᵤₜ/rᵢₙ; critical stress evaluation limited to hole edge points P₁ and P₂.

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Total circumferential stress at hole edge (point P₁) must not exceed allowable stress σₐₗ = 613.84 MPa (determined for n = 2000 cold starts); fluid must remain in saturated state (pressure-temperature dependency p = A + B(T_f/20)^C); heat transfer coefficient h = 3000 W/(m²·K) at inner surface; initial fluid temperature T₀ = 346.85°C (saturation temperature at 15.9 MPa); final temperature must reach ambient Tₐ = 20°C; stress concentration factors constrained to αₘ = 2.67 (pressure) and α_T = 1.615 (thermal); material constant φₘ = 4.172 MPa/K; Fourier number Fo* = 1 threshold for quasi-steady state formation; cooling time must prevent radial cracks at hole edge where thermal fatigue occurs.

- **Process/Manufacturing:** Optimum fluid temperature variation at cooling start must be simplified for practical implementation (stepwise reduction to minimum value at ~35s); rapid steam discharge capability required due to fluid boiling during depressurization; cooling process must accommodate thermal fatigue from repeated start-up/shutdown cycles; method must be applicable to both steam boiler drums and nuclear reactor pressure vessels; time step constrained to Δt = 0.5 s for Runge-Kutta method in verification calculations; optimization must not assume quasi-steady temperature distribution in pressure element wall.

10_1016_s0045_7825_01_00183_9.key_1:
• **Identity & Domain:** Scaled boundary finite-element method (SBFEM) applied to elastodynamics problems including cracked plates, tunnel structures, spherical domains, and embedded foundations.
• **Material / Medium:** Orthotropic plate with E₁=144.8 GPa, E₂=11.7 GPa, G₁₂=9.66 GPa, ν₁₂=0.21; transversely isotropic rock; materials with shear modulus G, Poisson's ratio ν=0.25, mass density ρ; half-space media with ν=0.25.
• **Application & Importance:** Combines advantages of finite-element and boundary-element methods; reduces spatial dimension by discretizing only the boundary; satisfies radiation condition exactly for unbounded media; handles anisotropic materials without fundamental solutions; avoids singular integrals; calculates stress intensity factors without crack-tip discretization; includes body loads without domain discretization.
• **Geometry / Domain:** Bounded media with 0≤ξ≤1 and unbounded media with 1≤ξ<∞ using dimensionless radial coordinate ξ; scaling center O from which entire boundary is visible; circumferential coordinates η, ζ; specific geometries include edge-cracked plate with crack perpendicular to edge, bimaterial plate with crack terminating at interface, railway tunnel intersecting fault, solid sphere, spherical cavity, cylinder (radius r₀, depth e=r₀) embedded in half-space, and square prism (e=b) embedded in half-space.
10_1016_s0045_7825_01_00183_9.key_2:
• **Boundaries & Constraints:** Displacements ({u}={\bar{u}}) and surface tractions ({t}={\bar{t}}) prescribed as boundary conditions; Bounded media: 0≤ξ≤1; Unbounded media: 1≤ξ<∞; Scaling center O positioned so entire boundary is visible; Side-faces (crack faces, free surfaces) not discretized; Radiation condition at infinity satisfied exactly for unbounded media.
• **Loads / Excitations:** Uniformly distributed shear stress τ₀ applied to edge-cracked plate fixed at base; Concentrated forces P from railway loads on tunnel; Uniform normal displacement u₀ on solid sphere boundary; Body loads included without domain discretization; Frequency domain analysis with displacement amplitudes {u}; Inertial forces represented by ω²ρ{u} term; Body load amplitudes {p} included.
• **Interactions / Interfaces:** Material interfaces between different media not discretized; Interface (boundary visible from scaling center) discretized with surface finite elements; Side-face defined as boundary part passing through scaling center; Analytical displacement solution around crack tip expressed as power series; No discretization required for free, fixed boundaries and interfaces between different materials.
• **Simulation Type:** Elastodynamics analysis; Frequency domain and time domain solutions; 2D and 3D problems addressed; Plane stress conditions for plate examples; Plane strain condition for tunnel example; Axisymmetric for cylinder embedded in half-space; Spherical symmetry for solid sphere and spherical cavity examples; Linear second-order ordinary differential equations solved analytically.

• **Physics Solved:** Linear elastodynamics; Wave propagation in bounded and unbounded media; Stress distribution around cracks; Displacement fields in elastic media; Dynamic response to harmonic excitation; Stress singularities at crack tips; Radiation condition satisfaction at infinity.

• **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Dynamic-stiffness coefficients S^b(ω) and S^∞(ω); Spring coefficients k(a₀); Damping coefficients c(a₀); Stress intensity factors K_I and K_II; Static-stiffness matrices [K^b] and [K^∞]; Mass matrices [M^b]; Powers of singularity at crack tips; Unit-impulse response matrices; Normalized stress intensity factors; Displacements relative to reference points; Equivalent dynamic-stiffness coefficients for spherical and cylindrical geometries.

• **Optimization Goal:** Accurate calculation of stress intensity factors without crack-tip discretization; Efficient computation by reducing spatial dimension by one; Exact satisfaction of radiation condition for unbounded media; Handling of general anisotropic materials without fundamental solutions; Avoidance of singular integrals; Elimination of domain discretization for body loads; Prevention of fictitious eigenfrequencies in unbounded media analysis.

• **Geometric/Design Space:** Scaling center O must be positioned so entire boundary is visible (achieved by subdividing domain into subdomains if necessary); Bounded media constrained to 0≤ξ≤1; Unbounded media constrained to 1≤ξ<∞; When scaling center on boundary, boundary decomposed into side-face A (spatial dimension reduced by one) and interface S; For tunnel example, scaling causes small deviations in interface locations between fault and rock.

• **Performance/Physics Limits:** [C^∞] must be positive definite to satisfy radiation condition (ensuring unbounded medium acts as energy sink); Real parts of eigenvalues [λ] must be smaller than zero for static solution; Sufficient degrees of freedom required to adequately represent wavelength when calculating mass matrix [M^b]; For dynamic analysis of unbounded media, high-frequency asymptotic expansion must be evaluated at high but finite frequency ω_h as starting value.

10_1007_s00211_020_01118_y.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Acoustic wave propagation modeled as a first-order hyperbolic system (wave equation) using mixed finite element methods with BDM1-P0 elements
- **Material / Medium:** Acoustic medium in a bounded Lipschitz domain Ω ⊆ R^d (d = 2 or 3) with velocity u and pressure p described by ∂t u + ∇p = 0 and ∂t p + div u = 0
- **Application & Importance:** Numerical simulation of wave propagation for applications in acoustics, elastodynamics, and electromagnetics; development of efficient explicit time integration methods on unstructured grids as a generalization of finite-difference time-domain methods
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Plane wave test case: Square domain Ω = (-1,1)² with time interval 0 ≤ t ≤ T = 5
  - Scattering test case: Ω = (-1,1)² \ {(x,y) | ‖(x,y+1)‖₂ ≤ 0.2} (square domain with circular obstacle)
  - Boundary conditions: Dirichlet (∂Ω_D), Neumann (∂Ω_N), and scattering (∂Ω_S) boundaries
  - Computational domain boundaries: (-1,1), (1,1), (1,-1), (-1,-1) with curved scattering boundary at bottom center
10_1007_s00211_020_01118_y.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition: p = 0 on ∂Ω × (0,T)
  - Scattering boundary condition: p = 0 on ∂Ω_S (circular obstacle boundary)
  - Dirichlet boundary condition: p = p^pw on ∂Ω_D (inflow boundary)
  - Neumann boundary condition: n · u = 0 on ∂Ω_N (no-flow boundary)
  - Domain boundaries: (-1,1), (1,1), (1,-1), (-1,-1) for the square domain
  - Mesh requirement: Uniformly shape regular mesh with γh_K ≤ ρ_K ≤ h_K for all elements K

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Plane wave excitation defined by u^pw(x,y,t) = (k1,k2)^T g(k1x + k2y - t), p^pw(x,y,t) = g(k1x + k2y - t)
  - Wave profile g(s) = e^-2(s+5)^2 for plane wave propagation test
  - Wave profile g(x) = 2e^-10(x+3)^2 for scattering test
  - Wave vector k = (1/√5)(2,1) for plane wave propagation test
  - Wave vector k = (1,0) for scattering test
  - Initial conditions: u(0) = u0, p(0) = p0 in Ω
  - Time interval: 0 ≤ t ≤ T = 5 for plane wave test
  - Time interval: 0 ≤ t ≤ T = 2 for scattering test

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Wave scattering at circular obstacle boundary ∂Ω_S
  - No-slip condition at solid boundaries (n · u = 0)
  - Plane wave entering computational domain from left boundary (∂Ω_D)

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Transient simulation in time domain
  - 2D computational domain (R^2)
  - First-order hyperbolic system for acoustic wave propagation
  - Unstructured simplicial mesh discretization
  - Time discretization using leapfrog method
  - CFL condition: τ ≤ h/c where c is the constant of the inverse inequality
  - Mass-lumped mixed finite element method with BDM1-P0 elements
10_1007_s00211_020_01118_y.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Acoustic wave propagation modeled as a first-order hyperbolic system (wave equation) with velocity and pressure fields governed by ∂t u + ∇p = 0 and ∂t p + div u = 0

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Velocity field (u) and pressure field (p) in L2(Ω) norm
  - Error metrics: |||e||| = max₀≤tₙ≤T ||e(tₙ)||L²(Ω)
  - Discrete solution errors: |||û - ûₕ|||, |||p - pₕ|||
  - Discrete error contributions: |||ûₕ - û*ₕ|||
  - Post-processed solution errors: |||u - ũₕ|||, |||p - p̃ₕ|||
  - Convergence rates (eoc) measured through mesh refinement studies

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Achieve second-order accuracy (O(h² + τ²)) in both space and time after post-processing
  - Enable efficient explicit time integration through mass-lumping while preserving second-order information
  - Overcome the formal first-order limitation of mass-lumped methods via super-convergence exploitation
  - Maintain computational efficiency with block-diagonal mass matrices while achieving optimal convergence rates
  - Prove and demonstrate that ||u(tₙ) - ũⁿₕ||L²(Ω) + ||p(tₙ) - p̃ⁿₕ||L²(Ω) ≤ C(h² + τ²) for the fully discrete scheme
10_1007_s00211_020_01118_y.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Domain must be a bounded Lipschitz domain Ω ⊆ R^d (d = 2 or 3)
  - Computational domain must be polyhedral for finite element discretization
  - Mesh must be uniformly shape regular: γh_K ≤ ρ_K ≤ h_K for all elements K with constant γ > 0
  - Quasi-uniform mesh requirement: γh ≤ h_K ≤ h for all elements K with constant γ > 0
  - Square domain Ω = (-1,1)² for plane wave propagation test case
  - Scattering domain Ω = (-1,1)² \ {(x,y) | ‖(x,y+1)‖₂ ≤ 0.2} with circular obstacle

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - CFL condition: τ ≤ h/c where c is the constant from inverse inequality ‖div v_h‖_L2(Ω) ≤ ch⁻¹‖v_h‖_L2(Ω)
  - Theoretical accuracy limitation: mass-lumped semi-discretization is formally only first-order accurate without post-processing
  - Convexity assumption (A2) required for certain theoretical results: "Ω is convex"
  - Time step constraint: τ = T/N with N > 1 and time steps t_n = nτ
  - Stability condition: τ ≤ 2/√λ_max where λ_max is the largest eigenvalue of (div v_h, div v_h)_Ω = λ(v_h, v_h)_h,Ω

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Finite element spaces constrained to BDM1-P0: V_h = P1(T_h)^d ∩ H(div;Ω) and Q_h = P0(T_h)
  - Mass-lumping strategy constrained to vertex rule integration: (u_h, v_h)_h,Ω = ∑_K ∫_K I_K(u_h · v_h)dx
  - Time discretization constrained to leapfrog scheme for explicit integration
  - Post-processing requires solution of local element problems for pressure and global system for velocity
  - Mesh refinement must project vertices at curved boundaries to exact geometry after each refinement step

10_1016_j_compstruc_2012_01_001.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Enriched finite element method for wave propagation problems in solids and structures; includes time harmonic and transient scalar wave equations, elastic bar impact, 2D elastic wave propagation (P, S, Rayleigh waves), and acoustic pressure wave propagation.

- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Elastic isotropic homogeneous medium with E=200×10⁹ N/m², ρ=8000 kg/m³ for bar impact problem
  - Semi-infinite elastic medium with P-wave velocity 3200 m/s, S-wave velocity 1847.5 m/s, density 2200 kg/m³ for Lamb problem
  - Inviscid fluid for acoustic pressure wave propagation
  - Material thickness=0.01 m in bar impact problem

- **Application & Importance:** Solving wave propagation problems where standard finite element method fails due to spurious oscillations, numerical dispersion, and dissipation errors; enables accurate wave propagation analysis with coarser meshes by embedding harmonic functions; critical for long-distance wave propagation where standard methods accumulate significant errors.

- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - One-dimensional elastic bar (0.5 m length, 0.01 m thickness)
  - Two-dimensional domain [0,1]×[0,1] with symmetry for scalar wave equation
  - Semi-infinite domain of 4000×2000 m² for Lamb problem
  - Unbounded domain containing circular cylinder (radius=1) for acoustic pressure wave problem
  - Mesh configurations include 4-node and 9-node elements with various distortion ratios
  - Receivers positioned at 640 m and 1280 m from force application point in Lamb problem
10_1016_j_compstruc_2012_01_001.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**  
  - Left end of bar: u=t m, v=1 m/s  
  - Right end of bar: u=0 m, v=0 m/s  
  - Dirichlet boundary: u = u_Su on S_u  
  - Neumann boundary: τ(u)·n = f_Sf on S_f  
  - Unbounded domain boundary: f_Sf = -c_Lρ[ν·n]n - c_Tρν_T where ν_T = ν - [ν·n]n  
  - Scalar wave problem: u(0,y) = 0, ∂u(x,2)/∂y = 0, ∂u(x,0)/∂y = 0, ∂u(2,y)/∂x = 4π (8π for case 2)  
  - Perfectly matched layer with γ₁ = 1 for |x| < 2; 1 + ik(3-|x|) for 2 ≤ |x| ≤ 3; γ₂ = 1 for |y| < 2; 1 + ik(3-|y|) for 2 ≤ |y| ≤ 3  

- **Loads / Excitations:**  
  - Ricker wavelet source: F(0,0,t) = 10[1 - 2π²f²(t-0.25)²]exp(-π²f²(t-0.25)²), c=1, f=6Hz  
  - Vertical force as Ricker wavelet with 14.5Hz central frequency applied at (2000m,2000m)  
  - Pressure boundary condition g = ∂P/∂n on cylindrical boundary (x₀=0.5, y₀=0, k=22.06)  

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**  
  - Boundary condition for infinite domain results in velocity dependent term in equations  
  - Perfectly matched layer used to model unbounded domains in acoustic wave problem  
  - No absorbing boundary conditions used in scalar wave problem as wave doesn't reach boundary within 0.95s  

- **Simulation Type:**  
  - Transient analyses with implicit time integration (trapezoidal rule)  
  - Time harmonic analyses  
  - Two-dimensional analyses  
  - Linear elastic analyses  
  - Real arithmetic (complex arithmetic used only for acoustic pressure wave with perfectly matched layer)  
  - Consistent mass matrix with α parameter for ill-conditioning (M = (1-α)M_consistent + αM_lumped)  
  - Mesh types: 4-node and 9-node elements with enrichment cutoff numbers (n,m) ranging from (0,0) to (4,4)
10_1016_j_compstruc_2012_01_001.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**  
  - Wave propagation phenomena including time harmonic and transient scalar waves  
  - Elastic wave propagation with P-waves, S-waves, and Rayleigh waves  
  - Impact-induced stress waves in elastic bars  
  - Acoustic pressure wave propagation in inviscid fluid  
  - Numerical dispersion and dissipation effects in wave propagation  

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**  
  - Displacement distributions in x and y directions  
  - Velocity distributions in impact problems  
  - Relative error in L² norm  
  - Solution error e_h = u(x,0) - u_h(x,0)  
  - Condition number of coefficient matrices  
  - Wavefront sharpness at impact boundaries  
  - Time history of displacements at receiver points (640m and 1280m from source)  
  - Spurious oscillations in numerical solutions  
  - Distortion ratio effects on solution accuracy  

- **Optimization Goal:**  
  - Minimize numerical dispersion (period elongation) and dissipation (amplitude decay)  
  - Reduce spurious high-frequency oscillations in stress and velocity predictions  
  - Control wavefront sharpness in impact problems  
  - Improve accuracy of wave propagation velocity representation  
  - Maintain solution accuracy with coarser meshes by increasing element degrees of freedom through harmonic enrichment  
  - Overcome ill-conditioning of algebraic equations while preserving solution accuracy
10_1016_j_compstruc_2012_01_001.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**  
  - Bar impact problem domain: 0.5 m length, 0.01 m thickness  
  - Semi-infinite elastic domain for Lamb problem: 4000×2000 m²  
  - Fundamental wavelengths constrained to Λx=2Δx and Λy=2Δy (where Δx and Δy are typical element sizes)  
  - Element types limited to 4-node and 9-node configurations  
  - Distortion ratio defined as ratio of longest element side to shortest element side in domain  
  - Cutoff numbers (n,m) for harmonic enrichment typically limited to values between 1 and 3 for optimal performance  

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**  
  - Time step constraints: Δt=0.00625s (CFL=0.5) for scalar wave equation; Δt=2.5×10⁻⁸s for bar impact; Δt=0.0008s for Lamb problem  
  - Condition number increases dramatically with cutoff numbers (2.8E+16 for (n,m)=(4,4) with α=0)  
  - P-wave reaches outer boundary during 1s solution time in Lamb problem  
  - Numerical dispersion and dissipation errors must be controlled through enrichment rather than mesh refinement  
  - Method currently limited to linear elastic analyses (not validated for nonlinear material behavior)  
  - Maximum cutoff numbers practically limited to (n,m)=(3,3) or (4,4) due to ill-conditioning  

- **Process/Manufacturing:**  
  - Computational cost increases rapidly with cutoff numbers (18, 50, 98 degrees of freedom per node for n=m=1,2,3 respectively)  
  - Bandwidth of assembled stiffness matrix becomes very large, especially in three-dimensional analyses  
  - Standard Gauss-Legendre integration requires increasing number of integration points as cutoff number increases  
  - Implicit time integration requires iterative solution methods for large bandwidth systems  
  - Method requires significant further research for nonlinear and multi-physics applications  
  - Current implementation limited to two-dimensional problems despite potential for 3D extension  
  - Complex arithmetic required for perfectly matched layer applications (whereas most analyses use real arithmetic)

10_1007_s12206_008_1204_0.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Unsteady scalar convection-diffusion-reaction equation in two dimensions, analyzed through four test cases: square pulse flow, rotation of two Gaussian pulses, triangular wave inflow convection, and skewed convection with reaction influence
- **Material / Medium:** Scalar quantity φ transported through convection (velocity field v), with diffusion coefficient ε (e.g., ε=10⁻⁴) and reaction coefficient κ (varied as 0, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10); no specific physical material is modeled
- **Application & Importance:** Solving transport phenomena in fluid dynamics where convection terms create discontinuities and high gradients; developing an explicit method that provides stabilized numerical solutions without requiring artificial diffusion
- **Geometry / Domain:** Four different test domains: unit square (0,1)×(0,1) for problems 4.1, 4.3, 4.4; square domain (-0.5,0.5)×(-0.5,0.5) for problem 4.2; uniform grids S1-S5 with 32×32 to 512×512 cells and an unstructured grid with 1,624 elements (20 cells per boundary) for problem 4.4
10_1007_s12206_008_1204_0.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**  
  - Square pulse flow (4.1): Inflow boundary condition at y=0 where φ=1 for 0.4≤x≤0.6, otherwise 0; outflow boundary at x=1 where spurious oscillations may occur  
  - Rotation of Gaussian pulses (4.2): Domain boundaries at ±0.5 in both x and y directions  
  - Triangular wave inflow (4.3): Inflow boundary at x=0 with φ(0,y)=100(y-0.25) for 0.25≤y≤0.5 and 100(0.75-y) for 0.5≤y≤0.75, otherwise 0; outflow boundary at x=1  
  - Skewed convection (4.4): φ=1 along boundaries x=0 and y=1; φ=0 along other boundaries  
  - Barth and Jespersen limiter function imposed at outflow boundaries to eliminate spurious oscillations  

- **Loads / Excitations:**  
  - Velocity fields: u=x, v=1-y (4.1); u=-4y, v=4x (4.2); u=0.05, v=0 (4.3); u=0.15, v=0.1 (4.4)  
  - Initial conditions: φ=0 for problems 4.1, 4.3, and 4.4; two Gaussian pulses for problem 4.2 with centers at (-0.25,0) and (0.25,0), standard deviation σ=0.0447  
  - Diffusion coefficient ε=10⁻⁴ for problems 4.2 (second test case) and 4.4  
  - Reaction coefficient κ=0, 0.01, 0.1, 1, and 10 for problem 4.4  

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**  
  - Convection-diffusion-reaction equation coupling: φ_t + ∇·(vφ) - ∇·(ε∇φ) + κφ = q  
  - Finite volume method discretizes the spatial domain while finite element technique determines gradient quantities at cell faces  

- **Simulation Type:**  
  - Unsteady (time-dependent) scalar transport problems  
  - 2D simulations on both uniform grids (S1:32×32, S2:64×64, S3:128×128, S4:256×256, S5:512×512) and unstructured grid (1,624 elements for problem 4.4)  
  - Explicit time integration with time step determined by Δt = C·min_i(|Ω_i|/max_j=1,2,3|v_n,ij|, |Γ_i^c|²/2ε) where 0<C≤1  
  - Final time t=2π for problem 4.2 (one rotation period); t=15 for problem 4.3
10_1007_s12206_008_1204_0.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Unsteady scalar convection-diffusion-reaction transport phenomena in two dimensions, including pure convection, convection-dominated diffusion, and reaction-influenced convection-diffusion problems

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**

- **Optimization Goal:**  
  - Develop an explicit method that provides stabilized numerical solutions without requiring artificial diffusion  
  - Achieve second-order spatial and temporal accuracy (O(Δt, Δx²))  
  - Maintain solution stability at outflow boundaries without spurious oscillations through Barth and Jespersen limiter  
  - Demonstrate convergence to exact solution as grid is refined

10_4028_www_scientific_net_amr_498_183.key_1:
• **Identity & Domain:** Vibration-assisted extrusion tapping process for internal thread formation in metal workpieces, using finite element method (FEM) simulation with simplified linear scratch models.

• **Application & Importance:** Reduces tapping torque and improves thread forming quality compared to traditional extrusion tapping; addresses defects like split crest formation and high torque requirements in internal thread manufacturing for aerospace, automotive, and instrument industries.

• **Geometry / Domain:** Multiple-tooth model simplified from M10 extrusion tap; geometric parameters: α₁=8°, α₂=30°, W=0.375 mm, L=1.2 mm, P=1.5 mm, Δh=0.084 mm; scratch speed=20 mm/sec; 15 scratch passes at 0.025 mm depth increments; vibration directions: axial (perpendicular to scratch) and screw-type (parallel to scratch).
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amr_498_183.key_2:

• **Loads / Excitations:** Torque (M) applied to extrusion tap; scratch speed=20mm/sec; sine wave vibration; vibration directions: axial (perpendicular to scratch) and screw-type (parallel to scratch); frequencies: 50Hz, 200Hz, 500Hz (low); 1000Hz, 2000Hz, 5000Hz (high); amplitudes: 2μm, 5μm, 10μm.

• **Interactions / Interfaces:** Frictional contact between multiple-tooth and workpiece; metal material flow along radial direction during extrusion; vibration transmitted to workpiece via clamp.

• **Simulation Type:** 3D transient analysis; simplified linear scratch model using DEFORM-3D; Johnson-Cook nonlinear material model accounting for strain hardening, strain-rate hardening and thermal softening; rigid tool with deformable workpiece.
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amr_498_183.key_3:

• **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Scratch force (proxy for tapping torque); thread forming geometry; split crest severity and size; material flow patterns; scratch force waveforms under different vibration parameters.

• **Optimization Goal:** Reduce tapping torque (measured by scratch force reduction); improve thread forming quality by minimizing split crest formation; determine optimal vibration parameters (frequency, amplitude, direction) for maximum torque reduction while maintaining thread integrity.
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amr_498_183.key_4:
• **Geometric/Design Space:** Multiple-tooth model parameters fixed: α₁=8°, α₂=30°, W=0.375 mm, L=1.2 mm, P=1.5 mm, Δh=0.084 mm; multiple-tooth simplified from M10 extrusion tap; lead hole diameter approximately equal to pitch-diameter of internal thread; 15 scratch passes at 0.025 mm depth increments; multiple-tooth placed at 0.025 mm depth under workpiece surface.

- **Material / Medium:** 304 stainless steel tube (6 mm outer diameter × 1 mm wall thickness); density 7.93 g/cm³; yield stress 260.01 MPa; Poisson ratio 0.3; elastic modulus 207.97 GPa; anisotropic properties characterized by Hill48 yield criterion with R₁₁=1, R₂₂=0.665, R₃₃=0.744
- **Application & Importance:** Tube formability research for aerospace, chemical, oil/liquid transport, shipbuilding, and medical equipment applications; enables production of tubes with varying bending radii without changing dies; reduces mold fabrication costs compared to traditional bending technologies
- **Geometry / Domain:** Cylindrical tube structure with planar bending; cross-section transforms from circular (D₀=6 mm) to elliptical (Dₘₐₓ, Dₘᵢₙ) during bending; free bending process consists of five sections: straight Section 1 (L1), transition Section 1 (S1), arc section (S2), transition Section 2 (S3), and straight Section 2 (L2); bending parameters include offset U, bending radius R, and bending angle θ
10_1007_s00170_024_14975_w.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Guide mechanism fixed (Figure 9)
  - Tube moved along Y-axis at constant speed V (Section 3.2)
  - Symmetry plane along X direction (Figure 13)
  - Offset U = 0 during straight sections L1 and L2 (Section 2.2)
  - Offset U increases to Umax during transition section S1 (Section 2.2)
  - Offset U = Umax during arc section S2 (Section 2.2)
  - Offset U decreases to 0 during transition section S3 (Section 2.2)
  - Tube modeled as deformable body, bending die and bearings modeled as rigid bodies (Section 3.2)

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Axial force PU applied to tube (Section 2.1)
  - Force PL causing displacement in X direction (Section 2.1)
  - Bending moment M = PU × A + PL × U (Section 2.1)
  - Distance A = 11.5 mm between bending die center and guiding mechanism front (Section 3.2)
  - Tensile test conducted at 1 mm/min rate (Section 3.1.1)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Coulomb friction with penalty contact method between tube and other components (Section 3.2)
  - Friction coefficient = 0.05 (fully lubricated parts) (Section 3.2)
  - Contact between tube and bending die (Figure 1)
  - Contact between tube and bearings (Figure 1)

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Abaqus/Explicit (Section 3.2)
  - Transient dynamic analysis (Section 2.2)
  - 3D model with solid elements (C3D8R) for tube (Section 3.2)
  - 5 nodes in tube thickness direction (Section 3.2)
  - Mass scaling factors tested from 1×10³ to 8×10³ (Section 4.2)
  - Relative mesh density values: 0.285, 0.428, 1, 1.711, 4.561 (Table 6)
  - Half-tube model with symmetry plane (Figure 13)
10_1007_s00170_024_14975_w.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Anisotropic tube deformation during free bending process
  - Material flow behavior under axial force and bending moment
  - Springback characteristics of 304 stainless steel tubes
  - Cross-section distortion (ellipticity) during bending
  - Wall thickness variation (thinning on outer bend, thickening on inner bend)
  - Contact mechanics between tube and bending components

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Bending angle (maximum error 3.77% between simulation and experiment)
  - Bending radius (maximum error 2.64% between simulation and experiment)
  - Wall thickness distribution (peak location inaccuracy of 1.16%)
  - Cross-section ovality ((Dmax - Dmin)/D0 × 100%)
  - Ratio of ALLKE/ALLIE (kinetic to internal energy) for model stability assessment
  - Computation time for different modeling approaches

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Balance computational accuracy and efficiency in finite element modeling
  - Achieve maximum simulation error < 10% for critical parameters while minimizing computation time
  - Identify optimal mass scaling factor (6000) where ALLKE/ALLIE ratio = 9.38% < 10%
  - Determine optimal relative mesh density (1.711) that balances accuracy (4.41% error) and efficiency
  - Establish finite element model with maximum error of 3.77% compared to experimental results
  - Reduce computation time by 51.4% using half-tube model with only 0.98% loss in accuracy
10_1007_s00170_024_14975_w.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Tube outer diameter fixed at 6 mm with 1 mm wall thickness (Section 3.1.1)
  - Distance A = 11.5 mm between bending die center and guiding mechanism front (Section 3.2)
  - Tensile specimen dimensions: φ4 × 55mm with Lc=34.5mm and L0=22.5mm (Figure showing tensile specimen)
  - Cross-section transformation limited to Dmax and Dmin from original D0=6mm (Figure 19)
  - Bending radius must be large enough to avoid excessive cross-section distortion (Figure 20)
  - Deformation zone length (A) affects bending radius (Section 2.2)

  - Maximum acceptable error for bending radius is 2.64% (Section 5.1)

  - Maximum acceptable cross-section ovality error is 0.51% (Section 5.3)
  - Friction coefficient fixed at 0.05 for fully lubricated parts (Section 3.2)
  - Anisotropic parameters constrained by R11=1, R22=0.665, R33=0.744 (Table 1)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**

  - Whole tube tensile testing required for tubes with outer diameter < 16mm (Section 3.1.1)
  - Guide mechanism must remain stationary throughout bending operation (Section 2.1)
  - Tube must be fed continuously in Z-direction at constant speed V (Section 2.2)
  - Bending process constrained to five specific sections (L1, S1, S2, S3, L2) with defined movement patterns (Section 2.2)
  - Cyclic loading-unloading tests required to characterize variable Young's modulus (Section 3.1.3)
  - Relative mesh density of 1.711 (0.5mm × 0.5mm element size) required to balance accuracy and efficiency (Section 4.4)

10_1016_j_finel_2010_03_001.key_1:
- Compressible inviscid flows governed by Euler equations for planar and axisymmetric cases
- Working medium is gas with specific heat ratio (γ) as parameter in energy equation
- Method combines Least Squares Finite Element Method (LSFEM) with spring analogy-based grid adaptation
- Four test cases analyzed: supersonic channel flow with 4% height-to-length bump, axisymmetric jet flow, nozzle flow with shock, and shock reflection problem
- Supersonic channel flow domain has parabolic arc bump with curved lower wall defined by y = {0 for -1.5 < x < -0.5, R² - x² + b for -0.5 < x < 0.5, 0 for 0.5 < x < 1.5}, where b = (α² - 0.25)/2α and R = 0.25 + b²
- Axisymmetric jet flow domain extends 70 Rj in axial direction and 20 Rj in radial direction
- Nozzle geometry defined by area function A(x) = {(0.1398 + 0.0347 tanh(-9x + 2.5))² for 0 ≤ x ≤ 0.5, (0.1398 + 0.0347 tanh(9(x-1) + 2.5))² for 0.5 ≤ x ≤ 1}
- Shock reflection problem domain has inlet conditions (ρ, u, v, p) = (1.0, 2.9, 0.0, 0.7143) and top boundary conditions (ρ, u, v, p) = (1.7, 2.6193, 0.5063, 1.5282)
- Initial coarse mesh for supersonic channel flow consists of 65×17 nodes
- Initial coarse mesh for shock reflection problem consists of 61×21 nodes
- Nozzle flow simulation uses 60×20 mesh
- Jet flow simulation uses 60×26 elements with clustering in normal direction to capture mixing layer variations
- Inlet boundary condition for supersonic channel flow: ρ = 1.0, u = 4M∞y(1-y), v = 0.0, p = 1/γ, M∞ = 1.65
- Back-pressure of p = 0.5 used to generate shock in nozzle flow
- Time step reduced from 0.1 to 0.05 during adaptation cycles to reduce artificial viscosity near shocks
- Steady state declared when maximum error (L₂ norm of ΔQ) reaches order of 1E-5 or less
- Potential core length of jet reaches 10 diameters in simulation, compared to experimental range of 8-10 diameters
- Sonic point in jet reached between 22-24 diameters in simulation, compared to experimental range of 18-20 diameters

10_1007_s00211_017_0884_8.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Mathematical framework for conforming approximation of convex functions using finite element methods, specifically for solving optimization problems with convexity constraints
- **Material / Medium:** Convex functions in finite element spaces P^k(T), triangulations/meshes (2D and 3D), convex domains Ω ⊂ R^d, optimization problems with convexity constraints
- **Application & Importance:** Solving optimization problems with convexity constraints including monopolist problem (economics), Newton's problem of least resistance (aerodynamics), projection on convex functions set, gradient flows in Wasserstein spaces, and computation of convex envelopes
- **Geometry / Domain:** Convex open bounded domain Ω ⊂ R^d (d ≥ 1) with various triangulations including Delaunay triangulations, Chevron meshes, uniform refinements, adaptive meshes, and cube triangulations into six tetrahedra; mathematical constraints include convexity conditions ∇²u_h(x) ⪰ 0 and [∇u_h^T n_E]_E ≥ 0 on interior edges

- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Convexity constraints: ∇²u_h(x) ⪰ 0 for all x ∈ int(T), T ∈ T 
  - Gradient jump constraints: [∇u_h^T n_F]_F ≥ 0 for all x ∈ relint(F), F ∈ F_i(T) 
  - Monopolist problem: u ≥ 0 on domain (1,2)² 
  - Newton's problem: 0 ≤ u ≤ L on domain Ω = {x ∈ R²: |x| < 1} 
  - Function value constraints: 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ 1 for constrained cases 
  - Gradient constraints: ∇u(x) ≥ 0 for constrained cases 
  - Non-degenerate triangulations: diam T ≤ h diam Ω, diam B_T ≥ ρ₁ diam T for all T ∈ T_h 
  - Assumption 3.1: [∇ψ_h^T n_F]_F ≥ c_kink h for all interior facets F 

- **Loads / Excitations:** 
  - Monopolist problem objective: ∫(1,2)² (1/2 |∇u(x)|² + u(x) - x^T∇u(x)) dx 
  - Newton's problem objective: ∫Ω 1/(1 + |∇u(x)|²) dx 
  - Projection problem objective: (1/2)∫Ω |∇(u - f)|² + (u - f)² dx 

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** 
  - Gradient discontinuities across element boundaries (interior facets) 
  - Relationship between mesh geometry and convexity constraints 
  - Interaction between Hessian conditions and gradient jump conditions 
  - Uniformly acute triangulations with interior angles < π/2 in A-scalar product

  - 2D and 3D domains with convex Ω ⊂ R^d

  - Projection onto the set of convex functions in H¹(Ω)
  - Solutions to monopolist problem and Newton's problem of least resistance

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**

  - L²(Ω) error norm between uh and target function

  - Number of unknowns (#UK), linear inequalities (#LI), linear matrix inequalities (#MI)

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Minimize projection error: (1/2)‖uh − f‖²_H¹(Ω)
  - Minimize monopolist problem objective: ∫(1,2)² (1/2|∇u(x)|² + u(x) − x^T∇u(x)) dx subject to u convex, u ≥ 0
  - Minimize Newton's problem objective: ∫Ω 1/(1 + |∇u(x)|²) dx subject to u convex, 0 ≤ u ≤ L

  - Enforce convexity constraints while minimizing objective function

10_1007_s00211_017_0884_8.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** 
  - Domain Ω must be open and convex
  - Triangulation must be non-degenerate: diam T ≤ h diam Ω, diam B_T ≥ ρ₁ diam T for all T ∈ T_h
  - For quasi-uniform meshes: diam T ≥ ρ₂ h diam Ω
  - Mesh must satisfy Assumption 3.1: existence of ψ_h ∈ P¹(T_h) with [∇ψ_h^T n_F]_F ≥ c_kink h for all inner facets F
  - For 2D meshes: uniformly acute triangulations (interior angles < π/2 in A-scalar product), δ-protected Delaunay triangulations, or uniform refinements of initial mesh satisfying Assumption 3.1
  - Chevron mesh family possibly violates Assumption 3.1
  - 3D meshes require tetrahedral elements with uniformly acute interior angles

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** 
  - Convexity constraints: ∇²u_h(x) ⪰ 0 for all x ∈ int(T), T ∈ T
  - Gradient jump constraints: [∇u_h^T n_F]_F ≥ 0 for all x ∈ relint(F), F ∈ F_i(T)
  - Monopolist problem constraint: u ≥ 0 on domain (1,2)²
  - Newton's problem constraints: 0 ≤ u ≤ L on domain Ω = {x ∈ R²: |x| < 1}
  - Constrained function values: 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ 1
  - Constrained gradients: ∇u(x) ≥ 0
  - Regularity requirement for convergence: u ∈ W^{k+1,∞}(Ω) for Theorem 3.2
  - For P³ elements, direct enforcement of gradient jump condition (5b) is impractical

- **Process/Manufacturing:** 
  - Finite element space must have polynomial degree k ≥ 2 (P¹ approximation is impossible per [10])
  - For k=2: Hessian is constant per cell (enabling (d+1)N_T^T semi-definite inequalities)
  - For constrained function values: use of Bernstein basis with coefficients in [0,1]
  - For gradient constraints: non-negative gradient requires ∇(f|_T)(v) ≥ 0 at all vertices
  - Augmented-Lagrangian method required for solving optimization with convexity constraints
  - Theoretical convergence rate in H¹(Ω) is O(h^{k-1}) for polynomial degree k
  - Heuristic error estimator η²_T used for adaptive mesh refinement: η²_T = ∑_F h²_F(|[∇u^T_h n_F]_F(x_F_1)|² + |[∇u^T_h n_F]_F(x_F_2)|²)

10_1007_s11666_022_01453_6.key_1:

10_1016_j_mtcomm_2025_111514.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Metal Inert Gas (MIG) welding process of 304L stainless steel butt joints, focusing on thermo-mechanical behavior and microstructural evolution.
- **Material / Medium:** 304L stainless steel base material (ASTM A240) with tensile strength 500–700 MPa, yield strength 200–350 MPa, elongation 30–60%, and hardness 92 HRB; SS308Si electrode wire filler material with chemical composition including 19.77% Cr and 10% Ni.
- **Application & Importance:** Optimizing welding parameters to achieve optimal mechanical properties for industrial applications in abattoirs and beverage industries where 304L stainless steel is widely used; understanding temperature distribution, cooling rates, residual stress, and microstructural evolution to enhance weld quality in repair and manufacturing of mechanical components.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Butt joint configuration with 100 mm × 100 mm × 5 mm stainless steel sheets; 1 mm welding gap between base metals; tensile test specimens prepared according to ASTM E8/E8M-13a standards; 3D finite element model with rectangular geometry featuring fusion and heat-affected zones at the center; Gaussian-distributed heat source model for thermal analysis.
10_1016_j_mtcomm_2025_111514.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Five contact areas identified: upper clamp face (A) contacting upper weld sample face 1; bottom clamp face (B) contacting lower weld sample face 2; left-side tag welding connecting workpieces 1 and 2 at points C and D; contact between weld samples and yellow fixture; frictionless contact between weld samples and supporting fixture; 1 mm welding gap between base metals; 3D rectangular geometry with fusion and heat-affected zone at center; temperature-dependent material properties (elastic modulus, yield strength, Poisson's ratio, thermal properties); density constant at 7.87 g/cm³.
- **Loads / Excitations:** Gaussian-distributed heat source model with heat flux q(r) = q_max·e^(-3r²/R²); welding current at 100 Amp, 120 Amp, and 140 Amp; welding voltage at 21 V, 22 V, and 23 V; welding speed at 3.33 mm/s, 3.57 mm/s, and 3.85 mm/s; heat transfer efficiency η = 70%; heat input calculated as Q = V·I·v·η; 3D heat source with 95% of heat concentrated within region R².
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Frictionless contact between weld samples and supporting fixture; heat loss through convection and radiation; temperature-dependent material properties updated during welding process; fine mesh at weld bed interface; sequential thermo-mechanical coupling between thermal and mechanical analysis.
- **Simulation Type:** 3D transient thermal analysis with time-stepped heat source movement; sequentially linked thermo-mechanical model; hexahedral mesh element type C3D8T; finite element method using ANSYS Workbench 2021 R2; temperature-dependent material properties with constant density; homogeneous and isotropic material assumption.
10_1016_j_mtcomm_2025_111514.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Transient thermal behavior and sequential thermo-mechanical response during MIG welding; temperature distribution and cooling rate dynamics; residual stress development (longitudinal and transversal); microstructural evolution in weld and heat-affected zones; phase transformation effects on mechanical properties.
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Temperature profiles over time at 5 mm from weld center; peak temperatures in fusion zone (1978.35–2613.35°C); cooling rates in 500–800°C range (2.54–6.08°C/s); longitudinal residual stress (σz); transversal residual stress (σx); equivalent stress distribution; heat input values (0.418–0.647 kJ/mm); yield strength (183.7–202.6 MPa); tensile strength (424.4–625.0 MPa); strain at fracture (22.28–35.92 mm/mm); hardness in weld zone (97.73–102.9 HRB) and heat-affected zone (101.1–105.5 HRB); microstructural characteristics including delta ferrite morphology and grain size.
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize yield strength, tensile strength, strain at fracture, and hardness in both weld and heat-affected zones; minimize residual tensile stress to improve fatigue life; achieve optimal microstructure with globular delta ferrite dispersed homogeneously in austenite matrix; identify optimal process parameters (100 Amp current, 23 V voltage, 3.85 mm/s welding speed) that provide the highest grey relational grade (0.6748) indicating best overall mechanical performance.

- **Geometric/Design Space:** 100 mm × 100 mm × 5 mm stainless steel sheets; 1 mm welding gap between base metals; tensile specimens prepared according to ASTM E8/E8M-13a standards; rectangular geometry with fusion and heat-affected zone at center in FEM model; 20 mm × 40 mm × 5 mm polished specimens for microstructural and hardness testing.
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Welding machine voltage limited to 60 V with current range of 5–300 Amp; heat transfer efficiency fixed at η = 70%; temperature-dependent material properties with density constant at 7.87 g/cm³; cooling rate calculated specifically for 500–800°C range critical for phase transformation; peak temperatures in fusion zone constrained between 1978.35°C and 2613.35°C; heat input constrained between 0.418–0.647 kJ/mm across experiments.

10_5516_net_01_2014_066.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Neutron transport calculation for nuclear reactor eigenvalue problems using Discontinuous Finite Element Method (DFEM) with discrete ordinate (Sₙ) angular discretization. Coarse Mesh Finite Difference (CMFD) acceleration applied to DFEM-Sₙ calculations. 3-D DFEM-Sₙ code FEDONA developed for general geometry applications.

- **Material / Medium:** UO₂ (Uranium dioxide), MOX (Mixed Oxide fuel), water reflector. Two-group cross sections (IAEA problem), seven-group cross sections (C5G7MOX problem). Macroscopic total cross section (Σₜ) and scattering cross section (Σₛ). Vacuum and reflective boundary conditions applied in benchmark problems.

- **Application & Importance:** Source convergence acceleration for eigenvalue calculations in large reactor problems. CMFD reduces number of fission source iterations from 175 to 9 for IAEA problem (reduction factor 19.4). Critical for practical analysis of fast neutron systems including fast liquid metal cooled reactors or fusion breeding blankets where general geometry handling is required.

- **Geometry / Domain:** IAEA3D problem: 170 cm × 170 cm × 380 cm rectangular domain with 189,684 tetrahedral elements (pitch=4.39 cm, CM size=20.0 cm). C5G7MOX problem: 64.26 cm × 64.26 cm × 214.2 cm rectangular domain with 157,021 tetrahedral elements (pitch=2.04 cm, CM size=10.71 cm). 2D test problems with 3×3, 5×5, 7×7, and 9×9 assembly arrays (widths 53.55 cm to 182.07 cm). Unstructured tetrahedral meshes combined into rectangular coarse mesh geometries for CMFD. Reflective boundary conditions at outer surfaces, vacuum boundaries in some configurations.
10_5516_net_01_2014_066.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Reflective boundary condition applied at outer surfaces of the domain and at top/bottom surfaces for 2D problem modeling; Vacuum boundary condition applied at some surfaces; Reflective boundary condition used for tetrahedron element classification (1 in/3 out, 2 in/2 out, 3 in/1 out element types); Element surfaces aligned with rectangular coarse mesh surfaces for CMFD calculation.

- **Loads / Excitations:** Fission source term as primary driver for eigenvalue calculations; Scattering sources including self-scattering and scattering from other energy groups; Angular quadrature set {Ω̂ₘ, ωₘ} for discrete ordinate calculations; Isotropic scattering term in the transport equation.

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Discontinuous angular fluxes at element interfaces requiring special treatment for current calculation; Coarse mesh surface current determined by element surface area ratio weighting; Alternating calculation scheme between CMFD and DFEM-Sn with restriction (coarse mesh average flux calculation) and prolongation (flux ratio-based update) processes; Node angular flux reconstruction using incoming partial current ratios at reflective boundaries.

- **Simulation Type:** Eigenvalue problems (not fixed-source); 3D and 2D simulations (2D problems modeled as 3D slices with reflective boundaries at top/bottom); Discrete Ordinate (Sₙ) method with S₄ angular quadrature set; Multigroup calculations (2-group for IAEA problem, 7-group for C5G7MOX problem); Steady-state neutron transport calculations; Unstructured tetrahedral mesh geometry with rectangular coarse mesh structure.
10_5516_net_01_2014_066.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Neutron transport equation solved using Discontinuous Finite Element Method (DFEM) with discrete ordinate (Sₙ) angular discretization; Eigenvalue (k-eff) calculations for nuclear reactor criticality; Source iteration convergence process for fission source distribution.

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** RMS error of fission source distribution; Number of transport sweeps/outer iterations; Eigenvalue (k-eff); Acceleration factor (ratio of iterations with/without CMFD); Computing time reduction factor; Residual reduction ratio for inner iteration termination; Spectral radius of CMFD iteration matrix; Coarse mesh average fluxes and net currents.

- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize number of fission source iterations required for convergence; Achieve RMS fission source error below 10⁻⁴ and eigenvalue convergence below 10⁻⁶; Maximize acceleration factor (demonstrated up to 27.3× for 9×9 2D problem); Maintain stable convergence for large dominance ratio problems; Reduce computing time while preserving accuracy (demonstrated 21.2× time reduction for IAEA problem).
10_5516_net_01_2014_066.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Rectangular coarse mesh geometries used for proof-of-principle demonstration (non-orthogonal geometries possible in general); Coarse mesh size must be sufficiently small to maintain stable convergence (21.42 cm maximum width tested); Coarse mesh size must be integer fraction of assembly size (1/16, 1/4, or full assembly); Element configuration must remain consistent across different coarse mesh sizes; Average element pitch constrained to ~2.5 cm for 2D test problems.

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Optical length in thermal energy group must remain below threshold (deterioration observed when >10); Eigenvalue convergence criterion limited to 10⁻⁶; Fission source RMS error criterion limited to 10⁻⁴; Residual reduction ratio for inner iteration termination limited to 10⁻⁴; Spectral radius of CMFD iteration matrix must remain <1 to avoid divergence; Acceleration effectiveness limited by problem size (2D lattice problems show deficient performance due to small dominance ratio).

- **Process/Manufacturing:** Tetrahedral element surfaces must align with rectangular coarse mesh surfaces; CMFD computing time must remain <1% of total calculation time for efficiency; Element-by-element calculation requires predetermined sweeping order based on angle-element surface relation; Angular quadrature set limited to S₄ in all test calculations; Original p-CMFD formulation required modification to include surface flux term for proper partial current calculation.

  - T2Q discretization (modified EI-FEM) multiplies mesh nodes by ≈3 for same number of elements to avoid volumetric locking

• Interactions / Interfaces: Frictional contact between die and tube; relative sliding between die and tube due to axial load; compression of urethane rod against tube in axisymmetric model; tube-die contact initiating immediately upon pressure application.

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109502.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Vertical Tuned Liquid Column Damper (VTLCD) system for structural vibration control
- **Material / Medium:** Water (liquid phase, density 998.2 kg/m³, viscosity 1.003×10⁻³ kg/(m·s)); air phase (density 1.2 kg/m³, viscosity 0.018×10⁻³ kg/(m·s)); container structure with 0.10 m × 2.24 m cross-section
- **Application & Importance:** Control of vertical vibrations in civil engineering structures under seismic loads; addresses limitation of conventional TLCDs that only control horizontal vibrations; critical for bridges, floors, and offshore structures experiencing vertical motion from earthquakes, vehicle traffic, or wave action
- **Geometry / Domain:** Inclined U-shaped container system with symmetrical slopes at 70° angle; long vertical tube initial liquid depth V₁ = 1.24 m; short vertical tube initial liquid depth V₂ = 0.37 m; inclined tube length H₁ = 0.93 m; container heights 1.61 m (long tube) and 0.74 m (short tube); dual-container configuration symmetric about XZ plane; liquid depth ratio χ = 0.3; mounted on wheels with springs (2759 N/m) and dashpots (173 N·s/m)
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109502.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Fixed support representing ground; frictionless support ensuring motion only in YZ-plane; containers slide along 70° inclined slopes without friction; structure constrained to vertical motion only; symmetrical dual-container configuration; liquid depth ratio χ = 0.3; container connected to bracket via springs (2759 N/m) and dashpots (173 N·s/m)
- **Loads / Excitations:** Six historical earthquake records (Coalinga 1983, Chi-Chi 1999, El Centro 1940, Kobe 1995, Loma Prieta 1989, Northridge 1994); horizontal PGA values: 4.5 m/s² (Coalinga), 3.8 m/s² (Chi-Chi), 3.4 m/s² (El Centro), 2.8 m/s² (Kobe), 6.2 m/s² (Loma Prieta), 2.7 m/s² (Northridge); vertical PGA values: 5.6 m/s² (Coalinga), 3.1 m/s² (Chi-Chi), 2.1 m/s² (El Centro), 3.7 m/s² (Kobe), 4.3 m/s² (Loma Prieta), 1.3 m/s² (Northridge); harmonic force (0.9 Hz, 2 N amplitude); stochastic force (0.5-1.5 Hz frequency range, 8 N amplitude)
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Two-way fluid-structure coupling; pressure and viscous forces transferred from fluid to solid domain; structural displacements transferred from solid to fluid domain; iterative solution updates; symmetrical container arrangement where horizontal forces cancel out
- **Simulation Type:** Two-way fluid-structure coupling with FVM for fluid domain and FEM for solid domain; time-domain and frequency-domain analysis; transient structural analysis; sweep-frequency calculation; nonlinear analysis with equivalent linearization for damping effects
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109502.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Vertical structural vibration dynamics coupled with liquid column oscillation in inclined U-shaped containers; fluid-structure interaction between vibrating structure and damper system; energy transfer from structure to liquid through container motion; dynamic response of VTLCD-structure system under harmonic and seismic excitations
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Dynamical Magnification Factor (DMF); structural displacement response; liquid natural frequency and tuning ratio; phase angles of structural, container, and liquid motions; normalized displacement amplitudes (û, ŷ); control efficiency (peak and RMS); optimized parameters including frequency tuning ratios (φf, φc), flow resistance coefficient (δ), container damping ratio (ζc), liquid depth ratio (χ), and inclination angle (θ)
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize the maximum structural displacement response (DMF_max) across all excitation frequencies; achieve three equal resonance peaks in the frequency response curve; optimize liquid depth ratio (χ ≈ 0.3) and maximize inclination angle (θ ≈ 70°); minimize vibration control efficiency loss while maintaining practical design constraints
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109502.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Liquid initial depth ratio constrained to 0.3 ≤ χ ≤ 0.7; angle of inclination constrained to 20° ≤ θ ≤ 70°; frequency tuning ratios constrained to 0.2 ≤ φf ≤ 3.0 and 0.2 ≤ φc ≤ 3.0; flow resistance coefficient constrained to 1 ≤ δ ≤ 120; container damping ratio constrained to 0 ≤ ζc ≤ 0.2; container height must exceed initial liquid depth to prevent splashing
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Liquid displacement must satisfy y/V₁ << 1 for analytical model validity; mass ratios μf and μc constrained by structural load-bearing capacity; liquid natural frequency varies in real-time based on structural and container vertical accelerations; optimized design requires three equal resonance peaks in frequency response; VTLCD must be tuned to specific structural vibration mode (e.g., 0.45 Hz for bridge application)
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Containers must slide freely along inclined slopes (cannot be fixed); symmetrical dual-container configuration required to ensure vertical-only reaction force; wheels necessary for container movement along slope; spring-dashpot system must provide specified stiffness (2759 N/m) and damping (173 N·s/m); geometric dimensions must allow practical manufacturing (e.g., 0.10 m × 2.24 m tube cross-section for bridge application)

10_1016_j_heliyon_2024_e24166.key_1:
- Identity & Domain: Aluminum honeycomb panel thermal analysis using representative volume element (RVE) and finite element method (FEM) for multiscale homogenization

- Material / Medium: Aluminum alloy as solid component with air-filled cells; Solid volume fraction: 0.02; Effective thermal conductivity tensor: [k_eff] = [1.3965 0 0; 0 1.389 0; 0 0 2.74] W/m/°C; Homogenized medium density: 55 kg/m³; Homogenized medium specific heat capacity: 830 J/kg/°C

- Application & Importance: Thermal behavior analysis under transient conditions; Validation shows maximum temperatures of 1101.9°C (real structure) vs 1096.4°C (homogenized medium) at t=600s; Achieves over 77°C temperature reduction with thickest panel under convective conditions; Modal analysis demonstrates frequency correlation between real and homogenized structures (0-72 Hz difference across 1013.8-9735.8 Hz range)

- Geometry / Domain: Hexagonal unit cell with side length: 5 mm; Cell angle: 60°; Thickness in z-direction: 10 mm; Overall dimensions: 105 × 60.6 × 10 mm³; Real structure mesh: 494,263 elements and 464,965 nodes; Homogenized medium mesh: 16,430 elements and 22,464 nodes; Orthotropic thermal conductivity with principal axes aligned to x, y, z directions
10_1016_j_heliyon_2024_e24166.key_2:
- Boundaries & Constraints: Time-dependent heat flux on upper surface; heat convection on bottom surface with ambient temperature 22 °C and heat transfer coefficient 8 W/m²/°C; other boundaries thermally insulated; bottom and top surfaces with convective boundary conditions; one side ambient temperature follows ISO 834 standard curve; thermal radiation with ambient included; Dirichlet boundary conditions for constant thermal gradient; RVE boundary temperatures defined by T(x₁,x₂,x₃) = T₀ + (∇T̅(i)·e→i)xᵢ

- Loads / Excitations: Time-dependent heat flux following half sine wave pattern with peak ~10,000 W/m²; ISO 834 standard temperature-time curve: T(t) = 20°C + 345*log₁₀(8*t + 1)°C; time-dependent ambient temperature on fire-exposed side

- Interactions / Interfaces: Computational domain contains high conductive metal and very low conductive air (only solid part contribution considered); heat transfer governed by heat conduction equation; RVE-based homogenization representing heterogeneous honeycomb structure as equivalent homogeneous orthotropic material; thermal performance characterized by effective thermal conductivity tensor

- Simulation Type: Transient thermal analysis; 3D analysis; nonlinear problem with Newton-Raphson solvers using arc-length method; FEM-based numerical solution; temperature-dependent material properties; orthotropic thermal conductivity tensor; RVE-based homogenization approach; structural modal analysis for natural frequencies
10_1016_j_heliyon_2024_e24166.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Transient thermal conduction in aluminum honeycomb structures; orthotropic thermal behavior using RVE-based homogenization; temperature-dependent material properties; natural vibration modal analysis

- Target Outputs (Metrics): Effective thermal conductivity tensor components (k_xx=1.3965, k_yy=1.389, k_zz=2.74 W/m/°C); temperature distribution at t=250s (545.75-572.91°C), t=600s (1062.3-1101.9°C), t=900s (498.8-507.8°C); temperature difference (ΔT) between upper and lower surfaces; natural frequencies for modes 1-6 (1013.8-9735.8 Hz for honeycomb structure); temperature rate of change (dT/dt); minimum temperature at bottom surface under varying panel thicknesses

- Optimization Goal: Validate homogenization approach through comparison with real structure (maximum temperature difference <5.5°C at peak heating); demonstrate computational efficiency (16,430 elements vs 494,263 elements); analyze thermal insulation performance with varying panel thicknesses (achieves >77°C temperature reduction with thickest panel); establish strong correlation between modal responses (frequency difference 0-72 Hz across 1013.8-9735.8 Hz range)
10_1016_j_heliyon_2024_e24166.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: Hexagonal unit cell side length constrained to 5 mm; Cell angle fixed at 60°; Thickness in z-direction constrained to 10 mm; Overall body dimensions constrained to 105 × 60.6 × 10 mm³; Solid volume fraction fixed at 0.02; Homogenized medium mesh limited to 16,430 elements (vs 494,263 elements in real structure)

- Performance/Physics Limits: Maximum temperature constrained by ISO 834 standard curve reaching ~900°C at 60 minutes; Temperature difference (ΔT) between surfaces constrained to ~90°C after 60 minutes; Analysis constrained to temperature range where aluminum properties remain valid (up to melting point); Thermal conductivity tensor constrained to orthotropic form due to honeycomb symmetry; Thermal model neglects internal convection and radiation contribution; Only solid part contribution considered in thermal behavior (air contribution ignored)

- Process/Manufacturing: Computational constraints requiring homogenization due to "enormous computing cost" of modeling entire honeycomb structure; Temperature-dependent material properties constrained by published aluminum data; Analysis constrained to 60-minute duration for ISO 834 fire test; Mesh refinement constrained by available hardware resources; Homogenization approach limited to representative volume element that must contain statistically representative microstructure while being computationally manageable

10_1016_j_compstruc_2004_03_024.key_1:
- The research develops a technique for prescribing displacements along side-faces in the scaled boundary finite-element method for static elasto-static problems
- Example 1 models a rigid circular footing of radius R on an elastic half-space with Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3 and shear modulus G
- Example 1 exact vertical stiffness: 4GR/(1-ν)
- Example 2 models an infinitely long strip footing of width 2b on a homogeneous half-space with Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3 and shear modulus G
- Example 2 rocking stiffness: M/φ = (1-ν)G/χ where χ = (1+λ)/2 with λ = (1-ν)/(1-2ν)
- Example 3 models a flexible bearing block bonded to a rigid underlying support with Young's modulus E and Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3 (plane stress)
- Example 3 determines 3×3 stiffness matrix relating horizontal force (H), vertical force (V), and moment (M) to horizontal displacement (u), vertical displacement (v), and rotation (φ)
- Error targets: 2% for Examples 1 and 2, 1% for Example 3
- Example 1 achieves ~1% error in stiffness with 28 degrees of freedom and <0.1% error with 60 degrees of freedom
- The method effectively handles stress singularities at the edges of rigid footings
- The scaled boundary finite-element method uses domains with two radial boundaries (side-faces) where boundary conditions can be satisfied with high accuracy
- Example 2 vertical stress distribution beneath footing follows σy = −M(1−ν)/[πb²(1−(x/b)²)½]

10_1016_j_tws_2024_111854.key_4:

10_1016_j_cej_2024_152109.key_1:

10_1016_j_cej_2024_152109.key_2:

- **Simulation Type:** 3D finite element analysis; Ogden hyper-elastic model for mechanical behavior; Transient dynamic analysis for impact testing; Steady shear and oscillatory modes for rheological characterization; Flow dynamics simulation of conical nozzles; Thermal gravimetric analysis (TGA) over 30-800 °C temperature range
10_1016_j_cej_2024_152109.key_3:

10_1016_j_cej_2024_152109.key_4:

10_1016_j_finel_2007_07_001.key_1:

10_1016_j_finel_2007_07_001.key_3:

10_1016_j_finel_2007_07_001.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Rotor system with L = 300 mm, L₁ = 8 mm, L₂ = 133 mm (simulation) or 188 mm (experiment), L₃ = 18 mm, d₁ = 9.5 mm, d₂ = 76 mm; crack location constrained to shaft segment L₂ (β = e/L₂); normalized crack parameters α, β ∈ [0.1, 0.9]; crack width = 0.2 mm; crack depths δ = 3.8 mm and 7.2 mm (corresponding to α = 0.2 and 0.4)

10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_345_346_8.key_1:
