10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_345_346_8.key_3:

10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_345_346_8.key_4:

10_1016_j_engappai_2024_109755.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Wave propagation in laminated composite structures using unified-input extended physics-informed neural networks (Uni-XPINNs)
- **Material / Medium:** Isotropic elastic materials including copper (E=65.79 GPa, ν=0.387, ρ=8800 kg/m³) and epoxy (E=4.07 GPa, ν=0.375, ρ=1142 kg/m³); materials arranged in layered configurations with different mechanical properties per layer
- **Application & Importance:** Nondestructive examination, ultrasonic testing, composite material optimization, and acoustic device design; critical for aerospace, marine, automotive, and civil infrastructure applications where wave propagation characteristics determine structural integrity assessment
- **Geometry / Domain:** Multilayered structures with layers numbered 1 to n from left to right; x-axis along thickness direction, y-axis along left surface; each layer has thickness h with layer-specific subscript; vertical dimensions greatly exceed horizontal dimensions; structures can be single-layered, double-layered, or four-layered with perfectly bonded interfaces between layers
10_1016_j_engappai_2024_109755.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Fixed boundary condition: u(x=0,t)=0 and u(x=h₁,t)=0 for fixed-fixed single-layer structures
  - Stress-free boundary condition: ∂u/∂x(x=0,t)=0 and ∂u/∂x(x=h₁,t)=0 for free-free single-layer structures
  - Left surface displacement excitation: u₁(x₁=0,t)=q(t)
  - Right surface fixed condition: uₙ(xₙ=hₙ,t)=0 for odd n, uₙ(xₙ=0,t)=0 for even n
  - Right surface stress-free condition: ∂uₙ/∂xₙ(xₙ=hₙ,t)=0 for odd n, ∂uₙ/∂xₙ(xₙ=0,t)=0 for even n
  - Initial displacement field: uᵢ(xᵢ,t=0)=Gᵢ(x)
  - Initial velocity field: ∂uᵢ/∂t(xᵢ,t=0)=gᵢ(x)

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Harmonic boundary excitation: u₁(x₁=0,t)=A₀sin(3πt) for single-layered structures
  - Harmonic boundary excitation: u₁(x₁=0,t)=A₀sin(t) for double-layered structures
  - Harmonic boundary excitation: u₁(x₁=0,t)=A₀sin(0.3t) for four-layered structures
  - Excitation amplitude: A₀=1 in all cases
  - Body forces: f=0, f=f₀×10⁵, f=f₀×10⁶, f=f₀×10⁷, f=f₀×10⁸ where f₀=ρᵢg
  - Initial conditions: u(x,t=0)=G(x)=0 and ∂u/∂t(x,t=0)=g(x)=3πsin(3πx)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Perfectly bonded interfaces between adjacent layers
  - Displacement continuity: u₂ₐ(x₂ₐ=h₂ₐ,t)=-u₂ₐ₋₁(x₂ₐ₋₁=h₂ₐ₋₁,t) for adjacent layers
  - Stress continuity: σ₂ₐ(x₂ₐ=h₂ₐ,t)=σ₂ₐ₋₁(x₂ₐ₋₁=h₂ₐ₋₁,t) for adjacent layers
  - Hybrid-handed coordinate systems with right-handed for odd layers and left-handed for even layers
  - Compatibility conditions applied at all interfaces between layers

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Transient wave propagation analysis
  - One-dimensional analysis along x-axis (thickness direction)
  - Nondimensionalized using first layer parameters (h₁, c₁₁, ρ₁)
  - Single-layered, double-layered, and four-layered structure configurations
  - Linear elastic analysis with homogeneous materials
  - Comparison with analytical solutions and FEM simulations
  - Three error metrics: relative root mean square error (RE1), relative absolute error (RE2), and mean square error (MSE)
10_1016_j_engappai_2024_109755.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Elastic wave propagation in laminated composite structures, specifically longitudinal wave mode along the thickness direction (x-axis), governed by Navier's equations with body forces included

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Time-varying displacement fields (u) across space (x) and time (t)
  - Wave incidence, reflection, and refraction characteristics at material interfaces
  - Relative root mean square error (RE1), relative absolute error (RE2), and mean square error (MSE) for validation
  - Wave velocity in different material layers
  - Energy reflection and conduction at interfaces between dissimilar materials

10_1016_j_cma_2024_117585.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Quasi-static fracture growth in brittle solids using Discontinuity-Enriched Finite Element Method (DE-FEM). The method models discrete crack propagation including branching and merging without remeshing.
- **Material / Medium:** Polymethylmethacrylate (PMMA) with E = 2.98 GPa, ν = 0.35, Gc = 285 N/m; material with E = 20.8 GPa, ν = 0.3, Gc = 1000 N/m; unit modulus material with E = 1, ν = 0; sandstone with ρ = 2650 kg/m³, E = 35 GPa, ν = 0.3, Gc = 16.64 N/m. Both plane stress and plane strain conditions applied depending on test case.
- **Application & Importance:** Modeling brittle fracture which poses significant hazard due to unpredictable and abrupt failure. The method enables prediction of crack paths in brittle materials without remeshing, particularly for complex crack patterns including multiple propagating cracks, branching, and merging.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Compact tension (CT) specimen with initial crack length a₀ = 2.74 mm; modified CT specimen with a₀ = 13.47 mm; asymmetric notched three-point bending test specimen; edge-notched plate for SIF verification; square specimen (2 mm side length) with 10 randomly distributed cracks for multiple crack propagation analysis. All specimens contain traction-free cracks within continuous domains with prescribed boundary conditions.

- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Prescribed displacement field ū on ΓD; prescribed traction t̄ on ΓN; traction-free cracks (σ · nΓ = 0 on ΓC); vertical displacement at points a and b with horizontal movement constrained (Δuy = 0.1 mm increment for CT specimen); vertical displacement increment of Δū = 0.02 mm at top edge center (asymmetric notched bending); asymptotic displacement field ūI prescribed to entire boundary of edge-notched plate; simply supported bottom boundary in multiple crack propagation example.
- **Loads / Excitations:** Monotonically increasing opening displacement at 4×10^-4 mm/s (CT specimen); uniform traction at top edge incremented by Δt̄ = 10 MPa per time step (multiple crack propagation); vertical displacement increment at loading points.
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Multiple traction-free cracks within domain; cracks defined as piece-wise line segments; interaction effects between cracks accounted for in SIF calculations; multiple cracks interacting within elements including parallel cracks and merging cracks; no contact modeling when cracks close (explicitly noted as a limitation).
- **Simulation Type:** Quasi-static crack propagation; small deformation kinematics; linear elasticity; proportional loading; plane stress condition (CT specimen); plane strain condition (multiple crack propagation example); 2-D analysis (with comparisons to 3-D models); displacement-controlled and load-controlled simulations (with snap-back behavior possible).
10_1016_j_cma_2024_117585.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Quasi-static fracture growth in brittle solids; discrete crack propagation including branching and merging; stress intensity factor calculation at crack tips; crack interaction effects (shielding and amplification); energy release rate determination; crack path evolution under mixed-mode loading.
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Reaction force (kN); crack opening displacement (COD) (mm); crack length (mm); stress intensity factors (K_I, K_II); energy release rate (G); nominal stress (MPa); nominal strain; displacement (mm); crack path trajectory; propagation direction angles; von Mises stress distribution.
- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve stable quasi-static crack growth satisfying Griffith's criterion (G = G_c); accurately reproduce experimental crack paths and load-displacement curves; maintain computational efficiency while modeling complex crack interactions; ensure accurate SIF calculations under crack shielding and amplification effects without requiring local mesh refinement.
10_1016_j_cma_2024_117585.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Initial crack length a₀ = 2.74 mm for standard CT specimen; a₀ = 13.47 mm for modified CT specimen; square specimen side length = 2 mm with 10 randomly distributed cracks; crack increment Δl = 0.5 mm (reduced to 0.05 mm when K_II/K_I > 0.01) for CT specimen; Δl = 2 mm (reduced to 0.2 mm when K_II/K_I > 0.01) for asymmetric bending test; Δl = 0.02 mm for multiple crack propagation; mesh size h₁ = 1 mm for CT specimen; structured mesh over 61×61 grid for multiple crack propagation; specific geometries for shielding (spacing b between microcracks) and amplification (distances c and d) configurations.
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Critical energy release rate G_c = 285 N/m (PMMA), 1000 N/m (asymmetric bending), 16.64 N/m (sandstone); quasi-static crack growth must satisfy G ≤ G_c with V_c > 0 if G = G_c; plane stress condition for CT specimen; plane strain condition for multiple crack propagation; tolerance ϵ = G_c/100 for determining active propagating cracks; linear finite elements undergo shear locking in bending; limited accuracy of linear elements in SIF evaluation causing oscillations; no contact modeling when cracks close; potential singular stiffness matrix from fragmentation due to crack merging.
- **Process/Manufacturing:** No explicit manufacturing constraints as this is a simulation study; computational constraints include requirement for mesh refinement to reduce oscillations in reaction-COD curves; zigzag crack patterns produced when crack increment is relatively large; linear finite elements require finer mesh for accurate SIF evaluation under mixed-mode loading; structured mesh required for accurate results with small crack sizes or closely spaced crack tips.

- **Material:** Ti-6Al-4V (Ti64) alloy in two forms: EB-PBF manufactured and wrought

  - EB-PBF: ε0.5 = 0.11918Z^0.06275

  - Wrought: Xdrx = 1 - exp[-4.75((ε-εc)/ε0.5)^1.81678]

- **Material / Medium:** Concrete with Young's modulus E=36,500 MPa, Poisson's ratio ν=0.1, cohesive strength f_u=3.19 MPa, and fracture energy G_F=50 N/m (three-point bending); concrete with E=28,000 MPa, ν=0.1, G_F=145 N/m, f_u=2.4 MPa (four-point shear); linear and rectangular cohesive traction-displacement laws implemented.
- **Application & Importance:** To model displacement discontinuities not conforming to interelement surfaces; to eliminate need for remeshing during crack propagation; to study size effect phenomenon; to determine minimum elements required per material characteristic length (N_c); to capture snap-back behavior in load-deflection curves.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Three-point bending specimen with depth b=0.15m, length l=4b, thickness t=b, initial crack length a=0, load distributed over d=0.01m; four-point shear specimen with depth b=0.2m, length l=4b, initial crack length a=0.2b, c/b=0.4, l1=l2=0.02m, thickness t=0.10m; cohesive zone defined between mathematical tip (zero crack opening) and physical tip (zero cohesive tractions); plane strain assumption used in simulations.
10_1016_s0013_7944_01_00128_x.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Prescribed displacements (zero) on boundary Γ_u; Point (0, b/2) in three-point bending specimen constrained to move only in y-direction; Point (l/2, −b/2) in four-point shear specimen fixed in both x and y directions; Point (−c/2, −b/2) in four-point shear specimen fixed in y-direction; Prescribed tractions on boundary Γ_F; Plane strain assumption applied in simulations
- **Loads / Excitations:** Load F applied at top center of three-point bending beam; Loads F₁ and F₂ applied on top and bottom of four-point shear beam; Load distributed over length d=0.01 in three-point bending specimen; Imposed tractions F depend linearly on load factor λ: F=λF₀; Cohesive strength f_u=3.19 MPa (three-point bending) and f_u=2.4 MPa (four-point shear)
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Cohesive traction-displacement relations on crack faces with linear and rectangular profiles; Neglected shear component of cohesive tractions; Cohesive zone (Γ_coh) between mathematical tip (zero crack opening) and physical tip (zero cohesive tractions); Cohesive traction at mathematical tip equals f_u; Crack opening at physical tip equals w_c; Fracture energy G_F=50 N/m (three-point bending) and G_F=145 N/m (four-point shear)
- **Simulation Type:** Small strain and displacement assumptions; Discrete crack growth steps with increment da; Iterative determination of load factor λ to satisfy K_I=0 at mathematical tip; Nonlinear analysis capturing snap-back behavior; Two-dimensional analysis; Plane strain formulation; Crack growth controlled by crack length parameter; 18 steps of crack growth at 0.01 m increments for four-point shear specimen
10_1016_s0013_7944_01_00128_x.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Cohesive crack growth in concrete specimens; displacement discontinuities not conforming to interelement surfaces; evolution of fracture process zone (FPZ) with traction-separation laws; stress intensity factor calculations at cohesive crack tips; snap-back behavior in load-deflection response; crack path trajectory determination
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Load-deflection curves for three-point bending and four-point shear specimens; cohesive zone length normalized by beam depth; stress intensity factors (K_I and K_II); number of elements per characteristic length (N_c); crack path trajectory; Mode I stress intensity factor (K_I) at mathematical crack tip; non-dimensional load-deflection curves; size effect behavior across different brittleness numbers
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize required elements per material characteristic length while maintaining accuracy (achieved with ~2 elements vs. 10 in classical methods); eliminate need for remeshing during crack propagation; accurately capture severe snap-back behavior; match experimental crack paths and load-deflection responses; determine optimal crack growth direction using maximum hoop stress criterion (θ=2arctan(K_II/K_I))
10_1016_s0013_7944_01_00128_x.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Minimum of approximately two elements per material characteristic length (N_c) required for reliable results; results for N_c below 0.5 show large oscillations and are not shown; characteristic element size da used for crack growth steps; J-integral domain limited to elements within radius of 2h_local from crack tip; three-point bending specimen geometry: depth b=0.15m, length l=4b, thickness t=b, initial crack length a=0; four-point shear specimen geometry: depth b=0.2m, length l=4b, initial crack length a=0.2b, c/b=0.4, l1=l2=0.02m, thickness t=0.10m
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Mode I stress intensity factor (K_I) must equal zero at mathematical tip of cohesive zone; cohesive strength f_u=3.19 MPa (three-point bending) and f_u=2.4 MPa (four-point shear); fracture energy G_F=50 N/m (three-point bending) and G_F=145 N/m (four-point shear); small strain and displacement assumptions applied; plane strain formulation used; material properties constrained to E=36,500 MPa, ν=0.1 (three-point bending) and E=28,000 MPa, ν=0.1 (four-point shear); shear component of cohesive tractions neglected in numerical studies
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Elements cut by crack require separate integration on each side of discontinuity; higher order quadrature required for elements near crack tip; node enrichment required (J set for jump function H, K set for branch functions); secant method used to update load factor λ; crack growth direction determined by maximum hoop stress criterion (θ=2arctan(K_II/K_I)); five-step flowchart for cohesive crack growth simulation; cohesive zone growth controlled by crack length parameter; 18 crack growth steps at 0.01m increments for four-point shear specimen; minimum 4 Gauss points used per cohesive segment for accurate integration

10_1016_j_finel_2004_01_005.key_1:

  - Young's modulus: 209
  - Poisson's ratio: 0.3
- **Application & Importance:** 
  - Transfers engine power to a driving shaft by hydraulic pressure
  - Subjected to hydraulic pressure (0.784) and centrifugal force loads at 2000 rpm rotational speed
  - Weight reduction target achieved: up to 13% after shape optimization
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Axisymmetric structure
  - Inner radius: 12 mm
  - Outer radius: 95 mm
  - Minimum thickness constraint: 0.6 mm
  - Boundary conditions: radial displacement fixed between points A and B; axial displacement fixed between points C and D
  - Excluded regions: flat region between D and E
  - Design boundaries: between B and C, and between F and G
10_1016_j_finel_2004_01_005.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Radial displacement fixed between points A and B (contact with rotating axis)
  - Axial displacement fixed between points C and D (contact with front cover)
  - Flat region between D and E excluded from design boundaries
  - Minimum thickness constraint of 0.6 mm
  - Design boundaries constrained to move only between B-C and F-G
  - Master nodes constrained to move along their normal directions on design boundaries
  - End nodes always assigned as master nodes

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Uniform pressure load of 0.784 applied on bottom surface between F and G
  - Centrifugal force with rotational speed of 2000 rpm
  - Density of 7850 kg/m³ for centrifugal force calculation
  - von Mises stress constraints: 40-65 MPa for pressure load case, 50-80 MPa for pressure and centrifugal load case

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Contact interface between disk and rotating axis (region A-B)
  - Contact interface between disk and front cover (region C-D)
  - Outer casing interface (region D-E)

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 2D axisymmetric finite element analysis
  - Plane stress condition assumed for verification cases (cantilever and fillet)
  - Sequential linear programming and Simplex method for optimization
  - B-spline curves used for boundary representation with fifth-order curves for spans of six data points
10_1016_j_finel_2004_01_005.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Structural stress distribution (von Mises stress)
  - Volume calculation of axisymmetric structures
  - Mesh distortion analysis

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - von Mises stress levels (with maximum values reported)
  - Volume in mm³ (initial volume 295,577.3 mm³)
  - Distortion metric D (quantitative mesh quality measure)
  - Axial displacement (maximum values reported)
  - Convergence ratio φ (volume change between iterations)

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Minimize volume (achieved 9.03% reduction for pressure load case, 13.3% for coupled loads case)
  - Maintain von Mises stress within specified ranges (40-65 MPa for pressure load, 50-80 MPa for pressure and centrifugal loads)
  - Reduce maximum von Mises stress (from 73.02 to 62.32 MPa for pressure load case; from 127.24 to 80.05 MPa for coupled loads case)
  - Maintain mesh quality through distortion metric control
  - Achieve smooth and continuous boundary surfaces using B-spline curves
10_1016_j_finel_2004_01_005.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Minimum thickness constraint of 0.6 mm to avoid extremely thin shapes
  - Design boundaries restricted to regions between B-C and F-G only
  - Contact regions A-B (rotating axis), C-D (front cover), and D-E (outer casing) excluded from design boundaries
  - Master nodes constrained to move only along their normal directions on design boundaries
  - End nodes always assigned as master nodes
  - B-spline curve requirement: p ≤ n+1 (where p is order of curve, n is number of data points)
  - Fifth-order B-spline curves employed for each span consisting of six data points

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - von Mises stress constraints: 40-65 MPa for pressure load case
  - von Mises stress constraints: 50-80 MPa for pressure and centrifugal load case
  - Cantilever maximum von Mises stress restricted to 1.8
  - Fillet maximum allowable von Mises stress set to 4.5
  - Convergence criterion: volume change ratio φ < 0.001 between iterations
  - Distortion metric D used to measure mesh quality (0 for ideal square element, increases with distortion)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Minimum thickness constraint of 0.6 mm to prevent manufacturing issues with extremely thin sections
  - Mesh smoothing applied to interior nodes to maintain finite element quality during optimization
  - Selection of master nodes (91 for torque converter disk) rather than all boundary nodes to maintain computational efficiency and smooth boundaries
  - Normal direction movement of master nodes to prevent discontinuous or unstable boundary surfaces

10_1016_j_engfailanal_2023_107890.key_4:

10_1016_j_jcrysgro_2004_02_112.key_1:
- Epitaxial island growth process modeled as a free boundary problem with diffusion equation for adatom density, boundary conditions for moving steps, and velocity law for step motion
- Single crystal film growth on substrate with lattice spacing "a" as unit of length
- Adatom density defined as number of adatoms per adsorption site
- Surface diffusivity D = 10⁵ (in units of lattice spacing a)
- Deposition flux rate F = 1
- Desorption rate τ⁻¹ > 0
- Thermodynamic equilibrium density ρ* = 10⁻⁴
- Step stiffness parameter μ = 0.1 (isotropic case) and μ(θ) = 1.0 - 0.8cos(3θ) (anisotropic case)
- Edge diffusion mobility ν = 0.1
- Kinetic attachment rates k⁺ and k⁻ with values of 10³ or 10⁴ used in simulations
- Two-dimensional projected domain Ω with terraces Ωᵢ(t) of different heights
- Circular islands on circular substrate in numerical test (initial radius R(0)=3 on substrate radius RΩ=10)
- Two concentric islands configuration with initial radii R₁(0)=5 and R₂(0)=4 on circular domain radius R₀=7
- Anisotropic growth produces "triangular" shaped islands while conserving Wulff shape during evolution
- Boundary conditions include Ehrlich-Schwoebel barrier (0 < k⁺ < k⁻), inverse Ehrlich-Schwoebel barrier (0 < k⁻ < k⁺), and symmetric case (k⁺ = k⁻)
- Step-edge diffusion of edge-adatoms along steps included in velocity law
- Adatom density discontinuity resolved at step edges with different densities on upper and lower terraces
10_1016_j_jcrysgro_2004_02_112.key_2:
- Kinetic boundary conditions on island boundaries: -D∇ρᵢ·nᵢ - vᵢρᵢ = k⁺(ρᵢ - ρ*(1+μκᵢ)) and D∇ρᵢ₋₁·nᵢ + vᵢρᵢ₋₁ = k⁻(ρᵢ₋₁ - ρ*(1+μκᵢ))
- Unit normal nᵢ points from upper to lower terrace at boundary Γᵢ(t)
- Ehrlich-Schwoebel barrier case defined as 0 < k⁺ < k⁻
- Inverse Ehrlich-Schwoebel barrier case defined as 0 < k⁻ < k⁺
- Symmetric attachment/detachment case defined as k⁺ = k⁻
- Thermodynamic boundary condition ρᵢ = ρᵢ₋₁ = ρ*(1+μκᵢ) when k⁺, k⁻ → ∞
- Deposition flux rate F = 1 (in units of atoms per site per time)
- Surface diffusivity D = 10⁵ (in units of lattice spacing a)
- Desorption rate τ⁻¹ > 0
- Thermodynamic equilibrium density ρ* = 10⁻⁴
- Step stiffness parameter μ = 0.1 (isotropic case)

- Kinetic attachment rates k⁺ and k⁻ with values of 10³ or 10⁴

- Normal velocity law for step motion includes step edge diffusion term ∂ₛ(ν∂ₛ(μκᵢ))
- Initial circular island radius R(0) = 3 (in units of lattice spacing a)
- Substrate radius RΩ = 10 (in units of lattice spacing a)
- Two concentric islands initial radii: R₁(0) = 5 and R₂(0) = 4 on circular domain radius R₀ = 7
- Transient simulation with first-order implicit time discretization
- Adaptive finite element method with mesh refinement near step edges
- Two independent meshes: 2D mesh for adatom diffusion and 1D mesh for boundary evolution
- Continuous in lateral directions but discrete in growth direction (terraces of different heights)
- Lattice spacing a used as unit of length throughout the paper
10_1016_j_jcrysgro_2004_02_112.key_3:
- Adatom diffusion on terraces of different heights solved via diffusion equation ∂ₜρᵢ - ∇·(D∇ρᵢ) = F - τ⁻¹ρᵢ
- Step boundary evolution with kinetic attachment/detachment asymmetry at moving boundaries
- Two-sided adatom flux at step boundaries from both upper and lower terraces
- Step edge diffusion of edge-adatoms along boundaries
- Adatom density distribution ρᵢ(x,t) on terraces as primary output

- Cross-sectional density profiles at step boundaries

- Comparison of growth behavior for three cases: Ehrlich-Schwoebel barrier (k⁺ < k⁻), inverse Ehrlich-Schwoebel barrier (k⁺ > k⁻), and symmetric case (k⁺ = k⁻)

  - Upper Limiter (UL): 8 limiters, 5.1 m² each, 1.83×1.49 m (polxtor), 6.9 MW stationary load, UVDE/disruption operation
  - Inboard Midplane Limiter (IML): 4 limiters, 2.45 m² each, 2.76×0.77 m (polxtor), 3.31 MW stationary load, L-H transition operation
  - Outboard Midplane Limiter (OML): 4 limiters, 4.25 m² each, 2.84×1.1 m (polxtor), 4.24 MW stationary load, Ramp-up operation
  - Outboard Lower Limiter (OLL): 4 limiters, 2.32 m² each, 1.37×0.98 m (polxtor), 3.14 MW stationary load, Ramp-down/DVDE/disruption operation
- **W lattice types:**
  - Type A: 49.2% density, 40% thermal conductivity reduction, 16% elastic modulus reduction
  - Type B: 53.1% density, 25% thermal conductivity reduction, 10% elastic modulus reduction
- **Optimized PFC layouts:**
  - Eurofer-based: Armour thickness (A) 14.5 mm, HS thickness (B) 1 mm, duct pitch (C) 10 mm, channel size (D) 7×7 mm, gap/2 (E) 1.5 mm, HS base (F) 2 mm
  - CuCrZr-based: Armour thickness (A) 10.8 mm, HS thickness (B) 1.5 mm, duct pitch (C) 17 mm, channel size (D) Ø12 mm, gap/2 (E) 2.5 mm, HS base (F) 3 mm
- **Operating conditions:**
  - Normal steady state: 0.5–1.5 MW/m² heat load
  - Ramp-up/down: Linearly varying load within 50 s, maximum ~4 MW/m²
  - U/DVDE-disruption thermal quench: ~1 GJ thermal energy in 1–4 ms, up to 100–300 GW/m² heat flux
  - Cooling water: 130 °C, 5 MPa
  - Heat transfer coefficient: 75–90 kW/m²K
- **Cooling channel variants:**
  - Circular: 12 mm diameter, 13 m/s water velocity for CuCrZr HS
  - Square: 7×7 mm, 9 m/s water velocity for Eurofer HS
- **Material properties:**
  - Eurofer at 300°C: Allowable stress intensity S_e=195 MPa, S_m=175 MPa
  - CuCrZr at 200°C: Allowable stress intensity S_e=97 MPa, S_m=86 MPa
  - W enthalpy function: ΔH_melt (~7% of ΔH_sub), ΔH_vap (~60% of ΔH_sub)
- **Erosion test conditions:**
  - 100 GW/m² heat flux for 1 ms duration
  - Initial vaporization occurs after 1e-5s
  - Total eroded volume: 0.5–0.8 mm³ per unit cell after 1 ms
- **Sample fabrication:**
  - Infiltration process: 1 hour at 1200°C in vacuum (<1e-5 mbar)
  - Cooling: 1200°C to 1000°C at 1 K/min, followed by inertial cooling
  - Supporting structure: W wires and W foil
  - Post-infiltration: Chemical removal of excess copper using diluted nitric acid

10_1016_j_fusengdes_2023_113742.key_3:

  - Thermal stress distribution under steady-state and transient conditions
  - Phase change phenomena (melting and vaporization) of tungsten
  - Heat transfer in lattice armor structures with orthotropic properties

  - Achieve compliance with ITER structural design criteria (K₁ < 1 and K₂ < 1)
  - Balance between steady-state heat exhaust capability and transient protection
  - Ensure pipe wall temperature remains below 300°C to maintain safety margin from critical heat flux
  - Minimize total pressure drop while meeting cooling requirements for integration with divertor CWS
10_1016_j_fusengdes_2023_113742.key_4:

  - Armour thickness range: 7.2–18 mm
  - Heat sink (HS) thickness range: 1–2.5 mm
  - Duct pitch range: 7–10 mm and 12–22 mm
  - Channel cross-section options: circular (12 mm diameter) or square (7×7 mm)

  - Ducts must be aligned with toroidal direction to mitigate electromagnetic loads
  - Gap/2 must compensate for rounding to ensure integer number of ducts

  - During disruption: armour temperature at ½ thickness must stay below W melting point
  - Maximum HS temperature during disruption: <1100°C
  - ITER SDC-IC criteria: K₁ < 1 and K₂ < 1 for structural integrity
  - Heat flux peaking must not exceed 1.3
  - Water temperature increase limited to maximum 33°C
  - Total pressure drop must remain below tolerable limits for divertor CWS integration
  - Allowable stress intensities: Eurofer at 300°C (S_e=195 MPa, S_m=175 MPa); CuCrZr at 200°C (S_e=97 MPa, S_m=86 MPa)

  - Infiltration temperature: 1200°C for 1 hour duration
  - Cooling profile: 1200°C to 1000°C at 1 K/min rate, followed by inertial cooling
  - Duct absolute roughness: ε = 0.01 mm for pressure loss calculations
  - Number of cooling circuits (N_circ) must be an integer value
  - Total number of ducts (N_tot) must be an integer value
  - Composite interlayer requires chemical removal of excess copper using diluted nitric acid
  - W wires and foil required as supporting structure to prevent sample contact with mould walls during infiltration

10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_741_262.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Swash plate component of an engine analyzed for inertial force and moment calculation using finite element method; studied for dynamic balance in high-speed rotating machinery.  
- **Material / Medium:** Material density 4500 kg/m³; rotational velocity 2050 r/min around X-axis.  
- **Application & Importance:** Dynamic balance calculation to mitigate vibration and noise in military engines where stringent noise requirements make unbalanced inertial forces critical.  
- **Geometry / Domain:** Circular plate inclined 20° around Y-axis; mass point coordinates (-14, -0.04, 5.09); discretized into 20,316 finite elements; coordinate origin near mass point.
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_741_262.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Swash plate inclined 20° around Y-axis; rotation constrained about X-axis.  
- **Loads / Excitations:** Rotational velocity of 2050 r/min around X-axis.  
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Total mechanism inertial force and moment calculated by summing individual part contributions.  
- **Simulation Type:** Transient 3D dynamic simulation with time step Δt for periodic motion analysis.
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_741_262.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Inertial force and inertial moment in rotating machinery under dynamic conditions.  
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Three-directional inertial forces (Fx, Fy, Fz) and moments (Mx, My, Mz) with units N and N·m.  
- **Optimization Goal:** Accurate calculation of inertial force and moment to enable dynamic balancing, reducing vibration and noise in high-speed rotating machinery.
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_741_262.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Element size must be sufficiently small to ensure accuracy, requiring discretization into thousands of elements per part (e.g., 20,316 elements for the swash plate component).  
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Calculation accuracy is dependent on element size, with smaller elements improving precision but increasing computational cost.  
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Requires separate finite element analysis (FEA) software for meshing and MATLAB for inertial force/moment calculations, with complex data conversion between tools. Manual calculation is infeasible due to the large number of elements.

10_1186_1471_2474_8_91.key_1:
- Custom-designed femoral component for knee replacement implants, compared with conventional design
- Cancellous bone (0.4 GPa modulus of elasticity, 0.3 Poisson ratio), cortical bone (15 GPa modulus of elasticity, 0.46 Poisson ratio), CoCr implant (220 GPa modulus of elasticity, 0.3 Poisson ratio)
- To evaluate stress distribution on bone-implant interface to reduce uneven bone remodeling and premature loosening
- Natural articulating surface mimicking distal femur geometry; smooth bone-implant interface created with spline curves in radial pattern; conventional design features five flat surfaces
- Three gait cycle positions analyzed: center (standing position), middle (end of normal walking), back (extreme climbing stairs position)
- Load levels: 2200 N (center), 3200 N (middle), 2800 N (back)
- Contact surface between femoral component and tibial tray defined as narrow surfaces approximately 2-3 mm width
- Bone-implant interface primarily cancellous bone with thin rim of cortical bone around edges
- Conventional implant center position stresses averaged 2.17 MPa at sharp edges; custom implant center position stresses averaged 2.53 MPa in contact regions
- Conventional implant contact edge stresses: 1.59 MPa (back position), 1.3 MPa (middle position)
- Stress distribution range for custom implant under second condition: 0.9 MPa to 3 MPa on contact surface
- Stress distribution range for conventional implant under third condition: 0.3 MPa to 15 MPa on contact surfaces
- Green contour stress levels defined at 2.5 MPa in comparative stress distribution analyses
- ABAQUS 6.4-3 CEA used for finite element analysis with tetrahedral mesh based on triangular surface mesh from Mimics
- Custom femur model contained 25,521 tetrahedral elements; custom implant contained 61,858 elements
- Standard femur model contained 19,657 tetrahedral elements; standard implant contained 49,724 elements
10_1186_1471_2474_8_91.key_2:

- Femurs fixed in the contact step and deactivated for loading

- Default stiffness used for contact calculation
- Finite sliding allowed with only overclosed nodes adjusted
- Load levels: 2200 N (center position), 3200 N (middle position), 2800 N (back position)
- Center position represents standing position or starting position of gait cycle
- Middle position represents end of normal walking gait cycle
- Back position represents extreme position for climbing stairs

- Bone-implant interface primarily cancellous bone with thin rim of cortical bone around edges
- 3D finite element analysis using ABAQUS 6.4-3 CEA
- Von Mises stress analysis

10_1186_1471_2474_8_91.key_3:
- Mechanical stress distribution on bone-implant interface
- Von Mises stress values at bone-implant interface
- Stress concentration patterns along interface edges
- Average stress measurements: 2.17 MPa (conventional implant at sharp edges), 2.53 MPa (custom implant in contact regions)
- Stress ranges: 0.9-3 MPa (custom implant contact surface), 0.3-15 MPa (conventional implant contact surfaces)
- Contact edge stresses: 1.59 MPa (conventional implant back position), 1.3 MPa (conventional implant middle position)
- Achieve more even stress distribution to reduce uneven bone remodeling
- Minimize stress concentrations at sharp edges to prevent premature aseptic loosening
- Reduce stress shielding in flat areas between edges to prevent bone loss
10_1186_1471_2474_8_91.key_4:
- Interface surface geometry must mimic distal femur but without undercuts to enable easy implantation
- Implant thickness must be adjustable based on material choice (titanium or cobalt-chromium), patient weight, and activity level
- Surgical tools and cutting guides historically limit bone-implant interface design to planar cuts
- Bone-implant interface must accommodate anatomical abnormalities at distal femur
- Conventional approach restricted to five flat surfaces creating sharp edges that cause stress concentrations
- Custom design requires surgical robot for bone resection due to complex freeform surfaces
- Time and cost associated with custom implant design represent significant constraints
- FDA approval limitations for orthopedic robots in United States
- Fabrication of custom implant components at reasonable cost has been historically problematic
- Current surgical methods result in only about 50% average contact surface between bone and implant
- Robotic systems can achieve 95% bone-implant contact surface but require specialized equipment
- Conventional design creates stress shielding in flat areas between sharp edges leading to bone loss
- Need to avoid uneven stress distribution that results in bone remodeling and implant loosening

10_1016_j_cmpb_2023_107376.key_1:

10_1016_j_cmpb_2023_107376.key_2:

- **Geometry / Domain:** Plane strain plate: 2m × 2m square with 0.40m × 0.1m flat hole; Cook's problem: tapered panel with 48mm base, 16mm/44mm heights, 5mm thickness; both modeled with tetrahedral elements (2538 elements for plate quarter, 3464 elements for Cook's panel) under plane strain conditions; Cook's panel clamped on one side with 1N shear load on opposite side

  - Stabilization of mixed finite element formulations for incompressibility

- **Optimization Goal:**

  - Achieve stable solutions matching quadratic/linear reference solutions using linear shape functions

10_2746_042516409x395688.key_1:

- **Material / Medium:** Osseous components (8000 MPa modulus); hoof wall (450 MPa horse, 300 MPa donkey); sole (150 MPa horse, 100 MPa donkey); frog (15 MPa); ungular cartilage (10 MPa); skin (5 MPa); articular cartilage (10 MPa); deep digital flexor tendon (nonlinear); superficial flexor tendon (nonlinear); common extensor tendon (nonlinear); suspensory ligament (nonlinear); collateral ligaments (nonlinear); ground concrete (31000 MPa modulus).

10_2746_042516409x395688.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Model realigned to weightbearing limb position with metacarpal bone within 5° to vertical; proximal structures constrained to prevent free body motion; tied surface contacts for most components; sliding contact algorithm for deep digital flexor tendon-sesamoid/middle phalanx interfaces, superficial/deep flexor tendon interface, articular cartilage surfaces, and hoof wall-ground interface.

- **Loads / Excitations:** Z-direction displacement of proximal superficial and deep digital flexor tendons to compensate for general anaesthesia relaxation; concentrated load equivalent to 1× body mass (400 kg horse, 190 kg donkey) applied through metacarpal bone center of mass.

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Sliding contact with static friction coefficient of 0.985 between hoof wall and ground; truss elements representing ligamentous structures connecting anatomical origin and insertion points; frictionless sliding contact at specified tendon-bone interfaces.

10_2746_042516409x395688.key_3:

- **Optimization Goal:** Accurate replication of prestrain in flexor tendons to compensate for anaesthesia relaxation; precise simulation of quasistatic weightbearing at mid-stance; validation of capsular deformation patterns against in vivo observations; measurement of tissue stress/strain levels unobtainable through experimental methods.

10_1016_j_finel_2009_03_008.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Cavity identification problem in geometric inverse heat conduction where unknowns are shape and location of internal cavity within a solid domain
- **Material / Medium:** Solid domain with thermal conductivity k; cavity assumed to have zero thermal conductivity (insulated boundary)
- **Application & Importance:** Industrial applications include blast furnace isotherm location estimation, furnace wall geometry determination, natural convection domain boundary identification, and frost growth shape estimation
- **Geometry / Domain:** 0.15 × 0.15 square domain with unknown internal cavity; upper boundary subjected to constant heat flux (q̄/k = 100), lower boundary with prescribed temperature (T̄ = 0 or T̄ = 100 sin(πx/0.15)), left/right boundaries insulated; cavity shapes include circular (radius 0.01–0.05), elliptical (major radius 0.04, minor radius 0.03), and egg-shaped; cavity boundary parameterized by closed cubic spline with 8 nuts
10_1016_j_finel_2009_03_008.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**

  - Lower boundary: Prescribed temperature (T̄ = 0 or T̄ = 100 sin(πx/0.15))
  - Left and right boundaries: Insulated (zero heat flux)
  - Cavity boundary: Insulated (zero heat flux) due to zero thermal conductivity assumption
  - Temperature measurement points on left and right boundaries

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Heat flux on upper boundary (q̄/k = 100)
  - Prescribed temperature distribution on lower boundary
  - Temperature measurements at specific boundary points for inverse problem solution

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Cavity boundary (ΓC) as interface between solid domain and zero-conductivity cavity
  - Non-boundary-fitted mesh with boundary intersecting elements (BIEs)
  - Overlapping and non-overlapping regions for shape sensitivity analysis

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Steady-state heat conduction
  - 2D analysis
  - Nonlinear inverse geometry problem
  - Square domain (0.15 × 0.15) with internal cavity
  - Measurement errors tested: ±3%, ±5%, ±8%, ±10%
10_1016_j_finel_2009_03_008.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Steady-state heat conduction governed by Laplace equation (∇²T(x) = 0) in multiply connected bounded domain with unknown internal cavity

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Temperature distribution in the domain (T)
  - Cavity shape parameters (P = [x_B, y_B, r_1, r_2, ..., r_Nn])
  - Objective function value (f = ∑(T_i^C - T_i^M)²)
  - Relative error between measured and computed temperatures (E_r = [∑(T_i^C - T_i^M)²/∑(T_i^M)²] × 100)
  - Number of iterations to convergence
  - Final identified cavity geometry

- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize the squared error between measured temperatures (T_i^M) at boundary measurement points and computed temperatures (T_i^C), with geometric regularization: f = ∑(T_i^C - T_i^M)² + α(1/r̄²)∑(r_i - r̄)², where α is regularization parameter and r̄ is average radius of spline nuts
10_1016_j_finel_2009_03_008.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Internal cavity cannot cross the outer surface of the object
  - Cavity shape parameterized by closed cubic spline with 8 nuts (10 total design parameters: base point coordinates and 8 radial distances)
  - Cavity radius constrained between 0.01 and 0.05 in size study
  - Maximum cavity size limited by domain dimensions (0.15 × 0.15 square domain)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Zero thermal conductivity inside cavity (insulated boundary condition)
  - Ill-posed nature of inverse problems requiring geometric regularization (zero-order regularization function)
  - High smoothing property of Laplace operator limits information transfer from small cavities to outer surface
  - Measurement errors constrained to ±3%, ±5%, ±8%, and ±10% in test cases
  - Steady-state heat conduction governed by Laplace equation (∇²T = 0)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Fixed non-boundary-fitted mesh used throughout optimization process (no mesh adaptation or re-meshing)
  - Single fixed mesh (0.15 × 0.15 domain) used for all test examples without modification
  - Conjugate gradient method used for optimization with golden section search for step length determination

10_1016_j_euromechsol_2023_105068.key_2:

  - CSFC (clamped-simply supported-free-clamped) boundary condition

  - Boundary conditions applied at x=0, x=a, y=0, and y=b edges

  - Perfect bonding conditions at interfaces between face sheets and core for intact regions
  - Point continuity method applied at delamination boundaries
  - Compatibility conditions between top face sheet and core (equation 30)
  - Compatibility conditions between bottom face sheet and core (equation 28)
  - Vertical distance parameters e₅ = (h_t - h₅)/2 and e₆ = (h_t - h₆)/2 for displacement continuity

  - Four distinct element types based on delamination location:
    * Intact sandwich element (15 DOF per node)
    * Laminated composite element (5 DOF per node)
    * Semi-sandwich element (13 DOF per node)
    * Inverse semi-sandwich element (13 DOF per node)

- **Loads / Excitations:** Darcy's law governing flow with hydraulic head gradient; Source term f_i in weak formulation; Sink fracture F₁ and source fracture F₂ with non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions on one edge; Homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions on remaining edges of sink and source fractures

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Fluid flow only through fractures and across traces (fracture intersections); No tangential flow along traces; Flux computed as jump of conormal derivative across traces; Global conformity achieved through VEM with matching nodes on traces between intersecting fractures; Hydraulic head continuous but with discontinuous derivatives across traces

- **Simulation Type:** Steady-state flow simulation; 3D domain with planar polygonal fractures; Virtual Element Method discretization; Polynomial orders from 1 to 4 tested; Weak formulation of Darcy's law; Saddle point linear system solved with Lagrange multipliers to enforce trace continuity
10_1016_j_finel_2015_10_003.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Steady-state fluid flow in Discrete Fracture Networks (DFNs) governed by Darcy's law; Hydraulic head distribution through interconnected planar fractures; Flow through fractures and across fracture intersections (traces) with no tangential flow along traces

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Hydraulic head distribution (H) across all fractures; Flux (u) across traces between fractures; L² and H¹ error norms for convergence analysis; Net flux in source (So) and sink (Si) fractures; Flux mismatch (Δ = So - Si); Convergence rates for Virtual Element Method (VEM) polynomial orders 1-4; Iteration counts for preconditioned conjugate gradient solvers

- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve global conformity of fracture meshes without modifying DFN geometry; Maintain hydraulic head continuity across all fracture intersections; Enable independent meshing of each fracture while ensuring trace conformity; Handle complex geometries with small angles (<1°), close parallel traces, high disparity in trace lengths (45:0.01), and multiple trace intersections; Minimize flux mismatch (Δ) between source and sink fractures; Reduce iteration counts through effective preconditioning (Dirichlet vs. Lumped); Demonstrate convergence for VEM polynomial orders 1-4 on complex DFNs with up to 130 fractures
10_1016_j_finel_2015_10_003.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Minimum angle of 0.41°; Maximum trace length ≈ 45, minimum trace length ≈ 0.01; Largest number of traces in a single fracture = 24; Elements with extreme aspect ratios (e.g., 10.26 length to 0.058 width, 177:1 ratio); Fractures with parallel traces very close to each other; Elements with angles less than 1 degree; Highly heterogeneous element areas; Complex trace intersections among multiple fractures

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** VEM order 4 and higher suffer from numerical instabilities on strongly distorted meshes; Fourth order approximation on mesh size 15 causes degenerate discrete solutions; Higher order VEM (order 4+) solutions can drastically change and fall below zero, incompatible with boundary conditions; Convergence is slower for flux variable with order 1 on coarse meshes; Hydraulic head continuity is guaranteed for the whole DFN by implementation; Exact DFN solutions generally lack high regularity, making cubic approximation of H and quadratic approximation for U potentially excessive

- **Process/Manufacturing:** Monomial basis for polynomial space is notoriously bad conditioned, with worsening condition as polynomial order increases; Mesh generation performed independently for each fracture regardless of trace positions; Baseline triangulation not necessarily conforming to trace disposition; Global conformity achieved through VEM without modifying DFN geometry; Higher order discretizations are much more computationally expensive with limited accuracy improvement; VEM order 2 recommended as optimal balance between accuracy and stability

10_1016_j_scriptamat_2003_11_061.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Cube-oriented face centered cubic (FCC) crystals under plane strain compression; orientational stability and in-grain microtexture evolution
- **Material / Medium:** FCC crystal structure with cube orientation (Bunge-Euler angles ϕ₁=0°, φ=0°, ϕ₂=0°); {111}〈110〉 slip systems; viscoplastic hardening behavior
- **Application & Importance:** Investigation of metastable behavior of cube-oriented FCC crystals under plane strain; study of how small initial orientation variations and friction conditions affect microtexture development and lattice rotations
- **Geometry / Domain:** 500 three-dimensional linear finite elements with eight integration points each; plane strain compression geometry mimicking channel die experiment; four boundary surfaces (Surfaces 1-4); 50% engineering thickness reduction; initial orientation distribution modeled as spherical Gaussian with 2.5° full width at half maximum
10_1016_j_scriptamat_2003_11_061.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Four boundary surfaces (Surfaces 1-4) in plane strain compression geometry; top and bottom surfaces (Surfaces 1 and 2) with friction coefficients of μ=0.1 or μ=0.3; side surfaces (Surfaces 3 and 4) with zero friction in some cases or μ=0.1 in surround friction cases; 50% engineering thickness reduction as final deformation state; initial orientation distribution modeled as spherical Gaussian with 2.5° full width at half maximum
- **Loads / Excitations:** Plane strain compression loading; linear Coulomb friction law applied to contact surfaces; three friction scenarios: (1) μ=0.1 on top/bottom only, (2) μ=0.3 on top/bottom only, (3) μ=0.1 on all four surfaces
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Frictional contact between sample and compression surfaces; shear distortion in elements due to friction effects; {111}〈110〉 slip systems activation; viscoplastic hardening behavior; 500 discrete orientations randomly distributed across elements
- **Simulation Type:** 3D crystal plasticity finite element simulation; implicit time integration of constitutive equations; quasi-static deformation to 50% engineering thickness reduction; nonlinear material behavior with 500 three-dimensional linear elements (4,000 integration points total)
10_1016_j_scriptamat_2003_11_061.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Orientational stability of cube-oriented FCC crystals under plane strain compression; lattice rotation behavior about normal direction (ND), rolling direction (RD), and transverse direction (TD); in-grain microtexture evolution; deformation structure development; effect of initial orientation scatter and friction conditions on crystal re-orientation
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Euler angle distributions (ϕ₁, φ, ϕ₂); orientation distribution function (ODF) sections at ϕ₂=0°; {111} pole figures showing orientation scatter; von Mises stress distribution; element distortion after deformation; quantitative orientation spread measurements (e.g., ∼22° about RD and ∼14° about ND at f(g)=10); in-grain orientation gradients
- **Optimization Goal:** Determine rotation axis dominance (ND, RD, or TD) as function of initial orientation scatter (2.5° spherical Gaussian) and friction conditions; quantify metastable behavior of cube orientation under plane strain; resolve contradictions in previous models regarding rotation axes in cube-oriented FCC crystals
10_1016_j_scriptamat_2003_11_061.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** 500 three-dimensional linear finite elements with eight integration points each (4,000 total integration points); plane strain compression geometry constrained to 50% engineering thickness reduction; four boundary surfaces (Surfaces 1-4) with fixed spatial arrangement mimicking channel die experiment
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** {111}〈110〉 slip systems activation exclusively; viscoplastic hardening behavior; initial orientation distribution limited to spherical Gaussian with 2.5° full width at half maximum; cube orientation defined strictly by Bunge-Euler angles ϕ₁=0°, φ=0°, ϕ₂=0°; linear Coulomb friction coefficients constrained to μ=0.1 or μ=0.3 on specified surfaces
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Implicit time integration using Kalidindi's crystal plasticity procedure; texture component method for initial orientation assignment; lateral random distribution of 500 discrete orientations across the mesh; simulation constrained to three specific friction scenarios (μ=0.1 on top/bottom, μ=0.3 on top/bottom, μ=0.1 on all four surfaces)

- Boundary Γ is the boundary of domain Ω
- H₀¹(Ω) space: functions in H¹(Ω) with trace vanishing on boundary Γ
- Space G defined with u̅_D = g̅ on Γ
- Volume force f̅ = (f₁, f₂) ∈ (L²(Ω))²
- Linear elasticity equation: −∑ⱼ ∂/∂xⱼ (σᵢⱼ(u̅)) = fᵢ in Ω, i = 1, 2
- Interelement boundaries handled via Lagrange multipliers
- Lagrange multiplier represents normal stress for linear elastic model
- Adjacent triangles K₁ and K₂ have K̄₁ ∩ K̄₂ as either empty, or an edge, or a vertex
- Two-dimensional linear elasticity problem
- Homogeneous isotropic elastic material
- Pure displacement boundary value problem
- Primal hybrid finite element method
- Crouzeix-Raviart nonconforming finite element space used
- Mesh size h varies from 1/2 to 1/32 in numerical examples
- Tested with Poisson's ratio values: ν = 0.4, ν = 0.499999, and ν = 0.49999999
10_1016_j_amc_2022_127462.key_3:
- Two-dimensional linear elasticity problem for homogeneous isotropic elastic material
- Displacement vector field u̅ = (u₁, u₂) and stress tensor σᵢⱼ(u̅) distribution
- Displacement error in (L²(Ω))² norm
- Displacement error in (H¹(Ω))² norm
- Lagrange multiplier (normal stress) error in M norm
- Order of convergence for displacement and stress errors
- Robustness against locking phenomenon as Poisson's ratio approaches 0.5
- Method provides optimal convergence rates independent of Lamé parameters
- Simultaneous approximation of both primal (displacement) and hybrid (normal stress) variables
- Quadratic convergence in (L²)² norm and linear convergence in H¹ norm for displacement
- Linear convergence for Lagrange multiplier error
- Validation of method robustness for Poisson's ratios ν = 0.4, ν = 0.499999, and ν = 0.49999999
10_1016_j_amc_2022_127462.key_4:
- Domain Ω is open, bounded, and convex polygonal Lipschitz in ℝ²
- Mesh consists of shape regular triangles K with max_K∈T_h h_K/ρ_K ≤ δ (h_K = triangle diameter, ρ_K = inscribed circle diameter)
- Lamé coefficients constrained by λ ≥ 0 and μ > 0
- Poisson's ratio ν approaches 0.5 (tested at ν = 0.4, ν = 0.499999, and ν = 0.49999999) to evaluate locking phenomenon
- Method designed to avoid deterioration of convergence rates as ν → 0.5
- Dirichlet boundary condition: u̅ = g̅ on Γ (with g̅ = 0̅ for analysis simplification)
- Homogeneous isotropic elastic material assumption
- Two-dimensional problem constraint (no 3D extension presented)
- Inter-element continuity requirement withdrawn, replaced with Lagrange multipliers
- Finite element spaces constrained to Crouzeix-Raviart nonconforming space for discrete formulation
- Mesh size h constrained to values 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16, and 1/32 in numerical examples
- Test domain has boundary Γ = ∪ᵢ₌₁ⁿ Γ̄ᵢ where Γᵢ are open line segments joining vertices
- The problem is formulated for pure displacement boundary value problem
- Method applies only to linear elasticity (not nonlinear elasticity)

10_1016_j_cma_2024_117681.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Solid elasticity mechanics problems using deep finite element method (DFEM) for structural analysis; specific test cases include plate with circular hole, non-symmetric stretching plate, and rock drill boom
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Young's modulus: 210 GPa (all test cases)
  - Poisson's ratio: 0.2 (plate with circular hole), 0.3 (non-symmetric stretching plate), 0.29 (rock drill boom)
- **Application & Importance:** Structural analysis with physics-informed neural networks; enables fast computation for digital twin applications; handles complex 3D geometries with high accuracy; integrates observational data with physical laws for high-fidelity modeling
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Plate with circular hole: 20 mm square plate with 5 mm radius hole; left side fixed; 1 MPa uniform load on right side
  - Non-symmetric stretching plate: Curved asymmetric plate; upper end fixed; -1 mm displacement applied to lower end
  - Rock drill boom: Complex 3D structure with multiple holes and connection points; 46,337 elements and 10,205 nodal points in mesh
  - Boundary conditions include fixed constraints, displacement constraints, and pressure loads (0.6-1.4 MPa in various tests)
10_1016_j_cma_2024_117681.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Fixed support on left side of plate with circular hole
  - Upper end fixed for non-symmetric stretching plate
  - u = 0 constraint on left boundary of non-symmetric stretching plate
  - Displacement constraint of v = -1 mm at lower end of non-symmetric stretching plate
  - Essential boundary conditions implemented through hard BCs (e.g., u = (x+20)uθ, v = (x+20)vθ for plate with hole; u = (20+y)(20-y)uθ, v = (20+y)(20-y)vθ + (y-20)/40 for non-symmetric plate)
  - Essential boundary conditions also implemented by modifying stiffness matrix (setting diagonal elements to 1, non-diagonal to 0, and load vector elements to 0)
  - Natural boundary conditions incorporated through nodal load vector P

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Uniform load of 1 MPa applied to right side of plate with circular hole
  - Pressure loads of P = 0.6 MPa, 0.8 MPa, 0.9 MPa, 1.1 MPa, 1.2 MPa, and 1.4 MPa tested in various examples
  - Applied loading of 1 MPa for rock drill boom analysis

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Essential boundary conditions introduced as observed data integrated into data loss term (soft BCs)
  - Neural network structure customized to automatically satisfy boundary conditions (hard BCs)
  - Natural boundary conditions considered through the nodal load vector P
  - Integration of observational data with physics-based modeling for high-fidelity digital twin applications

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Linear elasticity problems
  - Static analysis (not transient)
  - 2D and 3D simulations (2D for plate examples, 3D for rock drill boom)
  - Linear elastic constitutive relation with Lame constants
  - Neural network architectures: [2, 200, 200, 200, 2] for 2D problems, [3, 500, 500, 500, 3] for 3D problems
  - Optimization using l-BFGS and Adam algorithms
  - Mesh-based approach using finite element methodology with neural networks for displacement approximation
10_1016_j_cma_2024_117681.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Linear elasticity mechanics problems; solving boundary value problems of partial differential equations (PDEs) for solid structures; displacement field calculations under mechanical loads

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Displacement fields (u, v, and w components)
  - Potential energy values (J)
  - Loss function values during training iterations
  - Relative errors at specific test points (e.g., points 1-5 in various test cases)
  - Maximum absolute errors in displacement predictions (e.g., maximum error of u: 4.70×10⁻³ for DFEM vs. 3.62×10⁻² for DEM)
  - Average errors in displacement predictions
  - Convergence history of the optimization process

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Minimize the combined loss function: (1/2 N(θ)ᵀ·K·N(θ) - N(θ)ᵀ·P) + α∑||N(x_i;θ) - û(x_i)||²
  - Achieve stable training convergence (DFEM shows more stable loss evolution than DEM)
  - Reduce relative error compared to Deep Energy Method (DEM) by up to 99%
  - Reduce computation time by up to 7/8 compared to traditional FEM through pre-training
  - Enable fast structural response prediction for digital twin applications
  - Integrate observational data with physical laws to generate high-fidelity models when nominal values differ from actual conditions
10_1016_j_cma_2024_117681.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Plate with circular hole: 20 mm square plate with 5 mm radius hole
  - Rock drill boom: 46,337 elements and 10,205 nodal points in mesh
  - Complex geometries require "enormous number of points" for DEM but DFEM requires significantly fewer points due to structured meshing
  - Boundary conditions must be implemented either through neural network architecture modifications or stiffness matrix adjustments

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Potential energy cannot be lower than theoretical value (violation indicates incorrect solution)
  - Stiffness matrix K* must be symmetric positive definite for proper solution
  - |K*·N(θ)-P*| must equal zero when model converges to correct solution
  - Neural network must have sufficient parameters to ensure ∂N(θ)/∂θ is of full row rank
  - Method constrained to problems with variational formulation (required for energy-based approach)
  - Linear elastic constitutive relation assumed in all examples (λ and μ Lame constants)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - DFEM requires pre-training for optimal efficiency, reducing computation time by up to 7/8 compared to FEM
  - DEM fails to converge for complex 3D geometries (e.g., rock drill boom example)
  - Neural network architecture must be sufficiently complex (e.g., [2, 200, 200, 200, 2] for 2D, [3, 500, 500, 500, 3] for 3D)
  - Boundary conditions must be implemented using either soft BCs (through data loss) or hard BCs (through neural network structure)
  - Method currently validated only for linear elasticity problems (though authors note it can be extended to other PDEs with variational formulation)
  - Integration points for DEM require significantly more computational resources than DFEM's mesh nodes for complex geometries

10_1016_j_nucengdes_2011_08_052.key_3:
- High velocity impact dynamics with large deformation
- Material failure and perforation mechanics

10_1016_j_nucengdes_2011_08_052.key_4:
- Projectile diameter constrained to Φ0.02m and height to 0.08m
- Target plate constrained to 0.28m length, 0.04m width, 0.012m thickness
- Taylor impact rod constrained to 0.006m × 0.018m dimensions
- Beam constrained to 0.01m × 0.01m × 0.09m dimensions
- Particle spacing constrained to 10⁻³ m
- Mesh size near coupling interface constrained to 10⁻³ m
- Maximum time step constrained by Δt_SPH-FEM = min{Δt_SPH, Δt_FEM}
- SPH time step constrained by Δt_SPH = γh/c
- FEM time step constrained by Δt_FEM ≤ Δt_cr = L/c where L is smallest element length
- Damage variable D constrained between 0 (undamaged) and 1 (fully broken), with critical damage value D_C = 0.3

- Tensile instability limitation in SPH formulation requiring artificial stress correction
- Boundary effects limitation in SPH calculations near coupling interface
- Smoothing length constrained by support domain size
- Temperature constrained by homologous temperature T* = (T - T₀)/(T_m - T₀) with T_m = 1800 K
- Perforation time constrained to no more than 100 μs except for tests near ballistic limit
- Mesh coarsening toward boundary to reduce computational time
- Maximum strain rate constrained by Johnson-Cook model parameters

10_1007_s00202_020_01082_8.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Induction machine used as self-excited induction generator (SEIG) for magnetizing and leakage inductance calculation
- **Material / Medium:** Nonoriented 3% Si steel sheets for iron core; aluminum-skewed squirrel-cage rotor bars with 30°/m tilt angle
- **Application & Importance:** Determining magnetizing and leakage inductances in magnetic saturation region for accurate voltage build-up representation in SEIG; essential for implementing advanced control methods and modeling SEIG performance
- **Geometry / Domain:** Two-pole pair induction machines with different configurations: Case I (1.1 kW) with 24 stator slots, 14 rounded trapezoidal rotor bars; Case II (0.75 kW) with 36 stator slots, 24 skewed rectangular rotor bars; air gap between stator and rotor; 2D cross-section models with 3D multisliced representation to account for skewing effects
10_1007_s00202_020_01082_8.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Synchronous motor coupled to induction machine to rotate at synchronous speed (1500 rpm)
  - Slip equals zero, opening the rotor equivalent circuit
  - Rotor losses do not affect calculations
  - Aluminum-skewed squirrel-cage rotor bars with 30°/m tilt angle
  - Relative movement between stator and rotor modeled using moving mesh techniques

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Variable three-phase power supply connected to stator terminals
  - Excitation capacitors fixed to 100 μF (Case I) and 25 μF per phase (Case II)
  - Stator phases fed through three-phase voltage source
  - Ohmic loads connected when generator is loaded
  - No-load conditions during self-excitation process

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Magnetic field and electrical circuit equations coupled and solved simultaneously
  - Aluminum-skewed squirrel-cage rotor bars connected in parallel inside electrical circuit module
  - Rotor rotated at synchronous speed while stator connected to three-phase voltage source

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 2D finite element modeling using COMSOL Software
  - Multisliced FE model for skewed rotor bars (5 cross sections along motor)
  - Dynamic model of SEIG using d-q-axis equivalent circuit in stationary reference frame
  - Transient analysis for self-excitation process
  - Nonlinear analysis considering magnetic saturation effects
10_1007_s00202_020_01082_8.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Electromagnetic field distribution in induction machines
  - Magnetic flux density in air gap and cross-section of machine
  - Magnetic saturation effects in iron core
  - Magnetizing flux calculation based on radial component of magnetic flux density
  - Leakage flux calculation for stator slot and end-winding components

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Magnetizing inductance (LM) versus magnetizing current
  - Stator leakage inductance (Lls) including slot (Llss) and end-winding (Llsew) components
  - Rotor leakage inductance (Llr)
  - Sum of magnetizing and stator leakage inductances (LM + Lls)
  - Radial component of magnetic flux density in air gap
  - Stator voltage buildup during self-excitation process
  - Stator current waveforms during self-excitation
  - Stator voltage under varying resistive loads

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Accurate determination of magnetizing inductance using radial component of air gap magnetic flux density
  - Distinction between stator and rotor leakage inductances in magnetic saturation region
  - Improved modeling of self-excited induction generator (SEIG) voltage build-up and stabilization
  - Validation against experimental results showing closer match than existing methods (Ansari 2018)
10_1007_s00202_020_01082_8.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Case I: 24 stator slots, 14 rounded trapezoidal rotor bars
  - Case II: 36 stator slots, 24 rectangular rotor bars with 30°/m tilt angle
  - Mesh consists of 60,000 domain elements and 2,400 boundary elements for Case I
  - Multisliced FE model requires 5 cross-sections along motor axis to account for skewing effects
  - Simulation performed either on full motor geometry or averaged from multiple 2D cross-sections

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Rotor current is approximately zero at synchronous speed (1500 rpm)
  - Stator phases excited by balanced three-phase voltage source
  - Iron core made of nonoriented 3% Si steel sheets with defined saturation curve
  - Skin effect must be considered in outer layers of rotor bars
  - Magnetic saturation effects must be modeled in both magnetizing and leakage inductances
  - Stator flux linkage curve derived from synchronous speed test

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Aluminum-skewed squirrel-cage rotor construction
  - International standards define leakage inductance ratio (K ≈ 1 for class A, K ≈ 0.67 for class B)
  - DC resistance test used for stator resistance measurement (8.8 Ω for Case I, 10 Ω for Case II)
  - Locked-rotor test used to measure sum of stator and rotor leakage inductances
  - No-load test used to obtain magnetizing inductance
  - Self-excitation process requires specific excitation capacitor values (100 μF for Case I, 25 μF per phase for Case II)

10_1007_s00170_022_10210_6.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Planetary Roller Screw Mechanism (PRSM), a rolling screw transmission device that converts rotational motion to linear reciprocating motion through threaded engagement between screw, roller, and nut components.

- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Elastic modulus (E) for screw (ES), nut (EN), and roller (ER) materials
  - Poisson's ratio (ν) for component materials
  - Allowable shear and bending stresses ([τ], [σ]) for screw, nut, and roller materials
  - Equivalent modulus of elasticity (E*) for contact mechanics calculations

- **Application & Importance:**
  - Optimization of bearing capacity and transmission efficiency of PRSM
  - Improvement of thread load distribution to enhance reliability
  - Reduction of deformation while maintaining structural integrity
  - Achievement of balanced thread stiffness across screw, nut, and roller components

- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - Composed of screw, roller, nut, ring gear, carrier, and spring washer
  - Screw and nut feature multiple-start threads with equal number of starts
  - Roller has single-start thread with spur gears at both ends
  - Thread geometry parameters: pitch (P), thread height (h), root thickness (a), root height (hf = 0.5h), major diameter of nut (D0)
  - Constraint conditions: 3° ≤ αR ≤ 15°, 3° ≤ αS ≤ 15°, 34° ≤ βS ≤ 50°, 0.1 < a < 2.5mm, 0.1 < h < 1.5mm, 55 ≤ D0 ≤ 100mm
  - Thread count range: 20 ≤ nT ≤ 60
  - Number of rollers: nR (5-10 in optimization results)
10_1007_s00170_022_10210_6.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - 3° ≤ αR ≤ 15° (roller helix angle)
  - 3° ≤ αS ≤ 15° (screw helix angle)
  - 34° ≤ βS ≤ 50° (thread contact angle)
  - 0.1 < a < 2.5mm (thread root thickness)
  - 0.1 < h < 1.5mm (thread height)
  - 55 ≤ D0 ≤ 100mm (nut major diameter)
  - 20 ≤ nT ≤ 60 (number of threads)
  - Number of starts constraints: Starts = 4,5 ≤ nR; Starts = 5,5 ≤ nR; Starts = 6,5 ≤ nR
  - f1 ≥ 0
  - 2htan(90-βS) - aT < 0
  - a - P < 0
  - αS - αR > 0
  - Shear strength condition: τb = Fmax/(2aπCb·nrb) ≤ [τ]
  - Bending condition: σb = 3Fmaxh/(a²πCb·nrb) ≤ [σ]
  - Contact yield criterion: Q = 2·(πk*1k*2σS/√(3k*))³·cos(αR)·cos(90-βS)/(3·E*²·(∑σ)²)
  - Maximum thread load constraint: max(Fjk) ≤ Zb

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Axial force (F) applied to the nut
  - Axial load on thread (Fa)
  - Maximum equivalent stress of 460.32 MPa
  - Normal contact load between threads (Fn = Fa/(cosαR·cos(90-βi)))
  - Maximum deformation of 0.027 mm in finite element model
  - Maximum relative error on screw side of about 16%
  - Maximum relative error on nut side of about 15%

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Threaded contact between screw and roller (kIS contact stiffness)
  - Threaded contact between nut and roller (kIN contact stiffness)
  - Shaft segment stiffness between adjacent bearing threads (kBS, kBN, kBR)
  - Force projection to axial direction for analysis
  - Contact deformation follows perpendicular direction of common section
  - Equivalent spring model representing multi-body interactions
  - Thread load distribution between screw side and nut side

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Linearized Hertz contact stiffness using first-order Taylor series expansion
  - 3D finite element simulation for verification
  - Direct stiffness method for thread load distribution model solution
  - Multi-objective optimization using NSGA-II algorithm (population size 200, 100 iterations, crossover probability 0.9)
  - Steady-state static analysis (no dynamic behavior considered)
  - Comparison between thread load distribution model and finite element simulation results
10_1007_s00170_022_10210_6.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Thread load distribution across screw, nut, and roller components
  - Axial deformation of PRSM components under load
  - Contact mechanics between threaded surfaces
  - Thread stiffness characteristics of screw, nut, and roller
  - Force transmission through the threaded engagement

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Thread load distribution coefficient (ratio of actual load to average load)
  - Total deformation of PRSM (analytical solution: 0.0241 mm, FEA: 0.027 mm)
  - Maximum equivalent stress (460.32 MPa)
  - Thread stiffness values for screw (f9), nut (f10), and roller (f11, f12)
  - Transmission efficiency (f8)
  - Maximum relative error (16% on screw side, 15% on nut side)
  - Load distribution on screw side (f2) and nut side (f3)
  - Overall deformation (f1)

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Reduce overall deformation of PRSM by 10%
  - Reduce thread load distribution on screw side by 13.75%
  - Increase transmission efficiency by 45%
  - Increase screw thread stiffness by 45%
  - Increase nut thread stiffness by 50%
  - Increase roller thread stiffness by 50%
  - Achieve balanced thread profile parameters while maintaining structural integrity within constraint conditions
  - Minimize maximum relative errors between analytical model and finite element simulation
10_1007_s00170_022_10210_6.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - 3° ≤ αR ≤ 15° (roller helix angle)
  - 3° ≤ αS ≤ 15° (screw helix angle)
  - 34° ≤ βS ≤ 50° (contact angle of thread)
  - 0.1 < a < 2.5 mm (root thickness of thread)
  - 0.1 < h < 1.5 mm (thread height)
  - 55 ≤ D0 ≤ 100 mm (major diameter of nut)
  - 20 ≤ nT ≤ 60 (number of threads)
  - Number of starts constraints: Starts = 4,5 ≤ nR; Starts = 5,5 ≤ nR; Starts = 6,5 ≤ nR
  - Thread profile parameter limits for x1-x8 (helix angle of roller, helix angle of screw, contact angle of thread, root thickness of thread, thread height, major diameter of nut, number of threads, number of starts)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Shear strength condition: τb = Fmax/(2aπCb·nrb) ≤ [τ]
  - Bending condition: σb = 3Fmaxh/(a²πCb·nrb) ≤ [σ]
  - Contact yield criterion: Q = 2·(πk*1k*2σS/√(3k*))³·cos(αR)·cos(90-βS)/(3·E*²·(∑σ)²)
  - Maximum thread load constraint: max(Fjk) ≤ Zb
  - f1 ≥ 0 (deformation constraint)
  - 2htan(90-βS) - aT < 0
  - a - P < 0 (root thickness must be less than pitch)
  - αS - αR > 0 (screw helix angle must exceed roller helix angle)
  - Maximum relative error on screw side limited to about 16%
  - Maximum relative error on nut side limited to about 15%
  - Total deformation of PRSM must be less than 0.027 mm

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Thread load distribution model only considers axial deformation and load (ignores radial deformation)
  - First two threads and last three threads on screw side show larger errors due to boundary effects
  - First three threads and last four threads on nut side show larger errors due to boundary effects
  - The nut has the biggest shaft segment stiffness among the three parts, limiting improvement in load distribution on nut side
  - Contact angle tends to 45° under various optimum combinations
  - Helix angle of roller approaches the lower limit (3°)
  - Optimal solution obtained when number of starts equals 5
  - Thread profile must maintain proper engagement while meeting structural requirements

10_1016_j_mtcomm_2024_108595.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Laser welding process of SUS304 stainless steel butt-welded joint, specifically focused on predicting residual stress distribution
- **Material / Medium:** SUS304 austenitic stainless steel with composition (wt%): C 0.059, Mn 1.14, Ni 8.7, Cr 18.8, Mo 0.06; Temperature-dependent properties including Young's modulus (10⁴·MPa), Poisson's ratio, yield strength (10²·MPa), expansion coefficient (10⁻⁵·°C⁻¹), density (10⁻⁹·t·mm⁻³), thermal conductivity (mW·mm·10⁻¹·°C⁻¹), and specific heat (10⁸·mJ·t⁻¹·°C⁻¹)
- **Application & Importance:** Residual stress prediction to prevent weld joint failures caused by uneven thermal gradients, as tensile residual stresses can initiate cracks and accelerate pre-existing crack growth, deteriorating structural stability and quality; enables optimization of welding design and procedures
- **Geometry / Domain:** Butt-welded joint with dimensions 100 mm (length) × 50 mm (width) × 4 mm (thickness); welding path along longitudinal center; Goldak double ellipsoid heat source model with parameters a1, a2, b, and c; FE model mesh system with fine mesh at weld zone and coarser mesh at edges
10_1016_j_mtcomm_2024_108595.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Displacement/rotation constraints applied only to leftmost and rightmost planes of base material preventing displacement in x, y, and z directions; displacement-rotation constraint applied only to left and right surfaces of base material to avoid secondary residual stresses from over-constraints
- **Loads / Excitations:** Welding speed of 5 mm/s, voltage of 10 V, current of 190 A; Goldak double ellipsoidal moving heat source model with parameters a1, a2, b, c; heat source power Q = ηUI; thermal convection coefficient of 2.0×10⁻² mW·mm⁻²·°C⁻¹; ambient temperature of 20 °C; radiant emissivity of 8.0×10⁻⁴ mW·mm⁻²·°C⁻¹; energy grading parameters f₁ and f₂ where f₁ + f₂ = 2
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Four interaction types: deactivation of life-and-death elements, surface thermal convection, surface heat radiation, and reactivation of life-and-death elements; surface heat exchange interaction between weldment and surrounding environment; surface thermal radiation interaction between weldment and outside environment; reactivation of life-and-death elements at weld to simulate heating process; deactivation of remaining life-and-death elements at weld to simulate end of welding process
