10_1007_s00466_013_0860_9.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Imbricate Finite Element Method (I-FEM) for 2D solid mechanics analysis using low-order triangular meshes
- **Material / Medium:** Elastic material with Young's modulus E = 210 GPa and Poisson ratio ν = 0.3
- **Application & Importance:** Improvement of smoothness and accuracy in approximations for finite element discretizations using low-order triangular meshes; addresses poor approximation quality of standard linear triangular elements where strain/stress fields are homogeneous over each element
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Benchmark I: Quarter of quadratic slab (L = 100 mm) with central circular hole (a = 40 mm)
  - Benchmark II: Circular slab with straight crack cutting through half the domain
  - Three element types: tri3i6 (interior elements), tri3i5 (edge elements), tri3i4 (corner elements)
  - Mesh types include regular, irregular, and distorted meshes with varying element densities
  - Plane stress conditions assumed for all analyses
10_1007_s00466_013_0860_9.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Benchmark I: Displacement boundary conditions prescribed according to analytical solution for infinite slab with hole, with σ∞xx = 1 MPa, σ∞yy = 0, and σ∞xy = 0
  - Benchmark II: Displacement boundary conditions prescribed according to Westergaard solution for straight crack in infinite slab
  - Patch test: Six displacement fields applied: u = [1+x 0], [x 0], [y 0], [0 1+x], [0 x], [0 y]
  - Zero normal displacement constraints on certain boundary edges (shown in Fig. 33)
  - Stress boundary conditions applied to boundary edges (shown in Fig. 33)

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Asymptotic stress field σ∞ with σ∞xx = 1 MPa for Benchmark I
  - Stress intensity factors KI = 1 MPa and KII = 0 for Benchmark II
  - External forces (Fext) applied to the system as defined in the equilibrium equations

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Imbricate elements overlap with neighboring elements through shared integration domains
  - Parent-child element relationships where imbricate elements (parent) are supported by additional nodes from adjacent elements (child elements)
  - Three child meshes generated from a single background mesh, sharing the same set of nodes
  - Quadratic shape of integration domain boundaries for interior edges, linear shape for boundary edges

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 2D static linear elasticity analysis
  - Plane stress conditions assumed for all analyses
  - Material properties: Young's modulus E = 210 GPa, Poisson ratio ν = 0.3
  - Three integration methods: full integration (3 Gauss points), underintegration (1 Gauss point), smoothed FEM with one smoothing cell
  - Mesh types: regular meshes, irregular meshes, and distorted meshes
  - Direct solver used for system of equations
  - Linear elastic material behavior assumed throughout
10_1007_s00466_013_0860_9.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Linear elastic deformation in 2D solid mechanics, stress-strain field distribution, and displacement field approximation using finite element method
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Strain energy versus degrees of freedom
  - Error measures: Err(U) (nodal displacement error) and Err(σ) (stress field error)
  - Convergence rates (r values) for different element types and integration schemes
  - Computational time versus accuracy
  - Eigenvalues for stability analysis
  - Surface area calculations for patch test validation
- **Optimization Goal:** Improve smoothness and accuracy of approximations from low-order triangular meshes while maintaining computational efficiency; achieve better convergence rates than standard tri3 elements while using minimal additional computational resources (1.6-1.7x time increase with 3.1-10.2x accuracy improvement in displacement errors)
10_1007_s00466_013_0860_9.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Restricted to 2D problems only (not extended to 3D in this paper)
  - Requires triangular background meshes as the base discretization
  - Three element types with different formulations: tri3i6 (interior), tri3i5 (edge), tri3i4 (corner)
  - Mesh layouts significantly affect results when using underintegration (non-monotonic error convergence)
  - Benchmark I geometry: Quarter of quadratic slab (L = 100 mm) with circular hole (a = 40 mm)
  - Benchmark II geometry: Circular slab with straight crack cutting through half the domain

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Plane stress conditions assumed for all analyses
  - Material properties fixed at E = 210 GPa and ν = 0.3
  - Must pass patch test with errors at machine precision level (10⁻¹⁶) for full integration and S-FEM
  - Only three zero eigenvalues representing rigid body motions must be present (no hourglass modes)
  - Underintegration scheme shows surface area error of approximately 0.25% due to element mapping approximation
  - Error measures Err(U) and Err(σ) must be minimized while maintaining computational efficiency
  - Imbricate elements must satisfy standard FEM requirements: continuity, delta function property, and partition of unity

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Requires generation of three child meshes from a single background mesh
  - Numerical integration constrained to three methods: full integration (3 Gauss points), underintegration (1 Gauss point), and smoothed FEM with one smoothing cell
  - Boundary edges of integration domains must be linear, while interior edges have quadratic shape
  - Mesh distortion sensitivity: Imbricate elements are more sensitive to mesh quality than standard tri3 elements
  - Underintegrated imbricate elements show dependence on mesh layout (as shown in Fig. 18) where different layouts produce different area errors (0.25% vs. 0.41%)

10_1002_cjce_24571.key_1:
- Subject: Adiabatic isomerization of n-butane to i-butane in liquid phase
- Fluid composition: n-butane in 90% n-pentane at 2 MPa
- Reaction kinetics: First-order with rate constant k = 31.1 h⁻¹ at 360 K, activation energy 65.7 kJ·mol⁻¹, equilibrium constant KC = 3.03 at 60°C
- Reaction equation: r = k(CnC4 - CiC4/KC)
- Fluid properties: Constant density liquid-phase system
- Reactor geometries: 1D structured mesh, tubular reactor (5° wedge with 0.1 m/0.5 m diameters), notched reactor with sudden expansion-contraction
- Domain simplification: 5° wedge geometry using azimuthal symmetry to accelerate simulation
- Mesh specifications: 1000, 4000, and 16,000 cells for grid convergence study
- Boundary conditions: Fixed-value inlet, zero-gradient outlet, no-slip wall, symmetry axis, wedge boundaries
- Turbulence model: k-ω Shear Stress Transport (SST)
- Simulation software: OpenFOAM with rhoReactingFoam solver
- Grid convergence: Richardson extrapolation showed 7% underestimation with 16,000 cells
- Validation method: Comparison with 1D plug flow model solved in MATLAB
- Operating conditions: 2 MPa pressure, adiabatic temperature rise analysis
10_1002_cjce_24571.key_2:
- Inlet boundary: Fixed-value velocity (0, 0, 26 m/s), fixed-flux-pressure, fixed-value temperature, fixed-value species concentration (0.88 g/g n-butane)
- Outlet boundary: Zero-gradient velocity, fixed-pressure (2×10⁶ Pa), zero-gradient temperature, zero-gradient species concentration, inlet-outlet for k and ω turbulence parameters
- Wall boundary: No slip velocity condition, zero-gradient pressure, zero-gradient temperature, zero-gradient species concentration
- Symmetry boundary: Applied to reactor axis for tubular geometry
- Wedge boundary: Applied to planes along axis for rotational symmetry
- Default/empty boundary: Used in 1D mesh where no solution required
- Turbulence inlet: Turbulent intensity kinetic energy inlet (2-5% turbulence intensity), turbulent mixing length frequency inlet (0.07×hydraulic diameter)
- Turbulence modeling: k-ω Shear Stress Transport (SST) with kqR wall function and Omega wall function
- Operating pressure: 2 MPa
- Reaction conditions: First-order kinetics with k=31.1 h⁻¹ at 360 K, activation energy 65.7 kJ·mol⁻¹, equilibrium constant KC=3.03 at 60°C
- Simulation type: Transient (PISO algorithm with 3 inner correctors), 2D axisymmetric (5° wedge representation), turbulent flow regime
- Mesh type: Structured hexahedral meshes
- Time step constraint: CFL condition (NCFL = Δt·υ/Δx) respected with reduced time step for notched reactor
- Simulation duration: 0.2 s of simulated time
- Adiabatic conditions: No heat transfer to environment during isomerization reaction
10_1002_cjce_24571.key_3:
- Physics solved: Turbulent fluid flow, species transport (n-butane/i-butane), energy transport, and chemical reaction kinetics in liquid phase
- Target outputs: n-butane and i-butane mass fractions along reactor axis, temperature profiles, pressure distribution, velocity field, adiabatic temperature rise (63°C), conversion rates, grid convergence index
- Validation metrics: Comparison with 1D plug flow model (MATLAB), residuals monitoring, mass conservation (0.2% deviation), steady-state behavior
- Grid convergence assessment: Temperature at 0.35 m axial and 0.0075 m radial position used for Richardson extrapolation
- Simulation accuracy target: Within 7% error of Richardson extrapolation solution with 16,000 cells
- Geometric comparison: Conventional tubular reactor versus notched reactor with expansion-contraction effects
- Primary validation objective: Confirm correct implementation of chemical kinetics and thermophysical properties through 0.14% difference in i-butane mass fraction at outlet
10_1002_cjce_24571.key_4:
- Geometric constraint: 5° wedge simplification used for all reactor geometries to leverage azimuthal symmetry and accelerate simulation
- Volume constraint: Notched reactor designed to maintain identical total volume as conventional tubular reactor
- Time step constraint: Reduced time step required for notched reactor to satisfy CFL condition (NCFL = Δt·υ/Δx) due to higher velocities near notch
- Mesh quality constraint: Mesh quality defined by weakest cell with metrics including aspect ratio, skewness, orthogonality, and smoothness
- Convergence threshold: Mass conservation deviation limited to 0.2% for acceptable convergence
- Steady-state requirement: Simulation considered converged after 0.06 s (well below final 0.2 s time step)
- Grid independence constraint: 16,000 cells required to reach within 7% error of Richardson extrapolation solution
- Turbulence model constraint: k-ω SST model specifically selected for flows detaching from walls (notched reactor geometry)
- Computational time constraint: 392s (1000 cells), 1296s (4000 cells), and 6772s (16,000 cells) wall time for 0.2s simulated time on single Intel Core i7 (8th gen)
- Scalability limitation: CFD-DEM codes treat CFD and DEM parts sequentially, limiting parallelization efficiency
- Numerical error constraint: Errors compound as simulation proceeds from one step to the next
- Geometric convergence limitation: Not all areas of geometry converge at same rate, requiring targeted mesh refinement
- Simulation scale limitation: Small-scale phenomena like mass/heat transfer between catalyst particles and gas require fine mesh resolution
- Complex case limitation: Multiphase turbulent reacting flows can exceed weeks of computation time even with parallel computing
- Reaction constraint: Constant density liquid-phase assumption used (no pressure dependency on reaction rate)

10_1007_s12541_022_00706_2.key_1:

- **Geometry / Domain:** Modified Goldak's double ellipsoidal weld heat source (r = 5 mm, b = 3.2 mm); FEM model divides structure into upper plate, lower plate, and welded part; simplification model uses cylindrical welded part geometry; cross-sectional shape of weld matches experimental results with nugget diameter meeting KS B 0850 standard specifications
10_1007_s12541_022_00706_2.key_2:

  - Emission coefficient: 0.6
  - Stefan-Boltzmann constant: 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²·K⁴
  - Contact heat transfer coefficient: 1000 W/m²·K

10_1007_s12541_022_00706_2.key_3:

10_1007_s12541_022_00706_2.key_4:

10_1016_j_compstruc_2004_09_019.key_1:
- Method of finite spheres (MFS) is a meshfree numerical technique for solving boundary value problems on geometrically complex domains in R² and R³.
- MFS covers computational domain with intersecting/overlapping spheres where nodes are placed at sphere centers and interpolation functions are compactly supported on these spheres.
- Five coupling techniques between MFS and finite element method (FEM) are presented: Lagrange multipliers, penalty formulation, and three methods replacing Lagrange multipliers with physical significance (L₁, L₂, L₃).
- Test cases include: 1D elastic bar with distributed loading f(x)=4x², cantilever plate under uniform load of 12,000 psi, and plate with circular hole under tensile load of 1 unit magnitude.
- Material properties: cantilever plate (E=10,009,300 psi, ν=0.33, plane stress); plate with hole (E=100, ν=0.25, plane stress); elastic bar (E=1, cross-sectional area=1 for simplicity).
- Domain geometries analyzed: square domain with nine nodes, rectangular plate with two holes, S-shaped domain, L-shaped domain, cantilever plate, plate with central circular hole.
- Four integration sub-region types defined: Type A (T_A) with IR=0, OR=r_I; Type B (T_B) with IR=0, OR=E_i; Type C (T_C) with IR=E_i, OR=r_I; Type D (T_D) with IR=E_i1, OR=E_i2.
- Two integration methods for T_A/T_B sub-regions and one method for T_C/T_D sub-regions are developed using piece-wise midpoint quadrature rules.
- MFS demonstrates higher convergence rate than FEM for the same number of nodes in strain energy calculations.
- For equivalent accuracy, MFS delivers solutions faster than other methods for sufficiently large problems as shown in error vs. computational cost plots.
- Lagrange multipliers coupling technique provides the most accurate results with minimum computational effort compared to other coupling methods.
- Quadtree structure is used for hierarchical decomposition of 2D domains, with one-level adjusted trees ensuring open cover a priori and enabling adaptive local refinement.
- Valid cover requirements include: complete domain coverage, all nodal points within domain, finite overlap criterion (card{J: x∈B(x_J,r_J)}≤k_max), and volume overlap bounded by smaller sphere volume.
10_1016_j_compstruc_2004_09_019.key_2:
- Dirichlet boundary conditions: u(0)=0 and u(1)=0 for 1D elastic bar; upper and lower edges constrained from motion in y-direction for plate with circular hole
- Neumann boundary conditions: uniformly distributed load of 12,000 psi applied to top surface of cantilever plate; distributed loading f(x)=4x² for 1D elastic bar; uniformly distributed load of 1 per unit length in x-direction on both sides of plate with circular hole
- Interface conditions between MFS and FEM domains: displacement continuity u_MFS = u_FEM on Γ_INT; force equilibrium f_MFS + f_FEM = 0 on Γ_INT
- Material properties: Young's modulus E=10,009,300 psi and Poisson's ratio ν=0.33 (cantilever plate, plane stress); Young's modulus E=100 and Poisson's ratio ν=0.25 (plate with hole, plane stress); Young's modulus E=1 and cross-sectional area=1 (1D elastic bar for simplicity)
- Symmetry conditions applied to plate with circular hole (only quarter domain analyzed)
- Simulation types: linear elastic problems; plane stress conditions; 1D (R¹) and 2D (R²) static analyses; domain decomposed into Ω_MFS and Ω_FEM subdomains with interface Γ_INT
10_1016_j_compstruc_2004_09_019.key_3:
- Linear elasticity problems in R² and R³ (plane stress and plane strain conditions)
- Displacement fields (u), strain fields (ε), and stress fields (τ)
- Strain energy and its convergence with increasing refinement
- Error in strain energy as function of computational cost
- Relative error in integrals for numerical integration schemes
- CPU time and computational cost metrics
- Interface continuity and force equilibrium between MFS and FEM domains
- Optimization of numerical integration schemes for non-polynomial rational functions on complex domains
- Minimization of computational cost while maintaining solution accuracy
- Comparison of coupling techniques to achieve maximum accuracy with minimum computational effort
- Development of automated preprocessing for complex geometries with adaptive local refinement
- Validation of solution accuracy through comparison with exact solutions and pure FEM/MFS results
10_1016_j_compstruc_2004_09_019.key_4:
- Domain must be completely covered by spheres (Ω̄ ⊂ ∪ B(x_I, r_I)) - Condition 1 of valid cover

10_1016_j_finel_2006_01_010.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Quadrilateral finite element models for structural engineering objects, specifically reinforced concrete slabs.
- **Material / Medium:** Reinforced concrete (implied as application domain); no specific material properties provided.
- **Application & Importance:** Automatic calculation of element sizes to ensure mesh generation feasibility while minimizing element count; generation of local mesh refinement zones around stress concentrators (mechanical constraints and point loads) while avoiding highly distorted transition elements to preserve FEA result quality.
- **Geometry / Domain:** 2D multiply connected domains with external boundaries (closed sequences of entities), internal boundaries (openings/holes), and refinement zones; domains may contain T-type points (where mechanical constraints or point loads are applied) and P-type points (start/end points of entities); entity is defined as a line segment with start and end points; boundary entities must contain even number of steps for 100% quadrilateral mesh generation.
10_1016_j_finel_2006_01_010.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Mechanical constraints at T-type points where concentrated forces are applied; external boundary defined as a closed sequence of entities; internal boundaries (openings/holes) defined as closed sequences of entities inside the domain; boundary entities must contain an even number of steps for 100% quadrilateral mesh generation; aspect ratio lower limit for offsetting elements is set to 0.3; obtuse angles in boundary layer elements must be kept below 120° (with 125° as minor increase tolerance); domain boundaries commonly make 90° turns in structural engineering models.
- **Loads / Excitations:** Concentrated forces and point loads applied at T-type points (refinement zones).
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Transition zones between refinement zones and regular mesh must not contain highly distorted elements; neighboring layers offsetting entities can be "glued together" when step sizes are similar; artificial entities introduced for refinement points not connected to existing domain entities.
- **Simulation Type:** 2D structural engineering analysis; quadrilateral finite element mesh generation; 2D multiply connected domains; FEA models of reinforced concrete slabs.
10_1016_j_finel_2006_01_010.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Stress analysis in reinforced concrete slabs.
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Element step sizes along boundary entities; aspect ratio of elements (A = dₐ/s where dₐ is adjacent perpendicular edge length and s is boundary step size); obtuse angles in boundary layer elements; total number of elements in final mesh; element quality (distortion level in transition zones).
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize total element count while ensuring mesh generation feasibility; maintain element aspect ratios close to 1 (square elements) for optimal modeling properties; keep obtuse angles in boundary layer elements below 120° (with 125° as minor tolerance); prevent highly distorted elements in transition zones around stress concentrators to preserve FEA result quality.
10_1016_j_finel_2006_01_010.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Boundary entities must contain an even number of steps to enable 100% quadrilateral mesh generation; 2D multiply connected domains with external boundaries, internal boundaries (openings/holes), and refinement zones; artificial entities for interior refinement points (T-type) require exactly four entities at right angles with lengths equal to refinement zone radius $ R_T $; T-type points located within a predefined margin (several orders of magnitude smaller than user-defined step size) from the domain boundary are automatically moved to the boundary.
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Aspect ratio $ A = d_a/s $ for offsetting elements must be ≥ 0.3; obtuse angles in boundary layer elements must be ≤ 120° (with 125° tolerance when $ A = 0.3 $); step sizes within refinement zones must be ≤ user-defined average edge length $ S_T $; maximum step size ratio between perpendicular entities is capped at $ C = 3 $ to prevent excessive element size growth.
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Step sizes on boundary entities must be reduced to prevent overlap with P-type points and connected entities; step sizes outside refinement zones must be ≤ original values while remaining as close as possible to avoid distorted transitional elements; even number of steps required on all entities within refinement zones.

- **Geometric/Design Space:**

  - Fractures assumed to be fully penetrated and fully planar

  - Constant fracture gap assumption (simplification - actual gaps may vary along hydraulic fracture systems)
  - Fracture tips with closed (no-flow) boundary condition

  - Fracture boundaries discretized with linear elements
  - Reservoir thickness of 10m in low-permeability case (Table 3)

  - Fractures assumed to have constant permeability (200-10,000 μm² range)

  - Flow into wellbore only possible through hydraulic fracture system (not direct matrix flow)

  - The method assumes constant fracture gap despite noting "in reality, fracture gaps could vary along hydraulic fracture system due to residual opening effect" (ongoing work mentioned)

- Electron concentration governed by convection-dominated diffusion equation: ∂e/∂t = ∇·[De(x)∇e + μe(x)eu] - R(e,p)
- Hole concentration governed by convection-dominated diffusion equation: ∂p/∂t = ∇·[Dp(x)∇p - μp(x)pu] - R(e,p)
- Electric field intensity u = -∇ψ
- Diffusion coefficients related to mobilities by Ds(x) = UTμs(x), where UT is thermal voltage
- α = q/ε, where q is electron charge and ε is dielectric permittivity
- N(x) = ND(x) - NA(x) represents donor and acceptor impurity concentrations
- Insulating boundary conditions: ∂ψ/∂ν = ∂e/∂ν = ∂p/∂ν = 0 on ∂Ω
- Initial condition: e(x,0) = e0(x), p(x,0) = p0(x)
- Compatibility condition: ∫Ω(p0 - e0 + N)dx = 0
- Exact solution for test problem: ψ = (1/2π²)exp(-2π²t)cos(πx)cos(πy)

10_1016_j_parco_2011_05_007.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Finite element matrices from Poisson equation, linear elasticity, convection-diffusion equation, Stokes equations, and Maxwell cavity resonator problems.
- **Material / Medium:** Stainless steel with Lamé parameters μ = 80193.80, λ = 110743.82 for elasticity; ϵ = 1/200 for convection-diffusion; κ² = 0.01 for Maxwell cavity with first eigenvalue λ₁ ≈ 0.0028.
- **Application & Importance:** Solving large-scale finite element problems with millions/billions of unknowns; providing robust solutions for indefinite, unsymmetric, or ill-conditioned systems where iterative solvers fail; enabling efficient parallel computation on distributed memory systems.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Unit square/cube for Poisson problem; backward facing step configuration for Stokes problem; Ω = (-1,1)² for convection-diffusion; 3D geometries with surface meshes for elasticity and Maxwell cavity resonator; domain decomposed into 4 subdomains for 2D square example.
10_1016_j_parco_2011_05_007.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions on ∂Ω for Poisson problem; u = 0 on Γ_D (Dirichlet boundary) and σn = t on Γ_N (Neumann boundary) for linear elasticity; solution prescribed on ∂Ω for convection-diffusion; inflow boundary on left, no-flow condition on walls (top and bottom), Neumann condition on right side for Stokes problem; ν × u = 0 on ∂Ω for Maxwell cavity resonator.
- **Loads / Excitations:** Source term f in Ω for Poisson problem; surface traction t on Γ_N for linear elasticity; vector field b and source term f for convection-diffusion equation; given current density f for Maxwell cavity resonator.
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Non-overlapping domain decomposition with Ω = Ω_1 ∪ ... ∪ Ω_P where Ω_p = ∪_{c∈C_p} Ω_c; processor interfaces for parallel computation with P = 2^S processors; communication between processors for Schur complements.
- **Simulation Type:** Linear steady-state problems; 2D and 3D domains; symmetric positive definite (Poisson), symmetric positive definite but not M-matrix (linear elasticity), non-symmetric (convection-diffusion), symmetric indefinite (Stokes), and symmetric indefinite ill-conditioned (Maxwell) systems; parallel computation on distributed memory systems.
10_1016_j_parco_2011_05_007.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Linear system solutions from finite element discretizations of Poisson equation, linear elasticity, convection-diffusion equation, Stokes equations, and Maxwell cavity resonator problems; solution of distributed linear systems Ax = b with symmetric positive definite, symmetric indefinite, and non-symmetric matrices.
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Factorization time [s], solution time [s], number of degrees of freedom (d.o.f.), number of non-zero matrix entries, residual reduction (e.g., 2.8×10⁻¹⁴), comparison with MUMPS solver performance, parallel scaling behavior across 2^S processors (S=0 to 10).
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize factorization time for large-scale finite element problems; achieve optimal parallel efficiency with increasing processor count (P=2^S); outperform MUMPS for higher processor numbers; minimize communication overhead while maintaining numerical accuracy; handle distributed Schur complements efficiently in parallel computation.
10_1016_j_parco_2011_05_007.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Domain decomposition requires P=2^S processors; non-overlapping domain decomposition with Ω = Ω₁ ∪ ... ∪ Ω_P where Ω_p = ∪_{c∈C_p} Ω_c; efficiency depends on small processor interfaces for final steps; load balancing must use recursive coordinate bisection or spectral bisection algorithms; domain must be decomposable into cells C for cell-based additive decomposition of bilinear form.
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Residual reduction of ~10⁻⁵ is sufficient in most finite element contexts; sparse matrices only in initial elimination steps (s=0), becoming dense in subsequent steps; communication time dominates computation time for small problems on large processor counts; maximum processor count per cluster limited to p_max (64 for small problems, 128-256 for larger problems); factorization time increases when communication becomes too expensive (observed for level l=6 in 3D Poisson problem).
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Implementation requires MPI for inter-processor communication; algorithm uses BLAS/LAPACK via Intel Math Kernel Library for dense matrices; sparse matrix operations use MUMPS or SuperLU solvers; limited to hardware with Intel Xeon Quad Core processors (2.53GHz) connected by InfiniBand 4X QDR interconnect; requires non-overlapping domain decomposition with additive matrix representation.

- **Identity & Domain:** Time-dependent conduction-convection problems; specifically Bénard convection problem and thermal driven cavity flow problem

- **Geometry / Domain:** Bénard convection domain Ω = [0, 5] × [0, 1] with thermal insulation ∂ᵥT = 0 on lateral boundaries and fixed temperature difference between top (T=0) and bottom (T=1) boundaries; thermal driven cavity flow domain Ω = [0, 1]² with thermal insulation ∂ᵥT = 0 on top and bottom boundaries and fixed temperature difference between left (T=0.5) and right (T=-0.5) boundaries
- **Numerical Parameters:** Bénard convection: mesh size h = 1/16, time step τ = 0.01; thermal driven cavity flow: mesh size h = 1/32, time step τ = 10⁻⁴; Taylor-Hood finite element space used for both problems
- **Forcing Conditions:** Zero forcing functions (f = 0, b = 0) for both problems; initial conditions u₀ = 0, T₀ = 0 for both problems

10_1016_j_cma_2010_06_017.key_1:

- Geometry / Domain: 2D plate with circular hole (Ω=[-2,2]×[-2,2], hole radius=1m); Cook's membrane (48×60 tapered panel); axis-symmetric ring (inner radius=1, outer radius=2); 3D thick plate ([-2,2]×[-2,2]×[-0.5,0.5], cylindrical hole radius=1); hollow sphere (inner radius=1.3, outer radius=2.0); 3D Cook's membrane (yOz plane structure)

- Loads / Excitations: Time-dependent surface forces g(t)=500t at top/bottom edges (2D plate with hole); in-plane shearing load g(t)=e^(3t/40) at x=48 (Cook's membrane); surface forces g₁(t)=teᵣ on inner radius and g₂(t)=-teᵣ/4 on outer radius (axis-symmetric ring); time-dependent outer pressures g(t)=100t in y-direction (3D thick plate); uniform pressure g(t)=50teᵣ on inner radius (hollow sphere); time-dependent shear force g=90te_z (3D Cook's membrane)
- Interactions / Interfaces: No volume force in all examples; smoothing domains associated with nodes for NS-FEM; element mesh required for all S-FEM models; comparison between FEM-T3/T4, ES-FEM-T3, and FS-FEM-T4
- Simulation Type: Transient visco-elastoplastic analyses with time intervals from t=0.02 to t=1.0; time discretization with uniform steps (Δt=0.02-0.03); dual formulation with displacements and stresses; von-Mises yield function with Prandtl–Reuss flow rule; three material behaviors: perfect visco-elastoplasticity, visco-elastoplasticity with isotropic hardening, and visco-elastoplasticity with linear kinematic hardening
10_1016_j_cma_2010_06_017.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Visco-elastoplastic behavior of solids under time-dependent loading; elastic strain energy distribution; displacement field evolution; stress field distribution; plastic zone development; time-dependent material response with perfect visco-elastoplasticity, isotropic hardening, and linear kinematic hardening
- Target Outputs (Metrics): Elastic strain energy (E = ∫Ω σ_ϑ : e_ϑ dΩ); displacements at specific nodes (e.g., points A and B); error estimator η^h; global relative error in elastic strain energy; number of Newton-Raphson iterations; CPU time; elastic shear energy density (‖dev(σ̂_h)‖²/(4μ)); degrees of freedom (DOFs); computational efficiency (error estimator versus computational cost)
- Optimization Goal: Demonstrate NS-FEM's upper bound property for visco-elastoplastic analyses; prove NS-FEM provides higher accuracy than FEM despite higher computational cost; establish NS-FEM's superior efficiency (accuracy per computational time) compared to FEM; enable solution bounding using NS-FEM (upper bound) and FEM (lower bound); allow global relative error estimation without analytical solutions

10_1016_j_engfailanal_2024_108912.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Turbomachinery blade-disk fir-tree coupling connections
- **Material / Medium:** Blade and disk materials with Young's modulus of 200 GPa and density of 7.70×10³ kg/m³; materials assumed to have identical elastic properties in analysis
- **Application & Importance:** Optimization of load distribution across engaging teeth to prevent failure under extreme centrifugal forces during turbine operation; critical for structural integrity as blade-disk attachment failure can lead to catastrophic consequences
- **Geometry / Domain:** Multi-toothed "fir-tree" profile with 3-5 teeth; defined by throat cross-sections (TCS) at minimum area points; consists of circular arcs and segments with common tangents forming active (contact) and idle (non-contact) tooth surfaces; characterized by parameters including radial height H, frontal half width W_f, tooth pitch p, sub-pitch q, fillet radius r, and tooth aspect ratio A_r
10_1016_j_engfailanal_2024_108912.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Symmetry boundary conditions applied to blade and disk symmetry lines; Uniform radial displacement applied at the top of the blade section; Zero friction coefficient at contact interfaces; Displacement-controlled loading on the blade neck section; Fixed constraints at symmetry planes
- **Loads / Excitations:** Centrifugal force of airfoil-platform-neck assembly (F_apn = 8.04×10⁵ N); Blade-root centrifugal force (F_b-rt = 3.07×10⁵ N); Disk-post centrifugal force (F_d-pd = 2.45×10⁵ N); Disk angular speed of 4500 rpm; Total centrifugal force on joint inner radius (F_tot = 1.42×10⁶ N)
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Contact between blade-root and disk-post teeth; Augmented Lagrange contact method simulating normal pressure with zero friction; Spring model representation of radial contact stiffness (k_t) between tooth pairs; Radial displacement differences between corresponding blade and disk points
- **Simulation Type:** 2D plane strain finite element analysis; Second-order elements with adaptive meshing; Element size of 0.16 mm in contact regions; Static structural analysis; Parametric modeling with MATLAB and ANSYS APDL; Spring model with equivalent stiffness representation of blade-root and disk-post sections
10_1016_j_engfailanal_2024_108912.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Elastic deformation under centrifugal loads; contact mechanics between blade-root and disk-post teeth; stress distribution in throat cross-sections; load distribution across multiple engaging teeth pairs; tensile and bending stress analysis in fir-tree coupling structures
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Mean tensile stresses on throat cross-sections (TCS); mean contact pressure on full available contact area; maximum contact pressure (flat and Hertz cylindrical); mean shear stress on tooth bases; maximum tensile bending stress on tooth bases; radial displacement differences between corresponding blade and disk points; peak stresses at fillets with notch factors; indicator stresses and strains at critical locations
- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve uniform load distribution across all engaging teeth pairs; equalize mean tensile stresses on throat cross-sections between blade-root and disk-post; minimize peak stresses at contact surfaces and throat cross-sections; balance material distribution between blade-root, disk-post, and teeth to ensure equal contact forces on all teeth pairs while maintaining structural integrity against centrifugal forces
10_1016_j_engfailanal_2024_108912.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Number of teeth constrained to 3, 4, or 5; Radial height of joint H = 55.1 mm; Frontal joint width at outer radius 2Wf = 80.21 mm; Normal joint width at outer radius 2Wn = 72.64 mm; Teeth radial pitch p = 12 mm; Radial center-to-center of active profile q = 4.87 mm; Tip & fillet nominal radius r = 2 mm; Stagger angle ψ = 25°; Angle of teeth band to vertical η = 28.84°; Angle of contact surface to horizontal α = 28.1°; Reference profile assumes all teeth have identical shape; Radial axes of blade-root and disk-post approximated as parallel
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Young's modulus of blade and disk materials = 200 GPa; Density of blade and disk materials = 7.70×10³ kg/m³; Airfoil-platform-neck centrifugal force Fapn = 8.04×10⁵ N; Blade-root centrifugal force Fb-rt = 3.07×10⁵ N; Disk-post centrifugal force Fd-pd = 2.45×10⁵ N; Maximum allowable difference between spring model and FEM contact pressures: 5.8% (n=5 case); Maximum allowable difference for TCS stresses: 6.6% (blade-root, n=5 case); Contact forces must be uniform across all engaging teeth pairs; Mean tensile stresses on throat cross-sections must be equalized between blade-root and disk-post
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Actual geometry requires small clearances for assembly; Rounding radius at blade neck base required; Rounding at disk slot bottom and disk-post tip required; Clearances between idle profiles required; Clearances between bottom fillet and facing tooth tip required; Mesh element size in finest area = 0.16 mm (1/30 of contacting length); Contact simulated using augmented Lagrange method enabling separation and sliding; Tooth shapes must maintain uniform stiffness across all teeth-pairs; Friction coefficient set to zero in validation cases

10_1016_j_finel_2005_11_006.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** 2D Stokes flow problem, an approximation of incompressible Navier-Stokes equations for low Reynolds numbers
- **Material / Medium:** Incompressible fluid with kinematic viscosity ν (set to 1 in analytical example); body force per unit mass b
- **Application & Importance:** Stabilization of low-order finite element velocity-pressure interpolation pairs (Q₁Q₁ and P₁P₁) that fail to satisfy the LBB condition; development of a variational multiscale stabilized (VMS) method to enable stable computation using easily implemented low-order elements
- **Geometry / Domain:** Square domain Ω = [0,1] × [0,1] for analytical Stokes problem; square lid-driven cavity domain for benchmark test; 10×10 element meshes (100 total elements) used in analytical example; equivalent element domains Ωₑᶜ defined as smallest circle enclosing each finite element; upper boundary moves at unit speed while other boundaries are fixed in cavity problem; pressure singularities present at both corners of cavity domain
- **Boundary Conditions:** Zero velocity boundary conditions for analytical Stokes problem; u₁=1, u₂=0 on top boundary and u₁=u₂=0 on all other boundaries for cavity problem
- **Element Types:** Q₁Q₁ elements (bilinear velocity and bilinear pressure); P₁P₁ elements (linear velocity and linear pressure); 200 total elements used in some cavity problem meshes
- **Convergence Performance:** L2 norm of pressure errors decreases with increasing number of elements; VMS method shows similar convergence rate to MINI and GLS methods
- **Stabilization Parameter:** For GLS method, τₑ = (1/3)hₑ²/(4ν) where hₑ is characteristic element size
- **Analytical Solution:** For analytical Stokes problem, v₁ = x²(1-x)²(2y-6y²+4y³), v₂ = -y²(1-y)²(2x-6x²+4x³), p = x(1-x)
10_1016_j_finel_2005_11_006.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Pure Dirichlet boundary conditions with v = v₀ on Γ; zero velocity boundary conditions (v = 0) on all boundaries for analytical Stokes problem; u₁=1, u₂=0 on top boundary and u₁=u₂=0 on all other boundaries for cavity problem; pressure prescribed as p = 0 at point (0,0) to remove spurious constant pressure modes
- **Loads / Excitations:** Body force per unit mass b; specific analytical expressions for b₁ and b₂ in analytical Stokes problem; no body force in cavity problem; kinematic viscosity ν = 1 in analytical example
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Two-scale interaction between fine scale velocity and coarse scale pressure; stabilization term represents physical interaction between fine scale velocity and coarse scale pressure
- **Simulation Type:** 2D steady-state simulation; incompressible fluid flow; low Reynolds number regime (Stokes flow approximation)
10_1016_j_finel_2005_11_006.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Incompressible fluid flow governed by 2D Stokes equations (low Reynolds number approximation of Navier-Stokes equations); velocity and pressure fields calculation
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Velocity field distribution; pressure field distribution; L2 norm of pressure errors; convergence rates of different stabilization methods (VMS, MINI, GLS); pressure singularities at cavity corners; stabilization parameter matrix
- **Optimization Goal:** Stabilize low-order velocity-pressure finite element interpolation pairs (Q₁Q₁ and P₁P₁) that fail to satisfy LBB condition; achieve consistent convergence rate comparable to MINI and GLS methods; provide physically interpretable stabilization term representing interaction between fine scale velocity and coarse scale pressure
10_1016_j_finel_2005_11_006.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Square domain Ω = [0,1] × [0,1] used for analytical Stokes problem; equivalent element domains Ωₑᶜ defined as smallest circle enclosing each finite element; 10×10 element meshes (100 total elements) used in analytical example; 200 total elements used in some cavity problem meshes; square lid-driven cavity domain for benchmark test
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Low-order velocity-pressure elements (Q₁Q₁, P₁P₁) do not satisfy LBB condition without stabilization; pressure can only be determined up to a constant for pure Dirichlet problem (p = 0 prescribed at point (0,0) to remove spurious constant pressure modes); kinematic viscosity ν = 1 in analytical example; second derivatives of velocity vanish for low-order elements; stabilization parameter τₑ = (1/3)hₑ²/(4ν) where hₑ is characteristic element size
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Method designed specifically for low-order elements (interpolation order less than 2); approximation of neglecting fine scale solutions on element boundaries; use of infinite domain Green's functions rather than element-specific Green's functions; Taylor series expansion of coarse scale residual with only constant term retained; boundary integral terms neglected in local scale interaction calculations

  - Unit B: Cretaceous limestones and intrusive rocks (ρ = 2650 kg/m³, E = 3.6×10⁴ Pa, ν = 0.30)
- **Application & Importance:** Understanding stress field equilibrium of volcanic feeding system to explain long-lasting open conduit dynamics since 1913; assessing influence of geological data on numerical simulation reliability
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - 60 km × 30 km x-z Cartesian domain
  - Deep magma chamber: 2a = 14 km, 2b = 3.6 km at 15 km depth
  - Shallow magma chamber: 2a = 3.5 km, 2b = 2 km at 6 km depth
  - Feeder dykes with deep dyke 2ad = 2 km; shallow dyke width 2bd = 100 m
  - Fault damage zones: ca. 70° inclination, ca. 1 km thick, down to 10 km depth
  - Extensional far-field stress of 5 MPa applied at lateral boundaries
  - Magma overpressures: 10 MPa (deep chamber), 5 MPa (shallow chamber)
10_5194_se_11_2515_2020.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Zero normal displacements at bottom and lateral boundaries (except for extensional model case where zero displacement is removed from lateral sides)
  - Free-stress ground surface at upper boundary
  - Domain extends 60 km along x-axis and 30 km along z-axis
  - Unperturbed domain area extends approximately 30 km horizontally and 25 km vertically
  - Fault damage zones with 70° inclination, 1 km thickness, extending to 10 km depth

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Gravitational loading implemented via body forces
  - Magma overpressure: 10-20 MPa for 15 km deep chamber (ΔPe for isolated chambers, ΔPo for connected)
  - Magma overpressure: 5 MPa for 6 km deep chamber
  - Dyke overpressure: 10 MPa in deeper dyke, 5 MPa in shallower dyke
  - Conduit overpressure: 0.4 MPa in upper 500 m of conduit
  - Extensional far-field stress: uniform 5 MPa applied to lateral boundaries
  - Local extensive field simulated using reduced material properties in fault zones

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Magma chambers and dykes modeled as pressurized finite-size bodies in elastic crustal segment
  - Internal forces applied to chamber and dyke walls as boundary conditions
  - Deep magma chamber (15 km depth) connected to shallow chamber (6 km depth) via dykes
  - Shallow chamber connected to surface via conduit
  - Fault damage zones with degraded mechanical properties mimicking CR faults

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 2D plane strain approximation in x-z Cartesian coordinate system
  - E-W cross section (a-a') along the extension associated with the active Colima Rift
  - Linear Static Analysis (LISA) software version 8.0
  - Finite element discretization using three- and four-node elements (4660 plane continuum elements)
  - Stratified lithology models with four geological units (B, FC, GF, VD)
  - Multiple configurations: homogeneous vs. stratified lithology, single vs. dual magma chambers, with/without conduits, with/without extensional stress, with/without fault damage zones

  - Plane strain approximation used (deformation in third direction assumed negligible)
  - Mesh discretization with 4660 plane continuum elements, refined in high-gradient regions near magma system boundaries
  - Unperturbed domain area limited to approximately 30 km horizontal and 25 km vertical extent

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Magma overpressures constrained to 10-20 MPa for deep chamber and 5 MPa for shallow chamber (based on literature)

  - Material properties constrained by geological data (Table 2 values for density, Young's modulus, Poisson ratio)
  - Model accounts only for elastic regime (LISA software limitation)
  - Gravity included as body forces but no plastic deformation simulated
  - Dry rock masses assumption (pore pressure neglected)
  - Maximum stress variations limited to a few megapascals in equilibrium configuration

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - LISA software limitation: cannot include frictional law to represent fault movement

- **Material / Medium:** Magnesium AZ31B alloy; density 1780 kg/m³; Young's modulus 45 GPa; Poisson's ratio 0.34; Johnson-Cook constants A=238.5 MPa, B=252.6 MPa, n=0.4035, C=0.016; reference strain rate 1000 s⁻¹; Hall-Petch constants σ₀=75.66 MPa, k_HP=13.15 MPa·mm^(1/2); coefficient of friction μ=0.42; as-received average grain size 4.86-5.7 μm; SER-processed average grain size 4.2-4.487 μm
- **Application & Importance:** Overcome non-uniform grain refinement in conventional rolling where surface layers refine but core remains coarse; SER reduces grain sizes by up to 42% relative to conventional rolling; improves grain uniformity with non-uniformity value of 0.0914; enhances formability of Mg AZ31 which has inferior ductility compared to steel and aluminum alloys
- **Geometry / Domain:** Starting/ending rollers radius 125 mm; SER roller radius 75 mm; initial plate thickness t₀=100 mm; final thickness t_f=80 mm (20% reduction ratio); span distances S=450 mm and 900 mm (S/2=225 mm and 450 mm); SER-V transverse displacement 0-110 mm; SER angle φ 0°-13.74°; contact length formula L=Rθ; maximum contact angle θ_max=tan⁻¹(μ); plate thickness analysis range -40 mm to 40 mm; optimal SER4 configuration: S/2=225 mm, SER-V=40 mm, φ=10.08° with average grain size 3.127 μm, standard deviation 0.23, range 0.851 μm
10_1016_j_mtcomm_2023_106362.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Analytic-rigid roller model with R2D2 element type
  - 4-node bilinear plane strain quadrilateral CPE4R elements for AZ31 rod
  - Initial plate thickness t₀=100 mm, final thickness t_f=80 mm (20% reduction ratio)
  - 10 mm initial reduction equally divided over first roller pair (10% of initial thickness)
  - 10 mm final reduction equally divided over ending rollers (10% of initial thickness)
  - Coefficient of friction μ=0.42 between rollers and AZ31
  - Horizontal alignment maintained using water balance tool
  - Material fixed at both ends by holders attached to static steel frame

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Transverse load applied via SER roller with displacement up to 110 mm (110% of t₀)
  - Transverse displacement of 40% of AZ31 rod diameter in experimental prototype
  - Axial pre-tension applied to rod to approach nominal yield strength
  - Rolling speed of π rad/s in computational model
  - Experimental rolling speed of 1 m/min
  - Distributed transverse load w(x) generating horizontal shear force ΔH

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Frictional contact between rollers and AZ31 material
  - Material squeezing (wedge) effect observed before ending rollers
  - Unsymmetric material flow around SER roller
  - Contact length L = Rθ between rolled plate and upper-end rollers
  - Maximum contact angle θ_max = tan⁻¹(μ)
  - Horizontal shear force ΔH calculated from axial gradient in normal stress

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 2D dynamic/explicit analysis in ABAQUS
  - Adaptive Lagrangian Eulerian (ALE) method for mesh distortion control
  - Plane strain condition
  - Johnson-Cook viscoplasticity model for material behavior
  - Tresca yield criterion for stress analysis
10_1016_j_mtcomm_2023_106362.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Plastic deformation of Mg AZ31B under shear-enhanced rolling
  - Stress distribution (Tresca yield criterion) in rolled cross-section
  - Grain refinement mechanics using Hall-Petch relationship
  - Material flow with transverse shear stress induction
  - Contact mechanics between rollers and workpiece
  - Johnson-Cook viscoplastic material behavior

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Tresca yield stress distribution along plate thickness
  - Grain size distribution calculated from Hall-Petch equation
  - Average grain size (μm) along cross-sectional thickness
  - Standard deviation of grain sizes (μm)
  - Grain size range (μm) across thickness
  - Non-uniformity metric (d_max/d_average - 1)
  - Contact length (L) between rolled plate and end rollers
  - SER angle (φ) and SER-V displacement

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Maximize grain refinement (minimize average grain size to 3.127 μm, 42% reduction from NoSER 5.408 μm)
  - Maximize grain uniformity (minimize standard deviation to 0.23, 70% improvement from NoSER 0.746)
  - Minimize grain size range (0.851 μm, 65% improvement from NoSER 2.417 μm)
  - Optimize SER-V displacement and span distance to maximize contact length (L = Rθ) while respecting friction constraint θ_max = tan⁻¹(μ)
  - Achieve uniform grain structure across entire cross-section (core refined to match surface grain size)
10_1016_j_mtcomm_2023_106362.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Starting/ending roller radius fixed at 125 mm
  - SER roller radius fixed at 75 mm
  - Span distances (S) limited to 450 mm and 900 mm (S/2 = 225 mm and 450 mm) in computational study
  - SER-V displacement range limited to 0-110 mm (0-110% of initial thickness t₀=100 mm)
  - Contact length (L) constrained by L = Rθ with maximum L_max = R tan⁻¹(μ)
  - SER angle φ limited by maximum contact length constraint

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Maximum contact angle θ_max = tan⁻¹(μ) where μ = 0.42 (coefficient of friction)
  - Process becomes inoperable if it exceeds maximum roller contact length
  - Material squeezing (wedge) effect before ending rollers limits process viability
  - Unsymmetric material flow observed as a physical limitation in simulations
  - Tresca stresses higher near top surface than bottom surface due to bending
  - Thermal softening term was inactive as experiments conducted at room temperature

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Rolling speed maintained at 1 m/min in experimental prototype
  - Horizontal alignment must be maintained using water balance tool
  - Initial axial pre-tension required to approach nominal yield strength
  - No reduction ratio applied in prototype (all plasticity from transverse SER action)
  - Material fixed at both ends by holders attached to static steel frame
  - Differential speed rolling (DSR) identified as necessary to overcome wedging problem
  - Grain uniformity distribution differs for same SER angle at different span distances
  - SER-V must be adjusted considering practical rolling limitations rather than theoretical maximum
  - Prototype requires fixed number of turns to generate nominal axial strain
  - Transverse displacement limited to 40% of AZ31 rod diameter in experimental testing

- **Identity & Domain:** Countersunk blind riveting process for aluminum alloy components with 120° countersink angle
- **Material / Medium:**

  - Sleeve: 2A10 aluminum alloy (Yield Strength: 265.0 MPa, Tensile Strength: 418.4 MPa, Elastic Modulus: 73.8 GPa, Poisson's Ratio: 0.33)
  - Locking ring: 5056 aluminum alloy (Yield Strength: 301.8 MPa, Tensile Strength: 354.5 MPa, Elastic Modulus: 72.0 GPa, Poisson's Ratio: 0.33)
  - Connecting plates: 7075 aluminum alloy
- **Application & Importance:** Optimization of riveting process parameters to ensure high connection strength, reliability, and proper joint formation in automotive and aerospace industries
- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - Rivet nominal diameter: 4 mm
  - Hole diameter range: 4.10-4.30 mm (0.05 mm increments)
  - Interlayer thickness range: 3.20-4.80 mm (0.40 mm increments)
  - Components: mandrel, sleeve, locking ring, upper/lower connecting plates, puller
  - Critical features: breakneck groove, lock groove, 120° countersink
  - Mesh specifications: Mandrel (0.10 mm element size, 16,632 elements), Sleeve (0.10 mm, 1,276 elements), Locking ring (0.05 mm, 572 elements), Connecting plate (0.30 mm, 1,788 elements)

10_1016_j_mtcomm_2024_111078.key_2:

  - Puller movement: constant velocity of 2.3 mm/s until breakneck groove flushes with sleeve
  - Upper plate movement: constant velocity of 1.0 mm/s for locking
  - Friction coefficient: 0.2 (Coulomb friction)
  - Rigid molds: puller and upper plate (no heat transfer)
  - Deformable molds: sleeve, locking ring, upper/lower connecting plates

  - Locking force (Fβ) from locking ring on mandrel

  - Load stages: upset head formation (0-1.4s, max ~0.82 kN), void filling (1.4-2.8s, max ~2.75 kN), mandrel fracture (>2.8s, max ~2.85 kN)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**

  - Contact conditions: sleeve-mandrel, sleeve-plate, locking ring-mandrel, locking ring-sleeve
  - Mesh type: four-node quadrilateral elements for workpiece and deformable molds
  - Material interfaces: mandrel-sleeve, sleeve-plate, locking ring-sleeve

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Software: Simufact Forming
  - Model type: 2D axisymmetric finite element model
  - Analysis type: Transient (time-dependent) simulation of riveting process
  - Material behavior: Nonlinear (plastic deformation)
  - Analysis focus: Contact mechanics and deformation during riveting process
10_1016_j_mtcomm_2024_111078.key_3:

  - Contact mechanics between sleeve-mandrel, sleeve-plate, locking ring-mandrel, and locking ring-sleeve
  - Stress distribution and equivalent stress fields in all components

  - Protrusion size of mandrel relative to sleeve (A) and locking ring relative to sleeve (B) (mm)
  - Contact stress between sleeve-mandrel, sleeve-plate, locking ring-mandrel, and locking ring-sleeve (MPa)
  - Equivalent stress distribution in mandrel, sleeve, and locking ring (MPa)
  - Contact conditions (contact vs. uncontacted areas) across interfaces
  - Joint morphology measurements at specific points (1.2 mm from lower plate, 0.8 mm from upper plate)
  - Area of equivalent stress distribution in deformation regions

  - Maximize contact stress between sleeve-mandrel and sleeve-plate to enhance joint strength
  - Ensure proper locking ring engagement with mandrel and sleeve to prevent locking failure
  - Determine optimal hole diameter (4.15 mm) and interlayer thickness (4.00 mm) for best riveting quality
  - Minimize risk of locking failure by maintaining proper protrusion sizes (mandrel ~0.005 mm, locking ring ~0.10 mm)
  - Balance between hole diameter and interlayer thickness to optimize void filling and upset head formation

10_1016_j_finel_2019_07_004.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Crack propagation in 3D solid concrete using extended finite element method (X-FEM) combined with anisotropic damage-plasticity modeling
- **Material / Medium:** Concrete (quasi-brittle material) exhibiting sudden failure in tension, combination of crushing and plastic deformation under compression, and softening behavior
- **Application & Importance:** Accurate numerical simulation of concrete under multiaxial loading, capturing material degradation and discrete crack propagation; critical for structural integrity analysis where classical plasticity models fail to account for material degradation
- **Geometry / Domain:** Three test geometries: (1) Three-point bending beam (600×150×100 mm); (2) Double-notched shear specimen (200×200×50 mm with 25×5 mm notches); (3) Four-point shear beam (840×200×100 mm with 40×10 mm notch)
- **Mesh Specifications:** 8-node linear 3D elements with standard 8-point Gauss integration; fine mesh with minimum element size (ℓc)min = 12 mm (three-point bending), 7 mm (double-notched), and 10 mm (four-point shear)
- **Non-local Parameters:** Non-local averaging radius R = 30 mm (three-point bending), R = 25 mm (double-notched), R = 30 mm (four-point shear); typically 3 times minimum element size
- **Crack Direction Parameters:** Distance parameter ℓd = 1.7ℓc (three-point bending), 1.8ℓc (double-notched), 1.5ℓc (four-point shear)
- **Damage Switch-off:** Zone width ℓa = 3ℓc; distance from crack tip dtip = 10 mm
- **Crack Initiation Criterion:** Total equivalent damage parameter φeqtip ≥ critical value φcr = 0.5
- **Material Constants:** Young's modulus E = 28-32.8 GPa; Poisson's ratio ν = 0.1-0.2; tensile strength σ0+ = 35-38 MPa; compressive strength σ0- = 2.3-3.2 MPa; material constants B+ = 0.54, B- = 0.12, b = 2200
- **Numerical Implementation:** Enriched elements sub-divided into 4×4×4 cubic sub-elements with 8 Gauss points each; rectangular sub-division strategy used for cracked elements
- **Boundary Conditions:** Displacement-controlled approach used in all simulations to predict softening; three-point bending with two supports and central load; double-notched with horizontal shear force followed by vertical displacement; four-point shear with symmetric loading pattern
- **Crack Propagation Method:** Crack tip always intersects element edges (not allowed inside elements); direction determined by averaging normal unit vectors of damage tensor components from neighboring Gauss points within radius ℓd
10_1016_j_finel_2019_07_004.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Three-point bending beam: Two roller supports at bottom (600 mm span), displacement-controlled loading at top center
  - Double-notched shear specimen: Horizontal shear force (Pₛ) applied at vertical edges followed by vertical tensile displacement while maintaining shear force constant
  - Four-point shear beam: Symmetric loading with 10/11 P and 1/11 P force distribution as shown in Figure 24
  - Crack tip always intersects element edges (not allowed inside elements)
  - Displacement-controlled approach used in all simulations to predict softening behavior
  - Crack plane boundary condition where stress value must vanish

- **Loads / Excitations:** 
  - Three-point bending: Central vertical displacement (u) applied to top surface
  - Double-notched shear test: Horizontal shear force (Pₛ) with three loading paths: Pₛ = 5 kN, Pₛ = 10 kN, and Pₛ = 27.5 kN
  - Four-point shear test: Four-point loading pattern with applied forces (10/11 P and 1/11 P)
  - Vertical displacement applied incrementally to capture softening response

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** 
  - X-FEM implementation with Heaviside enrichment for elements fully split by crack
  - Damage/plasticity switch-off zone with width ℓₐ = 3ℓc near crack plane
  - Distance parameter d_tip = 10 mm from crack tip to end of active damage/plasticity zone
  - Data transfer between old and new Gauss points during element sub-division
  - Non-local averaging with radius R = 25-30 mm for damage calculation
  - Stress redistribution at crack boundary through relaxation steps without external loading

- **Simulation Type:** 
  - 3D nonlinear analysis using eight-node linear elements
  - Displacement-controlled incremental analysis
  - Newton-Raphson iterative method for nonlinear equations
  - Elastic predictor and plastic/damage corrector returning map algorithm
  - Enriched elements sub-divided into 4×4×4 cubic sub-elements with 8 Gauss points each
  - Non-local damage modeling with averaging radius R = 25-30 mm
  - Rectangular sub-division strategy for cracked elements
  - Mesh sensitivity analysis with coarse, medium, and fine meshes (minimum element size 7-12 mm)
10_1016_j_finel_2019_07_004.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Anisotropic damage-plasticity behavior of concrete under multiaxial loading
  - Discrete crack initiation and propagation in 3D solid concrete
  - Material degradation with softening response in tension and compression
  - Non-local damage modeling to prevent strain localization
  - Displacement field discontinuities at crack interfaces using X-FEM
  - Evolution of second order damage tensor components

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Force-displacement curves (vertical force vs. displacement u)
  - Crack mouth sliding displacement
  - Crack propagation paths (compared with experimental results)
  - Damage distribution (with values from 0.05 to 0.9 shown in color scales)
  - Total equivalent damage parameter (φ_eq) at integration points
  - Critical damage value (φ_cr = 0.5) for crack initiation
  - Crack growth direction vectors determined from second order damage tensor
  - Mesh sensitivity analysis results (coarse, medium, and fine meshes)
  - Comparison metrics against experimental data (Nooru-Mohamed, Carpinteri et al.) and other numerical methods

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Maximize agreement between predicted crack propagation paths and experimental results
  - Achieve mesh-independent results through non-local damage modeling (R = 25-30 mm)
  - Accurately predict force-displacement curves matching experimental softening behavior
  - Improve crack direction prediction using second order damage tensor in 3D space
  - Minimize zig-zag crack patterns through appropriate selection of ℓ_d (1.5-1.8ℓ_c)
  - Properly capture mixed-mode fracture behavior under different loading conditions (P_s = 5 kN, 10 kN, 27.5 kN)
10_1016_j_finel_2019_07_004.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Crack tip always intersects element edges (not allowed inside elements)
  - Minimum element size constraints: (ℓc)min = 12 mm (three-point bending), 7 mm (double-notched), 10 mm (four-point shear)
  - Specimen depth discretized into exactly 7 elements for all examples
  - Element size must be small enough to capture crack propagation (coarse mesh causes jumps in force-displacement curves)
  - Crack propagation element must be fully split (not partially split)
  - Damage/plasticity switch-off zone width ℓa = 3ℓc

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Critical damage value for crack initiation: φeqtip ≥ φcr = 0.5
  - Non-local averaging radius must be R > ℓc (element size) to prevent local averaging
  - Optimal non-local averaging radius: R = 25-30 mm (3 times minimum element size)
  - Crack direction parameter range: ℓd = 1.5ℓc to 1.8ℓc for smooth crack growth
  - Damage switch-off distance from crack tip: dtip = 10 mm
  - R > 5ℓc causes unnecessary computational cost and erroneous interaction between multiple crack paths
  - Maximum damage value φeq = 1.0 (complete failure)
  - Cannot accurately predict crack direction when multiple cracks meet each other

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Enriched elements sub-divided into 4×4×4 cubic sub-elements with 8 Gauss points each
  - Rectangular sub-division strategy required for cracked elements in 3D space
  - Data transfer between old and new Gauss points requires two-step process: (1) from Gauss points to nodal points, (2) from nodal points to new Gauss points
  - Dummy null step required with no new loading to achieve equilibrium
  - New crack traction must be removed through relaxation steps without external loading
  - Damage plasticity model must remain active during relaxation steps
  - Non-local averaging must exclude switched-off integration points near crack surface
  - Mesh sensitivity requires fine mesh to obtain smooth force-displacement curves (coarse mesh shows jumps)

10_1016_j_compstruc_2006_08_077.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** 1D linear elastostatics problem; unidirectional tension of an elastic bar analyzed using stochastic finite element method with random material properties
- **Material / Medium:** Elastic bar with Young's modulus as random variable (E[e] = 200E9 Pa); cross-sectional area A = 1E-4 m²; material treated as Gaussian random field despite noting this may not reflect real engineering statistics
- **Application & Importance:** To improve accuracy of stochastic perturbation techniques for problems with large input random field variations; specifically to overcome second-order perturbation limitations for input coefficients of variation exceeding 0.10-0.15
- **Geometry / Domain:** Prismatic bar discretized with 10 1D linear finite elements (11 nodes total); element length L = 1E-1 m; tension force P = 10E5 N applied at both ends; shape functions defined as φ₁ = ξ + 1/2 and φ₂ = ξ − 1/2 for 1D elements
10_1016_j_compstruc_2006_08_077.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Tension forces applied at both ends of the bar (P at nodes 1 and 11)
  - Displacement boundary condition: u_i(x; ω) = û_i(x; ω) on ∂Ω_u
  - Stress boundary condition: σ_ij(x; ω)n_j = t̃_i(x; ω) on ∂Ω_t
  - Shape functions defined as φ₁ = ξ + 1/2 and φ₂ = ξ − 1/2 for 1D elements
  - Bar discretized with 10 linear finite elements (11 nodes total)

- **Loads / Excitations:** 
  - Tensile force P = 10E5 N applied at both ends
  - Cross-sectional area A = 1E-4 m²
  - Element length L = 1E-1 m
  - Expected Young's modulus E[e] = 200E9 Pa
  - Young's modulus treated as random variable with coefficient of variation α(b) ∈ [0.0, 0.3]
  - Perturbation parameter ε ∈ [0.8, 1.2]

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** 
  - Single random variable (Young's modulus) affecting elastic properties
  - Stochastic perturbation applied to finite element formulation
  - Body forces effects neglected in final formulation

- **Simulation Type:** 
  - 1D linear elastostatics (static analysis)
  - Stochastic analysis with Gaussian input random field
  - Generalized perturbation method implemented up to 10th order
  - Statistically homogeneous continuum domain

- **Geometry / Domain:** Plane-strain model with 40.0m×80.0m calculation domain; Borehole radius=0.5m; Non-reflecting viscous boundaries; Symmetric left boundary; Faults with dips (20°, 50°, 80°) passing through point B (x=-5.0m, y=0); Fractured zone radius=7.0-9.0× borehole radius
- **Key Parameters:** Blast loading amplitude=15.0 m/s; Principal frequency=730.0 Hz; Critical damping fraction=0.02; Zone size=0.35m; Maximum modelable frequency=1093.0 Hz; Peak particle velocity correlates with damage
- **Fault Parameter Effects:** Maximum tensile failure occurs at fault dip≈45°; Higher fault friction angle reduces tensile failure percentage; Higher fault stiffness reduces total failure percentage
- **Failure Characteristics:** Crushed region near borehole from high radial compressive stresses; Fractured zone with severe cracking; Incipiently cracked region beyond fractured zone; Tensile failure causes radial cracking; Maximum compression stress on wavefront
- **Model Validation:** Coupled method results match LS-DYNA for peak velocity attenuation and velocity-time history at point A (x=6.2m, y=0)
10_1016_j_soildyn_2008_11_002.key_2:

- **Loads / Excitations:** Explosive column with radius 50.0 cm; Blast loading amplitude of 15.0 m/s; Principal frequency of 730.0 Hz; Critical damping fraction of 0.02; Velocity-time history applied to semicircular borehole boundary; TNT explosive modeled with JWL equation of state
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** LS-DYNA provides blast loading input to UDEC; Fault slip governed by Mohr-Coulomb criterion; Fault parameters: normal stiffness=2.0×10⁹ Pa, shear stiffness=2.0×10⁹ Pa, friction angle=35°; Wave reflection and dissipation at fault surfaces
- **Simulation Type:** Plane-strain dynamic analysis; Transient simulation; 2D domain; Calculation domain size 40.0m×80.0m; Zone size 0.35m; Maximum modelable frequency 1093.0 Hz; Simulated time duration up to 15 ms for velocity history
10_1016_j_soildyn_2008_11_002.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Peak particle velocity; Percentage of tensile failure zones; Percentage of total failure zones (tensile + compressive); Failure zone counts (at yield surface, yielded in past, tensile failure); Fractured zone radius (7.0-9.0× borehole radius); X-velocity at specific points; Velocity-time history; Peak velocity attenuation along X-axis; Principal frequency of blast wave (730.0 Hz); Wavefront stress distribution; Maximum compression stress on wavefront (131.4 MPa)

10_1007_s11831_016_9202_3.key_4:
- Bonded rubber block: Analysis stops when J = det F( ) ≤ 0 due to excessively element distortion; FEM-T10-SRI fails at torsion θ = 1.14π while FS/NS-FEM-T4 reaches θ = 2.15π

- Filler particle composite: Without mesh rezoning, computation fails at 147% nominal stretch due to excessively element distortion; with mesh rezoning, analysis lasts to 100% nominal stretch (4 rezonings) and 180% nominal stretch (8 rezonings)

- Volumetric locking: Standard FEM suffers when Poisson's ratio approaches 0.5 (incompressible solids); S-FEM models address this limitation

- Smoothing domain requirements: Minimum number of smoothing domains required for stability (Ns_min = nt for 1D, 2nt/3 for 2D, nt/2 for 3D where nt is total nodal unknowns)

- Temporal instability: NS-FEM models may be "temporally unstable" for dynamic problems due to competition between eigenvalues of stiffness and mass matrices

- Bandwidth limitations: NS-FEM has larger bandwidth in stiffness matrix compared to FEM (about double for NS-FEM-T3), increasing computational cost

- Computational limits: For the same computational cost, S-FEM models can be more accurate but may have higher computational cost for the same mesh structure due to larger bandwidth

- Element distortion: Standard FEM fails at lower deformation levels than S-FEM approaches due to Jacobian matrix becoming ill-conditioned with element distortion

10_1016_s0266_352x_00_00018_5.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Square plate on cross-anisotropic elastic foundation analyzed using finite element method
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Plate: Young's modulus E=0.343×10⁵ MPa, Poisson's ratio μ=0.167, thickness h=0.2 m
  - Foundation: Cross-anisotropic soil with five parameters (E_z, n, β, μ_rr, μ_rz); E_r=nE_z where n∈[0.5,2.0], β∈[0.8,1.5]
  - Isotropic foundation case: E_r=E_z=0.343×10³ MPa, μ_rr=μ_rz=0.4
- **Application & Importance:** Civil engineering foundation analysis where plate-soil interaction must account for soil anisotropy from deposition processes; enables analysis of special geometries, boundary conditions, and load distributions
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Square plate (4 m×4 m) with uniform loading q=0.98 MPa
  - Analysis uses quarter-plate symmetry
  - 8-noded isoparametric elements for plate discretization
  - Foundation modeled as elastic half-space
  - Plate thickness h=0.2 m (slenderness ratio L/h=20)
10_1016_s0266_352x_00_00018_5.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Symmetry boundary conditions applied to reduce analysis domain to quarter-plate (2m×2m)
  - Plate edges modeled as free (evidenced by stress concentration at corners)
  - Foundation modeled as elastic half-space (infinite horizontal extent, semi-infinite vertical domain)
  - Rotations of plate points treated as independent variables (Reissner-Mindlin plate theory)

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Uniform vertical loading q=0.98 MPa applied to plate top surface
  - Point load P used as fundamental solution for foundation displacement calculation

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Plate-foundation contact assumed to be perfectly bonded with full interaction
  - Foundation reaction treated as external forces to the plate
  - Interaction determined through fundamental solution of surface displacement due to point force
  - No separation between plate and foundation interface

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Static structural analysis (no time dependence)
  - 2D plate elements with 8-noded isoparametric formulation
  - Reissner-Mindlin plate theory applicable to both thick and thin plates
  - Reduced integration method used to eliminate fictitious shear deformation
  - Semi-analytical approach (analytical foundation solution coupled with numerical plate discretization)
  - Axisymmetric condition for fundamental solution, but 3D plate behavior analyzed
10_1016_s0266_352x_00_00018_5.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Structural response of plate-foundation system with cross-anisotropic soil behavior, incorporating shear deformations through Reissner-Mindlin plate theory

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - w_max: Maximum deflection at plate center (10⁻¹ m units)
  - p_max: Maximum contact pressure at plate corner (normalized as p_max/q)
  - M_max: Maximum bending moment at plate center (normalized as M_max/(q × l²), where l is half-plate length)
  - Contact pressure distribution beneath plate (non-dimensional p/q)
  - 3D deformation profile of plate

- **Optimization Goal:** Not explicitly stated as optimization; the analysis focuses on quantifying how foundation anisotropy parameters (n, μ_rr, μ_rz, β) affect structural response metrics. The method development aims to reduce computational effort while maintaining accuracy for plate-foundation interaction analysis.
10_1016_s0266_352x_00_00018_5.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Square plate with fixed dimensions: 4 m × 4 m (quarter-plate symmetry used for analysis)
  - Plate thickness constrained to h=0.2 m (slenderness ratio L/h=20)
  - Foundation modeled as elastic half-space (infinite horizontal extent, semi-infinite vertical domain)
  - Analysis limited to 8-noded isoparametric plate elements
  - Plate discretization mesh refined up to 8×8 elements (as shown in Table 1)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Soil anisotropy parameters constrained to moderate range: n ∈ [0.5, 2.0], β ∈ [0.8, 1.5]
  - μ_rr and μ_rz bounded by parabola corresponding to n (as referenced in Fig. 1 of Ref. [18])
  - Analysis restricted to linear elastic behavior of both plate and foundation
  - Maximum horizontal stiffness E_r = nE_z where n is the anisotropy factor
  - Contact pressure must remain positive (no plate-foundation separation considered)
  - Foundation solution based on Nayak's elastic surface settlement formulae (valid for cross-anisotropic materials)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - No manufacturing constraints specified (theoretical analysis only)
  - Method requires reduced integration to eliminate fictitious shear deformation
  - Solution assumes perfect bonding at plate-foundation interface
  - Analysis limited to static loading conditions (no dynamic effects considered)
  - Upper loading constrained to uniform distribution q=0.98 MPa in examples
