10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_117950.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Elastically supported (ES) beam subjected to successive moving loads for railway bridge design in high-speed rail systems
- **Material / Medium:** Beam with elastic modulus E (2.75×10¹⁰ N/m²), moment of inertia I (0.4 m⁴), mass per unit length m̅ (2500 kg/m); elastic supports with stiffness K; support stiffness ratio κ = EIπ³/(L³K)
- **Application & Importance:** Minimizing bridge vibrations caused by successive moving train loads to ensure passenger riding comfort and structural safety in elevated multi-span railway bridges; preventing vibration accumulation and resonance in high-speed rail systems
- **Geometry / Domain:** Beam of length L (20-50 m for typical railway bridges) supported by elastic springs of equal stiffness K at both ends; subjected to N concentrated loads of magnitude p spaced at interval d (typically ~25 m); bridge/vehicle length ratio L/d ∈ [0.5, 2]; vibration shape approximated as φ(x) ≈ sin(πx/L) + κ; load speed v with speed parameter S = πv/(Lω)
10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_117950.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Elastic supports with stiffness K at both beam ends
  - Bending moments at beam ends are zero: EI u''(x,t)|x=0,L = 0
  - Shear force at beam end balances elastic support force: EI u'''(x,t)|x=0,L = ∓Ku(x,t)|x=0,L
  - Support stiffness ratio κ = EIπ³/(L³K)
  - Bridge span length L ∈ [20, 50] m
  - Vehicle/load interval d ≈ 25 m
  - Bridge/vehicle length ratio L/d ∈ [0.5, 2]
  - Beam vibration shape approximated as φ(x) ≈ sin(πx/L) + κ
  - First mode vibration only considered (higher modes neglected)

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - N concentrated loads of magnitude p
  - Load spacing d (vehicle length or bogie interval)
  - Constant speed v of moving loads
  - N = 8 loads used in examples
  - Resonance speed parameter S_r = 1/(2n·d/L), n ∈ Z+
  - External cancellation speed parameter S_c^E = N·d/(2nL), N ≥ 2
  - First resonance condition S_r,1 = d/(2L) (n = 1)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - ES beam modeled as superposition of flexible beam with pinned supports and rigid beam with elastic supports
  - Vertical vibration equation: m̅ü + EIu'''' = p∑j=1^N δ(x-v(t-t_j))×H(t-t_j) - H(t-t_j-ΔT)
  - Beam displacement approximated as u(x,t) ≈ φ(x)q(t) = q(t)×(sin(πx/L) + κ)
  - Modal coordinate solution: q(t) = Δ_st[R sin(ωt+ψ)] for free vibration (t > t_N + ΔT)
  - Natural frequency relation: ω² = εω₀² where ω₀ = π⁴EI/(L⁴m̅)

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Free vibration analysis (t > t_N + ΔT)
  - Forced vibration analysis (t ≤ t_N + ΔT)
  - Comparison between theoretical solutions and FEM
  - Undamped cases (ξ = 0) and damped cases (beam damping ξ = 0.02, 0.04; support damping ξ_s = 0.06, 0.12)
  - Speed parameter S = πv/(Lω) as primary independent variable
  - Modal amplitude R as primary response parameter
  - Resonance and cancellation conditions analysis for various SSR values (κ)
10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_117950.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Vibration response of elastically-supported (ES) beams subjected to successive moving loads, specifically analyzing resonance and cancellation phenomena in free vibration

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Modal amplitude R of free vibration
  - Speed parameter S (S = πv/(Lω))
  - Support stiffness ratio κ (SSR) = EIπ³/(L³K)
  - Resonance speed parameter S_r = 1/(2n·d/L), n ∈ Z+
  - External cancellation speed parameter S_c^E = N·d/(2nL)
  - Internal cancellation speed parameter S_c^I
  - Optimal support stiffness ratio κ_opt = 2(d/L)sin(L/d·π/2)/[(4 - d²/L²)(1 - cos(L/d·π/2))]
  - Midspan displacement time histories
  - Cancellation function C = I_b + I_s
  - Vibration reduction percentage (90% reduction achieved with optimal SSR)

- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize bridge vibrations by selecting the optimal support stiffness ratio (SSR) to achieve resonance cancellation, specifically:
  - Achieve perfect cancellation when C = 0 (I_b + I_s = 0)
  - Suppress the first resonance (S_r,1) for railway bridges
  - Determine the optimal SSR based solely on bridge/vehicle length ratio L/d
  - For beams with L/d ∈ (0.5d, d] and (1.5d, 2d], select SSR closer to lower bound
  - For beams with L/d ∈ (d, 1.5d], select SSR as close to κ_opt as possible
  - Achieve near-perfect vibration cancellation for short to medium-span railway bridges
10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_117950.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Bridge span length L constrained to 20-50 m for typical railway bridges
  - Vehicle length/load spacing d fixed at approximately 25 m
  - Bridge/vehicle length ratio L/d constrained to [0.5, 2] for analysis
  - Support stiffness ratio (SSR) κ typically less than 0.3 for most railway bridges (0-0.5 range analyzed)
  - Perfect cancellation only achievable for L/d ∈ [1.25, 1.5]
  - Single-span beam configuration with elastic supports at both ends only considered
  - First mode vibration only analyzed (higher modes neglected)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Speed parameter S constrained to S < 1 (resonance analysis domain)
  - First resonance condition S_r,1 is primary focus for high-speed railways (>250 km/h)
  - For L/d = 1.5, optimal SSR κ_opt = 0 (simply supported beam condition)
  - Resonance cancellation depends solely on L/d ratio, independent of train speed
  - Damping ratios constrained to ξ = 0, 0.02, 0.04 (beam) and ξ_s = 0, 0.06, 0.12 (supports) in analysis
  - Maximum vibration reduction of 90% achieved with optimal SSR (compared to normal SSR)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Complete pin-pin support condition difficult to achieve in practice due to seismic and vibration isolation needs
  - Elastic support selection constrained by "material properties, seismic isolation and resistance, stability, and temperature"
  - For L/d ∈ (0.5d, d] and (1.5d, 2d], SSR must be selected closer to lower bound while meeting engineering requirements
  - For L/d = d, elastic supports have minimal vibration impact, allowing SSR selection based on practical considerations
  - For L/d ∈ (d, 1.5d], SSR must be selected to satisfy optimal condition while meeting other engineering constraints
  - When L/d = 1.5, supports should be designed as rigid as possible while meeting practical needs for seismic isolation

10_1007_s42235_024_00640_1.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Special Elastic Component (SEC) for passive flexible leg joints in hydraulic-driven quadruped robots, designed to enhance impact buffering and reduce energy consumption during locomotion.
- **Material / Medium:** 60Si2CrVA steel with yield strength >1665 MPa after quenching treatment; equivalent stress reaches 824.21 MPa at maximum deformation (3 mm).
- **Application & Importance:** Addressing challenges in hydraulic-driven quadruped robots including low energy efficiency, high non-linearity, and impact-induced component damage; specifically designed to buffer foot-ground impacts while improving motion energy efficiency.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Symmetrical multi-component structure consisting of turning-arms, leaf springs (4 leaves), pin rolls, center block, and center beam; SEC length |gh| = 85 mm with anti-torque arm |gf| = 188.5 mm; incorporates leaf spring deformation mechanism where force transmission through pin rolls causes turning-arms to pivot and elongate distance between end pin rolls.

10_1016_j_ijheatmasstransfer_2023_124205.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Heat source layout optimization for thermal management in electronic systems

- **Application & Importance:** Optimizing heat source placement to reduce hot spot temperature and improve heat dissipation in electronic systems, directly impacting equipment working state and service lifetime
- **Geometry / Domain:** Square layout domain (1×1 m); boundary conditions include VP problem (heat sink with width δ = 0.1 m on south boundary, other boundaries adiabatic) and VB problem (all four boundaries as Dirichlet type at 0 K); heat sources include rectangles (0.1×0.1 m), circles (radius 0.15 m), cross-shaped, and dumbbell-shaped components; analysis mesh discretizations of 10×10, 20×20, and 50×50 elements used in validation cases
10_1016_j_ijheatmasstransfer_2023_124205.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Dirichlet boundary: Constant temperature T₀ = 0 K at heat sink locations (entire bottom boundary in some cases, or small section with width δ = 0.1 m in VP problem)
  - Neumann boundary: Adiabatic (no thermal exchange) on boundaries not designated as heat sinks
  - Non-overlapping constraint: Any two components cannot intersect with each other and no component can protrude outside the layout domain
  - Layout domain boundary: Square domain of size 1×1 m with fixed perimeter

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Heat source intensity: 100 W/m² for all heat sources in multiple test cases
  - Heat source dimensions: 0.1×0.1 m square components (20 components in VP/VB problems), 0.2×0.2 m (two-component case), circular with radius 0.15 m (validation case)
  - Constant intensity model: Q_c(x) = Q_c (uniform heat generation across each source)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Component layout affects thermal load distribution in the design domain
  - Heat sources interact with the domain through the heat source intensity function Φ(x,y)
  - Non-overlapping constraint ensures no physical intersection between components
  - Fixed layout domain with moving heat sources

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Steady-state heat conduction analysis
  - 2D planar domain
  - Finite element analysis with structured quadrilateral elements
  - Mesh discretizations: 10×10, 20×20, and 50×50 elements used for validation
  - Adaptive multiresolution FEA with background elements for boundary analysis (n_g values from 1 to 40×40)
10_1016_j_ijheatmasstransfer_2023_124205.key_3:

  - Mean temperature (T_mean) in Kelvin
  - Temperature gradient (∂T/∂y) in K·m⁻¹
  - Temperature distribution across the domain

  - Minimize mean temperature (T_mean) for improved thermal performance
  - Optimize heat source placement to enhance overall heat dissipation
  - Achieve non-overlapping component layout while satisfying thermal objectives
  - Reduce T_max from initial values (e.g., 21.70 K to below 15 K in VP problem)
10_1016_j_ijheatmasstransfer_2023_124205.key_4:

  - Heat source intensity fixed at 100 W/m² for all test cases
  - Heat sink boundary maintained at constant temperature T₀ = 0 K
  - Adiabatic boundary conditions on non-heat sink boundaries
  - Heaviside regularization parameter constrained to 0 < ε ≤ 1 (due to LSF maximum value of 1)
  - Temperature field must satisfy the governing equation K·T = P from finite element analysis

- **Process/Manufacturing:**

  - Adaptive multiresolution FEA requires boundary analysis elements to be refined into background elements (n_g values from 1 to 40×40)
  - KS approximation parameter p = 40 used for max function approximation
  - Heaviside function parameter α can be set to 0 without affecting FEA calculation
  - Components maintain small separation distance in final layout due to conservative non-overlapping constraint calculation

10_1016_j_ijfatigue_2023_107594.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Fatigue crack initiation in oligocrystalline stent components under cyclic loading; microstructural modeling of X2CrNiMo-18-15-3 stainless steel using the Tanaka-Mura model implemented in Finite Element Method (FEM)
- **Material / Medium:** X2CrNiMo-18-15-3 (316LVM) stainless steel; chemical composition: Cr 17.30%, Ni 13.60%, Mo 2.67%, Mn 1.72%, Si 0.57%, Cu 0.14%, N 0.039%, P 0.021%, C 0.016%, S 0.001%; mechanical properties: E = 187.5 GPa, G = 70.3 GPa, ν = 0.33, Rm = 645 MPa, CRSS = 160 MPa, Wc = 69 kJ/m²

- **Geometry / Domain:** Microstructural model with dimensions ax = 2.0 mm, ay = 0.6 mm, az = 0.2 mm; oligocrystalline microstructure with coarse grain size of 200 μm and fine grain size of 90 μm; two surface conditions (rough for Model 1, smooth for Model 2); 3D deformable shell models with membrane elements; stent component geometry shown as mesh-like cylindrical structure with strut connections
10_1016_j_ijfatigue_2023_107594.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Fixed side on left boundary; dimensions ax = 2.0 mm, ay = 0.6 mm, az = 0.2 mm; two surface conditions (rough surface for Model 1, smooth surface for Model 2); 3D deformable shell model with membrane elements (M3D4R); mesh size 20 times smaller than grain size; remeshing after crack nucleation
- **Loads / Excitations:** Cyclic loading with stress amplitudes ranging from 100-700 MPa; blood pressure conditions: mean 13 kPa, maximum 16 kPa during Systole; stress amplitudes of 13 kPa, 14 kPa, and 16 kPa for fatigue life estimation; Diastole/Systole frequency of 1.2 Hz; 400 million cycles over 10 years (76 beats/minute)
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Oligocrystalline microstructure modeled based on EBSD map; pure elastic orthotropic behavior with material constants C11 = C22 = C33 = 277.8 GPa, C12 = C13 = C23 = 136.8 GPa, C44 = C55 = C66 = 70.3 GPa; slip band system with dislocations intersecting free surface; automatic remeshing upon micro-crack formation
- **Simulation Type:** Physically-based Tanaka-Mura model implemented in FEM (Abaqus); 3D shell membrane model; transient cyclic loading simulation for crack initiation; two models with four microstructures each (three with 200 μm average grain size, one with 90 μm grain size); automatic sequential remeshing for crack propagation; 3904 elements per submodel
10_1016_j_ijfatigue_2023_107594.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Fatigue crack initiation in oligocrystalline microstructures under cyclic loading; dislocation pile-up behavior on slip bands; micro-crack nucleation and propagation in X2CrNiMo-18-15-3 stainless steel; stress distribution in stent components with varying grain structures; energy balance of dislocations on slip band systems
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Number of cycles for crack initiation (N_ini); S-N (Wöhler) curves; fatigue endurance limit values (S_e); stress amplitude thresholds for crack initiation; accumulated cycle counts for broken segments; time to first micro-crack appearance in years; remeshing iterations; micro-crack formation sequence (e.g., "micro-crack in step 14", "micro-crack in step 15"); specific endurance limits: S_e = 390 MPa, 400 MPa, 510 MPa for different microstructures
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize fatigue endurance limit and number of cycles to crack initiation; identify optimal microstructure (grain size, orientation, surface condition) for stent components; achieve fatigue endurance limit as high as 510 MPa (from 400 MPa through grain orientation optimization); extend time to first micro-crack appearance under physiological loading (13-16 kPa blood pressure) to maximum possible duration; determine microstructure "h" as best performer with favorable grain size and surface roughness for fatigue performance
10_1016_j_ijfatigue_2023_107594.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Stent must be minimally invasive with small diameter; strut thickness must be minimized to avoid blood flow turbulence while maintaining sufficient radial strength; microstructural model dimensions fixed at ax = 2.0 mm, ay = 0.6 mm, az = 0.2 mm; microstructure must contain oligocrystalline arrangement with limited grain count; surface roughness must be less than 0.4 μm for biocompatibility
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Must withstand 400 million cycles (10 years at 76 beats/minute); stress amplitudes must remain below fatigue endurance limit (400 MPa for baseline X2CrNiMo-18-15-3); cyclic loading from blood pressure (13-16 kPa); fatigue endurance limit must be maximized to prevent in-stent restenosis; material must maintain structural integrity under pulsating blood pressure; stress concentration must be minimized to avoid premature crack initiation
- **Process/Manufacturing:** 316LVM stainless steel can only be hardened by cold working; surface roughness achievable through electropolishing; hyper-hardening treatment required (austenitization at 1050°C for 10 min, water quenching, tempering at 250°C for 1 hour); mesh size must be 20 times smaller than grain size for accurate FEM modeling; 3904 elements per submodel; vacuum melting required for 316LVM to increase corrosion resistance; microstructure must be oligocrystalline with either 200 μm or 90 μm grain sizes

10_1016_j_compstruc_2012_10_001.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Enriched finite element method using interpolation covers applied to structural mechanics and heat transfer problems; 3-node triangular elements for 2D analyses, 4-node tetrahedral elements for 3D analyses
- **Material / Medium:** Linear elastic materials with E = 7.2 × 10^9 (cantilever beam), E = 7.2 × 10^10 and ν = 0.3 (machine tool jig); thermal conductivity k₁ = 50, k₂ = 100 and heat transfer coefficient h̃ = 1 (heat transfer problem)
- **Application & Importance:** Improving convergence rates of low-order finite element solutions; capturing higher field variable gradients; smoothing inter-element stress jumps; enabling adaptive interpolation without mesh refinement; maintaining solution accuracy with distorted elements
- **Geometry / Domain:** 1D bar with variable cross-section (A₁ = 0.01, A₂ = 1, L = 1); 2D cantilever beam (L = 1, h = 0.1, r = 0.2 fillet radius); 2D heat transfer domain (10×10 with r = 3 circular hole and rectangular cutout); 3D machine tool jig (5×20×2.5 with r = 2 central hole); mesh configurations including non-distorted meshes and distorted Mesh I, II, III with specific distortion patterns
10_1016_j_compstruc_2012_10_001.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Linear elastic structural analysis
  - Steady-state heat transfer analysis
  - 2D plane stress analysis
  - 3D analysis
  - Linear time-independent analysis
  - Static analysis
  - Strain energy convergence studies
10_1016_j_compstruc_2012_10_001.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Linear elastic structural deformation
  - Steady-state heat transfer in solids
  - Strain energy distribution
  - Convergence behavior of finite element solutions
  - Stress field distribution in structural components

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Strain energy (E) and error (E - E_h)
  - Displacement fields (u, v, w)
  - Stress components (τ_xx, τ_yy, τ_xy, τ_yz, von Mises stress)
  - Temperature distribution (θ)
  - Convergence order (α) in energy norm
  - Condition numbers of stiffness matrices
  - Relative errors in strain energy calculations
  - Number of degrees of freedom (DOFs)
  - Maximum von Mises stress values
  - Longitudinal normal stresses along evaluation lines
  - z-displacement profiles along evaluation lines

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Increase convergence rates of low-order finite element discretizations (3-node triangular and 4-node tetrahedral elements)
  - Improve solution accuracy while maintaining coarse mesh configurations
  - Smooth inter-element stress jumps
  - Capture higher gradients of field variables without mesh refinement
  - Maintain solution accuracy with distorted elements
  - Reduce relative errors in strain energy calculations by factors of 10-100 compared to standard elements
  - Achieve higher-order convergence (theoretical α=4 for linear covers, α=6 for quadratic covers) with minimal additional DOFs
  - Minimize computational cost while maintaining accuracy through adaptive interpolation schemes
10_1016_j_compstruc_2012_10_001.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Base elements constrained to 3-node triangular elements for 2D and 4-node tetrahedral elements for 3D analyses
  - Element distortion constrained to specific patterns (Mesh I, II, III with defined distortion parameters: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 for different mesh types)
  - Domain size constraints in examples: 1D bar with L=1; 2D cantilever beam with L=1, h=0.1; 2D heat transfer domain 10×10 with r=3 circular hole; 3D machine tool jig 5×20×2.5 with r=2 central hole
  - Covers cannot be applied at boundaries where essential boundary conditions are imposed (prescribed displacements or temperatures)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Cover degrees of freedom must be removed at all nodes with prescribed displacements to avoid singular global stiffness matrices
  - Local coordinate systems required for proper matrix conditioning (global coordinates lead to poor conditioning)
  - Complete polynomial bases required for stable results (incomplete bases like F_D^{m,p} schemes become rapidly ill-conditioned as mesh is refined)
  - Method currently limited to linear time-independent analysis of solids and heat transfer (not applicable to dynamic or nonlinear problems)
  - The method cannot be directly applied to 4-node quadrilateral elements without modification (stated that "using the 4-node quadrilateral 2D element the above approach may not be sufficient to obtain a positive definite matrix K")

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Cover functions must be normalized by characteristic element length (ĥ = h) for reasonable matrix conditioning
  - Interpolation space enrichment requires maintaining original mesh topology (no mesh refinement allowed)
  - Cover interpolation orders limited to p ≤ 2 in practice due to increasing unknowns and condition numbers with higher orders
  - Computational cost is significantly higher than stress-improvement-only methods (e.g., Payen-Bathe scheme)
  - Mixed cover schemes require establishing first numerical solution to evaluate element gradients before determining proper cover regions
  - Cover interpolations must be removed at all boundaries with Dirichlet boundary conditions to maintain nonsingular global stiffness matrix

10_1016_j_jmrt_2022_07_120.key_1:
- Composite Helical Springs (CHSs) are the subject of analysis, used in transportation and aerospace applications including automobile suspension, railway bogies, and aircraft engine systems
- Materials include carbon fiber, glass fiber, Kevlar fiber, and Calotropis gigantea fiber reinforced polymer composites, with fiber volume contents ranging from 45% to 55%
- CHSs exhibit weight-reducing effects of 74.25-83.55% compared to steel springs, with stiffness decreasing in sequence: steel > carbon > Kevlar > glass > Calotropis gigantea fiber
- Geometric parameters include wire diameter (d), screw pitch (p), helical angle (α), spring diameter (D), spring height (h), and active number of turns (n)
- Hollow structure CHSs have inner wire diameter (d_i) as an additional parameter, with 13.33mm spacing between springs in test configurations
- Twistless CHS configurations include CMHS45%, CMHS50%, and CMHS55% with fiber volume contents of 45%, 50%, and 55% respectively
- Twisted CHS configurations include CMHS4 and CMHS6 with twist coefficients of 4 and 6 r/10 cm respectively, both at 55% fiber volume content
- Failure mechanisms include resin cracking, interfacial debonding, and fiber breakage, with cracks typically initiating at the opening end and inner rim delamination
- Manufacturing methods include hot press molding with ±45° laminates coiled around rubber core, Resin Transfer Molding (RTM), integrated forming, and lost mold method using plaster sacrificial molds
- Reinforcement structures include braided (with yarn directions), ply (with warp/weft directions), twisted, skin-core (with separate skin and core components), and hybrid configurations (AU, UR, BU, BUR)

10_1016_j_enganabound_2021_05_020.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Poisson equation solver using adaptive element free Galerkin (EFG) method
- **Material / Medium:** Mathematical model of Poisson equation (-Δu = f) with homogeneous and non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions
- **Application & Importance:** To improve computational efficiency of meshless methods by adaptively placing nodes where solution gradients are high while reducing nodes in smooth regions, addressing the low computational efficiency bottleneck of standard EFG methods
- **Geometry / Domain:** Multiple domain geometries including unit square [0,1]², circular sector (r < 1, -3π/4 < φ < 3π/4), L-shaped domain (-1,1)² ∖ (-0,0]², and 3D L-shaped domain (-1,1)³/(0,1)×(0,1)×(-1,1) with re-entrant corners causing singularities
10_1016_j_enganabound_2021_05_020.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition u = 0 on ∂Ω; Non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition u = (x² + y²)^(1/3)cos(2/3 atan2(y,x)) on ∂Ω for Example 2; Non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition u = (x² + y²)^(2/3)sin(1/3 atan2(y,x)) on ∂Ω for Example 5; Initial uniform nodal distributions: 9×9 nodes for Examples 1 and 3, 65 nodes for Example 4, 105 nodes for Example 5
- **Loads / Excitations:** Source term f = 4a²(1 - ar²)e^(-ar²) with a = 400 for Example 1; Source term f = 1 for Examples 3, 4, and 5; Anisotropic coefficient matrix A = [[1,0],[0,100]] for Example 3
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Gaussian quadrature points in each triangular/tetrahedral background integration element contribute only to nodes within that element; MLS shape function with arbitrary polygonal influence domain; Background integration elements (triangular for 2D, tetrahedral for 3D) serve dual purpose of numerical integration and grid adaptation
- **Simulation Type:** Steady-state elliptic problems; 2D domains for Examples 1-4, 3D domain for Example 5; Linear problems; Adaptive refinement with Dörfler marking strategy; Linear basis functions in MLS; 7 Gaussian quadrature points per triangular element (2D); 16 Gaussian quadrature points per tetrahedral element (3D); Stopping tolerances: 10 for Example 1, 2×10⁻³ for Example 3, 9×10⁻³ for Example 4; Marking parameter θ = 0.5 for Examples 1-4, θ = 0.4 for Example 5
10_1016_j_enganabound_2021_05_020.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Steady-state Poisson equation (elliptic partial differential equation) with homogeneous and non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions; includes problems with localized gradients, boundary layers, and singularities at re-entrant corners
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** A posteriori error estimates using three error estimation strategies (EES1-EES3); maximum absolute error of EFG and FEM solutions; convergence rate of error estimates; number of degrees of freedom (N); final nodal distribution patterns; error decay rate (O(N⁻⁰·⁵) for 2D problems, O(N⁻⁰·³²) for 3D problems); number of adaptive iterations required to reach stopping tolerance
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize computational cost by adaptively placing dense nodes only in regions with high solution gradients while using sparse nodes in smooth regions; achieve optimal convergence rate O(N⁻⁰·⁵) for 2D problems; ensure solution accuracy while reducing total node count; compare EFG performance against FEM with identical error estimation strategies
10_1016_j_enganabound_2021_05_020.key_4:

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Stopping tolerance constrained to 10 for Example 1, 2×10⁻³ for Example 3, 9×10⁻³ for Example 4; Marking parameter θ constrained to 0.5 for Examples 1-4 and 0.4 for Example 5; Linear basis functions required in MLS approximation; Error decay rate constrained to O(N⁻⁰·⁵) for 2D problems and O(N⁻⁰·³²) for 3D problems; Maximum node number constrained to 2×10⁴ for Example 5; 7 Gaussian quadrature points per triangular element (2D), 16 per tetrahedral element (3D)
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Adaptive refinement constrained to newest vertex bisection strategy; Marking strategy constrained to Dörfler strategy; Error estimation constrained to three specific strategies (EES1-EES3) borrowed from FEM; Implementation constrained to linear MLS approximation; Gaussian quadrature points constrained to contribute only to nodes within their background integration element; Method constrained to work with homogeneous and specific non-homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions

10_1007_s10443_023_10111_1.key_1:

- **Geometry / Domain:** 50 mm long circular thin-wall tube; radial flattening displacement: 90 mm; damage occurs at four symmetric positions (upper, bottom, left, right); cross-section transforms from circular to elliptical then to four-arched shape during flattening; multi-scale structure with 5.79 yarns/cm (warp) and 5.85 yarns/cm (weft) weaving density
10_1007_s10443_023_10111_1.key_2:

- **Loads / Excitations:** Displacement load of 1.2 mm at 0.05 mm/min in 3-point bending mode; Radial flattening displacement of 90 mm at 10 mm/min loading rate; Displacement load (Uy = -90mm) applied to upper plate; Temperature: heating to 100°C (20 min hold), cooling to 20°C at 2°C/min rate (20 min hold), re-heating to 100°C at 2°C/min rate
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Rigid body interaction between flattening plates and tube; Surface-to-surface contact between plates and tube; Multi-scale interactions between micro-scale RVE, meso-scale RUC, and macro-scale structure; Different failure criteria applied to pure matrix (Von-Mises) and yarns (3D Hashin); Homogenized progressive damage model for macro-scale SMPC
- **Simulation Type:** 3D nonlinear simulation with geometric nonlinearity enabled; 9000 S4R shell elements for tube model; 9 Simpson integration points through tube wall thickness; Multi-scale FEA with micro-scale RVE (55,800 elements), meso-scale RUC (282,194 elements), and macro-scale model (432,000 elements); Four-step process simulation: isothermal loading above Tg, cooling with constraint, constraint release, re-heating for recovery; Transient thermal-mechanical analysis with temperature-dependent properties
10_1007_s10443_023_10111_1.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Shape fixation ratio (85.6% experimental); shape recovery ratio (95.6% experimental); stiffness degradation factors (d₁₁ᵀ, d₁₁ᶜ, d₂₂ᵀ, d₂₂ᶜ, d₁₂); strain storage factor φ(T); stress ratio φ(T); load-displacement curves during flattening; temperature-displacement relationships during recovery; damage distribution at four symmetric positions; equivalent modulus values (22.73 GPa warp direction at 25°C); tensile modulus values; storage factor fitting parameters (A₁=-4.99×10⁻¹⁰, A₂=-9.7×10⁻⁴); stress ratio fitting parameters (A₃=0.98, A₄=0.13, A₅=13.19, T₀=43.37)
- **Optimization Goal:** Accurate prediction of shape memory behavior considering progressive damage; validation of homogenized progressive damage model combined with phase transition constitutive model; matching experimental results for shape fixation ratio (85.6%) and shape recovery ratio (95.6%) with simulation results (89.4% and 97.5% respectively); correct prediction of damage locations and their effect on final recovered shape
10_1007_s10443_023_10111_1.key_4:

10_1007_s00211_024_01446_3.key_1:
- Identity & Domain: Darcy flow in heterogeneous porous media modeled using mixed multiscale spectral generalized finite element method (mixed MS-GFEM)
- Material / Medium: Porous media with permeability coefficient A ∈ L∞(Ω) satisfying 0 < α₀ < A < α₁; examples include constant permeability (A=1), high-contrast permeability fields, and SPE10 benchmark top layer; fluid flow with source term f
- Application & Importance: Solving second-order elliptic equations for flow simulation in oil reservoirs and hydrology; provides locally mass-conservative Darcy velocity solutions; handles multiscale coefficient structures spanning non-separated length scales; efficiently models wells (source terms)
- Geometry / Domain: Unit square domain (0,1)²; partitioned into M = m² nonoverlapping subdomains; oversampling domains with l layers of fine mesh elements; fine FE mesh with h = 1/100 (Example 1) and h = 1/240 (Examples 2-3); SPE10 benchmark geometry used in Example 3

- Loads / Excitations: Source term f in divergence equation (div u_e = -f); Example 1: f(x,y) = 2π²cos(πx)cos(πy); Example 3: f(x,y) = {100 if x < 0.1 and y < 0.1, -100 if x > 0.9 and y > 0.9, 0 otherwise}; wells modeled as source terms in hydrology applications
- Interactions / Interfaces: Domain partitioned into M = m² nonoverlapping subdomains; overlapping subdomains extended by two layers of fine mesh elements; oversampling domains obtained by adding l layers of fine mesh elements; coefficient fields with high contrast heterogeneities (Example 2) and SPE10 benchmark geometry (Example 3)
- Simulation Type: Steady-state elliptic equations; 2D unit square domain (0,1)²; linear mixed formulation; fine-scale mesh resolutions of h = 1/100 (Example 1) and h = 1/240 (Examples 2-3); augmentation parameter γ varied from 10⁻⁶ to 10³ in Example 3
10_1007_s00211_024_01446_3.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Darcy flow in heterogeneous porous media governed by second-order elliptic equations in mixed formulation; specifically solving for velocity field (u) and pressure field (p) with A⁻¹u - ∇p = 0 and div u = -f
- Target Outputs (Metrics): Relative velocity error (error_v), relative pressure error (error_p), divergence error (error_div); logarithmic error metrics log₂(error_v) and log₂(error_p); degrees of freedom comparison between fine-scale and multiscale solutions
- Optimization Goal: Achieve exponential convergence with respect to local degrees of freedom; minimize computational cost while maintaining locally mass-conservative velocity solutions; efficiently solve problems with heterogeneous coefficients spanning multiple non-separated length scales; reduce system size while preserving accuracy (demonstrated 200x reduction in degrees of freedom in Example 3)
10_1007_s00211_024_01446_3.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: Unit square domain (0,1)²; partitioned into M = m² nonoverlapping subdomains; oversampling domains require l layers of fine mesh elements; mesh size h must be small enough to resolve fine-scale features of coefficient A; fine-scale mesh resolutions limited to h = 1/100 (Example 1) and h = 1/240 (Examples 2-3)
- Performance/Physics Limits: Permeability coefficient A must satisfy 0 < α₀ < A < α₁; compatibility condition ∫_Ω f dx + ∫_∂Ω g_N ds = 0 must be satisfied; inf-sup stability condition must be met (requiring velocity space enrichment as shown by Fig. 4 where method without enrichment is "highly unstable and inaccurate"); method requires augmentation parameter γ > 0 for theoretical analysis (though works for γ = 0 in practice)
- Process/Manufacturing: Local problems can be solved entirely in parallel; enrichment step remains fully parallel; local problems yield linear systems solvable by direct methods; 3D implementation requires efficient eigenproblem solvers due to complexity of harmonic and divergence-free constraints; method requires adaptive selection of local basis functions for practical applications (identified as future work)

- **Application & Importance:** Modeling flow and transport of concentration in porous media; FVM provides local flux conservation and convection stabilization while BEM handles unbounded exterior domains without domain truncation; designed for convection-dominated problems where conservation laws must be preserved
- **Geometry / Domain:**

  - Circular plate with radius Rp = 0.25 m and thickness h = 1.59 mm
  - Sphere with radius Rs = 9.53 mm
  - Plate composed of 5 patches (central patch square) and sphere composed of 7 patches (central patch cube)
  - Plate discretized with 320 cubic Bézier elements and 2929 control points
  - Sphere discretized with 56 cubic Bézier elements and 1651 control points
  - Minimum 25 nodes per patch edge (nd ≥ 25) required for convergence
  - Sphere edge patches divided into 2 cubic elements
  - Plate edge patches with 8-9 cubic elements corresponding to nd = 25-28
  - Original nondeformed geometry used for acoustic pressure calculation due to small plate deformation

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Linear elastic material behavior (no large deformations considered)
  - Frictionless contact condition (gN ≥ 0, qN ≤ 0, gN qN = 0)
  - Maximum sphere initial velocity of 0.22 m/s for simulations
  - Penalty parameter set to 100E (E = Young's modulus)
  - Time step Δt1 = 0.0154 μs for central difference scheme
  - Conditionally stable explicit integration requiring careful time step selection
  - Steel plate properties: Ep = 210 GPa, νp = 0.3, ρp = 7850 kg/m³
  - Acrylic sphere properties: Es = 3.1 GPa, νs = 0.37, ρs = 1190 kg/m³
  - Air properties: cf = 343 m/s, ρf = 1.021 kg/m³
  - Consistent mass matrix required for stability (vs. lumped mass matrix)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Bézier extraction extended to 3D problems for solid sphere elements
  - Only shape function routine needs modification for existing FE contact codes
  - Computational time increases significantly with KL method (3.2× CD) vs. NB method (1.3× CD)
  - Memory requirements increase with number of control points
  - Rayleigh integral equation requires plate embedded in rigid baffle
  - Model cannot handle plasticity, damping, or friction effects
  - Model cannot account for large deformations at contact point
  - Explicit scheme requires time step selection based on most finely meshed part (sphere)
  - Using consistent mass matrix increases computational time significantly

10_1016_j_cma_2009_02_018.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Dynamic crack growth simulations using eXtended Finite Element Method (X-FEM) with explicit time integration schemes; includes stationary/moving semi-infinite mode I crack, Kalthoff's experiment (mode II failure transition), and Grégoire's Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar test

- **Material / Medium:**

  - PMMA: E = 2.4 GPa, ν = 0.42, ρ = 1180 kg·m⁻³, c_L = 1426 m·s⁻¹, c_S = 846 m·s⁻¹, c_R = 800 m·s⁻¹, K_Ic_ini = 1.47 MPa·m¹/², K_Ic_propa = 1.33 MPa·m¹/²
  - Generic material: E = 210 GPa, ν = 0.3, ρ = 8000 kg·m⁻³, σ₀ = 500 MPa

- **Application & Importance:** Overcome critical time step reduction in explicit X-FEM when discontinuities approach nodes; enable standard critical time step usage regardless of enrichment position; reduce computational cost while maintaining accuracy for dynamic fracture mechanics; simulate moving interfaces with standard CFL condition

- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - Kalthoff's experiment: 200mm × 100mm × 75mm plate with two 50mm × 50mm edge notches; 50mm diameter projectile
  - Mode I crack problem: L = 10m, 2H = 4m, a₀ = 5m finite geometry approximating infinite medium
  - Grégoire's experiment: 70mm × 30mm PMMA specimen with 30mm diameter hole; 15mm offset initial notch (7.5mm height); φ40mm input/output bars (140mm input bar length)
10_1016_j_cma_2009_02_018.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Symmetry boundary conditions applied to upper half of plate in Kalthoff's experiment
  - Impedance boundary condition on contact surface between specimen and output bar: σ·n = -z(ü·n)n, where z = ρ_bar c_L_bar (ρ_bar = output bar density, c_L_bar = longitudinal wave speed)
  - Fixed bottom boundary in mode I semi-infinite crack problem
  - Tensile stress σ₀ applied to top boundary in mode I semi-infinite crack problem
  - Simulation time limited to t ≤ 3τ_c = 1.009 × 10⁻³ s for mode I crack problem
  - Crack remains stationary for 0 ≤ t < 1.5τ_c, then propagates at constant velocity for t ≥ 1.5τ_c

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Projectile impact velocity V₀ = 20 m/s in Kalthoff's experiment
  - Tensile stress wave with σ₀ = 500 MPa applied to top boundary in mode I crack problem
  - Experimental velocity imposed as loading on contact face between input bar and specimen in Grégoire's experiment
  - Impact velocity of 20 m/s for brittle propagation in Kalthoff's experiment

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Stable-explicit element group composed of elements enriched for crack representation and elements cut by hole
  - Initial notch moved upward from specimen's axis of symmetry to ensure mixed-mode loading
  - Crack initiation at ~200 μs, propagation at constant horizontal velocity ȧ_x ≃ 211 m/s (maximum curvilinear velocity ȧ ≃ 260 m/s), arrest for ~50 μs, then second propagation phase at ȧ_x ≃ 157 m/s (ȧ ≃ 160 m/s)
  - Elements completely contained inside holes are deleted from the mesh
  - As discontinuities move, new enriched elements are added to the stable-explicit (SE) group

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Plane strain conditions for all examples
  - Transient dynamic simulations
  - Explicit time integration schemes (central difference method and stable-explicit/explicit element-by-element partitioning)
  - Critical time step: Δt_c_x-fem = Δt_c_fem for proposed scheme (standard FE critical time step)
  - Mesh configurations: 40×80, 60×120, 80×80, and 27×51 piecewise bilinear quadrilateral elements
  - Fixed and evolving enrichment functions for discontinuities and crack tips
10_1016_j_cma_2009_02_018.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Dynamic crack growth in brittle materials; wave propagation and reflection effects; stress intensity factor evolution; displacement and stress field distributions during impact events; transient dynamic fracture mechanics with moving discontinuities

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Normalized mode I dynamic stress intensity factor (K_I^dyn / σ₀√H) vs. normalized time (t/τ_c)
  - Crack tip position (x-position, y-position) as function of time
  - Crack length evolution with time
  - Input and output bar velocities in Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar tests
  - Vertical displacement field (U_y) on deformed configuration
  - Von Mises stress field (Sigma VM) on initial configuration
  - Crack path trajectory and propagation angles
  - Crack initiation, arrest, and restart timing

- **Optimization Goal:** Recover standard FE critical time step (Δt_c_x-fem ≡ Δt_c_fem) independent of enrichment position; eliminate enrichment dependency of critical time step; reduce computational cost by enabling larger time steps (factor of 2 reduction in time steps compared to Δt_c/2 approach); minimize numerical oscillations while maintaining accuracy; enable explicit X-FEM simulations with arbitrary enrichments using classical CFL condition regardless of discontinuity position relative to mesh
10_1016_j_cma_2009_02_018.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Mode I crack problem: L = 10m, 2H = 4m, a₀ = 5m finite geometry approximating infinite medium
  - Kalthoff's experiment: 200mm × 100mm × 75mm plate with two 50mm × 50mm edge notches
  - Grégoire's experiment: 70mm × 30mm specimen with 30mm diameter hole; 15mm offset initial notch (7.5mm height); φ40mm input/output bars
  - Simulation time limited to t ≤ 3τ_c = 1.009 × 10⁻³ s for mode I crack problem (τ_c = H/c_d)
  - Mesh configurations constrained to 40×80, 60×120, 80×80, and 27×51 piecewise bilinear quadrilateral elements

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Critical time step constraint: 0 < Δt_c_x-fem ≤ Δt_c_fem with minimal ratio of 1/2 for standard X-FEM with mass lumping
  - Target constraint for proposed method: Δt_c_x-fem ≡ Δt_c_fem (standard FE critical time step)
  - Crack propagation velocity constraint: a˙ = 1500 m/s for moving crack tip in semi-infinite crack example
  - Material wave speed constraints: c_d = dilatational wave speed (3040 m/s for E=210GPa, ν=0.3, ρ=8000kg/m³), c_R = Rayleigh wave speed
  - Crack remains stationary for 0 ≤ t < 1.5τ_c, then propagates for t ≥ 1.5τ_c in moving crack simulation
  - Grégoire's experiment: crack initiation at ~200 μs, first propagation phase at ȧ_x ≃ 211 m/s (ȧ ≃ 260 m/s), arrest for ~50 μs, second propagation at ȧ_x ≃ 157 m/s (ȧ ≃ 160 m/s)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Element-by-element partitioning: stable-explicit scheme applied only to enriched and blending elements, central difference for other elements
  - Elements completely contained inside holes are deleted from the mesh
  - Partitioning must be updated as discontinuities evolve (new enriched elements added to SE group)
  - Required mass lumping formula: m_L_enr^e_ij = δ_ij m_L with m_L = [1/∑ψ²(x_i)]∫Ω^e ρψ² dΩ^e
  - SE group size must be maintained as small as possible to minimize computational cost
  - Impedance boundary condition constraint: z = ρ_bar c_L_bar for output bar interface modeling

- Slipping times: linear pressure (0.624 s), parabolic pressure (0.468 s), constant pressure (0.3121 s)
- Time step: Δt = 0.001 s

- Transient thermal analysis required due to high temperature gradient within less than 1 second
- Numerical scheme: Crank-Nicolson algorithm
- Element type: SOLID90 (20 nodes)
- Mesh: 268,675 elements (1,164,367 nodes)
- Isotropic and homogeneous materials used for numerical analyses
10_1007_s43069_025_00423_2.key_3:

10_1007_s43069_025_00423_2.key_4:

10_1016_j_finel_2024_104166.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Composite material structures with localized heterogeneity and nonlinearity analyzed using Generalized Finite Element Method with global-local enrichment functions (GFEM^gl)
- **Material / Medium:** Fiber composite with orthotropic properties (Single Ply: E₁₁=25.0 GPa, E₂₂=1.00 GPa, E₃₃=1.00 GPa, ν₂₃=0.25, ν₁₃=0.25, ν₁₂=0.25, G₂₃=0.20 GPa, G₁₃=0.50 GPa, G₁₂=0.50 GPa; [−45/45]ₛ layup: E₁₁=1.86 GPa, E₂₂=1.86 GPa, E₃₃=1.00 GPa, ν₂₃=0.036, ν₁₃=0.036, ν₁₂=0.860, G₂₃=0.29 GPa, G₁₃=0.29 GPa, G₁₂=6.39 GPa); Steel (E=210.0 GPa, ν=0.3, G=80.77 GPa) with linear isotropic hardening (K=210 MPa, σ_y=350 MPa)
- **Application & Importance:** Capturing stress concentrations and localized nonlinearity in composite structures, particularly for hypersonic aircraft applications where structural and material length scales may not be sufficiently separated
- **Geometry / Domain:** Square laminated plate (W=60 mm) with central hole (d=4 mm), 4-ply symmetric layup (t_ply=0.25 mm); Perforated plate with circular holes (r=L/4) and enlarged center hole (r_c=15L/32), uniform perforation spacing; Two local problem strategies: Strategy 1 (full heterogeneous local domain), Strategy 2 (heterogeneous core with homogenized ring)
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104166.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Fixed support on left end of plate (all three directions) for bearing load problem
  - Displacement ū_n = [-0.0001, 0, 0]^T applied to springs across thickness oriented normal to hole surface
  - Dirichlet boundary conditions on Γ_u where u(x) = ū(x)
  - Neumann boundary conditions on Γ_f where t(x) = (σ·n)(x) = t̄(x)
  - Spring boundary conditions on Γ_m where t(x) = K_s(ū(x) - u(x))
  - Global-local spring stiffness K_s^GL = E·V₀/(J·d) used at interface
  - Tie constraints used to enforce continuity between nonconforming approximations

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Uniaxial tensile traction in x₁ direction with magnitude σ̄₀
  - Biaxial traction with magnitude γ applied to boundary surfaces in thickness direction
  - Bearing load simulated through face-aligned linear springs with stiffness K_n = 2E_pin/(2r(1+ν_pin)(1-2ν_pin))
  - Linear isotropic hardening law with plastic modulus K = 210 MPa and yield stress σ_y = 350 MPa for steel

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Two-way communication between global and local problems in GFEM^gl framework
  - Global-local enrichment functions transferring local solution behavior to global problem
  - Buffer zones (B = 10 mm) tested for Strategy 1 GFEM^gl
  - Material transition handled at global-local interface (Strategy 1) or within local problem (Strategy 2)
  - Spring constraints used at global-local interface for boundary condition transfer

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Small deformation assumption for all problems
  - Linear elastic analysis for laminate plate problems
  - Materially nonlinear analysis with plasticity for perforated plate
  - 3D analysis using quadratic hexahedral elements for reference solutions
  - Two global-local iterations as standard procedure
  - Total global-local enrichment functions used for materially nonlinear problems
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104166.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Stress concentrations in composite structures with localized material heterogeneity and nonlinearity; strain energy distribution; stress-strain behavior under tension and bearing loads; plastic strain accumulation in perforated steel plates

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Strain energy (U_L) of local problem region
  - Relative error in strain energy: error(a) = |a_app - a_ref|/a_ref
  - Discrete L² error of through-thickness stress fields
  - von Mises stress contours
  - Equivalent plastic strain distribution
  - σ₁₁ stress component through plate thickness
  - Number of equations in global and local problems
  - Convergence behavior with mesh refinement (global H and local h)

- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve accurate representation of localized stress concentrations and material nonlinearity using coarse global discretizations with homogenized material properties while minimizing computational cost; enable on-the-fly incorporation of fine-scale material heterogeneity only where needed; maintain accuracy comparable to reference solutions with >85% of domain modeled using homogenized properties
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104166.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Plate width W = 60 mm, hole diameter d = 4 mm, ply thickness t_ply = 0.25 mm for laminate plate
  - Perforation radius r = L/4, center perforation radius r_c = 15L/32 for perforated plate
  - Local problem domain sizes L = 30, 25, 20 mm tested in GFEM^gl simulations
  - Buffer zone size B = 10 mm tested with L = 30 mm for Strategy 1
  - Global mesh uses single element through laminate thickness direction
  - Reference solutions use highly graded meshes with fine elements in localized regions

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Homogenization theory assumption violation when structural and material length scales are not sufficiently separated
  - Strategy 2 accuracy depends on quality of homogenized properties (less accurate than Strategy 1 when properties have errors)
  - All multiscale methods fail when global plasticity occurs (beyond localized nonlinearity)
  - Two global-local iterations found sufficient for convergence (rule of thumb)
  - Submodeling overestimates stress concentrations by nearly 100% in bearing load problem
  - Submodeling underestimates stress concentrations by more than 10% in tension problem
  - Material nonlinearity can be accurately captured only when localized, not when global

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Explicit modeling of all heterogeneity is computationally infeasible due to extreme analysis cost
  - User time for model creation grows "far too large" when explicitly modeling all heterogeneity
  - GFEM^gl maintains efficiency and scalability characteristics of the method
  - Local problems must be created where needed without prior knowledge of failure locations
  - Two-way communication between global and local scales required for accuracy (unlike Submodeling)
  - Global-local interface requires nested meshes (local problem mesh must be nested within global problem mesh)

10_1007_s10596_024_10322_w.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Fluid flow near multi-stage hydraulic fractures in horizontal wells using stream tube decomposition method
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Porous reservoir medium with absolute permeability kr(x,y,z)
  - Fractures filled with proppant with absolute permeability kf i ≫ kr (ratio kf/kr = 10³–10⁸)
  - Single-phase and two-phase fluids with viscosity μ
  - Reservoir porosity m
  - Formation height 2h ~ 10 m
  - Wellbore radius rw ~ 0.1 m
  - Fracture opening 2bi ~ 10⁻³–10⁻² m
  - Fracture half-length xfi
  - Half-distance between fractures Li ~ 10² m
  - Phase viscosity ratio Kμ
- **Application & Importance:** 
  - Calculating well productivity with multi-stage hydraulic fracturing
  - Modeling fluid flow near fractures for fast multivariate calculations
  - Enabling inverse problems for fracture parameter identification
  - Supporting tracer study interpretation
  - Reducing computation time for optimization and design of hydraulic fracturing
- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - Horizontal well with transverse fractures along y-axis
  - Fracture walls represented as plane rectangles orthogonal to borehole axis
  - Impermeable roof and bottom boundaries at z = ±h
  - Vertical cylindrical external boundary Σ with constant pressure pe
  - Two characteristic drainage sectors:
    * Utmost sector: elliptical external boundary for outer fractures
    * Inner sector: rectangular area between adjacent fractures with width LD and depth RD = 1 + 0.75LD
  - Fracture height equals reservoir height (hi = h)
  - Stream tubes extend from fracture edges to external boundary with variable cross-sectional area
10_1007_s10596_024_10322_w.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Impermeable top and bottom boundaries: z = ±h ∶ uz = -k/μ ∂p/∂z = 0
  - External boundary with constant pressure: (x,y,z) ∈ Σ ∶ p = pe
  - Wellbore with constant pressure: x² + z² = rw², ||y - yi|| < bi ∶ p = pw
  - Impermeable fracture ends: x = ±xfi, ||y - yi|| < bi ∶ ux = -k/μ ∂p/∂x = 0
  - Symmetry conditions on impermeable sections: (xD,yD) ∈ Γ1,Γ2,Γ3 ∶ ∂pD/∂n = 0
  - Fracture edges with pressure condition: |x| < xfi, y = yi ∶ p = pw

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Darcy law: u = -k/μ ∇p
  - Continuity equation: div u = 0
  - Transport equation for component/saturation: m ∂s/∂t + ∂(fuDx)/∂x + ∂(fuDy)/∂x = 0
  - One-dimensional transport in stream tubes: ∂(σU)/∂l = 0, m_r ∂s/∂t + (1/σ) ∂(fσU)/∂l = 0
  - Initial condition: t = 0 ∶ s = s0(x,y)
  - Boundary condition for transport: (x,y) ∈ Γ ∶ s = sΓ(x,y)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Fluid flow between reservoir and fracture: q±_i(x,z) = kr/μ (pe - p^f_i(x,z)) J±_i(x,z)
  - Continuity at fracture-reservoir interface: 2bi (∂u^f_x,i/∂x + ∂u^f_z,i/∂z) = q+ i + q- i
  - Dimensionless inflow expression: q±_Di = (1 - p^f_Di) J±_Di
  - Relative width of stream tubes: J±_Di = [∫(0 to λ±_Di) dlD/ω±_i(lD)]^-1

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Steady-state single-phase flow problems (3D and 2D plane flow)
  - Non-steady transport problems (transient)
  - One-dimensional transport problems in fixed stream tubes (transient)
  - Reservoir thickness-averaged flow (2D)
  - Dimensionless formulation for normalized analysis
  - Infinite conductivity fracture modeling (simplified case)
  - Finite permeability fracture modeling (more complex case)
10_1007_s10596_024_10322_w.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Single-phase flow in porous reservoir with multi-stage hydraulic fractures
  - Two-phase flow (water-oil displacement) in fractured reservoirs
  - Multi-component flow (tracer transport) near hydraulic fractures
  - Steady-state pressure distribution in reservoir-fracture systems
  - Non-steady fluid transport along fixed stream tubes
  - Inflow to horizontal wells with multiple transverse fractures

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Total well flow rate (QD)
  - Flow rate from individual fractures (QDi)
  - Inflow profile along fracture edges (q±_i(x,z))
  - Water cut (F = QDs/QD)
  - Pressure distribution in fractures
  - Saturation/concentration distribution
  - Relative error in flow rate (EQ = (QD - Qe_D)/Qe_D)
  - Relative error in water cut (eF)
  - Deviation between approximate and exact solutions (r±_i)
  - Production rate of wells with multiple fractures

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Reduce computational time by 1-2 orders of magnitude while maintaining solution error <1%
  - Enable practical solution of inverse problems for fracture parameter identification
  - Allow fast multivariate calculations for hydraulic fracturing design optimization
  - Make high-resolution grid simulations feasible for tracer study interpretation
  - Achieve accurate well productivity calculations for multi-stage fractured horizontal wells with minimal computational resources
  - Balance model simplicity with sufficient accuracy for short-term process analysis (not long-term field development)
10_1007_s10596_024_10322_w.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Formation height: 2h ~ 10 m
  - Wellbore radius: rw ~ 0.1 m
  - Fracture opening: 2bi ~ 10⁻³–10⁻² m
  - Distance between fractures: Li ~ 10² m
  - External boundary distance: R ~ 10²–10³ m
  - Fracture height equals reservoir height (hi = h)
  - For inner sector model: RD = 1 + 0.75LD
  - For circular drainage area: minimum RD = 1.65 to keep error <10% (when major/minor semiaxis difference <22%)
  - Fracture half-length normalized to maximum: typically 0.75–1.0 for practical applications

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Permeability ratio: kf/kr = 10³–10⁸
  - Pressure loss limits: <15% of total pressure drop at kf/kr > 10⁴, <2% at kf/kr > 10⁵
  - Incompressibility assumption valid for time scales exceeding pressure wave propagation
  - For finite permeability fractures: M = bkf/xfkr > 1 for flow rate error <0.13
  - For finite permeability fractures: M > 10 for flow rate error <0.022
  - Maximum error in flow rate calculation: <10% for LD < 1 (inner sector)
  - Applicable for layered-heterogeneous formation when relative fracture conductivity exceeds maximum formation conductivity by 10+ times
  - Error in stream tube model: <1% when NST > 20 stream tubes for both component transport and two-phase flow

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Model designed specifically for short-term processes, not long-term field development
  - Not suitable when surrounding well operating conditions significantly affect stream tube shape
  - Distance between fracturing intervals (LD) typically known in practice
  - Inverse problem for LD determination unstable to small deviations in initial data
  - Inverse problem for fracture length (xf) determination has same error as flow rate calculation
  - Requires minimum NST > 3 stream tubes for 10% error in component transport
  - Requires minimum NST > 10 stream tubes for 10% error in two-phase flow
  - Stream tube structure assumed fixed during simulation (valid for short-term processes)
  - Limited applicability when fracture lengths vary significantly (error increases when xf normalized to max <0.75)
  - Not applicable for very small LD values where flow structure differs significantly from model assumptions

10_1007_s13369_021_05597_5.key_1:
- Sandstone concrete composite pavement structure with oblique prestressing technology
- Argillaceous sandstone from Huangyan expressway construction site with 39% clay mineral, 10% Montmorillonite, 0.12 softening coefficient, 2.661 density, and 25% crushing value
- Four-layer pavement structure: AR-GM13 surface (4-10 cm), cross-tensioned prestressed sandstone concrete base (16-22 cm), C15 sandstone concrete base (22 cm), and C15 sandstone concrete subbase (20 cm)
- Elastic moduli: 1200 MPa (AR-GM13 surface), 23,600 MPa (prestressed sandstone concrete base), 15,800 MPa (C15 sandstone concrete base and subbase)
- Poisson's ratios: 0.25 (AR-GM13 surface), 0.27 (all concrete layers)
- Densities: 2000 kg/m³ (AR-GM13 surface), 2400 kg/m³ (prestressed sandstone concrete), 2200 kg/m³ (C15 sandstone concrete layers)
- Thermal contraction coefficients: 2.0×10⁻⁵/°C (surface), 1.5×10⁻⁵/°C (prestressed concrete and base), 1.0×10⁻⁵/°C (subbase)
- Mechanical constraints: interlayer shear stress ≤ 0.618 MPa, asphalt tensile stress ≤ 0.254 MPa, concrete bending tensile strength ≤ 4.0 MPa
- Optimal configuration: 5 cm rubber asphalt concrete single-surface layer and 18 cm cross-tensioned prestressed sandstone concrete base layer
- Load analysis locations spaced at 0.15 m intervals from pavement center to edge
- Tensile stress increases by 0.0138 MPa and interlayer shear stress increases by 0.0638 MPa when axle load moves closer to pavement edge
- Prestress applied using "cooling method" with negative temperature load calculated by ΔT = σ/(Eα)
- Objective function: Min f(x) = PV/t where PV is present value of total construction costs and t is pavement lifespan
- Maintenance period: 7.5 years for surface repaving at cost of 961,000 CNY/km
- Repaving of 4 cm modified asphalt concrete with 2 cm stress absorbing layer every 15 years at cost of 1.562 million CNY/km
10_1007_s13369_021_05597_5.key_2:
- C15 sandstone concrete cushion layers (22 cm and 20 cm thick) fixed during analysis
- Load application at 37 locations spaced at 0.15 m intervals from pavement center to edge
- Most unfavorable condition when axle load acts on pavement edge
- Interlayer shear stress constraint: τ ≤ 0.618 MPa
- Asphalt tensile stress constraint: σ ≤ 0.254 MPa
- Concrete bending tensile strength constraint: σ ≤ 4.0 MPa
- Standard axle loads applied at various positions on pavement surface
- Tensile stress increases by 0.0138 MPa when axle load moves closer to pavement edge
- Interlayer shear stress increases by 0.0638 MPa when axle load moves closer to pavement edge
- Adhesive layer with modified emulsified asphalt interface
- Seal coat as thin asphalt mixture layer interface
- Sliding layer with sand and polyethylene film interface
- Three-dimensional finite element modeling
- Prestress applied using "cooling method" with negative temperature load
- Concrete and rebars modeled separately with coupling through temperature load
- Mechanical analysis of pavement structure under vehicle loading conditions
10_1007_s13369_021_05597_5.key_3:
- Mechanical stress distribution in composite pavement structure under vehicle loading
- Interlayer shear stress between pavement layers
- Tensile stress in asphalt concrete surface layer
- Bending tensile stress in cross-tensioned prestressed concrete layer
- Maximum interlayer shear stress (τmax)
- Maximum tensile stress in asphalt layer (σmax)
- Bending tensile stress in concrete layer (σ)
- Pavement lifespan (t)
- Present value of total construction costs (PV)
- Objective function value (PV/t)
- Minimize the objective function f(x) = PV/t (ratio of total construction cost to pavement lifespan)
- Optimal thickness combination of rubber asphalt concrete surface (5-10 cm) and cross-tensioned prestressed sandstone concrete base (18-22 cm) satisfying mechanical constraints (τmax ≤ 0.618 MPa, σmax ≤ 0.254 MPa, σ ≤ 4.0 MPa)
10_1007_s13369_021_05597_5.key_4:
- Rubber asphalt concrete surface thickness range: 4-10 cm (optimized to 5-10 cm for single-layer)
- Cross-tensioned prestressed sandstone concrete base thickness range: 16-22 cm (optimized to 18-22 cm)
- C15 sandstone concrete base fixed at 22 cm
- C15 sandstone concrete subbase fixed at 20 cm
- Interlayer shear stress constraint: τmax ≤ 0.618 MPa
- Asphalt tensile stress constraint: σmax ≤ 0.254 MPa
- Concrete bending tensile strength constraint: σ ≤ 4.0 MPa
- When cross-tensioned prestressed sandstone concrete thickness is 16 cm or 17 cm, concrete bending tensile stress exceeds flexural strength
- Surface layer must be either single-layer (5-10 cm) or double-layer configuration
- Adhesive layer must use modified emulsified asphalt
- Sealing layer must be thin asphalt mixture
- Sliding layer must use sand and polyethylene film
- Maintenance required every 7.5 years for surface repaving
- Repaving of 4 cm modified asphalt concrete with 2 cm stress absorbing layer required every 15 years
- Finite element model must include concrete pavement slab, prestressed rebars, and foundation with consideration of prestress and slab bottom friction in both directions

10_1016_j_jcp_2024_113013.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Composite aero-structures, specifically: laminated beam under compression; C-shaped wing spar section (C-spar) with joggle region in center

- **Material / Medium:**
  - Carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) composite with carbon fibers embedded in resin
  - AS4/8552 elastic properties used for beam analysis
  - Beam: 3 layers (plies) of equal thickness (6 mm total thickness)
  - C-spar: 24 uni-directional layers (0.2 mm each)
  - Orthotropic elastic material with nine parameters and orientation vectors
  - Beam stacking sequence: [0°, 45°, -45°]
  - C-spar stacking sequence: [(45°, -45°)₃, (0°, 90°)₃]ₛ
  - Element aspect ratio of 15 for C-spar model

- **Application & Importance:**
  - Modeling interaction between meso-scale (ply level, sub-millimeter) and macro-scale (structural level, meter) behavior
  - Structural design and certification of composite aero-structures
  - Enabling efficient simulation for optimization and uncertainty quantification
  - Application to UK-EPSRC-funded CerTest project on composite structural certification

- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - Laminated beam: 500 mm length, 140 mm width, 6 mm thickness
  - C-spar: 500 mm long C-shaped structure
  - Dirichlet boundary conditions applied at x = 0 mm and x = 500 mm end surfaces
  - Maximum displacement of 20 mm observed on beam sides under unit displacement of -10 mm
  - Strain magnitude on order of 10⁻² in beam under compression
  - 24 elements through thickness (one per ply) in C-spar model
  - Displacement field shows characteristic out-of-plane deformation due to non-symmetric stacking sequence
10_1016_j_jcp_2024_113013.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Dirichlet boundary conditions applied at x = 0 mm and x = 500 mm end surfaces
  - Unit displacement of x(z) = -10 mm imposed at boundaries
  - Maximum displacement of 20 mm observed on beam sides under loading
  - Displacement field constrained to be zero on Γ_D (Dirichlet boundary)
  - Neumann boundary data g prescribed on Γ_N
  - Non-overlapping domain decomposition with 64 subdomains for beam model
  - Non-overlapping domain decomposition with 256 subdomains for C-spar model
  - Partition of unity with overlap size o = 1 or o = 3
  - Oversampling parameter o* = 3, 4, 5, 6, or 8 (depending on analysis)

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Uni-axial compression loading applied to both beam and C-spar
  - Body force per unit volume f(x) included in the formulation
  - Compression causes characteristic out-of-plane deformation due to non-symmetric stacking sequence

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Domain decomposed into non-overlapping subdomains with algebraic overlap construction
  - Oversampling subdomains normalΩ_j* created by adding layers of elements to overlapping subdomains normalΩ_j
  - Partition of unity operators used to "stitch" local approximation spaces together
  - A-harmonic condition enforced at subdomain interfaces through local eigenproblems
  - Subdomain communication via algebraic overlap construction with 1-8 layers of elements

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Linear elastic behavior analysis (no damage or non-linear effects considered)
  - 3D elasticity problems with orthotropic material properties
  - Finite element discretization with piecewise linear elements
  - Reduced integration used to avoid shear-locking
  - One element through thickness per ply layer
  - Element aspect ratio of 15 for C-spar model
  - Steady-state structural analysis (no time dependence)
  - Strain magnitude on order of 10⁻² in beam under compression
  - Mesh refinement with constant characteristic element size across different model sizes
10_1016_j_jcp_2024_113013.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Anisotropic linear elasticity in composite structures
  - Multiscale interaction between meso-scale (ply level) and macro-scale (structural level) behavior
  - Solution of symmetric positive-definite system from finite element discretization of elasticity equations
  - Local generalized eigenvalue problems (GEVPs) in A-harmonic subspaces for multiscale model reduction

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Displacement field (u_h) with maximum observed displacement of 20 mm
  - Strain field (ε_h,xx) with magnitude on order of 10⁻²
  - Relative L2 errors for displacement (e_d) and strain (e_ε) fields
  - Compressive failure criterion (φ₁₋) for structural design assessment
  - Reciprocal eigenvalues (1/λ_j^i) for local approximation spaces
  - Local basis size (m_j) ranging from 30 to 190
  - Oversampling parameter (o*) ranging from 3 to 8
  - Model order reduction ratios (32× for Set #1, 50× for Set #2, 170× for Set #3)
  - Computational time for GEVP solves and coarse space solutions

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Maximize model order reduction while maintaining accuracy in displacement and strain fields
  - Achieve nearly exponential decay of local approximation errors with respect to basis size
  - Accurately capture strains, stresses, and failure criteria with minimal coarse space dimension
  - Balance oversampling size (o*) and local basis size (m_j) to optimize computational cost
  - Enable efficient simulation for uncertainty quantification and optimization of composite structures
  - Achieve target relative L2 error below 10⁻⁷ for strain field with minimal computational resources
  - Reduce coarse space solve time while maintaining sufficient accuracy for engineering design (e.g., < 3.0×10⁻³ relative error on failure criterion)
10_1016_j_jcp_2024_113013.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Element aspect ratio constraint: High aspect ratios (15+) cause accuracy degradation in eigenvalue problems, leading to plateau in 1/λ_j^i values
  - Oversampling size trade-off: Larger oversampling (o*) reduces coarse space size but increases local problem dimensions and memory requirements
  - Subdomain size limitation: Subdomains with o* = 6 require >50,000 DoF, needing >8 GB RAM per subdomain
  - Domain decomposition constraint: C-spar model divided into 256 subdomains with constant dof(V_h)/P ≈ 10,000 per processor
  - Mesh resolution constraint: 24 elements through thickness (one per ply) with constant element size in other directions

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Strain magnitude constraint: Strains on order of 10⁻² in beam under compression
  - Error tolerance requirement: Target relative L2 error below 10⁻⁷ for high-accuracy solutions
  - Computational memory constraint: 4 GB RAM per subdomain required for local GEVP solves
  - Eigenvalue threshold constraint: Tolerance of t = 10⁻⁶ on 1/λ_j,m_j+1 used for accurate solutions
  - Model order reduction limits: 32× reduction for Set #1, 50× for Set #2, and 170× for Set #3
  - Failure criterion accuracy constraint: Relative error on compressive failure criterion must stay below 3.0×10⁻³ for engineering relevance
  - Coarse solve constraint: Final coarse space problem currently solved on one processor, limiting scalability for larger models

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Element type constraint: Quadratic serendipity elements still show accuracy loss with high aspect ratios
  - Integration domain constraint: Subdomain boundary integration limited to overlapping subdomain boundaries (process j requires integration only up to ∂Ω_j)
  - Boundary condition implementation: Dirichlet conditions enforced by setting A_ℓjℓj^H = 1, A_ℓjk^H = 0 for k ≠ ℓj, and b_ℓj^H = 1
  - HPC resource constraint: Model with 256 subdomains requires 4 nodes of Hamilton8 cluster (128 cores/node)
  - Computational trade-off: Single fine-scale solve is cheaper with GenEO-preconditioned Krylov methods than MS-GFEM for individual solutions
  - Interface error constraint: Oversampling required to handle interface errors at subdomain boundaries, with o* > 5 needed for smooth error distribution across domain

10_1016_j_engfailanal_2022_106952.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Solid rocket motor flexible joint structure; specifically uniform-thickness flexible joint (UTFJ) and variable-thickness flexible joint (VTFJ) as components of the thrust vector control system
- **Material / Medium:** Reinforcing parts (RP) with modulus of elasticity 2.100e5 MPa, Poisson ratio 0.300, density 7,850 kg/m³; Elastic parts (EP) with modulus of elasticity 0.520 MPa, Poisson ratio 0.499, density 1,240 kg/m³; EP uses Mooney-Rivlin five-parameter hyperelastic model (C₁₀=0.2590, C₀₁=-0.0042, C₁₁=0.0603, C₂₀=-0.0096, C₀₂=-0.1330)
- **Application & Importance:** Load-bearing safety and reliability analysis; addressing failure mechanisms in traditional uniform-thickness joints that cause local shear damage, high negative mass, and short system range; enabling lightweight design with improved swing performance
- **Geometry / Domain:** Concentric spherical annular structure with alternating layers of elastic and reinforcing parts; total thickness 25.10 mm; 7 elastic part layers and 6 reinforcing part layers; VTFJ has variable thickness with EP thickness increased up to 60.59% and RP thickness reduced up to 50% compared to uniform-thickness design; designed to move around common swing center with 5° swing angle capability
10_1016_j_engfailanal_2022_106952.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** FULL DOF on fixed body connected to combustion chamber; revolute pair between actuator sleeve and fixed body; translational pair between actuator sleeve and piston; revolute pair between piston and active body; total joint thickness constrained to 25.10 mm for assembly requirements
- **Loads / Excitations:** 12 MPa container stamping pressure; actuator driving displacement S = L sin(0.4·pi·time); 5° reciprocating swing angle; swing frequency of 0.2 Hz; 10,000 cycle fatigue testing
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Alternately adhesive spherical annular structures of composite rubber elastic parts and metal reinforcing parts; contact interfaces between elastic parts and reinforcing parts; fluid-structure interaction from container pressure
- **Simulation Type:** 3D nonlinear structural dynamics with material and geometric nonlinearity; total Lagrangian formulation; transient analysis with 5 s substeps; multi-axial stress fatigue analysis based on crack propagation; implicit Newmark integration (α=0.25, δ=0.5); Full Newton-Raphson iterative solution with 200 iteration limit
10_1016_j_engfailanal_2022_106952.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Nonlinear structural dynamics with coupled material and geometric nonlinearity; multi-axial stress fatigue analysis based on crack propagation; load-bearing swing performance under pressure and displacement loading
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Equivalent stress (max 562.235 MPa at 180° position); shear stress (max 2.207 MPa compressive, 1.895 MPa in stamping state); shear strain (max 1.002 at 0° position); swing center displacement (max 4.03 mm); swing moment (max 882.419 N·m theoretical, 1022.400 N·m experimental); fatigue life (minimum 9,376 cycles); convergence norms (2-norm tolerance 1E-06); stress-strain relationship for Mooney-Rivlin model
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize joint mass (achieved 22.27% reduction) while maintaining equivalent stress below 845 MPa yield limit; minimize shear stress in elastic parts (reduced from 3.670 MPa to 1.895 MPa); maximize swing flexibility through controlled shear deformation; ensure fatigue life exceeds 5,000 cycles; reduce swing moment below 1,500 N·m design limit
10_1016_j_engfailanal_2022_106952.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Total joint thickness constrained to 25.10 mm for system assembly requirements; 7 elastic part layers and 6 reinforcing part layers; maximum swing angle of 5° required for system operation; concentric spherical annular structure with alternating elastic and reinforcing parts
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Reinforcing parts (RP) yield strength limit of 845 MPa; elastic parts (EP) allowable shear stress of 3.4 MPa; maximum swing center displacement limited to 7 mm; system swing moment must remain below 1,500 N·m; fatigue life requirement of minimum 5,000 cyclic swings; safety factor requirement of 1.5 for both RP and EP; equivalent stress must remain below material yield limits during 12 MPa stamping pressure and swing conditions
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Elastic parts manufactured from vulcanized composite rubber material; actuator driving displacement defined as S = L sin(0.4·pi·time); finite element convergence criteria with 2-norm tolerance of 1E-06 for unbalanced force and 2E-06 for displacement; loading applied in five substeps with 5 s duration per substep; swing frequency constrained to 0.2 Hz for testing validation
