10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_118689.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Seismic Hold-Down (SHD) device for CLT building shear walls
- **Material / Medium:** S235JR steel (f_yk = 235 MPa, f_uk = 360 MPa, E = 200,000 MPa); GL24h glulam timber; C20/25 concrete; M20/M24 anchors; 5 mm diameter screws
- **Application & Importance:** Resists overturning moments in CLT shear walls during seismic events; promotes ductile failure at reduced steel flange segment (fuse) for controlled energy dissipation
- **Geometry / Domain:** Three configurations (SHD-440/540/620) with heights 440/540/620 mm, base widths 60/70/80 mm, thicknesses 2.5/3/3 mm; fuse segments with lengths 70/70/50 mm and widths 20/25/45 mm; 20/30/45 screws per device; concrete foundation 1500×750×500 mm
10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_118689.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Anchorage to concrete (Bonded, Sleeve) with concrete slab 1500×750×500 mm (C20/25)
  - T-Slot base plate on strong floor
  - Rollers at sides of test setup
  - Hard-contact between base plate and concrete foundation
  - Linear-elastic axial spring (30 kN/mm stiffness) modeling anchor connection
  - Base plate rotation assumed around toe (rigid rotation)
  - Kinematic constraints (master-slave) for screw connections

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Hydraulic cylinder with 300 kN capacity applying load at timber post center
  - Displacement-controlled testing with 0.08 mm/s stroke rate
  - Cyclic displacement protocol with target up-lift displacements at multiples of yielding displacement (d = 0.75-1.00-1.5-2.00·d_y up to 30 mm)
  - 30-ton ram with 300 mm stroke
  - Incrementally applied displacement in numerical model

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Steel-to-timber connection with 5 mm diameter screws
  - Mohr-Coulomb friction interface (c = 0.5 MPa, Φ = 30°) between steel plate and timber
  - Compression-only springs modeling hard-contact
  - Washer load cells (compression-only) for anchor force monitoring
  - Screw connections modeled with linear-elastic beams using master-slave constraints

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 3D finite element model with material and geometrical nonlinearities
  - Displacement-controlled static and cyclic tests
  - Monotonic and cyclic loading regimes
  - Nonlinear structural analysis using Newton-Raphson method
  - Series of nonlinear mechanical springs (component method) for analytical modeling
10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_118689.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Nonlinear axial tension behavior of hold-down connection
  - Buckling behavior of fuse segment during displacement recovery
  - Component interaction mechanics (steel-to-timber connection, anchor behavior)
  - Strain distribution in steel components under cyclic loading
  - Hysteretic response under cyclic displacement protocols

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Load-displacement curves for static and cyclic loading
  - Eccentricity ratio (k_t = F_a/F) ranging 1.5-2.5
  - Ductility (μ = d_u/d_y) with target >1.5
  - Strength reduction (k_deg = F_u/F_max) with minimum 0.8
  - Strength impairment (φ_imp = F_i/F_I) with maximum 30%
  - Equivalent viscous damping (ζ_eq) 0.05-0.10
  - Strain distribution at fuse reaching up to 25%
  - Buckling displacements during unloading cycles
  - Component displacement contributions (anchorage, steel segments, steel-to-timber)

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Achieve controlled ductile failure at the fuse segment (reduced steel flange)
  - Ensure adequate displacement capacity (μ > 3) for medium-to-high ductility CLT buildings
  - Maintain hysteretic behavior comparable to traditional hold-downs while changing failure mechanism
  - Design as "tension-only" member with buckling permitted during displacement recovery
  - Meet Eurocode requirements for dissipative connections (φ_imp ≤ 30%, k_deg ≥ 0.8)
  - Optimize overstrength ratios between fuse failure and other potential failure modes
10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_118689.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Device heights constrained to 440/540/620 mm (SHD-440/540/620)
  - Base widths limited to 60/70/80 mm with thicknesses of 2.5/3/3 mm respectively
  - Fuse segment length constrained to 50-70 mm with width 20-45 mm
  - Concrete foundation fixed at 1500×750×500 mm (C20/25)
  - Screw diameter fixed at 5 mm with penetration depth 40 mm and parallel-to-grain spacing of 44 mm
  - Timber post limited to GL24h glulam

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Minimum ductility requirement: μ = d_u/d_y > 1.5 (Eurocode requirement)
  - Maximum strength impairment: φ_imp ≤ 30% (per Eurocode for dissipative connections)
  - Minimum strength reduction factor: k_deg ≥ 0.8 (prescribed by Eurocode)
  - Steel strain limit: ε_max = 25% (assumed ultimate strain in numerical model)
  - Overstrength ratio for buckling must be <1 (no overstrength for fuse buckling)
  - Eccentricity ratio (k_t) must be considered between 1.5-2.0 for design purposes
  - Anchor force ratio (k_t = F_a/F) must account for base plate rotation around toe
  - Displacement protocol limited to 30 mm maximum (d = 0.75-1.00-1.5-2.00·d_y)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Steel material constrained to S235JR (f_yk = 235 MPa, f_uk = 360 MPa)
  - Anchors limited to M20/M24 diameter (Bonded or Sleeve types)
  - Testing equipment constrained to 300 kN capacity hydraulic cylinder with 300 mm stroke
  - Displacement control rate fixed at 0.08 mm/s for all tests
  - Base plate and stiffeners assumed rigid in analytical models
  - Screw connections modeled with effective number factor Ψ_eff ≤ 0.7
  - Anchor embedment depth constrained to 100-350 mm (100 mm for SHD-440, 150 mm for SHD-540, 350 mm for SHD-620)
  - SHD must be designed as "tension-only" member with compressed element contribution neglected

10_1007_s13239_022_00610_w.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Human heart model for external ventricular assist device (VAD) investigations, specifically focusing on ventricular mechanics and electrophysiology
- **Material / Medium:** Nonlinear anisotropic myocardial tissue described by Holzapfel-Ogden constitutive law with fiber and sheetlet directions; orthotropic active-strain model for muscle contraction; blood represented through lumped parameter circulation model
- **Application & Importance:** Design optimization of external cardiac assist devices that apply force patches to the epicardium; treatment of heart failure without direct blood contact or anatomical structure modification; addressing limitations of current VADs including surgical opening of closed systems and unnatural temporal actuation
- **Geometry / Domain:** Idealized ventricular structure consisting of strong ventricular muscles only; exclusion of great vessels, atria, coronary arteries, heart valves and papillary muscles; tetrahedral mesh domains with 160k, 250k, or 500k elements; fiber angles varying between -60° to +60° from endocardia to septum and epicardium; two circular epicardial regions for force patch application with radii ranging from 1.5-3.5 cm
10_1007_s13239_022_00610_w.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Endocardial surfaces: Pressure boundary conditions P · m = p m, with p from circulation coupling
  - Base around heart valve openings: Robin boundary conditions P · m = αu with α = αb = 750 mmHg cm⁻¹
  - Epicardium: Robin boundary conditions with α = αe = 0.75 mmHg cm⁻¹ to imitate surrounding tissue
  - Insulation boundary conditions applied to electrical potential, ionic model, and activation
  - Force patches: Dirichlet boundary conditions on circular epicardial regions (radii 1.5-3.5 cm) with displacement vectors normal to left ventricle centerline
  - Sliding allowed in direction of left ventricle centerline k underneath patches

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Initial preload pressures: 5.7 mmHg in left ventricle, 2.4 mmHg in right ventricle
  - Electrical wave initiation: Applied electric current I_app in lower third of both endocardial surfaces
  - Heartbeat duration: 800 ms with electrical signal spreading through ventricles within 60 ms
  - Force patch displacement: f̂ = 0.9 cm peak magnitude, t̂ = 250 ms peak time, T = 300 ms impact duration
  - Force patch motion: fi(X,t) = f̂i sin[2(t - (t̂i - 0.5Ti))/Ti π] ni with synchronous movement (T = T₁ = T₂, t̂ = t̂₁ = t̂₂)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Mechanical model coupled to circulation via ventricular pressure and volume
  - Implicit coupling of mechanics and circulation using same pressure boundary conditions p = [plv prv]T
  - Pressure boundary conditions updated through Newton's method to minimize ||Vfe - Vcirc||1
  - Lumped parameter circulation model provides pressure values for ventricular boundaries
  - Fiber and sheetlet directions (f, s, n) defined with n = f × s for anisotropic material behavior

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Transient 3D finite element simulation with tetrahedral elements (160k, 250k, or 500k elements)
  - Quadratic shape functions for all electromechanical fields
  - Multiscale temporal resolution: se = 0.05 ms for electrophysiology/activation, sm = sc = 1 ms for mechanics/circulation
  - Local load steps for mechanics: sls = 0.5 ms
  - Nonlinear anisotropic material model with active strain formulation
  - Coupled electromechanics and circulation model with implicit pressure-volume coupling
10_1007_s13239_022_00610_w.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Cardiac electromechanics including electrophysiology (transmembrane potential propagation), active strain-based muscle contraction, nonlinear anisotropic structural mechanics of myocardial tissue, and lumped parameter blood circulation modeling with pressure-volume interactions

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Ventricular pressure-volume (p-V) loops for left and right ventricles
  - Apex shortening (peaks at ~15%)
  - Wall thickening (peaks at ~45%)
  - Apex twist angle (peaks at ~12°)
  - Pressure and flow rate evolution over time
  - Calcium concentration distribution
  - Stroke work and cardiac power output (1.3 W total for healthy heart)
  - Ventricular volume changes
  - Deformation patterns during cardiac cycle

- **Optimization Goal:** Restore healthy cardiac output and p-V loop characteristics in pathological hearts using external force patches; optimize patch parameters (peak displacement magnitude f̂, peak time t̂, impact duration T, and radius r) to achieve equivalent power output as healthy hearts while minimizing tissue stress and controlling right ventricular pressure response; specifically target 0.9 cm peak displacement magnitude for 3 cm infarction radius to recover healthy stroke work in pathological hearts
10_1007_s13239_022_00610_w.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Idealized ventricular structure excluding great vessels, atria, coronary arteries, heart valves and papillary muscles
  - Force patch application limited to circular epicardial regions with radii ranging from 1.5 cm to 3.5 cm
  - Fixed 2 cm patch radius in primary demonstration
  - Fiber angles constrained to -60° to +60° from endocardia to septum and epicardium
  - Mesh resolution limited to 160k, 250k, or 500k tetrahedral elements

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Right ventricular pressure must not exceed physiological peak values (observed to rise above desired levels with simple actuation)
  - Tissue stress must remain below damage thresholds (not explicitly quantified but noted as critical constraint)
  - Wall thickening constrained to peak at approximately 45% (healthy baseline)
  - Apex shortening constrained to peak at approximately 15% (healthy baseline)
  - Apex twist angle constrained to peak at approximately 12° (healthy baseline)
  - Power output must be restored to healthy levels (1.3 W total for healthy heart)
  - 0.9 cm peak displacement required for 3 cm infarction radius to match healthy power output
  - Maximum infarction radius of 3.5 cm reduces left ventricular stroke work by almost 50%

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Force patch boundary conditions only account for normal force component (tangential forces ignored)
  - Cannot model potential patch sliding off slippery epicardial surface
  - Interactions between patches and coronary vessels not modeled
  - Long-term tissue damage from force patches cannot be assessed
  - Current implementation uses independent actuation without synchronization to electrical pulses (future improvement noted)
  - Simplified flow model cannot account for damaged heart valves or patch impact on valve function
  - Only normal displacement allowed underneath patches (sliding permitted along left ventricle centerline)

- Exponent α constrained to [0.2, 0.5]
- Pylon risk constraint: [1 + 2.86C_d - 2.42C_d² - 0.053C_dα]⁻¹·⁹²⁶ < 0.42
- Bearing risk constraint: [1 + 1.78C_d - 1.12C_d² - 0.315C_dα]⁻¹·⁹²⁶ < 0.43
- FVD risk constraint: [1 + 2.56C_d - 1.16C_d² - 1.32C_dα]⁻¹·⁹²⁶ < 0.43
- Acceptable failure probabilities: pylon (O_i = 0.05), bearing (O_i = 0.1), FVD (O_i = 0.1)
- Admissible domain defined by overlapping constraints for pylon, bearing, and FVD
- FVD deformation capacity (m_C-FVD) must be ≥ 0.5 m to achieve optimal system performance
- For m_C-FVD < 0.3 m, unconstrained optimal solution falls outside admissible range
- System risk minimization must occur within component-specific safety requirements
- The partial derivative of system risk with respect to C_d ranges from -5 to 1, while with respect to α it ranges from 0 to 0.1
- Optimal C_d for system risk is 0.82 when pylon acceptable failure probability is 0.05 or 0.045
- When pylon acceptable failure probability is < 0.04, optimal parameters differ from unconstrained solution
- The admissible domain narrows as the pylon protection level increases (O_i decreases)

10_1007_s00158_019_02353_0.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Hollow structural topology optimization using Moving Morphable Components (MMC) framework, analyzing square Mindlin cantilever plate, cantilever beam, and miniature bending beam (MMB) structures
- **Material / Medium:** Dimensionless material with Young's modulus = 1 and Poisson's ratio = 0.3; ersatz material model used for finite element analysis
- **Application & Importance:** Designing hollow structures with high stiffness-to-mass ratio for improved mechanical performance; addressing the limitation of traditional topology optimization that typically produces solid structures despite industrial preference for hollow components with mature joining technology
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Square Mindlin cantilever plate: 30×30×4 design domain with 90×90×12 mesh, V = 0.2|D| volume constraint, subjected to upward and downward forces
  - Cantilever beam: 30×4×20 design domain with 90×12×60 mesh, V = 0.3|D| volume constraint, subjected to in-plane and out-plane forces
  - Miniature bending beam: 40×4×20 design domain with 120×12×60 mesh, V = 0.3|D| volume constraint
  - Hollow components defined by internal and external topology description functions with parameters including rotation angles (α, β, θ), center coordinates (x₀, y₀, z₀), half-length (L), maximum half-width (a₁), width coefficients (c_b1), and thickness coefficient (c_t1)
  - Cross-sectional shapes include I-shaped, U-shaped, rectangular, dual rectangular, and L-shaped hollow components
10_1007_s00158_019_02353_0.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Dirichlet boundary condition: u = ū on Γu with ū = 0
  - Neumann boundary condition on Γt
  - Volume constraint: V = 0.2 |D| for square Mindlin cantilever plate
  - Volume constraint: V = 0.3 |D| for cantilever beam
  - Volume constraint: V = 0.3 |D| for miniature bending beam
  - Fixed support at one end of all cantilever structures (implied by cantilever designation)
  - Volume constraints satisfied at 500 iteration cycles
  - Body force density f = 0

- **Loads / Excitations:** 
  - Upward and downward forces on square Mindlin cantilever plate
  - In-plane and out-plane forces on cantilever beam
  - Surface traction t on Γt
  - Dimensionless material loading with Young's modulus = 1

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** 
  - Hollow component structure defined by combination of internal and external topology description functions (TDFs)
  - Hollow structure achieved by combining TDFs of internal and external structures through subtraction operation: ΩS = Ω²S \ Ω¹S
  - Ersatz material model used for element stiffness calculation

- **Simulation Type:** 
  - 3D topology optimization
  - Finite element analysis with eight-node solid elements
  - Mesh specifications:
    - Square Mindlin cantilever plate: 90×90×12 mesh
    - Cantilever beam: 90×12×60 mesh
    - Miniature bending beam: 120×12×60 mesh
  - Linear elasticity model
  - MMA (Method of Moving Asymptotes) optimizer
  - Heaviside function parameters: p = 6, ξ = 0.01, Δ = 0.4
  - Material properties: Young's modulus = 1, Poisson's ratio = 0.3
10_1007_s00158_019_02353_0.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Structural mechanics with linear elasticity, specifically compliance calculation using finite element analysis with eight-node solid elements and ersatz material model

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Structural compliance values (e.g., 145,000 for solid components vs. 83,144 for hollow components in square Mindlin cantilever plate)
  - Volume constraint satisfaction
  - Component layout and shape parameters (positions, inclined angles, dimensions)
  - Computational costs (FEA time, sensitivity analysis time, MMA optimization time)
  - Volume fraction of solid material (γe) calculated using Heaviside function

- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize structural compliance under volume constraints (V = 0.2 |D| for square Mindlin cantilever plate; V = 0.3 |D| for cantilever beam and miniature bending beam), with hollow structures demonstrating superior stiffness-to-mass ratio compared to solid structures (e.g., hollow cantilever beam compliance reduced by approximately 43% compared to solid counterpart)
10_1007_s00158_019_02353_0.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Volume constraints: V = 0.2 |D| for square Mindlin cantilever plate
  - Volume constraints: V = 0.3 |D| for cantilever beam
  - Volume constraints: V = 0.3 |D| for miniature bending beam
  - Mesh specifications: 90×90×12 finite element mesh for square Mindlin cantilever plate
  - Mesh specifications: 90×12×60 finite element mesh for cantilever beam
  - Mesh specifications: 120×12×60 finite element mesh for miniature bending beam
  - Hollow component parameterization: rotation angles (α, β, θ), center coordinates (x₀, y₀, z₀), half-length (L), maximum half-width (a₁), width coefficients (c_b1), thickness coefficient (c_t1)
  - Area ratio of non-differentiable region: 1.69% (4 components, 20×20 mesh) → 0.52% (2 components, 20×20 mesh) → 0.24% (2 components, 40×40 mesh)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Structural compliance minimization as objective function
  - Volume constraint satisfaction (g_i(P) ≤ 0) required for all optimization problems
  - Material properties: Young's modulus = 1, Poisson's ratio = 0.3
  - Heaviside function parameters: ξ = 0.01 (to avoid singularity), Δ = 0.4 (regularization parameter)
  - TDF parameter: p = 6 (even integer for topology description functions)
  - Optimization convergence at 500 iteration cycles
  - Dirichlet boundary condition: u = ū = 0 on Γu
  - Body force density: f = 0

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Hollow component representation requires more design variables (10 per component) than solid components
  - Numerical instability due to non-differentiable points in maximum/minimum operations (addressed by increasing mesh density and decreasing component count)
  - Computational costs of hollow components are slightly larger than solid components (e.g., 45.78s vs 43.39s for square Mindlin cantilever plate)
  - Non-differentiable region width must be less than mesh size to be ignored in MMC method
  - Constraint function must remain ≤ 0 throughout optimization process

10_1007_s11771_023_5460_z.key_3:
- Thermal-mechanical coupling analysis of multi-layer CAES cavern under high temperature and high pressure
- Circumferential strain (εθ) distribution, particularly εθmax at top points of lining layer

10_1007_s00158_024_03847_2.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** eCRM-001 wing structure of an electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) aircraft; permanent magnet synchronous motor (PMSM) with 12 magnets
- **Material / Medium:** Aluminum alloy (Young's modulus E = 6.8E10 Pa, Poisson's ratio ν = 0.35) for wing structure; Hiperco 50 alloy for motor rotor and stator; air density ρ = 1.225 kg/m³; overall wing thickness h_val = 0.003 m
- **Application & Importance:** Aeroelastic analysis and multidisciplinary design optimization (MDO) for eVTOL aircraft development; wing gust response simulation; motor shape optimization to minimize core losses; compliance sensitivity analysis with respect to thickness distribution
- **Geometry / Domain:** eCRM-001 wing with clamped boundary condition at root; permanent magnet synchronous motor with 12 magnets arranged in circular configuration; 80×40 structured quadrilateral mesh for cantilever beam topology optimization; sinusoidal gust profile Vgust = v₀ × (1 - cos(2π(t - T₀)/T₁)) with v₀ = 50 m/s, T₀ = 0.02 s, T₁ = 0.12 s
10_1007_s00158_024_03847_2.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Clamped boundary condition at wing root; left edge of cantilever beam clamped; homogeneous boundary condition Az = 0 for magnetic potential; displacements of boundary vertices imposed as Dirichlet boundary conditions; volume constraint C(ρ̃) = ∫Ω ρ̃ dΩ - V = 0; design variable bounds (ρmin = 10⁻⁴ for topology optimization, xmin ≤ x ≤ xmax for motor shape optimization); convergence tolerance for mesh updates below 10⁻⁶
- **Loads / Excitations:** Constant wind velocity V∞ = 50 m/s; angle of attack AoA = 6°; air density ρ = 1.225 kg/m³; sinusoidal gust profile Vgust = v₀ × (1 - cos(2π(t - T₀)/T₁)) with v₀ = 50 m/s, T₀ = 0.02 s, T₁ = 0.12 s; downward traction force with magnitude 0.25 on cantilever beam; body force assumed zero in hyperelastic model; 12 magnets in motor configuration; constant thickness of 0.03 m initial value for wing
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Aeroelastic coupling between VLM aerodynamic solver and FEniCSx structural solver; load mapping from aerodynamic to structural solver; displacement mapping from structural to aerodynamic solver; work-conservative aeroelastic coupling; mesh movement using hyperelasticity; free-form deformation for shape parametrization; iterative updates between structural displacements and VLM mesh coordinates
- **Simulation Type:** Static aeroelastic analysis; dynamic aeroelastic simulation; transient gust response simulation; nonlinear PDE for optimal control; linear elasticity for cantilever beam; two-way coupled aeroelastic model; implicit midpoint rule for time integration; steady-state VLM aerodynamic solver; 3D structural analysis; convergence studies with varying time steps (Nsteps=25,50,100,200) and mesh refinements
10_1007_s00158_024_03847_2.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Aeroelastic coupling between structural deformation and aerodynamic loads; wind gust response dynamics; magnetostatic field distribution in electric motor; linear elasticity for structural analysis; nonlinear PDE for optimal control; Reissner-Mindlin shell theory for structural analysis; Vortex Lattice Method (VLM) for aerodynamic analysis; hyperelastic mesh movement for shape optimization
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** von Mises stress distribution (9.2e-05 to 3.0e+07 Pa); distributed aerodynamic load (1.8e+02 to 5.8e+02 Pa); tip displacement under gust excitation; gust velocity profile; magnetic flux density (2.5e-04 to 2.3e+00); compliance (C = fᵀu); power losses (Pₗ = Pₑc + Pₕ); gradients of compliance with respect to thickness; optimized density distribution; tip displacement time history with different time step sizes (Nsteps=25,50,100,200); magnetic flux density magnitude comparison between initial and optimized motor configurations
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize structural compliance of the eCRM-001 wing; minimize natural core losses due to magnets during no-load operation; minimize compliance of cantilever beam under volume fraction constraint of 0.4; optimize density distribution for topology optimization; minimize power losses in motor by adjusting magnet position; optimize structural thickness distribution for improved wing performance; maximize aerodynamic efficiency while maintaining structural integrity
10_1007_s00158_024_03847_2.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Volume fraction constraint of 0.4 for cantilever beam topology optimization; minimum density constraint ρmin = 10⁻⁴; design variable bounds (xmin ≤ x ≤ xmax) for motor shape optimization; 12 magnets arranged in circular configuration for motor; initial constant thickness of 0.03 m for wing structure; cantilever beam with length 160 and height 80; volume constraint C(ρ̃) = ∫Ω ρ̃ dΩ - V = 0; thickness distribution represented as first-order continuous polynomial function; 13 nodes along span-wise direction selected for gradient validation
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Mesh coordinate update threshold below 10⁻⁶ for aeroelastic coupling convergence; optimization tolerances (optimality tolerance 10⁻⁸, feasibility tolerance 10⁻⁶); time step constraint Δt = 0.001 (Nsteps=50) for gust response simulation convergence; maximum relative error of 1.31% for adjoint validation; maximum magnetic flux density magnitude of 2.3 on undeformed mesh; power losses computed as sum of eddy current loss and hysteresis loss; von Mises stress range from 9.2e-05 to 3.0e+07 Pa; distributed aerodynamic load range from 1.8e+02 to 5.8e+02 Pa
- **Process/Manufacturing:** No explicit manufacturing constraints stated in the provided text; finite difference step size h = 10⁻⁴ selected for gradient validation after numerical experiments; structural deformation scaled by factor of 40 for visualization purposes; mesh deformation handled through hyperelastic equations rather than actual mesh regeneration

10_1007_s43236_025_01006_4.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Modulation-enhanced dual magnetic flux brushless dual-port (MDMF-BDP) machine; conventional brushless dual-port (BDP) machine; tidal power generation system component
- **Material / Medium:** Permanent magnets (spoke-type and radially magnetized); iron yoke material (DW310-35); copper windings; air gap (1 mm)
- **Application & Importance:** Tidal power generation; replaces "multiple machines + mechanical components"; enables dual-port cooperative operation; eliminates mechanical gearboxes and intermediate conversion mechanisms; operates during both flood and ebb tides with single machine
- **Geometry / Domain:** Dual mechanical ports and dual electrical ports; outer rotor and inner rotor structure; stator with 24 slots; modulator outside stator slots; composite outer rotor with spoke-type PMs and radially magnetized PMs; reluctance inner rotor; stator outer diameter 210 mm; stack length 80 mm; air gap length 1 mm; outer rotor pole pairs (Pro) = 22; inner rotor pole pairs (Pri) = 18; winding I pole pairs = 2; winding II pole pairs = 4; modulator thickness (a) = 2 mm; radial PMs width (b) = 1.5 deg; outer rotor height (h_RPM) = 15 mm; radial PMs height (h_SPM) = 3 mm; inner rotor tooth height (h_ri) = 13 mm; outer rotor pole pitch angle (θ_ro) = 8.18 deg; inner rotor pole pitch angle (θ_ri) = 10 deg; inner rotor tooth slot angle (θ_sl) = 4 deg
- **Performance Specifications:** Inner rotor torque increased from 23.15 Nm to 30.88 Nm (33.3% increase); outer rotor torque increased from 34 Nm to 137.17 Nm (303.4% increase); inner rotor torque ripple decreased from 27.7% to 16.9%; outer rotor torque ripple decreased from 23.4% to 3.3%; winding I back EMF in MDMF-BDP machine is 2.4× conventional BDP; winding II back EMF in MDMF-BDP machine is 1.1× conventional BDP; effective working harmonics increased by 46.1% (2nd, 4th, 22nd, 40th harmonics vs. 4th and 11th in conventional)
- **Operating Conditions:** Rated current of winding I = 6 A/mm³; rated current of winding II = 6 A/mm³; 40 turns per phase for both windings; outer rotor speed = -200 r/min; inner rotor speed = 300 r/min; volume of PMs = 511.6 cm³
10_1007_s43236_025_01006_4.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Air gap length = 1 mm for both inner and outer air gaps; stator outer diameter = 210 mm; stack length = 80 mm; slot number = 24; machine volumes and thermal loads remain unchanged for comparative analysis; mechanical volumes consistent between conventional BDP and MDMF-BDP machines
- **Loads / Excitations:** Rated current of winding I = 6 A/mm³; rated current of winding II = 6 A/mm³; 40 turns per phase for both windings; outer rotor speed = -200 r/min; inner rotor speed = 300 r/min; outer rotor rotates clockwise at 200 r/min; inner rotor rotates counter-clockwise at 300 r/min; excitation currents of 6 A for both windings during torque analysis
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Outer rotor directly connected to right-side hydraulic turbine; inner rotor directly connected to left-side turbine; magnetic field from outer rotor PMs modulated by both stator slot modulators and inner rotor; modulated magnetic field couples with stator armature; tidal flow drives left-side turbine during tide rise (inner rotor) and right-side turbine during tide recede (outer rotor); dual magnetic flux paths produce dual magnetic flux modulation effect
- **Simulation Type:** Two-dimensional finite element models; no-load conditions for flux density and back EMF analysis; rated operating conditions for torque performance analysis; comparison under different operating conditions including winding I in open circuit, winding II in open circuit, and both windings operating; finite element method used for electromagnetic characteristics comparison
10_1007_s43236_025_01006_4.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Electromagnetic field distribution; magnetic flux modulation effects; dual magnetic flux path interactions; air gap magnetic field harmonics; torque generation mechanisms
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Air gap flux density waveforms and FFT spectrums; back-EMF amplitude and waveforms for both windings; average torque values for inner rotor (Tri) and outer rotor (Tro); torque ripple percentages for inner rotor (fri) and outer rotor (fro); effective working harmonics of air gap magnetic field; transmission ratios between rotors and windings; magnetic flux density distribution in stator and rotors
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize inner rotor torque (Tri); maximize outer rotor torque (Tro); minimize inner rotor torque ripple (fri); minimize outer rotor torque ripple (fro); improve effective working harmonics of air gap magnetic field; achieve 46.1% increase in effective working harmonics; optimize modulator thickness (a), outer rotor height (h_RPM), outer rotor pole arc coefficient (K_ro), and inner rotor pole arc coefficient (K_ri) using BBD multi-objective optimization with weight coefficients λ1=0.3 (outer rotor torque), λ2=0.3 (inner rotor torque), λ3=0.2 (outer rotor torque ripple), λ4=0.2 (inner rotor torque ripple)
10_1007_s43236_025_01006_4.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Inner and outer air gaps set to 1 mm; modulator thickness (a) constrained to [1, 4] mm; radial PMs width (b) constrained to [1, 4] deg; outer rotor height (h_RPM) constrained to [10, 16] mm; radial PMs height (h_SPM) constrained to [1, 4] mm; inner rotor tooth height (h_ri) constrained to [5, 20] mm; outer rotor pole arc coefficient (K_ro) constrained to [0.2, 0.8]; inner rotor pole arc coefficient (K_ri) constrained to [0.2, 0.8]; inner rotor tooth slot angle (θ_sl) constrained to [2, 8] deg; stator outer diameter fixed at 210 mm; stack length fixed at 80 mm; slot number fixed at 24; models maintain consistent overall dimensions and mechanical volumes for fair comparative study
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Magnetic flux density distribution must remain below saturation flux density of iron yoke material (DW310-35); machine volumes and thermal loads must remain unchanged for comparative analysis; volume of permanent magnets constrained (501.1 cm³ for conventional BDP vs 511.6 cm³ for MDMF-BDP); torque ripple must be minimized with weight coefficients λ3=0.2 (outer rotor) and λ4=0.2 (inner rotor) in optimization function; rated current of 6 A/mm³ for both windings
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Optimization process requires layered sequential approach where weakly sensitive parameters (b, h_SPM, h_ri) are optimized using finite element single-variable scanning method before highly sensitive parameters (a, h_RPM, K_ro, K_ri) are optimized using Box-Behnken Design (BBD) multi-objective optimization; response surface model must achieve R² > 0.9288 and relative root mean square error Re < 0.0872 for acceptable accuracy; optimization requires 29 sets of experiments for BBD method; geometric parameters must satisfy flux modulation theory relationships: Qs = Pro + PW1 and Pro = Pri + PW2

10_1016_j_mechmachtheory_2023_105322.key_1:
- Planetary Roller Screw Mechanism (PRSM)
- GCr15 steel for screw, roller, and nut (E=212 GPa, ν=0.29, ρ=7810 kg/m³)
- Load distribution analysis to determine performance characteristics including load-carrying capacity, stiffness, and service life; critical for applications in space stations, aircraft, oil drilling, and medical instruments where non-uniform load distribution causes premature wear and reduced operational life
- Central screw with helical threads surrounded by 10 rollers (typically), enclosed by a nut; threaded interfaces between screw-roller and nut-roller with pitch=1 mm, nominal diameters of 19.5 mm (screw), 6.5 mm (roller), and 32.5 mm (nut); 5 starts on screw and nut, 1 start on roller; 30 threads per roller; flank angle=45°; helix angles of 4.66° (screw) and 2.8° (roller/nut)
10_1016_j_mechmachtheory_2023_105322.key_2:
- Fixed constraint on screw end face; axial displacement released for screw, roller, and nut while rotation and movement in other directions constrained
- Symmetric constraints applied to symmetric plane of PRSM
- External load of 50 kN applied on nut end face to simulate installation and loading conditions
- Tension-compression (T-C) loading condition where screw is under tension and nut is under compression
- Contact between nut-roller interface and screw-roller interface following Hertz contact theory
- Elastic contact deformation only occurring in contact area
- Deformation compatibility relationships between adjacent thread contact pairs
- Thread contact pairs with axial backlash defined as L(i,j) = LNR(i,j) + LSR(i,j)
- 3D FE model using implicit solver scheme of ABAQUS 6.14
- Iterative solution approach for non-linear contact deformation-load relationship
- Static analysis considering multiple machining errors (pitch error, roller nominal diameter error, screw eccentricity error, nut eccentricity error)
10_1016_j_mechmachtheory_2023_105322.key_3:
- Load distribution characteristics among rollers and threads in Planetary Roller Screw Mechanism considering multi-coupled machining errors
- Axial contact force distribution along threads (N)
- Load Sharing Coefficient (LSC) defined as k_Ri = F_Ri / F_avr where F_Ri is load shared by each roller and F_avr = F/N_R is average load
- Relative importance values of machining errors (ε_R=19%, ε_S=34%, ε_N=47%)
- LSC prediction formula: k_R = 0.0138ε_R + 0.0352ε_S + 0.0409ε_N + 1
- Achieve uniform load distribution among rollers to maximize load-carrying capacity, minimize uneven wear, and extend service life of PRSM by rigorously controlling eccentricity errors of screw and nut in engineering practice
10_1016_j_mechmachtheory_2023_105322.key_4:
- Geometric parameters fixed per Table 1: screw nominal diameter (19.5 mm), roller nominal diameter (6.5 mm), nut nominal diameter (32.5 mm), pitch (1 mm), flank angle (45°), helix angle (4.66° for screw, 2.8° for roller/nut), 10 rollers, 30 threads per roller
- ISO 286-1 grade 7 tolerance limits: roller nominal diameter error (15 μm), screw eccentricity error (10.5 μm), nut eccentricity error (12.5 μm)
- Operating under rated dynamic load of 50 kN with tension-compression (T-C) loading condition
- Maximum measured pitch error of 2.2 μm (6# roller), roller nominal diameter error ranging 1.8-12.3 μm, screw eccentricity error average 6.4 μm, nut eccentricity error average 8.5 μm
- Contact deformation follows Hertz contact theory with elastic behavior only in contact area (F = (δ/K)^(3/2))
- Analytical model does not consider small radial and torsional deformations, causing slight discrepancies at roller ends
- Pitch error has negligible influence on load distribution among rollers (only affects thread-level distribution)
- Excessive positive nominal diameter error leads to premature roller wear and failure
- Machining error directions constrained: 1# roller angle set to zero, screw eccentricity error along positive X-axis, nut eccentricity error along negative X-axis
- Measurement limitations: 5 μm sampling point spacing, 3 mm/s scanning speed using optical probe on Leitz PMM-C coordinate measuring machine

10_1007_s12008_024_01790_6.key_1:
- Convex spherical surface drilling process of Ti6Al4V titanium alloy
- Ti6Al4V material with constitutive model parameters: σ0 = 1.569 × 10^9, n = 6.413, ε0p = 1, c0 = 1.0131, c1 = -5.838 × 10^-4, c2 = -3.795 × 10^-8, c3-c5 = 0, m = 78.125, ε'0 = 1

10_1016_j_cam_2024_116275.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Discrete network (graph) models representing pore networks in reservoir simulation, with time-dependent behavior and highly varying connectivity.

- **Material / Medium:**

  - Connection weights w_ij ranging from 0.0001 to 0.5085 in Test-1a, and 6.14 to 6.14×10⁴ in high-contrast tests

- **Application & Importance:** 
  - Reducing computational complexity of large-scale network simulations through coarse-scale approximation
  - Enabling simulation of pore network models in reservoir simulation with significant system size reduction
  - Providing accurate solution reconstruction from coarse to fine scale for highly heterogeneous networks
  - Handling networks with varying connectivity patterns from structured regular to unstructured irregular

- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Networks embedded in rectangular cuboid domain Ω = [0, L₁] × ⋯ × [0, L_d]
  - Three network structures analyzed: structured regular, structured irregular, and unstructured irregular
  - 2D networks: 200×200 structured grid (40,000 nodes, 79,600 connections) and 240×240 irregular grid (46,006 nodes, 62,538 connections)
  - 3D networks: 25×25×25 structured grid (15,625 nodes, 45,000 connections) and 30×30×30 irregular grid (22,092 nodes, 43,075 connections)

- **Identity & Domain:** Parabolic evolution problem in moving spatial computational domains, specifically heat conduction/diffusion processes modeled by ∂tu − Δu = f with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions
- **Material / Medium:** Not explicitly specified; general mathematical model applicable to diffusion processes and heat conduction in arbitrary media
- **Application & Importance:** Numerical solution of parabolic initial-boundary value problems in deforming domains; enables analysis of processes like heat transfer in moving geometries where standard time-stepping methods are inadequate
- **Geometry / Domain:** 2D space-time domain Q = Ω(t) × [0,1] with deforming spatial cross-section Ω(t) = {x ∈ R : a(t) < x < b(t)}, where a(t) = −t/2 and b(t) = 1 + t/2; unstructured triangular mesh discretization as shown in Fig. 2; space-time cylinder with boundaries Σ (lateral), Σ₀ (initial time), and Σₜ (final time)
- **Discretization:** Continuous finite element method with polynomial degrees p = 1 (linear) and p = 2 (quadratic); quasi-uniform triangulations of space-time domain
- **Parameters:** θ = 0.1 and δ = 10 used in all numerical experiments; GMRES solver without preconditioning
- **Convergence:** For smooth solution u(x,t) = sin(πx)sin(πt), optimal convergence rates O(hᵖ) observed; for singular solution u(x,t) = (1−t)¹/²sin(πx), convergence rates of 0.75 for p = 1 and 0.5 for p = 2
- **Error Measurement:** Discrete norm ‖·‖ₕ defined as (‖∇ₓvₕ‖²_L₂(Q) + θh‖∂ₜvₕ‖²_L₂(Q) + ½‖vₕ‖²_L₂(Σₜ) + θh/2‖∇ₓvₕ‖²_L₂(Σₜ) + θh/2∑‖⟦∇ₓvₕ⟧ₜ‖²_L₂(Fᵢⱼ) + δθh∑‖⟦∂ₜvₕ⟧ₓ‖²_L₂(Fᵢⱼ))¹/²

- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition u = 0 on Σ (lateral boundary ∂Ω(t) × (0,T)); homogeneous initial condition u = 0 on Σ₀ (Ω(0) × {0}); homogeneous boundary condition u = 0 on ΣT (Ω(T) × {T}) for test functions; deforming spatial domain boundaries defined by a(t) = −t/2 and b(t) = 1 + t/2 for 1D spatial domain
- **Loads / Excitations:** Source term f in the equation ∂tu − Δu = f; exact solutions u(x,t) = sin(πx)sin(πt) (Example I) and u(x,t) = (1−t)¹/²sin(πx) (Example II); stabilization parameters θ = 0.1 and δ = 10
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Interior facets Fi j between mesh elements with jump operations ⟦·⟧ and average operations {·}; upwind test functions at interfaces; continuous finite element spaces with C⁰ continuity across element boundaries
- **Simulation Type:** Transient parabolic evolution problem; 2D space-time domain (Q ⊂ R²); moving/deforming spatial computational domain; continuous finite element method with polynomial degrees p = 1 and p = 2; unstructured triangular mesh discretization; space-time finite element formulation with simultaneous discretization in space and time
10_1007_s10092_018_0261_8.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Error estimates in the discrete norm ‖·‖ₕ; convergence rates of the numerical solution; solution contours in the space-time cylinder; degree of freedom versus error estimate plots; specific convergence rates (0.75 for p=1 and 0.5 for p=2 in Example II with singular solution)
- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve optimal convergence rates O(hᵖ) for smooth solutions as predicted by Theorem 2; validate the theoretical a priori discretization error estimates; demonstrate feasibility of the stable space-time finite element method for both smooth (Example I) and singular (Example II) solutions in deforming domains
10_1007_s10092_018_0261_8.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Space-time domain Q = Ω(t) × [0,T] with deforming spatial cross-section Ω(t) ⊂ Rᵈ (d = 1,2,3); quasi-uniform triangulations of space-time domain with non-degenerate (d+1)-simplices; Lipschitz continuous space-time domain; specific example uses 1D spatial domain with time-dependent boundaries a(t) = −t/2 and b(t) = 1 + t/2
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Solution must belong to H²(Q) for consistency; for a priori error estimate, solution must satisfy 2 ≤ s ≤ p + 1 and s > (d + 1)/2 where s is regularity parameter; stabilization parameter θ ≤ (C²_inv,0 C²_u)⁻¹; δ must be positive constant; reduced convergence rates for non-smooth solutions (e.g., O(h⁰·⁵) instead of optimal O(hᵖ) for singular solution at t=1)
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Continuous finite element method with C⁰ basis functions; limited to polynomial degrees p = 1 and p = 2 in numerical examples; GMRES solver without preconditioning used for linear systems; method requires piecewise polynomial approximation with Pᵖ elements; quasi-uniform mesh assumption (hK ≤ h ≤ CuhK for all K ∈ Kh)

10_1016_j_compstruc_2008_09_003.key_1:
- Subject: Node-based smoothed finite element method (NS-FEM) for solid mechanics problems
- Test cases: Cantilever beam, infinite plate with circular hole, semi-infinite plate under uniform pressure, crack problem in linear elasticity
- Cantilever dimensions: Length L=48m, height D=12m, unit thickness (plane stress)
- Cantilever material: E=3.0×10⁷ kPa, ν=0.3, loaded with P=1000N parabolic traction at free end
- Infinite plate with hole: Central circular hole radius a=1m, modeled quarter domain (5.0×5.0), E=1.0×10³ N/m², ν=0.3 (plane strain)
- Semi-infinite plate: 5a×5a square domain with a=0.2m, c=100, p=1MPa uniform pressure, plane strain condition
- Crack problem: E=1.0 N/m², ν=0.3, t=1m thickness
- Element types: n-sided polygonal (Voronoi), 4-node quadrilateral, triangular elements
- Mesh types: Regular discretization and extremely irregular discretization (α_ir=0.5)
- NS-FEM properties: Provides upper bound in strain energy with reasonably fine mesh, immune from volumetric locking, works with arbitrary polygonal elements, insensitive to element distortion
- Comparison methods: Standard FEM (FEM-Q4, FEM-T3), element-based SFEM
- Boundary conditions: Prescribed displacements using analytical solutions, traction boundary conditions from exact solutions
- Domain discretization: Voronoi diagram for polygonal elements, regular and distorted quadrilateral meshes
- Analytical solutions: Timoshenko beam theory for cantilever, Kirsch solution for infinite plate with hole
- Strain energy reference: Exact strain energy used as reference for convergence studies
- Poisson's ratio range: Tested from 0.4 to 0.499999 in volumetric locking studies
- Mesh refinement: Number of nodes varies from hundreds to thousands across test cases
10_1016_j_compstruc_2008_09_003.key_2:
- Cantilever left boundary: Constrained using exact displacements from Timoshenko beam theory (Eq. 37)
- Cantilever right boundary: Distributed parabolic shear stresses (Eq. 38) with P=1000N
- Infinite plate with hole: Symmetric conditions on left and bottom edges; traction-free inner boundary of hole; traction boundary conditions on right (x=5.0) and top (y=5.0) edges based on exact solution (Eq. 40)
- Semi-infinite plate: Left and bottom sides constrained using exact displacements (Eq. 43); right side subjected to tractions from Eq. (42); uniform pressure within range -a ≤ x ≤ a with p=1MPa
- Crack problem: Symmetry about y-axis (only half domain modeled)
- Plane stress condition: Applied to cantilever (uniform unit thickness)
- Plane strain condition: Applied to infinite plate with hole (E=1.0×10³ N/m², ν=0.3), semi-infinite plate, and crack problem
- Unidirectional tensile load: σ=1.0 N/m² at infinity in x-direction for infinite plate with hole
- Poisson's ratio range: Tested from 0.4 to 0.499999 for volumetric locking studies
- Mesh irregularity: α_ir ranging from 0.0 (regular mesh) to 0.5 (severe distortion)
- Domain symmetry: Exploited in infinite plate with hole (quarter model) and crack problem (half model)
- 2D linear elasticity: Assumed for all problems
- Homogeneous essential boundary conditions: Required for upper bound property in strain energy
- Traction boundary conditions: Applied on specific edges based on exact analytical solutions
- Exact displacements: Used for constrained boundaries in all test cases
- Regular and extremely irregular discretizations: Used for quadrilateral element tests (α_ir=0.5)
10_1016_j_compstruc_2008_09_003.key_3:
- Physics solved: Linear elasticity in solid mechanics
- Target outputs: Strain energy, displacement error norm, stress distributions, displacement fields
- Upper bound verification: Strain energy comparison against exact/reference solution to confirm upper bound property
- Volumetric locking assessment: Displacement error norm versus Poisson's ratio (0.4 to 0.499999)
- Convergence analysis: Strain energy and displacement error norm versus number of nodes
- Element distortion testing: Performance evaluation with irregularity factor α_ir from 0.0 to 0.5
- Mesh flexibility demonstration: Results using regular discretization, extremely irregular discretization, and Voronoi polygonal elements
- Boundary condition validation: Comparison with analytical solutions for cantilever, infinite plate with hole, and semi-infinite plate problems
- Zero-energy mode verification: Rank testing of stiffness matrix to confirm absence of spurious modes
- Stress field accuracy: Direct comparison of computed stresses (σ_xx, σ_yy, τ_xy) with analytical solutions
- Displacement field accuracy: Comparison of computed displacements (u, v) with exact solutions along specific boundaries
10_1016_j_compstruc_2008_09_003.key_4:
- NS-FEM provides upper bound in strain energy only when "a reasonably fine mesh is used" and with homogeneous essential boundary conditions
- FEM fails with severely distorted elements (α_ir > 0.3) due to negative Jacobian determinant, while NS-FEM remains functional
- Poisson's ratio range constrained to 0.4-0.499999 for volumetric locking studies
- Irregularity factor α_ir limited to 0.0-0.5 range for mesh distortion testing (0.0 = regular mesh, 0.5 = severe distortion)
- Cantilever dimensions fixed at L=48m, D=12m with unit thickness (plane stress condition)
- Infinite plate with circular hole modeled as quarter domain with 5.0×5.0 size and hole radius a=1m
- Semi-infinite plate uses 5a×5a domain with a=0.2m and c=100
- NS-FEM requires linearly independent columns/rows in stiffness matrix to avoid spurious zero-energy modes
- Plane strain condition applied to infinite plate with hole, semi-infinite plate, and crack problem
- Voronoi diagram elements have varying numbers of sides per element
- For crack problems, discontinuity fields along crack path require incorporation with XFEM for complete solution
- NS-FEM does not require elements to be convex, though Voronoi elements are generally convex polygons
- Triangular and quadrilateral elements from FEM can be used directly in NS-FEM without modification
- Upper bound property applies specifically to strain energy in linear elasticity problems
- FEM shows decreasing accuracy with increasing element distortion (α_ir = 0.1-0.3), while NS-FEM maintains stable accuracy

10_1016_j_cma_2010_01_021.key_2:

10_1016_j_cma_2010_01_021.key_3:

10_1016_j_cma_2010_01_021.key_4:

10_1016_j_jsv_2022_117174.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Coupled rectangular panels subjected to time-harmonic point force, specifically thin steel plates and cross-laminated timber (CLT) panels connected by L-shaped joints, analyzed using hybrid finite element/wave and finite element (FE/WFE) method

- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Steel plates: density 7800 kg/m³, Young's modulus 2×10¹¹ N/m², Poisson's ratio 0.3, damping loss factor 0.02, thickness 0.0018 m
  - CLT panels: 6-layer construction with stacking sequence 0°/90°/0°/0°/90°/0°, density 450 kg/m³, Eₓ 1.1×10¹⁰ N/m², Eᵧ/E_z 3.67×10⁸ N/m², Gₓᵧ/Gₓz 6.9×10⁸ N/m², G_yz 6.9×10⁷ N/m², ν_yx/ν_zx 0.014, ν_zy 0.030, damping loss factor 0.020, thickness 0.198 m

- **Application & Importance:** Predicting structure-borne vibration and sound transmission in lightweight building structures (e.g., high-speed train carriages, aircraft fuselages, CLT buildings); mitigating structural vibration and reducing structure-borne noise; developing improved energy models for sound transmission prediction without statistical energy analysis (SEA) assumptions

- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Two coupled thin plates: 1 m width, 1.5 m and 2 m lengths
  - Two coupled CLT panels: 2 m × 1.2 m × 0.198 m dimensions
  - L-shaped joint connections with arbitrarily complex cross-sections
  - Boundary conditions: free ends, simply supported edges
  - Analysis considers both infinite and finite panel configurations
  - Trace wavenumber components (m = ±1, ±3, ±5, ±7) used for finite width panels
  - Point force excitation at (x₁ = 1.9 m, y₁ = 0.6 m, z₁ = 0 m) for CLT panels
  - Response measured at (x₂ = 2 m, y₂ = 0.6 m, z₂ = 0 m) for CLT panels
  - FE model segments: 0.002 m × 0.002 m for thin plates, 0.005 m thick joint segment with 2394 DOFs for CLT panels
10_1016_j_jsv_2022_117174.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Ends of panels are free
  - Edges of panels are simply supported (zero translations in x-, z-directions, zero rotation around y-axis, and zero bending moment in positive x-axis for thin plates)
  - Sliding boundary conditions (zero slope and zero shear force for thin panels)
  - Simply-supported boundaries defined by series of image forces producing stress distribution f(x₁, y₁) = fₑδ(x₁ − xₑ) Σ[δ(y₁ − yₑ − 2mL_y) − δ(y₁ + yₑ − 2mL_y)]
  - Sliding boundary conditions defined by stress distribution f(x₁, y₁) = fₑδ(x₁ − xₑ) Σ[δ(y₁ − yₑ − 2mL_y) + δ(y₁ + yₑ − 2mL_y)]
  - Discrete trace wavenumber components (m = ±1, ±3, ±5, ±7) used for finite width panels

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Time-harmonic point force with complex magnitude fₑ acting normal to panel surface
  - Point force of unit amplitude at (x₁ = 1.5 m, y₁ = 0.25 m, z₁ = 0 m) for thin steel plates
  - Point force of unit amplitude at (x₁ = 1.9 m, y₁ = 0.6 m, z₁ = 0 m) for CLT panels
  - Time-harmonic line force Fₘ exp(−ik_y y) with amplitude Fₘ = ifₑ/L_y sin(πm/L_y yₑ) and trace wavenumber k_y = πm/L_y
  - Damping loss factor of 0.02 for panels and joint

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Panels coupled by L-shaped joint with arbitrarily-shaped cross-section
  - Continuity of displacement and force equilibrium at panel-joint interfaces
  - Reflection and transmission matrices determined using hybrid FE/WFE method
  - Scattering matrix S relating incident negative-going waves to reflected/transmitted positive-going waves (d⁺ = S d⁻)
  - Wave amplitudes at joint defined by d⁺ = S d⁻, g⁻ = r g⁺

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Time-harmonic analysis (exp(iωt) dependence assumed throughout)
  - Wave-based deterministic approach modeling response as sum of discrete propagating waves
  - Hybrid FE/WFE method combining finite element modeling of joint with wave and finite element analysis of panels
  - Analysis of both infinite and finite panel configurations
  - Superposition of responses to individual trace wavenumber wave components
  - Linear elastic analysis with frequency-dependent damping
10_1016_j_jsv_2022_117174.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Wave propagation in coupled rectangular panels
  - Vibration transmission through structural joints
  - Time-harmonic forced response of coupled panel systems
  - Structure-borne sound transmission between connected panels
  - Wave scattering and reflection at panel-joint interfaces

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Wavenumbers (k_x) of propagating and nearfield waves as function of frequency
  - Power transmission (τ(T)) and reflection (τ(R)) coefficients for incident wave modes
  - Transverse velocity magnitude at specific points in panels
  - Out-of-plane displacement magnitude at response points
  - Wave amplitudes at various locations in the system (d⁺, d⁻, g⁺, g⁻)
  - Frequency response functions for coupled panel systems
  - Magnitude and phase of displacement/velocity responses

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Develop accurate prediction method for structure-borne vibration and sound transmission in coupled panel systems
  - Enable computationally efficient analysis of complex panel constructions (e.g., cross-laminated timber)
  - Provide foundation for developing improved energy models without Statistical Energy Analysis (SEA) assumptions
  - Understand wave propagation mechanisms between coupled complex panel systems for vibration mitigation in lightweight structures
10_1016_j_jsv_2022_117174.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Panels must be rectangular with constant width L_y in the y-direction
  - Joints must have constant cross-section in the y-direction
  - Analysis is exact only for simply-supported or sliding boundary conditions; otherwise an approximation
  - Thin steel plates: 1 m width, 0.0018 m thickness, 1.5 m and 2 m lengths
  - CLT panels: 2 m × 1.2 m × 0.198 m dimensions
  - 6-layer CLT construction with specific stacking sequence (0°/90°/0°/0°/90°/0°)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Boundary conditions limited to free ends with simply-supported or sliding edges
  - Method assumes time-harmonic excitation with form exp(iωt)
  - Response representation requires decomposition into discrete trace wavenumber components
  - Wave propagation analysis constrained to linear elastic behavior with frequency-dependent damping
  - Simply-supported boundary condition requires zero translations in x-, z-directions, zero rotation around y-axis, and zero bending moment
  - Sliding boundary condition requires zero slope and zero shear force for thin panels

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Method is constrained to structures where "the response of the finite system is identical to that of the system of semi-infinite panels excited by a series of image forces"
  - Numerical issues can arise for complicated applications, requiring "careful formulation, the use of alternative eigensolvers for the wave modes or using a reduced wave basis"
  - "Including very short 'stubs' in the model of the joint" is recommended to improve numerical stability
  - Method is not applicable to structures where "boundary conditions need to be defined for every DOF over the cross-section" beyond the defined simply-supported or sliding conditions
  - Full FE analysis becomes impractical at high frequencies due to "dramatic" increase in computational cost and sensitivity to "indeterminate construction details"

10_1017_pds_2023_34.key_1:

- Material / Medium: Isotropic material with density of 1350 kg/m³; Young's modulus values tested: 1 MPa, 2.5 MPa, 5 MPa, 7.5 MPa, and 10 MPa; structure modeled as a rod with 1 cm diameter; non-linear material effects not considered in the use case

- Geometry / Domain: Structure attached between tibia and foot; rigid approximations of bones with same dimensions and weights as actual bones; fixed at knee; 20° plantarflexion motion analyzed (determined as maximal value during gait); rod-shaped support structure with 1 cm diameter; required simulation nodes include contact/force application points (red dots) and approximation points (blue dots) for model order reduction

- Loads / Excitations: Gravity as the only external force in the use case; steady plantarflexion motion up to 20°; force applied by patient; external forces acting on the foot; dorsiflexors maximal applicable force decreased by 90% in weakened model (10% remaining strength); linear elastic material behavior considered
- Interactions / Interfaces: Kinematics and forces at interaction points transferred from musculoskeletal model to FEA; reaction forces transferred from FEA to musculoskeletal model; comparison between target muscle activation and muscle activation with assistance; boundary conditions from multibody simulation (MBS) used in FEA; external force applied by orthosis/supporting structures used in musculoskeletal model

10_1017_pds_2023_34.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Musculoskeletal human model inverse dynamics for gait analysis; finite element structural response calculation; interaction between orthosis structures and lower leg muscles during ankle motion; linear elastic structural behavior of orthosis components
- Target Outputs (Metrics): Muscle activations (particularly tibialis anterior); joint reaction forces; gait kinematics; structural stresses; displacements; reaction forces from orthosis structures; target muscle activation vs. actual activation comparison; force applied by orthosis/supporting structures
- Optimization Goal: Match muscle activation of weakened model with assistance to target (healthy model) muscle activation; provide "assistance-as-needed" where orthosis only supplies force that weakened muscles cannot provide; prevent further muscle impairment by ensuring weakened muscles maintain appropriate contribution; achieve optimal structural design of force-generating orthosis components for patient-specific gait requirements
10_1017_pds_2023_34.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: Rod-shaped support structure with 1 cm diameter; motion limited to 20° plantarflexion (maximal value during gait); model fixed at knee; 2D motion analysis (vs. full 3D walking); lightweight design requirement for passive AFO; node selection for model order reduction with red dots at contact/force application points and blue dots for solution approximation
- Performance/Physics Limits: Dorsiflexors' maximal applicable force decreased by 90% (10% remaining strength); material must have low stiffness to enable deformation by foot force; linear elastic material behavior considered (non-linear effects neglected); small forces/torques in use case vs. walking (1x body weight forces, 1.5x body weight torques on ankle during actual walking); activation of tibialis anterior must not reach 0% to prevent further muscle impairment; gravity as only external force in use case
- Process/Manufacturing: Material distribution via catalogs and optimization techniques; foot and calf plate lightening via topology optimization with stiffness objective function; truss model planned for evaluation instead of full AFO model; structure adjustment through material selection and dimensioning; model order reduction required for feasible calculation time; implementation via MATLAB as bilateral interface between OpenSim and ANSYS

- Angle of attack (α) as primary input parameter

- Slotted flap tested at 0° and 25° deflection
- RAE2822 airfoil profile

- Boundary layer calculations performed from stagnation point to trailing edge along upper and lower sides of wing sections
- Wake aligned with free stream flow with no vortex roll-up calculated

- Turbulent boundary layer calculated using Head's model after transition
- Flow detachment predicted when boundary layer shape factor reaches 2.2

- Steady-state aerodynamic analysis for moderate to high angles of attack including stall regions

10_4028_www_scientific_net_msf_963_788.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** 650V, 45mΩ SiC Power MOSFET under short-circuit test conditions
- **Material / Medium:** 4H-SiC, SiO₂, Polysilicon, Platinum, Aluminum
- **Application & Importance:** Power conversion in automotive, aircraft, industry and renewable energy applications; understanding failure mechanisms during short-circuit events which are critical for safety in power converters
- **Geometry / Domain:** Layered MOSFET structure with vertical cross-section showing gate oxide interface; 3D thermal domain covering die and neighboring layers with temperature range 25.644°C–965.53°C
10_4028_www_scientific_net_msf_963_788.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**  
  - Gate resistance R<sub>g</sub> = 4.7Ω (external) for both switching characterization and short-circuit tests  
  - V<sub>DD</sub> = 400V for short-circuit tests and switching characterization  
  - V<sub>GS</sub> = -5/20V (switching), 0/20V (short-circuit test)  
  - Load current = 20A for switching characterization  
  - Pulse width increment of 250ns with 5s delay between pulses in short-circuit test sequence  
  - 5V supply for gate driver circuit  
  - Ground potential at source terminal in equivalent circuits  

- **Loads / Excitations:**  
  - Short-circuit pulse duration t<sub>sc</sub> = 5.75µs (survivable), 6µs (failure)  
  - Power profile P<sub>off</sub> = 2kW, E<sub>off</sub> = 25µJ (initial switching), E<sub>off</sub> = 220µJ (post-failure)  
  - Waveform amplitudes: V<sub>DS</sub> = 100V/10V, I<sub>D</sub> = 5A/100A, V<sub>GS</sub> = 5V/10V  
  - Time-dependent power distribution from Silvaco structural simulation as input to thermal model  

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**  
  - Gate oxide/SiC interface with density of states energy profile  
  - Thermal coupling between SiC die and neighboring layers (substrate, front metal, die attach)  
  - Polysilicon layer melting at failure location (observed in physical analysis)  

- **Simulation Type:**  
  - Transient thermal analysis for microsecond-scale events (short-circuit duration ≤ 6µs)  
  - 3D Finite Element Method (FEM) with temperature-dependent material properties  
  - Nonlinear thermal model (thermal conductivity and heat capacity as function of temperature)  
  - Static structural simulation in Silvaco for power distribution extraction
10_4028_www_scientific_net_msf_963_788.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**  
  - Transient thermal behavior during microsecond-scale short-circuit events  
  - Power dissipation distribution within SiC MOSFET structure  
  - Temperature-dependent thermal conductivity and heat capacity propagation  
  - Structural response to high-energy short-circuit pulses  

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**  
  - Temperature profiles vs time for gate oxide, SiC die, front metal, substrate, and die attach layers  
  - Peak temperature values (up to 965.53°C in thermal maps)  
  - Short-circuit pulse duration at failure point (t<sub>sc</sub> = 6µs)  
  - Switching energy (E<sub>off</sub> = 25µJ pre-failure, 220µJ post-failure)  
  - Power distribution across device width (0-3.0 µm)  
  - Gate-source resistance degradation (R<sub>GS</sub> = 3.3kΩ for Sample 1, 18Ω for Sample 2)  
  - Thermal map showing heat flux propagation through layers  

- **Optimization Goal:**  
  - Correlate temperature distribution with experimentally observed failure modes (polysilicon layer melting)  
  - Identify critical temperature thresholds that cause gate oxide failure  
  - Map power dissipation hotspots to physical defect locations  
  - Validate thermal model against experimental short-circuit waveforms and failure analysis
10_4028_www_scientific_net_msf_963_788.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**  
  - Layered structure with fixed material composition: 4H-SiC, SiO₂, Polysilicon, Platinum, Aluminum  
  - Device width constrained to 0-3.0 µm for power distribution analysis  
  - Vertical cross-section geometry as shown in Silvaco simulated structure (Fig. 5a)  
  - 3D thermal domain limited to die and immediate neighboring layers  

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**  
  - Maximum short-circuit pulse duration: 5.75µs (survivable) vs 6µs (failure threshold)  
  - Operating voltage V<sub>DD</sub> = 400V for short-circuit tests  
  - Gate voltage range V<sub>GS</sub> = 0/20V for short-circuit conditions  
  - Critical temperature threshold: polysilicon layer melting at approximately 965.53°C (maximum observed in thermal map)  
  - Gate oxide failure when short-circuit energy exceeds critical value (E<sub>off</sub> increases from 25µJ to 220µJ)  
  - Model cannot predict current filamentation due to lack of electro-thermal interaction implementation  

- **Process/Manufacturing:**  
  - Limited thermal monitoring capability for microsecond-scale power pulses (few specialized equipment available)  
  - Conduction model requires fine-tuning of interface parameters (density of state energy profile at gate oxide/SiC interface)  
  - Anisotropic mobility values and electron saturation velocity must be calibrated using experimental data  
  - Temperature-dependent thermal properties (conductivity, heat capacity) required for accurate simulation  
  - Gate oxide integrity must be verified prior to short-circuit testing as prerequisite

10_1016_j_rineng_2025_104972.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** 3D-printed polylactic acid (PLA) crash box components for mechanical energy absorption
- **Material / Medium:** Red PLA filament (Color Plus brand); density 1.24 g/cm³; Young's Modulus 3.5 GPa; Tensile Strength 60 MPa; Shear Modulus 1287 MPa; Poisson's ratio 0.36; melting temperature 190-230°C
- **Application & Importance:** Energy dissipation in low-speed impact scenarios; automotive crash boxes; protective gear; packaging systems; converts kinetic energy to deformation energy during impacts
- **Geometry / Domain:** Thin-walled square cross-section crash box; honeycomb lattice optimized structure; initial weight 30 g increasing to 155 g (5x) in optimized version; printed with 0.4 mm nozzle diameter and 0.1 mm layer thickness; raster angle ±45°
- **Thermal Treatment:** Annealing temperature 50-55°C; duration 7 minutes to 120 hours; optimal treatment 50°C for 90 minutes; increases peak crushing force (PCF) by 40.6% (1403.3 N to 1974 N)
- **Testing Parameters:** Displacement rates 1 mm/min and 70 mm/min; crushing tests measured with Instron universal machine; sampling frequency 0.2 s
- **Performance Metrics:** PCF (Peak Crushing Force) and MCF (Mean Crushing Force) measured; energy absorption calculated as ∫F(δ)⋅dδ from force-displacement curves
- **Finite Element Model:** 30,400 first-order quad elements (1 mm size); rigid wall with 5 mm enforced displacement; Johnson-Cook material model; density 1.24e−9 tonne/mm³; Young's Modulus 3.986 GPa; Poisson ratio 0.332; Yield Strength 41 MPa; Ultimate Tensile Strength 59.903 MPa
- **Optimization Results:** Honeycomb structure increased PCF 32-fold (1403 N to 45,143 N) with only 5x weight increase; 12.5% PCF improvement in honeycomb with thermal treatment
10_1016_j_rineng_2025_104972.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Fixed base constraint on bottom surface; rigid wall with enforced displacement on top surface; spatial constraint on base; symmetry planes not explicitly mentioned; no elements violating mesh quality thresholds (max size, aspect ratio, warpage, skew, jacobian, angle metrics all at 0.0%)
- **Loads / Excitations:** Uniaxial displacement rates of 1 mm/min and 70 mm/min; 5 mm enforced displacement; crushing force measured in Newtons; 70 mm/min rate used for FE simulation; sampling frequency of 0.2 s for measurements
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** General-purpose contact to prevent mesh penetration during deformation; rigid wall contact with top surface; physical contact between testing machine and component during crushing tests
- **Simulation Type:** Transient finite element analysis; 3D model; quasistatic load case; Radioss solver with Hypermesh preprocessing; 30,400 first-order quadrilateral elements (1 mm size); Johnson-Cook material model (referred to as "Johns Zeril"); time history analysis (0-2.0 seconds)
10_1016_j_rineng_2025_104972.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Crushing behavior of 3D-printed PLA components under uniaxial compression; energy transformation from kinetic to deformation energy; stress distribution during collapse; quasistatic mechanical response of thin-walled structures
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Peak Crushing Force (PCF); Mean Crushing Force (MCF); Energy absorption (E = ∫F(δ)⋅dδ); Force-displacement curves; Von Mises stress distribution; PCF values ranging from 1403.3 N (raw) to 45,143 N (optimized)
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize Peak Crushing Force (PCF) while maintaining energy absorption efficiency; achieve 32-fold PCF increase (from 1403 N to 45,143 N) with minimal weight penalty (5x weight increase from 30 g to 155 g); improve energy absorption by 40.6% through thermal treatment (1403.3 N to 1974 N PCF); optimize geometry to enhance mechanical performance for low-speed impact applications
10_1016_j_rineng_2025_104972.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Nozzle diameter constrained to 0.4 mm; layer thickness constrained to 0.1 mm; build direction fixed to "Flat, printed through the thickness"; raster angle constrained to ±45°; initial crash box weight 30 g with maximum 5x weight increase (155 g) for optimized honeycomb structure; thin-walled square cross-section maintained during optimization
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Thermal treatment temperature constrained between glass transition temperature (~60°C) and melting temperature (190-230°C); optimal annealing temperature determined as 50°C; maximum PCF improvement limited to 40.6% for simple crash box; honeycomb structure shows maximum 12.5% PCF improvement with thermal treatment; enforced displacement limited to 5 mm in FE simulation; warpage observed after 24 hours of thermal treatment
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Extruder temperature constrained to 200°C; bed temperature constrained to 50°C; printing rate constrained to 50 mm/min; thermal treatment duration constrained between 7 minutes and 120 hours; cooling to room temperature required after thermal treatment; residual thermal stresses generated during printing process; anisotropic structure formation due to interlayer bonding limitations; solid-melt-solid phase transition inherent to material extrusion process; warpage effect constrains maximum thermal treatment duration at higher temperatures

- **Loads / Excitations:** Uniform external hydrostatic pressure applied to outer pipe surface; rotation angle (θ) applied to reference point to simulate pure bending; two loading paths: P-κ (pressure applied first then curvature with pressure held constant) and κ-P (curvature applied first then pressure with curvature held constant); external pressure range 0 to maximum collapse pressure; bending curvature range (κ/κI) from 0 to 2.0
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** External pressure directly applied to pipe outer surface; bending simulated via rotation at reference point; parametric variations in outer diameter (101.6-610 mm), t/D ratio (1.48-6.62%), yield strength (295, 375, 431, 535 MPa), and initial ovality (0.5-3.0%); interaction between bending curvature and external pressure causing cross-sectional ovalization
- **Simulation Type:** 3D nonlinear FEM analysis; half-model due to symmetry; C3D8R solid elements; 7 layers through pipe thickness; 26 elements across width; 60 elements along half-length; ABAQUS Standard solver; two-step analysis per loading path; parametric studies for P-κ loading path (identified as more critical than κ-P path)
10_1016_j_oceaneng_2025_121607.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Collapse pressure (Pc) corresponding to specific bending curvature; normalized collapse pressure (Pc/Py); normalized curvature (κ/κI); pressure-curvature interaction diagrams; collapse envelopes; bending moment-curvature relationships; ovalization progression; moment at collapse; pressure at collapse; statistical metrics (R², RMSE, MAE, A10-index) for model performance
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize prediction accuracy of collapse pressure under combined bending-external pressure loading; minimize MAE and RMSE; maximize R² (target >0.99) and A10-index (target >0.94); develop interpretable model through SHAP analysis; create practical GUI tool for engineering design within parameter ranges (D: 101.6-610 mm, t/D: 1.48-6.62%, Δₒ: 0.5-3.0%, σₒ: 295-535 MPa)

10_1016_j_tws_2023_110865.key_1:
- Thin-walled cylinders for shape sensing using inverse Finite Element Method with Generalized Beam Theory (iFEM/GBT)
- Material: Steel with Young's modulus E = 210 GPa and Poisson's ratio μ = 0.3
- Application: Structural Health Monitoring for ocean engineering (ship hulls, submarines), civil engineering (bridges, wind turbines), and aerospace engineering (aircraft wings)
- Geometry: Cylindrical with radius r, length L, and wall thickness t; Example 1: L = 300 mm, r = 50 mm, t = 1 mm; Example 3: L = 5 m, r = 1 m, t = 20 mm
- Global coordinate system X, Y, Z with local coordinate system x (longitudinal, 0 to L), θ (angular, 0 to 2π), and z (normal, -t/2 to t/2)
- Shell-type deformation modes include 12 in-plane shapes with varying circumferential wave patterns
- Additional deformation modes: axial extension (u=1), axisymmetric extension (w=1), and torsion (v=r)
- Cross-section constrained to behave as rigid-body with respect to translational degrees of freedom in some test cases
- Boundary conditions include fixed end (constrained translations and rotations) and free end with rigid cross-section constraint
- Loading conditions include end loads (FX = -5 kN, FY = 5 kN, FZ = 15 kN, MX = -1 kNm, MY = 2 kNm, MZ = 1 kNm), distributed line load (30 N/mm), and concentrated forces (F = 100 kN at multiple locations)
10_1016_j_tws_2023_110865.key_2:
- Fixed end with constrained translations and rotations
- Free end with rigid cross-section constraint (linked to reference point at center of gravity)
- Fully fixed ends (Example 3)
- Uniformly distributed force of 30 N/mm along the cylinder length (Example 2)
- Concentrated force of F = 100 kN applied at twelve locations (Example 3)
- End loads: FX = -5 kN, FY = 5 kN, FZ = 15 kN, MX = -1 kNm, MY = 2 kNm, MZ = 1 kNm (Example 1)
- Strain sensors placed on inner surface of cylinder (z = t/2)
- Static analysis with geometric nonlinearity in shell FE analysis (Abaqus)
- iFEM/GBT formulation assumes geometrically and materially linear behavior
- Simulated measured strains extracted from shell FE analysis at sensor locations
- Cross-section constrained to behave as rigid-body with respect to translational degrees of freedom
- Symmetry planes utilized in some analyses (reduced model for Example 2 and Example 3)

10_1016_j_tws_2023_110865.key_3:
- Physics solved: Shape sensing of thin-walled cylinders using inverse Finite Element Method combined with Generalized Beam Theory (iFEM/GBT); reconstruction of displacement fields based on measured strains; minimization of differences between theoretical and measured strains
- Target outputs: Total displacement magnitude Ut = √(U² + V² + W²); maximum relative error in cross-section with maximum displacements; Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) values; modal participation factors; reconstructed displacement field (Uinv)
- Optimization goal: Minimize number of strain sensors while maintaining accuracy (maximum relative error < 1% and 1-MAC < 0.1%); identify optimal sensor placement locations; select only relevant deformation modes (sum of participations > 99%); achieve significant reduction in required strain rosettes compared to inverse shell finite elements (e.g., 66 rosettes vs. 320 for equivalent accuracy)
10_1016_j_tws_2023_110865.key_4:
- Geometric constraint: Method applicable only to thin-walled cylinders where Kirchhoff's thin plate assumption holds
- Geometric constraint: Shell-type deformation modes cannot capture membrane shear effect, leading to underestimation of maximum displacements for short members (cylinder diameter and length having same order of magnitude)
- Performance constraint: iFEM/GBT assumes geometrically and materially linear behavior (no geometric nonlinearity)
- Performance constraint: Relevant deformation modes must have sum of participations > 99% for accurate reconstruction
- Performance constraint: Maximum relative error tolerance set to 1% (tolU = 1%)
- Performance constraint: 1-MAC tolerance set to 0.1% (tolMAC = 0.1%)
- Performance constraint: Axial extension mode must be included in analysis when axial loads are present
- Design space constraint: Current implementation limited to circular cross-sections (though extension to arbitrary cross-sections mentioned as future work)
- Process constraint: Requires strain sensors to be placed at specific optimized locations determined by iterative procedure
- Process constraint: Requires modal identification from shell FE analysis before applying iFEM/GBT
- Performance constraint: Existing inverse beam/frame finite elements cannot describe cross-sectional distortions of thin-walled members
- Design constraint: Displacement field must be representable as superposition of orthogonal deformation modes
- Process constraint: Sensor placement must avoid linear dependency in the system of equations for modal identification
