10_1016_j_physb_2025_417195.key_1:
- Identity & Domain: Indium Nitride (InN) nanosheets under tension, analyzed using spring-based finite element method for size-dependent nonlinear mechanical behavior
- Material / Medium: Hexagonal InN monolayer; thickness t = 0.32 nm; III-V nitride semiconductor; modeled using Stillinger-Weber potential with parameters: A = 2.476875 nN nm, B = 0.699, σ = 0.1879 nm, b = 1.8, λ = 5.919947 nN nm, γ = 1.2, k = 0.5, equilibrium angle θ₀ = 2π/3, bond length r₀ = 0.2156 nm
- Application & Importance: Advanced optoelectronic devices including biosensors and laser diodes; high-performance applications requiring structural integrity at sub-micrometer scale; overcoming experimental characterization challenges at nanoscale; mechanical behavior prediction for nanoscale engineering applications
- Geometry / Domain: 2D hexagonal monolayer nanosheets with dimensions Lₓ and Lᵧ ranging from 1-3 nm to ~24 nm; armchair orientation (x-direction) and zigzag orientation (y-direction); 97 different sized models analyzed; periodic boundary conditions not used; one edge fully constrained while opposite edge subjected to uniform axial displacement
10_1016_j_physb_2025_417195.key_2:
- Boundaries & Constraints: One edge fully constrained (all translational DoFs fixed); Opposite edge subjected to uniform axial displacement; Lateral edges unconstrained to allow free transverse deformation; Clamped-free loading scenario; No periodic boundary conditions implemented
- Loads / Excitations: Uniform axial displacement to induce uniaxial tension; Displacement-controlled loading protocol; Quasi-static loading scheme; Convergence criterion set to relative residual force norm of 10⁻⁶
- Interactions / Interfaces: Bond stretching and bond angle bending interactions modeled through translational spring-like elements; Two-noded straight spring-like 2D line finite elements connecting bonded In-N atoms; Stillinger-Weber potential used for two-body and three-body interatomic interactions
- Simulation Type: Nonlinear finite element analysis; Deterministic simulations; Incremental-iterative solution using Newton-Raphson algorithm; Quasi-static analysis; 2D plane stress analysis; Molecular mechanics based finite element method; 2D InN nanosheet modeled as nanoplate with thickness t = 0.32 nm
10_1016_j_physb_2025_417195.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Nonlinear elastic and plastic deformation of InN nanosheets under uniaxial tension; Bond stretching and bond angle bending mechanics; Size-dependent mechanical behavior at nanoscale; Anisotropic stress-strain response in hexagonal lattice structures
- Target Outputs (Metrics): Young's modulus (Eₓ, Eᵧ); Ultimate tensile strength (σᵤₓ, σᵤᵧ); Strain at ultimate strength (εᵤₓ, εᵤᵧ); Stress-strain curves; Size-dependent mechanical properties as functions of Lₓ and Lᵧ; Semi-empirical expression coefficients for mechanical property prediction
- Optimization Goal: Development of a predictive framework for size-dependent mechanical behavior; Rapid estimation of mechanical properties as function of structural dimensions; Understanding anisotropic mechanical response in different crystallographic orientations (armchair vs. zigzag); Validation of spring-based FEM against DFT and MD results for InN nanostructures
10_1016_j_physb_2025_417195.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: Nanosheet dimensions Lₓ and Lᵧ range from 1-3 nm to ~24 nm; Analysis limited to monolayer InN structures only; 97 different 2D structures analyzed; Principal crystallographic orientations restricted to armchair (x-direction) and zigzag (y-direction); Fixed nanoplate thickness t = 0.32 nm for all models; Maximum model size of Lₓ = 23.716 nm and Lᵧ = 23.562 nm
- Performance/Physics Limits: Defect-free ideal structure assumption; Athermal conditions with no thermal fluctuations; Stillinger-Weber potential parameters specific to InN (A = 2.476875 nN nm, B = 0.699, σ = 0.1879 nm, b = 1.8, λ = 5.919947 nN nm, γ = 1.2, k = 0.5, θ₀ = 2π/3, r₀ = 0.2156 nm); Displacement-controlled loading with convergence criterion of relative residual force norm 10⁻⁶; Quasi-static analysis with no dynamic effects; Assumption of linear elastic behavior followed by sharp transition at ultimate stress
- Process/Manufacturing: Experimental validation challenges due to chemical instability and lattice mismatch of InN nanosheets; Method limited to monolayer structures with non-trivial extension to multilayered systems; Semi-empirical expression specific to InN requiring recalibration for other III-V nitrides; Computational framework based on Stillinger-Weber potential with no incorporation of thermal effects or structural imperfections; No consideration of edge roughness, vacancies, or grain boundaries in the model

10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_638_183.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Bone mechanical adaptation simulation using finite element method to model bone remodeling under mechanical loads
- **Material / Medium:** Bone tissue with initial apparent density of 1 g/cm³ (half of cortical bone maximum density), Young's modulus updated by E = 3790·ρ³ relation, minimum density set to 0.01 g (later increased to 0.1 g to prevent excessive deformations)
- **Application & Importance:** Comparative analysis of three bone remodeling mathematical models (Nijmegen, cellular accommodation, Manchester quadric term) to understand differences in predicted density distributions under mechanical loading
- **Geometry / Domain:** 2D rectangular test geometry with L = 50 mm, H = 20 mm, meshed with eight-noded quadrilaterals of 1 mm side length; horizontal beam supported at both ends with central distributed load (p·l_b = 1000 N)
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_638_183.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Fixed support at left end; roller support at right end; 2D rectangular domain with L = 50 mm, H = 20 mm; meshed with eight-noded quadrilaterals of 1 mm side length
- **Loads / Excitations:** Central distributed load with p·l_b = 1000 N; higher load case with p·l_p = 3000 N; reference stimulus S₀ = 0.25 [(N·cm³)/(mm²·g)]; remodeling rate constant B = 1 [(g·cm⁻³)²·(MPa·time)⁻¹]; quadric term constant D = 60 [(g·cm⁻³)³·MPa⁻²·time⁻¹]; cellular accommodation time Tₐ = 25 iterations; initial apparent density = 1 g/cm³; minimum density set to 0.01 g (increased to 0.1 g for QT model)
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Young's modulus updated by E = 3790·ρ³ relation; MATLAB-ANSYS coupling for remodeling algorithm; load application on finite elements where remodeling is active
- **Simulation Type:** 2D finite element simulation; transient simulation with forward Euler integration scheme; integration step h = 1; iteration-based time stepping; 1 mm side length quadrilateral elements
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_638_183.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Bone remodeling process (adaptation of bone density distribution to mechanical loads); strain energy density distribution; cellular accommodation response; quadric term effects on density accumulation at high loads
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Apparent density distribution; total bone mass convergence; comparative density patterns across different remodeling models; iteration-based evolution of density distributions (at iterations 10, 20, 36, 57, 74, 111, 148, 275); density accumulation/resorption patterns at load application points
- **Optimization Goal:** Comparative analysis of three mathematical bone remodeling models (Nijmegen, cellular accommodation, Manchester quadric term) to identify differences in predicted density distributions; evaluation of model performance under different load conditions (1000 N and 3000 N); assessment of model applicability for different simulation purposes and structural scales
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_638_183.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Rectangular test geometry with fixed dimensions L = 50 mm and H = 20 mm; mesh restricted to eight-noded quadrilaterals with 1 mm side length; minimum density threshold set to 0.01 g (increased to 0.1 g for QT model simulations)
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Young's modulus constrained by E = 3790·ρ³ relation; initial apparent density limited to 1 g/cm³ (50% of cortical bone maximum); reference stimulus S₀ = 0.25 [(N·cm³)/(mm²·g)]; remodeling rate constant B = 1 [(g·cm⁻³)²·(MPa·time)⁻¹]; quadric term constant D = 60 [(g·cm⁻³)³·MPa⁻²·time⁻¹]; cellular accommodation time Tₐ = 25 iterations; load magnitudes restricted to p·l_b = 1000 N and p·l_p = 3000 N cases

10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_827_288.key_1:
• Subject of analysis: Cylinder liners of an eight-cylinder V-type four-stroke turbocharged internal combustion engine
• Material composition: Generic steel for liners and bolts; generic aluminium for engine head and block; generic steel for connecting rod and piston pin; generic aluminium for piston
• Functional requirements: Sealing of combustion pressure gas; resistance to piston thrust forces; fatigue durability assessment
• Geometry characteristics: Cylindrical structure with interference fit areas at top and bottom; simply supported beam configuration between interference fits; four combustion chambers per bank as shown in Fig. 1(a); critical regions at upper liner portion corresponding to piston/liner interface
• Analysis purpose: Fatigue behavior prediction using multiaxial Dang Van criterion; evaluation of stress-strain state under thermal and mechanical loads; identification of critical areas with minimum safety factor
• Operating conditions: Maximum and minimum combustion gas pressures; cyclic piston thrust forces; thermal boundary conditions averaged over engine cycle
• Critical locations: Upper liner portion at piston/liner interface during absolute maximum bending stress load-case; normalized von Mises stress distribution shows correspondence between complete and simplified models
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_827_288.key_2:
• Boundary constraints: Symmetry plane; bolt tightening; contact with lower engine block; simply supported beam configuration between interference fit areas

10_1016_j_matdes_2025_113908.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Thermally-activated twisted and coiled polymer actuators (TATCPAs) for soft robotics and smart textiles applications
- **Material / Medium:** Ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene fishing line; 1-9 ply configurations; spring index of 4.3 for all samples; thermally responsive material with actuation triggered by temperature changes
- **Application & Importance:** Optimization of actuation strain (ε = (lh - l0)/l0) for artificial muscle applications; achieving high mechanical actuation in smart textiles and soft robotics; expansionary movement under heating for heterochiral actuators
- **Geometry / Domain:** Heterochiral structure with Z-direction twisting and S-direction coiling; helical/coiled geometry that expands under heat; identical internal diameter across all samples due to same mandrel usage; cross-sectional areas maintained similar across 1-9 ply configurations; discrete design space with 11 stress values from 1-10 MPa for both twist and coil stresses
10_1016_j_matdes_2025_113908.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Spring index maintained at 4.3 across all samples
  - Thermosetting temperature of 110°C for 150 minutes
  - Maximum heating temperature limit of 140°C to prevent thermal degradation
  - Identical internal diameter for all samples due to same mandrel usage
  - Cross-sectional areas kept similar across different ply counts
  - Samples secured horizontally with mercerized cotton sewing thread that does not significantly restrict movement

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Applied twisting stress: 11 discrete values from 1 to 10 MPa
  - Applied coiling stress: 11 discrete values from 1 to 10 MPa
  - Ply number: 1-9 discrete values
  - Infrared heating at 1500 W from above sample
  - Weights placed on sled to control applied stress during fabrication
  - Three actuation cycles per sample with first cycle for training and average of last two cycles for measurement

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Z-direction twisting followed by S-direction coiling around mandrel
  - Line manually tied to motor head and mandrel for twisting process
  - Coiled line secured with locking device before thermosetting
  - Ice water container placed behind samples to create temperature contrast for thermal imaging
  - Friction-based mechanism used for twisting and coiling (applied stresses not equal to internal sample stresses)

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Discrete Bayesian optimization with discretized Gaussian process surrogate model
  - 3D design space (ply number, twist stress, coil stress) with 1089 total possible combinations
  - Iterative process with 16 total iterations
  - Batch acquisitions using Kriging Believer method (4 samples per iteration)
  - Exploration-modified lower confidence bound (eLCB) acquisition function
10_1016_j_matdes_2025_113908.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Thermal actuation of twisted and coiled polymer structures
  - Reversible shape-memory effect triggered by temperature changes
  - Strain development in heterochiral actuator configurations due to thermal expansion
  - Internal stress distribution from twisting and coiling processes

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Actuation strain (ε = (lh - l0)/l0), where l0 is initial length and lh is maximum length after heating
  - Maximum obtained actuation value of 1.25 ± 0.34 (2 standard deviations)
  - Temperature distribution during actuation (measured up to 140°C)
  - Actuation strain as function of ply number, twist stress, and coil stress

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Maximize actuation strain of thermally-activated polymer actuators
  - Achieve highest possible expansionary movement under thermal stimulation
  - Identify optimal processing conditions (ply number, twist stress, coil stress) for maximum strain response
  - Reach maximum actuation with minimal experimental samples (62 unique combinations out of 1089 possible)
10_1016_j_matdes_2025_113908.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - 3D design space with 1089 total points (9 ply numbers × 11 twist stress values × 11 coil stress values)
  - Ply number constrained to discrete values 1-9
  - Twist stress constrained to 11 discrete values from 1-10 MPa
  - Coil stress constrained to 11 discrete values from 1-10 MPa
  - Spring index fixed at approximately 4.3 for all samples
  - Identical internal diameter maintained across all samples through use of same mandrel
  - Cross-sectional areas kept similar across different ply configurations

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Maximum heating temperature capped at 140°C to prevent thermal degradation
  - Actuation strain defined as ε = (lh - l0)/l0 where l0 is initial length and lh is maximum length after heating
  - Stress limits set to maximum permissible levels without breaking the sample
  - Maximum actuation strain achieved was 1.25 ± 0.34 (2 standard deviations)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Thermosetting performed at 110°C for 150 minutes
  - Twisting performed at 400 rpm until onset of over-twisting
  - Discrete weights pre-determined for practical implementation (not continuous values)
  - Friction-based twisting/coiling mechanism (applied stresses not equal to internal sample stresses)
  - Maximum weights determined beforehand to prevent sample snapping during fabrication
  - 9-ply samples with high stresses faced difficulty maintaining tension before curing
  - Multi-ply samples risked over-twisting due to length variations between individual plies
  - Commercial ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene fishing line used as base material
  - Experimental processing conditions inherently discrete rather than continuous
  - Samples secured with mercerized cotton sewing thread that does not significantly restrict movement during testing

10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_747_36.key_1:

- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - Square panel with side length L=H=3 m and thickness 250 mm
  - Central rectangular opening with dimensions width Lw=0.75 m and height Hw=1.5 m
  - Lower edge fully constrained (fixed boundary condition)
  - Upper edge subjected to uniform vertical pressure σyy and uniform shear stress σxy
  - Two load cases analyzed: Case A (σyy=0.10 MPa, σxy=0.020 MPa) and Case B (σyy=0.025 MPa, σxy=0.013 MPa)
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_747_36.key_2:

  - Lower edge fully fixed (constrained boundary with zero displacement)
  - Upper edge free boundary with prescribed tractions
  - Side edges free (no constraints explicitly mentioned)
  - Settlements u0 prescribed over constrained boundary Γu
  - Tractions t0 prescribed over free boundary Γt

  - Uniform vertical pressure σyy on upper edge: 0.10 MPa (75 kN resultant) for Case A; 0.025 MPa (18.75 kN resultant) for Case B
  - Uniform shear stress σxy on upper edge: 0.020 MPa (15 kN resultant) for Case A; 0.013 MPa (10 kN resultant) for Case B

  - Same discretization used for both underlying masonry body and reinforcing layer
  - Four-node plane elements sharing the same degrees of freedom for both materials

  - Linear elastic with nonlinear constraints (no-tension for masonry, no-compression for reinforcement)
  - Finite element method with regular mesh of bi-linear square elements
  - Topology optimization using volume constrained minimum compliance formulation

10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_747_36.key_3:

  - Structural mechanics of no-tension masonry walls with fiber reinforcement under in-plane loading

- **Geometry / Domain:** First case: square blank dimensions 1 mm × 1 mm × 0.8 mm with 100 N normal force applied; Second case: circular blank with Φ100 mm diameter, 2.5 mm initial thickness; die with Φ50 mm diameter, 10 mm depth, and R5 corner radius; edge constraints prevent material flow into deformation area; 2382 nodes and 2305 shell elements used in simulation

- **Loads / Excitations:** 100 N normal force applied by rigid bodies; stretching 0.3 in x and y directions; hydraulic pressure applied from 0.0 MPa to 80.0 MPa proportionally; pressure P applied to blank; force F applied to blank

10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_639_435.key_3:

- **Optimization Goal:** Improve accuracy of thickness prediction compared to traditional shell elements while maintaining computational efficiency; achieve results closer to solid element simulations without significantly increasing computation time; accurately predict material behavior under large applied pressure (up to 80.0 MPa) where normal stress in thickness direction significantly affects formability

10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_770_419.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Highly stressed steel castings parts for mechanical engineering, specifically case distribution and valves with complex geometry.
- **Material / Medium:** Low-alloy cast steel; yield strength 360 MPa for steel with 0.45% C; elastic modulus 200-210 GPa for low shrinkage porosity (<3%); shrinkage porosity affects mechanical properties with 5-10% porosity causing 30% reduction in short-term indicators and 50% reduction in fracture toughness.
- **Application & Importance:** Assessment of quality and service life calculation for cast details; shrinkage porosity directly impacts structural strength and fatigue resistance; heterogeneity in mechanical properties leads to 20-30% increase in extreme stress when 5-10%.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Complex geometry with curved crossings at junction flange design; wall thickness >50 mm associated with 5-10% shrinkage porosity; high-stress areas identified at curved crossings reaching 140 MPa; wall stress up to 90 MPa.
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_770_419.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Elastic modulus 210 GPa for uniform elastic properties; elastic modulus 200-210 GPa for shrinkage porosity <3%; wall stress up to 90 MPa; stress intensity values reaching up to 140 MPa in curved crossings; yield strength 360 MPa for steel with 0.45% C; shrinkage porosity thresholds: <3% (no significant change), 5-10% (significant reduction), >15% (serious decline).
- **Loads / Excitations:** None explicitly stated.
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Interaction between casting and mold during solidification; heterogeneity of mechanical properties interacting with stress-strain state.
- **Simulation Type:** FEM analysis of stress-strain state; FEM analysis of heterogeneity of mechanical properties; stress intensity used as parameter for risk evaluation.
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_770_419.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Stress-strain state distribution; heterogeneity of mechanical properties due to shrinkage porosity; fatigue resistance; solidification process effects on mechanical property formation.
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Stress intensity (up to 140 MPa in curved crossings); elastic modulus (200-210 GPa for <3% porosity, reduced at higher porosity); shrinkage porosity volume percentage; fracture toughness (K_IC); short-term mechanical indicators (σ, δ); wall stress (up to 90 MPa).
- **Optimization Goal:** Directed formation of high mechanical properties in high-stress local areas (e.g., curved crossings) by minimizing shrinkage porosity to increase technical resource (service life) of cast steel parts.
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_770_419.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Wall thickness >50 mm corresponds to 5-10% shrinkage porosity; curved crossings at junction flange design identified as high-stress regions.
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Shrinkage porosity must not exceed 3% to maintain elastic modulus at 200-210 GPa; 5-10% porosity causes 30% reduction in short-term mechanical indicators and 50% reduction in fracture toughness; porosity >15% leads to rejection due to critical mechanical property degradation.
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Feeding conditions must limit shrinkage porosity to <3% for acceptable mechanical properties; solidification must be directionally controlled to minimize porosity in high-stress areas; rejection of castings with >15% shrinkage porosity per technical requirements.

- **Identity & Domain:** Small low-speed wind tunnel contraction section; comparison of five different contraction curve designs.

- **Geometry / Domain:** Square cross-section contraction with inlet side B = 3000 mm, outlet side b = 1000 mm, contraction length L = 3000 mm (3:1 contraction ratio).
- **Contraction curves analyzed:** Witozinsky, Batchelor-Shaw, 3-power curve (Xm=0.5), improved 3-power curve (Xm=0.5), 5-power curve (Xm=0.5, n=7).

- **Velocity unevenness metric:** Defined as β = √[Σ(ui - U)² / (n - 1)], where ui is local velocity and U is mean velocity.

- **Optimal design criteria:** 5-power curve preferred for low turbulence and energy efficiency; improved 3-power curve provides better flow uniformity than Witozinsky/Batchelor-Shaw.

10_1016_j_ymssp_2022_109167.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Shell structures with holes for displacement field reconstruction using inverse Finite Element Method (iFEM) in structural health monitoring applications
- **Material / Medium:** Aluminum alloy (E = 70,000 MPa, ν = 0.3) with thickness values of 2 mm, 3 mm, and 5 mm across different case studies
- **Application & Importance:** Structural health monitoring of aircraft fuselages and similar structures where holes (for rivets/bolts) create stress concentration points that can lead to crack nucleation; enables displacement field computation with sparse sensor networks
- **Geometry / Domain:** Four primary configurations analyzed: (1) infinite plate (300×200 mm) with centered 10 mm diameter hole, (2) strip (50 mm width) with centered 20 mm diameter hole (λ = a/b = 0.4), (3) plate with hole near edge (300×200 mm, 10 mm diameter hole 20 mm from edge), and (4) strip (350 mm length, 50 mm width) with three equally spaced 20 mm diameter holes; hole influence region defined as 8× hole radius; validity region for physics-based pre-extrapolation varies (coincident with influence region for infinite plate, limited to strip width for holed strip)
10_1016_j_ymssp_2022_109167.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Ux = Uz = 0 (fixed in X and Z directions)
  - θx = θy = θz = 0 (all rotational degrees of freedom constrained)
  - Uy = 0 (fixed in Y direction at specific locations)
  - Left side grounded/clamped for plate and strip models
  - Discrete strain gauge rosettes on both top and bottom surfaces of shell structures
  - Mesh discretization with 11,020 to 21,896 elements for different case studies

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Tension distributed load of 100 N/mm (infinite plate case)
  - Tension distributed load of 200 N/mm (strip in tension case)
  - Normal distributed load q_n = 150 N/mm (multiple holes case)
  - Transverse distributed load q_t = 0.05 N/mm (multiple holes case)
  - Distributed load q = 100 N/mm (plate with hole near edge case)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Strain gauge rosettes on both top and bottom surfaces measuring ε⁺ and ε⁻ strain fields
  - Membrane and bending strain components computed from surface measurements
  - 4 strain gauge rosettes per side (top and bottom) in reduced sensor network configurations
  - Physical sensor network located 10-20 mm from structural edges

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Static analysis (no time-dependent effects mentioned)
  - 3D shell structures with thickness 2h
  - Direct FEM using S8R elements with quadratic shape functions
  - iFEM using iQS4 inverse elements
  - Plane-stress condition assumed for stress-strain calculations
  - Same mesh used for both direct FEM and iFEM models for accurate node-to-node comparison
10_1016_j_ymssp_2022_109167.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Displacement field reconstruction of shell structures with holes using inverse Finite Element Method (iFEM) based on strain measurements; strain field pre-extrapolation incorporating physics-based knowledge of stress concentration near discontinuities

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Displacement field magnitude (U) in mm
  - Strain field components (εₓₓ, εᵧᵧ, γₓᵧ) in microstrain (με)
  - Percentage error on displacement field magnitude (U_err) normalized to maximum FEM displacement
  - Percentage error on strain field (ε_err) normalized to maximum FEM strain
  - Maximum displacement error values (e.g., 0.68%, 3.84%, 12.07%)
  - Far-field displacement error values (e.g., 0.47%, 7.45%, 1.23%)
  - Strain field reconstruction accuracy near holes

- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize displacement field error near structural discontinuities (holes) using sparse sensor networks by incorporating physics-based strain pre-extrapolation, reducing errors from data-driven methods (e.g., from 12.07% to 4.83% maximum error for strip with hole) while approaching ideal case accuracy where all elements are covered by sensors (0.50% error)
10_1016_j_ymssp_2022_109167.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Ratio constraint λ = a/b ≤ 0.5 for strip with hole in tension (a = hole radius, b = semi-strip width)
  - Physics-based pre-extrapolation validity region limited to r ≤ b for strip in tension (r = radial distance from hole center)
  - Hole influence region defined as 8 times the hole radius for infinite plate cases
  - Sensor placement constrained to be 10-20 mm from structural edges in all case studies
  - Maximum of 4 strain gauge rosettes per side (top/bottom) used in reduced sensor network configurations

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Howlard analytical solution only valid for 0.1 ≤ λ ≤ 0.5 (for strip with hole in tension)
  - For λ < 0.1, Kirsch solution for infinite plate can be reasonably adopted
  - Physics-based pre-extrapolation requires knowledge of Poisson ratio (assumed ν = 0.3 for aluminum)
  - Plane-stress condition assumed for stress-strain calculations
  - Analytical solutions provide correct strain field only in specific regions (e.g., validity region ≠ influence region for strip in tension)
  - Physics-based pre-extrapolation cannot provide exact solution for multiple holes in series due to unaccounted collaborative effects

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Sensors cannot be applied to entire structure due to hardware limitations, economic reasons, and physical installation constraints
  - Strain gauge rosettes must be placed on both top and bottom surfaces to capture full 2D strain tensor
  - Data-driven pre-extrapolation (bi-linear) insufficient for high strain gradient regions near discontinuities
  - Physics-based pre-extrapolation requires knowledge of discontinuity characteristics (hole size and position)
  - Weighting coefficients must be adjusted (e.g., increased to 10⁻²) in physics-based region when validity region ≠ influence region

- **Loads / Excitations:** Internal source of manufacturing errors represented by function E in Poisson equation; Deviations of measured points (other than boundary points) considered as internal source of errors dominating pattern of geometric deviations
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Parametric space defined by u, v (parameters to define substitute geometry) and d (spatial axis for geometric deviations); Skin model covers ideal substitute geometry to produce actual manufactured surface; Transferred points to parametric space called "sites" with triple coordinates (u, v, d)

- **Material / Medium:** Carbon Fiber-Reinforced Plastics (CFRP); bending strength 289 MPa; bending modulus 31.6 GPa; test specimen dimensions length l=140mm, breath b=15mm, thickness t=3.0mm; 12 ply laminate; anisotropic material with complex laminate structure
- **Application & Importance:** Achieve weight reduction while maintaining structural integrity; original wooden structure was "too heavy and the carrying is difficult"; establish new design technique for high design quality products with lightness and high strength; address displacement and torsional rigidity issues
- **Geometry / Domain:** Four straight-line panels (backrest, seat, chair support, floor support); fold structure model with zigzag profile; three comparative structural models (rib structure, hollow structure, fold structure); load condition 580N to seat and 100N to backrest simulating 60kg person; displacement measurement at rear seat central point
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_749_231.key_2:

  - Three-point bending test: Penetrator radius 5 mm, Support point radius 2 mm, Distance between support points 100 mm
  - Displacement measurement point at rear seat central position
  - Fixed support points in bending test setup as shown in Figure 9
  - 12 ply laminate configuration for test specimens
  - Boundary condition for chair analysis: load applied to seat and backrest surfaces

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Static load condition: 580 N applied to seat and 100 N applied to backrest (simulating 60 kg person)
  - Bending test rate: 5 mm/min
  - Load increased until delaminating fracture occurred with plosive sound

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Interlayer shear observed at fracture section of test pieces
  - Compression destruction mechanism between laminate layers
  - Wooden mold interface with CFRP sheet during manufacturing

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Structural analysis comparing analytical displacement with experimental measurements
  - Stress distribution analysis shown in Figure 7
  - Linear elastic analysis as evidenced by proportional load-displacement relationship in Figure 8
  - Comparative analysis of three structural models: Rib structure, Hollow structure, and Fold structure
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_749_231.key_3:

  - Stress distribution in CFRP structures
  - Displacement behavior under bending loads
  - Interlayer shear effects in laminate structures
  - Torsional rigidity characteristics of folded composite structures

10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_681_214.key_3:

- **Loads / Excitations:** Load Case 1 (partial loading on girders 2# and 3#); Load Case 2 (approximately symmetrical loading on girders 2# and 3#); Loading truck configurations with 70kN, 140kN, and 140kN loads at 4.35m and 1.4m spacing; Mid-span vertical displacement measurements used as input for model updating.

10_1016_j_powtec_2019_01_086.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Granular material segregation in rotating drums and conical hoppers; binary mixtures of granular materials; shear-driven percolation segregation; transient two-dimensional multi-scale modeling

- **Application & Importance:** Prediction of percolation segregation magnitude and rate; analysis of granular material processing in chemical, food, and pharmaceutical industries; prevention of heterogeneous powder blends that cause processing inconsistencies and product quality issues; design and management of unit operations for better product quality

- **Geometry / Domain:** Rotating drum with 150 mm diameter; 10 mm width for computational efficiency; rotational speed 0.75 rad/s (7.2 rpm); conical hoppers with 15° and 55° angles; 55° hopper: Ø125 mm top diameter, 125 mm height, 35 mm cone height, Ø25 mm outlet; 15° hopper: Ø100 mm top diameter, 50 mm height, 165 mm cone height, Ø13 mm outlet; Eulerian-Lagrangian approach with EC3D8R elements; half-geometry modeling with symmetry boundary conditions; initial fill height 105 mm for 55° hopper and 210 mm for 15° hopper

- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Symmetry boundary condition on front side of Eulerian mesh for hopper simulations; free-flow Eulerian boundary condition at hopper outlet after opening; both front and back sides of Eulerian mesh treated as symmetry planes for rotating drum; axisymmetric boundary condition not used due to numerical errors along axis; rigid shell elements for hopper walls fixed in all degrees of freedom; material concentration threshold set between 0 and 1 to prevent numerical errors; segregation and diffusion fluxes set to zero on boundary to ensure mass conservation

- **Loads / Excitations:** Gravity of 9.8 m/s² directed in negative y-direction; rotational speed of 0.75 rad/s (7.2 rpm) for rotating drum; gradual gravity increase to fill drum before rotation; hopper outlet initially closed then opened after material settles

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Coupled Eulerian-Lagrangian (CEL) approach for Eulerian-Lagrangian element interactions; penalty method to prevent material penetration and ensure mass conservation; rounded corners (10 mm radius) to prevent severe penetration; contact between granular material and hopper walls with specified wall friction coefficient (0.31 for hoppers, 0.324 for rotating drum); material outflow at hopper outlet; Eulerian Volume Fraction (EVF) used to determine material volume within elements

- **Simulation Type:** Transient three-dimensional FEM simulations; two-dimensional advection-diffusion-segregation (ADS) equation model; explicit time integration in Abaqus/Explicit; one-way coupled model (bulk flow field unaffected by local particle species concentration); second-order Taylor Lax-Wendroff finite difference scheme for ADS equation; 500,000 elements for rotating drum simulation and 176,000 elements for hopper simulations
10_1016_j_powtec_2019_01_086.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Shear-driven percolation segregation in dense, sheared granular flows; gravity-driven segregation; binary mixture segregation of granular materials; advection-diffusion-segregation phenomena; bulk-level granular velocity field; particle-level diffusion and segregation correlations

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Small particle concentration profiles as function of dimensionless distance (δ/R₀); normalized fines mass fraction (xᵢ/x_f) versus fractional mass discharged (M/M_total); steady-state concentration distributions; surface velocity in streamwise direction; segregation patterns at different discharge stages; averaged absolute differences between experimental and model predictions; small particle concentration spatial and temporal evolution

- **Optimization Goal:** Quantitative prediction accuracy matching DEM and experimental segregation data; reproduction of experimentally-observed normalized mass fraction of fines; validation of multi-scale model against published experimental results for cohesionless granular materials; accurate prediction of segregation patterns in rotating drums and conical hoppers with different geometries
10_1016_j_powtec_2019_01_086.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Rotating drum width limited to 10 mm for computational efficiency; only half-geometry modeled for hopper simulations to save computational time; axisymmetric boundary condition cannot be applied due to numerical errors along axisymmetric axis; mesh size constrained to 500,000 elements for rotating drum and 176,000 elements for hopper simulations

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Minimum dilation angle of 0.1° required in Abaqus for Mohr-Coulomb model; material concentration constrained to remain between 0 and 1; model does not accurately describe final stage of discharge process due to material attaching to wall; one-way coupled model (bulk flow field unaffected by local particle species concentration); cannot predict shear band formation without considering shear localization; Drucker-Prager model mathematically ill-posed; μ(I) model ill-posed at high and low inertial numbers; diffusion coefficient simplified to constant value despite being anisotropic tensor quantity

- **Material / Medium:** Protection glass layer (E-modulus 83 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.23, thermal expansion coefficient 6.75×10⁻⁶/°C RT-600°C); platinum tracks (12μm thick, E-modulus 153 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.38, thermal expansion coefficient 9.52×10⁻⁶/°C RT-600°C); alumina substrate (E-modulus 340 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.23, thermal expansion coefficient 7.30×10⁻⁶/°C RT-600°C); adhesion particles mixed in platinum matrix
- **Application & Importance:** Monitoring vehicle emission control system performance; addressing aggressive working environment with extreme temperatures (to 900°C) and rapid temperature changes (400°C/sec); analyzing thermal expansion mismatch between layers; preventing crack propagation in protective glass layer; improving mechanical reliability of sensor design
- **Geometry / Domain:** Three-layer structure (protection layer, platinum tracks, alumina substrate); symmetric 2D model about sensor chip centerline; discontinuous bonding areas representing adhesion particles at track-substrate interface; four stress concentration areas with two located next to edge on each side of track; 12μm thick platinum tracks screen printed on substrate; protective glass layer deposited over platinum tracks
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_644_96.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Symmetric analysis about sensor chip centerline; discontinuous bonding areas representing adhesion particles at track-substrate interface; cohesive zone modeling for de-bonding analysis; contact analysis at interfaces between layers
- **Loads / Excitations:** Manufacturing thermal cycle: heated to 750°C then cooled to 25°C; operational thermal cycle: heated to desired temperature then cooled to 25°C; working environment: extreme temperatures up to 900°C; rapid temperature changes of 400°C/sec; thermal shock test with accelerated and extreme thermal loading
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Contact between protection glass layer, platinum tracks, and alumina substrate; track-substrate bonding interface with discontinuous adhesion particles; thermal expansion mismatch between layers; four stress concentration areas with two located next to edge on each side of track
- **Simulation Type:** 2D FEA model using ANSYS mechanics package; non-linear material properties to simulate platinum plastic deformation; transient thermal analysis with sequential heating/cooling cycles; validated by laboratory thermal shock test
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_644_96.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Thermal stress distribution; plastic deformation of platinum tracks; stress concentration due to thermal expansion mismatch between layers
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Von Mises stress; first principle stress distribution; stress concentration areas; stress levels at track-substrate bonding interface; plastic strain in platinum tracks; crack positions in protection glass layer; stress curve profiles along track width
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize thermal expansion mismatch between sensor chip layers; reduce stress at track-substrate bonding interface; prevent crack propagation in protection glass layer; balance protection layer thickness to mitigate stress while maintaining defect resistance; optimize adhesion particle volume in platinum tracks to switch stress from tensile to compressive
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_644_96.key_4:

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Stress must not exceed platinum yield strength at 20°C and 500°C; thermal expansion mismatch between layers must be minimized to prevent stress generation; crack formation in protection glass layer must be avoided as it accelerates track buckling; operational temperature must not exceed 900°C
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Manufacturing process requires thermal cycle: heating to 750°C followed by cooling to 25°C; adhesion particle volume in platinum tracks has upper limit to prevent excessive compressive stress; platinum tracks must be screen printed on alumina substrate; residual stress from manufacturing must be incorporated in simulation through thermal cycling

10_1016_j_tws_2021_107926.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Full-flexible membrane spacecraft with no rigid supporting structure; hexagonal symmetry; six independent flexible beams supporting six flexible membranes; structural dynamic modeling under large deformation
- **Material / Medium:** Membranes: Young's modulus 1×10⁶ N/m², Poisson's ratio 0.2, density 1×10³ kg/m³, thickness 1 mm; Beams: stiffness 2×10⁵ N/m; Center particle: mass 1 kg
- **Application & Importance:** Required for control system design and spacecraft safety; addresses modern spacecraft utilizing flexible structures and payloads leading to non-rigid-body tendency and large deformation; solves structural motion of large deformation under concentrated forces, body forces and torques
- **Geometry / Domain:** Hexagonal symmetry; beam length 6 m; discretized into 216 triangular elements; time-domain response calculated for up to 9 s under gravity; concentrated forces tested at 10 N, 20 N, 30 N, and 50 N; torques tested at 10 Nm, 15 Nm, and 20 Nm
10_1016_j_tws_2021_107926.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Displacement constraint at connecting nodes on membranes; central body regarded as a particle; spacecraft assumed in static equilibrium without external force at time t₀; hexagonal symmetry with six flexible beams supporting six flexible membranes
- **Loads / Excitations:** Concentrated force on center (10 N, 30 N, 50 N, parallel to membrane normal at t₀); Concentrated force on membrane (10 N, 20 N, 30 N, parallel to membrane normal at t₀); Body force (constant gravity); Torque at center (10 Nm, 15 Nm, 20 Nm, perpendicular to initial membrane normal, equivalent to pair of opposite forces)
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Membranes discretized into 216 triangular nonlinear finite elements; support function and flexible motion of beams treated as displacement constraints for connecting nodes; no rigid supporting structure (full-flexible spacecraft)
- **Simulation Type:** Transient nonlinear analysis; 3D structural dynamics; explicit Newmark integration method; time-domain response calculated for 2.7s (force/torque cases) and 9s (gravity case); triangular element-based finite element method with area coordinate system
10_1016_j_tws_2021_107926.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Structural dynamics of full-flexible spacecraft under large deformation; nonlinear behavior of triangular finite elements including displacement, strain, and stress distributions; coupling between rigid-body motion and elastic deformation
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Time-domain displacement responses at specific intervals (e.g., t=0.3s to 2.7s for force/torque cases, 9s for gravity); deformation shapes and magnitude under concentrated forces (10–50 N), body forces (gravity), and torques (10–20 Nm); relative node displacements; comparison of deformation features with ABAQUS
- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve accurate structural dynamic modeling with reduced degrees of freedom while maintaining physical fidelity; enable efficient simulation of large deformation in full-flexible spacecraft where traditional hybrid coordinate methods fail due to lack of rigid bodies or small deformation assumptions
10_1016_j_tws_2021_107926.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Hexagonal symmetry with six flexible beams (length 6 m) supporting six flexible membranes; membrane thickness 1 mm; discretization into 216 triangular elements; spacecraft modeled without rigid supporting structure
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Traditional hybrid coordinate methods encounter divergence with large-range rotation and large deformation; maximum external forces tested: 50 N concentrated force on center/membrane; maximum torque tested: 20 Nm; time-domain response validated for up to 9 s under gravity; deformation magnitude increases with external input magnitude
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Accuracy and computation time both increase with number of elements; requires triangular element discretization before calculation; existing nonlinear FEM methods become difficult to implement due to high degrees of freedom of elements; method is a theoretical finite element approach requiring pre-calculation discretization into triangular elements

- **Material / Medium:** Structure concrete (Young's modulus 36,000 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.20, density 2,500 kg/m³, tensile strength 2.85 MPa, compressive strength 38.50 MPa); Foundation concrete (Young's modulus 32,500 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.20, density 2,500 kg/m³, tensile strength 2.39 MPa, compressive strength 26.80 MPa); Steel liner (Young's modulus 206,000 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.30, density 7,850 kg/m³, yield strength 265 MPa); Steel bar layer (Young's modulus 195,000 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.30, density 7,850 kg/m³, yield strength 500 MPa)
- **Application & Importance:** Seismic response reduction of nuclear power plants during safe-shutdown earthquake (SSE) loadings; minimizing relative displacement and absolute acceleration of internal containment; preventing damage to pipelines and equipment; addressing excessive relative displacement issues in base isolation systems
- **Geometry / Domain:** Total height 87.9 m (inner containment height 84.6 m); base diameter 27.4 m (inner diameter 24.7 m); 121 base-isolation bearings uniformly arranged under foundation with total horizontal stiffness 1.23×10⁶ kN/m and damping coefficient 6.62×10⁴ kN·s/m; TIDs installed between outer and inner containments with 1,800 mm spacing and maximum stroke capacity ±400 mm; base isolation target period 1.70 s; inner structure mass 8.96×10⁴ ton
10_1016_j_soildyn_2025_109438.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Translational degrees of freedom in Z directions of isolation bearings constrained; horizontal stiffness k_h in X and Y directions assigned; TID devices installed with 1800 mm spacing between inner and outer containments; maximum stroke capacity of TIDs set to ±400 mm; 121 base-isolation bearings uniformly arranged under foundation; outer structure fixed to ground in theoretical models; inner structure elevated by 0.30 m using isolation bearings
- **Loads / Excitations:** Safe-shutdown earthquake (SSE) loading; peak ground acceleration (PGA) adjusted to 0.30 g for analysis; PGA of 0.60 g used for high-level seismic motion cases; earthquake records matching US Nuclear Regulatory Commission Regulatory Guide 1.60 (RG 1.60) spectrum; selected from Pacific Earthquake Engineering Research Center database including Chi Chi, Taiwan (CHY024), Superstition Hills (Kornbloom Road), Northridge (Lawndale Osage Ave), and other near-field/far-field motions; stationary Gaussian white noise excitation used in frequency domain analysis
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** TIDs installed horizontally between outer containment and inner containment at 44.0 m height; inner structure isolated from ground through base isolation system (BIS); no consideration of vertical seismic motion effects; no soil-structure interaction considered; four reference points (RP1-RP4) defined for monitoring structural responses; theoretical models simplified as mass-spring-damper systems with outer structure fixed to ground
- **Simulation Type:** Nonlinear time-history analysis; frequency-domain response analysis; 3D finite element modeling in Abaqus; stationary Gaussian white noise excitation; random vibration analysis; modal analysis; 30 earthquake waves used for time-history validation; parameter optimization through frequency analysis with time-history verification; structural damping ratio of fixed base model set to 5%; BIS model damping ratio calculated as 12%; BIS-TID model damping ratio increased by approximately 4%
10_1016_j_soildyn_2025_109438.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Seismic response of base-isolated nuclear power plants under earthquake excitation; random vibration analysis of structures subjected to stationary Gaussian white noise; energy dissipation characteristics of tuned inerter dampers; structural vibration behavior under near-field and far-field earthquake motions; modal analysis of base-isolated structures with hybrid vibration control systems
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Relative displacement (u_i^rms, u_i^max) between inner structure and ground; absolute acceleration (a_i^rms, a_i^max) of inner structure; frequency response functions; objective functions (f1: relative displacement variance, f2: absolute acceleration variance, f3: filtered energy index, F: hybrid objective function); optimal parameters (γ_opt: circular frequency ratio, κ_opt: damping coefficient ratio, μ_b: mass ratio); spectral acceleration and displacement responses; TID stroke capacity; energy dissipation metrics; RMS values and peak values of structural responses
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize relative displacement of inner structure by 27.54% (RMS) and 25.57% (peak) on average; minimize absolute acceleration by 19.20% (RMS) and 17.16% (peak) on average; reduce filtered energy index to maximize energy dissipation; achieve lightweight design of TID components with optimal parameters (SPIS-II: γ=1.50, κ=0.67; SPIS-I: γ=0.94, κ=0.36; SIS: γ=1.19, κ=1.33 at μ_b=0.20); maintain TID stroke within ±400 mm capacity; reduce spectral acceleration and displacement while increasing structural period and damping ratio
10_1016_j_soildyn_2025_109438.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** TID installation space limited to 1800 mm between inner and outer containments; maximum stroke capacity constrained to ±400 mm; inner structure elevated by 0.30 m using isolation bearings; 121 base-isolation bearings uniformly arranged under foundation; total structure height 87.9 m with base diameter 27.4 m; TIDs installed at 44.0 m height; upper limit for SPIS-II γ_opt restricted to 1.5; optimization variable ranges: γ ∈ [0.20, 2.00], κ ∈ [0.05, 8.00]; time-history analysis ranges: γ_opt ∈ [0.1, 1.6], κ_opt ∈ [0, 4]
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Target period of base-isolation system fixed at 1.70 s; structural damping ratio of fixed base model limited to 5%; BIS model damping ratio calculated as 12%; BIS-TID model damping ratio increases by approximately 4%; inner structure mass constrained to 8.96×10⁴ ton; total horizontal stiffness of isolation bearings limited to 1.23×10⁶ kN/m; maximum stroke for SIS measured at 185.52 mm under worst-case earthquake; vertical seismic motion not considered; soil-structure interaction not considered; PGA adjusted to 0.30 g for standard analysis and 0.60 g for high-level seismic cases
- **Process/Manufacturing:** TIDs designed as compact models with minimum 400 mm stroke capacity; space-saving parallel configurations adopted for SPIS-I and SPIS-II; inerter elements simulated using user-defined element subroutines with negligible physical mass; numerical model complexity too high for direct parameter optimization; inertial coefficients of all TIDs assumed equal for comparative analysis; theoretical models simplified by neglecting height characteristics and vertical ground motion

10_1016_j_precisioneng_2025_02_023.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Dual-stage force sensor integrated fast tool servo (FS-FTS) for diamond turning of optical microstructures
- **Material / Medium:** 7075 aluminum alloy (Poisson's ratio 0.33, Young's modulus 71 GPa) for compliant mechanisms; laminated electrical steel (saturation flux density 1.96 T, relative permeability 18000) for armatures/yokes; Nd-Fe-B permanent magnet (remanence 1.22 T); brass workpiece; piezoelectric actuators (7 mm × 7 mm × 12 mm, 16.5 μm nominal stroke)
- **Application & Importance:** Integrated machining and in-process measurement of optical microstructures; resolves stroke-bandwidth conflict in traditional fast tool servos; eliminates remounting errors from offline measurement; enables high-efficiency fabrication of complex optical surfaces like 2D water drop structures
- **Geometry / Domain:** Dual-stage structure with primary stage driven by normal-stressed electromagnetic actuator and secondary stage driven by piezoelectric actuator; primary stage features double parallelogram mechanism (DPM); secondary stage uses double parallel eight-par linkage mechanisms (DPELMs); target geometry includes 2D water drop surface with spatial frequencies λ=400 μm, n=6 and amplitudes A₁=2.5 μm, A₂=2.5 μm, A₃=5 μm
10_1016_j_precisioneng_2025_02_023.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Primary stage fixed on base; symmetric flexure mechanism enhances stiffness in x-direction for primary stage and y-direction for secondary stage; target stroke of primary stage >250 μm; target natural frequency of secondary stage >8000 Hz; spindle speed 1600 r/min for machining; feed rate 1 μm/rev; scanning speed 150 μm/min for line A and 18°/min for line B during in-process inspection; maximum cross-coupling displacement from secondary to primary stage is 0.33 μm (0.11% of primary stroke)
- **Loads / Excitations:** Maximum excitation current 2 A for NSEAs; sinusoidal signal 2 A amplitude/1 Hz frequency for primary stroke testing; chirp signal 0.1 A amplitude/1-2000 Hz for primary dynamic properties; sinusoidal signal 200 V amplitude/1 Hz for secondary stroke testing; chirp signal 10 V amplitude/1-20000 Hz for secondary dynamic properties; oscillation signal 5 nm amplitude at 200 Hz, 400 Hz, 800 Hz, 1600 Hz, 3200 Hz, and 6400 Hz for tool setting; 800 Hz selected as suitable oscillation frequency; multi-sinusoidal trajectory with 10 Hz, 30 Hz, and 60 Hz for controller testing
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Secondary stage embedded into primary stage; laser interferometer measures displacements of both stages; piezoelectric force sensor senses contact force between cutting tool and workpiece; linear servo amplifier (gain 0.4 A/V) drives NSEAs; high-voltage amplifier (gain 20) drives PEAs; charge amplifier processes force signal; lock-in amplifier used for in-process inspection; cutting tool serves as both machining tool and measurement probe with constant contact force maintained
- **Simulation Type:** Finite element analysis (FEA) for electromagnetic and mechanical validation; discrete domain modeling of closed-loop system; FRD-based optimization for controller design; chirp signal testing for frequency response analysis; transient simulation for toolpath tracking; linear modeling of closed-loop system after addressing hysteresis, resonance, and disturbances
10_1016_j_precisioneng_2025_02_023.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Mechanical-electromagnetic behavior of normal-stressed electromagnetic actuator (NSEA); mechanical-piezoelectric behavior of piezoelectric actuator (PEA); dynamic properties of compliant mechanisms (stiffness, natural frequencies); hysteresis nonlinearity in piezoelectric actuation; frequency response characteristics of control systems; force-sensing dynamics for in-process inspection
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Primary stage stroke (288 μm); primary stage first-order resonant frequency (408 Hz); secondary stage stroke (11.2 μm); secondary stage first-order resonant frequency (8520 Hz); RMS tracking error (0.1521 μm for PSCC); -3 dB bandwidth (392 Hz for optimized controller); cross-coupling displacement (0.33 μm max); surface roughness (Sa=4.9 nm); form error (PV=242.8 nm, Erms=55.7 nm for in-process inspection); current coefficient (KI=50.71 N/A); negative stiffness (Kz=-0.459 N/μm); z-directional stiffness (Kcomp1=2.48 N/μm, Kcomp2=37.35 N/μm)
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize primary stage resonant frequency while maintaining stroke >250 μm; maximize secondary stage stroke while maintaining natural frequency >8000 Hz; flatten frequency response curve within working bandwidth to achieve higher control bandwidth; minimize RMS tracking error for complex toolpaths; minimize form error of fabricated optical microstructures; maximize force sensing sensitivity for in-process inspection with minimal surface scratch (13 nm amplitude)
10_1016_j_precisioneng_2025_02_023.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Primary stage stroke constraint >250 μm; secondary stage natural frequency constraint >8000 Hz; PM size preset as 6.5 mm × 9.9 mm × 20 mm; S_yoke = 9.9 mm × 20 mm and S_pm = 6.5 mm × 20 mm; w and h preset as 12 mm and 30 mm; PEA size 7 mm × 7 mm × 12 mm with 16.5 μm nominal stroke; optimization parameter intervals: z0 [0.15,0.4] mm, R1 [2,3.5] mm, t1 [0.5,2] mm, l1 [2,8] mm, w1 [7,10] mm, b1 [25,40] mm, l2 [2,4] mm, w2 [0.4,1] mm, b2 [5,10] mm

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Maximum excitation current 2 A; sampling frequency 50 kHz; linear servo amplifier gain 0.4 A/V; high-voltage amplifier gain 20; spindle speed 1600 r/min; feed rate 1 μm/rev; oscillation frequency 800 Hz for force sensing; cross-coupling displacement <0.33 μm (0.11% of primary stroke); cross-coupling effect <−30 dB below primary stage resonant frequency; contact force must be very small for in-process inspection; maximum surface scratch amplitude 13 nm during tool setting

- **Process/Manufacturing:** 7075 aluminum alloy for compliant mechanisms (Poisson's ratio 0.33, Young's modulus 71 GPa); laminated electrical steel for armatures/yokes (saturation flux density 1.96 T, relative permeability 18000); Nd-Fe-B PM with remanence 1.22 T; in-process inspection limited to rough and semi-finish machining; method invalid if tool wear changes tool radius; analytical vs. experimental errors: primary stroke +12.1%, primary frequency −10.1%, secondary stroke −9.8%, secondary frequency −2.4%; fabrication errors acknowledged as source of model-experiment discrepancies

10_1016_j_undsp_2018_05_002.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Buried damaged polyethylene gas pipe with circular and elliptical defects under mechanical and thermal loading

- **Material / Medium:**
  - Medium Density Polyethylene (MDPE) pipe material (PE80 type) with elasticity modulus 427 MPa, yield stress 19.3 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.35, thermal expansion coefficient 2×10⁻⁴ mm/mm/°C
  - Asphalt layer with elasticity coefficient 173 MPa, density 2,200 kg/m³, Poisson ratio 0.35
  - GW soil layers (90% compaction: 6.90 MPa elasticity, 1,700 kg/m³ density; 95% compaction: 15 MPa elasticity, 2,000 kg/m³ density; 85% compaction: 4.80 MPa elasticity, 1,600 kg/m³ density)
  - SM soil layer with 90% proctor density (6.90 MPa elasticity, 1,900 kg/m³ density, 0.35 Poisson ratio)
  - Internal gas pressure of 4 bar (405,300 Pa)

- **Application & Importance:**
  - To evaluate stress distribution in damaged buried polyethylene gas pipes for safe operation with 50-year life expectancy
  - To determine if damaged pipes require immediate repair or replacement by comparing maximum Von Mises stresses with allowable stress limits
  - To design proper repair methods that reduce stress values to allowable limits
  - To investigate stress concentration effects from circular and elliptical defects under combined loads

- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - 4-inch nominal diameter MDPE pipe with 114.3 mm outside diameter and 94.44 mm inside diameter (SDR 11.5)
  - Burial depth of 125 cm with pipe center at 114.3 mm below trench base
  - Trench width of 415 mm
  - Damage types: circular holes (5-20 mm diameter) and elliptical holes (diameter ratios a/b from 0.2 to 1.0, major diameter 25.4 mm)
  - Soil layers above pipe: 100 mm asphalt, 300 mm GW soil (90% compaction), 700 mm SM soil (90% proctor density)
  - Surrounding soil: 150 mm GW soil (95% proctor density) below pipe, 150 mm GW soil (85% proctor density) on sides
  - Model dimensions: 1.5 m × 1.5 m × 1.5 m with symmetric boundary conditions (only half modeled)
10_1016_j_undsp_2018_05_002.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Symmetry plane at x=0 (u_x=0)
  - Fixed boundary at y=-207.15 mm (u_x=u_y=u_z=0)
  - Fixed boundary at z=±l/2 (u_z=0)
  - Plane strain constraint applied in pipe axis direction
  - Half-model symmetry (only half of problem modeled due to geometric and loading symmetry)
  - Pipe at hole location encased by soil (same as undamaged part)
  - Effects of gas leakage to trench ignored

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Internal gas pressure: 4 bar (405,300 Pa)
  - H20 highway traffic load: 112,869 N wheel load (544,780 Pa for half model)
  - Soil column weight above pipe
  - Temperature variations: maximum 5°C increase (from 8°C to 13°C), maximum 15°C decrease (from 50°C to 35°C)
  - Soil temperature at 125 cm depth: constant at 35°C (summer), 13°C (winter)
  - Thermal expansion coefficient: 2×10⁻⁴ mm/mm/°C
  - Soil and pipe temperature considered equal at specific depth

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Soil-pipe interaction modeled using Conta172 and Target170 elements (face-to-face contact)
  - Linear elastic, isotropic material assumption for soil, pipe, and surrounding materials
  - Soil layers (asphalt, GW soil, SM soil) with defined elasticity coefficients, densities, and Poisson ratios
  - No-slip condition at soil-pipe interface

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 3D finite element analysis using ANSYS V12 software
  - Half-model symmetry due to geometric and loading symmetry
  - SOLID95 20-node hexahedral elements for all components
  - Linear elastic material behavior (for calculation purposes, despite polyethylene's viscoelastic nature)
  - Static structural analysis
  - Model dimensions: 1.5 m × 1.5 m × 1.5 m
  - Fine mesh in damage region with gradual coarsening in areas further from damage
  - Convergence verified through multiple mesh configurations (82,994 elements total)
10_1016_j_undsp_2018_05_002.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Stress distribution in buried polyethylene pipes with geometric discontinuities
  - Von Mises stress calculation in damaged pipe walls under combined mechanical and thermal loading
  - Soil-structure interaction effects on buried pipes
  - Stress concentration around circular and elliptical defects in pipe walls

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Maximum Von Mises stress values in pipe (measured in MPa)
  - Stress concentration factors around defects
  - Comparison of computed stresses against allowable stress limits (4.3 MPa at 35°C for 50-year life)
  - Effect of hole diameter (5-20 mm) on stress values
  - Effect of elliptical hole diameter ratio (a/b from 0.2 to 1.0) on stress values
  - Temperature variation effects (-15°C to +5°C) on stress distribution
  - Combined effects of soil column weight, internal pressure (4 bar), and traffic loads on stress values

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Determine when pipe damage requires repair (when Von Mises stress exceeds 4.3 MPa at 35°C)
  - Identify critical damage parameters that exceed safety limits for 50-year life expectancy
  - Provide basis for designing effective pipe repair methods that reduce stress to allowable levels
  - Establish relationship between defect geometry and stress concentration to guide repair decisions
  - Evaluate which combinations of loading conditions produce maximum stress values requiring immediate intervention
10_1016_j_undsp_2018_05_002.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - 4-inch nominal diameter MDPE pipe with 114.3 mm outside diameter and 9.93 mm wall thickness (SDR 11.5)
  - Burial depth fixed at 125 cm (optimum depth where daily weather changes don't affect pipe temperature)
  - Trench width of 415 mm
  - Damage size constraints: circular holes (5-20 mm diameter), elliptical holes with major diameter 25.4 mm and diameter ratios (a/b) from 0.2 to 1.0
  - Model dimensions limited to 1.5 m × 1.5 m × 1.5 m

  - Maximum allowable stress of 4.3 MPa at 35°C for 50-year life expectancy
  - Internal gas pressure fixed at 4 bar (405,300 Pa)
  - Temperature variations constrained to maximum 5°C increase (winter) and 15°C decrease (summer)
  - Design coefficient (factor of safety) of 1.5
  - Minimum required strength (MRS) used to calculate design stress
  - Stress values must remain below allowable limits to prevent damage propagation
  - Material properties fixed for MDPE PE80 (427 MPa modulus, 19.3 MPa yield stress, 0.35 Poisson ratio)

  - Finite element modeling using ANSYS V12 with SOLID95 20-node hexahedral elements
  - Maximum element count of 82,994 for computational efficiency
  - Mapped mesh with finer elements in damage regions and gradual coarsening away from damage
  - Soil layers must conform to ASTM standards for compaction and properties
  - Pipe material must be MDPE type PE80 for gas distribution
  - Linear elastic material assumption despite polyethylene's viscoelastic nature (for calculation purposes)
  - Model must include all four load types: soil column weight, internal pressure, H20 traffic load, and temperature variations
  - Pipe at hole location encased by soil (same as undamaged part) with gas leakage effects to trench ignored

10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_665_281.key_1:
• Identity & Domain: Crack tip deformation behavior under Mode-II shear stress loading in single crystal superalloy

• Material / Medium: Ni-base single crystal superalloy CMSX-4; two-phase microstructure with γ matrix phase and cuboidal γ' precipitate phase; γ' phase volume fraction ≈70%; γ' phase has L12 lattice structure; γ' phase exhibits anomalous temperature dependence of yield strength (increases with temperature up to ~800°C); at lower temperature, yield strengths of γ/γ' phases are nearly equal; at higher temperature, yield strength of γ' phase is significantly higher than γ phase

• Application & Importance: Gas turbine first-stage blade applications; thermal stress from thermal gradients through blade thickness causes fatigue cracks; essential for assessing component reliability; understanding temperature-dependent fatigue crack propagation behavior

• Geometry / Domain: Cuboidal γ' precipitates in γ matrix microstructure; crack direction [110]; crack plane normal [1̄10]; octahedral slip systems with <110> slip directions and {111} slip planes; specific slip systems: (1̄11)[110], (1̄11)[011̄], (1̄11)[101]; equivalent inclusion model with three γ channel phases (γx, γy, γz) embedded in γ' phase; simulation represents post-shearing mode cracking propagated to <110> slip direction
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_665_281.key_2:
• Boundaries & Constraints: Crack direction [110]; crack plane normal [1̄10]; simulation represents post-shearing mode cracking propagated to <110> slip direction

• Loads / Excitations: Mode-II shear stress applied to crack; temperatures 400°C and 800°C

• Interactions / Interfaces: γ/γ' microstructure modeled using Eshelby’s inclusion theory; three γ channel phases (γx, γy, γz) embedded in γ' phase

• Simulation Type: Crystal plasticity finite element analysis; static regime; 3D model; nonlinear material behavior due to plastic deformation
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_665_281.key_3:
• Physics Solved: Crystal plasticity deformation at crack tip under Mode-II shear stress; interaction between γ/γ' microstructure and crack tip deformation; temperature-dependent slip system activation

• Target Outputs (Metrics): Slip deformation distribution in γ' phase; equivalent plastic strain distribution in γ' phase; equivalent plastic strain distribution in γ phase; activation levels of specific slip systems ((1̄11)[110], (1̄11)[011̄], (1̄11)[101]); crack tip deformation patterns at 400°C and 800°C; plastic strain distribution relative to γ channel <100> directions

• Optimization Goal: Evaluate temperature dependence of fatigue crack propagation behavior in single crystal superalloys; correlate crack tip deformation mechanisms with experimental observations of shearing mode (at lower temperature) and opening mode (at higher temperature) crack propagation
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_665_281.key_4:
• Geometric/Design Space: Cuboidal γ' precipitates with volume fraction ≈70%; three γ channel phases (γx, γy, γz) embedded in γ' phase; crack direction [110]; crack plane normal [1̄10]; octahedral slip systems with <110> slip directions and {111} slip planes; microstructure scale with 1μm reference; slip systems limited to (1̄11)[110], (1̄11)[011̄], and (1̄11)[101]

• Performance/Physics Limits: Yield strength of γ' phase increases with temperature up to ~800°C; at 400°C, yield strengths of γ/γ' phases are nearly equal; at 800°C, yield strength of γ' phase is significantly higher than γ phase; analysis constrained to Mode-II shear stress condition only; slip deformation restricted in γ' phase at higher temperature due to increased yield strength

• Process/Manufacturing: Material is CMSX-4 single crystal superalloy; application is gas turbine first-stage blades; thermal gradients from internal cooling system cause fatigue cracks; analysis does not include Mode-I loading (previously studied separately); crystal orientation constrained to specific slip systems relevant to crack propagation behavior

10_1016_j_nucengdes_2021_111541.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Reinforced concrete structural elements in nuclear power plant (NPP) buildings, specifically addressing B-regions (non-disturbed strain regions) and D-regions (discontinuity/disturbance regions) with focus on wall-slab connections and massive structural components.

- **Material / Medium:** C40 concrete (fck = 40 MPa), B500B reinforcement steel, 5 cm concrete cover; hard soil with shear modulus = 6 GPa, Poisson's ratio = 0.3, shear wave velocity Vs = 1550 m/s; structural elements with wall thicknesses ranging 30-80 cm and slab thicknesses 10-60 cm.

- **Application & Importance:** Optimization of reinforcement design in nuclear civil structures to improve constructability, reduce excessive reinforcement (25% saving on bending reinforcement sections), enhance seismic response accuracy, and address modeling inaccuracies in D-regions where traditional shell element approaches lead to overestimation of reinforcement requirements.

- **Geometry / Domain:** 5-story building (10.6m × 6.6m × 25m) with 1.5m thick raft, walls with variable thickness, and floors (0.2-0.6m thick); 5m × 10m clamped slab example; Voronoi-tessellated panels for local-global analysis; wall-slab connections with clear span (l-t) versus center-to-center span (l); structural domain including soil-structure interaction modeled with spring mat.
10_1016_j_nucengdes_2021_111541.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Clamped boundaries on upper and left borders for 5m×10m slab; fixed supports at beam ends for Case #1 (clamped-clamped) and fixed-free for Case #2; kinematic relations between brick connection elements and plate elements (u_x^n5 = (u_x^n1 + u_x^n2)/2, u_y^n5 = (u_y^n1 + u_y^n2)/2, u_z^n5 = (u_z^n1 + u_z^n2)/2, θ_z^n5 = (u_y^n2 - u_y^n1)/e_x); spring mat representing soil in three translational directions; clear span (l-t) versus center-to-center span (l) modeling; Voronoi tessellation with influence areas extending beyond polygon boundaries by 30 cm.

- **Loads / Excitations:** Vertical load on opposite sides of slab (0.25 MN/m magnitude); distributed load (p) and concentrated load (F) on beams; floor loads between 10 kN/m² and 20 kN/m²; seismic excitation using EUR spectrum with ZPA value of 0.4 g (horizontal direction), scaled to 2/3 for vertical shaking; 24 Newmark seismic load combinations for accidental Ultimate Limit State; gravity loads applied to structural elements.

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Kinematic constraints transferring average translations and rotations between brick connection elements and plate/shell elements; soil-structure interaction modeled with spring mat; energy conservation between local and global scales; Voronoi tessellation defining panels with weighted least square regression for homogenization; connection elements representing homogenized behavior within shared volume between connected walls and slabs.

- **Simulation Type:** Linear elastic FEM analysis; 3D structural modeling with both plate/shell and brick elements; modal analysis for dynamic behavior; response-spectrum method for seismic analysis; linear static analysis for gravity loads; energy-conserving local-global design method for reinforcement calculation; 24 Newmark seismic load combinations for accidental Ultimate Limit State.
10_1016_j_nucengdes_2021_111541.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Linear elastic structural behavior of reinforced concrete elements; bending, membrane, and shear forces in plate/shell elements; modal vibration characteristics; seismic response through response-spectrum method; reinforcement calculation based on Ultimate Limit State design; energy conservation between local and global scales.

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Reinforcement density (A_sup,x, A_sup,y) in cm²/m; reinforcement ratio in kg/m³; bending moments (m_xx, m_yy, m_xy); membrane forces (n_xx, n_yy, n_xy); out-of-plane shear forces (v_x, v_y); natural frequencies; deflection values; curvature indicators (κ_xx² + κ_yy²); potential energy distribution; reinforcement section distributions; maximum reinforcement values; modal participation factors.

- **Optimization Goal:** Reduce bending reinforcement sections by 25% for outer walls; decrease maximum reinforcement values due to bending by 40%; eliminate local reinforcement peaks through energy-conserving smoothing; improve constructability by reducing reinforcement density in B-regions; minimize modeling errors in D-regions (particularly wall-slab connections); achieve optimal reinforcement distribution while maintaining structural safety; reduce overestimation of reinforcement requirements caused by inappropriate modeling practices.
10_1016_j_nucengdes_2021_111541.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Wall thicknesses range 30-80 cm; slab thicknesses range 10-60 cm; 1.5 m thick raft; floor thickness 0.2-0.6 m; concrete cover 5 cm; influence areas extend 30 cm beyond Voronoi polygon boundaries (15× diameter of 20 mm rebar); clear span (l-t) versus center-to-center span (l) with ρ = t/l; building dimensions 10.6 m × 6.6 m × 25 m with 5 stories (5 m average height per story).

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** C40 concrete (fck = 40 MPa); B500B reinforcement steel; hard soil with shear modulus = 6 GPa, Poisson's ratio = 0.3, shear wave velocity Vs = 1550 m/s; floor loads between 10 kN/m² and 20 kN/m²; EUR spectrum with ZPA value of 0.4 g (horizontal direction), scaled to 2/3 for vertical shaking; reinforcement calculations follow EN1992-1-1:2004 and RCC-CW, 2019 standards; Ultimate Limit State design requirements must be met.

- **Process/Manufacturing:** Mandatory rebar arrangements based on RCC-CW, 2019 standard; reinforcement continuity requirements at connections; need for overlapping and anchorage lengths in reinforcement drawings; deliberate design reinforcement provisions required for future seismic retrofitting; no minimum reinforcement criteria considered in the example but acknowledged as necessary in practice; excessive reinforcement density complicates fabrication; constructability limitations due to rebar congestion from inappropriate modeling practices.

10_1038_s43588_024_00749_7.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Shape optimization problems in soft matter physics using the Morpho computational framework, with specific focus on filaments on spherical substrates, swelling hydrogels, nematic liquid-crystal tactoids, and soap films/membranes.
- **Material / Medium:** Nematic liquid crystals (with elastic constant κ and anchoring parameter ω), hydrogels (with Flory-Huggins mixing parameter χ), lipid membranes, flexible filaments (with Young's modulus E, area moment of inertia I, density ρ), and soap films; all modeled as soft materials that deform significantly at room temperature.
- **Application & Importance:** Predicting shape changes in soft materials under mechanical, electromagnetic, or chemical stimuli; enabling design of soft robotics, structured fluids, biological materials, and particulate media; providing computational tools for shape-optimization problems that lack accessible general-purpose simulation software.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Spherical substrates for filament studies, initially ellipsoidal soap bubbles converging to spheres, spherical hydrogel beads under confinement by hard spheres (with r = 0.3 and r = 0.9 ratios), nematic tactoids transitioning from spherical to elongated/cusped shapes, and 1D filaments with fixed length L constrained to spherical surfaces of radius R (characterized by dimensionless arc-length Φ = L/R).

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Aspect ratio of tactoids (ranging from 1 to 7+ as shown in Fig. 2)
  - Energy values for nematic tactoids (ranging from 5 to 8+ in Fig. 2b)
  - Volume ratio Vf/Vi for hydrogels (up to 5x expansion in Fig. 3e)
  - Fraction of filament length on longitude (α, 0-1 range in Fig. 4b)
  - Curvature distribution along filaments (1.0-2.2 range in Fig. 4c)
  - Relative error in minimal surface problems (10⁻³ to 10⁰ in Fig. 5c)
  - Number of degrees of freedom (10³ to 10⁵ in Fig. 5d)
  - Fraction of boundary nodes (0.1-0.7 in Fig. 5e)
  - Runtimes for different processor cores (Table 1)

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Minimize surface area for soap films under fixed volume constraint
  - Minimize Helfrich energy for lipid membranes under fixed boundary conditions
  - Minimize free energy of nematic tactoids including elastic and anchoring terms
  - Minimize Helmholtz free energy for hydrogels (ΔF = ΔFmix + ΔFel)
  - Minimize energy functional for filaments (F = ∫[χ²(s) + ΩgS(s)·ẑ]ds) with fixed length on spherical surface
  - Minimize perimeter while maintaining fixed enclosed area in level-set problems
  - Achieve convergence criteria of relative energy change <10⁻⁸ for most problems
  - Maintain fixed volume constraints with specified tolerance through projection methods
10_1038_s43588_024_00749_7.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Filament fixed length L constrained to sphere of radius R (dimensionless arc-length Φ = L/R)
  - Coiling transition occurs for Φ > 4 (sharp transition from vertical to coiled morphology)
  - For Φ ≲ π, filament lies vertically along a line of longitude of the sphere
  - Fixed enclosed volume constraint for soap bubbles (∫_C dV = V₀)
  - Outside boundary of membrane disks held fixed during minimization
  - Confining spherical obstacles with r = 0.3 and r = 0.9 (ratio of confining particle radius to undeformed hydrogel bead radius)
