  - Fixed gravitational parameter Ωg⁻¹ = 0.1 for filament studies
  - Aspect ratio of 2 for tactoids when ω = 1 with homogeneous nematic orientation
  - Convergence criteria of relative energy change <10⁻⁸ (or <10⁻¹² for filament studies)
  - Tolerance for constraint maintenance during optimization
  - For large membrane indentations, tether approaches cylindrical shape with radius r₀ = √ε/2
  - Hydrogel volume ratio Vf/Vi (final volume to initial volume) as key performance metric
  - Dimensionless fields H(φ) and φ maintained in level-set formulations
  - Fixed volume constraints maintained through projection methods with specified tolerance

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Mesh regularization required to prevent vertex bunching at solution ends (without regularization, vertices cluster)
  - Interleaved optimization steps with ~2:1 ratio (surface tension to regularization)
  - Discrete refinement steps (splitting/merging elements, edge flips) for complex problems
  - Adaptive refinement with β = 1.5 threshold (elements refined if contribution to F exceeds 1.5× average)
  - Partial parallelization with varying serial fractions (5.6-100% depending on problem type)
  - Mesh quality control through adaptive refinement to maintain element distribution
  - Level-set re-initialization required to satisfy |∇φ| = 1 constraint
  - Area re-projection steps to maintain fixed enclosed area during level-set optimization

10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_828_119.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Discrete Element Method (DEM) modeling of damage mechanisms in composite materials and dry fabrics. Specific subjects include Representative Elementary Volumes (REV) with single fibers, Statistical Elementary Volumes (SEV) with multiple fibers, and woven fabric structures under impact loading.

- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Carbon fiber composites: E_M = 260 GPa, ρ_M = 1750 kg/m³, ν_M = 0.3
  - Epoxy matrix: E_M = 3.45 GPa, ρ_M = 1200 kg/m³, ν_M = 0.3
  - Kevlar fibers for impact simulation: Yarn modulus E₁ = 62 GPa, density = 1310 kg/m³
  - Discrete element properties: Carbon fiber discrete bounds (BBF process) E = 8272 GPa, ν = 0.3, r = 0.307; Epoxy matrix discrete bounds (BBF process) E = 89 GPa, ν = 0.3, r = 0.33
  - Fiber diameter = 10 μm, matrix domain size = 28 μm in REV

- **Application & Importance:** 
  - Modeling damage mechanisms: matrix cracking, debonding, fiber break, and delamination in composite materials
  - Simulating ballistic impact on dry fabrics with projectile velocities of 60 m/s, 92.1 m/s, and 245 m/s
  - Addressing aeronautical safety requirements for composite structures
  - Capturing contact effects and yarn realignment until rupture in textile impact scenarios
  - Reducing experimental testing through numerical simulations of impact events

- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - REV: Cubic domain containing cylindrical carbon fiber in epoxy matrix with 51.3% fiber volume fraction
  - SEV: Volume with randomly distributed fibers using bi-disperse medium (larger fiber DE than matrix DE)
  - Impact simulation domain: 5 cm × 5 cm plain weave ply with two clamped edges and two free edges
  - Projectile: Rigid sphere with diameter of 5.35 mm impacting at fabric center
  - Yarn geometry: Section width = 0.59 mm, section height = 0.115 mm, woven thickness = 0.265 mm
  - REV model: 80,000 discrete elements with 130,516 fiber bonds, 115,096 matrix bonds, and 8,282 fiber-matrix bonds
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_828_119.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Plain weave ply with two clamped edges and two free edges
  - Double symmetry used to model only a quarter of the domain
  - Displacement-controlled loading for tensile tests
  - Loading for elasticity tests and loading for failure tests with different displacement profiles
  - Boundary conditions for elementary tests including longitudinal (L), transversal (T), in-plane (LT), and out-of-plane (TT') configurations

- **Loads / Excitations:** 
  - Projectile velocities: 60 m/s, 92.1 m/s, and 245 m/s
  - Rigid sphere projectile with 5.35 mm diameter impacting at fabric center
  - Tensile loading at macroscopic strains: ε_M = 8.82·10^-3, 9.00·10^-3, 9.25·10^-3, 9.50·10^-3 (BBF criterion) and ε_M = 10.00·10^-3, 10.25·10^-3, 10.50·10^-3, 12.00·10^-3 (RDEF criterion)
  - Strain rates in transverse tension tests

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** 
  - Cohesive beams between fiber DE and matrix DE
  - 130,516 fiber bonds, 115,096 matrix bonds, and 8,282 fiber-matrix bonds in REV
  - Contact force calculation: F_r = δ·K_μ·n where δ is interpenetration between DE
  - Contact stiffness assumed equal to microscopic stiffness
  - Fiber-matrix cohesive contact with normal and shear behavior
  - Linear by piece contact laws for normal and shear behavior
  - Fracture energy release rates: G_I=0.5·σ_n^max·u_n^p and G_II=0.5·σ_s^max·u_s^p
  - Interface cohesive bonds initially chosen identical to matrix bonds

- **Simulation Type:** 
  - Explicit time integration using Verlet scheme
  - Transient dynamic simulations
  - 3D simulations with 80,000 discrete elements for REV
  - Time step of approximately 10^-9 s
  - No numerical or physical damping introduced
  - Energy conservation error never exceeding 0.7%
  - Bi-disperse medium for SEV modeling (larger fiber DE than matrix DE)
  - Discrete element simulations with 50,000-200,000 iterations shown in results
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_828_119.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Matrix cracking in composite materials
  - Fiber-matrix debonding
  - Fiber breakage
  - Delamination in composite structures
  - Impact response of dry woven fabrics
  - Contact effects and yarn realignment during impact
  - Crack propagation through different failure criteria (BBF and RDEF)
  - Energy transfer during impact events

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Elastic moduli (EL, ET) for unidirectional composite
  - Stress-strain curves for composite specimens
  - Macroscopic failure properties (σ_failM, ε_failM)
  - Percentage of broken bonds in fiber, matrix, and fiber/matrix interface
  - Energy balance components (Total Energy, Strain Energy, Contact Energy, Friction Energy, Woven Kinetic Energy, Impactor Kinetic Energy)
  - Energy conservation error (never exceeding 0.7%)
  - Projectile velocity during impact simulation
  - Displacement fields at different time intervals (27 μs, 45 μs, 63 μs, 90 μs)
  - Crack propagation paths in composite specimens
  - Theoretical macroscopic failure strain values (ε^fib_M = 9.6·10^-3 and ε^mat_M = 20.3·10^-3)

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Reduce physical experiments through accurate numerical simulation
  - Improve prediction of damage initiation and propagation in composite materials
  - Enhance simulation efficiency (CPU time between 2.5-7 hours for impact simulations, lower than FEM's 8-17 hours)
  - Develop parameter identification for cohesive contact laws using reverse approach
  - Implement variability of cohesive contact properties and defects due to elaboration
  - Capture damage mechanisms at microscopic/mesoscopic scale in the damage area while maintaining structural effects at macroscopic scale
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_828_119.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - REV (Representative Elementary Volume) has cubic domain with cylindrical carbon fiber in epoxy matrix
  - Fixed fiber volume fraction of 51.3% in REV
  - Fiber diameter = 10 μm, matrix domain size = 28 μm in REV
  - Impact simulation domain: 5 cm × 5 cm plain weave ply with two clamped edges and two free edges
  - Only a quarter of the domain modeled due to double symmetry of plain weaving
  - Projectile: rigid sphere with 5.35 mm diameter impacting at fabric center
  - Yarn section width = 0.59 mm, height = 0.115 mm, woven thickness = 0.265 mm
  - Discrete element radius = 0.118 mm for Kevlar impact simulations
  - REV model uses 80,000 discrete elements
  - Bi-disperse medium requires larger fiber DE than matrix DE
  - Length of REV cell in fiber direction determined from sensitivity analysis

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Energy conservation error never exceeds 0.7% during simulations
  - Time step of approximately 10^-9 s used for simulations
  - Theoretical macroscopic failure strain values: ε^fib_M = 9.6·10^-3 and ε^mat_M = 20.3·10^-3
  - Contact stiffness assumed equal to microscopic stiffness
  - No numerical or physical damping introduced
  - Explicit integration scheme (Verlet) used in DEM method
  - Isotropic properties adopted for carbon fiber (convenience assumption)
  - Interface cohesive bonds initially chosen identical to matrix bonds
  - Minimum coordination number (contacts per DE) of 6 required
  - Optimal compaction rate of 6.3 (ratio between volume of spherical DE and enveloping volume)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Spherical DE shape used for efficiency reasons
  - DE size varies according to Gaussian distribution
  - Only brittle elastic behavior considered (viscous behavior of epoxy matrix neglected)
  - Transverse isotropy of carbon fiber not yet implemented (planned for future work)
  - Implementation of variability of cohesive contact properties and defects due to elaboration is planned but not yet implemented
  - Fiber DE geometrically overlap in bi-disperse medium to best represent fiber continuity
  - Maximum elongation criterion used for spring failure in yarn modeling
  - No numerical damping introduced for simulations

10_1016_j_jmbbm_2020_104302.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Human skull bone specimen under uniaxial compression, analyzed using finite element modeling of deformation and failure response
- **Material / Medium:** Human skull bone with sandwich structure (dense outer/inner tables surrounding porous diploe); Bone Volume Fraction (BVF) ranges from 0.00-1.00; Modulus (E) follows power relationship E = 8.528(f_BV)^1.585 GPa; Failure criteria: σ_f = 175(f_BV)^2 MPa for both tension and compression; Poisson's ratio = 0.3 for all elements; Pure bone density = 1.8 g/cm³
- **Application & Importance:** To develop biofidelic simulations for evaluating head injury from external loading, enabling identification of realistic fracture patterns (linear/tensile, depressed/compressive, penetration/shear); addresses challenge of modeling skull's heterogeneous mesostructure for improved clinical relevance in head injury prediction
- **Geometry / Domain:** 8×8 mm outer surface specimen including full skull thickness; Rectangular volume of interest (VOI) meshed with 16,683 tetrahedral elements; Average element volume = 2.20×10⁷ μm³ ± 1.32×10⁷ μm³; Specimen dimensions: 7.8×9.6 mm (left camera view), 8.4×9.6 mm (right camera view); FE mesh dimensions: 5.8×9.3 mm (x-y), 6.9 mm (z-y); Micro-CT resolution: 84.9 μm (downsampled from 5.3 μm original); Inscribed sphere diameter distribution peaks at ~0.2 mm; Element voxel mapping: mean=37 voxels, max=237 voxels
10_1016_j_jmbbm_2020_104302.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Top and bottom compression platens modeled as analytical rigid surfaces; Bottom platen fixed in y-direction; Top platen displaced in through-thickness (y) direction; Apparent simulation strain (ε_app) defined as v_y/d_sim where v_y is y-displacement and d_sim is original mesh depth; Tangential friction coefficient μ = 0.1 between platens and specimen; Linear simulation displaced to ε_app = 0.4%; Failure simulation displaced to ε_app = 0.6%
- **Loads / Excitations:** Uniaxial compressive loading via top platen displacement; Failure simulation platen speed = 11.1 mm/s (nominal strain rate of 1.2/s); Experimental quasi-static strain rate was 0.001/s; Applied stress calculated by normalizing reaction force on top platen by undeformed cross-sectional area
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Surface-to-surface contact pair formulation with penalty method (linear simulation); General contact formulation (failure simulation); Micro-CT dataset mapped to FE mesh at 84.9 μm resolution (downsampled from 5.3 μm); Element-specific material properties assigned based on local Bone Volume Fraction (BVF)

  - Hole pattern forms regular triangular distribution with hexagonal periodic unit
  - Projection of Plate B holes on Plate A located at center of triangular units formed by Plate A holes
  - Key dimensions: Hole diameter (1–1.5 mm), hole distance (3–5 mm), plate distance (1–3 mm)
  - Initial configuration with 10 plates (5 of each type), optimized to 40 layers in final design

- **Material / Medium:** Cortical bone (elastoplastic Johnson-Cook), trabecular bone, intervertebral disc (nucleus pulposus, annulus fibrosus), ligaments; PEEK cage (E=3.4 GPa, ν=0.4), titanium cage (E=115 GPa, ν=0.34), titanium pedicle screws; 400 N gravitational load with 10 Nm moments in flexion/lateral bending/axial rotation
- **Application & Importance:** Optimization of cage parameters to balance indirect decompression, spinal realignment, and subsidence risk reduction; critical for minimizing cage subsidence (7-53% clinical incidence) while achieving desired spinal correction
- **Geometry / Domain:** L4-L5 functional spinal unit with 52 mm vertebral width, 33 mm anterior-posterior dimension; cages with 22 mm width, 10-14 mm height, 6°-12° lordosis, 40-60 mm length; cage positions defined by center point ratio (anterior CPR=0.65, central CPR=0.5, posterior CPR=0.35) relative to superior endplate length
10_1016_j_spinee_2025_04_009.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** L5 inferior endplate constrained in all rotations and translations; 0.5 mm initial gap at facet joints; minimum 0.5 mm separation at cage-endplate interface; cortical layer thickness varying from 0.4 mm at endplates to 2 mm at upper pedicle
- **Loads / Excitations:** 400 N gravitational load applied to superior endplate of L4; combined 10 Nm moments applied in flexion, lateral bending, or axial rotation; distractive force applied between L4 and L5 during cage insertion
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Node-to-surface contact with 0.2 Coulomb friction coefficient between cage and endplates; tied contact conditions for ligament attachments; screw-bone interface with 0.2 Coulomb friction coefficient; node-to-surface contact with 0.2 Coulomb friction coefficient for pedicle screws; tied contacts between screws and rods
- **Simulation Type:** Quasi-static 3D finite element analysis using explicit dynamic solver (RADIOSS 2020) with kinetic relaxation (kinetic energy <1% of total energy, strain rates <1/s); 172 simulations covering 4 loading conditions across various cage configurations
10_1016_j_spinee_2025_04_009.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Biomechanical response of L4-L5 spinal segment with grade I spondylolisthesis under OLIF procedures, including stress distribution, displacement patterns, and geometric changes in spinal structures
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Disc height (mm), foraminal height (mm), spinal canal diameter (mm), foraminal area (mm²), spinal canal anteroposterior area (mm²), spinal canal axial area (mm²), segmental lumbar lordosis (SLL) (°), facet joint gap (mm), vertebral slip (%), maximum Von-Mises endplate stress (MPa), maximum endplate displacement (mm)
- **Optimization Goal:** Balance between achieving optimal indirect decompression (maximizing foraminal height/area and spinal canal dimensions), spinal realignment (maximizing segmental lordosis restoration), and minimizing cage subsidence risk (minimizing endplate stresses and displacements) across varying cage parameters
10_1016_j_spinee_2025_04_009.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Cage length limited to 40-60 mm (77-115% of L4/L5 maximum width); cage height limited to 10-14 mm; cage lordosis limited to 6° or 12°; cage position constrained to anterior (CPR=0.65), central (CPR=0.5), or posterior (CPR=0.35); vertebral width of 52 mm serves as practical upper limit for cage length; 22 mm fixed cage width (anteroposterior dimension)
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Cortical bone yield stress threshold >130 MPa; kinetic energy maintained <1% of total system energy; strain rates limited to <1/s to ensure quasi-static conditions; maximum recorded stress in extreme case (14 mm height, 40 mm length, 6° lordosis, titanium, stand-alone) was 134 MPa, approaching cortical bone compressive strength (130-180 MPa)
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Partial discectomy preserving 25-30% of initial disc elements; all ligaments maintained intact during surgical simulation; endplate smoothing required for cage insertion; pedicle screw diameter constrained to 6.5 mm; rod diameter constrained to 6 mm; 0.5 mm minimum separation maintained at cage-endplate interface; pedicle screw length constrained to 45 mm

10_1016_j_tws_2024_112258.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Cast steel tubular (CST) joints used in steel structures including tree-like structures, grid shells, and coastal structures
- **Material / Medium:** G20Mn5N cast steel with elastic modulus 2.06×10⁵ MPa, yield strength 235 MPa, density 7850 kg/m³, and Poisson's ratio 0.3; linear elastic material model used in FEA
- **Application & Importance:** To reduce material redundancy and improve stress distribution in CST joint design; addresses lack of standard verification formulas for diverse CST joint configurations; provides efficient alternative to trial-and-error design approaches; ensures manufacturability through conventional casting processes
- **Geometry / Domain:** Multi-branch tubular joints with intersecting members including tree-like 4-branch joints (D500×40 mm lower member, three D360×35 mm upper members) and grid shell 6-branch joints (D88.9×4 mm chords, D101.6×4 mm braces); modeled using subdivision surface techniques with middle surface offset inward/outward to create inner/outer surfaces; geometric parameters include member diameters, angles between members (120°, 140°, 58.8°), and dimensional measurements (640 mm, 890 mm, 209.46 mm)
10_1016_j_tws_2024_112258.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Fixed boundary condition applied to joint's bottom; Hinged boundary condition at RP-1 permitting rotation only around Z axis of local coordinate system; Translational degrees of freedom at RP-4 restrained along Y and Z axes of local system while allowing translational movement along X axis and all rotations; End vertices of control mesh fixed during geometric modeling; Boundary conditions applied at reference points (RPs) with local coordinate systems aligned with members' axes

- **Loads / Excitations:** Vertical force of 615 kN applied to each upper member of tree-like joint (total 1845 kN); Axial load of 20 kN applied to chord members of grid shell joint; Axial load of 20 kN and shear force of 20 kN applied to each brace member of grid shell joint

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Reference points (RPs) established at ends of each member and coupled with respective supporting regions; Support regions applied at end of each member; Local coordinate systems defined at RPs aligning with members' axes

- **Simulation Type:** 3D finite element analysis; Linear elastic material model; Tetrahedral mesh and sweep technique used for mesh generation; Mesh sizes of 20 mm (tree-like joint) and 8 mm (grid shell joint) selected based on sensitivity analysis; Material properties: elastic modulus 2.06×10⁵ MPa, yield strength 235 MPa, density 7850 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio 0.3
10_1016_j_tws_2024_112258.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Linear elastic structural mechanics of cast steel tubular joints under static loading conditions, calculating stress distribution and deformation

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Joint volume (V) and volume fraction (V_f = V/V₀)
  - Maximum Mises stress (σ_max)
  - Stress distribution patterns
  - Structural response for optimization fitness evaluation

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Tree-like joint: Minimize volume fraction with stress penalty term (target: 39.2% volume reduction while keeping maximum Mises stress below 100 MPa)
  - Grid shell joint: Minimize maximum Mises stress with volume penalty term (target: 49.0% stress reduction while volume fraction constraint set at 1.20)
  - Overall: Achieve optimal balance between material efficiency and stress distribution while maintaining continuous, smooth surfaces suitable for conventional casting processes
10_1016_j_tws_2024_112258.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Tree-like joint: Deformation parameters d_i constrained to [-200, 200] mm; thickness parameters t_i constrained to [10, 50] mm; member dimensions: D500×40 mm (lower), D360×35 mm (upper); heights: 640 mm (lower section), 890 mm (upper section); 140° angle between members
  - Grid shell joint: Deformation parameters d_i constrained to [-80, 80] mm; thickness parameters t_i constrained to [1, 15] mm; member dimensions: D88.9×4 mm (chords), D101.6×4 mm (braces); effective length: 209.46 mm; angles: 3.3° to horizontal plane, 58.8° between braces in horizontal projection
  - Symmetry constraints reducing design variables to 4 vertices for both joint types
  - Wall thickness dimensions preserved at member ends (26.04 mm for upper members, 30.20 mm for lower member in tree-like joint; 4.9 mm for all members in grid shell joint)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Tree-like joint: Stress limit of 100 MPa (based on topology-optimized joint results from literature)
  - Grid shell joint: Volume fraction constraint V̄_f = 1.20
  - Maximum Mises stress as primary performance indicator for structural integrity
  - Optimization formulation includes stress penalty term for tree-like joint (max(0, σ_max/σ̄ - 1)) and volume penalty term for grid shell joint (max(0, V_f - V̄_f))

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Requirement for continuous and smooth surfaces compatible with conventional casting processes
  - Avoidance of complex topologies with holes that would complicate casting (unlike topology optimization results)
  - Preservation of simple, continuous topology throughout optimization process
  - No need for extensive post-processing (unlike topology-optimized joints which require mesh smoothing and inverse modeling)
  - Design must maintain connectivity with structural members (achieved by fixing end vertices of control mesh)
  - Horizontal trimming of upper members to maintain consistent joint configuration with literature examples

- Target Outputs (Metrics): Utilization adhesion coefficient (φ1, φ2) for front/rear wheels; braking strength (z); regenerative braking torque (Tm); total energy consumed on brakes (kJ); recovery energy (kJ); energy recovery efficiency (%); optimized braking torque at different vehicle speeds, braking strengths, and battery states of charge (SOC).
- Optimization Goal: Minimize J = y1J1 - y2J2 where J1 = √(φ1 - z) + (φ2 - z) (braking stability) and J2 = FmVηmηbηt (energy recovery efficiency); balance between braking stability (prioritized when 0.4 < z ≤ 0.7) and energy recovery efficiency (prioritized when 0.1 < z ≤ 0.4); increase braking stability while improving energy recovery efficiency (achieved 0.94% efficiency gain in FTP75 cycle).
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_872_331.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: Braking force distribution (Fb1, Fb2) must be within safety area POABC defined by Line I (ideal braking curve), Line M (ECE R13 compliant), Line f (front wheel lock curve), Line DE (tangent to Line M), and Line EF (front wheel lock curve); Point D corresponds to braking strength 0.1; Point E corresponds to maximum regenerative braking force.
- Performance/Physics Limits: Regenerative braking torque Tm ≤ available motor torque Tavail; regenerative braking power FmVηmηbηt ≤ maximum battery charging power Pcmax; regenerative braking force Fm ≤ front wheel braking force Fb1; braking strength z constrained to 0.1 < z ≤ 0.7; utilization adhesion coefficient must be close to braking strength for optimal performance; different weighting coefficients applied for braking strength ranges (0.1<z≤0.4 and 0.4<z≤0.7).
- Process/Manufacturing: Optimization validated across multiple driving cycles (FTP75, NEDC, 1015); initial vehicle speed fixed at 100 km/h; braking intensity increased from 0 to 0.7 within 8s; no explicit manufacturing constraints mentioned as the study focuses on control strategy rather than physical component manufacturing.

10_1016_j_jmbbm_2024_106830.key_1:
- Human knee joint with meniscus implants being analyzed via finite element method
- Bone material: elastic modulus 300,000 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.3
- Cartilage material: elastic modulus 20 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.46
- Native meniscus material: elastic modulus 59 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.48
- Hydrogel implant material: silk fibroin/gelatine/decellularised meniscus-derived extracellular matrix, elastic modulus 0.1 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.5
- Polyurethane implant materials: PU 54 (elastic modulus 54 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.48) and PU 205 (elastic modulus 205 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.48)
- Hybrid implant configurations: hydrogel core with either PU 54 or PU 205 shell
- Simulation domain: human knee joint at full extension (0° flexion) based on OpenKnee(s) patient data
- Boundary conditions: tibia and fibula fixed at lower ends, quadriceps tendon fixed at upper end, axial compressive load of 1150 N and anterior-posterior compressive load of 135 N applied to femur
- Analysis focuses on Tresca shear stress, Von-Mises stress, peak contact pressure, and displacement distributions across femoral cartilage, menisci, and tibial cartilage
- Five implant configurations tested: hydrogel-only, PU 54-only, PU 205-only, hydrogel/PU 54 core-shell, and hydrogel/PU 205 core-shell
- Load application: short-term gait load at full knee joint extension with 1150 N axial compressive load and 135 N anterior-posterior compressive load
- Meniscus implant geometry based on patient-specific medial meniscus from OpenKnee(s) model
- Core-shell implant design features hydrogel core with PU shell replicating circumferential collagen fiber volume proportions of native meniscus

- Fixed constraints at lower ends of tibia and fibula

10_1016_j_jmbbm_2024_106830.key_4:

- Meniscus implant geometry derived from native medial meniscus of the same patient
- Core-shell implant design constrained to replicate circumferential collagen fiber volume proportions of human menisci

- Analysis restricted to five specific implant configurations (hydrogel-only, PU 54-only, PU 205-only, hydrogel/PU 54, hydrogel/PU 205)

- Analysis constrained to short-term gait load without considering complex movements like flexion and rotation

10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_852_525.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Gear trolley for material handling in engine manufacturing plant; comparative analysis of mild steel and E-glass fiber composite trolleys with electro pneumatic braking system.

- **Material / Medium:** Mild steel (AISI 1020) with strength 294 MPa and density 7.87 g/cc; E-glass fiber composite with strength 3440 MPa, density 2.45 g/cc, tensile strength 3.44 GPa, compressive strength 1.08 GPa, tensile modulus 72.3 GPa, composition 52-56% SiO₂, 12-16% Al₂O₃, 16-25% CaO, 8-13% B₂O₃.

- **Application & Importance:** Carrying engineering components (turbochargers, fuel injection pumps, cam shafts); current mild steel trolleys cause damage due to lack of braking mechanism and excessive weight; analysis focuses on stress, strain, and deformation under load to enable weight reduction and improved vibration damping.

- **Geometry / Domain:** Dimensions 1000mm length × 1000mm breadth × 1230mm height; gear placement rod length 500mm with 50mm diameter; profile thickness 3mm; supported on four 150mm diameter wheels; nine load-bearing rods; three composite layers of 1mm thickness for E-glass trolley; 3mm thickness for mild steel trolley; mesh with 123751 elements, minimum size 3mm, maximum face size 5mm.
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_852_525.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Fixed constraint applied to nine corner edges of the trolley; fixed support at corner edges for static structural analysis.
- **Loads / Excitations:** Uniform distributed load of 1500N applied on the top face of nine rods (representing 5× typical operational load); electro pneumatic braking system with 6 bar applied braking pressure; kinetic energy of 514.95J at 5 km/hr for braking analysis.
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Frictional contact between brake pads and disc (coefficient of friction 0.28–0.38); load transfer from applied force to structural frame through nine rods; electro-pneumatic actuation of double-acting piston cylinder.
- **Simulation Type:** Static structural analysis; 3D domain; linear material behavior; shell mesh with minimum size 3mm and maximum face size 5mm.
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_852_525.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Static structural deformation, stress distribution, and strain behavior under mechanical loading; vibration damping characteristics of composite vs. metal materials.
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Stress (MPa), strain (dimensionless), deformation (m), braking force (540N), kinetic energy absorption (514.95J), weight reduction percentage (68.86%–69%); extreme values: E-glass stress (35.165 to -43.755 MPa), strain (0.00080209 to -0.00095918), deformation (0.0017397 m); mild steel stress (35.133 to 0.00000758 MPa), strain (0.00021875 to 0.00000000014252), deformation (0.00017316 m).
- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve 69% weight reduction while maintaining stress/strain/deformation within permissible limits under 5× typical load (1500N); enable vibration damping improvement via E-glass composite; ensure safe emergency braking via electro pneumatic system with 6 bar pressure and 540N braking force.
10_4028_www_scientific_net_amm_852_525.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Trolley dimensions constrained to 1000mm length × 1000mm breadth × 1230mm height; gear placement rod length 500mm with 50mm diameter; profile thickness fixed at 3mm; 150mm diameter wheels; E-glass trolley composite layers limited to three 1mm-thick plies; ergonomic requirement for arm rest height at human hip level with foot clearance below bottom plate.
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Maximum allowable stress must remain within permissible limits under 1500N load (5× typical operational load); deformation limited to ≤0.0017397 m for E-glass and ≤0.00017316 m for mild steel; strain constrained to ≤0.00080209 for E-glass and ≤0.00021875 for mild steel; braking system must absorb 514.95J kinetic energy with 1.3 safety factor; impact factor ≥2 requires design to withstand ≥2× static stress.
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Mesh generation constrained to 123751 elements with minimum size 3mm and maximum face size 5mm; E-glass fiber orientation fixed at 45°/90°/45° cross-ply stacking sequence; electro-pneumatic braking system limited to 40mm piston diameter, 25mm stroke length, and 6 bar operating pressure; composite layer thickness restricted to 1mm per ply for E-glass trolley.

  - Stress wave propagation in homogeneous isotropic materials
  - Displacement-velocity field interactions in time-dependent structural dynamics
  - Dynamic soil-structure interaction in plate load testing

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Displacement field (u) and velocity field (v) distributions
  - Stress field (σ) distributions
  - L2 norm of errors in displacement and velocity fields (E_u(t_n), E_v(t_n))
  - Maximum plate deflection (d_max = 0.33 mm for E=65 MPa, 0.67 mm for E=32 MPa)

  - Spectral radius (ρ(A))
  - Convergence rates in space (nearly second-order) and time (third-order)
  - Error in displacement and velocity at specific points (e.g., midpoint P1)

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Achieve unconditional stability (spectral radius ρ(A) ≤ 1 for all time steps)
  - Maintain third-order temporal accuracy with minimal numerical dissipation
  - Reduce numerical dispersion (low relative frequency error)
  - Localize oscillations near discontinuities rather than propagating throughout domain
  - Minimize system size compared to two-field formulations while maintaining accuracy

  - Axisymmetric model with dimensions 5m × 3m for dynamic plate load test

  - Time domain requires non-uniform subdivision with intervals I_n = (t_n, t_{n+1}) and Δt_n = t_{n+1} - t_n

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** 
  - Method is constrained to small strain theory (where displacement-based and rate-form stress recovery techniques are equivalent)
  - No parameter to control numerical dissipation (unlike HHT-α method with parameter α)
  - Attenuates only middle band of frequencies while leaving low and high-frequency components practically unaffected (ρ_∞ = 1)
  - Velocity field discontinuity at time steps creates jump conditions that add artificial viscous damping
  - The method is limited to third-order accuracy in time (cannot achieve higher order with the current formulation)
  - For shock problems, Gibbs phenomenon causes overshooting/undershooting around discontinuities
  - The method requires strong satisfaction of displacement-velocity compatibility condition and displacement continuity in time
  - Velocity field time-continuity is satisfied only in a weak sense using kinetic energy norm

- **Process/Manufacturing:** 
  - Not applicable (computational method rather than physical manufacturing process)

- **Material**: Carbon Fiber Reinforced Plastic (CFRP) with density 1600 kg·m⁻³, elasticity modulus 71 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.30
- **Preparation**: Mixture of 8 parts polycaprolactam, 50 parts phenolic resin, 25 parts carbon fiber yarn, 1 part potassium persulfate, 10 parts antimony trioxide, 0.2 parts fatty alcohol polyoxymethylene ether, and 0.5 parts vinyl trimethoxy silane
- **Geometry**: Rectangular box structure with front and rear cover plates; internal modules; simplified model removed round holes, grooves, and non-bearing parts
- **Stress analysis**: Maximum equivalent stress 3.9012 MPa (Figure 4); maximum stress 1.091 MPa at bottom end of box (Table 2)
- **Deformation analysis**: Maximum deformation 7.5201×10⁻⁶ m (Figure 3); maximum deformation 0.00099 mm at bottom center (Table 2)
- **Weight**: 469.1 g for CFRP box body (Table 2)
- **Failure criteria**: Hashin failure criterion with four failure modes (fiber tensile, fiber compressive, matrix tensile, matrix compressive)
- **Assembly structure**: Three levels - component level, PCB/module level, plug-box level
- **Application focus**: Lightweight design for aviation equipment with emphasis on stress and deformation characteristics

- **Loads / Excitations**: None explicitly stated beyond equivalence to actual loads

- **Optimization Goal**: Verify feasibility of CFRP for aviation equipment lightweight design while maintaining mechanical performance within operational limits (stress below material yield strength, minimal deformation)
10_4028_www_scientific_net_kem_871_234.key_4:

- **Process/Manufacturing**: Preparation requires specific material ratios (8:50:25:1:10:0.2:0.5 for polycaprolactam:phenolic resin:carbon fiber:potassium persulfate:antimony trioxide:fatty alcohol polyoxymethylene ether:vinyl trimethoxy silane), curing at 150°C followed by 100°C, and injection molding process

- **Identity & Domain:** Lamellar bone tissue at sub-tissue level, specifically investigating elastic properties related to intra- and extra-fibrillar mineralization

- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Hydroxyapatite (HA) mineral with anisotropic elastic tensor (C₁₁=137 GPa, C₃₃=172 GPa, C₄₄=39.6 GPa, C₁₂=42.5 GPa, C₁₃=54.9 GPa)
  - Collagen matrix (E=1.2 GPa, ν=0.35)
  - NCP-water composite matrix (E=0.6 GPa, ν=0.35)
  - Mineralized collagen fibrils (MCFs) with 50 nm diameter

- **Application & Importance:** Understanding the mechanical implications of mineral distribution between intra- and extra-fibrillar phases on bone's elastic properties, as the relative contribution of each phase to tissue-level behavior remains poorly understood

- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Multiscale hierarchical structure spanning macroscale (trabecular/cortical bone), microscale (osteons), sub-microscale (lamellar bone), and nanoscale (HA crystals)
  - Representative Volume Elements (RVEs) at nanoscale for MCFs (based on Jäger-Fratzl and Landis models) and extra-fibrillar matrix
  - Extra-fibrillar matrix modeled as unidirectional HA platelets (L=150 nm, W=60-80 nm, T=5 nm)
  - Lamellar bone RVE as 250 nm cube with unidirectional MCFs embedded in extra-fibrillar matrix
  - Mineral distribution parameter (α) defined as Vfᴴᴬᴹᶜᶠ/Vfᴴᴬ, ranging from 0.1 to 0.3
  - Mineral volume fraction in lamella (Vfᴴᴬ) varying from 0.33 to 0.52
  - MCF volume fraction in lamella (Vfᴹᶜᶠ) varying from 0.37 to 0.69
10_1016_j_jmbbm_2022_105139.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Periodic boundary conditions (PBC) applied to all RVE models using four master nodes: Master-O (0,0,0), Master-X (W₀,0,0), Master-Y (0,L₀,0), Master-Z (0,0,H₀)
  - Boundary equations: u→(0,Y,Z) − u→(W₀,Y,Z) = U→_X_Master; u→(X,0,Z) − u→(X,L₀,Z) = U→_Y_Master; u→(X,Y,0) − u→(X,Y,H₀) = U→_Z_Master; u→(0,0,0) = (0,0,0)_Master
  - Perfectly bonded interface between mineral and collagen components (no interphase region considered)
  - Cylindrical material orientation near each fibril to simulate wrapping nature of mineral platelets around MCFs

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Axial tension with U→_Z = (0,0,δ) where δ is relative displacement in z-direction
  - Pure shear in XY plane with U→_x = (0,γL₀/2,0) and U→_Y = (γW₀/2,0,0) where γ is applied shear strain
  - Applied strain of ε₃₃ = 0.1% in MCFs axial direction (3-direction) for stress analysis
  - Applied strain of 0.1% in transverse direction for transverse stress analysis
  - Six loading modes applied to characterize anisotropic elastic constants: three axial tensions and three pure shear cases

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Perfectly bonded interface between mineral and collagen components
  - Material orientation in cylindrical coordinates near each fibril to represent wrapped mineral platelets
  - Discrete representation of mineral platelets within NCP-water matrix
  - Staggered arrangement of mineral crystals within collagen matrix in MCFs

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Two-scale homogenisation scheme (nanoscale and sub-micron scale)
  - 3D finite element analysis with periodic geometries and meshes
  - Linear elastic analysis in the elastic regime
  - Transversely isotropic material behavior for lamellar bone
  - Instantaneous property determination (no time-dependent effects considered)
  - Static analysis (no dynamic loading)

- **Material / Medium:** Coefficient function A ∈ L∞(Ω,ℝd×d) that is symmetric and positive definite with 0 < α ≤ β < ∞ satisfying α|η|2 ≤ (A(x)η) · η ≤ β|η|2 for x ∈ Ω, η ∈ ℝd. High-contrast channeled coefficients with maximum contrast up to 107 are specifically analyzed.
- **Application & Importance:** Solving elliptic PDEs with non-periodic coefficients having oscillations on multiple non-separated scales where classical finite element methods yield unsatisfactory approximations. The method addresses stability issues present in previous approaches like SLOD while maintaining super-localization properties.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Polygonal/polyhedral Lipschitz domain Ω ⊂ ℝd with d ∈ {2,3}. Numerical experiments conducted on Ω = (0,1)2 with Cartesian meshes. Domain contains high-contrast channels that may touch boundaries or stop before boundaries.

- **Simulation Type:** Non-Equilibrium Green's Function (NEGF) formalism; 2D simulation for cases without RDF/SR; 2.5D simulation for cases with RDF/SR; Real-space NEGF method for complex device structures; Coupled Mode Space (CMS) method as preconditioning; Steady-state DC analysis; Room temperature (300 K) quantum transport simulations

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** On-current (drain current at VDS = VGS = 0.6 V); Drain current per micrometer (A/μm); Standard deviation of on-current (device variability); Conduction band energy profiles; Electron density distributions; Current spectrum at source contact; Normalized on-current; I-V characteristics; Doping-dependent carrier injection efficiency; Comparison with IRDS HP specifications
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize on-current by minimizing quantum access resistance through optimal device geometry; Achieve on-current close to IRDS HP specifications for single nanosheet channel; Reduce device variability from 19.9% to 14.1% through quantum geometrical optimization; Optimize extension length (Lext) to balance carrier injection and extension resistance; Determine optimal contact depth to maximize carrier injection while minimizing Schottky barrier-induced depletion effects

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Constriction doping density threshold of ~10²⁰/cm³ for reflectionless contact; doping density at constriction constrained to range from 5×10¹⁷ to 5×10²⁰/cm³; scattering rate constrained to balance carrier injection (increases with moderate scattering) versus mobility degradation (at high scattering); on-current constrained to be below IRDS HP specifications for non-optimized devices; variability constrained to 19.9% for dumbbell-shaped devices versus 14.1% for optimized devices

- Subject: Gradient recovery method for finite element analysis using polygonal elements

- Domain: Convex polygonal regions with n vertices (P1, P2, ..., Pn) arranged counterclockwise
- Polygon types: Pentagons, hexagons, heptagons, and octagons demonstrated in numerical examples
- Superconvergence points: Centroids of sub-triangles formed by dividing canonical polygonal elements

- Boundary segments: ΓD and ΓN with ΓD ∪ ΓN = ∂Ω
- Interpolation method: Wachspress interpolation with rational function form
- Convergence rates: R≈2 for L2 norm; R≈1 for energy norm (original); R≈2.08/2.01 for energy norm with SPR
- Adaptive threshold: ηmax = 0.01 for error percentage in whole domain
- Gradient recovery: Superconvergent patch recovery (SPR) and polynomial preserving recovery (PPR) methods
- Physical applications: Topology optimization, large deformation, contact-impact, nearly incompressible material, crack propagation, polycrystalline ferroelectrics
10_1002_nme_6698.key_2:
- Dirichlet boundary condition: u = gD on ΓD
- Neumann boundary condition: ∂u/∂n = gN on ΓN with ΓD ∪ ΓN = ∂Ω
- Case 1 exact solution: u = (1 − x²)(1 − y²), f = 2(1 − x²) + 2(1 − y²) in Ω = [−1, 1]²
- Case 2 exact solution: u = −16e−(x²+y²)/0.32, f = 64(x² + y² − 0.32)e−(x²+y²)/0.32/0.34 in Ω = [−1, 1]²
- Adaptive analysis domain: Ω = [0, 1]² with ΓN = φ, ΓD = ∂Ω
- Adaptive Dirichlet boundary: u = x²(x − 1)²(e¹⁰ˣ² − 1)y²(y − 1)²(e¹⁰ʸ² − 1)
- Error threshold for adaptive refinement: ηmax = 0.01
- Initial adaptive mesh: 441 nodes (Figure 13(A))

- Analysis method: Finite element method with polygonal elements
- Mesh types: Uniform polygonal meshes and quadtree adaptive meshes
- Solution continuity: C⁰ continuous finite element solution with discontinuous gradient at element boundaries
- Error estimation: A posteriori error estimator using recovered gradients (η) with convergence criterion η ≤ ηmax

10_1016_j_polymertesting_2021_107181.key_2:

10_1002_eng2_70138.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Material flow in Friction Stir Welding (FSW) and Friction Stir Processing (FSP)
- **Material / Medium:** Aluminum alloys (6061, 2024-T3, 7075-T6, 5083-H111, 7050-T7651), stainless steel (304 L, 6005-T6), magnesium alloys (AZ31B), copper, transparent polymers (PMMA, PVC, polycarbonate), plasticine (analog material)
- **Application & Importance:** Understanding microstructural refinement and mechanical properties of welds, identifying defect formation mechanisms, optimizing tool design and welding parameters, improving weld quality and structural integrity, enabling dissimilar metal joining
- **Geometry / Domain:** FSW tool with non-consumable shoulder and pin; material flow zones including stir zone (SZ), heat-affected zone (HAZ), pin-affected zone (PAZ), and shoulder-affected zone (SAZ); advancing side (AS) and retreating side (RS) flow regions; various pin geometries (circular, threaded, square, triangular, hexagonal, tapered); shoulder geometries (flat, concave, convex, scrolled); weld cross-sections showing flow patterns at top, center, and bottom regions
10_1002_eng2_70138.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Mixed sticking/sliding contact state at tool-workpiece interface with material flow rate to tool rotation rate ratio ranging from 0.4 to 0.8
  - Sliding fraction ranging from 0.43 to 0.83 depending on welding parameters
  - Tool tilt angles varying from 0° (perpendicular to weld plate) to 2.5°
  - Zero tilt angle resulting in regular streamline patterns, while 2.5° tilt angle causing denser streamlines at retreating side
  - Tool tilt toward trailing side enhancing forging effect on material in that area
  - Shoulder end surface geometries: flat, convex, or concave (6°-10° inclined concave preferred)

- **Loads / Excitations:** 
  - Rotational speeds from 200 to 3000 rpm
  - Traverse speeds from 50 to 375 mm/min
  - Preheating treatment to reduce material viscosity
  - Tool tilt angle as process parameter (0° to 2.5°)
  - Axial force applied by tool shoulder

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** 
  - Mixed sticking/sliding conditions at tool-pin interface
  - Material flow differences between advancing side (AS) and retreating side (RS)
  - Shoulder-affected zone (SAZ) and pin-affected zone (PAZ) with distinct flow mechanisms
  - SAZ flow: stirring along downward circular trajectory affecting upper 1/3 of workpiece thickness
  - PAZ flow: shearing around pin lateral surface with downward motion
  - Transition zone requiring convergence and merging of SAZ and PAZ flows
  - Tool shoulder generates frictional heat and provides backing support

- **Simulation Type:** 
  - Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) for 2D and 3D metal flow modeling
  - Computational Solid Mechanics (CSM) approaches
  - Arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) method
  - Coupled Eulerian-Lagrangian (CEL) method for severe plastic deformation
  - 3D simulations for material flow analysis
  - Steady-state and transient analyses depending on specific application
10_1002_eng2_70138.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Material flow patterns and velocity distribution in FSW/FSP
  - Strain rate and strain distribution in welded materials
  - Temperature distribution and heat transfer during welding
  - Defect formation mechanisms (voids, tunnels, kissing bonds)
  - Material mixing behavior in similar and dissimilar metal welding
  - Intermetallic compound formation in dissimilar welding

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Material flow velocity (2-20 mm/s on advancing side, 1-5 mm/s on retreating side)
  - Strain rate distribution patterns
  - Temperature distribution across weld zones
  - Defect prediction (tunnel defects, voids, kissing bonds)
  - Material flow streamlines and patterns
  - Intermetallic compound thickness (0-10 μm range)
  - Stress distribution (485.6-582.7 MPa at flash roots)
  - Material flow continuity and filling cavity behavior

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Minimize defect formation (tunnel defects, voids, kissing bonds)
  - Maximize material flow uniformity across weld thickness
  - Optimize welding parameters (rotational speed, traverse speed, tilt angle)
  - Improve tool design for enhanced material flow (pin geometry, shoulder design)
  - Achieve defect-free welds with optimal mechanical properties
  - Minimize intermetallic compound thickness in dissimilar welding
  - Maximize material flow continuity to prevent void defects
  - Optimize heat input for balanced temperature distribution
10_1002_eng2_70138.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Tool pin diameter must exceed half the plate thickness to prevent lack of penetration defects
  - Tool tilt angle constrained to 0°-3° range (0° causes void defects, 1° causes voids/cavities, 2° yields defect-free welds, 3° produces defective welds)
  - Shoulder end surface geometries limited to flat, convex, or concave designs (6°-10° inclined concave preferred)
  - BTFSW requires pre-existing holes for tool entry due to inability to plunge directly into workpiece
  - Tool axis offset constrained to ±1 mm range when welding dissimilar aluminum alloys

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Nodal force must exceed 200 N and flow velocity must exceed 0.25 mm/s to avoid cavity defects in USSFSW
  - Material flow rate to tool rotation rate ratio constrained between 0.4 to 0.8
  - Rotational speed must exceed 300 rpm for tracer material to rotate around the pin
  - Intermetallic compound thickness must be minimized as excessive thickness from low traverse speeds reduces tensile strength
  - Thermal conductivity must be accurately calibrated to prevent erroneous temperature predictions
  - Maximum stress at flash roots reaches 485.6-582.7 MPa

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Tracer materials must match base material thermo-mechanical properties to avoid distorted flow results
  - CEL method requires tailored mass scaling factor with maximum 0.75 mm discrepancy for tunnel defects
  - Dissimilar welding requires accurate modeling of different physical/mechanical properties
  - Fine mesh size required for accuracy leads to long simulation times
  - BTFSW creates entry/exit zone discontinuity defects that must be managed
  - Tool wear alters geometry over time, changing flow characteristics (threaded tools lose vertical flow capability, circular tools reduce pin diameter)

10_1016_j_apacoust_2024_110196.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Sonic Black Hole (SBH) structure for broadband sound absorption; consists of five Basic Absorption Units (BAUs), each containing micro-perforated plate, folded cavity, micro-slit, and trapezoidal cavity
- **Material / Medium:** ABS 3D-printed structure; air as propagation medium; micro-perforated plate with hole radius 0.4 mm, thickness 2 mm, perforation rate 5%; duct radius 50 mm; SBH diameter 100 mm
- **Application & Importance:** Achieve near-perfect broadband sound absorption in low-frequency range; optimized structure achieves absorption coefficient >0.9 within 100-1600 Hz frequency band
- **Geometry / Domain:** Cylindrical structure with total length 570 mm; five BAUs with optimized cavity lengths (Lc1=132 mm, Lc2=121 mm, Lc3=104 mm, Lc4=113 mm, Lc5=100 mm); folded cavity widths (w1=9.2 mm, w2=7.3 mm, w3=6.0 mm, w4=5.9 mm); slit width 1.5 mm; partition inclination angle 5°; conical shell with power-law decaying radius
10_1016_j_apacoust_2024_110196.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Rigid end condition at SBH tip (U_l = 0)
  - Hard boundary conditions applied to non-perforated surfaces
  - Perfect matching layer connected to background pressure field at inlet section
  - Boundary layers with 6 layers and 1.2 stretch factor at micro-perforated plate and micro-slit edges
  - Duct divided into N equal-length segments for transfer matrix analysis

- **Loads / Excitations:** 
  - Incident planewave with 100-1600 Hz frequency range and 20 Pa amplitude
  - Harmonic excitation for theoretical analysis (p(x,t) = A e^(j(ωt-k0x)) + B e^(j(ωt+k0x)))
  - Unit amplitude incident wave for reflection coefficient calculations

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** 
  - Connection boundary conditions between adjacent sub-domains (i and i+1)
  - Coupling between folded cavity domain A, micro-slit domain B, and trapezoidal cavity domain C
  - Micro-perforated plate boundary condition at perforated areas
  - Interface conditions based on pressure continuity and velocity integration across boundaries

- **Simulation Type:** 
  - 3D acoustic finite element model with free tetrahedral mesh (235,647 domain elements)
  - Transient simulation for wave propagation analysis (Pressure Acoustics-Transient)
  - Narrow area acoustic physics in SBH structure, pressure acoustics in duct
  - Theoretical analysis using transfer matrix method (TMM) and volume decomposition and coupling method (VDCM)
  - Kriging surrogate modeling for parameter optimization within 100-1600 Hz frequency range
10_1016_j_apacoust_2024_110196.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Sound wave propagation through SBH structure with slow-sound effect
  - Acoustic energy dissipation in micro-perforated plates and micro-slits
  - Resonance behavior of folded cavities and trapezoidal cavities
  - Wave energy concentration at conical tip
  - Particle velocity distribution and power dissipation density
  - Pressure field transformation in duct with varying cross-section

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Absorption coefficient (α) across 100-1600 Hz frequency range
  - Sound pressure distribution (Pa) at specific frequencies
  - Total power dissipation density (W/m³) at resonance frequencies
  - Wave propagation distance versus time
  - Impedance of individual BAUs and overall SBH structure
  - Reflection coefficient for theoretical calculations
  - Particle velocity field magnitude and direction

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Maximize absorption coefficient to achieve near-perfect broadband sound absorption (>0.9) within 100-1600 Hz frequency range
  - Minimize objective function f_r = Σ(1-α) across 151 frequency points in 100-1600 Hz range
  - Implement weighted absorption coefficient (α_w) with priority for α > 0.95: α_w = α^0.6 (α > 0.95), 0.9 (0.9 < α ≤ 0.95), α (α < 0.9)
  - Optimize cavity dimensions (Lc1-Lc5, w1-w4) to achieve uniform absorption peak distribution across target frequency band

10_1016_j_rineng_2025_105372.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Aircraft hydraulic piston pump thermal distribution analysis
- **Material / Medium:** Hydraulic oil (density 770 kg/m³, dynamic viscosity 7.73E-4 Pa·s); Solid components include piston, slipper, swash plate, rotor, valve plate; Friction coefficients: piston pair (0.05), slipper pair (0.2), distribution pair (0.1), sealing surface (0.05)
- **Application & Importance:** Thermal distribution analysis to prevent performance degradation, material strength reduction, lubricant viscosity loss, oil film thinning, and structural damage from thermal cracks; critical for real-time monitoring and service life extension of aircraft hydraulic systems
- **Geometry / Domain:** Axial piston pump configuration with 10 pistons; includes housing, piston oil region, cylinder oil region, and solid heat source regions (piston, slipper, swash plate); complex geometry with friction interfaces at slipper-swash plate, piston-cylinder, and distribution plate; non-critical components like pump shell excluded from simulation to improve computational efficiency
10_1016_j_rineng_2025_105372.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Inlet temperature = 25°C; Initial temperature of other nodes = 50°C; Inlet flow speed = 1 m/s; Inlet pressure = 0.5 MPa; Outlet pressure = 20.6 MPa; Chamber oil pressure = 0.2 MPa; Boundary heat transfer coefficients defined at fluid-solid interfaces using empirical formulas; Inlet and outlet fluid temperatures, flow velocities, and environmental temperatures determined from experimental data
- **Loads / Excitations:** Rated speed = 4000 rpm; Swash plate angle = 14.5°; Piston suction flow rate = 2150 mm³/s; Frictional heat sources: slipper pair (10-15 W/mm²), piston pair (3-5 W/mm²), shear flow (0.5 W/mm²), slipper inner surface (3-5 W/mm²), outlet pressure differential (2-3 W/mm²), piston chamber leakage (2 W/mm²), sealing pair (0.6 W/mm²), housing radiation (0.1 W/mm²); Cooling effects: chamber suction cooling (200-240 W), piston suction cooling (20-30 W)
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Fluid-structure interaction between hydraulic oil and solid components; Frictional contact at slipper-swash plate interface; Frictional contact at piston-cylinder interface; Frictional contact at distribution plate-rotor interface; Heat exchange at fluid-solid interfaces; Oil film effects in clearance gaps with defined thickness (4 μm for distribution pair); Pressure distribution at contact surfaces
- **Simulation Type:** Transient thermal analysis; 3D spatial domain with equidistant hexahedral meshes; Finite difference method for coupled thermal-fluid-structure analysis; Time step-based iteration for temporal behavior; Spatial domain discretized with equidistant square grids; Boundary conditions applied at fluid-solid interfaces with heat transfer coefficients
10_1016_j_rineng_2025_105372.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Thermal conduction in solid domains; Fluid diffusion and heat transfer in fluid domains; Frictional heating mechanisms at solid interfaces; Coupled thermal-fluid-structure interaction; Temperature-dependent oil film behavior in clearance gaps; Pressure-induced heating from fluid flow
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Temperature distribution matrix; Sliding shoe temperature; Cavity oil temperature; Shell temperature; Outlet temperature; Return temperature; Shoe bottom temperature; Rotor outer surface temperature; Piston seal oil area temperature; Temperature gradients across friction interfaces; Flow field distribution; Concentration distribution of cooling flow; Temperature distribution heatmaps
- **Optimization Goal:** Reduce simulation duration to ~10% of conventional finite element methods while maintaining <5% temperature discrepancy; Enable real-time thermal monitoring under dynamic operating conditions; Provide rapid responsiveness to parameter variations (flow rate, rotational speed); Enhance operational performance and service longevity of hydraulic systems through accurate thermal field prediction; Minimize computational resources while maintaining engineering-relevant accuracy for fault diagnosis and performance optimization
10_1016_j_rineng_2025_105372.key_4:

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Solid friction interfaces reach ~300°C at high loads (4000 rpm, 30 MPa); Fluid regions stabilize at 70-80°C under high load; Slipper-swash plate junction temperatures can rise to 310°C; Maximum acceptable error <5% for 5-10s simulations; Cumulative errors exceed 2°C when simulation time >15s; Error must remain within 10% for engineering applications; Correction factor requires calibration using experimental data; Time step selection constrained by computational accuracy and available computation time
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Oil film thickness for distribution pair approximated as uniform 4μm; Friction coefficients determined through specialized testing or estimated values; Heat exchange coefficient requires adjustment to match measured values; Friction coefficient and contact thermal resistance must be redefined for high-temperature regions; Boundary heat transfer coefficients at fluid-solid interfaces require empirical formulas; Pump material and lubrication oil selection directly influence heat concentration; Meshing strategy selected based on model complexity, boundary size, and required computational precision

10_1016_j_mtchem_2024_101972.key_1:

- Five distinct designs (A-E) with three strut thicknesses (0.10 mm, 0.15 mm, 0.20 mm), featuring open-cell (A-D) and closed-cell (E) configurations, 2.8 mm inner diameter, and varying strut crown geometries and connector patterns
10_1016_j_mtchem_2024_101972.key_2:

- Displacement of the balloon reduced to zero to simulate deflation
- Frictionless contact between inner surface of stent (contact) and outer surface of balloon (target)
- Target elements: Targe 170; Contact elements: Conta 174
- Balloon modeled with 0.10 mm thin surface
- Mooney-Rivlin 2 hyperplastic model for balloon (C₁₀ = 1.07 MPa, C₀₁ = 0.71 MPa, D₁ = 0 MPa)
- Multilinear isotropic hardening elastic-plastic model for thermoplastic materials

10_1016_j_mtchem_2024_101972.key_3:

- Radial recoil ratio (RRR), foreshortening percentage, von Mises stress (peak and residual), equivalent plastic strain

10_1016_j_mtchem_2024_101972.key_4:

10_1016_j_finel_2018_04_001.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Graphene-based nanostructures, specifically graphene sheets, carbon nanotubes (CNTs), and carbon nanocones (CNCs)
- **Material / Medium:** Graphene with hyperelastic properties; Material constants for GGA: α̂=1.53, ε=93.84 N/m, μ₀=172.18 N/m, μ₁=27.03 N/m, β̂=5.16, η₀=94.65 N/m, η₁=4393.26 N/m; For LDA: α̂=1.38, ε=116.43 N/m, μ₀=164.17 N/m, μ₁=17.31 N/m, β̂=6.22, η₀=86.9 N/m, η₁=3611.5 N/m; Bending stiffness: FGBP=0.133 nN·nm, SGBP=0.225 nN·nm, QM=0.238 nN·nm
- **Application & Importance:** Analysis for sensor applications, energy storage devices, healthcare, corrosion-resistant coatings, and composite material enhancement; Specifically demonstrates CNCs as superior AFM tips with 18.44× higher buckling force than CNTs; Focus on buckling/post-buckling behavior under mechanical loading
- **Geometry / Domain:** CNTs: Cylindrical structures defined by chirality parameters (n,m) with specific examples CNT(10,10) length 10 nm, CNT(12,6) length 6.74 nm, CNT(15,15) length 38.19 nm; CNCs: Conical structures with apex angle θ_apex and length L, examples CNC(19.2°) length 12.04 nm tip radius 1 nm, CNC(38.94°) length 38.19 nm; Apex angles discrete values: θ_apex = 2·arcsin(1 - dθ/360); Buckling geometry shows 180° rotational symmetry below θ=10° and 120° symmetry above θ=10°
10_1016_j_finel_2018_04_001.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** End faces of CNTs/CNCs kept rigid and planar; CNTs/CNCs allowed axial deformation to avoid net axial force; For twisting simulations, axial length kept fixed; CNCs simply supported in contact simulations; Wall is rigid; Quadratic NURBS meshes used with specific element counts (200×200 for CNT bending, 100×100 for CNT twisting, 320×120 for CNT contact convergence study, 120×120 for CNC bending, 180×180 for CNC twisting, 250×150 for CNC contact)
- **Loads / Excitations:** Bending angle applied equally at both faces; Twisting angle applied equally at both faces; Wall displacement (u_wall) as loading parameter; Lennard-Jones potential: Ψ(VdW)(h) = -Γ[3/2(h₀/r)³ - 1/2(h₀/r)⁹] with h₀ = 0.34 nm, Γ = 0.14 N/m; Contact angle θ_w = 17.45°
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Coarse grained contact model (CGCM) with equivalent half space potential; Relation between axial force F_A and normal force F_N: F_N = F_A / cos(θ_w); Buckling points identified by membrane energy/total energy ratio; Two instabilities present: buckling/unbuckling (points B & C) and jump-to/jump-off-contact (points A & D); CNT/CNC with identical tip radius for comparable measurement precision
- **Simulation Type:** Rotation-free isogeometric shell formulation; Quadratic NURBS elements; Nonlinear analysis with modified arc-length method and line-search for convergence; No special treatment against locking; Mesh convergence studies performed; Buckling and post-buckling behavior captured; Wall displacement controlled loading (loading/unloading paths)
10_1016_j_finel_2018_04_001.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Nonlinear hyperelastic behavior of graphene-based structures; Buckling and post-buckling phenomena; Contact mechanics with Lennard-Jones wall; Bending and twisting deformation; Membrane and bending energy distribution; Stress-strain response under uniaxial tension and pure shear
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Strain energy per atom (eV/atom); Membrane energy/total energy ratio; Axial force (nN); Normal contact force (nN); Perpendicular force (nN); Stress components σ₁₁ and σ₂₂ (N/m); Buckling angles (bending: θ=3.48° at tip, θ=3.9° at end; twisting: θ≈7° and θ≈9.85°); Relative error of energy; Deformed geometries; Contact force vs wall displacement; Twist/bending angle vs strain energy
- **Optimization Goal:** Develop material model that is 1.5× faster than previous model while maintaining accuracy; Demonstrate CNCs as superior AFM tips with buckling force 18.44× higher than CNTs; Accurately capture buckling points and post-buckling behavior; Enable efficient simulation of graphene-based structures for sensor applications, energy storage, and composite material enhancement
10_1016_j_finel_2018_04_001.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** CNTs defined by chirality parameters (n,m) with specific examples: CNT(10,10) length 10 nm, CNT(12,6) length 6.74 nm, CNT(15,15) length 38.19 nm; CNC apex angles limited to discrete values: θ_apex = 2·arcsin(1 - dθ/360) where dθ ∈ {60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300°}; Examples: CNC(19.2°) length 12.04 nm tip radius 1 nm, CNC(38.94°) length 38.19 nm; Contact angle θ_w = 17.45°; CNTs/CNCs with identical tip radius selected for comparable measurement precision
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Valid for strains up to 25% (experimental limit); Buckling force of CNC is 18.44× higher than CNT (23.41 nN vs 1.27 nN); Extremum axial force 1.21 nN and perpendicular force -0.38 nN for CNT contact; Membrane energy/total energy ratio used to identify buckling points; CNT buckles at 3.48° at tip and 3.9° at end for bending; CNC buckles at approximately 7° and 9.85° for twisting; Material model calibrated for GGA/LDA parameters with specific constants (α̂, ε, μ₀, μ₁, β̂, η₀, η₁)
- **Process/Manufacturing:** CNTs have discrete chiralities and radii that can be mass-produced with precise dimensions; No special treatment against locking - requires sufficiently fine quadratic NURBS meshes; Minimum mesh requirements: 200×200 elements for CNT bending (0.1% energy error), 100×100 for CNT twisting (0.01% energy error), 320×120 for CNT contact; Convergence requires modified arc-length method and line-search even with small load steps; Material behavior validated up to 25% strain where deformation remains elastic and reversible

10_1016_j_finel_2017_01_001.key_1:
- Identity & Domain: Space structural component for thermal analysis; specifically the Back Telescope Assembly (BTA) of Meteosat Third Generation Infrared Sounder instrument
- Material / Medium: Aluminum with thermal conductivity k = 170 W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹ and specific heat cₚ = 900 J·kg⁻¹·K⁻¹; emissivity ε = 1 (assumed for test cases); radiative environment temperature of -100°C
- Application & Importance: Thermal control of precision optical instruments where temperature must be accurately computed to maintain mirror alignment; reducing computational burden of finite element thermal analysis with radiation; enabling thermo-structural analysis through detailed temperature recovery
- Geometry / Domain: Complex 3D space structure with 35,217 nodes in detailed mesh; includes beam-like components and mirror support structures; analyzed as 1D cantilever beam (1m long, 1cm square cross-section), 2D radial radiating fin, and full 3D BTA assembly
10_1016_j_finel_2017_01_001.key_2:
- Boundaries & Constraints: Fixed temperature of 20°C at x=0 for 1D beam; insulated boundary condition (dT/dx|L=0) at beam tip; fixed temperature of 20°C on inner edge of radial fin; insulated boundary condition (dT/dr|r=r_e=0) at fin outer edge; fixed temperature of 20°C at one end of BTA structure; radiative environment temperature of -100°C for all test cases
- Loads / Excitations: 1W thermal load spread uniformly along 1D beam; 10W applied at opposite mounting interface of BTA structure; radiative exchange with environment (emissivity ε=1); constant thickness for radial fin
- Interactions / Interfaces: Radiative heat exchange between external surfaces and environment; conductive heat transfer within structures; thermal load uniformly distributed over super nodes
- Simulation Type: Steady-state and transient thermal analysis; 1D cantilever beam, 2D radial fin, and 3D BTA structure; conductive-radiative coupled heat transfer; nonlinear analysis due to radiative heat transfer (T⁴ term); temperature-dependent properties handling similar to ESATAN-TMS
10_1016_j_finel_2017_01_001.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Conductive-radiative heat transfer in space structures; temperature field distribution; radiative exchange between surfaces with Monte Carlo ray-tracing; coupled thermal analysis involving both conduction and radiation mechanisms
- Target Outputs (Metrics): Temperature distribution throughout structures; RMS error (ΔT,RMS) between detailed and recovered solutions; temperature gradients; radiative exchange factors (REFs); detailed mesh temperatures recovered from super nodes; reduction factor (ratio of #nodes/#super-nodes)
- Optimization Goal: Reduce computational burden by decreasing number of radiative exchange factors by four orders of magnitude and number of nodes by two orders of magnitude while maintaining temperature accuracy (target error <0.3K); enable direct use of structural FE mesh for thermal analysis without separate thermal model creation; facilitate thermo-structural analysis through detailed temperature recovery; achieve accurate results with 4× fewer nodes than ESATAN-TMS (0.3K error vs. 2.6K)
10_1016_j_finel_2017_01_001.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: Clusters cannot cross sharp edges or junctions (edges sharing more than 2 elements) for 2D parts; 3D clusters may contain faces on different sides; user-defined number of clusters for each model part; 1D cantilever beam has 1m length with 1cm square cross-section; radial fin has defined inner and outer edges; Back Telescope Assembly structure has 35,217-node detailed mesh
- Performance/Physics Limits: Uniform thermal load assumption required on each super node for exact reduction/recovery; super nodes must be independent (no linear combinations between them making matrix singular); for 3D clusters with expected large thermal gradients between center and external faces, dedicated 2D surface super nodes must be added; emissivity assumed to be 1 in test cases; maximum error tolerance of 0.3K demonstrated for BTA structure (vs. 2.6K with LPM)
- Process/Manufacturing: CAD model requires cleaning and structural FE mesh adaptation; thermal properties must be provided; critical surfaces require quadric fitting for accurate ray-tracing; structural mesh needs minor modifications to integrate thermal components like MLI and thermo-optical properties; selective quadric fitting and FE mesh clustering required as preprocessing steps; Monte Carlo ray-tracing used for computing radiative exchange factors between super nodes

- Initial condition: u(x,y,0) = u₀(x,y) for (x,y) ∈ Ω̄
- Computational domain: Ω = [xₗ, xᵣ] × [yₗ, yᵣ] (rectangular domain)

- Conservative properties: Q(t) = ||u(·,t)|| = ||u₀|| = Q(0) (charge conservation) and E(t) = ||u(·,t)||²_H¹ + (1/2)||u(·,t)||⁴_L⁴ = E(0) (energy conservation)

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109458.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Composite laminates analyzed using 3-D finite element (FE) method with port-reduced static condensation (PR-SC) and port-reduced static condensation reduced basis element (PR-SCRBE) techniques
- **Material / Medium:** Unidirectional transversely isotropic composite materials characterized by five independent properties: fiber-directional Young's modulus (E₁), fiber-perpendicular-directional Young's modulus (E₂), in-plane shear modulus (G₁₂), in-plane Poisson's ratio (ν₁₂), and out-of-plane Poisson's ratio (ν₂₃); specific materials include CCF300/5228A, IM7/8552, T700/epoxy, and T300/M21; parameter ranges: E₁ [105,180] kN/mm², E₂ [7.5,15.5] kN/mm², G₁₂ [3.5,7.0] kN/mm², ν₁₂ [0.20,0.36], ν₂₃ [0.20,0.60], fiber angle θ [-90,+90]°
- **Application & Importance:** Parametric studies and design optimization of composite laminates in automotive, shipbuilding, and aerospace industries; addresses computational demand of traditional 3-D FE analysis for repetitive simulations requiring changes in layer materials (including fiber angles), number of layers, and stacking sequence
- **Geometry / Domain:** Two test configurations: (1) Three-point bending test with 65 mm length, 10 mm width, 0.225 mm height composite plate, simply supported at ±12.5 mm from center, with distributed load over ±1 mm from center; (2) Tensile test with 60 mm length, 30 mm width, 0.125 mm height composite plate with 5 mm diameter central hole, outer edges fixed in e₃ direction, right edge stretched by u₁ = 0.6 mm; test systems include 4-12 layers for bending test and 4-8 layers for tensile test; domain of interest for tensile test is 12 mm × 12 mm square region around the hole
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109458.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Three-point bending test: Simply supported along lines at ±12.5 mm from plate center; left edge constrained with u₁ = u₂ = 0; right edge constrained with u₂ = u₃ = 0
  - Tensile test: Outer edges fixed in e₃ direction; constrained at x₁ = -30 mm and y₁ = -15 mm in e₁ and e₂ directions respectively; right edge displacement u₁ = 0.6 mm at x₁ = +30 mm
  - Top component (bending test): û_top,1 = û_top,2 = 0
  - Bottom component (bending test): û_bottom,2 = û_bottom,3 = 0
  - Tensile test component: û_lamina,1 = û_lamina,3 = 0 and û_lamina,2 = û_lamina,3 = 0 at different boundaries

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Three-point bending test: Uniformly distributed load p over rectangular region within ±1 mm from center; load range p ∈ [0,1] N/mm² for top layer
  - Tensile test: Displacement-controlled loading with u₁ = 0.6 mm applied at right edge
  - Lifting function for tensile test: u_L = (0.01x₁ + 0.3, 0, 0) mm to satisfy Dirichlet boundary condition

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Component ports with geometric compatibility requirements: (i) Instantiated components should not overlap; (ii) Connected ports must perfectly align; (iii) System assembly must remain invariant under parametric variation
  - Port connections between layers defined by index set π where π_p = {(i',j')} for non-shared ports and π_p = {(i',j'), (i'',j'')} for shared ports
  - System assembly using archetype components with upper and lower ports for connection

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 3-D linear elastostatic analysis
  - Steady-state conditions (no time-dependent effects mentioned)
  - Static analysis with no dynamic considerations
  - Linear material behavior with parameterized constitutive tensor depending on material properties and fiber angle
  - Weak form formulations solved using finite element method with static condensation techniques
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109458.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 3-D linear elastostatic behavior of composite laminates under mechanical loading, including displacement fields and stress distributions with particular focus on interlaminar stresses at layer interfaces

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Displacement magnitude fields (u) in mm
  - Stress magnitude fields (σ) in kPa including σ₁₁, σ₂₂, σ₃₃, σ₁₂, σ₁₃, σ₂₃
  - Interlaminar shear stresses (σ₁₃, σ₂₃) and normal stresses (σ₃₃)
  - Mean and maximum absolute errors (AEs) of displacement and stress magnitudes compared to full FE analysis
  - Computational time and dimension reduction ratios
  - Through-the-thickness stress distributions at specific locations

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Achieve Lego-like flexibility to rapidly change layer materials (including fiber angles), number of layers, and stacking sequence while maintaining high accuracy
  - Balance between computational speedup (up to 75.85× for PR-SCRBE) and accuracy for composite laminate analysis
  - Enable many-query applications (design optimization, virtual testing) through rapid parametric analysis of composite structures
  - Provide option to select between PR-SC (for accuracy) and PR-SCRBE (for efficiency) based on application requirements
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109458.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Three-point bending test: 65 mm length, 10 mm width, 0.225 mm height composite plate with supports at ±12.5 mm from center
  - Tensile test: 60 mm length, 30 mm width, 0.125 mm height composite plate with 5 mm diameter central hole
  - Domain of interest for tensile test limited to 12 mm × 12 mm square region around the hole
  - Material parameter ranges constrained to: E₁ [105,180] kN/mm², E₂ [7.5,15.5] kN/mm², G₁₂ [3.5,7.0] kN/mm², ν₁₂ [0.20,0.36], ν₂₃ [0.20,0.60], fiber angle θ [-90,+90]°
  - System-based training requires minimum n layers matching target system (Model C in Fig. 3 is invalid with fewer layers)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Geometric compatibility requirements: (i) Instantiated components must not overlap; (ii) Connected ports must perfectly align; (iii) System assembly must remain invariant under parametric variation
  - PR-SCRBE accuracy degrades when component-level PDE solutions are highly nonlinear with respect to parameters (e.g., fiber angle)
  - PR-SCRBE shows significantly higher errors for tensile test compared to three-point bending test due to "chaotic bubble functions" with parameter-dependent changes and significant fluctuations across the domain
  - Maximum computational speedup for PR-SCRBE is limited to factors of 17.91-75.85 (bending test) and 6.00-12.60 (tensile test)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**

  - Offline PR-SCRBE training requires approximately 128.77 hours (6.7× longer than PR-SC training)
  - PR-SCRBE analysis is "significantly demanding" for offline training compared to PR-SC
  - Port reduction requires 6 additional DOFs to account for rigid body motions beyond the base 100 DOFs obtained by pivoted Cholesky decomposition

10_1016_j_ymssp_2018_07_013.key_1:

  - Ballast: Vertical translational stiffness 9×10⁷ N/m, lateral translational stiffness 1×10⁸ N/m, longitudinal translational stiffness 9.5×10⁸ N/m, vertical rotational stiffness 2.5×10⁸ N·m/rad, lateral/longitudinal rotational stiffness 2×10⁸ N·m/rad
  - Half-sleeper mass: 122 kg

- **Application & Importance:**

  - Required for acoustic radiation prediction from rail and wheel vibrations
  - Addresses rail and wheel roughness as displacement excitation sources

- **Geometry / Domain:**

  - Deformable cross-section with 137-node mesh
  - Periodic generic element: longitudinal rail section with half-sleeper attachments
  - Support modeled as mass-spring system with 6 degrees of freedom for ballast
  - Pads modeled with 3 translation springs (x, y, z axes)
  - Excitation at upper rail head surface, response measured below rail foot
  - Frequency range: 50-5000 Hz with 10 Hz linear spacing
  - Vibration modes: in-phase rail/sleeper (Mode 1), 180° out-of-phase (Mode 2), foot flapping (high-frequency vertical), web bending (high-frequency lateral)
10_1016_j_ymssp_2018_07_013.key_2:

  - Continuity of stress and displacement imposed between generic elements i and i+1
  - Floquet's theorem applied to express periodicity hypothesis in longitudinal direction
  - Force applied between two generic elements or on a generic element between sleepers
  - Displacement continuity enforced at junctions between consecutive generic elements

  - Second-Order Arnoldi Reduction (SOAR) used for model reduction

10_1016_j_finel_2024_104165.key_1:
