- **Loads / Excitations:** Incident plane wave from 7×7 loudspeaker array (transducers spaced 100 mm apart); audio signal at specific frequency amplified by amplifier; stepper displacement mechanism (SDM) driving microphone at 8 mm step size (≈1/12 wavelength); reference sound pressure P_ref = 20 μPa
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Acoustic waves emitted from loudspeaker array pass through ACCM and measured by microphone; 3D printed photosensitive resin metasurface with 16×16 unit array (256 total units); reconfigurable units with rotational inner/outer cylinders for phase modulation
- **Simulation Type:** 3D finite element simulation using COMSOL Multiphysics; full-wave simulation; far-field approximation for radiation pattern analysis; discrete particle swarm optimization (DPSO) with 50 particles, 500 iterations termination condition, and 16×16 coding units per particle; free-field environment in anechoic chamber
10_1016_j_ymssp_2025_112710.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Acoustic wave propagation and scattering from arbitrarily curved coding metasurfaces; 3D far-field radiation pattern calculation using Huygens-Fresnel principle
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Sound pressure field (P); normalized energy intensity field (P̄² = P/||P_max||²); sound pressure level (L = 20log₁₀(P/P_ref) with P_ref = 20 μPa); radiation patterns in elevation (θ) and azimuth (φ); normalized diffusion coefficient Z ∈ [0,1] for omnidirectional scattering; side lobe energy intensity (E_SL)
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize Z = min(E(φ₁,θ₁), E(φ₁,-θ₁), ..., E(φₙ,θₙ), E(φₙ,-θₙ)) for symmetric beamforming; maximize Z = min(E(φ₁,θ₁), E(φ₁,-θ₁), ..., E(φₙ,θₙ), E(φₙ,-θₙ)) - E_SL for asymmetric beamforming; maximize radiation uniformity through normalized diffusion coefficient Z for omnidirectional scattering; achieve specific beam directions including (0°, ±30°), (30°, ±41°), (0°, 60°), and multi-beam configurations
10_1016_j_ymssp_2025_112710.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** 16×16 unit array (256 total units); unit spacing of 0.4λ to prevent aliasing; spinning paraboloid shape function z(x,y) = a(x² + y²) with a > 0 (convex) and a < 0 (concave); arbitrary surface example z(x,y) = 0.3λ(sin x + sin y); metasurface placed 800 mm from loudspeaker array; measurement area 300 mm from metasurface; microphone step size = 8 mm (≈1/12 wavelength)
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Transmittance values ξmn = 0.89 (unit "0") and 0.71 (unit "1"); cross-sectional angles β0 = 2° (unit "0") and β1 = 31° (unit "1"); reference sound pressure P_ref = 20 μPa; normalized diffusion coefficient Z ∈ [0,1]; side lobe recognized only when E_SL > 0.4 × minimum target direction intensity; 1-bit coding restricts to phase shifts of 0 or π; incident plane wave assumption in theoretical derivation

10_1016_j_finel_2021_103692.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Sound propagation in rigid-walled ducts with uniform and slowly varying cross-sections
- **Material / Medium:** Subsonic gas flow with density ρ₀(z), sound celerity c(z), ratio of specific heats γ; Mach numbers up to 0.3; irrotational flow conditions
- **Application & Importance:** Acoustic analysis for industrial applications including aircraft engines; reducing computational time of finite element models while maintaining accuracy for duct acoustics
- **Geometry / Domain:** Cylindrical duct with circular cross-section; uniform ducts with 0.1 m radius; slowly varying ducts with radius linearly decreasing from 0.1 m at z=0 to 0.06 m at z=1.5 m; axial length up to 1.5 m; 3D domain with axial coordinate z as propagation direction
10_1016_j_finel_2021_103692.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Hard-walled duct (infinite wall impedance); uniform duct with circular cross-section of 0.1 m radius; slowly varying duct with radius linearly decreasing from 0.1 m at z=0 to 0.06 m at z=1.5 m; pressure vector with L2 norm ||p₀||₂ = 1 applied at z=0; totally reflecting termination at z=L; reflection coefficient R imposed at z=L; axial coordinate z as propagation direction; duct length 1.5 m for varying cross-section case
- **Loads / Excitations:** Harmonic time-dependent acoustic perturbations; pressure excitation at z=0; input mode (2,0) for slowly varying duct cases; frequency range up to 7000 Hz with 400 frequency steps; frequencies from 50 Hz to 5000 Hz for uniform duct validation
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Subsonic irrotational flow described by v̄ = U(z) + ve^(iωt); continuity equation ∇(ρ₀U) = 0; energy equation (1/2)|U|² + c²/(γ-1) = E; forward and backward propagating waves; local wavenumber calculation at Gauss-Legendre integration points; no intermodal scattering due to slow geometry variation; no reflection throughout varying cross-section except at termination
- **Simulation Type:** Frequency domain analysis; linear acoustic analysis with small perturbations; 3D finite element modeling; reduced-order modeling using wave finite element method; steady-state harmonic analysis; uniform ducts treated as periodic waveguides; slowly varying ducts analyzed using local eigenvalue problems with Gauss-Legendre quadrature integration; Mach numbers up to 0.3 for validation
10_1016_j_finel_2021_103692.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Sound wave propagation in ducts with mean flow; solution of the convected Helmholtz equation for acoustic field; wave propagation in rigid-walled ducts with uniform and slowly varying cross-sections
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Axial wavenumbers (k_z) for various modes (0,0), (1,0), (2,0), (0,1); frequency response functions (FRFs); pressure amplitude distributions; iso-pressure contours; Mach number distribution; density distribution; wave mode shapes; wave amplitudes; cut-on/cut-off transitions; forward and backward propagating wave characteristics
- **Optimization Goal:** Reduce computational time of finite element analysis while maintaining accuracy (407s vs 3863s for full FE model); minimize model size through reduced-order modeling; enable analysis of complex geometries where analytical solutions are unavailable; maintain less than 3% average error compared to analytical solutions for wavenumbers
10_1016_j_finel_2021_103692.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Duct geometry must be slowly varying (change on length scale much larger than wavelength); circular cross-sections used for validation (0.1 m radius for uniform duct); linear radius variation from 0.1 m at z=0 to 0.06 m at z=1.5 m for varying duct case; identical mesh distribution required for cross-sectional interfaces; no abrupt geometry changes permitted; maximum frequency limited by minimum wavelength (requiring at least 6 elements per wavelength)
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Subsonic flow conditions (Mach numbers up to 0.3 validated); modes must remain cut-on throughout entire duct length; no cut-on/cut-off transitions allowed; no intermodal scattering considered; irrotational flow assumption; transversal mesh density must scale with minimum wavelength/largest cross-section dimensions; method breaks down at transition points where reflection of cut-on modes and transmission of cut-off modes occur; maximum frequency limited by mesh resolution
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Structured mesh of 84 hexahedron elements with linear interpolation for reduced model; full 3D FE model requires 42,000 elements; eigenvalue problem solved 400 times per evaluation point; frequency analysis performed over 400 frequency steps; Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 3 points used for numerical integration; 9 Wave Finite Element evaluations required for slowly varying duct case; minimum of 6 elements per wavelength required for numerical stability; method cannot handle sudden geometry changes or trapped modes phenomena

10_1016_j_finel_2021_103558.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Topology optimization for structures manufactured via laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing, with focus on part distortion prediction and mitigation
- **Material / Medium:** AlSi10Mg alloy with Young's modulus 75 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.34; inherent strain components ε_x = ε_y = -0.0025, ε_z = 0
- **Application & Importance:** Reducing dimensional inaccuracy and residual stress in AM parts; enabling high-performance structural designs while accounting for manufacturing-induced distortion; validating through experimental measurement of vertical deformation and residual stress
- **Geometry / Domain:** Cantilever specimens (beam thickness t = 3 mm and 5 mm); cubic specimens (10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm); fixed design domains for optimization (100×50 for cantilever model, 300×50 for MBB beam model); layer-by-layer building process with 0.03 mm material layer thickness; mesh models with element sizes of 0.25 mm and 1.0 mm; laser scan pattern with 67° rotation between layers
10_1016_j_finel_2021_103558.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Fixed displacement boundary condition at bottom surface (Γ_u); fixed displacement at bottom of left column during cutting process; traction boundary condition (Γ_t) with applied traction t = 10; zero traction on boundaries other than Γ_t and Γ_v; volume constraint limited to 50% of fixed design domain volume; inactive domain (Ω_I) with Young's modulus of 0.01 MPa; boundary conditions defined for fixed design domains (Γ_v for cantilever model, corner supports for MBB beam model)
- **Loads / Excitations:** Inherent strain components (ε_x = ε_y = -0.0025, ε_z = 0); applied traction t = 10; laser scanning pattern with 67° rotation between layers; material layer thickness of 0.03 mm; elastic strain released by cutting
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Ersatz material approach with smooth transition between material and void domains (width parameter w = 0.5); active domain (Ω_A) and inactive domain (Ω_I) interface; boundary between material and void domains with transition width; fixed displacement boundary at substrate interface
- **Simulation Type:** 2D topology optimization; linear elastic analysis using inherent strain method; multi-scale modeling (analysis domain divided into fewer layers than actual manufacturing layers); layer-by-layer domain activation process; steady-state elasticity problems; transient analysis for level set function update; topology optimization using level set method with reaction-diffusion equation
10_1016_j_finel_2021_103558.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Linear elastic analysis using inherent strain method to predict residual stress and distortion in additive manufacturing; layer-by-layer domain activation with inherent strain application; structural deformation analysis; topology optimization with level set method
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Vertical deformation (mm); residual stress distribution (MPa); normalized objective function values (F, F_MC, F_AM); volume fraction; maximum displacement (|u_max|); distortion distribution (mm); convergence history of objective functions; optimal configurations for different weighting coefficients (γ) and regularization parameters (τ)
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize the combined objective function F = (1-γ)F_MC + γF_AM, where F_MC represents mean compliance and F_AM represents part distortion; achieve minimum mean compliance while controlling part distortion in additive manufacturing; maintain volume constraint at 50% of fixed design domain; optimize geometric complexity through regularization parameter τ while balancing distortion reduction and structural performance through weighting coefficient γ
10_1016_j_finel_2021_103558.key_4:

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Inherent strain components ε_x = ε_y = -0.0025, ε_z = 0; material properties fixed at Young's modulus = 75 GPa and Poisson's ratio = 0.34; active domain Young's modulus = 75 GPa, inactive domain Young's modulus = 0.01 MPa; maximum displacement values reported for different γ settings (e.g., |u_max| = 0.135 for γ = 0 in cantilever model); weighting parameter β = 5 for distortion objective function
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Laser powder bed fusion process with 67° layer rotation between successive layers; actual material layer thickness = 0.03 mm; element size per layer set to 0.25 mm (10× actual layer thickness) or 1.0 mm (30× actual layer thickness) for computational efficiency; analysis domain divided into fewer layers than actual manufacturing layers due to computational costs; fabrication using EOSINT M280 machine with 400 W fiber laser (beam diameter ≈ 0.1 mm); wire electric discharge machining (WEDM) used for cutting specimens to measure elastic strain release; regularization parameter τ examined at values 1×10^-4 and 1×10^-3

10_1016_j_cad_2014_11_011.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Adaptive meshing for finite element analysis (FEA) of heterogeneous materials, specifically 2D planar regions with spatially varying material compositions. Case studies include turbine blade geometries and arch-shaped domains.
- **Material / Medium:** Heterogeneous material systems including ceramic (blue) and metal (red) composites; Functionally Graded Materials (FGMs); Al₂O₃ and Ni with properties: thermal conductivity (Al₂O₃: 35 W/m/K, Ni: 90.7 W/m/K), elastic modulus (Al₂O₃: 393 GPa, Ni: 199.5 GPa), Poisson ratio (Al₂O₃: 0.25, Ni: 0.3), thermal expansion coefficient (Al₂O₃: 7.4×10⁻⁶/K, Ni: 15.4×10⁻⁶/K).
- **Application & Importance:** To minimize mesh complexity while maintaining FEA accuracy for heterogeneous materials by distributing material composition variation across elements as equally as possible; enables significant mesh reduction without sacrificing analysis quality (e.g., 32% reduction demonstrated in case study 4).
- **Geometry / Domain:** 2D planar domains with curved boundaries including arch-shaped profiles, turbine blade geometry, and domains with internal cutouts; material distribution follows power functions (e.g., f(P) = (b-yP/b)²), exponential variations, or Heterogeneous Feature Tree (HFT) structures; mesh adaptivity governed by material threshold δ₀ (e.g., 0.1, 0.05, 0.03 values used in examples).
10_1016_j_cad_2014_11_011.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Top boundary (LMN) constrained to room temperature (273.15 K); node A completely constrained; node H constrained against vertical displacement; semicircular regions C_BCD at 1173.15 K and C_EFG at 873.15 K serve as heat sources.
- **Loads / Excitations:** Thermal loads applied as temperature boundary conditions (1173.15 K, 873.15 K, and 273.15 K) at specified geometric locations; six test points (P₁: (0.04, 0.045), P₂: (0.04, 0.035), P₃: (0.04, 0.025), P₄: (0.12, 0.045), P₅: (0.12, 0.035), P₆: (0.12, 0.025)) for stress measurement.
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Thermal-structural coupling between temperature distribution and mechanical deformation; material composition varies spatially according to power function f(dₚ) = cdₚ² or Heterogeneous Feature Tree (HFT) structure with interface curves where material composition changes.
- **Simulation Type:** Steady-state thermal conduction; plane strain assumption; linear elastic and isotropic material behavior; 2D analysis domain; von Mises stress calculations at test points.
10_1016_j_cad_2014_11_011.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Thermal conduction and structural mechanics (thermal-structural coupling); steady-state thermal conduction with linear elastic and isotropic material behavior under plane strain assumption.
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Von Mises stress at six test points (P₁-P₆); mesh quality parameters (q_min, q_max, q_avg); material composition variation metrics (δ_min, δ_avg); number of nodes (N_p) and elements (N_e); material composition variation distribution across elements.
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize the number of mesh elements while satisfying the material threshold requirement (δ_max < δ₀); distribute material composition variation over mesh elements as equally as possible; maintain high mesh quality (avoiding "skinny" triangles) through centroidal Voronoi tessellation-based refinement.
10_1016_j_cad_2014_11_011.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Mesh must conform to curved boundaries (e.g., turbine blade geometry, arch profiles); no triangle elements may straddle material interface curves where composition is discontinuous; initial triangulation must approximate geometric domain boundaries with denser points on curved boundaries.
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Material composition variation constraint: δ_max < δ₀ (maximum material composition variation must be below predefined material threshold); mesh quality constraint: avoid skinny triangles with large aspect ratios that degrade FEA accuracy; minimum angle criterion must be satisfied for all triangles after geometry-oriented refinement; density function must follow ρ ≈ g^(d+2) where g is material composition changing rate and d=2 for 2D domains.
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Initial triangulation generated using SolidWorks; thermal-mechanical analysis conducted with COMSOL Multiphysics; adaptive sampling uses mesh vertices as sample points to calculate material composition variation within elements; material composition variation calculated as δ(T) = max(δ_ij) where δ_ij = ||M_i - M_j|| between vertices.

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2016_10_009.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Refined beam and plate structural models based on Carrera Unified Formulation (CUF) with Hierarchical Legendre Expansion (HLE)
- **Material / Medium:** Isotropic Aluminium alloy (Young's modulus E = 75 GPa, Poisson ratio ν = 0.33) used in all numerical assessments
- **Application & Importance:** Development of accurate structural analysis models for slender bodies in aerospace/civil engineering applications; overcoming limitations of classical beam theories by capturing cross-sectional deformations, warping, and torsion effects with lower computational cost than 3D models
- **Geometry / Domain:** Square cross-section beams (0.2m × 0.2m), C-section beams (h=1m, b₂=1m, b₁=0.5m, t=0.1m), hollow square cross-section beams (h=1m, t=0.1m), and open hollow square cross-sections; plate structures with 1m sides and thicknesses of 0.1m, 0.01m, and 0.001m; analysis covers both solid and thin-walled structures with open/closed cross-sections
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2016_10_009.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Clamped-free boundary condition for square section beam
  - Both ends clamped for hollow square cross-section beam
  - One end clamped and opposite end free for open hollow square cross-section beam
  - Plates with boundary conditions: two opposite sides clamped, two opposite sides simply-supported, all sides clamped, all sides simply-supported
  - Physical boundary conditions applied at any point of 3D geometry on physical sides along beam axis

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Two point loads of −25N applied at lower corners [±b/2, L, −h/2] for square cross-section beam
  - Two opposite vertical point forces at [0, L, ±0.4] (−1N at upper flange middle, +1N at lower flange edge) for C-section beam
  - Vertical force of −1N applied at lower right corner [b₁, L, −h/2] for C-section flexural-torsional load case
  - Vertical point load of 1N applied at center of lower edge at mid-span [0, L/2, h/2] for hollow square beam
  - Four point loads at cut location: two at [0, L, −0.4] with ±0.5N and two at [0, L, −0.5] with ±0.5N for open hollow square beam
  - Pressure load of p = 1Pa applied on upper face of plate structures

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Multi-domain cross-sections with local expansion sub-domains (6, 9, 11 sub-domains configurations)
  - Cross-section domain divided into multiple local expansions for HLE and LE models
  - MSC Nastran solid models used as reference for comparison
  - 10 B4 elements used for longitudinal beam discretization
  - 10×10 MITC elements mesh for 2D plate models

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Linear analysis with small deformations and rotation angles
  - Slenderness ratios: L/h = 10 (square beam), L/h = 20 (C-section and hollow beams)
  - Height-to-thickness ratios: h/t = 10 (hollow sections)
  - Plate thicknesses: 0.1m, 0.01m, and 0.001m with 1m side length
  - Polynomial expansion orders from 1 to 8 for HLE models
  - Cubic Lagrange-type B4 elements used for longitudinal discretization
  - Linear to seventh-order hierarchical Legendre-type expansions used for HLE models
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2016_10_009.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Structural deformations and stress distributions in beam and plate structures, including cross-sectional deformations, warping effects, and shear stress distributions; small deformation linear elasticity analysis with focus on refined structural behavior beyond classical beam theory limitations

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Vertical displacements (u_z) at specific locations (e.g., loaded points, free edges)
  - Normal stresses (σ_yy) along the z-axis at mid-span sections
  - Shear stresses (σ_yz) along the z-axis, particularly at section edges
  - Dimensionless displacement and stress components (u_z*, σ_xx*, σ_yy*, σ_yz*) for plate analysis
  - Number of degrees of freedom (DOFs) for different model configurations
  - Stress-free condition satisfaction at free borders
  - Convergence characteristics with increasing polynomial order and element refinement

- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve high-accuracy structural analysis with computational efficiency by developing a beam model that captures 3D-like behavior while maintaining 1D model simplicity; validate that Hierarchical Legendre Expansion (HLE) models can represent physical boundary conditions at structural edges without geometric approximation; demonstrate that the methodology requires fewer degrees of freedom than equivalent 3D solid models while maintaining accuracy comparable to MSC Nastran reference solutions
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2016_10_009.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Square cross-section beam: height (h) and width (b) = 0.2m, length-to-height ratio L/h = 10 (length = 2m)
  - C-section beam: height (h) = 1m, upper flange width (b₂) = 1m, lower flange width (b₁) = 0.5m, thickness (t) = 0.1m, length-to-height ratio L/h = 20
  - Hollow square cross-section: height (h) = 1m, thickness (t) = 0.1m, height-to-thickness ratio h/t = 10, length-to-height ratio L/h = 20
  - Plate structures: side length = 1m, thicknesses of 0.1m, 0.01m, and 0.001m
  - Cross-section domain configurations limited to 6, 9, or 11 sub-domains for multi-domain analysis

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Isotropic Aluminum alloy with Young's modulus E = 75 GPa and Poisson ratio ν = 0.33
  - Small deformations and small rotation angles assumption (stated in geometrical relations)
  - Stress-free boundary conditions at edges (though solid model mesh was not refined at free borders)
  - Polynomial expansion orders constrained to 1-8 for HLE models in analyses
  - Longitudinal discretization limited to 10 B4 elements for square beam (ensuring convergence)
  - For C-section beam stress analysis, 40 B4 elements required along longitudinal axis to satisfy stress-free conditions at edges

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - MSC Nastran solid models used as reference with six-sided brick elements (CHEXA)
  - Convergence requirements dictate minimum element count (10 B4 elements for square beam displacement analysis)
  - Computational resource constraints related to degrees of freedom (DOFs): HL8 model with 9 sub-domains requires 32,643 DOFs compared to 84,600 for solid model
  - Expansion order serves as free input parameter determining number of unknowns to be solved
  - Cross-section domain division must maintain compatibility between sub-domains for multi-domain theories

10_1016_j_jmbbm_2024_106790.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Biodegradable R-shaped hemostatic clips for vascular ligation in minimally invasive surgery; two designs: no teeth (NT) and staggered teeth (ST)
- **Material / Medium:** Mg-2.8Nd-0.2Zn-0.4Zr alloy (ρ = 1.78 g/cm³, E = 4.2e10 Pa, ν = 0.35); blood vessel modeled with Mooney-Rivlin 5 model; artificial plasma corrosion medium (NaCl 6.8 g/L, CaCl₂ 0.2 g/L, KCl 0.4 g/L, MgSO₄ 0.1 g/L, NaHCO₃ 2.2 g/L, Na₂HPO₄ 0.126 g/L, NaH₂PO₄ 0.026 g/L)
- **Application & Importance:** Vascular closure in laparoscopic surgery requiring mechanical strength for ≥2 weeks; must exceed physiological blood pressure (23.99 kPa for severe hypertension); needs to minimize stress concentration to prevent premature failure; biodegradable alternative to titanium/polymer clips
- **Geometry / Domain:** R-shaped clip with double-arc transition at apex; total length 8.80 mm, width 6.20 mm, thickness 0.80 mm; curvature radius R1.55, inner radius R2.20, 190° angle, arm length 5.20 mm; ST clip features 0.20 mm height staggered teeth with 0.10 mm spacing; blood vessel model: 2 mm inner diameter, 0.2 mm wall thickness, 8 mm length
10_1016_j_jmbbm_2024_106790.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Both ends of the blood vessel completely fixed; artificial plasma at pH 7.4; thermostat water bath at 37 °C ± 0.5 °C; open circuit potential (OCP) held for 10 min before electrochemical measurements; volume of artificial plasma to clip surface area ratio of 0.5 mL/mm²; artificial plasma as etching solution for electrochemical tests
- **Loads / Excitations:** Displacement changes applied to both clip arms; impact force (F_impact) perpendicular to clip arms; constant flow pump injection rate of artificial plasma at 3 ml/min; EIS scan starting at −250 mV below OCP; physiological pressure requirement of 23.99 kPa (severe hypertension level)
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Inner sides of clip arms in contact with outer blood vessel surface; frictional contact between clip and blood vessel; multiple micro-gripping points between staggered teeth clip and vascular tissue; clip-rubber tube interaction through corrosion products after immersion; vessel closed by Mg-Nd-Zn-Zr alloy clip
- **Simulation Type:** 3D nonlinear finite element analysis using ANSYS Workbench 19.2; transient immersion tests (14 days with artificial plasma replaced every 24 h); long-term immersion tests (4 weeks with artificial plasma replaced every 48 h); electrochemical measurements including polarization curves and EIS; burst pressure tests with constant flow rate
10_1016_j_jmbbm_2024_106790.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Structural mechanics (stress-strain distribution during clip closure); corrosion behavior (hydrogen evolution, weight loss, electrochemical degradation); fluid-structure interaction (vessel occlusion under fluid pressure)
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Maximum equivalent elastic strain (NT: 0.00639, ST: 0.00636); maximum equivalent stress on blood vessels (NT: 1.645 MPa, ST: 1.237 MPa); burst pressure (NT: 79.83 ± 1.65 kPa, ST: 88.73 ± 2.58 kPa); corrosion rate (open: 0.082 ± 0.016 mm/y, closed: 0.088 ± 0.013 mm/y); hydrogen evolution volume (<0.3 ml/cm²); corrosion potential (open: -1.229 V, closed: -1.319 V); corrosion current density (open: 9.58e-3 A/cm², closed: 4.85e-2 A/cm²); vascular strain (0.26135 maximum)
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize stress concentration at clip apex during closure (achieved 24.8% reduction in vessel stress with ST design); maintain burst pressure >23.99 kPa (3.67× physiological requirement); balance corrosion rate to ensure mechanical integrity for ≥2 weeks while enabling complete degradation within clinical timeframe; reduce mechanical damage to vascular tissue during clamping
10_1016_j_jmbbm_2024_106790.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Total clip length 8.80 mm; width 6.20 mm; thickness 0.80 mm; curvature radius R1.55; inner radius R2.20; 190° apex angle; arm length 5.20 mm; 35° angle between arms; R0.20 radius at clip bottom; staggered teeth height 0.20 mm with 0.10 mm spacing for ST design; designed for blood vessels with 2 mm inner diameter and 0.2 mm wall thickness
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Minimum burst pressure requirement of 23.99 kPa (severe hypertension level); must maintain mechanical integrity for ≥2 weeks for vessel healing; maximum hydrogen evolution volume <0.3 ml/cm²; corrosion rate must not exceed 0.088 ± 0.013 mm/y; mechanical support duration of ~2 months; complete degradation timeframe of ~9 months; stress concentration at apex must be minimized to prevent stress corrosion cracking; equivalent elastic strain must remain below 0.00639
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Laser cutting of extruded Mg-2.8Nd-0.2Zn-0.4Zr alloy sheet; ground to 0.8 mm thickness using SiC papers #3000, #5000, #7000; polished and ultrasonically washed in anhydrous ethanol for 5 min; dried in constant temperature oven for 24 h; etched with nitric acid alcohol solution; artificial plasma replacement every 24 h for 14-day immersion tests; artificial plasma replacement every 48 h for 4-week immersion tests; electrochemical measurements with 10 min OCP stabilization before testing

- **Identity & Domain:** Heterogeneous composite materials with inclusions, analyzed using Phantom Domain Finite Element Method (PDFEM) for numerical homogenization and effective property calculation
- **Material / Medium:** Two-phase heterogeneous systems consisting of matrix and inclusions with isotropic properties; thermal conductivity contrast (c_thermal = λ_inc/λ_mat) and elastic contrast (c_elastic = k_inc/k_mat); 100:1 contrast ratio used in 3D fiber analysis; Poisson's ratio maintained equal for both phases in elastic tests
- **Application & Importance:** Efficient calculation of effective material properties for composite materials; handling complex inclusion geometries (particularly fibers) that challenge traditional FEM meshing; thermal conductivity and linear elasticity analysis; global property prediction without requiring precise interface resolution
- **Geometry / Domain:** 2D square domain Ω = [0,1]^2 with disk inclusions (diameter 0.3) and square inclusions (side length 0.3); 3D periodic RVE with fiber-like inclusions defined by spline curves with circular sections; structured mesh resolutions from N_mat = 15 to 75 (element sizes from 6.7×10^-2 to 1.3×10^-2); 2D domain discretized with 3721 nodes and 3600 quadrilateral elements at N_mat = 60 resolution
10_1016_j_apples_2025_100218.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Kinematic Uniform Boundary Conditions (KUBC): u(x) = g⋅x for thermal problems; u = E̅x for elastic problems (with E̅ = [[1,0],[0,0]] as example)
  - Static Uniform Boundary Conditions (SUBC): q(x)⋅n = Q⋅n for thermal problems; σ̅(x)n = Σ̅n for elastic problems (with Σ̅ = [[0,0],[0,1]] as example)
  - Dirichlet boundary (Γ_D): imposed temperature u₀ for thermal problems
  - Neumann boundary (Γ_N): imposed heat flux F for thermal problems
  - Periodic boundary conditions applied to RVE faces for homogenization calculations
  - Domain Ω = [0,1]^d with d = 2, 3

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - External heat source f in thermal problems
  - Uniform temperature gradient (g ∈ R²) for KUBC thermal problems
  - Uniform heat flux (Q ∈ R²) for SUBC thermal problems
  - Uniform traction tensor (Σ̅) for SUBC elastic problems

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Matrix-inclusion interfaces where weak continuity is expected but not enforced
  - Independent meshes for matrix domain and inclusions coupled via substitution matrix
  - Periodic repetition of fibers in 3D RVE analysis

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Steady-state boundary value problems
  - Linear elasticity and thermal conductivity analyses
  - 2D and 3D computational domains
  - Numerical homogenization of composite materials
  - Single inclusion cases (disk with diameter 0.3, square with side length 0.3) and periodic RVE with fiber inclusions
  - Contrast ratios up to c = 100 between matrix and inclusions for 3D elastic analysis

- **Physics Solved:**
  - Linear thermal conduction in heterogeneous materials
  - Linear elasticity in heterogeneous composite materials
  - Numerical homogenization of composite materials with inclusions
  - Energy minimization for boundary value problems with non-conforming meshes

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - PDFEM/FEM relative difference for displacement, strain, and Von Mises stress
  - L² norm of the solution
  - H¹ semi-norm of the solution
  - Temperature distribution in thermal problems
  - Displacement fields in elastic problems
  - Effective material properties including stiffness tensor components (C₁₁, C₂₂, μ), conductivity tensor (k), and homogenized Young's modulus (E_hom)
  - Maximum relative differences at material interfaces (up to ~0.02 for displacement, ~0.5 for strain/stress in elastic cases)

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Achieve efficient computation of global effective properties of composite materials without requiring conforming meshes
  - Maintain linear convergence while handling complex inclusion geometries (particularly fiber-like structures)
  - Reduce computational complexity for heterogeneous material analysis compared to standard FEM
  - Enable analysis of complex geometries that would require extremely fine meshes in traditional FEM (e.g., "meshing such fine structures requires an extremely high number of elements")
  - Preserve computational efficiency while ensuring sufficient pixelization of inclusions (with η = h_mat/h_inc > 1)

  - Implementation requires sufficient pixelization of inclusions as a key method step

- **Material / Medium:** Implicit porous structures represented mathematically as Φ = {(x, y, z) | φ(x, y, z) ≤ c(x, y, z)}, with three defined types: rod type (φ ≤ c), pore type (φ ≥ c), and sheet type (c₁ ≤ φ ≤ c₂). The material properties mentioned in simulations include Young's modulus of 210,000 MPa and Poisson's ratio of 0.3.
- **Application & Importance:** Designing manufacturable heterogeneous porous models for bone tissue engineering, biomimetic scaffolds, and high-stiffness mechanical structures; eliminating topological errors (isolated connected components and isolated holes) that prevent additive manufacturing; enabling smooth transitions between different porous structures while maintaining structural integrity.
- **Geometry / Domain:** 3D implicit porous structures with complex internal geometries, featuring blending regions (BR) between existing regions (ER₁, ER₂); structures include P-TPMS, IWP-TPMS, Rod-P, Rod-G, Rod-D, and Sheet-type configurations; domain boundaries can be Cartesian, cylindrical, or spherical; designed to avoid topological errors while controlling relative density, stiffness, and anisotropy through threshold distribution fields.

  - Blending region defined as [0.4, 0.6] × [0, 0.125] × [0, 0.125] or [0.35, 0.55] × [0, 0.125] × [0, 0.125] for specific test cases

10_1016_j_jmbbm_2015_08_032.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Auricular silicone scaffold for reconstructive surgery; modeled for thickness optimization using finite element analysis (FEA) to simulate transplant process.

- **Material / Medium:** SY-1 medical silicone with 100:1 base:curing agent ratio; Shore A hardness 27; elasticity modulus 2.14 MPa; density 1.17 g/cm³; tearing strength 18.0 kN/m; breaking strength 4.2 MPa; curing time 60 min at 80°C.

- **Application & Importance:** Determine minimal scaffold thickness that maintains structural integrity during skin wrapping/vacuumization; accounts for variable skin thickness (0.83–4.34 per 10,000 births for pediatric microtia); ensures sufficient hardness to resist deformation while matching normal auricle appearance.

- **Geometry / Domain:** 3D auricle model derived from CT scans of 25-year-old adult; offset values from -0.25mm to -2.0mm applied inward from original model; critical features: helix, auricular concha, cavum conchae, cymba conchae; minimal thickness criterion of 0.4mm for supporting structures; maximum offset value of -1.75mm maintains structural integrity (deformation 1.8967mm at 1atm pressure).
10_1016_j_jmbbm_2015_08_032.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Edges at bottom of skin and around cochleae fixed to simulate surgical sutures; no penetration condition between scaffold and skin (S_ear ∩ S_skin = ∅); gap distance between scaffold and skin constrained to tolerance (f_gap(P_ear, P_skin) < ε).

- **Loads / Excitations:** Standard atmospheric pressure (1 atm = 10135 Pa) linearly applied to outer skin surface from 0 to 0.5s; constant 1 atm maintained on skin surface during deformation.

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Augmented Lagrange formulation for contact between scaffold and skin; hyper-elastic material definition for both scaffold and skin; large deflection switch enabled due to significant skin deformation during vacuuming.

- **Simulation Type:** Nonlinear transient 3D analysis; tetrahedral mesh for scaffolds and quadrilateral-dominant mesh for skin; large deformation regime with Young's modulus increasing with deformation; iterative computation of pressure-deformation variation.
10_1016_j_jmbbm_2015_08_032.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Nonlinear large deformation mechanics of hyper-elastic materials under atmospheric pressure; contact mechanics between scaffold and skin during vacuum-assisted wrapping; stress-strain behavior with strain-dependent Young's modulus increase.

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Maximum deformation (mm) of scaffold (1.8967mm at -1.75mm offset); minimal thickness (mm) of helix, auricular concha, cavum conchae, and cymba conchae; offset-error values (e.g., +0.147mm error at 0.00mm offset); deformation threshold where structural failure occurs (15.986mm deformation at -2.00mm offset).

- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize negative offset value (minimize scaffold thickness) while maintaining supporting structures above 0.4mm minimal thickness threshold and preventing large deformation (>1.8967mm) during 1atm pressure application; determine maximum offset value of -1.75mm as transition point where scaffold maintains structural integrity.
10_1016_j_jmbbm_2015_08_032.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Offset values applied inward from original model in decrements of −0.25mm (range −0.25mm to −2.0mm); minimal thickness threshold of 0.4mm for helix, auricular concha, and cavum conchae; original auricle features maintained during offsetting; sharp angles eliminated in offset models; cymba conchae thickness unconstrained as it is a feature structure (not supporting structure).

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Maximum deformation tolerance of ≤1.8967mm (3% of total dimension) at −1.75mm offset; structural failure threshold at >15.986mm deformation (−2.00mm offset); scaffold must resist 1 atm pressure without collapse; thickness of helix, auricular concha, and cavum conchae must not drop below 0.38mm, 0.14mm, and 0.17mm respectively to avoid large deformation; SY-1 silicone material properties fixed (Shore A hardness 27, elasticity modulus 2.14 MPa).

- **Process/Manufacturing:** Offset step accuracy of 0.25mm deemed sufficient for medical application; PLA 3D-printed molds generated via Boolean subtraction of scaffold from cube geometry; silicone curing at 80°C for 60 minutes; error between theoretical and actual offset values acceptable (P >0.05) despite increasing with offset magnitude.

• Material / Medium: Aluminum base material with density ρ₀ = 2700.0 kg/m³, Young's modulus E₀ = 69.0 GPa, Poisson's ratio µ₀ = 0.33, thermal conductivity κ₀ = 237.0 W/(mK); air used for cooling with convection coefficient h_f = 32 W/(m²K), airflow speed v_f = 5 m/s, specific heat capacity c_p = 1218 J/(m³K)

• Application & Importance: Battery housing must simultaneously fulfill competing requirements of high mechanical stiffness (to prevent deformation and fracture) and effective thermal management (to avoid overheating and thermal runaway) while being lightweight; addresses multidisciplinary objectives of mechanical vibration, thermal conduction, and thermal convection for electric vehicle battery systems

• Geometry / Domain: Battery housing with dimensions a = 27.0 mm (ξ-axis), c = 1309.5 mm (η-axis), b = 135.0 mm (ζ-axis); lattice unit cell edge length e = 6.75 mm; relative density bounds 0.1 ≤ ρ ≤ 0.5; cuboid volume for modal analysis 2106.0 mm × 1309.5 mm × 135.0 mm; SP lattice structure with parametrized relative density as design variable; design domain discretized into hexahedral elements with 30×30×30 voxel resolution for homogenization
10_1038_s41598_024_60124_4.key_2:
• Boundaries & Constraints: Spring foundation on lower surface Ŵ⁻ζ with spring constant kₛ = 1 N/m³; no heat conduction at battery housing tips (dTₗ/dy|y=±c/2 = 0); airflow inlet temperature T_f(-c/2) = 280 K; relative density bounds 0.1 ≤ ρ ≤ 0.5; global volume constraint with target volume fraction V*ₚ = 30%; heat generation on battery cell surfaces excluding η = ±1 boundaries; airflow direction along η axis

• Loads / Excitations: Torsional vibration load based on first eigenfrequency ω₁ = 155.8 Hz; equivalent distributed force field F(ξ, η) = F₀·(p₀₀ + p₁₀·ξ + p₀₁·η + p₂₀·ξ² + p₁₁·ξ·η + p₀₂·η²) with F₀ = 130,000 kN/m²; heat dissipation per battery cell q̇ = 200 W; airflow speed v_f = 5 m/s; initial airflow temperature 280 K; airflow temperature field T_f(η) = 289.85 + 9.85η

• Interactions / Interfaces: Airflow temperature field linearly related to η coordinate; lattice structure temperature consistently 4 K higher than airflow temperature; heat transfer through convection at lattice-airflow interface; cross-sectional area of airflow channel A_f = 4.62e² m²; heat convection surface area per meter A_h = 203.28e m; thermal conductivity of lattice κₗ = 0.1334κ₀ when ρ = 0.2

• Simulation Type: Steady-state thermal analysis; modal analysis for vibration; 3D finite element analysis; multi-scale approach with homogenization; linear tetrahedral elements for modal analysis; eight-node hexahedral elements with full integration for structural analysis; steady-state fluid analysis; vibration analysis based on torsional deformation mode
10_1038_s41598_024_60124_4.key_3:
• Physics Solved: Modal vibration analysis; steady-state thermal conduction; thermal convection with airflow cooling; structural mechanics; multi-physics coupling of mechanical deformation and thermal dissipation; eigenvalue problem for vibration modes; heat transfer through convection and conduction

• Target Outputs (Metrics): Mechanical compliance (Cm = F^T U); thermal compliance (Ct = Q^T T); normalized mechanical compliance (Cm-Cmin_m)/(Cmax_m-Cmin_m); normalized thermal compliance (Ct-Cmin_t)/(Cmax_t-Cmin_t); relative density distribution (ρ); displacement field wζ(ξ,η); temperature fields for airflow (Tf(η) = 289.85 + 9.85η) and lattice structure; first eigenfrequency ω₁ = 155.8 Hz; Pareto front showing trade-offs between mechanical and thermal objectives

• Optimization Goal: Minimize weighted sum of normalized mechanical compliance and thermal compliance; minimize deformation under torsional vibration (mechanical objective); maximize heat dissipation during operation (thermal objective); achieve optimal balance between structural stiffness and thermal management through multi-objective optimization with weight pairs ranging from 0.00-1.00 in 0.25 increments; maintain battery operating temperature under 323 K while ensuring mechanical integrity
10_1038_s41598_024_60124_4.key_4:
• Geometric/Design Space: Relative density bounds 0.1 ≤ ρ ≤ 0.5 to ensure minimum wall thickness for printability; target volume fraction V*ₚ = 30%; battery housing dimensions a = 27.0 mm (ξ-axis), c = 1309.5 mm (η-axis), b = 135.0 mm (ζ-axis); lattice unit cell edge length e = 6.75 mm; dimensions adjusted to ensure even division by lattice unit cell edge length

• Performance/Physics Limits: Battery operating temperature must stay under 323 K; lattice structure temperature consistently 4 K higher than airflow temperature; airflow temperature field constrained by T_f(η) = 289.85 + 9.85η; no heat conduction at battery housing tips (dTₗ/dy|y=±c/2 = 0); initial airflow temperature at inlet T_f(-c/2) = 280 K; spring foundation constraint with kₛ = 1 N/m³

• Process/Manufacturing: Minimum wall thickness requirement for additive manufacturing printability (enforced through relative density bounds); self-supportive geometry enabling fabrication by additive manufacturing; SP lattice unit cell discretized with 30×30×30 voxel resolution for homogenization analysis; thermal convection requirements necessitating sufficient porosity for airflow

10_1016_j_compstruct_2023_116798.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Textile Reinforced Mortar (TRM) composites, specifically steel fiber textile reinforced mortar (STRM) and carbon fiber textile reinforced mortar (CTRM) composites, analyzed for tensile properties and interfacial bonding behavior.

- **Material / Medium:**
  - Mortar: Compressive strength 55 MPa, flexural strength 12 MPa, splitting tensile strength 7 MPa, density 2.05 g/cm³, moisture content 15-17%, tested at curing times of 7, 14, and 28 days
  - Steel fiber textile: Cross-sectional area 0.537 mm², spacing 5 mm, tensile strength 3084.171 MPa, elastic modulus 188,900 MPa, thickness 0.84 mm, mass density 670 g/cm²
  - Carbon fiber textile: Cross-sectional area 0.888 mm², spacing 20 mm, tensile strength 2399.55 MPa, elastic modulus 138,900 MPa, thickness 0.044 mm, mass density 80 g/cm²
  - Epoxy resin: Used as gradient interface coating with O-H stretching vibration at 3372.84 cm⁻¹

- **Application & Importance:** External strengthening of damaged buildings; improving structural integrity against collapse; sustainable development applications; overcoming limitations of traditional strengthening materials; investigating tensile properties, interfacial bonding performance, and failure mechanisms.

- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - Tensile specimens: 140 mm layer length, 40 mm width, 10 mm bottom layer thickness, 5 mm top layer thickness
  - Double-lap shear specimens: 150 mm × 60 mm × 10 mm mortar with 20 mm clearance at top edge
  - Steel fiber textiles: 5 mm spacing between fibers, 0.84 mm thickness
  - Carbon fiber textiles: 20 mm spacing between bundles in both directions, 0.044 mm thickness
  - FE models: STRM model with 37,642 elements, CTRM model with 27,678 elements
  - Critical area measurements around fiber bundles ranging from 4.241 mm² to 34.747 mm² depending on textile type and loading condition
10_1016_j_compstruct_2023_116798.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Tensile test gauge length set to 140 mm
  - Bottom nodes of mortar completely fixed in FE simulation
  - Reference point created to couple to all surface nodes of each fiber bundle for load application
  - Curing conditions: Initial curing in customized chamber for 7 days, followed by room temperature curing for at least 14 days
  - Cameras positioned 1 m away from specimen surface for DIC monitoring
  - Mortar specimens cured for different times: 7, 14, and 28 days
  - Mortar layer dimensions: 140 mm length, 40 mm width, 10 mm thickness for bottom layer; 5 mm thickness for top layer

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Tensile loading speed of 2 mm/min
  - Double-lap shear testing loading speed of 2 mm/min
  - Applied force (F) in tensile testing configuration
  - Displacement-controlled loading in FE simulation
  - Compression applied on top of gradient interface model for stress distribution examination

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Interface between textile and mortar with chemical bonding (O-H absorption peak at 3350.14 cm⁻¹ for mortar/epoxy resin hybrid)
  - Contact angles: 74.21° for steel fiber, 50.78° for carbon fiber
  - Bond-slip law extracted from experimental data with critical slip (S_crit) and maximum slip (S_max)
  - Bond shear stress interface with critical stress (τ_crit) and maximum stress (τ_max)
  - Three interface regions: bonding, debonding, and sliding zones during pull-out process
  - Gradient interface (epoxy transition layer) between textile and mortar

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 3D FE simulation using ABAQUS software
  - Solid elements C3D8R for discretization of geometry
  - Linear isotropic elastic constitutive model for mortar, steel fibers, and carbon fiber bundles
  - Connector elements with spring-like behavior to simulate pull-out process
  - One axial degree of freedom activated along interface direction
  - Mesh sizes: 37,642 elements for STRM model, 27,678 elements for CTRM model
  - Simulation of double-lap shear tests with 7 days curing time
  - Nonlinear bond-slip behavior implementation using experimental data
10_1016_j_compstruct_2023_116798.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Tensile behavior of textile reinforced mortar composites
  - Interfacial bonding behavior in double-lap shear configuration
  - Crack initiation and propagation mechanisms in TRM composites
  - Stress distribution and load transfer between textile and mortar
  - Bond-slip behavior at textile-mortar interface
  - Failure mechanisms of steel fiber (STRM) and carbon fiber (CTRM) reinforced composites

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Peak load values (kN) for both STRM and CTRM composites
  - Initial stiffness (N/mm) from load-displacement curves
  - Critical area measurements around fiber bundles (4.241-34.747 mm²)
  - Transition points between stages (ε_I, σ_I), (ε_II, σ_II), (ε_III, σ_III)
  - Load-displacement curves for tensile and shear tests
  - Stress-strain curves for TRM composites
  - Equivalent stress (von Mises) distributions in FE models
  - Bond shear stress (τ) and slip displacement (S)
  - Contact angles (74.21° for steel fiber, 50.78° for carbon fiber)
  - FTIR peak values (3403.78 cm⁻¹ for mortar, 3372.84 cm⁻¹ for epoxy resin, 3350.14 cm⁻¹ for mortar/epoxy hybrid)
  - Surface roughness (60 μm for steel filament, 20 μm for carbon fiber bundle)

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Improve interfacial bonding performance using gradient interface (epoxy transition layer)
  - Maximize peak load and initial stiffness through proper curing time (14 days recommended)
  - Optimize textile selection (STRM shows stiffer and stronger response than CTRM)
  - Prevent premature debonding by addressing stress concentration at interface
  - Enhance load transfer efficiency from textile to mortar matrix
  - Achieve approximately 30% improvement in interfacial bonding performance with gradient interface

  - Mortar top layer thickness: 5 mm

  - Critical slip (S_crit) and maximum slip (S_max) parameters defining bond-slip behavior
  - Critical stress (τ_crit) and maximum stress (τ_max) thresholds in bond-shear relationship

  - Carbon fiber surface must be coated with epoxy resin

10_1016_j_eswa_2025_127123.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Railway turnout switch rails, specifically analyzing tractive location selection to control insufficient displacement (ID) during conversion

- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Switch rail material: density 7860 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio 0.25, elastic modulus 2×10⁵ MPa
  - Weight per unit length: 60 kg/m
  - Cross-sectional area: 5145 mm² (head) to 8918 mm² (cutting point) for 10.8m rail; variable for 19.7m rail
  - Moments of inertia: 231.3 cm⁴ (head) to 756.3 cm⁴ (cutting point)
  - Frictional coefficient: uniform distribution [0.2, 0.3] with expected value 0.25

- **Application & Importance:** 
  - Controlling insufficient displacement (ID) between actual and designed switch rail shape after conversion
  - Ensuring maximum ID remains below 2 mm engineering requirement
  - Critical for train passage safety, smoothness, and preventing structural damage
  - Tractive locations directly influence ID and remain fixed throughout operational phase

- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Two case studies: 10.8 m and 19.7 m switch rails
  - Cantilever beam with linearly varying cross-section (4755 mm variable section for 10.8m rail)
  - Heel rigidly fixed with fasteners modeled as linear springs
  - Supported by sleepers and sliding chairs underneath
  - Feasible tractive regions (Rᵢ,ᵢ₊₁) defined between sleepers
  - Finite element mesh: 20 mm (10.8m rail) and 40 mm (19.7m rail)
  - 10.8m rail: 3245×3245 stiffness matrix; 19.7m rail: 2954×2954 stiffness matrix
10_1016_j_eswa_2025_127123.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Rigid fixation at the heel (root) of the switch rail
  - Displacement Boundary Condition (DBC) applied at tractive points: u_iy = 0
  - Tractive force constraint: f_max ≤ f_iy^t ≤ 0, where f_max = 3500 N (hydraulic machine overflow pressure)
  - All non-y directional degrees of freedom constrained to zero at tractive points: f_ix^t = f_iz^t = f_iθx^t = f_iθy^t = f_iθz^t = 0
  - Fasteners modeled as linear elastic springs with one end rigidly fixed

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Frictional resistance from sliding chairs (modeled as concentrated force opposite to rail movement direction)
  - Frictional coefficient: uniform distribution [0.2, 0.3] with expected value E[μ_s] = 0.25
  - Tractive force applied at selected nodes (f_iy^t < 0)

10_1007_s00211_021_01243_2.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Elliptic interface problems with discontinuous coefficients across arbitrary interfaces
- **Material / Medium:** Piecewise constant diffusion coefficient with values a₁ and a₂ in subdomains Ω₁ and Ω₂; examples use coefficient contrasts of 10:1 (Examples 1 and 3) and 100:1 (Example 2)
- **Application & Importance:** Solving partial differential equations with complex or moving interfaces without body-fitted mesh generation; enables efficient computation for multiphase systems where interface geometry is complex or changes over time
- **Geometry / Domain:** Computational domain Ω = (-2,2) × (-2,2); interface geometries include: circular interface (r=1.1), two closely spaced circles (r=0.51, d=0.02 separation), and non-smooth interface |y| = (4√2/9)cos(√2πx/3) + (2√2/9) with singularities at (±√2, 0)
10_1007_s00211_021_01243_2.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Dirichlet boundary condition u = g on ∂Ω; g = 0 in all numerical examples; interface conditions [[u]]_Γ = 0 (continuity of solution) and [[a∇u · ν]]_Γ = 0 (continuity of normal flux) across interface Γ
- **Loads / Excitations:** Right-hand side f ∈ L²(Ω); f = 1 in Examples 2 and 3; f computed to match exact solution in Example 1; exact solution defined as u(x) = {e^{|x|²-r²} + 10r² - 1 for |x| ≤ r, 10|x|² otherwise} in Example 1
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Interface Γ divides domain into Ω₁ and Ω₂; jump condition [[v]]_Γ = v|_Ω₁ - v|_Ω₂; unit outer normal ν to Ω₁; diffusion coefficient a = a₁χ_Ω₁ + a₂χ_Ω₂ with a₁, a₂ > 0
- **Simulation Type:** 2D steady-state elliptic PDE; computational domain Ω = (-2,2) × (-2,2); Cartesian meshes with hanging nodes; K-meshes satisfying Assumption (H3) for adaptive refinement; unfitted finite element method with polynomial degrees p = 1, 2, 3
10_1007_s00211_021_01243_2.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Elliptic interface problems with discontinuous diffusion coefficients; specifically the model problem -div(a∇u) = f in Ω with interface conditions [[u]]_Γ = 0 and [[a∇u · ν]]_Γ = 0 across arbitrary interfaces
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Discrete error in DG norm: ||u-U||_DG
  - A posteriori error estimate η = (∑_K∈M ξ²_K)^(1/2)
  - Effectivity index: eff = η/||u-U||_DG
  - Quasi-optimal decay rate of error with respect to degrees of freedom (O(N^(-p/2)))
  - Local error estimators ξ_K for each element K
  - Number of degrees of freedom (#DoFs)
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize degrees of freedom required to achieve target error tolerance through adaptive mesh refinement while maintaining quasi-optimal convergence rates for polynomial degrees p=1,2,3; specifically achieving O(N^(-p/2)) error decay where N is number of degrees of freedom
10_1007_s00211_021_01243_2.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Computational domain Ω must be a union of bounded rectangles (to be partitioned by Cartesian meshes)
  - Interface Γ must be Lipschitz and piecewise C²-smooth
  - Each interface element K must intersect Γ at most twice at different sides
  - Each interface element K can include at most one singular point where Γ is not C²-smooth
  - Elements must satisfy "large element" conditions with respect to Ω₁ and Ω₂ (Definition 2.1)
  - For interface elements, η_K ≤ max(1/2, (1-δ₀)/(1+δ₀)) where η_K is the interface deviation
  - Mesh must satisfy Assumption (H3): diam(supp(ψ_P)) ≤ C min_{K∈M_P} h_K for all conforming nodes P
  - Each side of the mesh can include at most N₀ = 3 hanging nodes

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Coefficient a(x) must be positive and piecewise constant (a = a₁χ_Ω₁ + a₂χ_Ω₂, a₁, a₂ > 0)
  - Domain must be divided into two non-intersecting subdomains Ω = Ω₁ ∪ Ω₂ with Ω₁ ⊂ Ω̄₁ ⊂ Ω
  - Uniform polynomial degree p is used across the mesh (p = 1, 2, 3 in examples)
  - Penalty parameter α₀ > 0 (set to 1 in all numerical examples)
  - Interface must satisfy jump conditions [[u]]_Γ = 0 and [[a∇u · ν]]_Γ = 0
  - For stability, mesh must satisfy interface resolving conditions related to η_K

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Mesh must be generated by local successive quad-refinements of an initial conforming mesh
  - For adaptive refinement, elements are marked when ∑_{K∈M̂} ξ²_K ≥ (1/2)η²
  - Interface elements must be merged with neighboring elements to satisfy large element conditions
  - Parameter δ₀ ∈ (0, 1/2) must be chosen (natural choice δ₀ = 1/4 used in examples)
  - The method requires that the interface is sufficiently resolved (elements sufficiently refined) to satisfy Assumption (H2)
  - Maximum number of hanging nodes per side is fixed at N₀ = 3 for all examples

- Implant length (H) = 1/3*Y where Y = length between lesser trochanter and epiphyseal plate
- Implant width (W) = X where X = width at one-sixth of Y length proximally from epiphyseal plate
- Defect height constrained to Y/3 (one-third of Y length above epiphyseal plate)
- Defect width constrained to 3X/4 (three-quarters of X)
- Volume retention set at 15% to match original bone weight after topology optimization
- Implant weight reduction target: 30% of original solid core implant while maintaining structural integrity
- Rhombic mesh pattern size constrained to 5 mm × 5 mm on excavated areas
- Hole diameter for fixation: 5.3 mm (screw diameter)
- YM lattice parameters: unit size 2.7 mm, average pore size 500 μm, porosity 65%, pillar diameter 0.6 mm
- Maximum allowable dimensional manufacturing error: 2% (actual measured errors 0.98-1.16%)
- Layer thickness maintained at 30 μm during 3D printing
- 3D printing parameters: laser power 200 W, scanning speed 0.6 m/s, exposure time 125 s

- Failure criterion: medial-lateral displacement difference must not exceed 5 mm (maximum observed was 2.355 mm)

10_1007_s12206_017_0110_8.key_1:
- Flexible-disk rotor system with grouped blades connected by lacing wires
- Shaft material: Density 7850 kg/m³, Shear modulus 75 GPa; Disk material: Density 7850 kg/m³, Young's modulus 200 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.3; Blade material: Density 7850 kg/m³, Young's modulus 200 GPa
- Analysis of coupled vibration characteristics to understand stability and reliability of rotating machinery systems, particularly examining effects of lacing wire parameters and flexible disk on natural frequencies and system stability
- Shaft (length 0.6 m, radius 0.04 m) with flexible disk (outer radius 0.2 m, thickness 0.03 m) mounted at 0.3 m position, multiple blades (outer end 0.4 m) with stagger angle 30°, blades grouped by lacing wires at various connection positions
10_1007_s12206_017_0110_8.key_2:
- Boundary condition of shaft-torsion vibration: fixed-free
- Disk boundary condition: fixed inside (inner radius), free outside (outer radius)
- Blade configuration: cantilever (fixed at root)
- Rotational speed range: 0 to 123,000 rpm
- Lacing wire stiffness range: k* = 0 to 10⁴
- Lacing wire position range: xw* = 0.005 to 1 (normalized from blade root to tip)
- Lacing wires modeled as massless springs connecting blades
- Coupled vibration between shaft-torsion, disk-transverse, and blade-bending subsystems
- Kinematic relations between shaft torsion displacement, disk transverse displacement, and blade bending displacement
- New vibration modes: lacing wires-blade (LB) and lacing wires-disk-blade (LDB)
- Analysis type: Free vibration (eigenvalue problem)
- Solution methods: Assumed Mode Method (AMM) and Finite Element Method (FEM)
- FEM implementation: ANSYS (3D hexahedral solid elements for shaft/disk, 3D tetrahedral solid elements for blades, spring elements for lacing wires) and Hyperworks (3D hexahedral solid elements for shaft/disk, 2D shell elements for blades, spring elements for lacing wires)
- Results normalized to first-order natural frequency of cantilever blade (ω* = ω/ω₁b, Ω* = Ω/ω₁b, k* = kw/(Eb·Ib/Lb³))
- Mode shape analysis for different rotational speeds and spring parameters
10_1007_s12206_017_0110_8.key_3:
- Coupled shaft-torsion, disk-transverse, and blade-bending vibrations in a flexible-disk rotor system
- Natural frequencies (in Hz) of coupled vibration modes (SDB, DB, BB, LB, LDB)
- Mode shapes of different vibration modes at various rotational speeds
- Frequency bifurcation patterns with respect to rotational speed
- Error percentages between AMM and FEM results (ANSYS: <1%, Hyperworks: -2% to -6% for blade modes, 33.62% for shaft modes)
- Instability thresholds at specific rotational speeds (e.g., Ω* = 7.5 Hz for 1a mode, Ω* = 17 Hz for 1f mode)
- Effects of lacing wire stiffness (k* = 0-10⁴) and position (xw* = 0.005-1) on natural frequencies
- Comparison of vibration characteristics between rigid-disk (previous studies) and flexible-disk rotor systems
- Validation of Assumed Mode Method against Finite Element Method results
- Identification of new vibration modes: lacing wires-blade (LB) and lacing wires-disk-blade (LDB)
10_1007_s12206_017_0110_8.key_4:
- Shaft length constrained to 0.6 m, radius to 0.04 m
- Disk outer radius constrained to 0.2 m, thickness to 0.03 m, located at 0.3 m from shaft end
- Blade outer end constrained to 0.4 m, cross-sectional area to 1.2×10⁻⁴ m², area moment of inertia to 1.92×10⁻⁹ m²

- Rotational speed limited to 0-123,000 rpm

- Shaft-torsion vibration boundary condition fixed to fixed-free
- Flexible disk boundary condition fixed inside, free outside
- Blade boundary condition constrained to cantilever (fixed at root)

10_1039_d5mh00502g.key_1:
- Energy-absorbing metamaterials based on self-locking bistable structures
- Fabricated from nylon with Young's modulus E = 807 MPa, Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3, and friction coefficient μ = 0.29
- Designed for impact protection in industrial production, mechanical operations, and safety-critical applications requiring high absorption capacity and self-locking mechanisms
- Curved beam geometry follows y(x) = h/2(1 - cos(2πx/l)) with height h = 10 mm, span l = 100 mm, width b = 20 mm
- Snap-fit structure parameters include inclination angle θ, sliding groove height hs, lower width ts, vertical beam thickness tb, and height hb
- Sample 1 has target force plateau Fe1 = 7.5 N; Sample 2 has target force plateau Fe2 = 10 N
- Four metamaterial types tested: Type I (3×2 units of sample 1), Type II (3×2 units of sample 2), Type III (3×1 units each of samples 1 and 2), Type IV (3×2 identical curved beams)
- Energy absorption values: Type I = 608.3 mJ, Type II = 774.2 mJ, Type III = 699.6 mJ, Type IV = 442.1 mJ
- Drop tower test parameters: mass M = 1460 g dropped from 40 mm height (564 mJ impact energy)
- Miniature trailer test: mass 1.86 kg traveling at 2.1 m/s
- Quasi-static compression testing conducted at 2 mm/min displacement rate
- Unit cells arranged in series, parallel, or series-parallel configurations to tune force-displacement response
- Force plateau error between designed and experimental results less than 8.55%
- Maximum principal strains during testing: 0.0397 (sample 1) and 0.0241 (sample 2), below material yield strain
- Impact tests show 47.03% reduction in peak acceleration compared to baseline (Type IV)
10_1039_d5mh00502g.key_2:

- Cyclic loading tests performed to evaluate reusability of metamaterial
- Three identical structures arranged in parallel for drop tests, resulting in force measurement three times that of a unit cell
- Symmetric arrangement of units within layers to ensure structural stability in multi-unit configurations

10_1016_j_matdes_2025_114006.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB) induced crystalline patterns in additively manufactured components, specifically analyzing how laser scanning strategies influence crystallographic texture and mechanical properties.
- **Material / Medium:** IN718 nickel-based superalloy; FCC crystalline structure; relative density >99.8%; material exhibits high Zener ratio; studied in as-printed condition without heat treatment.
- **Application & Importance:** Predicting strength-enhancing orientations for mechanical performance optimization; integrating manufacturing considerations into early design stages; enabling alignment of stress fields with favorable crystalline orientations to improve component performance in aerospace, oil/gas, and automotive applications.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Columnar grain structures aligned with building direction (BD); melt pool boundaries forming hierarchical dendritic patterns; three primary crystalline orientation groups (<001>, <011>, <111>); azimuthal coordinate system (α, β angles) for mechanical property mapping; analyzed at microstructural scale (grain boundaries, dislocation networks) and macroscopic scale (component orientation).
10_1016_j_matdes_2025_114006.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Fixed manufacturing parameters: Material IN718, hatch distance 90 μm, layer thickness 60 μm, laser power 200 W
  - Varied parameters: Scan speed (500 mm/s, 1000 mm/s), scanning strategies (R0, R67, R90), elevation angle (0°, 45°, 90°), azimuthal angle (90°, 180°, 225°)
  - Unheated build plate
  - No post-build heat treatment
  - Tensile specimens cut at 0°, 45°, 90° using EDM
  - Relative density >99.8% to avoid porosity effects

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Tensile testing using INSTRON 8801
  - Laser power of 200 W with Gaussian energy distribution
  - Volumetric energy density controlled by scan speed (500 mm/s, 1000 mm/s)
  - Strain levels up to 2.5×10⁻³ in elastic range testing

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Melt pool boundaries and side branching growth patterns
  - Columnar grain structure with epitaxial growth through layers
  - Grain boundaries with geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs)
  - Dendritic cellular structures with interdendritic zones containing statistical stored dislocations (SSDs)
  - Dislocation networks interacting with grain boundaries and Nb/Ti particles
  - Competitive grain growth level between crystalline orientations

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 3D mechanical property mapping in azimuthal coordinate system (α, β angles)
  - Orientation Distribution Function (ODF) analysis with Typical Crystalline Orientation (TCO) and Main Crystalline Orientation (MCO)
  - Texture index J calculation using ODF
  - Grain morphology represented as equivalent ellipsoids with major/minor axes
  - Voigt-Reuss-Hill theory for Young's modulus calculations
  - Taylor factor calculations for yield strength using tensile and shear strain tensors
  - Mechanical property contour maps for stiffness and yield strength prediction
10_1016_j_matdes_2025_114006.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Crystalline texture development during Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB)
  - Relationship between laser scanning strategies and crystallographic orientation formation
  - Mechanical property anisotropy in additively manufactured IN718
  - Dislocation dynamics (GNDs and SSDs) within columnar grain structures
  - Orientation Distribution Function (ODF) and texture index calculation

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Young's modulus in azimuthal coordinate system (α, β angles)
  - Yield stress as function of crystalline orientation
  - Texture index (J) values for different scanning strategies
  - Misorientation angle (λ) between TCO and MCO (3°-8.5°, mean 5.6°)
  - Misorientation around MCO (ψ)
  - Grain boundary density (GBD)
  - Geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density (median ~0.005 μm⁻¹)
  - Taylor factor for tensile and shear deformation
  - Grain morphology parameters (major/minor axes, aspect ratio)

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Maximize mechanical strength by aligning stress fields with favorable crystalline orientations
  - Identify high-strength orientations (<111> direction showing 15% higher stiffness than isotropic IN718)
  - Achieve strength variations exceeding 90% between <111> and <001> orientations
  - Enable early-stage integration of crystallographic texture in component design
  - Optimize component performance through strategic orientation selection of stress fields relative to crystalline patterns
10_1016_j_matdes_2025_114006.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Tensile specimens must follow ASTM E8 subsize specifications
  - Plate dimensions of 160 mm × 120 mm for tensile specimen preparation
  - Specimens cut at specific angles (0°, 45°, 90°) using EDM
  - Azimuthal angles (α) limited to 90°, 180°, 225° for specimen orientation
  - Elevation angles (β) constrained to 0° and 90° for tensile testing
  - Microstructural characterization samples sized 10 × 5 × 5 mm
  - Minimum of two tensile specimens per crystalline direction required

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Relative density must exceed 99.8% to eliminate porosity effects on mechanical properties
  - Tensile testing limited to elastic range up to strain of 2.5×10⁻³
  - Maximum observed strength variation between <111> and <001> orientations cannot exceed 90%
  - Misorientation angle (λ) between TCO and MCO ranges from 3° to 8.5° (mean 5.6°)
  - Young's modulus reduction (ΔE) ranges from 2.5% (horizontal) to 9.5% (vertical) at v=500 mm/s

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Fixed parameters: IN718 material, hatch distance 90 μm, layer thickness 60 μm, laser power 200 W
  - Scan speed limited to 500 mm/s and 1000 mm/s
  - Scanning strategies restricted to R0 (0°), R90 (90°), and R67 (67°) rotation angles
  - Unheated build plate condition (no preheating)
  - No post-build heat treatment applied
  - Laser scanning strategy limited to meander type with Gaussian energy distribution
  - EBSD analysis with 2 μm step size and 12° misorientation threshold
  - GND density calculated from Nye's tensor using EBSD data and ATEX software
  - Relative density constraint (>99.8%) to avoid porosity effects on mechanical properties
  - Minimum of six tensile specimens per scanning strategy and speed combination required

10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120088.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Double-feature bio-inspired gradient lattice structure (DBGLS) combining spider web bidirectional gradient distribution and peacock mantis shrimp dactyl club impact-resistant features
- **Material / Medium:** AlSi10Mg aluminum alloy with density 2.67 g/cm³, Young's modulus 62.9 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.30, initial yield stress 125 MPa, limit stress 325 MPa; strain rate effect ignored in simulation
- **Application & Importance:** Impact resistance and energy absorption under multi-angle loads (0°-30°); designed for lightweight structural applications in rail transit, aerospace, and civil engineering where protection from impact loads is critical
- **Geometry / Domain:** 48 mm × 48 mm × 52.8 mm lattice structure partitioned into 9 sections (①-⑨) with wall thickness ranging from 0.5-0.9 mm in 0.1 mm increments; features both longitudinal (vertical) and lateral (horizontal) bidirectional gradients; unit cell parameters include number of corrugations (N), amplitude (A), and wall thickness (t); fabricated via selective laser sintering with 0.1-0.2 mm precision
10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120088.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Lower rigid plate fully fixed with all degrees of freedom constrained; static friction coefficient 0.3 and dynamic friction coefficient 0.2 at contact interfaces; impact angle θ ranging from 0° to 30°
- **Loads / Excitations:** Moving rigid plate velocity of 30 m/s; quasi-static compression test at strain rate of 10⁻³/s (3 mm/min); impact angles of 0°, 10°, 20°, and 30°; axial and oblique impact loading conditions
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Automatic single contact algorithm between rigid plate and lattice structure; automatic single surface contact for self-interacting interfaces of lattice structure; automatic surface contact nodes for lattice structure-rigid plate interaction
- **Simulation Type:** Explicit dynamic analysis using LSDYNA solver; 3D nonlinear modeling; mesh size of 0.3 mm selected after convergence analysis; oblique impact loading simulations with velocity 30 m/s
10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120088.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Dynamic impact mechanics of lattice structures under multi-angle loading conditions, including stress distribution, deformation patterns, energy absorption characteristics, and crushing behavior
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Specific energy absorption (SEA), crushing force efficiency (CFE), peak crushing force (PCF), mean crushing force (MCF), plateau stress, densification strain, force-displacement curves, stress-strain diagrams at impact angles (0°, 10°, 20°, 30°), and deformation failure modes
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize specific energy absorption (SEA) while minimizing peak crushing force (PCF) to enhance crashworthiness performance, with design variables being thickness parameters t₁, t₂, and t₃ (0.5 mm ≤ tᵢ ≤ 1.0 mm) of the bidirectional gradient structure
10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120088.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Wall thickness parameters constrained to 0.5 mm ≤ tᵢ ≤ 1.0 mm (i=1,2,3); overall structure dimensions of 48 mm × 48 mm × 52.8 mm; partitioned into 9 sections (①-⑨) with 0.1 mm thickness increments; mesh size limited to 0.3 mm for computational efficiency after convergence analysis
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Moving rigid plate velocity constrained to 30 m/s; impact angle range limited to 0°-30°; static friction coefficient of 0.3 and dynamic friction coefficient of 0.2 at contact interfaces; lower rigid plate fully fixed with all degrees of freedom constrained; quasi-static compression test conducted at strain rate of 10⁻³/s (3 mm/min)
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Fabrication via selective laser sintering (SLM 280) with precision of 0.1-0.2 mm; AlSi10Mg powder feedstock; pulsed laser scanning speed of 4 m/s; strain rate effect ignored due to aluminum alloy insensitivity; optimization impact conditions fixed at 30 m/s velocity and 10° angle for consistency

10_1007_s12206_015_0815_5.key_1:
- Water wave propagation in numerical wave tanks using level set finite element method
- Incompressible water and air as immiscible fluids with density (ρ) and kinematic viscosity (ν) as key properties
- Generation and propagation of linear and second-order Stokes waves for numerical wave tank development and wave force evaluation
- 2D domain: 10 m length (5 ≤ x ≤ +5), 0.24 m height, 0.2 m water depth, 1.5 m sponge layers at both ends
- 3D domain: 10 m length, 0.24 m height, 0.4 m width (-0.2 m ≤ y ≤ +0.2 m), 0.2 m water depth, 1.8 m sponge layers at both ends
- Wave generation source region: 0.06 m width (Sw), 0.0665 m height (Sh), located 0.0048 m below still water level
- Wave parameters: H = 0.01 m, T = 1.0 sec, C = 1.21 m/s, kd = 1.04 (L = 1.21 m) for intermediate water depth cases
- Wave force evaluation domain: 1.0 m water depth, 1.0 m width with 0.1 m height opening under vertical wall
- Mesh specifications: 65,050 nodes and 63,700 quadrilateral elements for 2D; 1,229,445 nodes and 1,144,000 hexahedral elements for 3D
- Numerical sponge layer parameters: α = 200.0, n = 10 for energy absorption at open boundaries
10_1007_s12206_015_0815_5.key_2:
- Walls at all domain boundaries except ends
- Numerical sponge layers at both ends (1.5 m thickness for 2D simulations, 1.8 m thickness for 3D simulations)
- Sponge layer damping coefficient defined by cs = [exp{(xs-x)/α}^n - 1]/[exp(1) - 1] with α = 200.0 and n = 10
- Wave generation source region: 0.06 m width (Sw), 0.0665 m height (Sh), located 0.0048 m below still water level
- Mass source function for linear waves: s(x,t) = CH/A sin(σt)
- Mass source function for 2nd-order Stokes waves with phase shift constant ps
- Linear wave parameters: H = 0.01 m, T = 1.0 sec, C = 1.21 m/s, kd = 1.04 (L = 1.21 m)
- 2nd-order Stokes wave parameters: H = 0.10 m, 0.15 m, and 0.20 m for wave force evaluation
- Air-water interface treated as immiscible fluids with level set method
- Level set advection equation: ∂φ/∂t + ui∂φ/∂xi = 0 for interface tracking
- Incompressible Navier-Stokes equations for fluid flow
- Transient simulations with time integration using fractional four-step method
- 2D domain for linear wave propagation and 3D domain for wave force evaluation
- Linear wave and 2nd-order Stokes wave simulations in intermediate water depth
10_1007_s12206_015_0815_5.key_3:
- Incompressible Navier-Stokes flow for water wave propagation with free surface tracking
