10_1007_s40997_025_00856_4.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Snap-fit mechanical metamaterial (SMM) with multistable characteristics for energy absorption
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Snap-fit material: Elastic-plastic with density 1.1×10³ kg/m³, Poisson's ratio 0.35, Young's modulus 3580 MPa, yield stress 79 MPa
  - Baseplate: Rigid body (020-*MAT_RIGID)
- **Application & Importance:** Reusable energy absorption for robotics collision prevention, impact protection devices, and precision instrument packaging; addresses limitation of single-use energy absorbers that rely on plastic deformation
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Two main components: deflecting member (cantilever beam) and retaining member
  - Retaining member features triangular insertion face matching baseplate wedge
  - Cantilever beam dimensions: T_b=3 mm (beam thickness), T_w=5 mm (wall thickness), W_b=8 mm (beam width)
  - Parametric ranges studied: L_b=16-24 mm (beam length), L_r=3-7 mm (retention feature length), α=20°-50° (insertion face angle)
  - Multistable operation with two stable states; energy absorbed through friction between insertion face and wedge face during deflection
  - Optimized parameters: L_b=16 mm, L_r=3.5 mm, α=37.14°
  - Multi-level assembly configuration enables programmable energy absorption across vertical layers
10_1007_s40997_025_00856_4.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Baseplate bottom surface completely fixed
  - Cantilever beam fixed at one end (modeled as Euler cantilever beam)
  - Rigid body assumption for baseplate (020-*MAT_RIGID material model)
  - Chamfer design at contact edge position between retaining member and base wedge to prevent stress concentration

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Quasi-static compression loading at 10 mm/s
  - Impact test with steel ball: m=5 kg, v₀=2.5 m/s
  - External load exceeding specific threshold value required for deformation process
  - Assembly force calculated as Fa = {(μ+tan α)/(1-μ tan α) Fd, (n-1)Lr < d ≤ nx; (1-μ tan θ)/(μ+tan θ) Fd, nx < d ≤ nLr}

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Frictional contact between insertion face and wedge face (friction coefficient μ)
  - Energy absorption through friction generated by bending of deflecting member and relative movement of insertion face and wedge face
  - Contact interaction modeled with chamfered edges at contact points
  - Multiple contact interfaces in multi-level assembly structure

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Quasi-static analysis (loading velocity 10 mm/s, kinetic energy <10% of total energy)
  - Explicit dynamic simulations using LS-DYNA
  - 3D finite element model with hexahedral elements, reduced integration and hourglass control
  - Material model 024-*MAT_PIECEWISE_LINEAR_PLASTICITY for snap-fit
  - Multi-level assembly configuration with four vertical layers for impact testing
10_1007_s40997_025_00856_4.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Elastic deformation behavior of cantilever beam structure
  - Multistable transition between stable states during assembly/disassembly
  - Frictional contact mechanics between insertion face and wedge face
  - Energy transformation during impact (kinetic to internal and frictional energy)
  - Force-displacement relationships during compression and recovery

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Specific Energy Absorption (SEA) in J/kg (total energy absorbed per unit mass)
  - Peak Crushing Force (PCF) in N (initial peak load in force-displacement curve)
  - Assembly force-displacement curves
  - Internal energy and frictional energy components
  - Total absorbed energy
  - Force response at different parameter configurations (Lb, Lr, α)
  - Pareto optimal solution sets for multi-objective optimization

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Maximize Specific Energy Absorption (SEA)
  - Minimize Peak Crushing Force (PCF)
  - Achieve optimal balance between high energy absorption capacity and low peak impact load
  - Multi-objective optimization using NSGA-II algorithm with design variables: beam length (Lb), retention feature length (Lr), and insertion face angle (α)
  - Target improvement: 175.7% increase in SEA and 64.3% reduction in PCF compared to original design (from SEA=7.86 J/kg to 21.67 J/kg, PCF=47.0 N to 77.23 N)
10_1007_s40997_025_00856_4.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Beam length constrained to 16-24 mm (Lb)
  - Retention feature length constrained to 3-7 mm (Lr)
  - Insertion face angle constrained to 20°-50° (α)
  - Beam thickness at wall: T_b=3 mm
  - Wall thickness at beam: T_w=5 mm
  - Beam width at wall: W_b=8 mm
  - Total snap-fit length: L_t=25 mm
  - Multi-level assembly limited to 4 vertical layers in tested configuration
  - Chamfer radius options tested: 0 mm, 0.25 mm, and 0.5 mm

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Kinetic energy must remain below 10% of total energy for quasi-static analysis validity
  - Loading velocity constrained to 10 mm/s for quasi-static simulation
  - Material yield stress limit: 79 MPa (exceeding this at 50° insertion angle causes zigzag load curve)
  - Stress at cantilever beam root must remain below yield strength to prevent damage
  - Insertion face angle must be 25°-40° to balance energy absorption and structural integrity
  - Assembly force must exceed threshold value to initiate deformation process
  - Maximum deflection must not cause permanent deformation to maintain reusability

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Chamfer design required at contact edge position to prevent stress concentration
  - Insertion face angle must be carefully selected to avoid damage during assembly
  - Retention feature length must be selected based on material properties of snap-fit
  - Beam length must be determined considering installation space limitations
  - Theoretical model simplification ignores chamfer effects, creating discrepancy in contraction stage analysis
  - Manufacturing must maintain precise wedge face geometry to ensure proper insertion mechanics
  - Contact interface requires precise manufacturing to maintain consistent friction coefficient (μ)

10_1016_j_cscm_2025_e04480.key_1:
- Identity & Domain: Concrete mixture design for fire-resistant reinforced concrete structures, focusing on compressive strength prediction at elevated temperatures and multi-objective optimization of mixture proportions
- Material / Medium: Concrete (cement, water, sand, gravel, fly ash, slag, superplasticizer); Ordinary Portland cement PO42.5; Fly ash (specific surface area >400 kg/m³); Slag (specific surface area >400 kg/m³); Water-to-binder ratio (0.27–0.90); Fly ash replacement ratio (0–0.55); Slag content (0–0.61); Aggregate-to-binder ratio (2.64–9.85); Fire exposure temperature (24–700 °C)
- Application & Importance: To address concrete's susceptibility to fire-induced performance degradation in multi-story buildings (13.85% fire likelihood over 10 years); optimize mix designs balancing high-temperature mechanical properties, production cost, and carbon emissions; achieve up to 40% carbon emission reduction and 30% cost reduction while maintaining structural integrity
- Geometry / Domain: Square columns (300 mm and 500 mm side lengths) exposed to ISO834-standard fire for 2 hours; concrete specimens (150 mm diameter × 300 mm height cylinders); temperature distribution in 1/4 cross-sections (150×150 mm and 250×250 mm); equivalent compressive strength calculations accounting for non-uniform temperature distribution within sections

10_1016_j_conbuildmat_2025_141685.key_1:

  - Track slab: C60 concrete (2500 kg/m³ density, 36.5 GPa Young's modulus, 0.2 Poisson's ratio)
  - Base plate: C40 concrete (2500 kg/m³ density, 32.5 GPa Young's modulus, 0.2 Poisson's ratio)

- **Application & Importance:** SCC casting quality directly affects track smoothness which influences high-speed train operations; improper casting causes slurry overflow, incomplete casting, and excessive slab uplift
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - NPST structure comprising track slab, isolation layer, SCC layer, and base plate
  - 24 sets of portal rebars and 2 sets of spiral rebars within SCC layer
  - Track slab with 9 rail support platforms (1#-9#) for rail installation
  - Full-scale experimental dimensions: 1550 mm × 1210 mm × 1550 mm layout
  - Section A-A dimensions: 250 mm, 1010 mm, 160 mm, 110 mm, 110 mm, 1010 mm, 250 mm (total 2890 mm width)

10_1016_j_conbuildmat_2025_141685.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**

  - Normal direction prevents interpenetration while allowing fresh separation for contact interfaces
  - Other contact relationships prevent both penetration and separation
  - CFD module mesh size: 2.5-20.0 mm

  - PRESTO interpolation scheme for pressure calculations across cell faces

- **Loads / Excitations:**

  - SCC hydration times: 5, 30, 60, 90, and 120 minutes
  - Anti-overflow tube heights: 10, 15, 20, 25, and 30 cm
  - Clamping device stiffness coefficient (Sc): 0.75, 1.00, 1.25, and 1.50
  - SCC yield stress and plastic viscosity varying with hydration time
  - Gravitational acceleration in Navier-Stokes equations

  - Arbitrary Lagrange-Eulerian (ALE) method for coordinate information transfer between FSI interface
  - SCC-air interface tracked by volume of fluid model

  - Pressure-based solver for CFD module

10_1016_j_compstruct_2024_118594.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Composite pressure vessel with unequal polar openings, designed for storage and heating water. The analysis focuses on multi-objective optimization of filament-wound composite structures with non-symmetrical polar openings.

- **Material / Medium:** Three composite material systems: Glass Fiber reinforced Polypropylene (GF-PP), Carbon Fiber reinforced Polyamide (CF-PA), and Flax Fiber reinforced Polylactide (FF-PLA). The liner material is Polypropylene (PP). Key properties include: fiber volume fraction (0.45 for all composites), Young's moduli (E₁₁: 34,500 MPa for GF-PP, 90,296 MPa for CF-PA, 30,643 MPa for FF-PLA), tensile strength in fiber direction (Xₜ: 765 MPa for GF-PP, 1710 MPa for CF-PA, 295 MPa for FF-PLA), and density (ρ: 1.47×10⁻⁹ t/mm³ for GF-PP, 1.3×10⁻⁹ t/mm³ for CF-PA).

- **Application & Importance:** Domestic hot water storage alternative to metallic vessels (stainless/enamel steel), requiring durability with optimal thermal properties, low energy consumption, and recyclability. The optimization addresses the lack of global methodology for non-symmetrical pressure vessels with unequal openings, aiming to minimize composite mass and thickness while maximizing strain energy and satisfying failure criteria.

- **Geometry / Domain:** Cylindrical pressure vessel (180 L volume) with domed ends, featuring: cylinder height (Hc) of 819 mm, cylinder radius (R) of 250 mm, upper and lower dome heights (h_up, h_d) of 123 mm each, and liner thickness of 4 mm. The design includes four hoop layers and three helical layers with paired ±α winding angles. Polar opening radii vary per layer (r₀upᵢ, r₀dᵢ), with r₀up₁ = 20 mm and r₀d₁ = 125 mm fixed as manufacturing constraints. The model accounts for geodesic and non-geodesic fiber trajectories with piecewise linear fiber angle distribution along the cylindrical section.

10_1016_j_energy_2025_135712.key_1:
- Liquid-based cooling plate for lithium-ion battery packs in electric vehicles
- Fluid: 50% ethylene glycol water (ρf = 1051 kg/m³, kf = 0.411 W/m/K, cpf = 3054 J/kg/K, μf = 0.00137 Pa·s)
- Solid: Aluminum (ρs = 2700 kg/m³, ks = 237 W/m/K, cps = 900 J/kg/K)
- Designed to maintain battery temperature within 15-35°C with <5°C deviation between cells to prevent 1.5-2.0% capacity loss
- Bi-directional fluid pattern with inlet and outlet on same side for shortest coolant circulation path
- Design domain: 2200 mm × 1060 mm with 100 mm inlet width, symmetric about center line
- Inlet conditions: constant velocity (0.0021 m/s) and temperature (25°C)
- Outlet condition: zero-gauge pressure with zero heat flux
- No-slip boundary condition applied to domain walls with thermal insulation on exterior surfaces
10_1016_j_energy_2025_135712.key_2:
- Inlet: Constant velocity (u_in = 0.0021 m/s) and constant temperature (T_in = 25 °C)
- Outlet: Zero-gauge pressure (P_out) and zero heat flux
- Walls: No-slip boundary condition applied to design domain and exterior walls
- Exterior walls: Thermal-insulation condition
- Symmetry: Design symmetry considered about center line (dashed blue line in Fig. 7)
- Heat generation: Normalized heat flux based on C-rates (0.5 C, 1.0 C, 2.0 C)
- Flow rates: 10-30 LPM investigated for thermofluid analysis; 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 LPM tested experimentally
- Volume constraint: V* = 0.35 (35% volume fraction)
- Experimental conditions: 100 W heat source, ambient temperature of 22.8 °C
- Simulation type: Two-dimensional, steady-state, incompressible, laminar flow
- Coupled physics: Continuity equation, Navier-Stokes equation, and heat-balance equation solved simultaneously
- Material properties: 50% ethylene glycol water (fluid) and aluminum (solid) with specified thermal and fluid properties
10_1016_j_energy_2025_135712.key_3:
- Two-dimensional thermofluid behavior under steady-state, incompressible, laminar flow conditions
- Velocity distribution, pressure distribution, and temperature distribution calculated via continuity equation, Navier-Stokes equation, and heat-balance equation
- Power dissipation (pressure drop between inlet and outlet)
- Thermal compliance (combination of conduction and convection compliances)
- Temperature difference (ΔT = T_outlet - T_inlet)
- Maximum temperature deviation ((ΔT)_max)
- Average temperature (T_avg)
- Flow rate effects on thermal performance (10-30 LPM)
- C-rate effects on thermal performance (0.5 C to 2.0 C)
- Minimize power dissipation (pressure drop) while satisfying cooling requirements
- Minimize thermal compliance
- Achieve uniform temperature distribution (target <5°C deviation between cells)
- Eliminate intermediate densities (achieve clear solid/fluid phase distinction)
- Balance trade-off between fluid performance (low power dissipation) and thermal performance (high thermal compliance)
- Satisfy volume constraint (35% volume fraction)
- Suppress locally high temperatures to prevent battery hardware damage
10_1016_j_energy_2025_135712.key_4:

- Symmetric design region about center line (dashed blue line)
- Volume fraction constraint: V* = 0.35 (35% maximum allowable volume of fluid)

- Maximum temperature deviation between cells: ≤ 5 °C (to prevent 1.5-2.0% capacity loss)
- Flow rate range: 10-30 LPM investigated for thermofluid analysis

- HIP temperature range: 920-950°C
- HIP pressure range: 120-150 MPa
- HIP time range: 0-180 minutes
- Optimized HIP parameters: 950°C, 120 MPa, 60 minutes
- Tensile strength: As-cast 1033 MPa, HIP-treated 1013 MPa (1.94% reduction)
- Elongation: As-cast 7.0%, HIP-treated 13.5% (92% increase)
- Thermal conductivity range: 6.7085-24.23 W/m/K (25-1000°C)
- Young's modulus range: 36-112 GPa (25-1000°C)
- Yield strength range: 5.22-887 MPa (25-1000°C)
- Low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs): As-cast 7.58%, HIP-treated 10.7%

- Pore closure criterion: Volume reduction to <0.001 mm³
- Heating rate: 10°C/min
- Pressurization rate: 1.2-1.3 MPa/min
- Tensile testing: Room temperature, strain rate 10^-3 s^-1
- Energy savings: >60% compared to conventional HIP (150-minute hold time)
- Post-treatment efficiency increase: >300% by omitting solution aging
10_1007_s40962_024_01522_2.key_2:

10_1002_batt_202400539.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Lithium-ion battery (LIB) manufacturing processes and components, including anodes, cathodes, separators, and complete cells with focus on high-energy density configurations for electric vehicles, portable electronics, and grid storage
- **Material / Medium:** Cathode materials: NMC (LiNi1-x-yCoxMnyO2), NCA (LiNi1-x-yCoxAlyO2), LMO (LiMn2O4), LFP (LiFePO4); Anode materials: graphite, silicon, lithium metal, hard carbon, LTO (Li4Ti5O12); Solvents: NMP (N-Methyl-2-pyrrolidone), water-based alternatives; Current collectors: copper foil (anode), aluminum foil (cathode); Electrolyte: lithium salts in organic solvents
- **Application & Importance:** Optimization of battery performance, reliability, safety, and cost-effectiveness; reduction of energy consumption (20.3-37.5 kWhprod per 1 kWhcell) and greenhouse gas emissions in manufacturing; prediction of state-of-charge (SOC), state-of-health (SOH), and remaining useful life (RUL) with MAE < 1.3% and RMSE < 2%; enabling sustainable manufacturing practices for electric vehicles and grid storage
- **Geometry / Domain:** Cell types: coin cells, pouch cells, cylindrical cells, prismatic cells; Modeling scales: micro (10^-8 to 10^-5 m), meso (10^-5 to 10^-2 m), macro (10^-2 to 10^3 m); Physical domains include electrode particles, separator, electrolyte, and current collectors; Manufacturing process stages: mixing, coating, drying, vacuum drying, calendering and slitting, assembling and testing; Contact areas in crushed cells: 6.15 mm², 4.125 mm², 2.775 mm²
10_1002_batt_202400539.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Contact areas in mechanically crushed pouch cell: 6.15 mm², 4.125 mm², 2.775 mm²; 740 mAh LIB capacity; Anode surface at SOC=50%; Current rates: 1 C and 4 C; SOC range: 2%-98%; Constant current: ±0.5 C/1 C; Boundary conditions primarily applied to cathode (infinite Li-ion supply in half-cells); Material constraints: Young's modulus (E), fully compacted value modulus (Emax), strain (ε), strain when material is fully compacted (εp), fitting parameter (b)
- **Loads / Excitations:** Indentation-induced short-circuit; Lithium ion flow governed by Fick's diffusion equations; Electrochemical reactions represented by Butler-Volmer equation; C-rate tests; Open Circuit Potential (OCP) measurements; Impedance spectroscopy; Driving cycle with non-uniform current distribution; Constant current discharge under varying discharge rates; Electrochemical-thermal model simulations
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Mechanical-electrical-thermal coupling; Explicit representation of active material, current collector, and separator components; Mechanical deformation under quasi-static indentation; Strain components: mechanical loading (εmeij), thermal expansion (εeiTij), Li intercalation (εeicij); Time-temperature superposition principle with thermo-viscoelastic modeling; Transferred structural parameters between manufacturing process models and battery cell simulation
- **Simulation Type:** Quasi-static settings; 3D multiphysics modeling; Pseudo-two-dimensional (P2D) model; Single-particle model (SPM); Stochastic modeling; Monte Carlo (MC) and Kinetic Monte Carlo (kMC); Brownian dynamics; Coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD); Two-level framework (electrode submodels and cell submodels); Reduced electrochemical submodel validated up to 4 C discharge rate
10_1002_batt_202400539.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Electrochemical processes including lithium-ion diffusion mechanisms governed by Fick's diffusion equations; coupled thermal-electric-mechanical responses; stress-strain relationships under mechanical deformation; electrochemical reactions described by Butler-Volmer equation; multiphysics interactions between electrochemical, thermal, and mechanical domains; lithium plating kinetics; electrode slurry aggregation behavior; drying process dynamics
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** State of Charge (SOC) with MAE < 1.3% and RMSE < 2%; State of Health (SOH) with error < 3%; Remaining Useful Life (RUL) with RMSE < 5.03%; Cell voltage prediction; Relative solid lithium concentration on anode surface; Temperature distribution and local temperature increase (up to 22.75 K); Electronic conductivity, thickness, and capacity predictions; Energy consumption (421 kWh per 10 kWh battery pack); Cost per kWh ($/kWh) for different cell types and materials; Classification error for electrode quality assessment
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize manufacturing energy consumption (currently 20.3-37.5 kWhprod per 1 kWhcell); Reduce greenhouse gas emissions; Improve prediction accuracy for SOC, SOH, and RUL; Optimize solvent selection (NMP alternatives); Reduce electrode thickness to lower manufacturing costs; Maximize energy density while minimizing cost; Achieve optimal trade-offs between cost, energy density, and environmental impact; Minimize classification error in electrode quality assessment (e.g., 0.02% error for LFP capacity with 3 decision trees)
10_1002_batt_202400539.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Electrode thickness constraints (doubling thickness reduces costs by 25%); Cell form factor limitations (pouch, cylindrical, prismatic, coin cells); Theoretical capacity constraints (graphite anodes limited to 372 mAhg⁻¹, LTO limited to 175 mAhg⁻¹, silicon to 3579 mAhg⁻¹); SOC operational range constrained to 2%-98%; Current rate constraints (±0.5 C/1 C); Material-specific energy density limitations (LFP/LMO have lower energy density per kg/cm³)
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Thermal constraints (5% energy increase when ambient temperature rises from 0°C to 40°C); NMP classified as reproductive toxicant with health/safety risks; Lithium metal anodes limited by dendrite formation leading to "dead lithium" and reduced Coulombic efficiency; Water-based electrodes have lower binding effectiveness for active material-active material (AM-AM) and active material-current collector (AM-CC) compared to NMP-based; GWP constraints (recovery of lithium results in 38-45% greater energy consumption and 16-20% more air emissions than initial manufacture)
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Drying process consumes majority of energy in electrode production; NMP energy requirements (10.2 kWh per kg vaporized, 421 kWh per 10 kWh battery pack, total energy 45x vaporization heat); Manufacturing process sequence constraints (mixing → coating → drying → vacuum drying → calendering/slitting → assembly/testing); Solvent selection limitations (NMP vs. water-based alternatives); Electrode volume constraints (water-based coating has lower ultimate volume than NMP-based); Production scale constraints (500,000 packs annually for cost analysis); Manufacturing cost constraints (reducing electrode thickness lowers costs)

10_1016_j_cad_2022_103232.key_1:
- Identity: Automotive sheet metal components, specifically engine hood sub-structure of BMW E46
- Material: Steel with Young's modulus of 210 GPa and Poisson's ratio of 0.3
- Application: Creating digital twins for sheet metal assembly optimization in automotive manufacturing
- Geometry: Surface meshes of sheet metal parts with thicknesses of 0.7 mm and 2 mm
- Target accuracy: ±0.05 mm (matching measurement uncertainty of optical measurement devices)
- Component types: Outer skin, inner parts, and reinforce structure
- Mesh type: First-order shell elements
- Measurement method: 3D scanning with structured light scanner
- Perimeter characteristics: Topological boundaries with center of mass and length parameters
- Mesh elements: Ranging from 4,039 to 120,381 elements across different parts
- Validation: Performed on single parts and full assembly (7 components totaling 365,152 shell elements)
10_1016_j_cad_2022_103232.key_2:
- Perimeter boundaries with prescribed movement in all three dimensions (blue in figures)
- Displacement boundaries applied only in surface normal direction (green in figures)
- Restriction of boundary placement to perimeter boundaries only for a user-defined number of element rows next to mesh perimeters
- Class a boundaries: nodes within 0 mm to 0.05 mm distance range with displacement set to zero (only normal direction restricted)
- Class b boundaries: nodes within 0.05 mm to 1 mm distance range with dense boundary placement (every 2nd node)
- Class c boundaries: nodes beyond 1 mm distance with coarse boundary placement (every 2nd node)
- Boundary displacement magnitudes weighted by function f(x) = 1/(0.5x+2) + 0.5
- Maximum normal angle between source vertex and target triangle: 10° for Part 1, 30° for Parts 2 and 3
- Maximum search distance: 10 mm for all parts
- Perimeter displacement vectors calculated via coherent point drift (CPD) registration algorithm
- Linear elastic FE problem with Young's modulus of 210 GPa and Poisson's ratio of 0.3
- Iterative process until RMS error below threshold (target of ±0.05 mm)
- First-order shell elements used throughout the simulation
- Boundary conditions updated in each iteration based on current mesh position
- FE solver: ABAQUS from Dassault Systèmes
- Element quality criteria per ABAQUS standards (shape factor <0.01 for triangles, corner angles between 5°-170° for triangles, etc.)
- Measurement setup using HP pro S3 structured light scanner
- Aluminum-profile frame with dial gauge for positioning during measurement
10_1016_j_cad_2022_103232.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Linear elastic deformation field calculation for mesh morphing
- Target Outputs: RMS error between current mesh and target geometry, signed distance to target geometry (in mm), percentage of bad shaped elements
- Optimization Goal: Approximate target geometry within ±0.05 mm (matching measurement uncertainty of optical measurement devices)
- Termination criterion: Iteration stops when RMS error falls below threshold value
- Convergence metric: RMS error per iteration converging toward zero
- Mesh quality target: Maintain elements within ABAQUS quality criteria (shape factor <0.01 for triangles, corner angles between 5°-170° for triangles, etc.)
- Final accuracy requirement: Error values below ±0.05 mm for morphed geometry
- Iterative process: Repeated until geometries of FE-model and measurement match within specified tolerance
10_1016_j_cad_2022_103232.key_4:
- Geometric constraints: Method designed and validated only for surface meshes (not volume meshes)
- Mesh resolution limitation: Element edge deviations occur even when nodes are close to target surface
- Perimeter matching requirement: Target mesh must accurately represent perimeter curves for boundary condition application
- Measurement coverage limitation: Areas not visible to both scanner cameras cannot be captured
- Maximum error tolerance: Target accuracy of ±0.05 mm (matching optical measurement uncertainty)
- Material constraints: Linear elastic model with Young's modulus of 210 GPa and Poisson's ratio of 0.3 (geometric non-linearity not considered)
- Normal angle thresholds: 10°-60° depending on iteration phase (used to filter mismatched normals)
- Search distance limit: 5-10 mm for thresholding distance calculations
- Element quality criteria: ABAQUS standards (shape factor <0.01 for triangles, corner angles 5°-170° for triangles, aspect ratio <10, edge length >0.01 mm)
- Boundary placement constraints: "Remove rows" parameter (1-3 rows) defining exclusion zone next to perimeters
- Boundary density constraints: Class-specific coarsening parameters (n values: 1-5) for boundary placement
- Computational constraint: FE pre-processing time dominates overall computation time
- No implemented mesh quality controls during morphing process
- Partial measurement limitation: Sub-structure not captured in scans shows higher errors (up to ±0.5 mm)

- Fixed constraint at spar roots connected to fuselage

- Distributed load on free end of L-shaped cantilever beam
- Concentrated downward load at center of simply supported beam top

- Concentrated load (engine weight) at center of wing
- Biomedical implant interface with bones
- Material orientation specification for anisotropic lattice structures
- 3D Finite Element Analysis
- Linear elasticity and small deformations assumption

- Steady-state mechanical analysis
- Topology optimization framework

- Displacement magnitude, Mises stress distribution, and strain energy values
- Structural compliance (F⊤U), force-displacement curves, and volume fraction distribution
- Relative Young's modulus (E/E*), shear modulus, and Poisson's ratio for lattice structures
- Minimize structural compliance while satisfying volume fraction constraints
- Reduce maximum displacement response (27.9-57.3% reduction demonstrated across examples)

10_1007_s40430_023_04213_x.key_1:
- Polymer spur gear tooth analyzed for crack propagation effects on mesh stiffness
- Material: Polyamide 12 (PA12) with elastic modulus E = 1650 MPa, Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3, density = 1.01 g/cm³
- Gear parameters: Module = 2 mm, teeth number = 30, pressure angle = 20°, face width = 17 mm, pitch circle diameter = 60 mm, addendum circle diameter = 64 mm, dedendum circle diameter = 55 mm, base circle diameter = 56.3816 mm, shaft diameter = 48 mm, whole depth = 4.5 mm, rim thickness = 3.5 mm, contact ratio = 1.6
- Initial crack parameters: lengths of 0/0.1/0.5 mm, angles of 70°/50°, positioned at fillet root tooth area
- Crack propagation studied under loads of 100/150/200 N at rotational speed of 400 rpm
- Backup ratio (rim thickness/whole depth) = 0.77, where crack propagates through tooth thickness
- Gear mesh stiffness (GMS) measured in N/mm with maximum value 3543 N/mm (double pairs contact) and minimum 1971 N/mm (single pair contact) for 150 N load
- Crack growth direction depends on backup ratio, with crack propagating through tooth thickness when backup ratio ≥ 0.5
- Mesh cycle period = 0.0083 s, GMS cycle period = 0.005 s at 400 rpm (frequency f = 200 Hz)
- Crack initiation occurs at tooth root in contact side where tensile root stress reaches maximum critical stress
- For 0.5 mm initial crack length, stiffness reduction of 5.3% (70° case) and 4.6% (50° case) at 200 N load
- Crack length ratio (total crack length/available region length) reaches 13.49% (50°) and 14.1% (70°) with 0.5 mm initial crack at 200 N load
10_1007_s40430_023_04213_x.key_2:
- Fixed boundary conditions at gear root (red edges in Fig. 5 representing regions fixed to ground)
- Applied normal pressure load moving along contact regions during mesh cycle
- Loads: 100 N, 150 N, and 200 N (Table 4)
- Rotational speed: 400 rpm (Table 4)
- Contact ratio: 1.6 (Table 2)
- Initial crack parameters: lengths of 0 mm, 0.1 mm, and 0.5 mm; angles of 70° and 50° (Table 4)
- Linear mixed-mode softening traction-separation law for cohesive behavior (Fig. 7)
- Cohesive parameters: Mode I fracture toughness GIc = 1.1 N/mm, cohesive strength σn max = 16 MPa, interfacial stiffness Kn = 1E+6 N/mm³ (Table 3)
- Damage initiation criterion: f = max(⟨σn⟩/σn max, ⟨τs⟩/τs max, ⟨τt⟩/τt max) ≤ 1 (Equation 11)
- Propagation criterion: (GI/GIC)α0 + (GII/GIIC)α0 + (GIII/GIIIC)α0 = 1 with α0 = 1 (Equation 12)
- Quasi-static procedure for one mesh cycle
- 3D numerical model using linear hexahedron 8-nodes brick elements
- Contact region length |AB| defined by equation: |AB| = 0.5[√(da1² - db1²) + √(da2² - db2²) - (d1 + d2)sin(ψn)] (Equation 9)
- Load moves from points A to B for driven tooth model and from B to A for driving model
- Backup ratio (rim thickness/whole depth) = 0.77 (3.5 mm / 4.5 mm)
10_1007_s40430_023_04213_x.key_3:

10_1016_j_compstruc_2017_09_011.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Bearing bracket structural component analyzed as a 3D elasticity problem with parametric uncertainty using stochastic finite element method; governed by elliptic stochastic partial differential equation -∇·[κ(x,θ)∇u(x,θ)] = f(x,θ)
- **Material / Medium:** Coefficient κ modeled as Gaussian random field with mean μ = 200 units, standard deviation σ = 10 units, and exponential covariance kernel C(x,y) = σ²e^(-|x-y|/lc); structural material with restrained boundary degrees of freedom at bolt holes
- **Application & Importance:** Uncertainty quantification for engineering systems requiring prediction of behavior under parametric uncertainty; addresses computational challenges of simultaneous large degrees of freedom (25,023 active DOF) and high stochastic dimensionality (L = 25)
- **Geometry / Domain:** Complex 3D mechanical component with bolt holes; discretized with 8,463 nodes, 34,667 linear strain tetrahedral elements; domain decomposed into subdomains using FETI-DP method; square domain of 0.5 × 0.5 used in numerical studies
10_1016_j_compstruc_2017_09_011.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Dirichlet boundary condition u(x) = 0 on ∂D; all boundary DOF near bolt holes are restrained; interface compatibility enforced via ∑ᵢ₌₁ᴺˢ Bᵢᴿ Uᵢᴿ = 0; corner nodes and remaining nodes classification in FETI-DP subdomain decomposition
- **Loads / Excitations:** Deterministic point load applied on one end of the bracket; right-hand side term f(x,θ) in the governing elliptic stochastic PDE
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Subdomain-level equilibrium equations with Lagrange multipliers (Λ) enforcing compatibility at boundary nodes; global coarse problem combining subdomain contributions; interface problem requiring solution of FᴵᴿᴿΛ + FᴵᴿᶜKᴵᶜᶜ⁻¹FᴵᴿᶜᵀΛ = dᴿ - Fᶜ
- **Simulation Type:** 3D elasticity problem; linear stochastic analysis; hybrid method combining stochastic Galerkin (subdomain level) and Monte Carlo simulation (interface problem); elliptic stochastic partial differential equation; steady-state analysis; weak and strong scalability studies with fixed chaos order p = 2
10_1016_j_compstruc_2017_09_011.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Elastic deformation under parametric uncertainty; solution of elliptic stochastic partial differential equation with random field coefficient κ(x,θ); uncertainty propagation in mechanical systems with stochastic material properties
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Displacement field u(x,θ); computational time for interface problem, subdomain problem, and total solution; number of PCG iterations; global stochastic dimensionality (L); local stochastic dimensionality (L_s); wall clock time; weak and strong scalability metrics
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize computational time for large-scale stochastic problems; maximize scalability with increasing degrees of freedom and stochastic dimensionality; find optimal combinations of subdomains (N_s) and Monte Carlo bins (N_b); reduce total PCG iterations through proposed initial iterate strategy; minimize communication overhead in parallel implementation
10_1016_j_compstruc_2017_09_011.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Square domain of 0.5 × 0.5 used for numerical studies; bearing bracket model with 8,463 nodes, 34,667 linear strain tetrahedral elements, and 25,023 active DOF; correlation length (l_c) of random field affects stochastic dimensionality; domain decomposed into N_s subdomains using METIS
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** FETI is not numerically scalable for fourth order problems (plates and shells); computational cost becomes prohibitively large when degrees of freedom and stochastic dimensionality increase; communication cost grows with number of subdomains; stochastic Galerkin suffers from curse of dimensionality; Amdahl's law limits parallelization efficiency; ideal weak scalability requires horizontal time curve but observed steep rise after N_b = 30 due to communication bottleneck
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Limited to 12-node Linux cluster with 8 GB RAM and 8 processors (2.6 GHz) per node; communication bottleneck occurs when too many processors simultaneously access storage; process-processor mapping must be explicitly managed to reduce inter-node communication; default compiler mapping shows poor weak scalability compared to proposed mapping; bin size must be kept constant for weak scalability studies

- Application & Importance: Understanding interlayer bonding shear performance is critical as 3DPC structures exhibit interlayer bonding weak interfaces that significantly impact safety, durability, and mechanical performance; the research establishes constitutive models for theoretical and numerical simulations of 3DPC interlayer shear mechanics
- Geometry / Domain: Rectangular specimens measuring 600 mm (length) × 40 mm (width) × 240 mm (height) printed, later cut to 100 mm (length) × 40 mm (width) × 120 mm (height) for double shear testing; testing focuses on layer interface with vertical loading configuration; specimens analyzed include single-graded aggregates (0.6mm, 1.18mm, 2.36mm, 4.75mm) and continuous-graded aggregates with Fuller curve exponents (n=0.4, 0.45, 0.5, 0.55)

- Loads / Excitations: Shear force applied parallel to interlayer interface; Loading rate of 0.5 mm/min; Maximum shear stress values ranging from 4.10 MPa to 7.76 MPa depending on aggregate gradation; Shear stress calculated as τ = F/(2LH) where F is bearing capacity, L = 40 mm, H = 120 mm
- Interactions / Interfaces: Interlayer interface between printed concrete layers; Aggregate-matrix interface at microstructural level; Localized crack formation at interfaces; Single-graded and continuous-graded specimen interfaces analyzed separately

10_1016_j_conbuildmat_2025_142024.key_3:

10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120329.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Automotive chassis S-rail with three-dimensional curved axis and variable cross-sections (depth and width profiles)

- **Manufacturing constraints:** Compressive strain limit ε̂c = -0.04; tensile strain limit ε̂t = 0.2 for DP780 steel with 2 mm thickness
- **Optimization results (without constraints):** Strain energy decreased from 0.14 to 0.01 J (92.6% reduction); mass reduced from 3.54 to 2.66 kg (25.1% reduction); converged at 108th iteration
- **Optimization results (with constraints):** Strain energy decreased from 0.14 to 0.02 J; mass reduced from 3.54 to 2.91 kg; converged at 64th iteration
- **Design variables:** 18 parameters (six triplets) controlling left width, right width, and depth profiles including coordinates (xo, zo/yo) and radii (ro)

10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120329.key_2:

- **Loads / Excitations:** Compression load applied on the right end of flange and web edges in negative x-direction; objective to minimize strain energy (compliance)
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** FEA model established with reduced integration shell elements (S4R); structure remeshed in each iteration after geometric modifications; Flexible Roll Forming (FRF) manufacturing process with longitudinal strain constraints in flange edges

10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120329.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Strain energy (compliance) in joules; mass in kilograms; displacement magnitude in millimeters; von Mises stress in megapascals; longitudinal strain in flange edges; maximum displacement (23.91 mm initial, 3.59 mm optimized in Case 1); maximum stress (142.83 MPa initial, 29.93 MPa optimized in Case 1)
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize strain energy (compliance) while maintaining structural mass below initial design and satisfying manufacturing constraints of Flexible Roll Forming process (longitudinal strain within -0.04 to 0.2 limits for DP780 steel)
10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120329.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** 
  - Overlapping constraint: |ro_k^d| + |ro_{k+1}^d| - √[(xo_{k+1}^d - xo_k^d)² + (yo_{k+1}^d - yo_k^d)²] ≤ 0 to prevent circle overlap
  - Sequence constraints: X_{k-1,1}^d - X_{k,0}^d ≤ 0 and X_{k,0}^d - X_{k,1}^d ≤ 0 to prevent crossover/reverse relationships
  - 18 design variables (six triplets) controlling the geometry
  - Thickness maintained at uniform 2 mm throughout optimization

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Area constraint: A_3D(ξ) ≤ A_3D(ξ_input) to prevent mass increase
  - Compressive strain limit: ε̂_c = -0.04 for DP780 steel with 2 mm thickness
  - Tensile strain limit: ε̂_t = 0.2 for DP780 steel with 2 mm thickness
  - Maximum iteration limit set to 500
  - Convergence criteria threshold of 10e-7 for auxiliary function change ratio

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Flexible Roll Forming (FRF) manufacturing constraints:
    - Longitudinal strain in concave depth section: ε_d^c = ln(1 - h sinθ / rd_init^c)
    - Longitudinal strain in convex depth section: ε_d^t = ln(1 + h sinθ / rd_init^t)
    - Longitudinal strain in concave width section: ε_w^c = ln(1 - h(1 - cosθ) / (rw_init^c + h))
    - Longitudinal strain in convex width section: ε_w^t = ln(1 + h(1 - cosθ) / (rw_init^t - h))
  - Flange perpendicular to web maintained at θ = 90° throughout process
  - Strain must remain within material limits to prevent wrinkling (compression) and tearing (tension) defects

10_1007_s00339_025_08633_5.key_1:

10_1016_j_finel_2024_104169.key_1:

10_1016_j_finel_2024_104169.key_2:

10_1016_j_finel_2024_104169.key_3:

10_1016_j_finel_2024_104169.key_4:

10_1016_j_finel_2022_103794.key_1:

10_1016_j_finel_2022_103794.key_2:

- Small strain-displacement relations used

- Linear analysis (no mention of nonlinear effects)
10_1016_j_finel_2022_103794.key_3:

10_1016_j_finel_2022_103794.key_4:
- Uniform structured background mesh with rectangular/cuboid elements required for the immersed boundary approach
- Small-deformation and plane stress assumptions limit analysis to linear regime
- Quadratic B-spline elements require C¹ continuous displacement field approximation
- Elements have only three translational degrees of freedom per node with no rotational degrees of freedom
- Transverse shear strains vary only as allowed by the element shape functions (not constant assumption)
- For extremely thin shells, quadratic B-spline elements show reduced convergence rate (shear locking effect)
- Cubic B-spline elements required for maintaining convergence rate in very thin shells (t=0.001)
- Composite modeling approach does not permit zig-zag effects in stiff-soft layups
- Transverse shear continuity between layers is not ensured in the composite model
- Analysis limited to small strain-displacement relations (no large deformation capability)
- The method assumes the transverse shear stress varies through thickness only as permitted by the displacement field
- The equivalent single layer model does not capture full layer-wise behavior of composite laminates
- Step boundary method required for applying boundary conditions without nodes on boundaries
- Mesh-independent approach requires accurate geometric representation of shell mid-surface
- The method is limited to linear analysis with no nonlinear material or geometric effects considered
- Quadratic convergence rate is observed for most cases but slows for very thin shells with quadratic elements

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109583.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Biaxial non-crimp-fabric (NCF) composite material under compressive loading, analyzed using multi-scale finite element modeling (micro-scale fiber/matrix, meso-scale tow/resin, macro-scale laminate)
- **Material / Medium:** Carbon fiber (TORAY T700S, 12K tow) with epoxy resin (MTM57); fiber volume fraction 0.61 ± 0.01; composite thickness 2.4 mm ± 0.2 mm; tow imperfection angles up to 6°; interfacial strengths: tow-tow 70 MPa, fibre-matrix 100 MPa
- **Application & Importance:** Analysis of compressive behavior to understand failure mechanisms in NCF composites; critical for aerospace applications (e.g., Airbus A380 rear pressure bulkhead, A400M cargo door) where NCF composites provide cost-effective alternatives to traditional prepregs but exhibit different mechanical behaviors due to heterogeneous internal structures
- **Geometry / Domain:** Multi-scale geometry: micro-scale RVE (single fiber model with 7μm diameter, 35,200 elements); meso-scale 3D RUC (7.2×7.2×2.4 mm³ with in-phase S0/out-of-phase S1/S2 tow placements); meso-scale 2D RUC (900 μm width with 56,880 elements); layered structure with 0°/90° tows; tow waviness modeled with imperfection angles (φ₀); resin-rich areas with diamond-shaped geometry; layups A [0/90]₄ₛ and B [90/0]₄ₛ
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109583.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Periodic Boundary Conditions (PBCs) applied to lateral surfaces of 3D RUC models; bottom and top surfaces free in 3D RUC models; X-motion constrained at left surface (Uₓ=0) in 2D RUC models; Z-motion constrained at left bottom nodes (U_z=0) in 2D RUC models; top and bottom surfaces free in 2D RUC models; rigid motion in Y-direction constrained with transverse expansion allowed in 2D RUC models; PBCs applied to opposite surfaces of micro-RVE models; free expansion in Z-direction for 90° tow micro-RVE model; Z-motion of end tabs constrained in macro-scale model; left ending X-motion constrained in macro-scale model
- **Loads / Excitations:** Uniform compressive displacement (Δu) applied to right surface along X-direction in 2D RUC models; constant out-of-plane shear stresses τ₁₃ uniformly applied at Uₓ=0 and Uₓ=L₀ in 2D RUC models; compressive displacements applied in X-direction for 0° tow micro-RVE models; compressive displacements applied in Y-direction for 90° tow micro-RVE models; transverse tension σ₃₃ and transverse compression σ₂₂ applied to 90° tow micro-RVE model; 1 mm/min loading rate in compression tests
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Cohesive surfaces inserted at tow-tow interfaces; cohesive surfaces inserted at fibre-matrix interfaces; delamination modeled by Option 9 of tiebreak contact; interfacial normal and shear strengths set equal (tₙ₀ = tₛ₀); Mode II fracture dominates interfacial debonding
- **Simulation Type:** Quasi-static compression analysis; nonlinear implicit integration; 2D and 3D meso-RUC models; micro-RVE models; implicit solver in LS-DYNA; *MAT_ORTHOTROPIC_ELASTIC for tows in 3D RUC models; *MAT_ELASTIC for resin-rich areas in 3D RUC models; *MAT_ENHANCED_COMPOSITE_DAMAGE for tows in 2D RUC models; *MAT_MOHR_COULOMB for resin-rich areas in 2D RUC models
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109583.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Compressive behavior of biaxial non-crimp-fabric composites including stress distributions, failure initiation, and propagation; fiber kinking and crushing mechanisms; interfacial debonding under compression; out-of-plane shear stress effects; pressure-dependent matrix behavior
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Compressive strength values (MPa); stress-strain curves; failure modes (fibre crushing vs. fibre kinking); X-stress and XZ-stress distributions; cohesive yield stress (c) values; imperfection angle effects; mesh-dependent strength predictions; out-of-plane shear stress τ₁₃ effects; elastic modulus E₀; failure envelopes between compressive strength σ₁₁ and shear stress τ₁₃
- **Optimization Goal:** Identify key factors controlling compressive strength to guide development of NCF composites with optimal compressive strength; determine how misaligned resin-rich areas contribute to higher compressive strength; establish relationship between tow waviness and failure mode transition; validate homogenized properties from meso-scale to macro-scale models
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109583.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** 3D RUC model dimensions 7.2×7.2×2.4 mm³; 2D RUC width L₀ = 900 μm (minimum in-plane RUC 1800×1800 μm²); mesh sizes: 10 μm (X-direction) and 3.5 μm (Z-direction) for fiber elements; single fiber RVE with 7 μm diameter and 7.21 μm cross-section dimensions; two layers of elements stacked in tow thickness direction; imperfection angles up to 6° analyzed; 56,880 elements used in 2D RUC model (difference <1% vs. 113,760 elements)

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2015_11_024.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Cyclic plasticity behavior of 304 stainless steel at microstructural level with crystal plasticity finite element modeling (CPFEM)
- **Material / Medium:** 304 stainless steel (austenitic, FCC crystal structure) with composition: Fe (69.7%), C (0.062%), Si (0.366%), Mn (1.98%), P (0.023%), S (0.17%), Cu (0.671%), Cr (17%), Mo (0.41%), Ni (9.37%); average grain size 19 μm; lattice parameter 0.3584 nm; Burgers vector 0.2534 nm; dislocation density order of magnitude 1×10⁸ mm⁻²
- **Application & Importance:** Predicting crack initiation sites in chemical plant pipes subject to cyclic loading; understanding microstructural effects on fatigue failure; identifying locations of high local plastic deformation and plastic dissipation energy
- **Geometry / Domain:** 3D cuboid FE model (76 μm × 76 μm × 19 μm) with 25 grains constructed via Voronoi tessellation; cylindrical fatigue specimen with gauge diameter 7 mm, parallel length 14 mm, radius 30 mm, grip diameter 14 mm, grip length 50 mm; boundary conditions: strain-controlled y-directional loading on Face 1 (top), fixed in x/y/z directions on Face 2 (bottom)
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2015_11_024.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Strain-controlled loading within ±0.2% in y-direction on Face 1; Face 2 fixed in x, y, and z directions to prevent rigid body motion; grain boundaries coincident with element boundaries; displacement-controlled loading at strain of 2% for tensile tests
- **Loads / Excitations:** Strain-controlled cyclic loading at room temperature (20°C); strain ranges of ±0.2%, ±0.4%, ±0.5%, ±0.6%; frequency of 0.1 Hz; strain rate of 4×10⁻³ s⁻¹; fatigue tests stopped when maximum cyclic load drops by 99% compared to reference cycle number 10
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** 25-grain polycrystalline structure with Voronoi tessellation; 3D four-node tetrahedral elements (C3D4 in ABAQUS); grain interaction considered to satisfy stress equilibrium and strain compatibility; grain boundaries act as sites for stress/strain concentration
- **Simulation Type:** 3D nonlinear transient analysis; ABAQUS implicit solver with Newton-Raphson method; small deformation range analysis; crystal plasticity finite element method (CPFEM); strain-controlled displacement loading; UMAT subroutine implementation for material behavior
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2015_11_024.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Cyclic plasticity behavior of 304 stainless steel at microstructural level; dislocation density evolution; slip system activation; grain boundary effects; stress-strain distribution heterogeneity; microcrack initiation mechanisms under fatigue loading
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Maximum principal stress/strain distributions; accumulated plastic deformation (SDV133); local plastic dissipation energy (ELPD); dislocation densities for specific slip systems (e.g., SDV121 for slip system C5); hysteresis loops at different cycle numbers; grain-specific stress-strain responses; microcrack initiation indicators; Schmid factors for slip systems
- **Optimization Goal:** Predict crack initiation sites based on local accumulated plastic deformation and local plastic dissipation energy criteria; determine material constants for crystal plasticity model through inverse method; identify relationship between grain orientation and local mechanical behavior to understand fatigue failure mechanisms
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2015_11_024.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** 3D cuboid FE model dimensions constrained to 76 μm × 76 μm × 19 μm with 25 grains; Voronoi tessellation method with mean seed point distance of 19 μm; element size constrained to 3.8 (dividing geometry into 20 equal segments); model limited to 25 grains (instead of recommended 10³–10⁴ grains) due to computational constraints; grain boundaries must coincide with element boundaries
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Analysis constrained to small deformation range; strain-controlled loading limited to ±0.2% strain range; room temperature conditions only; cannot predict crack initiation caused by precipitates; transition from elastic to plastic region in FE results is less smooth than experimental results; crack initiation indicator accuracy requires further experimental validation; fatigue tests stopped when maximum cyclic load drops by 99% compared to reference cycle number 10
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Specimen geometry constrained to British Standard BS ISO 12111:2011 requirements (gauge diameter 7 mm, parallel length 14 mm, radius 30 mm, grip diameter 14 mm, grip length 50 mm); material exhibits pre-hardening from manufacturing processes; precipitate effect (MnS, FeS, CrS inclusions) not incorporated in current model despite being observed as crack initiation sites in experiments

10_1007_s40430_018_1380_5.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Laser welding process for butt joints of thin metal sheets; three-dimensional transient temperature distribution simulation; similar (304L-304L, St37-St37) and dissimilar (304L-St37) material combinations

- **Material / Medium:** AISI 304L austenitic stainless steel (0.0270% C, 0.4250% Si, 0.7200% Mn, 18.49% Cr, 8.17% Ni); St37 low carbon steel (0.102% C, 0.15% Si, 0.4900% Mn); temperature-dependent properties including specific heat (510.70-619.60 J/kg°C for 304L, 465-840 J/kg°C for St37), density (7920-7210 kg/m³ for 304L, 7850-7100 kg/m³ for St37), and thermal conductivity (15.93-36.37 W/m°C for 304L, 48.07-34.28 W/m°C for St37) across 20-1600°C range

- **Application & Importance:** Evaluation of transient temperature distribution in dissimilar laser welding; comparison of similar and dissimilar material welding under identical process parameters; validation of temperature profiles, peak temperatures, molten pool shape, and weld bead geometry; automotive weight reduction applications requiring precise temperature control

- **Geometry / Domain:** Butt-welded specimen with 50 mm length × 25 mm width × 1.4 mm thickness; 82,530 nodes and 78,750 elements in full 3D model; 0.2 mm × 0.2 mm × 0.2 mm element size near weld line; conical Gaussian heat source distribution; thermocouple positions at 3, 6, 9, and 12.5 mm from weld line; 1.4 mm sheet thickness with welding direction along Y-axis; Cartesian coordinate system (X, Y, Z) with weld line at X=0
10_1007_s40430_018_1380_5.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Initial workpiece temperature of 39 °C; convection heat transfer coefficient of 50 W/m²°C for top and lateral surfaces, 200 W/m²°C for bottom surface; convection not applied in heat source moving region; radiation heat loss calculated using Stefan-Boltzmann law with emissivity parameter; temperature-dependent thermal properties

- **Loads / Excitations:** Laser parameters: 425 W average power, 17 J pulse energy, 25 Hz frequency, 5 mm/s welding speed, 5 ms pulse duration, 0.75 mm spot diameter, 1060 nm wavelength; 70% of laser power absorbed by workpiece (30% lost); 17.3% of absorbed power distributed as surface heat source; 52.7% of absorbed power distributed as volumetric heat source; moving Gaussian conical heat source with specified spatial distribution

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Heat conduction through workpiece material; convection and radiation heat loss from workpiece surfaces; moving heat source traveling along Y-axis at 5 mm/s; no fluid flow considered in molten weld pool; K-type thermocouples positioned at 3, 6, 9, and 12.5 mm from weld line for temperature measurement

- **Simulation Type:** 3D transient thermal analysis; nonlinear (temperature-dependent material properties); finite element method using ANSYS APDL; moving heat source analysis with 82,530 nodes and 78,750 elements; element size of 0.2 mm × 0.2 mm × 0.2 mm near weld line
10_1007_s40430_018_1380_5.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Temperature profiles at 3, 6, 9, and 12.5 mm from weld line; peak temperature values; temperature field contours; weld pool geometry (depth, width, shape); temperature gradient distribution; element-specific temperature values; full penetration threshold power (355 W for dissimilar 304L-St37 welding); comparison between FEM and experimental thermocouple measurements

- **Optimization Goal:** Validation of numerical temperature distribution against experimental K-type thermocouple measurements; determination of minimum power for full penetration in dissimilar welding; comparison of thermal behavior between similar (304L-304L, St37-St37) and dissimilar (304L-St37) material combinations; accurate prediction of asymmetric weld pool geometry in dissimilar material welding; establishment of power-threshold relationship for complete weld penetration
10_1007_s40430_018_1380_5.key_4:

- **Process/Manufacturing:** Nd:YAG laser welding with fixed parameters (425 W average power, 5 mm/s welding speed, 25 Hz frequency, 5 ms pulse duration); argon gas shielding at 6 l/min flow rate; K-type thermocouples used for validation with ±1% accuracy; butt joint configuration only; 1.4 mm sheet thickness limitation; experimental validation constrained to discrete thermocouple measurement points; conical Gaussian heat source distribution modeling constraint

10_1016_j_fusengdes_2025_115058.key_1:

- **Material / Medium:** Probe (CuCrZr); Sleeve (AISI316 stainless steel); Adapter (CuCrZr); Beryllium sub-sample for DT retention; Beryllium coating via CX sputtering; Reference indicator (molybdenum)
- **Application & Importance:** Measurement of erosion caused by Charge Exchange Neutral (CXN) particles and fuel retention on First Wall; structural integrity assessment under Major Disruptions (MD) and Vertical Disruption Events (VDE) which generate intense electromagnetic stresses; ensuring diagnostic functionality during plasma disruptions
- **Geometry / Domain:** Standardized removable components with different adapters for Enhanced Heat Flux (4 MW/m²) and Normal Heat Flux (2 MW/m²) First Wall Panels; samples distributed both poloidally (vertically) and toroidally (horizontally) across the First Wall; sub-modeling focused on adapter region where over 90% of total load is experienced
10_1016_j_fusengdes_2025_115058.key_2:

- **Loads / Excitations:** Current flowing into Poloidal Field Coils (PF) and Toroidal Field Coils (TFC); Secondary excitations related to plasma currents (PFV for poloidal field variation, TFV for toroidal field variation); Halo current (HC) excitations; Disruption scenarios including MD down exp16ms, MD UP exp16ms, VDE down lin36ms, and VDE UP lin36ms; Time-dependent current from DINA code scaled for toroidal amplitude
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Sub-modeling technique transferring magnetic vector potential and electric scalar potential from global model to sub-model boundary nodes; Material interfaces between Probe (CuCrZr), Sleeve (AISI316), and Adapter (CuCrZr); Sample adapter bears over 90% of total load; Beryllium sub-sample for DT retention and beryllium coating via CX sputtering
- **Simulation Type:** Transient 3D electromagnetic analysis; Two-stage approach with global model followed by sub-modeling; Time-dependent simulation with specific time steps (e.g., TIME=10.8318, TIME=0.687); Analysis of plasma disruption events including Major Disruptions (MD) and Vertical Disruption Events (VDE)
10_1016_j_fusengdes_2025_115058.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Radial forces (Fx, Fy, Fz) in Newtons; Torque moments (Mx, My, Mz) in Newton-meters; Current density distribution (A/m²); Peak force values on inboard and outboard samples; Peak moment values on inboard and outboard samples; Time-dependent force and moment profiles during disruption events
- **Optimization Goal:** Ensure structural integrity of First Wall Samples Diagnostic under Major Disruptions (MD) and Vertical Disruption Events (VDE); Achieve accurate prediction of electromagnetic loads on individual components; Identify critical load-bearing components (sample adapter bearing over 90% of total load); Validate sub-modeling technique for precise calculation of current distribution and resulting forces/moments; Guide design improvements for diagnostic functionality and durability under extreme operating conditions
10_1016_j_fusengdes_2025_115058.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Standardized removable components with variations only at the interface between removable part of FWS and First Wall Panels (FWP); Different adapter designs required for Enhanced Heat Flux (4 MW/m²) and Normal Heat Flux (2 MW/m²) FWPs; Sub-modeling focused specifically on adapter region where over 90% of total load is experienced; Two distinct adapter types (standard adapter and FW8-9 adapter) for different panel configurations
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Must withstand loads from Major Disruptions (MD) and Vertical Disruption Events (VDE); Maximum torque observed reached 700 Nm at 687 ms; Sample adapter experiences over 90% of total electromagnetic load; Radial forces and torque forces identified as dominant stress factors; Analysis constrained to specific disruption scenarios: MD down exp16ms, MD UP exp16ms, VDE down lin36ms, and VDE UP lin36ms; Structural integrity must be maintained during plasma disruptions generating intense electromagnetic stresses
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Samples designed for Remote Handling removal; Beryllium coating applied via CX sputtering process; Material properties constrained by ITER Materials Properties Handbook; Computational constraints requiring sub-modeling approach due to resource-intensive nature of full-sector models; Mesh shape differences between global model (squared) and sub-model (rounded and refined) affecting force predictions; Analysis limited to time-dependent electromagnetic effects without including beryllium sub-sample in electromagnetic calculations

10_1016_j_ijpharm_2025_125474.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Microneedle hierarchical structures for multi-stage wound healing applications
- **Material / Medium:** Polymer-based (PVA, HA, chitosan, PLGA), metal-based (stainless steel, titanium), and inorganic non-metallic (silicon, ceramics); with properties including biocompatibility, biodegradability, mechanical strength (yield force), and drug loading capacity
- **Application & Importance:** Optimizing transdermal drug delivery efficiency for wound treatment by overcoming skin mechanical barriers; addressing chronic inflammation, infection, and scarring through precise structural design to prevent "bed of nails" effect and ensure adequate skin penetration
- **Geometry / Domain:** Microneedle arrays with length 500-1400 μm, aspect ratio >2, tip diameter 10-15 μm, spacing >450 μm; featuring conical, pyramidal, candle-flame, and bio-inspired shapes (e.g., bee sting, thorny-headed worm); skin penetration domain includes epidermis (50-130 μm) and dermis (>1000 μm) layers
10_1016_j_ijpharm_2025_125474.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Skin layer thickness: Epidermis (50–130 μm), Dermis (>1000 μm)
  - Microneedle length range: 500–1400 μm to avoid subcutaneous tissue/nerve contact
  - Microneedle spacing: >450 μm to prevent "bed of nails" effect
  - Microneedle aspect ratio: >2 for adequate penetration
  - Needle tip diameter: 10–15 μm
  - Wound microenvironment parameters: pH levels, temperature, metabolites, and immune signaling molecules
  - Microneedle base diameters: 200, 300, 400 μm
  - Center spacing: 1800 μm and 2400 μm for penetration testing

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - External insertion force for microneedle penetration
  - Visible red/near-infrared light with power output of hundreds of milliwatts and energy density <10 J/cm²
  - Endogenous electric fields produced when skin integrity is compromised
  - Exogenous electrical stimulation (alternating current, direct current, pulsed current)
  - Drug loading: antimicrobial peptides, simvastatin, triamcinolone acetonide, quercetin nanocrystals
  - Oxygen generation from calcium oxide and catalase in microneedle tips

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Microneedle-skin mechanical interaction with stress distribution
  - Porous/hollow microneedle structures for interstitial fluid absorption
  - Bio-inspired mechanical interlocking: eagle claw-shaped, bee sting-like, thorny-headed worm-inspired structures
  - Octopus suction cup-like adhesion structures for wet/dry environment adhesion
  - Hydrogel dressing interface enabling mechanical wound contraction
  - Microneedle array patterns: square, diamond, triangular, rectangular substrates

- **Simulation Type:**
  - In vitro testing on human cadaver skin
  - In vivo animal models: rat, rabbit, pig skin
  - Finite element method for mechanical analysis of penetration
  - Trypan blue assay for skin puncture visualization
  - Drug flux measurements with z-axis (flux), y-axis (microneedle density), x-axis (microneedle length)
  - Needle tip angle variations: 45°, 30°, 20°, 10° for penetration testing
10_1016_j_ijpharm_2025_125474.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Mechanical skin penetration dynamics of microneedle arrays
  - Drug diffusion through skin layers (epidermis, dermis)
  - Stress distribution in microneedle arrays during insertion
  - Biofilm disruption mechanics in infected wounds
  - Tissue adhesion mechanics for bio-inspired structures
  - Wound contraction mechanics with hydrogel-based systems
  - Photothermal conversion in light-responsive microneedles
  - Electrical stimulation effects on tissue healing

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Penetration depth (500-1400 μm range)
  - Drug flux (g/cm²/h) measured against microneedle length and density
  - Percent penetration rates across different skin models (rat, human, pig)
  - Insulin concentration increase (1.80-2.57× based on microneedle length)
  - Pore diameter in epidermis (75-180 μm for 150-1500 μm microneedles)
  - Cell activation volume relative to microneedle spacing
  - Aspect ratio effects on penetration performance
  - Tip angle effects (10-45°) on insertion force
  - Bacterial killing efficiency for infected wounds
  - Scar elevation index for anti-scar applications

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Maximize drug delivery efficiency while preventing "bed of nails" effect through optimal spacing (>450 μm)
  - Achieve sufficient skin penetration (500-1400 μm length) without reaching nerve endings
  - Maintain aspect ratio >2 and tip diameter 10-15 μm for optimal penetration force
  - Maximize tissue adhesion for long-term drug release in inflammatory wounds
  - Minimize scar formation through mechanical intervention (1000 μm length, 690 μm spacing, 15×15 array)
  - Enhance biofilm penetration for infected wound treatment
  - Optimize multi-stage wound healing through structural design parameters
10_1016_j_ijpharm_2025_125474.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Microneedle length constrained to 500-1400 μm to avoid nerve endings while ensuring sufficient skin penetration
  - Aspect ratio must exceed 2 for optimal penetration performance
  - Needle tip diameter limited to 10-15 μm for effective skin penetration
  - Microneedle spacing must exceed 450 μm to prevent "bed of nails" effect
  - Optimal anti-scar configuration: 1000 μm length, 690 μm spacing, 15×15 array
  - Tip angle generally restricted to less than 45°, with better performance at ≤30°
  - Base diameter typically 200-400 μm based on penetration testing data
  - Microneedle density limited to prevent reduced individual needle force (e.g., 5625 needles/cm² was ineffective)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Maximum penetration depth constrained by epidermis (50-130 μm) and dermis (>1000 μm) layer boundaries
  - Mechanical strength must exceed wound bed biofilm resistance for anti-infection applications
  - Anti-scar microneedles must maintain sufficient structural integrity to pierce hardened scar tissue
  - Wound monitoring microneedles require hollow/porous structures to absorb tissue exudate
  - Minimum aspect ratio threshold required to concentrate stress for effective skin penetration
  - Maximum drug loading capacity limited by microneedle size and structural design

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - 3D printing requires 2-10 μm precision for hollow microneedle fabrication
  - Traditional manufacturing techniques struggle to replicate intricate bio-inspired microstructures
  - Micro molding is primary method for soluble microneedles but has geometric limitations
  - Dip coating, ink jet, and drip coating methods face challenges with uniform coating distribution
  - Hollow microneedle microchannel processing presents greater complexity than solid microneedles
  - Current research primarily at animal experiment stage with clinical translation challenges for large wound areas
  - Limited patch area for multi-parameter monitoring systems due to patient comfort considerations

10_1016_j_ijhydene_2025_02_390.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Rubber seals (O-ring and backup ring assembly) in high-pressure hydrogen environments
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Nitrile-Butadiene Rubber (NBR) O-ring (87 phr carbon black, 15 phr PVC, 7 phr dioctyl adipate, 5 phr epoxidized soybean oil, 2 phr zinc oxide, 1 phr stearic acid, 2 phr sulfur; Shore A hardness 72 HA)
  - High-density PTFE backup ring (elastic modulus 1800 MPa, Poisson's ratio 0.46, thermal conductivity 0.25 W/(m·K))
  - Hydrogen gas (10-70 MPa pressure, 298.15-358.15 K temperature)
- **Application & Importance:** Ensuring safety of high-pressure hydrogen storage and filling equipment by analyzing combined effects of pressure, hydrogen swelling, and temperature on sealing performance to prevent hydrogen leakage or explosion
- **Geometry / Domain:** 2D axisymmetric model with O-ring diameter 5.30 mm, sealing clearance 0.03 mm, groove width 9.00 mm, groove depth 4.05 mm, backup ring axial width 1.80 mm, fillet radius 0.50 mm, and radial width 4.05 mm
10_1016_j_ijhydene_2025_02_390.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Dirichlet thermal boundary conditions: T₁ = Tᵢ (hydrogen temperature) at O-ring/H₂ interface, T₂ = Tₒ = 298.15 K at backup ring/external environment interface
  - Neumann thermal boundary condition at O-ring/backup ring contact surface
  - Hydrogen concentration boundary: c = 0 ppm at low-pressure side (LS) and initial concentration
  - Hydrogen concentration at high-pressure side (HS) varies with pressure/temperature (498.73 ppm at pᵢ=35 MPa, Tᵢ=298.15 K; 512.81 ppm at pᵢ=35 MPa, Tᵢ=323.15 K; 529.72 ppm at pᵢ=35 MPa, Tᵢ=358.15 K)
  - Friction coefficients: O-ring/back-up ring (0.02), O-ring/groove (0.1), O-ring/shaft (0.1), back-up ring/groove (0.04), back-up ring/shaft (0.04)
  - Face-to-face contact with augmented Lagrange method for all seal interfaces

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Hydrogen pressures: pᵢ = 10, 35, 70 MPa
  - Hydrogen temperatures: Tᵢ = 298.15, 323.15, 358.15 K
  - Environmental temperature: Tₒ = 298.15 K
  - Radial displacement load for pre-compression to achieve set compression ratio
  - Thermal expansion coefficient: α_T = 0.00017 K⁻¹
  - Hydrogen-induced expansion coefficient (varies with temperature, proportional to solubility coefficient)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Thermal-mechanical-diffusion multi-field coupling with cyclic iteration
  - Contact pairs: O-ring/back-up ring, O-ring/groove, O-ring/shaft, back-up ring/groove, back-up ring/shaft
  - Hydrogen diffusion driven by concentration, temperature, and stress-strain gradients
  - Stress-strain field affects hydrogen diffusion through stress influence factor kₚ
  - Temperature field affects hydrogen diffusion through Soret influence factor kₛ
  - Hydrogen concentration field affects mechanical deformation through hydrogen expansion coefficient

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 2D axisymmetric model
  - Steady-state temperature field with transient hydrogen diffusion
  - Nonlinear analysis (hyperelastic material behavior with Mooney-Rivlin model)
  - Thermal-mechanical-diffusion coupled field simulation
  - Cyclic coupling process until node changes in concentration, temperature, and stress < 0.001
  - Finite element formulation using CAX4RHT (rubber O-ring) and CAX4RT (backup ring) elements
  - Grid: global size 0.05 mm, locally densified to 0.03 mm near sealing gap and backup ring
10_1016_j_ijhydene_2025_02_390.key_3:

  - Thermal-mechanical-diffusion multi-field coupling behavior of rubber seals
  - Hydrogen permeation and diffusion in rubber materials
  - Stress-strain response under high-pressure hydrogen conditions
  - Temperature distribution in rubber seals with thermal gradients
  - Hydrogen swelling effects on rubber deformation

  - Maximum contact stress (p_cm)
  - Maximum Von Mises stress (σ_mm)
  - Maximum temperature difference (ΔT_m)
  - Total contact width (L_st)
  - Effective sealing rate
  - Average hydrogen concentration (c_a)
  - Hydrogen concentration distribution
  - Contact pressure distribution
  - Temperature distribution along sealing surfaces
  - Material deformation under multi-field coupling

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Minimize maximum contact stress (p_cm)
  - Minimize maximum Von Mises stress (σ_mm)
  - Minimize maximum temperature difference (ΔT_m)
  - Achieve optimal balance between sealing performance and structural reliability in high-pressure hydrogen environments
  - Reduce failure risk while maintaining adequate contact pressure above hydrogen pressure
10_1016_j_ijhydene_2025_02_390.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Axial width of backup ring (b): 1.4–2.0 mm
  - Fillet radius of backup ring (R₂): 0.2–0.8 mm
  - Sealing clearance (h): 0–0.1 mm
  - Concave arc radius of backup ring (R₃): 3–7 mm
  - Diameter of O-ring (Dₒ): 1.8–5.3 mm

  - Effective sealing rate (ratio of contact width with pressure > hydrogen pressure to total contact width) must be maintained

  - Compression ratio must maintain adequate sealing while avoiding excessive compression under hydrogen swelling
  - Maximum temperature difference must be minimized to reduce thermal deformation effects
  - Hydrogen pressure range: 10–70 MPa
  - Hydrogen temperature range: 298.15–358.15 K

  - Recommended compression ratio range: 15–30%
  - Sealing gap should be minimized as much as possible
  - Multiple rubber seals required for ultra-high-pressure hydrogen applications
  - Sealing surface roughness and flatness must be controlled to strengthen reliability
  - Material composition constrained to NBR with 87 phr carbon black, 15 phr PVC, 7 phr dioctyl adipate, 5 phr epoxidized soybean oil, 2 phr zinc oxide, 1 phr stearic acid, and 2 phr sulfur

Critical for applications requiring performance over broad frequency windows, such as hearing aid devices where acoustic transmission must be precisely controlled.

  - Absorbing boundary conditions on left (inlet) and right (outlet) boundaries

  - Structural domain boundaries: Fully clamped condition (u = 0)
  - Structural traction-free boundaries: nₛ·σ = 0
  - Left boundary (inlet): Absorbing boundary condition (nₐ·∇p + (1/cₐ)∂p/∂t = (2/cₐ)∂pᵢₙ/∂t)
  - Right boundary (outlet): Absorbing boundary condition (nₐ∇p = 0)
  - Non-designable regions at inlet and outlet (by construction)

  - Time duration of 0.02 s for transient analysis
  - Time step size Δt = 2×10⁻⁵ s
  - Broad frequency excitation achieved through white noise input

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Acoustic-structural coupling at interface Γₐₛ with:
    - Structural traction equals acoustic pressure: nₛ·σ = p nₐ
    - Acoustic normal gradient equals structural acceleration: nₐ·∇p = ρₐ ∂²nₛ·u/∂t²
  - Fictitious domain approach with:
    - Void phase (10⁻⁸ stiffness) in acoustic region for structural solution
    - Rigid phase (10⁻⁸ stiffness) in structural region for acoustic solution

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Transient vibroacoustic analysis in time domain with frequency-domain optimization
  - 2D plane stress linear elasticity coupled with linear acoustic wave equation
  - Implicit Newmark time integration scheme (unconditionally stable with β̃ = 1/4, γ̃ = 1/2)
  - Spatial discretization using Q4 elements with cut element method for interface
  - Fixed background mesh with element edge length of 2×10⁻³ m (12,500 total elements)
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104123.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Transmission coefficient S(f) = p̂(f)/p̂₀(f) where p̂(f) is transmitted acoustic pressure frequency response and p̂₀(f) is reference from empty duct
  - Sound Pressure Level (SPL) at duct outlet
  - Constraint functions Φ₁ and Φ₂ measuring deviation from target transmission profiles
  - Displacement magnitude |u| [m] of structural components
  - Frequency response of coupled system obtained via FFT of transient response

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Minimize Φ₁: Achieve full transmission (S(f) ≈ 1) in designated pass-band frequency ranges
  - Minimize Φ₂: Achieve zero transmission (S(f) ≈ 0) in designated stop-band frequency ranges
  - Design broadband acoustic filters (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, band-stop) with 60 dB difference between pass-bands and stop-bands
  - Create structures that act as wave stoppers in specific frequency ranges while allowing transmission in other predefined frequency sets through internal reflections and acoustic-structural interactions

  - No volume constraint imposed on structural material (as a solid slab does not trivially solve the optimization problem)
  - No minimum length scale control, leading to unbounded material amount in optimization
  - Design domain restricted to central 0.3 m × 0.1 m region of the 0.5 m total duct length
  - Non-designable regions at inlet and outlet boundaries by construction
  - Filter radius set to 8×10⁻³ m for design smoothing

  - Time step size Δt = 2×10⁻⁵ s required for adequate time resolution of coupled system
  - Total calculation time of 0.02 s for transient analysis
  - White noise excitation with pressure values between -1 Pa and 1 Pa at inlet
  - Parameter b must be set as a small positive number (1×10⁻³ found most effective) to avoid division by zero in constraint function Φ₂
  - Small features become transparent to filter performance when sufficiently small, causing sensitivities to approach zero

- **Process/Manufacturing:**

  - Optimizer cannot remove small transparent features as sensitivities approach zero
  - No manufacturing constraints considered in current study (identified as future work)
  - Small features adversely affect oscillatory behavior of objective function history during optimization
  - No explicit length scale control, with minimum feature size bound by element size rather than manufacturing capabilities

- Simulation Type: 3D clash detection; BIM-driven structural analysis; BIM-based moisture mapping simulations; 3D modeling for interference checks; AI-augmented BIM simulations for HVAC system optimization
10_1007_s41062_025_01986_z.key_3:
- Physics Solved: MEP system interference detection; structural load distribution analysis; solar energy harvesting performance; drainage slope optimization; thermal performance of BIPV-integrated facades
- Target Outputs (Metrics): 95% elimination rate of MEP clashes; 25% reduction in rework; 40% of annual electricity generated by BIPV; 1.5% drainage slope for water flow; 10–20% cooling load reduction from BIPV-integrated facades; 92% of conflict-prone pipe junctions re-routed; 12 drainage slope errors and 16 pipes-to-column clashes identified through 3D clash detection
- Optimization Goal: Minimize water leakage incidents through BIM-facilitated drainage slope optimization; eliminate MEP system interferences; achieve 40% renewable energy self-sufficiency via BIPV integration; reduce operational costs by 20% through HVAC system optimization; minimize construction rework by 25% through early-stage clash detection
10_1007_s41062_025_01986_z.key_4:
