10_1016_j_ast_2025_110304.key_1:
- Inflatable wing for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), focusing on mechanical properties and buckling failure mechanisms
- Vectran fiber/thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) composite material (skin and ribs); Young's modulus: 14,204 MPa; Shear modulus: 305 MPa; Thickness: 0.1 mm; Internal pressure range: 10–35 kPa
- Analysis addresses structural reliability and safety concerns under extreme conditions due to limited research on buckling failure mechanisms; provides theoretical foundation for structural design optimization and dynamic pressure regulation strategies
- Full-size wing: 1.2 m length, 0.6 m chord length, NACA4318 airfoil profile; Cross-section consists of 13 circular cavities tangent to baseline airfoil curve; Ribs at circle intersections; Three-point bending test setup with 1 m support span; Finite element model: 1 m wing length (excluding spherical end caps), global mesh size 8 mm (4 mm refined in central region), 46,845 membrane elements (M3D4R)
10_1016_j_ast_2025_110304.key_2:
- Simply supported boundary conditions at both ends with 1 m spacing (providing vertical reaction forces while allowing free in-plane rotation)
- Displacement control at constant rate of 80 mm/min
- Six inflation pressure conditions: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35 kPa
- Lever transmission system with 1.2-meter aluminum alloy lever arm fixed at one end through hinged support (permitting rotation while restricting translation)
- Loading rod positioned 0.5 m from hinge point on lever arm
- Displacement load applied to reference point (RP) coupled with rectangular tube
- Loading mechanism follows lever ratio 1:2 (P_wing = 2 × P_measured, w_wing = w_measured/2)
- Analytical rigid body treatment for rectangular loading tube
- Twelve internal ribs running spanwise through wing interior for aerodynamic profile maintenance
- Explicit dynamic simulation method with total loading duration of 10 s
- Finite element model uses membrane elements (M3D4R) with global mesh size of 8 mm (refined to 4 mm in central region)
- Three-point bending test configuration as per ASTM C203–05a standard
10_1016_j_ast_2025_110304.key_3:
- Buckling failure mechanisms and load-bearing characteristics of inflatable wings under static loading
- Bending stiffness (N·m²), critical buckling load (N), stress distribution, strain evolution, force-displacement curves, compressive stress on upper surface, shear strain in ribs, and material properties (Young's modulus: 14,204 MPa, shear modulus: 305 MPa)
- Establish quantitative relationship between internal pressure (10-35 kPa) and structural stability to enable pressure optimization for inflatable-wing UAVs, with specific targets of predicting buckling loads (3.0% error) and bending stiffness (6.89% error) to support dynamic pressure regulation strategies during flight operations
10_1016_j_ast_2025_110304.key_4:
- Wing dimensions constrained to 1.2 m length and 0.6 m chord length
- Airfoil cross-section limited to 13 circular cavities tangent to NACA4318 baseline airfoil curve
- Support spacing fixed at 1 m in experimental three-point bending setup
- Internal pressure range limited to 10–35 kPa (typical operational range from low-stiffness buckling-prone to high-stiffness bending-resistant states)
- Material thickness constrained to 0.1 mm for Vectran fiber/TPU composite
- Displacement rate constrained to 80 mm/min to satisfy quasi-static conditions
- Internal pressure limited by membrane material strength and interface connection strength
- Twelve ribs required for maintaining aerodynamic profile along spanwise direction
- Material constrained to Vectran fiber/TPU composite for both skin and ribs
- Experimental setup uses spherical end caps for sealing the inflatable wing
- Simulation uses membrane elements (M3D4R) rather than shell elements due to structural differences from traditional wings
- Static loading tests constrained to concentrated midpoint force application rather than distributed aerodynamic loads
- Computational cost constraints led to mesh size selection (8 mm global, 4 mm refined central region) to balance accuracy and efficiency (49,493–180,068 s computation time depending on mesh size)

10_1016_j_compstruct_2025_119176.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Turbine disk and L-bracket structures for stress-related multi-material topology optimization with gradient interfaces
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - MAT1 (density=1.00, elastic modulus=1.00, E/ρ=1.00)
  - MAT2 (density=0.50, elastic modulus=0.20, E/ρ=0.40)
  - Single gradient: GRA1 (density=0.75, elastic modulus=0.41, E/ρ=0.55)
  - Double gradient: GRA2 (density=0.83, elastic modulus=0.53, E/ρ=0.64), GRA3 (density=0.67, elastic modulus=0.32, E/ρ=0.48)
  - Triple gradient: GRA4 (density=0.88, elastic modulus=0.61, E/ρ=0.69), GRA5 (density=0.75, elastic modulus=0.41, E/ρ=0.55), GRA6 (density=0.63, elastic modulus=0.29, E/ρ=0.46)
  - Poisson's ratio=1/3 for all materials
- **Application & Importance:** Minimize global stress in aerospace components (turbine disks) that endure complex loads and extreme thermal conditions; gradient interfaces reduce stress concentration and enhance structural strength
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Turbine disk: Dimensionless domain (length=2, width=1), discretized into 200×100 elements (0.005×0.005 each), fixed left end as rotational axis, force F=1 applied to six nodes on right end
  - L-bracket: Dimensionless domain discretized into 200×200 elements (0.005×0.005 each), fixed top constraint, vertical load F=1 applied to four top-right nodes
  - Mass constraint=0.3, filtering radius r_min=8, p-norm parameter P=8, maximum iterations=197
10_1016_j_compstruct_2025_119176.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Fixed displacement constraint at left end (turbine disk) and top (L-bracket)
  - Mass constraint = 0.3 (30% of design domain)
  - Minimum design variable x_min = 0.001 to prevent singularity
  - Density filter radius r_min = 8
  - Maximum iterations = 197 or convergence when objective function difference ≤ 0.001 between consecutive iterations

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Turbine disk: Vertical force F = 1 applied to six nodes at right end
  - L-bracket: Vertical load F = 1 N applied to four nodes at top-right end
  - Material density range: 0.50 (MAT2) to 1.00 (MAT1)
  - Elastic modulus range: 0.20 (MAT2) to 1.00 (MAT1)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Multi-gradient material interpolation based on SIMP method and piecewise Heaviside projection
  - Gradient ratio ξ defines volume fraction of MAT1 in mixed material (ξ ∈ [0,1])
  - Single design variable represents multi-material density field
  - Material interfaces achieve smooth gradient transitions between parent materials
  - Stress relaxation using SIMP-like method with relaxation coefficient q = 0.8

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 2D plane stress topology optimization
  - 4-node quadrilateral finite elements
  - Stress minimization using p-norm aggregation (P = 8)
  - Method of Moving Asymptotes (MMA) optimizer with move limit = 0.12
  - Convergence assessed using objective function difference between iterations
  - Global stress evaluated using p-norm function to approximate maximum von Mises stress
10_1016_j_compstruct_2025_119176.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Stress distribution in multi-material structures with gradient interfaces
  - Finite element analysis of von Mises stress
  - P-norm stress aggregation to approximate maximum stress

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - P-norm stress (σ^PN)
  - Maximum von Mises stress (σ^vM_max)
  - Total mass (constrained to 0.3)
  - Material volume fractions for MAT1, MAT2, and gradient materials (GRA1-GRA6)
  - Stress distribution maps showing stress concentration areas

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Minimize the p-norm stress (σ^PN = (∑(σ^vM_e)^P)^(1/P)) while maintaining mass constraint ≤ 0.3
  - Reduce maximum stress in multi-material structures through gradient interface design
  - Achieve 99.1-99.3% reduction in stress levels as demonstrated in turbine disk examples
10_1016_j_compstruct_2025_119176.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Turbine disk domain: length=2, width=1, discretized into 200×100 elements (0.005×0.005 each)
  - L-bracket domain: discretized into 200×200 elements (0.005×0.005 each)
  - Right end of turbine disk has non-designable area (slender rectangular region)
  - Minimum design variable constraint: x_min = 0.001 to prevent singularity
  - Density filter radius: r_min = 8 to prevent checkerboard patterns
  - Mass constraint: total mass ≤ 0.3 (30% of design domain)
  - Single design variable representation for multi-material density field

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - P-norm stress aggregation parameter: P = 8 (optimal value for stress approximation)
  - Stress relaxation coefficient: q = 0.8 for stress interpolation
  - Elastic modulus penalty exponent: p = 3 in SIMP interpolation
  - Poisson's ratio fixed at 1/3 for all materials
  - Maximum iterations: 197 or convergence when objective function difference ≤ 0.001 between consecutive iterations
  - Optimization terminates when convergence criterion is satisfied

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Design compatible with additive manufacturing technologies:
    - 5-axis Directed Energy Deposition (DED) for prototype production
    - Selective Laser Melting (SLM) for high-precision components with minimal post-processing
  - Multi-gradient material interfaces designed to be manufacturable through AM
  - Structure topology designed to be "exact" and "compact" to benefit additive manufacturing
  - Material distribution avoids complex geometries that would require excessive support structures
  - Gradient transition achieved at multi-material interfaces for improved manufacturability

10_1016_j_cocom_2024_e00957.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Al₂Cu precipitate (θ phase) with elemental doping
- **Material / Medium:** Al₂Cu intermetallic compound with doping elements (Fe, Mn, Mg, Sc, Zr); tetragonal crystal structure (space group I4/mcm); lattice parameters a = 6.067 nm, c = 4.877 nm
- **Application & Importance:** Strengthening phase in Al-Cu alloys; critical for mechanical properties; doped precipitates improve structural stability, mechanical properties, and address brittleness issues limiting industrial applications
- **Geometry / Domain:** Tetragonal crystal structure with Al atoms at (0.1581 0.6581 0) and Cu atoms at (0 0 0.25); 2×2×2 supercell model for doping studies (2.08 at% concentration); high-symmetry points (Γ, X, W, L) for phonon spectrum analysis
10_1016_j_cocom_2024_e00957.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Plane wave cut-off energy: 500 eV
  - K-point grid: Monkhorst-Pack with K-spacing ~0.1 Å⁻¹ (1800k points)
  - Structural relaxation convergence criteria: total energy < 10⁻⁸ eV, residual forces < 0.01 eV/Å
  - Exchange-correlation functional: GGA-PBE
  - Projected Augmented Wave (PAW) method for electron-ion interactions
  - 2×2×2 supercell model with periodic boundary conditions
  - Lattice parameters for pure θ phase: a = 6.067 nm, c = 4.877 nm

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Doping concentrations: 2, 4, 6, and 8 atoms of dopant elements
  - Dopant elements: Fe, Mn, Mg, Sc, and Zr
  - Structural relaxation to equilibrium configuration

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Electronic interactions between dopant atoms and host Al/Cu atoms
  - Charge transfer analysis using Bader charge method
  - Atomic positions: Al at (0.1581 0.6581 0), Cu at (0 0 0.25) in Wyckoff positions
  - Doping site preferences: Fe/Mn substitute Cu sites; Mg/Sc/Zr substitute Al sites

- **Simulation Type:**
  - First-principles DFT calculations (ground state)
  - 3D periodic boundary conditions
  - Structural relaxation
  - Phonon spectrum calculations using density functional perturbation theory
  - Elastic constant calculations via stress-strain relationship
  - Density of states calculations using modified linear tetrahedral Blöchl method
  - Charge density analysis in (001) plane
10_1016_j_cocom_2024_e00957.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Structural stability assessment through formation energy, cohesive energy, and phonon spectrum calculations
  - Mechanical properties analysis via elastic constant determination and derived moduli
  - Electronic structure characterization through density of states and charge distribution analysis
  - Lattice dynamics through phonon dispersion relationship calculations
  - Charge transfer mechanisms via Bader charge analysis

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Formation energy values for dopant substitution at Al/Cu sites
  - Cohesive energy values as function of doping concentration
  - Phonon dispersion curves with frequency range 0-10 THz
  - Elastic constants (C₁₁, C₁₂, C₄₄)
  - Bulk modulus (B), shear modulus (G), Young's modulus (E), Poisson's ratio (ν)
  - B/G ratio for ductility assessment (1.75 threshold)
  - Elastic anisotropy index (Aᵤ) with reference to isotropic value of 0
  - Density of states (DOS) and partial density of states (PDOS) across -12 to 4 eV range
  - Charge density distributions in (001) plane with values 0.02-0.04 e
  - Bader charge values showing electron transfer (ranging from -1.4722 e to 2.8766 e)
  - Lattice parameters (a, c), c/a ratio, and equilibrium volume

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Enhance structural stability of θ phase while maintaining thermodynamic and dynamic stability
  - Improve mechanical properties: increase hardness and stiffness through Fe doping
  - Enhance ductility by controlling Mn content and adding Zr
  - Increase shear modulus through Mg doping
  - Optimize elastic anisotropy (minimize Aᵤ) using Sc doping
  - Strengthen covalent interactions between dopant elements and host atoms to improve overall stability
  - Address brittleness issues of pure θ phase while preserving its strengthening effect in Al-Cu alloys
10_1016_j_cocom_2024_e00957.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - 2×2×2 supercell model with fixed doping concentration (2.08 at%)
  - Lattice parameters constrained to tetragonal structure (a = 6.067 nm, c = 4.877 nm)
  - Doped atoms must maintain sufficient distance to avoid strong local stress fields (prevents convergence issues)
  - Atomic positions fixed at Al (0.1581 0.6581 0) and Cu (0 0 0.25) Wyckoff positions
  - Doping limited to discrete concentrations (2, 4, 6, 8 atoms per supercell)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Must satisfy Born-Huang mechanical stability criteria for tetragonal structures
  - Cohesive energy must remain negative for thermodynamic stability (all calculated values were negative)
  - Phonon spectrum must show no imaginary frequencies for dynamic stability (all doped phases satisfied this)
  - B/G ratio threshold of 1.75 for ductility assessment (B/G > 1.75 indicates ductile behavior)
  - Poisson's ratio threshold of 0.26 (values > 0.26 indicate ductile behavior)
  - Formation energy must be negative for favorable doping (only cases with negative formation energy were considered)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Practical Fe content in Al-Cu alloys strictly limited (< 0.07% in aerospace applications)
  - Mn content must be strictly controlled as excessive amounts consume and corrode θ phase
  - Experimental equipment limitations for analyzing small θ phase structures
  - Doping limited to specific elements (Fe, Mn, Mg, Sc, Zr) only
  - Study constrained to low concentration doping (2.08 at%) with no consideration of dopant interactions at higher concentrations

10_1016_j_finel_2021_103533.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Flat plate wing and sensorcraft wing structures for topology optimization under boundary condition uncertainty
- **Material / Medium:** Aluminum (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.3, ρ = 2700 kg/m³, t = 0.001 m) for flat plate; Aircraft-grade aluminum (E = 73.1 GPa, ν = 0.33, ρ = 2780 kg/m³) with spar thickness 2.9-5.8 mm, rib thickness 0.51-0.57 mm, skin thickness 0.15-0.45 mm for sensorcraft
- **Application & Importance:** Maximizing frequency gap between first two natural frequencies to prevent aeroelastic instabilities for flat plate; Minimizing compliance for structural stiffness in sensorcraft wing
- **Geometry / Domain:** Flat plate: 1 m × 0.25 m rectangular plate with 100×25 element mesh, cantilevered on bottom edge, non-design regions along boundaries, V* = 0.75; Sensorcraft: Joined wing configuration with front and rear wings, 10,000 N load on leading edge, design area includes three central spars and twenty rib sets, V* = 0.5; BC uncertainty: ne = N(0,0.1nx) for flat plate (nx=100), ne = N(0,0.15nx) for sensorcraft (nx=8)
10_1016_j_finel_2021_103533.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Cantilevered on bottom edge for flat plate (1 m × 0.25 m); Non-design regions along boundaries; BC uncertainty: ne = N(0,0.1nx) where nx = 100 grid points for flat plate, ne = N(0,0.15nx) where nx = 8 for sensorcraft; Grid points freed starting from corners with symmetry maintained; Volume constraint V* = 0.75 for flat plate, V* = 0.5 for sensorcraft; Upper and lower surface points freed together in pairs for sensorcraft
- **Loads / Excitations:** Static load of 10,000 N applied to sensorcraft leading edge; Impulse hammer with aluminum tip striking normal to surface at 20 predefined locations; Eigenvalue problem for natural frequency analysis
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Front and rear wings joined in the middle for sensorcraft; Plate clamped to anti-vibration table using three G-clamps; Cantilevered wings connected to fuselage (not shown in model)
- **Simulation Type:** Dynamic analysis for frequency optimization (flat plate); Static analysis for compliance minimization (sensorcraft); BESO algorithm for flat plate; SIMP algorithm for sensorcraft; Experimental hammer testing with FRF analysis; Modal analysis with eigenvalue problem (K−ω²M)u=0
10_1016_j_finel_2021_103533.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Modal vibration analysis for natural frequency calculation; Static structural analysis for compliance; Uncertainty quantification via Non-Intrusive Polynomial Chaos Expansion (NIPC); Eigenvalue problem solution for dynamic analysis (K−ω²M)u=0
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Frequency gap (ω₂ - ω₁) between first two natural frequencies; Compliance (C); Frequency Response Functions (FRFs); Probability Density Functions (PDFs) of compliance; Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC); Mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) of objective functions; 95% confidence intervals for compliance
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize weighted sum of mean and standard deviation of frequency gap (μ(ω₂ - ω₁) + βσ(ω₂ - ω₁)) for flat plate to prevent aeroelastic instabilities; Minimize weighted sum of mean and standard deviation of compliance (μ(C) + βσ(C)) for sensorcraft to maintain structural stiffness under boundary condition uncertainty; Achieve flatter performance curves with reduced variance across uncertain boundary conditions
10_1016_j_finel_2021_103533.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Volume fraction constraint V* = 0.75 for flat plate (1 m × 0.25 m, 100×25 element mesh); Volume fraction constraint V* = 0.5 for sensorcraft; Non-design regions along boundaries of flat plate; Design area limited to three central spars and twenty rib sets for sensorcraft; BESO uses discrete density variables (x_i ∈ {x_min, 1}); SIMP uses continuous density variables (x_i ∈ [x_min, 1]); Non-design regions ensure structural connectivity; nx = 100 grid points along fixed edge for flat plate; nx = 8 for sensorcraft cantilever (4 upper + 4 lower surface points)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Frequency gap (ω₂ - ω₁) maximization objective; Compliance minimization objective; Boundary condition uncertainty: ne = N(0,0.1nx) for flat plate, ne = N(0,0.15nx) for sensorcraft; Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) threshold of 0.9 for mode validation; 10,000 N static load applied to sensorcraft leading edge; 800 spectral lines with 100 Hz bandwidth (0.125 Hz resolution) for FRF measurements; Convergence criteria: |(∑J_itr-k - ∑J_itr-5-k)/∑J_itr-k| ≤ δ for last 10 solutions (BESO); Maximum density change ≤ 0.01 per element (SIMP)

- **Process/Manufacturing:** Aluminum sheet metal (2700 kg/m³, 0.001 m thickness) for flat plate experiments; Aircraft-grade aluminum for sensorcraft; Three G-clamps used for plate mounting; 20 predefined hammer strike locations along free edges; Experimental validation with six-channel Bruel and Kjaer Model 3160-A-042 system; Freeing grid points starting from corners with symmetry maintained; Paired upper/lower surface grid points freed together for sensorcraft; Polynomial order 6 and oversampling factor 2 for NIPC analysis

10_1016_j_compstruct_2017_05_064.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** 3D braided composites analyzed using multiscale finite element method at representative unit cell (RUC) scale and tow architecture scale
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Carbon fiber (12K T300): Longitudinal modulus 220 GPa, transverse modulus 13.8 GPa, shear modulus G₁₂ 9.0 GPa, shear modulus G₂₃ 4.8 GPa, longitudinal CTE -0.3×10⁻⁶/°C, transverse CTE 3.1×10⁻⁶/°C
  - Epoxy resin (TDE-85): Young's modulus 4.5 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.34, CTE 31.7×10⁻⁶/°C
  - Fiber volume fraction 57.1% in experimental specimens
- **Application & Importance:** 
  - Analysis of thermo-mechanical properties for aerospace and automobile applications
  - Study of bending mechanical response under thermal and mechanical loading
  - Investigation of effects of braiding angle and temperature difference on performance
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - 4-step braided composites with 1×1 pattern containing ten yarn segments in RUC
  - Specimen dimensions 80mm×15mm×5mm for three-point bending tests
  - Yarns modeled as straight columns with elliptical cross-section in XY plane
  - Braiding angles studied ranging from 20° to 60°
  - Three-point bending test configuration with environmental chamber
  - Representative unit cell with periodic boundary conditions for homogenization analysis
10_1016_j_compstruct_2017_05_064.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Periodic boundary conditions imposed on outer surface boundaries of RUC: χᵢₖₗ(0,y₂,y₃) - χᵢₖₗ(g₁,y₂,y₃) = 0, χᵢₖₗ(y₁,0,y₃) - χᵢₖₗ(y₁,g₂,y₃) = 0, χᵢₖₗ(y₁,y₂,0) - χᵢₖₗ(y₁,y₂,g₃) = 0
  - Fixed rotations and displacements at one arbitrary point of RUC to avoid rigid body motion
  - Three-point bending test configuration with environmental chamber
  - Constant crosshead speed of 0.2mm/min for bending tests

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Temperature difference ΔT ranging from 0°C to 80°C
  - Experimental temperature T = 80°C
  - Mechanical load P = 650 N for stress distribution analysis
  - Three-point bending loads with peak values of 1753N (experimental) and 1847N (predicted)
  - Thermal loading with temperature rise ΔT as shown in multiple figures
  - Room temperature as control condition

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Thermo-mechanical coupling between thermal and mechanical loading
  - Yarn-matrix interface interactions with different thermal expansion coefficients
  - Stress transfer between yarn regions (higher modulus) and matrix regions
  - Thermal mismatch stress between components due to different CTE values
  - Multiscale interaction between RUC scale and tow architecture scale

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Multiscale finite element method combining MAEH (multiscale asymptotic expansion homogenization) and MPFE (multiphase finite element) approaches
  - 3D analysis of braided composite structures
  - Static equilibrium analysis under thermo-mechanical loading
  - Linear elastic analysis with 99% compliance matrix degradation after failure
  - Representative Unit Cell (RUC) scale analysis with periodic boundary conditions
  - Macroscale structural analysis with homogenized properties
10_1016_j_compstruct_2017_05_064.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Thermo-mechanical behavior of 3D braided composites
  - Coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) under temperature variation
  - Stress distribution in representative unit cells (RUC) under combined thermal and mechanical loading
  - Bending mechanical response of composite structures
  - Thermal mismatch stress between yarn and matrix components

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Bending strength (MPa) at various temperature differences and braiding angles
  - Longitudinal CTE (α_z) ranging from -15×10⁻⁶/°C to 15×10⁻⁶/°C
  - Transverse CTE (α_x=α_y) ranging from 6×10⁻⁶/°C to 36×10⁻⁶/°C
  - Stress distribution (σ_z) in RUC under P=650N and ΔT=80°C conditions
  - Load-deflection curves with peak loads (1753N experimental, 1847N predicted)
  - Elastic correctors (χ) and thermal corrector (ψ) for RUC analysis
  - Temperature rise effects on material degradation (28.54% strength reduction at 20° braiding angle)

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Determine optimal braiding angle for maximum bending strength under thermal conditions
  - Establish relationship between braiding angle (20°-60°) and thermo-mechanical performance
  - Quantify temperature difference (0-80°C) effects on bending strength degradation
  - Validate prediction method for thermo-mechanical performance of 3D braided composites
  - Characterize anisotropic thermal expansion behavior for aerospace and automotive applications
10_1016_j_compstruct_2017_05_064.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Braiding angle range constrained to 20°-60° for analysis
  - Specimen dimensions fixed at 80mm×15mm×5mm for three-point bending tests
  - RUC dimensions defined by g₁, g₂, g₃ in periodic boundary conditions
  - Yarns modeled as straight columns with elliptical cross-section in XY plane
  - 4-step braided composites with 1×1 pattern containing ten yarn segments in RUC

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Element count must exceed 2835 for numerical convergence (per mesh sensitivity analysis)
  - Fiber volume fraction constrained to 57.1% in experimental specimens
  - Temperature rise limited to maximum ΔT=80°C (80°C above room temperature)
  - After damage initiation, compliance matrix degraded by 99% while maintaining linear elastic response
  - Material properties constrained to carbon fiber (12K T300) and TDE-85 epoxy resin values listed in Table 1
  - Analysis limited to static loading conditions at constant crosshead speed of 0.2mm/min

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Fabrication constrained to four-step braiding process with 12K-carbon fiber and TDE-85 epoxy resin
  - Numerical model constrained to periodic boundary conditions on RUC outer surfaces
  - Analysis limited to 3D four-directional braided composites configuration
  - Yarn architecture simplified to straight columns (not capturing actual curved paths)
  - Homogenization analysis limited to representative unit cell scale with periodic assumptions

10_1016_j_jcsr_2024_109020.key_1:
- Strengthened T-shaped concrete-filled steel tubular (CFST) column-steel beam joint for structural building applications
- Q355B steel with yield strength ranging from 380-522 MPa and ultimate strength from 489-635 MPa depending on thickness (6-20 mm)
- C40 concrete with average compressive strength of 48.6 MPa

- **Geometry / Domain:** Multiple configurations including: cantilever beam (5L × 2.5L × 2.5L) with fixed left end and bottom surface traction; wheel-like structure with fixed inner surface and five counter-clockwise torsion loads on outer surface; bracket-like structure with fixed top-right ring and traction on bottom-left ring; airplane bearing bracket with fixed bottom and 45° inclined traction; bridge (L × 3L × 10L) with fixed bottom ends and top surface traction; all models incorporate design domains with non-design domains at boundaries

10_1016_j_compstruc_2020_106327.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Progressive damage evolution in composite laminates under large deformation including intra-ply matrix cracking, fiber rupture/kinking, inter-ply delamination, and their nonlinear coupling; geometrically nonlinear behavior with finite rotation and translation of crack surfaces

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Load-deflection curves for center-loaded plates and four-point-bending specimens
  - Stress-strain curves for open-hole tension specimens
  - Progressive damage states at different load levels (40%, 70%, 100% of ultimate load)
  - Crack initiation locations and propagation paths (transverse cracks, splitting cracks)
  - Delamination regions and growth patterns
  - Final failure load/strength (e.g., 860.4 MPa for OHT specimen, 349.1 N for FPB specimen)
  - Relative error between predicted and experimental peak loads (within 2% for center-loaded plate)
  - Damage visualization showing fiber fracture, matrix transverse cracks, and delamination

- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve high-fidelity prediction of progressive damage evolution from early-stage multiple crack initiations through nonlinearly coupled progression with delamination to final catastrophic failure; enable accurate damage tolerance design by capturing post-peak load behavior; maintain computational efficiency by eliminating need for additional nodes/DOFs while handling multiple interactive cracks; ensure mesh-independent results with element size smaller than cohesive zone size (lₑ < l_coh)
10_1016_j_compstruc_2020_106327.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Mesh size must be smaller than the smallest cohesive zone size (lₑ < l_coh) among all relevant crack types
  - Open-hole tension specimen modeled as 1/8 due to symmetry (with symmetric boundary conditions)
  - Center-loaded plate modeled as 1/4 due to symmetry
  - Typical composite lamina thickness of 0.1-0.2 mm constrains crack orientation assumption
  - 3D cohesive crack assumed to be locally perpendicular to mid-plane of lamina
  - OHT specimen discretized with Mesh A (lₑ~0.3 mm), Mesh B (lₑ~0.15 mm), or Mesh C (lₑ~0.12 mm) around the hole

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Ultimate strains for fiber reinforced composites typically no more than 1-2%, justifying linear constitutive model
  - Crack initiation occurs when max{F_FT, F_FC, F_MT, F_MC} ≥ 1 (Hashin criterion)
  - Mixed-mode CZM failure criterion: G_I*/Γ_I + G_II*/Γ_II + G_III*/Γ_III = 1
  - Cohesive strength limits: σ̂_t = X_t (2170 MPa for HTA/6376), σ̂_c = X_c (1551 MPa), τ̂_s = S_L (83 MPa), τ̂_t = S_T (83 MPa)

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Yield stress (σy) at 0.2% offset; true flow stress as function of true inelastic strain; flow stress curves for ferrite and bainite phases; R² (92.24%) and modified R² (87.53%) for regression model; variance inflation factors (VIFs); optimal parameter combinations for maximum yield stress
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize yield stress (σy) of API 5L steel; achieve optimal yield stress of approximately 521.4 MPa; determine optimal microstructural parameters: void size (0.5 μm), void volume fraction (0.5%), ferrite grain size (2 μm), bainite grain size (5 μm), and bainite volume fraction (50%)
10_1007_s13632_024_01139_1.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Ferrite grain size (FGS) constrained to 2–15 μm; bainite grain size (BGS) constrained to 5–15 μm; bainite volume fraction (BVF) constrained to 15–50%; void size (VS) constrained to 0.5–20 μm; void volume fraction (VVF) constrained to 0.5–10%
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Offset yield point defined at 0.2% inelastic deformation; peak strain value limited to 0.14 at onset of necking under static tension load conditions; analysis conducted under quasi-static strain conditions; yield stress optimization target of approximately 521.4 MPa
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Void volume fraction (VVF) optimized to 0.5% to meet stringent steel casting cleanliness requirements; microstructural parameters controllable through chemical composition, thermomechanical control process (TMCP), and accelerated cooling (ACC) processes; manufacturing practices during hot working must ensure low void content for optimal mechanical properties

10_1016_j_ijrmms_2025_106036.key_1:
- Identity & Domain: Simultaneously-stimulated hydraulic fractures in two-hole configuration
- Material / Medium: PMMA (polymethyl methacrylate) with Young's modulus 3.90 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.35, uniaxial compression strength 85.80 MPa, Brazilian tensile strength 13.50 MPa; water with green fluorescent dye
- Application & Importance: Optimization of hydraulic fracturing design in hydrocarbon reservoir stimulation, enhanced geothermal systems, and block caving mining; understanding fracture competition to address non-uniform growth where "a large proportion of perforation clusters do not contribute to production"
- Geometry / Domain: Cubic PMMA sample with 200 mm side length; two vertical holes (10 mm diameter, 75 mm depth) spaced 40 mm apart along center line; 65 mm packer length leaving 10 mm open-hole; boundary stress conditions with σH fixed at 1.69 MPa while varying σh to achieve stress ratios k (σh/σH) from 0 to 0.8; water injection rate of 200 ml/s; high-speed camera recording at 1000 frames per second
10_1016_j_ijrmms_2025_106036.key_2:
- Boundaries & Constraints: Cubic PMMA sample (200 mm × 200 mm × 200 mm); two vertical holes (10 mm diameter, 75 mm depth) spaced 40 mm apart; 65 mm packer length leaving 10 mm open-hole; σH fixed at 1.69 MPa with σh varied to achieve stress ratios k (σh/σH) from 0 to 0.8; third direction free for observation; hydraulic actuators applying boundary stresses in two directions; porosity and permeability considered infinitesimal (mimicking no pore pressure diffusion)
- Loads / Excitations: Water with green fluorescent dye injected at 200 ml/s; pressure monitored every 0.2 s; high-speed camera recording at 1000 frames per second; two flat lights illuminating sample from both sides; boundary stresses applied through hydraulic actuators
- Interactions / Interfaces: Competition between boundary stress (σH, σh) and internal stress from holes; stress ratio k = σh/σH; injection pressure idealized as boundary stress uniformly applied on hole periphery; stress interference between adjacent fractures; stress repulsion from primary fracture affecting secondary fracture propagation
- Simulation Type: Transient analysis; two-dimensional XFEM model with plane strain assumption for cross-section perpendicular to open-hole segment; 3D fracture geometry reconstructed from high-speed camera images; numerical simulations conducted for stress ratios k = 0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, and 0.8; pumping pressure linearly applied according to experimental trends
10_1016_j_ijrmms_2025_106036.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Dynamic propagation and interaction of multiple hydraulic fractures under simultaneous stimulation; stress interference effects between adjacent fractures; competition between boundary stress and internal stress fields; fracture initiation, propagation, and reorientation mechanisms
- Target Outputs (Metrics): Fracture geometry (planar vs. spiral); breakdown pressure; stress distribution (σxx, σyy, σmax) along hole connection line; turning radius of fracture deflection; propagation stages (hole connection/deflection/rapid propagation for spiral fractures; upward/bilateral synchronization/downward propagation for planar fractures); fracture initiation sequence; stress ratio (k = σh/σH) effects; injection pressure-time curves; maximum principal stress at fracture initiation points
- Optimization Goal: Understand fracture competition mechanisms to optimize hydraulic fracturing design; identify conditions that prevent "non-production perforation clusters"; determine optimal stress ratio conditions for desired fracture patterns; explain why "a large proportion of perforation clusters do not contribute to production" to improve stimulation efficiency in hydrocarbon reservoirs, geothermal systems, and mining applications
10_1016_j_ijrmms_2025_106036.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: Cubic PMMA sample with 200 mm side length; two vertical holes (10 mm diameter, 75 mm depth) with 40 mm spacing; packer length of 65 mm leaving 10 mm open-hole; fixed σH at 1.69 MPa with stress ratio k (σh/σH) limited to range 0-0.8; third dimension free for observation
- Performance/Physics Limits: PMMA material properties constrained to Young's modulus 3.90 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.35, uniaxial compression strength 85.80 MPa, Brazilian tensile strength 13.50 MPa; porosity and permeability considered infinitesimal (no pore pressure diffusion); stress ratio k cannot exceed 0.8 in experimental design; breakdown pressure varies with stress ratio (decreases when k > 0.6)
- Process/Manufacturing: Water injection rate fixed at 200 ml/s; pressure monitoring every 0.2 s; high-speed camera recording at 1000 frames per second; PMMA cannot reflect mineral composition and heterogeneity of real rock; experimental model simplifies adjacent perforations into two holes; sample size limitation prevents direct field-scale application; stress ratio of 0.4 identified as upper limit for single-hole planar fracture formation

10_1016_j_engfailanal_2020_104829.key_1:

- Materials: Austenitic stainless steel stem (E=205 GPa, ν=0.3), ceramic ball (E=380 GPa, ν=0.26), polyethylene cup (E=1 GPa, ν=0.4), PMMA cement (E=2.8 GPa, ν=0.33), bone (E=20 GPa, ν=0.25)
- Ball outer radius: 16 mm
- Acetabular cup inner radius: 16 mm, outer radius: 26 mm
- Cement layer thickness: 2 mm
- Acetabular cup positioning angle (θ) range: -40° to 40° in 10° increments
- Boundary conditions: M-I (stem fixed), M-II (pelvis fixed), M-III (pelvis fixed with femoral shaft fixed to collar)
- Hip joint movement range: 45° abduction, 30° adduction in coronal plane
- Applied load: 500 N force or 0.1 mm displacement
- Crack initiation site: Horizontally diagonal to acetabular cup, at outer ring
- Crack path: Initiates in acetabular cup, propagates to cement layer
- Maximum contact pressure location varies with θ: α≈90° at θ=-40°, α≈125° at θ=-20°, α=180° at θ=0°, 20°, 40°
- Hip joint components modeled with C3D8R 8-node linear brick elements with reduced integration
10_1016_j_engfailanal_2020_104829.key_2:

- Fixed constraints: Femoral shaft fixed in all directions up to collar in M-III condition
- Tied interfaces: Cement outer surface tied to bone inner surface; cement inner surface fixed to cup outer surface; stem joined to ball
- Contact interface: Master-slave algorithm used between cup inner surface and ball outer surface
- Finite sliding tracking: Allowed arbitrary relative separation and rotation between cup and ball surfaces
- Loading: Vertical load applied on pelvis transmitted to hip joint components
- Load magnitude: 500 N force or 0.1 mm displacement control
- Acetabular cup positioning angle (θ) range: -40° to 40° in 10° increments

- Material behavior: Linear elastic analysis (model applied in elastic state)

- Stress analysis: Von-Mises stress and S22 stress component evaluation
- Crack analysis: Maximum principal stress criterion for crack initiation
10_1016_j_engfailanal_2020_104829.key_3:

10_1016_j_dt_2024_12_016.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Box-type Multiple Launch Rocket System (BMLRS) launch dynamics with slider-guide plane clearance contact modeling
- **Material / Medium:** 45 Steel (209 GPa Young's modulus, 0.269 Poisson ratio), alternative materials with 170 GPa Young's modulus (0.269 Poisson ratio) and 0.209 GPa Young's modulus (0.22 Poisson ratio); launch canister with bending stiffness EI; rocket treated as 6-DOF rigid body
- **Application & Importance:** Ensuring launch stability and safety, minimizing control costs, and improving guidance precision by accurately calculating rocket launch attitude and angular velocity; developing novel launch modeling theory adapted to box-type launch technology where conventional tube launching methodology is inapplicable
- **Geometry / Domain:** Complex multi-rigid-flexible-body system comprising 15 rigid bodies, 3 elastic beams, and 12 boundary ends connected by 24 spatial elastic hinges; launch canister divided into three Euler-Bernoulli beam segments with two massless rigid bodies; rocket with square sliders interacting with guides in launch canister; two slider pairs (front and rear) constraining rocket movement; rectangular contact surfaces with clearances (c_i,yu, c_i,yl, c_i,z) between sliders and guides
10_1016_j_dt_2024_12_016.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Connection points between road wheels and ground, head and rear ends of launch canister defined as system boundaries (numbered 0)
  - Boundary ends with fixed displacement (X=Y=Z=Θx=Θy=Θz=0) for i=1,4,7,10,13,16,19,22,25,28
  - Boundary ends with fixed internal forces/moments (Mx=My=Mz=Qx=Qy=Qz=0) for i=38+7l, 42+7l
  - Firing angle set to 60° through pitch body during static equilibrium simulation
  - Fixed excitation point at rear of chassis beam for modal testing
  - Observation point at connection between vehicle body and rotation body for modal convergence verification

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Gravity acting on the system during static equilibrium simulation
  - Rocket thrust that gradually increases after ignition to counteract gravity
  - Force hammer with rubber-tipped head for modal test excitation
  - Rocket subsystem experiences gravity, propulsion from engine, and slider-guide contact forces
  - Integration step size of 0.0001 s for numerical simulation

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Slider-guide plane clearance contact with three potential contact surfaces (upper, lower, side)
  - Initial clearances: c_i,yu, c_i,yl = 2 mm (upper/lower), c_i,z = 2.5 mm (side)
  - Contact dimensions: b_i,zu, b_i,zl = 2.25 cm (contact length), b_i,y = 3 cm (slider thickness)
  - Normal contact force modeled with Lankarani-Nikravesh contact model: f_n^c = Kδ[1 + (3(1-c_e^2)/4)(δ̇/δ̇^(-))]
  - Modified Coulomb friction model for tangential force with parameters: μ_s=0.10, v_s=0.3 m/s, μ_d=0.08, v_d=0.6 m/s
  - Restitution coefficient c_e = 0.75
  - Data exchange between launch platform and rocket subsystem only at displacement and velocity levels

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Transient analysis with simulation time less than 0.9 s for launch dynamics
  - 6-DOF rigid body model for rocket
  - Linear time-invariant system modeling for launch platform subsystem (LPS)
  - Nonlinear ordinary differential equation solved using fourth-order Runge-Kutta algorithm
  - Modal analysis using first 10 modes for convergence
  - Multibody system transfer matrix method (MSTMM) for dynamics modeling
  - Closed-loop topology converted to tree-shaped topology for analysis
10_1016_j_dt_2024_12_016.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Coupled multibody system dynamics of launch platform and rocket
  - Slider-guide plane clearance contact mechanics with normal force and friction effects
  - Vibration characteristics of complex multi-rigid-flexible-body launch platform subsystem
  - Rocket motion with 6-DOF rigid body dynamics within launch canister
  - Modal behavior of the launch platform under static conditions

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Eigenfrequencies (natural frequencies) of LPS (experimental vs. simulation max relative error 3.29%)
  - Rocket attitude parameters: pitch angle δ₁^I, yaw angle δ₂^I, roll angle γ and their angular velocities
  - Contact forces between sliders and guides (normal and tangential)
  - Penetration depth and velocity at contact interfaces
  - Vertical displacement of launch canister head
  - Time histories of rocket motion parameters under various conditions
  - Frequency-domain responses of angular velocities
  - Modal convergence verification using first 10 modes

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Determine optimal slider-guide clearance values (2 mm lower clearance minimizes guide influence on rocket)
  - Identify preferred slider layout (shorter distance between front and rear sliders recommended)
  - Select appropriate materials with smaller elastic modulus within strength constraints
  - Maintain launch canister bending stiffness within appropriate range to prevent excessive vibration
  - Reduce yaw angle and yaw angular velocity through reduced side clearance
  - Minimize vibration and attitude oscillations while ensuring safe launch dynamics
10_1016_j_dt_2024_12_016.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Initial clearances constrained to extremely narrow values: c_i,yu, c_i,yl = 2 mm (upper/lower), c_i,z = 2.5 mm (side)
  - Contact dimensions fixed at: b_i,zu, b_i,zl = 2.25 cm (contact length), b_i,y = 3 cm (slider thickness)
  - Slider-guide clearance parameter range: c_i,y_l tested at 1.5-2.5 mm, c_i,z tested at 1.5-2.5 mm
  - Slider length (l_s) constrained to 4.8-5 mm range for testing
  - Front-to-rear slider distance (l_2) constrained to 6-10 cm range for testing
  - Rocket movement limited to small range inside launch canister except for axial movement

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Integration time step constrained to 0.0001 s for numerical stability
  - Firing angle fixed at 60° for static equilibrium simulation
  - Front slider pairs must exit guides before 0.591 s and rear slider pairs before 0.861 s
  - Penetration depth must remain within acceptable limits to validate contact model
  - Rocket attitude angle δ_B must remain relatively modest during entire motion
  - Restitution coefficient fixed at c_e = 0.75 for contact modeling
  - Friction parameters constrained: μ_s=0.10, v_s=0.3 m/s, μ_d=0.08, v_d=0.6 m/s
  - Natural frequency relative error must not exceed 3.29% for model validation

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Slider and guide must be constructed from same material
  - Material selection constrained by strength requirements: Young's modulus tested at 0.209 GPa, 170 GPa, and 209 GPa
  - Material with smaller elastic modulus prioritized within strength constraints
  - Slider length reduction must not compromise launch safety due to stiffness reduction
  - Manufacturing must ensure extremely narrow initial clearances to prevent slider from breaking away from guide
  - Contact surface shape assumed to be approximately rectangular when slider contacts guide

10_1016_j_energy_2025_136006.key_1:
- Solar receiver heat-absorbing tube row for supercritical CO₂ power cycle
- Heat transfer fluid: Supercritical CO₂ (S-CO₂); Tube material: Inconel 600 (density 8470 kg/m³, specific heat cₚ = -1.415×10⁻⁹·T⁴ + 4.129×10⁻⁶·T³ + 0.004251·T² + 2.025·T + 114.4 J/(kg·K), thermal conductivity λ = -4.498×10⁻¹⁰·T³ + 3.694×10⁻⁶·T² + 0.01197·T + 10.93 W/(m·K))
- Analysis of thermal efficiency, stress-strain characteristics, and entropy generation to improve receiver safety and performance in high-temperature solar thermal power generation
- 17 parallel heat-absorbing tubes (1600 mm length, 35 mm outer diameter, 7.5 mm wall thickness) with 3 mm spacing; three tube configurations: circular tube, straight ribbed tube (1 mm rib height, 8 ribs, 60° top angle), and internal spiral ribbed tube (1 mm rib height, 8 ribs, 60° top angle, 62.8 mm thread pitch); manifold length 726 mm, 180 mm outer diameter; non-uniform Gaussian heat flux distribution on heating surface with σ values from 0.4 to 0.8
10_1016_j_energy_2025_136006.key_2:
- Heating surface: Non-uniform Gaussian heat flux with q_max values of 818.57 kW/m² (σ=0.4), 677.11 kW/m² (σ=0.5), 602.30 kW/m² (σ=0.6), 588.21 kW/m² (σ=0.7), and 530.10 kW/m² (σ=0.8)
- Other external surfaces: Adiabatic boundaries
- Inlet: Mass inlet with 7.96 kg/s flow rate (base case), inlet temperature 823 K
- Outlet: Pressure outlet at 20 MPa
- Gravity: Applied along negative z-axis
- Convergence criteria: Continuity/momentum equation residuals < 10⁻⁴, energy equation residual < 10⁻⁷
- Wall treatment: Dimensionless wall distance (y⁺) ≈ 1
- Heat loss modeling: Radiative loss q_loss,r = εσ(T_w⁴ - T_∞⁴) and convective loss q_loss,c = 0.81(T_w - T_∞)^0.426
- Ambient temperature: 295.85-309.05 K (8:00-18:00)
- Time-varying conditions: q_max from 342.94-863.49 kW/m² (8:00-18:00)
- Mass flow rate variation: 5.57-10.34 kg/s in parametric studies
- Turbulence model: SST k-ω model for flow characteristics
- Numerical scheme: Second-order upwind discretization with SIMPLEC algorithm for pressure-velocity coupling
- Domain: 3D tube row with 17 parallel tubes
- Material interface: Inconel 600 tube wall with S-CO₂ working fluid
- Steady-state thermal-fluid analysis coupled with structural mechanical analysis
10_1016_j_energy_2025_136006.key_3:
- Turbulent flow of supercritical CO₂, conjugate heat transfer under non-uniform solar irradiation, thermal stress-strain behavior, and entropy generation analysis
- Thermal efficiency (η), equivalent stress (σ_eq), equivalent elastic strain (ε_eq), heat absorption (Q_ab), heat loss (Q_loss), Nusselt number (Nu), mass flow rate distribution (m), total entropy generation (S_tot), heat transfer entropy generation (S_ht), viscous dissipation entropy generation (S_fr), temperature distribution (T), temperature gradient (T_grad)
- Minimize total entropy generation (11.5% reduction target), reduce equivalent stress (15.4% reduction target), reduce equivalent elastic strain (17.4% reduction target), and maximize thermal efficiency (1.03% improvement target) while ensuring structural integrity under non-uniform solar irradiation and high-temperature operation
10_1016_j_energy_2025_136006.key_4:
- Tube length: 1600 mm; Tube outer diameter: 35 mm; Tube wall thickness: 7.5 mm (per ASME Pressure Piping B31.1 Code); Space between tubes: 3 mm; 17 parallel tubes per row; Manifold length: 726 mm; Manifold outer diameter: 180 mm; Manifold wall thickness: 20 mm
- Inlet temperature: 823 K; Outlet pressure: 20 MPa; Inlet mass flow rate: 7.96 kg/s (base case); Maximum equivalent stress: ~700 MPa; Wall temperature range: 823-1475 K; Non-uniform heat flux with σ values from 0.4-0.8 (q_max from 530.10-818.57 kW/m²); Maximum heat flux at 12:00 (823.68 kW/m²); Heat loss calculation constrained by q_loss,r = εσ(T_w⁴ - T_∞⁴) and q_loss,c = 0.81(T_w - T_∞)^0.426
- Wall thickness determined by ASME Pressure Piping B31.1 Code; Only three tube configurations permitted: circular tube, straight ribbed tube (1 mm rib height, 8 ribs, 60° top angle), and internal spiral ribbed tube (1 mm rib height, 8 ribs, 60° top angle, 62.8 mm thread pitch); Only tubes No.6 and No.12 can be replaced with reinforced tube types; Tube material limited to Inconel 600; Heat flux distribution constrained to Gaussian form q_h = q_max·exp[-1/2((y-0.3215)²/σ_y² + (z-0.8)²/σ_z²)]

10_1007_s10338_018_0061_3.key_1:
- Graphene nanopores with different geometries (circular (CR), horizontal rectangular (RH), vertical rectangular (RV), and square (SQ))
- Monolayer graphene sheet of 9.628 × 9.845 nm²
- Pore sizes range from approximately 0.7-5 nm (sub-5nm)
- Carbon atoms treated as nodes and C-C bonds as beam elements in atomistic finite element model
- Four sides of graphene sheet are clamped as boundary condition
- Uniaxial tensile loading normal to graphene plane applied on pore-lining carbon atoms
- C-C bond failure stress of 123 GPa
- Pore dimensions defined by La (length in armchair direction) and Lz (length in zigzag direction)
- Critical load per atom ranges from 0.025 to 0.25 nN depending on pore size and geometry
- Critical displacement decreases with increasing pore area
- Two corner configurations observed: C-like (armchair) and V-like (zigzag) corners
- Strength order for comparable sizes: CR > RH > RV > SQ
- V-like (zigzag) corners experience higher tensile stress than C-like (armchair) corners
- Maximum stress concentration occurs at pore corners in all cases
- Pore mechanical properties depend on size, geometry, and orientation relative to graphene lattice directions
10_1007_s10338_018_0061_3.key_2:
- Four sides of graphene sheet are clamped (fixed boundary condition)
- Uniaxial tensile loading normal to the graphene plane applied on pore-lining carbon atoms
- Force applied on each surface node (carbon atom at pore edge)
- Loading mimics impact force from fluid flow through nanopore
- DNA translocation forces up to 0.01 nN on pore edge (experimental reference)
- C-C bond failure stress of 123 GPa (used as failure criterion)
- Atomistic finite element method simulation
- 3D elastic BEAM4 element used for modeling
- Carbon atoms treated as nodes and C-C bonds as beam elements
- Load per atom ranging from 0 to approximately 0.2 nN (as shown in stress-strain curves)
- Pore areas ranging from 0.4 to 18.5 nm²
- Critical load per atom ranging from 0.025 to 0.25 nN depending on pore geometry and size
10_1007_s10338_018_0061_3.key_3:
- Mechanical stress distribution in graphene nanopores under normal loading
- Critical load per atom that carbon atoms can tolerate before fracturing
- Critical displacement of graphene sheet under load
- Stress concentration patterns at pore edges and corners
- Comparison of mechanical strength between different pore geometries (CR, RH, RV, SQ)
- Effect of pore size (0.7-5 nm) on mechanical properties
- Maximum stress values (GPa) as function of load per atom
- Failure analysis based on C-C bond strength (123 GPa)
- Effect of corner configuration (C-like armchair vs V-like zigzag) on stress concentration
- Deflection behavior of graphene sheet with different pore orientations
- Critical load per atom ranging from 0.025 to 0.25 nN depending on pore geometry and size
- Displacement values showing different deflection patterns for various pore shapes
- Stress concentration at corners identified as origin of pore fracture
- Strength ranking for comparable pore sizes: CR > RH > RV > SQ
- Mechanical property comparison between pores with long sides aligned along zigzag vs armchair directions
10_1007_s10338_018_0061_3.key_4:
- Pore sizes constrained to sub-5nm range (0.7-5 nm) as this promotes high-resolution molecular sensing
- Graphene sheet size fixed at 9.628 × 9.845 nm² for all simulations
- Only four pore geometries studied: circular (CR), horizontal rectangular (RH), vertical rectangular (RV), and square (SQ)
- CR pores not perfectly round due to discrete carbon network, more hexagonal-like
- Failure criterion based on C-C bond stress limit of 123 GPa
- Critical load per atom must exceed DNA translocation forces (0.01 nN) for functional nanopores
- Maximum critical load per atom ranges from 0.025 to 0.25 nN depending on pore geometry and size
- Simulation limited to atomistic finite element method without electronic phenomena (bond forming/breaking)
- Pore reconstruction and damage phenomena difficult to capture with finite element technique
- Only mechanical properties of experimentally fabricable nanopores studied
- Analysis limited to normal load on pore rim, omitting real solution/fluid flow conditions
- Pore sizes constrained to those commonly used for single-stranded DNA sequencing (1-5 nm)
- Study focuses on mechanical properties rather than pore selectivity which also plays dominant role in nanofiltration
- Corner configurations limited to C-like (armchair) and V-like (zigzag) types based on graphene lattice structure

10_1016_j_cej_2025_161385.key_2:
- Electrolyte composition: EC : DMC : EMC = 1 : 1 : 1 + 5% FEC

- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Isotropic elastic materials with Young's modulus E=2, Poisson's ratio ν=0 (non-dimensional) or E=5/2, ν=1/4 (non-dimensional)

  - Characteristic material length l ranging from 10⁻⁴ to 10³ in non-dimensional form; l=300 nm for copper single crystal
- **Application & Importance:** Capturing mechanical response at micro/nano scales where classical elasticity fails; analysis of stress concentration factors, stiffness size-dependence, and energy partitioning for micro-scale components, graphene sheets, and carbon nanotubes
- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - Cantilever beam with L=20h, fixed left end, downward uniform traction on right end (t̂₂=-1)
  - Square plate with central circular hole (2L×2L dimensions, hole diameter=1)
  - Quarter-plate symmetry models for hole problems with zero rotation and normal displacement boundary conditions
  - Characteristic length ratios (h/l or L/l) defining classical regime (large ratio), transition regime, and couple stress saturation regime (small ratio <0.1)
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106497.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Left side of cantilever fully constrained with zero displacements
  - Symmetry boundaries with zero rotation and zero normal displacement for quarter-plate models
  - Displacements specified on Γ_u boundary portion
  - Rotations specified on Γ_ω boundary portion
  - Rotation boundary condition: 1/2 ε_ijk u_k,j = ω_i on Γ_ω
  - Normal component of couple-traction vector must be zero on all surfaces

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Uniform downward force-traction with unit magnitude (t̂_2 = -1) on right side of cantilever
  - Uniform traction T_0 = 1 applied to boundaries of square plate (all boundaries for case one, opposite sides only for case two)
  - Applied body-force density f̂_i
  - Force-traction t̂_i specified on Γ_t boundary portion

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Couple-traction relation: m_i = μ_ji n_j
  - Force-traction relation: t_i = σ_ji n_j
  - Divergence-free nature of couple-stress vector enforced in finite element representation

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Planar (2D) quasistatic elastostatic analysis
  - Linear elastic isotropic media and cubic single crystal materials
  - Size-dependent mechanics using skew-symmetric couple stress theory
  - Two distinct regimes: classical regime (large characteristic length ratio) and couple stress saturation regime (characteristic length ratio <0.1)
  - C⁰ continuous finite element formulation with linear three-node triangles for displacements and tangential edge elements for couple-stresses
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106497.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Size-dependent elastic behavior using skew-symmetric couple stress theory; planar quasistatic elastostatic response of linear elastic isotropic media and cubic single crystals at micro/nano scales

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Non-dimensional stiffness (kL²/3EI) for cantilever beam
  - Displacements at specific points (P₁ and P₂) in square plate with central hole
  - Stress concentration factor (σ₂₂/σ_nom on hole surface at minimum cross-section)
  - Internal energy partitioning (strain energy, curvature energy, total energy)
  - Relative energy error for convergence studies
  - Axial stress distributions (σ₁₁, σ₂₂)
  - Couple-stress distributions (μ₁, μ₂)
  - Deformation shapes under different characteristic length ratios
  - Force-stress distributions across critical cross-sections

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Validate mixed variational principle against boundary element method solutions
  - Demonstrate convergence rates of approximately order two in internal energy
  - Capture transition from classical to couple stress saturation regimes
  - Show reduction in stress concentration factors from classical values (3.2 for isotropic, 2.7 for cubic crystal) to saturated values (1.2 for isotropic, 1.1 for copper single crystal)
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106497.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Element size must be comparable to characteristic material length l to capture size effects (ξ ~ l)
  - Mesh refinement required such that element size is "reduced to the order of l, or perhaps a few times larger"
  - Characteristic length ratio (h/l or L/l) defines analysis regimes: classical (large ratio), transition (ratio ~1), and saturation (ratio <0.1)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Theory restricted to infinitesimal deformations (finite element displacements in figures are scaled for visualization)
  - Valid only for the smallest scales where continuum mechanics applies
  - Limited to centrosymmetric materials in the current implementation
  - Two distinct response regimes exist: classical elasticity regime (large characteristic length ratio) and couple stress saturation regime (ratio <0.1)
  - Maximum stress concentration factor reduction from classical values (3.2 for isotropic, 2.7 for cubic crystal) to saturated values (1.2 for isotropic, 1.1 for copper single crystal)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Computational limitation: couple-stress variables (μ̄) are continuous across elements and cannot be eliminated at individual element level
  - Convergence studies require multiple mesh refinement levels (60×3, 120×6, 240×12, 480×24 blocks)
  - Current implementation restricted to two-dimensional problems (though framework can be extended to 3D)

10_1016_j_advwatres_2022_104129.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Single-phase Darcy flow in fractured porous media using a hybrid-mixed finite element method (HM-DFM)
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Porous matrix with permeability tensor Kₘ
  - Conductive fractures with permeability tensor Kc ≫ Kₘ (e.g., Kc = 10⁴ m²)
  - Blocking fractures with permeability Kᵦ ≪ Kₘ (e.g., Kᵦ = 10⁻⁴ m²)
  - Fracture thickness ε (e.g., ε = 10⁻⁴ m)
  - Matrix porosity φₘ (e.g., 0.1-0.2)
  - Fracture porosity φc (e.g., 0.4-0.9)
- **Application & Importance:** 
  - Simulation of flows in porous media with conductive and blocking fractures
  - Applications in contaminant transportation, oil recovery, and underground radioactive waste deposit
  - Accurate modeling of complex fracture networks without requiring mesh conformity to blocking fractures
- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - 2D and 3D domains with various fracture configurations
  - Benchmark 1: Polygonal domain (vertices at A=(0,150), B=(400,100), etc.) with two conductive fractures
  - Benchmark 2: Square domain (unit dimensions) with regular fracture network
  - Benchmark 5: Cube-shaped domain (100m × 100m × 100m) with a single conductive planar fracture
  - Benchmark 6: Unit cube domain (1m × 1m × 1m) with 9 regularly oriented fractures
  - Benchmark 8: Realistic 3D domain (−500m to 350m in x, 100m to 1500m in y, −100m to 500m in z) with 52 fractures
  - Fractures treated as (d-1)-dimensional interfaces within d-dimensional domains (d=2,3)
10_1016_j_advwatres_2022_104129.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Dirichlet pressure conditions: p = height on top boundary (Benchmark 1), p = 4 m at inlet (Benchmark 5), p = 1 m at outlet (Benchmark 5), p = 1 m on Γ_D = {(x,y,z) ∈ ∂Ω: x,y,z > 0.875 m} (Benchmark 6)
  - Neumann boundary conditions: u·n = -1 m/s on ∂Ω_in = {(x,y,z) ∈ ∂Ω: x,y,z < 0.25 m} (Benchmark 6), u·n = -1 m/s on inlet boundary (Benchmark 7), uniform unit inflow u·n = 1 m/s on inlet (Benchmark 8)
  - Homogeneous Neumann conditions on remaining boundaries (Benchmark 1)
  - No-flow conditions (q^N = 0) on remaining boundaries (Benchmarks 5,6,7)
  - Pressure continuity: p = p_c on Ω_c (conducting fractures)
  - In-plane no-flow condition: u_c · η_Γ = 0 on Γ_c_b ∪ Γ_c_m_N ∪ Γ_c_i

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Inflow through narrow bands: {0 m} × (0 m,100 m) × (90 m,100 m) (Benchmark 5)
  - Outlet through narrow bands: (0 m,100 m) × {0 m} × (0 m,10 m) (Benchmark 5)
  - Source term f in flow equations
  - Inflow concentration c_B = 1 on left boundary (Benchmark 2 transport)
  - Initial concentrations: c_0 = c_c,0 = 0 (Benchmark 2)
  - Velocity input: ū = -1 m/s (from figures)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Conductive fractures: pressure continuity across fracture interfaces (p = p_c)
  - Blocking fractures: normal component of Darcy velocity continuity across interfaces
  - Conductive fracture intersections: mass conservation enforced through jump conditions
  - Fracture-matrix mass exchange: [u] = (u⁺ - u⁻)·n_Γ
  - Matrix-fracture concentration continuity: c = c_c on Ω_c

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Steady-state flow simulations with transient transport
  - 2D and 3D domains (d = 2,3)
  - Fitted mesh required for conductive fractures, unfitted mesh allowed for blocking fractures
  - Time stepping: implicit Euler method with Δt = 2^-l × 5×10^-3 s (Benchmark 2), Δt = 10^7 s (Benchmark 5), Δt = 2^-l × 2.5×10^-3 s (Benchmark 6)
  - Final simulation times: T = 0.1 s (Benchmark 2), T = 10^9 s (Benchmark 5), T = 0.25 s (Benchmark 6)
10_1016_j_advwatres_2022_104129.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Single-phase Darcy flow in fractured porous media with hybrid-dimensional modeling, treating conductive fractures (Kc ≫ Kₘ) and blocking fractures (Kb ≪ Kₘ) differently; coupled with scalar transport of passive tracers
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Piezometric/hydraulic head distribution along specified lines
  - Pressure profiles across fracture networks (e.g., along (0m,100m,100m)-(100m,0m,0m) in Benchmark 5)
  - Matrix and fracture concentration distributions
  - L² errors in velocity (‖uₕ - uᵣₑ𝒻‖), postprocessed pressure (‖pₕ* - pᵣₑ𝒻*‖), and concentration (‖cₕ(T) - cᵣₑ𝒻(T)‖)
  - Match percentages (e.g., "match: 66", "match: 81" in figure captions)
  - Convergence rates for mesh refinement studies
- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Achieve locally conservative velocity approximations with nonconforming meshes for blocking fractures
  - Minimize degrees of freedom while maintaining accuracy (symmetric positive definite system with pressure DOFs on mesh skeleton only)
  - Demonstrate competitive performance with existing methods in benchmark test cases
  - Maintain accuracy with reduced computational cost compared to methods requiring mesh conformity to all fractures
10_1016_j_advwatres_2022_104129.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Mesh must be conforming to conductive fractures (fracture boundaries must align with mesh interfaces)
  - Mesh can be nonconforming to blocking fractures (no requirement for fracture alignment with mesh interfaces)
  - Background mesh must be tetrahedral for 3D implementations (as described in mesh immersing technique)
  - Fractures are assumed to be hyperplanes with smooth boundaries
  - The domain Ωₘ is assumed to be a bounded open domain in ℝᵈ, d=2,3

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Pressure continuity must be enforced across conductive fractures (p = p_c on Ω_c)
  - Normal component of Darcy velocity must be continuous across blocking fractures
  - The method is limited to single-phase flow (not multi-phase flow)
  - For conductive fractures: Kc ≫ Kₘ (e.g., Kc = 10⁴ m² vs Kₘ = 1 m²)
  - For blocking fractures: Kb ≪ Kₘ (e.g., Kb = 10⁻⁴ m² vs Kₘ = 1 m²)
  - The fracture thickness ε must be small (e.g., ε = 10⁻⁴ m)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - The linear system after static condensation is symmetric positive definite but requires pressure DOFs on mesh skeleton only
  - Computational cost is higher than TPFA schemes but lower than saddle point systems like UiB-MVEM
  - The method requires specialized mesh handling for conductive fractures (fitted mesh) but not for blocking fractures
  - The immersed mesh technique creates highly anisotropic elements when background mesh is independent of fracture geometry
  - The number of global unknowns is roughly N_F (total number of mesh faces), approximately 2N_C where N_C is number of cells
  - The method requires implementation of Dirac-δ function approach for blocking fractures

10_1016_j_finel_2015_05_002.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Thermal field analysis of concrete with embedded cooling pipes using extended finite element method (XFEM)
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Concrete (heat conduction coefficient λ = 185.0 kJ/md°C, density ρ = 2663.0 kg/m³, specific heat capacity c = 0.943 kJ/kg°C)
  - Metal cooling pipes (radius = 0.0084m, wall thickness ≈ 2mm)
  - Water (cooling medium with variable temperature)
- **Application & Importance:** 
  - Mitigation of thermal cracks in mass concrete structures caused by temperature gradients from cement hydration heat
  - Avoidance of thermal cracking through active pipe cooling systems
  - Elimination of requirement for extremely refined conforming meshes around pipes in conventional FEM
- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - 2D cross-sectional plane normal to pipe axis
  - Single pipe case: 1.5m × 1.5m concrete square with center-embedded pipe
  - Multiple pipe case: 7×7 pipe grid with 1.5m spacing between adjacent pipes
  - Analytical model: Hollow cylinder with inner radius r₀ (pipe radius) and outer radius r_b (half distance between neighboring pipes)
  - Reference case: r_b/r₀ = 100 (e.g., r_b = 0.75m, r₀ = 0.0075m)
10_1016_j_finel_2015_05_002.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Dirichlet boundary condition on pipe wall: T = T_w(τ) on Γ_p
  - Adiabatic boundary condition on concrete edges (in single pipe verification case)
  - Robin boundary condition approximation: ∂T/∂n = β[T - T_w(τ)] on Γ_β (concrete circle with radius r_0 + Δr)
  - Initial condition: Uniform temperature field T = T_0(x) when τ = 0
  - Reference temperature at r = r_b used for enrichment function

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Internal heat source Q(τ) = ρcχ(τ) where χ(τ) = χ_0(1 - e^(-mτ))
  - Hydration heat parameters: χ_0 = 20°C, m = 0.1 (in internal heat source case)
  - Constant cooling water temperature: T_w = 4°C for 100 days (first verification case)
  - Varying cooling water temperature: T_w = 10°C for first 50 days, then 4°C for remaining 50 days
  - Multiple pipe cooling temperature: T_w(x,y,τ) = (16-0.1τ) + 0.1(y-0.75/1.5)^2 + 0.1(x-0.75/1.5)
  - Time-dependent water temperature changes in Table 5: 0-20d: 12°C, 21-40d: 10°C, 41-60d: 8°C, 61-80d: 6°C, 81-100d: 4°C

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Thermal resistance of pipe walls (≈2mm thickness) completely omitted (concrete temperature at pipe wall = water temperature)
  - Conversion parameter β = λ/(r_0·ln[(r_0+Δr)/r_0])
  - Pipe location within elements without mesh conformity requirement
  - Enrichment shape function based on radial distance from pipe center: r = ||x - x_O||

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Transient thermal analysis with implicit backward-Euler time-integration scheme (ξ = 1)
  - 2D analysis in cross-section normal to pipe axis
  - Time increment: 1 day per step in all verification cases
  - Regular regime analysis for ε ≥ 0.12 (ε = λτ/(ρcr_b²))
  - Multiple verification cases: constant cooling boundary, varying cooling boundary, internal heat source, and multiple-pipe cases
10_1016_j_finel_2015_05_002.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Transient heat conduction in concrete with internal heat source (cement hydration), modeling discontinuous temperature gradient fields around embedded cooling pipes

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Temperature field distribution in concrete domain
  - Temperature versus time curves at specified radial distances from pipes (0.05m, 0.10m, 0.20m, 0.35m, 0.50m)
  - Correlation coefficients between XFEM and conventional FEM results (ranging from 99.3% to 100.0%)
  - Relative errors between first-term analytical solution and full series solution (0.005% to 3.475% depending on ε and r_b/r_0)
  - Temperature differences at specific coordinate points (e.g., Point 1: x=2.25, y=6.85 with 0.10m radial distance to pipe 30)

- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve comparable accuracy to conventional FEM with refined conforming meshes while eliminating the requirement for mesh conformity to pipe geometry, enabling analysis with coarse meshes (e.g., 7×7 grid for multiple pipe case versus 6728 nodes in refined mesh)
10_1016_j_finel_2015_05_002.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Pipe diameter (20-40mm) must be significantly smaller than concrete structure dimensions (1-2m length)
  - Analytical model limited to hollow cylinder geometry with inner radius r₀ (pipe radius) and outer radius r_b (half distance between neighboring pipes)
  - Verification cases constrained to 1.5m × 1.5m concrete square with 0.0084m radius pipe
  - Multiple pipe case restricted to 7×7 grid with 1.5m spacing between adjacent pipes
  - Enrichment function requires radial distance calculation from pipe center (r = ||x - x_O||)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Thermal resistance of pipe walls (≈2mm thickness) completely omitted (concrete temperature at pipe wall = water temperature)
  - Temperature variation along pipe axis considered negligible compared to radial direction
  - Method validity limited to regular regime (ε ≥ 0.12) where first-term analytical solution error < 1%
  - Analytical solution approximation uses only first term of infinite series for computational efficiency
  - Method developed specifically for 2D cross-sectional analysis normal to pipe axis (3D extension noted as future work)
  - Initial temperature field must be uniform for analytical solution validity

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Conventional FEM requires extremely refined meshes conforming to pipe geometry with acceptable aspect ratios
  - Mesh generation becomes "demanding and cumbersome" due to huge difference between pipe diameter (20-40mm) and length (1-2m)
  - 3D grid-like coil pipe arrangements make meshing procedure significantly more difficult, especially for complex structures like arch dams
  - Multiple pipe arrangements make analysis "very costly in time and computable resources"
  - Conventional FEM requires mesh refinement specifically around pipe axis to capture sharp temperature gradients
  - Standard post-processing software cannot directly plot enriched element contours without sub-element division

10_1016_j_energy_2025_136161.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Pipe-type energy piled raft foundation with embedded heat exchange devices in layered transversely isotropic media. The system consists of hollow cylindrical pipe piles connected by a concrete raft, functioning as both structural foundation and geothermal heat exchanger.
- **Material / Medium:** Pipe piles (steel with Eₚ=200 GPa, αₚ=1.2×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹; concrete with Eₚ=30 GPa, αₚ=1×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹); raft (concrete with Eᵣ=Eₚ); soil (layered transversely isotropic media with Gᵥ, Eᵥ, Eₕ, μᵥ, μₕ, thermal conductivity K, thermal expansion coefficients αᵥ=2αₕ). Specific soil layers include silty clay (1.5m thick, Gᵥ=4.44 MPa, Eᵥ=11.10 MPa) and silty clay with silt (1.6m thick, Gᵥ=3.30 MPa, Eᵥ=8.25 MPa).
- **Application & Importance:** Analyzing thermo-mechanical performance to optimize foundation design and enhance energy utilization efficiency. Pipe-type energy piles provide dual functionality as structural support and heat exchangers, with hollow space facilitating heat exchange tube installation and backfill material optimization.
- **Geometry / Domain:** 3×3 square pile arrangement (10m×10m raft); pile spacing Sₚ=3.75m; pipe piles with outer diameter R₂=0.6m, inner diameter R₁=0.32m, length Lₚ=20m; raft thickness hᵣ=3R₂; layered soil domain modeled with radius=30m and depth=60m in validation cases. The system features two pile-soil boundary interfaces (inner and outer) unlike solid piles which have only one interface.

- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Bottom of raft in close contact with geotechnical media surface
  - Soil treated as continuum, neglecting space occupied by pipe piles
  - Two pile-soil boundary interfaces for pipe piles (inner and outer)
  - Soil domain with radius = 75R₂ = 30 m and depth = 3Lₚ = 60 m to simulate half-space
  - Pile node calculation depth defined as distance from center point to ground
  - Raft-soil interface modeled in "hard" contact

- **Loads / Excitations:**

  - Concentrated load of 25.97 kN at raft center
  - Temperature increments: T_p = +20 K, +10 K, 0 K, -10 K, -20 K
  - Stable temperature distribution uniformly applied along pile length
  - Uniform surface load of 60.74 kPa from foundation weight and covering soil
  - Heating (+10K) and cooling (-10K) conditions for thermal analysis

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**

  - Pipe pile-soil interface modeled as two boundary surfaces (inner and outer)
  - Simplified approximation of two pile boundary forces as single force at mid-surface (a = (R₁+R₂)/2)
  - Pile-raft-soil coupling interaction
  - Boundary forces consist of side friction and end reaction forces

  - Layered transversely isotropic soil media
  - 3D analysis of pipe-type energy piled raft foundation
  - Steady-state thermal conditions (temperature stabilization)
  - Thermo-mechanical analysis considering both thermal and mechanical loads
  - Linear elastic analysis for foundation components

10_1007_s42452_025_07158_z.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Tangentially Magnetized Reverse-Salient Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motor (TM-RSPMSM)
- **Material / Medium:** Permanent magnets (PM I, PM II, PM III), stator core, rotor core, copper windings; permanent magnet permeability similar to air
- **Application & Importance:** Electric vehicle propulsion; achieves wider constant power speed regulation range (3.6× rated speed), strong overload capacity, high efficiency at high speeds, reduced permanent magnet demagnetization risk, improved flux-weakening capability
- **Geometry / Domain:** 8-pole 18-slot fractional slot winding; stator outer diameter 190 mm, stator inner diameter 120 mm, axial length 115 mm, air-gap length 0.4 mm; rotor eccentricity design with d-axis air-gap shorter than q-axis air-gap; magnetic bridges, magnetic barriers, and segmented permanent magnets; PM thickness 4.5 mm; rated power 7.5 kW, rated speed 1000 rpm, rated voltage 380 V
10_1007_s42452_025_07158_z.key_2:

- **Loads / Excitations:** Rated voltage 380 V; rated power 7.5 kW; rated speed 1000 rpm; d-axis current (id) and q-axis current (iq) maintained constant during magnetic flux analysis; limiting voltage and limiting current maintained constant during flux-weakening analysis
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** D-axis magnetic circuit includes permanent magnet magnetic resistance (RPMI, RPMII), magnetic bridge resistance (Rcq1, Rcq2), small air-gap resistance (Rδmin), and d-axis magnetic motive force (Fd); q-axis magnetic circuit includes large air-gap resistance (Rδmax), magnetic barrier resistance (Rcz), and q-axis magnetic motive force (Fq); magnetic flux passes through magnetic bridge rather than permanent magnets when id and iq are constant
- **Simulation Type:** Finite Element Method (FEM) analysis; 2D electromagnetic field simulation; performance characterization under constant voltage and current limits; comparative analysis of multiple motor topologies (TM-RSPMSM, TM-PSPMSM, "-" type-PSPMSM, "V" type-PSPMSM, SPM motor) with identical motor rating parameters, size, and material utilization

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Direct-axis inductance (Ld), quadrature-axis inductance (Lq), reverse-salient ratio (ρ = Ld/Lq), electromagnetic torque (75.2 Nm average for TM-RSPMSM), torque ripple (3.0% for TM-RSPMSM), efficiency (92.25% at rated speed), constant power speed range (3600 rpm, 3.6× rated speed), maximum speed (5000 rpm), air-gap flux density, no-load back EMF (185 V for TM-RSPMSM), dq-axis current characteristics, power density (0.23 kW/kg), torque density (23.1 kN·m/m³)
- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve reverse-salient characteristic (Ld > Lq); maximize constant power speed range (achieved 3.6× rated speed); minimize irreversible demagnetization risk by reducing required flux-weakening current; optimize magnetic bridge length (0.75 mm), PMI thickness (4.5 mm), magnetic barrier width (1.35 mm), and magnetic barrier angle (35°) to balance electromagnetic torque, efficiency, and constant power speed range while maintaining high overload capacity and reducing torque ripple
10_1007_s42452_025_07158_z.key_4:

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Rated power constrained to 7.5 kW; rated speed constrained to 1000 rpm; rated voltage constrained to 380 V; constant power speed range limited to maximum of 3.6× rated speed (3600 rpm); maximum operational speed limited to 5000 rpm where electromagnetic torque equals no-load friction torque (3.5 Nm vs 2.86 Nm); no-load back EMF constrained to 185 V for TM-RSPMSM; reverse-salient characteristic requires Ld > Lq; d-axis resistance must be less than q-axis resistance to maintain reverse-salient characteristic; efficiency must remain above 80% in most operating states; electromagnetic torque must exceed 75.2 Nm average
