  - Adiabatic boundary conditions on lateral (short dimension) directions for 5 mm × 5 mm × 100 mm domain
  - Periodic boundary conditions on domain boundaries normal to x and y directions
  - Neumann (no-flux) boundary conditions on front and back boundaries along z direction ("empty" BCs in OpenFOAM)
  - Isothermal boundary conditions on bottom (y-) and right (x+) boundaries
  - Constrained boundary conditions on top (y+) and left (x-) boundaries
  - Imposed boundary condition at lower end (z = 0) of the ingot
  - Heat flux of 3000 W/m² applied to top boundary for t ≤ 900s to account for heat losses

- **Loads / Excitations:** 
  - Thermal gradient of G = 250 K/m in z-direction
  - Cooling rate of Ṫ = -0.1 K/s
  - Initial undercooling of ΔT = 2 K
  - Pulling velocity of v_pull = 86 µm/s for 2D case
  - Directional solidification velocity of v_pull = 100 µm/s for 3D case
  - Linear cooldown at constant cooling rate dT/dt = 10⁴ K/s
  - Nuclei seeding density of ρ_nuc = 10¹³ m⁻³
  - Nucleation undercooling with ΔT_min = 0 K, ΔT_max = 10 K, ΔT_μ = 5.19 K, and ΔT_σ = 0.25 K

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** 
  - One-way coupling: solidification solver receives phase distribution (solid, liquid, gaseous metal, ambient gas) and temperature distribution from CFD solver
  - Two-way coupling between volume-averaged finite volume solver and particle-based envelope tracking solver
  - Solid-liquid interface formed by grain envelopes located within mushy zone (liquid fraction between 0 and 1)
  - Melt flow (arrows) and evaporated metal (translucent pink shading) interaction in welding simulations

- **Simulation Type:** 
  - Three-dimensional (3D) computational domain for grain structure modeling
  - Quasi-2D thin sample for directional solidification cases
  - Quasi-two-dimensional case for melting test
  - Transient simulations with time steps as small as 0.01 s
  - Diffusive thermal field coupled with particle-based solidification model (without convection in Section 3 cases)
  - Non-iterative coupling scheme for enthalpy method
  - Laser beam welding simulations with moving heat source
10_1016_j_commatsci_2025_113918.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Grain microstructure evolution during solidification
  - Competitive growth of dendritic grains
  - Columnar-to-equiaxed transition (CET)
  - Particle-based grain envelope tracking along crystallographic directions
  - Temperature field evolution during solidification
  - Solute concentration distribution and segregation
  - Grain boundary formation and orientation
  - Melting and re-solidification of grain structures

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Temperature evolution at specific probe locations (x = 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 mm)
  - Solid fraction evolution over time
  - Grain boundary angle between competing grains
  - Number of surviving grains as a function of solidified length
  - Solute concentration maps in cross-sectional and longitudinal sections
  - Grain structure evolution in 3D cylindrical ingots (173 mm height, 70 mm diameter)
  - Grain envelope shape compared to analytical solutions
  - Orientation of grains (θ_y, θ_z) represented by color maps
  - Melt pool shape and temperature field in laser welding simulations
  - Microstructure model spatial discretization effects on grain boundary angle

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Accurate prediction of grain microstructures at macroscopic scale for solidification processes
  - Validation of the particle-based approach against analytical solutions, experimental measurements, and phase-field/CA-FE numerical results
  - Development of a computationally efficient method that requires less active tracking points (413,766 peak vs. 43×10⁶ cells in CA-FE)
  - Enable coupling with multiphysics models for realistic process simulations (e.g., laser beam welding)
  - Achieve similar accuracy to cellular automaton methods with more data- and computation-efficient implementation
  - Predict columnar-to-equiaxed transition height in ingot casting (targeting ≈108-118 mm in Al-7wt.%Si experiments)
10_1016_j_commatsci_2025_113918.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Unidirectional solidification domain: 5 mm × 5 mm × 100 mm with adiabatic lateral boundaries
  - Cylindrical ingot dimensions: 173 mm height and 70 mm diameter for Al-7wt.%Si simulations
  - Laser welding simulation uses 2 mm thick 316L stainless steel sheet
  - Lateral dimensions of 768 μm for solid-liquid interface simulations at G = 10 K/mm and 100 K/mm
  - Microstructural length scale λ₀ must be ≥ secondary dendrite arm spacing (SDAS) for convergence
  - Peak active tracking points limited to 413,766 in simulations (vs. 43×10⁶ cells in CA-FE approach)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Model limited to stationary grains (excludes floatation or sedimentation of grains)
  - Kinetic undercooling not considered (focus on moderate cooling rates with growth velocity ≪ 1 m/s)
  - Dendrites assumed to grow perfectly aligned with <100> crystallographic directions
  - Melting assumed to result in well-mixed interdendritic liquid
  - Local undercooling estimated with respect to local solute concentration
  - Cannot capture detailed mechanisms of dendrite impingement at converging grain boundaries
  - Simplified (nearly linear) grain boundary morphology due to lack of explicit dendritic branch resolution
  - Model does not account for fluid flow effects on grain structure in certain validation cases

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - λ₀ ≤ 48 μm needed for reasonable convergence (vs. experimentally measured SDAS λ₂ = 8.4 ± 0.4 μm)
  - Grid element size Δx must be small compared to primary dendrite arm spacing for detailed results
  - Computational time of ~80 hours for coupled laser welding simulation on 8 CPU cores
  - Discrepancies with experiments attributed to excluded effects: sedimentation, fragmentation, shrinkage, and macrosegregation driven by fluid flow
  - Uncertainty in grain boundary angle measurement of ±1° to ±2° for coarser grids (λ₀ > 55 μm)
  - One-way coupling used in welding application (CFD to solidification solver only), rather than full two-way coupling
  - Non-iterative coupling scheme used for enthalpy method, leading to small oscillations near liquidus/eutectic temperatures

- **Material / Medium:** Carbon Fiber Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) with properties: E₁=106.33 GPa, E₂=E₃=28.44 GPa, G₁₂=G₃₁=11.02 GPa, G₂₃=39 GPa, μ₁₂=μ₁₃=0.306, μ₂₃=0.1, S₁ₜ=2640.76 MPa, S₁c=1122.1 MPa, S₂ₜ=S₃ₜ=78.3 MPa, S₂c=S₃c=164.4 MPa, S₁₂=S₁₃=88.6 MPa, S₂₃=61.9 MPa, density=1750 kg/m³
- **Application & Importance:** Failure mechanism analysis under service conditions (300 km/h on 100 km straight track) to provide design guidance for lightweight bogie frames that reduce energy consumption and improve train efficiency
- **Geometry / Domain:** Bogie frame comprising two weathering steel cross beams and two CFRP side beams with curved geometry; ply thickness=0.5 mm; stacking sequence [45°/-45°/0°/90°/0°/90°/0°/-45°/45°]; mesh size=10 mm (in-plane); failures concentrated in curved side beam regions (FM3/FM4) and near primary suspension connections (FM5)
10_1016_j_engfailanal_2025_109701.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Element thickness direction set to single CFRP ply thickness (0.5 mm); 100 km straight track with no curved track conditions, superelevation, or additional variations; connection points P1 and P2 defined as primary suspension connection points on bogie frame; bogie frame consists of two weathering steel cross beams and two CFRP side beams
- **Loads / Excitations:** Track irregularity characterized by power spectral density function S(f) = Ã/f^k where Ã = 3.9488 × 10^-4 and k = 3.4516; constant train speed of 300 km/h; dynamic wheel-rail forces transmitted through primary suspension to bogie frame
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Car body connected to bogie frame via secondary suspension (stiffness: 160/160/240 kN/m; damping: 0/40/20 kNs/m along x/y/z axes); wheelsets connected to bogie frame via primary suspension (stiffness: 980/980/1176 kN/m; damping: 0/0/10 kNs/m along x/y/z axes); rigid-flexible coupling between car body/wheelsets (rigid) and bogie frame (flexible)
- **Simulation Type:** Transient 3D rigid-flexible coupled vehicle model; progressive fatigue damage analysis with real-time updates of material properties; hexahedral 8-node element meshing with 10 mm in-plane element size; generalized α method for time integration; Newton-Raphson method for solving equations; 100 km track distance simulation at 300 km/h constant speed
10_1016_j_engfailanal_2025_109701.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Rigid-flexible coupled dynamics of high-speed train system with progressive fatigue damage analysis of CFRP bogie frame; stress distribution calculation using geometric and constitutive equations; stiffness and strength degradation based on gradual and sudden damage mechanisms; failure mode identification using 3D Hashin criteria
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Vertical displacement of bogie frame centroid; mesh convergence results at critical points P1 and P2; failure elements with corresponding failure modes (FM1-FM7); reduction percentages of stiffness parameters (E₁₁, E₂₂, E₃₃, E₁₂, E₂₃); reduction percentages of strength parameters (S₂ₜ, S₂c, S₃ₜ); critical failure distances (l̄_failure); residual percentages of material parameters during service; MAE = 1.5×10⁻⁵ and RMSE = 4.5×10⁻⁵ for model validation; three primary failure modes with specific trigger thresholds
- **Optimization Goal:** Develop damage-tolerant CFRP bogie frame designs through practical guidance including: incorporating symmetric ±45° ply orientations in shear-critical regions (curved side beams) to enhance shear stiffness and delay matrix-dominated failure; applying localized reinforcements (interlayer resin) near suspension areas to mitigate delamination risk; providing foundation for fatigue prediction and optimization of CFRP bogie frames in high-speed rail applications
10_1016_j_engfailanal_2025_109701.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Single CFRP ply thickness constrained to 0.5 mm; in-plane mesh size constrained to 10 mm for computational efficiency; fixed stacking sequence [45°/-45°/0°/90°/0°/90°/0°/-45°/45°]; analysis limited to 100 km straight track with no curved track conditions or superelevation; curved regions of side beams identified as shear-critical areas
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Element considered completely failed when stiffness/strength degrades to 0.01 times initial values; FM3 triggered at 46%-48% reduction in E₁₂; FM4 triggered at 21%-23% reduction in E₁₂; FM5 triggered at 85%-87% reduction in interlaminar tensile strength S₃ₜ; train speed constrained to constant 300 km/h; track irregularity characterized by specific PSD function (Ã = 3.9488 × 10⁻⁴, k = 3.4516)
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Hexahedral 8-node element meshing required for CFRP side beam; stacking configuration provided by CRRC Group Co., Ltd. to ensure balanced mechanical performance; only symmetric ply orientations considered in analysis; no manufacturing defects or process variations included in model; no temperature effects or environmental degradation factors incorporated in current analysis

10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_119996.key_1:

- Aluminum alloy Al6061-O material with density ρ = 2700 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3, elastic modulus E = 68.5 GPa, initial yield stress σy = 94.2 MPa, ultimate strength σu = 194.8 MPa
- Thin-walled tube height L = 200 mm with inner and outer polygons inscribed in circles of diameters 150 mm and 75 mm
- Cross-sectional configurations: quadrilateral (QT), hexagonal (HT), octagonal (OT) traditional multi-cell tubes; biomimetic variants with forward (F), reverse (R), balanced (B) configurations (B-QF/B-QR/B-QB, B-HF/B-HR/B-HB, B-OF/B-OR/B-OB)
- Diamond angle α = 60°, circumferential radius R = 75 mm, ratio coefficient λ = 0.6 (forward/reverse), λ = 0.5 (balanced)
- Equal mass design with total mass = 0.369 kg, B-QF wall thickness t0 = 0.4 mm
- Loading conditions: impact velocity V = 10 m/s, impact mass = 500 kg, loading angles θ = 0°, 10°, 20°, 30°, compression distance = 120 mm
- Crashworthiness metrics: Specific Energy Absorption (SEA) in kJ/kg, Mean Crushing Force (MCF) in kN, Peak Crushing Force (PCF) in kN, Crushing Force Efficiency (CFE) in percentage
- Dynamic enhancement coefficient k = 1.55 (B-QB), 1.60 (B-HB), 1.4 (B-OB) for theoretical mean crushing force prediction
- Finite element model with grid size 1.5 mm, dynamic/static friction coefficients 0.2/0.3
- Theoretical model based on Simplified Super Folding Element (SSFE) theory with effective compression distance coefficient η = 0.73

- Rigid body modeling for mobile and fixed walls

- Aluminum alloy Al6061-O material properties: density ρ = 2700 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3, elastic modulus E = 68.5 GPa, yield stress σy = 94.2 MPa, ultimate strength σu = 194.8 MPa

10_1016_j_engstruct_2022_114993.key_1:
- Marine concrete filled CFRP-aluminum alloy tube columns (CFRP-CFAT) under axial compression
- Marine concrete (28-day compressive strength 49.5 MPa, characteristic strength f_ck 37.9 MPa); aluminum alloy (150 mm outer diameter, 3 mm thickness, 600 mm height, yield strength 190.0 MPa, ultimate strength 217.3 MPa, elastic modulus 69.8 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.3); CFRP (ultimate tensile strength 3667.5 MPa, elastic modulus 240 GPa, thickness 0.167 mm); epoxy resin adhesive (ultimate tensile strength 48.5 MPa, elastic modulus 3200 MPa)
- Marine infrastructure development requiring durable structural components resistant to chloride corrosion while maintaining high load-bearing capacity; addresses ecological concerns of using seawater and sea sand instead of fresh water and river sand
- Cylindrical geometry (600 mm height, 150 mm outer diameter); cross-section consists of marine concrete core surrounded by aluminum alloy tube with optional CFRP layers on inner and/or outer surfaces; multiple configurations tested with 0-2 outer CFRP layers and 0-1 inner CFRP layers
10_1016_j_engstruct_2022_114993.key_2:
- Boundary conditions: Top steel ring constrained with U1=U2=U3=0, UR1=UR2=UR3=0; Bottom steel ring constrained with U1=U2=0, UR1=UR2=UR3=0 (longitudinal displacement freedom released)
- Loading method: Displacement-control mode with loading rate of 2 mm/min
- Termination condition: Test terminated when axial displacement reached 5% of specimen height (30 mm)
- Contact interactions: "Tie" contact between aluminum alloy tubes and CFRP; "Surface-to-surface contact" between aluminum alloy tubes and concrete for specimens without inner CFRP; "Surface-to-surface contact" between CFRP and concrete for specimens with inner CFRP
- Contact behavior: "Hard contact" for normal direction, "penalty" for tangential direction with friction coefficient of 0.25
- Preloading: Specimens preloaded and unloaded until load reached 100 kN before testing
- Analysis step: "Dynamic, Explicit" in ABAQUS
- Element types: C3D8R for confined concrete and aluminum alloy tube, S4R for CFRP
- Instrumentation: Two LVDTs on both sides of specimen to measure axial displacement; circular and longitudinal strain gauges at middle height of aluminum alloy tube and CFRP
- End condition: Pair of steel clamps set to prevent end failure
- Mesh size: D/10 (diameter divided by 10)
10_1016_j_engstruct_2022_114993.key_3:
- Axial compression behavior of marine concrete filled CFRP-aluminum alloy tube columns including stress-strain response, failure mechanisms, confinement effects, and material interactions
- Ultimate bearing capacity (N_u), load-displacement curves, strain development (ε_h, ε_v), Poisson's ratio (ν), energy absorption capacity (W), damage field variable (D), confinement factors (ξ_a, ξ_f,i, ξ_f,o), increase coefficient of bearing capacity (η_cap,o, η_cap,i)
- Quantify enhancement of ultimate bearing capacity (up to 60.0%) and energy absorption capacity (up to 37.3%) through CFRP confinement; develop accurate calculation model for ultimate bearing capacity that accounts for different CFRP pasting positions (inner vs. outer) with minimal deviation from experimental results
10_1016_j_engstruct_2022_114993.key_4:
- Geometric constraints: Specimens maintained fixed dimensions of 600 mm height and 150 mm outer diameter; aluminum alloy tubes had fixed 3 mm thickness; diameter-thickness ratio (D/t) limited to 30-60 in parametric study; circular cross-section geometry only; maximum axial displacement termination point set at 5% of specimen height (30 mm)
- Performance limits: Relative deviation of ultimate load data capped at 15% for representative curve calculation; aluminum alloy yield strength constrained at 190.0 MPa; concrete characteristic strength limited to 37.9 MPa; CFRP tensile strength fixed at 3667.5 MPa; test termination condition when longitudinal displacement reached 30 mm (5% of height)
- Manufacturing constraints: Aluminum alloy tubes cut from same batch; inner CFRP pasting required specific sequence (ethanol cleaning, adhesive application, steel tube assistance); epoxy resin adhesive properties fixed (48.5 MPa tensile strength, 3200 MPa modulus); only 18 specimens (6 groups of 3) manufactured to eliminate dispersion; loading rate fixed at 2 mm/min; preloading to 100 kN before testing; test terminated when cracks appeared or displacement reached 5% height

10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120155.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** DTU 10-MW offshore wind turbine blade structural model, specifically focusing on trailing edge buckling analysis
- **Material / Medium:** Sandwich glass fiber-reinforced composites with balsa wood core; uniaxial ply properties: E₁=41.63 GPa, E₂=14.93 GPa, G₁₂=5.047 GPa, ν₁₂=0.241, ρ=1915.5 kg/m³; balsa wood properties: E₃=2.730 GPa (axial), E₁=E₂=0.050 GPa, G₁₃=G₂₃=0.150 GPa, ρ=110 kg/m³
- **Application & Importance:** Analysis of trailing edge buckling failure mechanisms in large wind turbine blades to improve design optimization frameworks; verification of geometrically nonlinear beam models against shell models for structural assessment; evaluation of linear vs. nonlinear buckling analysis methodologies
- **Geometry / Domain:** Cantilever beam structure with box girder configuration, two main shear webs and aft web from first quarter to tip; shell model contains ~35,000 elements and 104,000 nodes; beam model meshed with 101 nodes and 50 quadratic elements; blade exhibits large deformations at service loads with trailing edge buckling as primary failure mechanism
10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120155.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Cantilever beam fixed at blade root; kinematic coupling constraints applied to spar cap nodes in shell model; volume-proportional damping coefficient of 1×10⁻⁴ in ABAQUS automatic stabilization; blade root clamped boundary condition; no blade pre-bending initially included in models (added posteriorly)
- **Loads / Excitations:** 12 combined flapwise and edgewise bending load cases; pointwise forces applied across axes' nodes at sections' semi-chords; distributed uniform loads ranging from 7.0 kN/m (design) to 41.7 kN/m (extreme); Pressure side Towards Suction side (PTS) and Leading edge Towards Trailing edge (LTT) certification load cases; extreme load levels up to 610% of design loads; edgewise gravity effects
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Shell model uses 8-node layered shell elements (S8R) with 20-node hexahedra (C3D20) for trailing edge adhesive connection; spar cap nodes coupled to reference nodes; cross-sections defined by twist vector (t) and bending vector (b); director vectors defined at shear webs to account for local deformations; equivalent cross-sections created in shell model to match beam model
- **Simulation Type:** Quasi-static nonlinear structural analysis; geometrically nonlinear finite element analysis; modal vibration analyses; nonlinear static equilibrium path analysis; linear eigenvalue buckling analysis; vibration method for stability analysis; 3D shell modeling; geometrically exact Timoshenko beam modeling; nonlinear buckling strength assessment
10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120155.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Geometrically nonlinear structural behavior of composite wind turbine blades; buckling phenomena (particularly trailing edge buckling); vibration characteristics; stress distribution; load-deflection relationships; mode interaction; imperfection sensitivity; nonlinear stability analysis
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Natural frequencies (eigenfrequencies) of first six vibration modes; displacements (u_x, u_y, u_z) at control section (z=80.5 m); rotations (bend, twist) at control section; maximum/minimum principal stresses; out-of-plane stress (σ_33) and σ_33/σ_max ratio; tangent stiffness (K_T = Δq_x/Δu_x); non-dimensional eigenvalues (β = ω²/ω₀²); critical buckling load (P_crit = 12.69 kN/m for perfect model); load-deflection curves; local sectional deformations; vibration mode shapes; displacement deviations between beam and shell models
- **Optimization Goal:** Verify geometrically exact beam model against shell model for offshore-sized blades; demonstrate vibration method effectiveness for nonlinear buckling strength assessment; establish that nonlinear methods provide more accurate buckling predictions than linear eigenvalue analysis; validate that beam models are sufficient for global behavior but shell models are required for local phenomena like trailing edge buckling; quantify the 25.9% buckling load reduction in imperfect structures (P_crit^ξ = 9.41 kN/m) compared to perfect model (P_crit = 12.69 kN/m)
10_1016_j_engstruct_2025_120155.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Control section fixed at z = 80.5 m for displacement and rotation assessments; beam model meshed with 101 nodes and 50 quadratic elements; shell model contains ~35,000 elements and 104,000 nodes; geometric imperfection magnitude of ξ = 8.75 mm (1/400 of critical buckle wavelength) applied to imperfect structure
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Critical buckling load for perfect model at P_crit = 12.69 kN/m (85% of extreme load); imperfect model buckling load at P_crit^ξ = 9.41 kN/m (25.9% lower than perfect model); nonlinearity onset observed at approximately 85% of extreme load level; partial safety factors lower than γ_MD = 2.042 reported in turbine definition report; linear eigenvalue buckling overestimates critical loads for shell structures
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Manufacturing imperfections inevitable during mold preparation, composite layup, curing, or bonding; beam model lacks adhesive trailing edge bond modeling present in shell model; difficulties in identifying corresponding vibration mode shapes along equilibrium path, especially when local modes couple with other modes; bend-twist coupling modeling limitations in beam compared to shell; 1/400 of critical buckle wavelength used as imperfection scaling factor per certification standards

10_1016_j_finel_2019_103348.key_1:
- Free-surface incompressible fluid flow problems
- Incompressible Newtonian fluid with density ρ = 1000.0 kg/m³ (square tank), ρ = 1.0 kg/m³ (sloshing), ρ = 1000 kg/m³ (wave propagation)
- Dynamic viscosity μ = 0.01 N·s (square tank, sloshing), μ = 1 Pa·s (wave propagation)
- Gravity acceleration g = 10.0 m/s² (square tank), g = 9.81 m/s² (wave propagation)
- Square tank geometry: 1.0 m width × 1.0 m height
- Sloshing container: 1.0 m width, 1.0 m fluid height at rest, wave amplitude a = 0.01 m
- Dam break initial conditions: H₀ = 0.7 m fluid height, L₀ = 0.35 m width
- Wave propagation domain: d = 10 m depth, H = 2 m initial wave height, L = 80 m length
- Boundary conditions: slip walls, free surface with zero traction, no-slip walls
- Time step Δt = 0.01 s (square tank), Δt = 0.05 s (sloshing), Δt = 0.005 s (dam break), Δt = 0.001 s (wave propagation)
- Newmark parameters: β = 0.25, γ = 0.5 for time integration
- Pressure stabilization parameter α = 0.001 for dynamic contribution scaling
- Mesh configurations: structured 10×10, 100×100, and unstructured 10×10 element discretizations
- Fluid domain deformation tracked using total Lagrangian description with position as primary variable
- Maximum pressure values: 115.33 Pa (t=0.0 s), 134.46 Pa (t=7.61 s), 132.61 Pa (t=22.83 s)
- Velocity magnitude range: 0.00-1.98 m/s at t=0.0 s, 0.00-0.12 m/s at later time steps
- Wave run-up height R = 14.25 m for solitary wave propagation case
10_1016_j_finel_2019_103348.key_2:
- Slip wall boundary conditions applied to container walls
- Free surface with zero traction boundary condition
- No-slip wall conditions enforced by setting position correction to zero (Δyₐ = 0)
- Slip wall conditions enforced by setting only normal component of position correction to zero: (n·Δyₐ)n = 0
- Initial fluid at rest condition for dam break problem
- Gravity acceleration g = 10.0 m/s² acting downward (square tank)
- Gravity acceleration g = 1.0 m/s² (dam break)
- Gravity acceleration g = 9.81 m/s² acting downward (wave propagation)
- Initial free surface shape for sloshing: η(x₁,0) = a sin(π/b x₁) + h with a = 0.01 m, b = 1.0 m, h = 1.0 m
- Initial velocity conditions for wave propagation: ẋ₁ = √(gd)(H/d)sech²[x₁√(3H/(4d³))], ẋ₂ = 3√(gd)(H/d)^(3/2)(x₂/d)sech²[x₁√(3H/(4d³))]tanh[x₁√(3H/(4d³))]
- Dam break initial geometry: H₀ = 0.7 m fluid height, L₀ = 0.35 m width
- Wave propagation initial geometry: d = 10 m depth, H = 2 m initial wave height, L = 80 m length
- Total Lagrangian description for fluid domain
- Transient analysis with time steps: Δt = 0.01 s (square tank), Δt = 0.05 s (sloshing), Δt = 0.005 s (dam break), Δt = 0.001 s (wave propagation)
- 2D planar analysis for all examples
- Nonlinear problems with finite deformations
- Static analysis for square water tank example
- Dynamic analysis for sloshing, dam break, and wave propagation examples
- Equal-order mixed finite elements with pressure stabilizing Petrov-Galerkin technique
- Newmark-β time integration with parameters β = 0.25, γ = 0.5
10_1016_j_finel_2019_103348.key_3:
- Free-surface incompressible Newtonian fluid flow under total Lagrangian description
- Pressure field distribution (Pa) in fluid domain
- Velocity magnitude and direction (m/s) throughout fluid domain
- Free surface height/position over time (m)
- Fluid domain deformation ratio (L/L₀)
- Volume conservation (V/V₀)
- Wave run-up height (m)
- Position and pressure correction vectors during Newton-Raphson iterations
- Convergence metrics: ||e||_L2 (relative error over fluid domain), ||e_a||_2 (position error at specific nodes)
- Maximum horizontal fluid domain dimension (L/L₀) vs. non-dimensional time (t*)
- Pressure at bottom left corner and free-surface center
- Euclidean norm of position and pressure correction vectors vs. accumulated iterations
- Stable pressure field without spurious oscillations
- Accurate free surface tracking with finite deformations
- Quadratic convergence in spatial and temporal discretization
- Volume conservation within 10⁻⁵ error
- Agreement with experimental results (Martin and Moyce), numerical solutions (Nithiarasu), and theoretical solutions (Byatt-Smith)
10_1016_j_finel_2019_103348.key_4:
- Total Lagrangian description limited to problems where initial mesh can accommodate all deformations without remeshing
- Ladyzhenskaya-Babuška-Brezzi (LBB) conditions must be satisfied for stable pressure solutions when using mixed finite elements
- Equal-order interpolation of positions and pressure requires pressure stabilizing Petrov-Galerkin (PSPG) technique to avoid spurious oscillations
- Newmark-β time integration parameters constrained: β = 0.25 and γ = 0.5 with α < 1 required for stable pressure field (α = 0.001 used in validation cases)
- Time step size constrained by convergence requirements (e.g., Δt = 0.0005 s used as reference solution for sloshing problem)
- Mesh dependence requiring careful selection of discretization pattern (structured vs. unstructured) to avoid pressure oscillations
- Computational cost limitations demonstrated by mesh sizes: 34-273 nodes (dam break), 2207 nodes/4072 elements (wave propagation)
- Volume conservation constrained to 10⁻⁵ maximum variation as shown in dam break analysis
- Spatial discretization must achieve quadratic convergence as demonstrated in convergence studies
- Pressure stabilization parameter τ_PSPG must be calculated with dimensional consistency for position-based problems
- Dynamic contribution to pressure stabilization must be scaled (α < 1) to avoid oscillatory pressure behavior while maintaining second-order time integration accuracy

10_1016_j_jcp_2025_113976.key_1:
- Identity & Domain: Brain tumor growth model for glioblastoma, specifically a reaction-diffusion system constrained by partial differential equations
- Material / Medium: Brain tissue (gray matter and white matter regions); tumor volume fraction u(x,t) ∈ [0,1]; diffusion parameter D with log(D_gm) = -0.9937 and log(D_wm) = -0.3006; growth rate parameter G as log-normal random field log(G) = m ~ N(m_prior, C_prior) with Matérn covariance C_prior = (-γΔ + δI)^(-2)
- Application & Importance: Optimal MRI imaging time point selection for monitoring tumor growth; addresses clinical need to identify most informative time points for MRI acquisition to balance diagnostic value against time/cost constraints
- Geometry / Domain: 2D brain domain extracted from rat T2-weighted MRI slice with 14,003 FEM degrees of freedom; homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions; time domain T = 10 days with Δt = 0.1 (K = 100 time steps)
10_1016_j_jcp_2025_113976.key_2:
- Boundaries & Constraints: Homogeneous Neumann boundary condition (D∇u⋅n = 0 on ∂Ω×(0,T]); Initial condition u(x,0) = u₀ (tumor implantation at t=0); Tumor volume fraction constraint u(x,t) ∈ [0,1]; Brain domain Ω is a 2D slice extracted from rat T2-weighted MRI image
- Loads / Excitations: Nonlinear reaction term G(1-u)u representing tumor growth; Diffusion parameter D constant within regions (log(D_gm) = -0.9937, log(D_wm) = -0.3006); Growth rate G as log-normal random field; Time domain T = 10 days with uniform time step Δt = 0.1 (K = 100 time steps)
- Interactions / Interfaces: Distinct gray matter and white matter regions with different diffusion characteristics; Parameter D constant within each region; Spatial correlation lengths for G: ρ_gm = 6.0 mm, ρ_wm = 12.0 mm
- Simulation Type: Transient 2D simulation; Nonlinear reaction-diffusion PDE; FEM with piecewise linear finite elements (14,003 degrees of freedom); Implicit time stepping; Matérn covariance operator C_prior = (-γΔ + δI)^(-2) with γ = ρ/(4√(2π)σ) and δ = 2/(σρ√π)
10_1016_j_jcp_2025_113976.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Reaction-diffusion dynamics of tumor volume fraction; Bayesian inference for parameter estimation in infinite-dimensional space; Sequential experimental design for parameter uncertainty quantification
- Target Outputs (Metrics): Tumor volume fraction u(x,t) ∈ [0,1]; MAP (Maximum a Posteriori) points; Eigenvalues of generalized eigenvalue problem; Pointwise standard deviation of parameter field; Conditional Expected Information Gain (cEIG); Relative errors for PtO map (8.05% peak on day 1, decreasing to 2.27% by day 10) and reduced Jacobian (4.05% to 1.57%); Computational speed-up metrics (180× amortized total speed-up)
- Optimization Goal: Select 4 optimal observation times from 10 days to maximize cumulative information gain; Minimize parameter uncertainty in tumor growth model; Achieve adaptive global optimality in experimental design with terminal formulation of optimality criterion

10_1007_s40997_024_00825_3.key_1:
- Bulge formed joint (free-form surface thin-wall structure for truss systems)
- Steel pipe construction (inferred from "steel pipe truss systems" context)
- Optimized for enhanced aesthetic appearance (smoothness) and increased bearing capacity of truss structures
- Consists of convex hull generated by semi-cylinder deformation
- Global parameters: length Lb (0.85 m), radius Rb (0.226 m), spread angle θb (140°)
- Local parameters: convex hull height Hb (0.05 m), convex hull length ratio Tb1 (0.62), transition region ratio Tb2 (0.2), center position (u,v) (0.5,0.5)
- Semi-cylindrical surface fixed to fit with string bars, convex hull connects to belly bars
- T-type and K-type configurations with multiple load application points

10_1007_s40430_025_05666_y.key_1:
- Orthogonal Staggered Star Honeycomb (OSSH) structure, a 3D auxetic metamaterial with negative Poisson's ratio properties
- Acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) material with density 1040 kg/m³, Young's modulus 1830 MPa, yield strength 50 MPa, and Poisson's ratio 0.394
- Designed to overcome limitations of traditional Star-Shaped Honeycomb (SSH) structures, providing enhanced mechanical properties for aerospace, automotive, and impact-resistant applications
- Geometric parameters include transverse beam length l₁ (2.73-4.92 mm range), longitudinal beam length l₂ (4.74-6.85 mm range), beam thickness t (1.0-2.5 mm), lateral angle θ₁ (15°-35°), vertical angle θ₂ (15°-35°), and connecting axis width b
- Staggered (orthogonal) stacking configuration rather than beam-to-beam connection, improving structural stability under compression
- Unit cell exhibits negative Poisson's ratio effect, contracting toward the middle area under compression in the elastic stage
- Relative density ranges from approximately 0.15 to 0.45 depending on geometric parameters
- Equivalent Young's modulus ranges from approximately 10 MPa to 90 MPa depending on geometric parameters
- 3D printed samples with dimensions including 42.0 mm height and base dimensions varying from 29.5 mm to 45.5 mm
- Quasi-static compression tests performed at 1 mm/min displacement rate using MTS-300 universal material testing machine
- Structure maintains stability during compression due to inward contraction characteristic of auxetic structures
- Equivalent Young's modulus decreases with increasing l₁ and θ₂, increases with increasing l₂, θ₁, and t
- Equivalent Poisson's ratio absolute value decreases with increasing l₁, increases with increasing l₂ and θ₁, and shows parabolic variation with θ₂
- Relative density positively correlates with equivalent Young's modulus for length and thickness parameters, but not for angle parameters
- OSSH structure exhibits prolonged stress plateau in stress-strain curves, indicating energy absorption potential
10_1007_s40430_025_05666_y.key_2:

10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_119154.key_1:

- 3D printed steel tube specimens with particle size range 15-53 µm
- System characterized by length L, width W, height H, layer number Nₗ, tube number Nₜ
- Tube parameters: unit number n, wall thickness t, maximal external diameter D, minimal external diameter d, unit length l
- Vertical section contour consists of circular arcs with radius R and central angle α
- Geometric relationships: L = W = nl, l = 4R sin α, D - d = 4R(1 - cos α), with l ≈ D
- Parameter ranges studied: d/D = 0.5-0.65, l/D = 1-1.15, t/D = 1.5%-3.5%
- Designed for crashworthiness applications with specific energy absorption exceeding 12.9 J/g and efficiency exceeding 47%
- System dimensions in experiments: H = 87.9 mm, L = W = 80-83.2 mm, Nₜ = 14-28, Nₗ = 7
- Single sphere diameter D = 20 mm in theoretical analysis
- Bamboo-inspired system shows four deformation phases: interspace squeezing, global deforming, snap-through, and densifying
- Self-locking capability with stable deformation mode under loads up to 50 m/s velocity
- Designed to avoid sharp impact peaks while maintaining structural integrity during energy absorption

10_1016_j_aiepr_2024_05_002.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Fiber-reinforced topology optimization (FRTO) for advanced polymer composites using automated manufacturing techniques, specifically addressing concurrent and sequential optimization of structural topology and fiber reinforcement path design
- **Material / Medium:** Carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites with thermoplastic matrix; fiber content typically ~30% for MEX systems; anisotropic material properties dependent on fiber orientation; continuous carbon fiber bundles with controlled tension during placement
- **Application & Importance:** Minimizing material consumption while maximizing strength-to-weight ratio; enabling complex geometries unattainable with conventional manufacturing; optimizing fiber placement to align with principal stress directions; addressing design freedom limitations in automated fiber placement (AFP), automated tape placement (ATP), and material extrusion (MEX) systems
- **Geometry / Domain:** Predefined design space with boundary conditions; benchmark geometries include MBB structure, cantilever beam, L-shear structure, Michell-truss, and Kirsch geometry; optimization domain features void regions and material regions with varying fiber orientation; fiber paths follow curvilinear trajectories along structural load paths with minimum bending radius constraints
10_1016_j_aiepr_2024_05_002.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Fixed support (clamped boundary) on left side of cantilever beam; Force application point at L/2 from fixed end; Minimum bending radius constraint for fiber bundles; Minimum cutting length constraint for fibers; Nozzle size control integrated into optimization process; Boundary fitting constraint for medial axis extraction; Filter radius constraint applied to orientation vector fields; Manufacturing constraints including closest proximity of reinforcement placement and support material requirements
- **Loads / Excitations:** Applied force (F) on right side of cantilever beam; Bending load case for MBB structure; Shear and bending load cases for cantilever beam and L-shear structures; Compression load case for Michell-truss; Tension load case for Kirsch geometry; Multi-directional force application in structural examples; Load path directions as input for reinforcement orientation
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Filter interaction between topology and morphology optimization phases; Medial axis extraction process connecting geometric boundaries to reinforcement paths; Material orientation field interaction with fiber path planning; Neural network representation enabling simultaneous optimization of matrix topology, fiber density, and fiber orientation; Filter application to orientation vector fields to remove numerical errors; Integration of nozzle size control with path planning; Interaction between collimated fiber band and mold surface in AFP/ATP systems
- **Simulation Type:** Iterative optimization process with convergence criteria; Concurrent optimization of material density (ρi) and orientation (θi); Sequential optimization approach where topology and morphology are optimized separately; 2D planar geometry optimization; 2.5D extruded profile optimization; 3D spatial geometry optimization; Finite Element Analysis (FEA) integration with optimization process; Benchmark environments including MBB structure, cantilever beam, L-shear, Michell-truss, and Kirsch geometries
10_1016_j_aiepr_2024_05_002.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Structural mechanics with anisotropic material behavior; finite element analysis for stress/strain distribution; principal stress field calculation; load path determination; fiber orientation optimization; topology optimization with material density distribution
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Strength-to-weight ratio; structural stiffness; compliance; strain energy distribution; principal stress directions; material density distribution (ρi); material orientation angles (θi); fiber path trajectories; volume fraction of material; load path directions; matrix density; fiber density; fiber orientation fields
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize strength-to-weight ratio; minimize structural compliance; align fiber reinforcement with principal stress directions; optimize fiber path continuity while satisfying manufacturing constraints (minimum bending radius, minimum cutting length); maximize structural stiffness with minimal material usage; achieve continuous reinforcement paths for automated manufacturing; optimize both topology (geometrical structure) and morphology (reinforcement structure) simultaneously or sequentially
10_1016_j_aiepr_2024_05_002.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Minimum bending radius constraint for fiber bundles; Minimum cutting length for fibers; Closest proximity constraint for reinforcement placement; Filter radius applied to orientation vector fields; Nozzle size control integrated into optimization process; Micro-scale unit cell edge size constraints (a₁, a₂); Cell orientation constraints (θ); Requirement for continuous fiber paths; Transformation of closed loops into continuous paths; Adaptive width selection for segmented central axis; Elimination of fibers shorter than minimum cutting length
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Strength-to-weight ratio maximization; Structural stiffness maximization; Compliance minimization; Principal stress direction alignment; Separation of tensile and compressive stress components; Multi-load condition optimization for enhanced robustness; Strain energy distribution optimization; Load path direction optimization; Volume fraction constraints on material distribution
- **Process/Manufacturing:** MEX systems limited to planar reinforcement placement; AFP/ATP systems have higher spatial freedom due to increased robotic arm degrees of freedom; Fiber content limited to ~30% in MEX due to two-step impregnation process; Support material requirements; Total number of reinforcement cuts limitation; Co-extrusion mechanism limitations in MEX systems; Prepreg tapes/tows used in AFP/ATP systems; Manufacturing constraints integrated into optimization (minimum bending radius, minimum cutting length); Requirement for continuous paths in automated fiber placing processes; Porosity constraints (typically ~10% due to lack of consolidation step in MEX)

10_1007_s40430_022_03544_5.key_1:

10_1016_j_cma_2024_117503.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Coated structure topology optimization for additive manufacturing (AM) processes, with focus on modeling material heterogeneity between surface/perimeter regions and interior/infill regions in both metal (powder bed fusion) and polymer (fused filament fabrication) AM processes
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Metal AM: Ti-6Al-4V with directional microstructure (columnar grains in bulk, different grain structures in surface regions from contour beam pass)
  - Polymer AM: PLA and ABS with orthotropic properties (coating region: isotropic E=3765.08 MPa; bulk region: Ex=1694.285 MPa, Ey=55.43 MPa, Gxy=144.275 MPa at 50% infill density)
  - Two distinct material regions: coating material (surface/perimeter) and bulk material (interior/infill)
- **Application & Importance:** Addressing the performance mismatch between topology optimization predictions and actual AM-fabricated parts by integrating AM process-induced material anisotropy and heterogeneity into the optimization framework, improving correlation between simulated and as-built mechanical performance
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Multiple test cases: 2D MBB beam, curved beam, serpentine beam, and 3D cantilever beam
  - Optimized structures feature distinct coating (red) and bulk (blue) regions where coating forms a shell around bulk material
  - Filter radii (R₁, R₂) control coating thickness (e.g., R₁=0.15, R₂=0.03-0.08 in various cases)
  - 3D designs show characteristic features like walls merging at loading regions or I-beam cross-sections depending on material directionality
10_1016_j_cma_2024_117503.key_2:

  - Prescribed volume fraction limits (v̄): 0.4 (MBB beam), 0.3 (curved beam), 0.2 (3D cantilever case c), 0.1 (partial constraint case)
  - Filter radii constraints: R₁ = 0.15, R₂ = 0.04; R₁ = 0.15, R₂ = 0.08; R₁ = 0.15, R₂ = 0.03; R₁ = 0.1, R₂ = 0.02

  - Force applied at center of specimen top surface during three-point bending tests

  - Distinct coating region (perimeter/surface) and bulk region (interior/infill) with different material properties

  - Contour beam pass vs. infill hatching regions in metal AM processes

10_1016_j_cma_2024_117503.key_3:

  - Coating volume (Vc) and bulk volume (Vb)

  - Improving correlation between simulated and as-built mechanical performance for AM-fabricated parts
  - Achieving optimal structural performance given the constraints of AM processes (e.g., distinct properties in perimeter vs. infill regions)

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Error indicator (convergence criterion); Von Mises stress (MPa); longitudinal displacement (mm); sliding magnitude after load cycles; preload stress (σ_zz); computation time/CPU time; number of iterations required for convergence; stress distribution patterns; interface forces
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize computation time through parallelization and load balancing (achieved 6.6× speedup); achieve convergence with minimal iterations (target error indicator < 10⁻⁵ for spatial launcher, < 10⁻⁶ for Airbus model); demonstrate scalability of the non-invasive domain decomposition method with increasing subdomains; optimize subdomain decomposition to balance computational load across processors
10_1016_j_finel_2019_01_004.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Conforming meshes required; semi-industrial scale models only (extremely fine models requiring HPC are out of reach); subdomain decomposition must avoid non-connected subdomains as bounding boxes become non-representative; spatial launcher model limited to 3 million DOFs; Airbus model limited to 300,000 DOFs; subdomain decomposition constrained by maximum M=10 subdivisions for largest subdomains
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Quasi-static and infinitesimal strain assumptions only; convergence criterion target of error indicator <10⁻⁵ for spatial launcher and <10⁻⁶ for Airbus model; automatic parameter setting ineffective for non-representative bounding boxes; single Young modulus assumption ineffective for heterogeneous materials; limited to isotropic linear elastic materials; multiscale approach effectiveness reduced by numerous non-linearities
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Non-invasive implementation constraint requiring no source code modification; limited to Python-driven commercial software (code_aster); mesh format constrained to MED format; parallel implementation requires MPI protocol through mpi4py; subdomain decomposition must support Robin condition implementation via sole elements; frictional contact interfaces must be explicitly defined in subdomain decomposition

10_1016_j_cad_2025_103864.key_4:

10_1016_j_cscm_2025_e04777.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** 3D printed concrete (3DPC) grid components with W-shaped and Y-shaped patterns subjected to bending performance analysis
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - 3DPC mixture: Portland cement (713.1 kg/m³), silica fume (79.2 kg/m³), water (237.7 kg/m³), sand (1290.0 kg/m³), superplasticizer (9.5 kg/m³), HPMC (15.8 kg/m³)
  - Compressive strength: 55 MPa
  - Tensile strength: 4.6 MPa
  - Young's modulus: 2.52×10⁴ MPa
  - Poisson's ratio: 0.23
  - Filament interface tension: max traction 1.52 MPa, initial stiffness 4.27 N/mm³, fracture energy 0.28 N/mm
  - Layer interface tension: max traction 1.30 MPa, initial stiffness 3.80 N/mm³, fracture energy 0.29 N/mm
- **Application & Importance:** Analysis of how printing patterns and interfacial anisotropy affect bending performance of unreinforced 3DPC structures to optimize structural design and mitigate layer-by-layer deposition anisotropy effects
- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - Specimen dimensions: 502 mm length × 200 mm width × 140 mm height
  - W-grid and Y-grid patterns with different nozzle sizes (10 mm and 20 mm)
  - 10 mm nozzle specimens: 28 layers of 5 mm thick printed filaments
  - 20 mm nozzle specimens: 11 layers of 13 mm thick printed filaments
  - Fifth-point bending test configuration with nodal loading
  - Average moment of inertia: Y-grid 2.6% higher than W-grid
  - Failure mode: brittle fracture with cracks at lower chords near supports and web members near loading points
10_1016_j_cscm_2025_e04777.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Fifth-point bending test configuration with nodal loading via four steel bars
  - High-strength gypsum leveling between steel bars and specimen surface
  - Displacement loading rate of 0.05 mm/min
  - Fixed supports at bottom of specimens
  - White matte coating with black speckle pattern for DIC measurement
  - Ambient curing conditions for 28 days prior to testing

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Hydraulic servo universal testing machine applying displacement-controlled loading
  - Nodal loads applied at two points on upper surface
  - Uniaxial compression tests along printing direction
  - Splitting tension tests in x-, y-, and z-directions
  - Inclined shear tests at 60° angle with loading speed of 0.05 mm/min

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Inter-layer interface: boundary between adjacent printed layers
  - Filament interface: boundary between adjacent parallel printed strips within same layer
  - Bilinear cohesive zone model (CZM) with traction-separation relationship
  - Inter-layer element thickness: 1 mm
  - Inter-filament element thickness: 2 mm
  - Concrete Damaged Plasticity (CDP) model for printed filaments
  - Layer interface tensile strength: 1.30 MPa average
  - Filament interface tensile strength: 1.52 MPa average

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 3D nonlinear finite element analysis
  - Quasi-static displacement-controlled loading
  - Refined finite element model (RFEM) combining continuum elements for filaments and cohesive elements for interfaces
  - Numerical simulations with less than 10% error in predicting failure loads and displacements
  - Simulation validated against experimental results from DIC measurements
10_1016_j_cscm_2025_e04777.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:**
  - Structural response of 3D printed concrete under bending loads
  - Interfacial damage mechanics between printed filaments and layers
  - Anisotropic material behavior in orthotropic 3DPC structures
  - Tensile damage progression and failure mechanisms in grid components
  - Stress-strain distribution in W-shaped and Y-shaped grid patterns

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Ultimate load capacity (kN) with relative error <10% between simulation and experiment
  - Failure displacement (mm) with 6.8-11.8% error between simulation and DIC measurements
  - Stiffness (kN/mm) comparison between grid patterns and nozzle sizes
  - Load-to-weight ratio (77% higher for Y-grid vs W-grid)
  - Moment of inertia (2.6% higher for Y-grid)
  - QUADSCRT parameter for interface damage assessment (0 at all interfaces before failure)
  - Tensile damage factor distribution patterns

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Maximize load-bearing capacity by optimizing printing patterns (Y-grid demonstrated 80% higher capacity than W-grid)
  - Enhance structural efficiency through load-to-weight ratio improvement (Y-grid showed 77% higher ratio)
  - Minimize interfacial defects by reducing nozzle size (10mm nozzles increased ultimate loads by 10-24% compared to 20mm)
  - Achieve uniform stress distribution to prevent premature failure (Y-grid showed more extensive damage in upper web)
  - Mitigate anisotropy effects through pattern design (demonstrated interfacial integrity prior to structural failure)
10_1016_j_cscm_2025_e04777.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Specimen dimensions constrained to 502 mm length × 200 mm width × 140 mm height
  - W-grid and Y-grid patterns with identical overall dimensions
  - Cross-sectional filling ratios maintained as similar between different specimens
  - Printing pattern geometries limited to hollow grid configurations (W-shaped and Y-shaped)
  - Nozzle diameter constrained to 10 mm and 20 mm sizes
  - Layer height constrained to 5 mm for 10 mm nozzle and 13 mm for 20 mm nozzle

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Compressive strength limited to approximately 55 MPa for printed matrix
  - Tensile strength limited to approximately 4.6 MPa (about one-twelfth of compressive strength)
  - Interfacial tensile strength constraints: filament interface (1.52 MPa max traction), layer interface (1.30 MPa max traction)
  - Specimens exhibit brittle failure with no ductility after peak load
  - Interfacial damage must remain absent prior to structural failure (observed in experiments)
  - Maximum displacement loading rate of 0.05 mm/min for bending tests
  - Young's modulus constrained to 2.52×10⁴ MPa

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Printing speed constrained to 30 mm/s across all specimens
  - Screw speed constrained to 60 rpm across all specimens
  - Curing time constrained to 7 days initial curing plus 21 days additional curing
  - Layer height must be much smaller than nozzle size and tightly controlled
  - Material composition constrained by specific mix proportions (713.1 kg/m³ cement, 79.2 kg/m³ silica fume, etc.)
  - Layer-by-layer deposition process inherently introduces anisotropy
  - Printing process constrained by layer interface quality limitations (porosity at interfaces tends to be relatively high)
  - Smaller nozzles constrained by reduced printing speed for same material output rate

10_1016_j_cad_2024_103730.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Immersed finite element analysis of complex CAD models; Poisson equation solution on arbitrary 3D geometries; tested on sphere, unit cube with internal layer, handle block, fan disk, and 11 engineering/computer graphics models (armadillo, bracket, bunny, dragon, engine, gripper, quadcopter, robo, spanner, turbo, cover)
- **Material / Medium:** General physical medium for Poisson equation (e.g., heat transfer); no specific material properties stated; numerical grids defined by geometry resolution (h_g), finite element resolution (h_f), and quadrature resolution (h_q)
- **Application & Importance:** Automated analysis of complex CAD models without boundary-fitted meshing; overcomes CAD model defects (gaps, overlaps, self-intersections) and eliminates manual defeaturing of small geometric details (fillets, holes); enables high-order accuracy on non-boundary-conforming grids
- **Geometry / Domain:** Arbitrary 3D domains represented via implicit signed distance functions from STL meshes; domain boundaries defined by zero isocontour ϕ⁻¹(0); includes sharp edges, curved surfaces, and small features; geometry grid refined in narrow band (δ = 3h_g) around boundary; FE grid octree-refined toward boundary with 2:1 level constraint; quadrature grid octree-refined in cut cells (r_Q = 0-4)
10_1016_j_cad_2024_103730.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Dirichlet boundary conditions (u = u_true on Γ_D) enforced via Nitsche's method; Neumann boundary conditions (n ⋅ ∇u = g_true on Γ_N); critical basis functions with support overlap below threshold ϵ = 1/8 stabilized via extrapolation; boundary defined by zero isocontour ϕ⁻¹(0) of signed distance function; domain boundaries represented by piecewise-linear reconstruction from signed distance function
- **Loads / Excitations:** Forcing function f in Poisson equation (-∇⋅∇u = f); prescribed analytical solutions including u = cos(x₃) for sphere and complex geometries; prescribed internal layer solution u = arctan(60(r - π/3)) for unit cube problem
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Domain boundaries embedded in non-boundary-fitted grids; cut cells identified by signed distance function evaluation; quadrature cells created through octree refinement of cut finite element cells; tetrahedralization of cut quadrature cells for integration; subdomain interfaces managed via BDDC preconditioner with coarse degrees of freedom at selected interface nodes
- **Simulation Type:** Steady-state analysis; 3D domain with 2D representations in figures; linear elliptic partial differential equations (Poisson equation); high-order analysis with polynomial degrees p = 1 and p = 2; both uniform and adaptive grid refinement approaches; strong and weak scalability testing with processor counts from 128 to 1024
10_1016_j_cad_2024_103730.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Poisson equation (-∇⋅∇u = f) for scalar field problems; representative of heat transfer applications; tested on multiple complex 3D domains including sphere with analytical solution u = cos(x₃) and unit cube with internal layer solution u = arctan(60(r - π/3))
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Relative L₂ norm error (||u - u_h||_L₂/||u_h||_L₂); relative H¹ seminorm error (|u - u_h|_H¹/|u_h|_H¹); volume and surface area errors for geometric representation; number of PCG iterations; computational time components (assembly, BDDC setup, PCG iterations); degrees of freedom; strong/weak scalability performance
- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve optimal convergence rates for both linear (p=1) and quadratic (p=2) basis functions; maintain robustness for complex CAD models with geometric defects; minimize computational time while preserving accuracy; ensure strong scalability with increasing processor count; reduce degrees of freedom through adaptive refinement while maintaining error bounds
10_1016_j_cad_2024_103730.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Minimum geometry grid resolution h_g defines smallest resolvable feature size; geometric details smaller than ≈ h_g are automatically discarded; narrow band width δ = 3h_g for geometry grid; finite element grid maintains 2:1 refinement level constraint between neighboring cells; quadrature grid resolution h_q ≥ h_g; FE grid resolution h_f typically larger than geometry grid resolution h_g; octree refinement levels constrained to r_Q = 0-4 for quadrature cells; cut-cell identification requires supersampling with resolution ≤ h_g to detect small geometric features
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Critical basis function threshold ϵ = 1/8 for support overlap with physical domain; Nitsche method stability parameter γ = γ₀/h_f; quadratic basis functions (p=2) require h_q = h_f/4 or finer for optimal convergence; linear basis functions (p=1) achieve optimal convergence with h_q = h_f; boundary surface must be approximated with polynomials of degree p to achieve order p+1 approximation; minimum 3 octree refinements required for extraordinary cut cells containing sharp features; volume and surface errors plateau when h_q < h_g, bounded by geometry grid resolution
- **Process/Manufacturing:** CAD models contain unavoidable defects (gaps, overlaps, self-intersections); small geometric features (fillets, holes) typically require manual defeaturing in traditional meshing; immersed method provides automatic defeaturing by discarding subgrid geometry details; system matrix for entire problem is never assembled in parallel implementation; requires STL mesh conversion from CAD models for robust signed distance computation; quadrature grid uses bottom-up octree construction to merge non-cut cells for integration efficiency; parallel implementation requires dual graph analysis to handle subdomain fragmentation

10_1016_j_apradiso_2024_111632.key_1:
- Identity & Domain: 35 MeV high-power electron accelerator driven white neutron source target for photoneutron production
- Material / Medium: Tungsten target (high atomic number, thermal conductivity 173 Wm⁻¹K⁻¹, melting point ~3695 K, Young's modulus 411 GPa); Light water (H₂O) coolant; 35 MeV/2 mA@70 kW electron beam
- Application & Importance: Neutron science research requiring thermal management analysis to overcome limitations in high-current accelerator-driven neutron sources; applications include neutron capture/fission cross-section research, isotope production, neutron therapy, material irradiation modification, and neutron activation analysis
- Geometry / Domain: Cylindrical tungsten target with 2.5 cm radius and 6 cm thickness; multi-layer stacked structure with layer thicknesses of 2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 15 mm along electron incidence direction; 1.5 mm water channels between layers; 2.5 cm inner diameter electron flight pipeline; 1 mm cooling water channel between 1 mm thick aluminum windows at end
10_1016_j_apradiso_2024_111632.key_2:
- Boundary conditions: Inlet water flow rates of 2 m/s, 4 m/s, 6 m/s, and 8 m/s; initial coolant temperatures of 5°C, 10°C, 15°C, and 20°C; velocity inlet boundary condition; pressure outlet boundary condition; 1.5 mm water channel width between target layers; 1 mm cooling water between 1 mm thick aluminum windows
- Operating environment: 35 MeV/2 mA@70 kW electron beam with Gaussian distribution; electron beam spot radius of 1.5 cm; full width at half maximum in Y and Z directions of 1.5 cm; 1.0 × 10⁸ incident electrons; cylindrical tungsten target with 2.5 cm radius and 6 cm thickness; multi-layer target structure with thicknesses of 2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 15 mm along electron incidence direction
- Simulation configuration: Monte Carlo algorithm for neutron physics and radiation damage analysis; ANSYS finite element analysis for thermal analysis; ANSYS CFX CFD module; steady-state thermal analysis with varying flow rates and temperatures; transient analysis for radioactivity decay evaluation
- Interface conditions: Cooling water enters through the middle and flows out around the sleeve; energy deposition primarily within 6 mm at front end of target with peak around 2 mm; gamma radiation concentrated in first 10 mm with peak around 3 mm; heat transfer from tungsten target plates to coolant water
10_1016_j_apradiso_2024_111632.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Neutron production via photoneutron reactions; electron energy deposition; gamma fluence distribution; thermal conduction and fluid flow; radiation damage (displacement per atom); radioactive activation; neutron angular and spatial distribution
- Target Outputs: Neutron yield per electron (7.62 × 10⁻³ n/e for H₂O cooling); total neutron yield (9.53 × 10¹³ n/s); neutron energy spectrum (0.001 eV–30 MeV); target maximum temperature (226°C at 6 m/s flow rate, 15°C inlet); coolant maximum temperature (51°C at 6 m/s flow rate, 15°C inlet); displacement per atom rate (4.288 dpa/y); radioactivity levels of induced isotopes; neutron flux distribution at various angles and distances
- Optimization Goal: Maximize neutron yield while maintaining target temperature below melting point; determine optimal target dimensions (2.5 cm radius, 6 cm thickness); achieve target lifespan exceeding one year (4.288 dpa/y < 10 dpa limit); select appropriate coolant (H₂O preferred for wider energy spectrum); optimize multi-layer target thicknesses (2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 15 mm) to manage thermal strain; ensure coolant temperature remains below 100°C (achieved at ≥6 m/s flow rate)
10_1016_j_apradiso_2024_111632.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: Target cross-sectional radius fixed at 2.5 cm; target thickness fixed at 6 cm; multi-layer target thicknesses configured as 2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 15 mm along electron incidence direction; water channel width fixed at 1.5 mm; electron beam spot radius of 1.5 cm with FWHM of 1.5 cm in Y and Z directions; inner diameter of electron flight pipeline at 2.5 cm; cooling water channel maintained at 1 mm thickness between 1 mm aluminum windows
- Performance/Physics Limits: Maximum target temperature must remain below tungsten melting point (~3695 K); coolant temperature must stay below 100°C (achieved at ≥6 m/s flow rate); displacement per atom (dpa) rate limited to 4.288 dpa/y (well below 10 dpa lifespan threshold); maximum target temperature constrained to 226°C at 6 m/s flow rate with 15°C inlet; energy deposition peak constrained to ~2 mm from target front; gamma distribution peak constrained to ~3 mm from target front; electron beam energy fixed at 35 MeV; maximum water flow velocity constrained to 60 m/s
- Process/Manufacturing: Inlet cooling water flow rate must be ≥4 m/s for effective cooling; cooling water temperature must be below 20°C for optimal performance; light water (H₂O) selected as coolant despite 3.3% lower total neutron yield compared to heavy water (D₂O) due to better neutron spectrum characteristics; annual operation time limited to 5000 hours; target material constrained to tungsten due to high atomic number, thermal conductivity (173 Wm⁻¹K⁻¹), melting point (~3695 K), and Young's modulus (411 GPa); flow rates above 6 m/s accelerate tungsten target corrosion; water channel geometry constrained to avoid target positions at 3 mm where neutron production peaks

10_1016_j_actbio_2025_02_017.key_1:
- Identity: Keratinous avian feather shaft structures exhibiting hydration-driven shape memory effect
- Material: β-keratin composite with amorphous matrix and crystalline fibers
- Matrix properties (dry): Elastic-perfectly plastic with Young's modulus E_M^D and yield stress σ_y^D
- Matrix properties (hydrated): Elastic-perfectly plastic with reduced Young's modulus E_M^H (< E_M^D) and reduced yield stress σ_y^H (< σ_y^D)
- Fiber properties: Linearly elastic with Young's modulus E_F (> E_M^D), unaffected by hydration
- Hierarchical structure: β-keratin filaments (~3 nm), β-keratin fibrils (~20 nm), macro-fibrils (50-400 nm), fibers (3-5 μm)
- Matrix-fiber volume fractions: Variable in models, with 40% fiber volume fraction used in benchmark testing
- CFSC model: 31-layer configuration (16 matrix layers, 15 fiber layers) showed convergence
- Recovery ratio: 97.6% without swelling, 99.7% with swelling at 31 layers under flexural bending
- Pipe geometry for benchmark: Thickness-to-diameter ratio of 0.1, diameter-to-length ratio of 0.05
- Bending test results: 97.8% recovery with swelling, 96.3% without swelling
- Twisting test results: 99.4% recovery without swelling, 98.1% with swelling
- Fiber volume fraction range studied: 1% to 25% in flower application model
- Deformation requirement: Applied deformation must increase exponentially with fiber volume fraction to maintain constant permanent plastic deformation
- Mechanical symmetry: Both matrix and fibers exhibit symmetric behavior under tension and compression
- Hydration effects: Matrix softening (reduced stiffness and strength) is primary driver of shape recovery; swelling effect is conditionally beneficial
- Swelling directionality: Beneficial under tensile loading/bending, detrimental under compressive loading/twisting
- Shape recovery parameter: Defined as ε_r = 1 - (ε_c'/ε_c) where ε_c represents persistent plastic deformation
- CFSC application: Modeled as flexible hinges connecting rigid petals to base in flower structure demonstration

10_1007_s12206_022_1011_z.key_1:
- Self-healing resin mineral composites with microcapsule
- Material composition: resin matrix, aggregate (Ji Nan Qing stone), and microcapsules
- Aggregate composition: CaAl2Si2O8 (79%) and mica (21%), compressive strength 189-210 MPa, flexural strength 28-32 MPa
- Material parameters: aggregate E=128 GPa, μ=0.28, σs=251 MPa; epoxy E=3.1 GPa, μ=0.30, σs=67 MPa; microcapsule E=2.12 GPa, μ=0.30, σs=41.45 MPa
- Microcapsule diameter: 300 μm
- Microcapsule proportions studied: 1%, 3%, 5%, 7%, 9%
- Cohesive element tensile strength: 4 MPa
- Cohesive element fracture energy: 0.1 N/mm
- Double line constitutive model used for cohesive elements
- Damage evolution process divided into four stages: damage accumulation, bond interface crack appearing, matrix crack appearing, fracture surface formation
- Self-healing efficiency defined as η = (V'/V) × 100%, where V' is repaired area and V is total crack area
- For 1% microcapsule proportion: V'=0.126 mm², V=1.033 mm², η=12%
- For 3% microcapsule proportion: V'=0.280 mm², V=0.660 mm², η=42%
- For 5% microcapsule proportion: V'=0.280 mm², V=0.571 mm², η=49%
- For 7% microcapsule proportion: V'=0.840 mm², V=1.425 mm², η=59%
- For 9% microcapsule proportion: V'=0.672 mm², V=0.932 mm², η=72%
- Optimal microcapsule proportion: 1.68%
- At 1.68% microcapsule proportion: elastic modulus E=30.92 GPa (2.9% reduction), self-healing efficiency=25.38%, Poisson's ratio=0.25
- Relationship between self-healing efficiency and microcapsule proportion is nonlinear positive correlation
- Relationship between elastic modulus and microcapsule proportion is nonlinear negative correlation
- Self-healing efficiency increased from 0 to 38.66% when microcapsule proportion was 0-3%
- Elastic modulus decreased from 31.85 to 30.22 GPa when microcapsule proportion was 0-3%
- Crack area V not directly related to microcapsule proportion but to aggregate distribution position

10_1016_j_finel_2019_05_002.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** 1.5 MW 25-strake metal wind turbine support tower
- **Material / Medium:** Structural steel with Young's modulus of 210 GPa, Poisson ratio of μ = 0.3, and yield stress of 355 MPa
- **Application & Importance:** Structural assessment for buckling and plastic collapse resistance under global transverse shear and torsion loads; enables optimization of multi-strake tower design
- **Geometry / Domain:** 22 truncated-conical shell strakes (β < ~1.1°, nearly cylindrical) with 3 cylindrical flanges; strakes exhibit stepwise varying wall thicknesses (upper strakes thinner than lower strakes); total height of 72.8 m; strake heights ranging from 80 mm (flanges) to 2,940 mm; radii from 1,477.5 mm to 2,017.5 mm; thicknesses from 9 mm to 25 mm
10_1016_j_finel_2019_05_002.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Base edge fully clamped; regular nodal continuity between adjacent shell strakes; rigid kinematic coupling to reference point for shell strake to global boundary; rigid kinematic coupling to beam node for shell-to-beam strake connection; edge-to-edge tie constraint for shell-to-rigid strake connection; "ring" conditions (u = w and v = 0) and "pinned" conditions (w = v = u = 0) for conical shell boundaries
- **Loads / Excitations:** Transverse point load of 2 MN applied through top flange centroid; point torque of 4 MNm applied at top flange centroid; no mass or gravity loading applied
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Hybrid beam-shell modeling with shell strakes connected to beam strakes via rigid kinematic coupling; shell strakes connected to rigid bodies via edge-to-edge tie constraints; connection of discrete strakes through nodal continuity or rigid kinematic couplings at interfaces; point loads applied directly to top reference point or node
- **Simulation Type:** Linear bifurcation analysis (LBA); materially nonlinear analysis (MNA); geometrically and materially nonlinear analysis with imperfections (GMNIA); bilinear elastic-plastic material law with no hardening; Riks modified arc-length algorithm for equilibrium path following; eigenmode imperfections and weld depression imperfections (Fabrication Tolerance Quality Class C); bi-quadratic thick-shell reduced-integration S8R elements; linear B31 beam elements for flange/beam strakes; 4-node R3D4 rigid elements for rigid bodies
10_1016_j_finel_2019_05_002.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Structural buckling behavior and plastic collapse of thin-walled metal shells under combined meridional compression, bending, and torsion; linear and nonlinear structural response of multi-strake wind turbine towers
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** LBA load factors; MNA load factors; GMNIA load factors; characteristic resistances (Rk); normalized buckling loads; critical buckling locations (strake identifiers); load proportionality factors; wave numbers (m, n) for buckling modes; relative criticality distributions along tower height
- **Optimization Goal:** Identify globally critical strakes for buckling and plastic collapse; determine underutilized strakes that may be candidates for thickness reduction; optimize overall tower design by balancing structural resistance across all strakes while minimizing material usage; enable efficient LBA-MNA design assessment according to EN 1993-1-6
10_1016_j_finel_2019_05_002.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** 22 truncated-conical shell strakes (β < ~1.1°) with 3 cylindrical flanges; strake thicknesses ranging from 9-25 mm; strake heights from 80-2,940 mm; radii from 1,477.5-2,017.5 mm; meshing constraints requiring minimum 10 elements per buckling half-wave; meridional element size ≤ 0.173·√(ρ̄·t̄); circumferential element size ≤ 0.346·√(ρ̄·t̄); maximum dimensionless parameter Ω ≈ (L/r₀)·√(t/r₀) ≤ 1.6 to prevent significant cross-sectional ovalisation
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Material properties: E = 210 GPa, μ = 0.3, yield stress = 355 MPa; buckling resistance must exceed design loads; Fabrication Tolerance Quality Class C (highest codified imperfection amplitudes) used for GMNIA; characteristic resistance Rₖ must be ≥ 1 for structural adequacy; LBA load factors must be evaluated for each strake; EN 1993-1-6 LBA-MNA design procedure requirements
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Weld depression imperfections modeled as Type 'A' axisymmetric circumferential deviations; piecewise cylindrical approximation required (incompatible with spiral welded structures); near-cylindrical geometry necessary (apex half-angle β < ~1.1°); cannot model detailed distributed surface pressure loading; requires sufficient intermediate stiffening rings/flanges to prevent pre-buckling cross-sectional ovalisation under bending; must be treatable as shells of revolution; incompatible with strongly non-cylindrical geometries
