10_1016_j_finel_2024_104306.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Equivalent macro-elements (μ elements) representing microstructures with non-uniform material distribution for finite element analysis in topology optimization
- **Material / Medium:** Elastic isotropic material in plane stress; Young's modulus E = 1 (consistent units); Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3 (unless specified); linear material interpolation Dₑ(xₑ) = xₑD̂; power law scheme Dₑ(xₑ) = xₑᵖD̂ with p ≥ 1
- **Application & Importance:** Improving boundary representation in topology optimization; eliminating intermediate elements at solid-void boundaries without remeshing; enhancing stress calculation accuracy near jagged boundaries; achieving smoother designs while maintaining computational efficiency
- **Geometry / Domain:** n×n microstructure grids converted to equivalent 4-node quadrilateral (Q4) macro-elements; trapezoidal elements with node coordinates x = [-1, 1, 1, -1], y = [-1, -1, 1, a] (-1 ≤ a ≤ 1); plate with circular hole (r ∈ [0.09, 0.11]) in 2×1 domain; MBB beam with 60×20 coarse mesh (60×20 elements) and 240×80 fine mesh (240×80 elements); hole radius r ∈ [0.09, 0.11] in circular hole test case
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104306.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Left edge fixed for 3×3 element test; bottom left corner fixed with top edge rollers for MBB beam; node 1 pinned with horizontal sliding constraint at node 2 (DoFs 1, 2, 4 constrained) for trapezoidal element tests; symmetry boundary conditions for plate with circular hole (quarter-domain modeling); all degrees of freedom constrained except unit displacement at DoF 5 for trapezoidal element displacement test; fixed left edge for cantilever beam
- **Loads / Excitations:** Downward point load at bottom right corner of 3×3 element problem; uniaxial tension for plate with circular hole; unit load P = 0.1 for Q4/Q9 element comparison; unit load P = 1 for checkerboard test; unit displacement at DoF 5 (horizontal direction at node 3) for trapezoidal element tests; point load P at end of cantilever beam
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** D0, D1, and D2 displacement mappings define relationships between microscale and macroscale displacements; D0 mapping cannot maintain continuity between adjacent macro-elements; force equilibrium along edges for lumping edge forces to corner nodes; linear material interpolation Dₑ(xₑ) = xₑD̂; power law scheme Dₑ(xₑ) = xₑᵖD̂ with p ≥ 1
- **Simulation Type:** 2D plane stress; linear elasticity; quasi-static; topology optimization with volume fraction constraint (v_f = 0.5 for MBB beam); coarse mesh (60×20) and fine mesh (240×80) analyses; symmetry boundary conditions (half-domain for MBB beam, quarter-domain for circular hole); comparison of Q4, Q9, and μ element formulations
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104306.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Linear elasticity in 2D plane stress; structural response of microstructures represented as equivalent macro-elements (μ elements); displacement and stress fields in finite element models; topology optimization with material distribution
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Mean compliance (C = PᵀU); maximum normal stress in loading direction (max(σ̃₁₁)); nodal forces at specific degrees of freedom; displacement values at constrained nodes; sensitivity values for topology optimization; stress distributions near boundaries; density fields; objective function values in optimization iterations; stress concentration factors
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize mean compliance while maintaining volume constraints; enhance boundary resolution in topology optimization; eliminate intermediate elements at solid-void boundaries without remeshing; achieve smoother design boundaries; improve stress calculation accuracy near jagged boundaries; reduce computational cost compared to fine mesh solutions (e.g., 23% of time for post-processing solution vs. fine mesh)
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104306.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Volume fraction constraint of v_f = 0.5 for MBB beam topology optimization; hole radius constrained to r ∈ [0.09, 0.11] in circular hole test case; trapezoidal element with parameter range -1 ≤ a ≤ 1; square-shaped microstructures only; half-domain modeling for MBB beam due to symmetry; 3×3 element test domain with specific boundary conditions
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Minimum density value x_true̲ > 0 to prevent singular stiffness matrices; ε-relaxation parameter range: ε = 0.010, 0.020, 0.030, 0.040 for stress calculation; theoretical stress concentration factor of 3 for circular hole in infinite plate; abrupt stiffness changes in μ₁ elements when a ≈ 1 - 4/n due to void micro-elements near node 4; intermediate micro-elements eliminated using penalty factor p ≥ 1
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Q4-based μ₂ elements limited to shape optimization only (cannot handle topology changes within microstructure); filtering radius r_min must be ≥ macro element size to eliminate checkerboard patterns; computational cost increases exponentially with mesh refinement; n=8 (8×8 micro-elements) threshold where μ elements become more economical than fine mesh solutions; sensitivity issues in Q4-based μ₂ elements require filtering techniques for resolution; intermediate elements at boundaries unavoidable without remeshing or special techniques in standard topology optimization

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2016_05_004.key_1:
• Identity & Domain: Structural cables with helical wire construction, specifically semi-parallel wire cables and spiral strands (Galfan strands) for bending analysis
• Material / Medium: Steel wires (elastic modulus 2.1×10¹¹ Pa), HDPE sheath (elastic modulus 150 MPa, thermal expansion coefficient 1.4×10⁻⁴ C⁻¹), Galfan anti-corrosion coating, Coulomb friction coefficient μ=0.5
• Application & Importance: Understanding complex bending behavior in structural applications (bridges, cable-supported structures); predicting flexural stiffness variations between fully stuck and fully slipped wire states (differing by up to two orders of magnitude); assessing stress concentrations near cable ends to prevent fatigue failure
• Geometry / Domain: Helical wire arrangements with 37-91 wires; 1050mm total length, 820mm bending span; semi-parallel cables with uniform winding direction; spiral strands with alternating layer winding; wire diameters of 5mm; cable diameters ranging from Φ38 to Φ63; FE model using helically arranged short-beam elements, radial rigid beams, and directional spring elements
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2016_05_004.key_2:
• Boundaries & Constraints: Free-end condition with rigid plane restraint on X,Y displacements while releasing Z direction; Welded-end condition with restraint on all three displacement freedoms creating rigid plane section; Prestressed end with steel blocks welded to cable ends, cable end nodes connected to short beams with rigid plane couplings; Supporting pad locations with X,Y displacement constraints; Rigid plane restraint on all three displacement freedoms for Galfan strand end clamping

• Loads / Excitations: Lateral displacement at midsection (4mm bending deflection standard); Axial traction of 100 MPa (1963.5 N point force); Pretension levels of 5, 8, and 10 Ton; HDPE sheath compaction as centripetal forces (28.15 N for 37Φ7 cable, 25.07 N for 55Φ7 and 61Φ7 cables); Thermal contraction from HDPE sheath fabrication with 24°C temperature difference

• Interactions / Interfaces: Three-directional coupling between wires (X,Y springs for contact extrusion, Z spring for friction); Two-directional coupling for free-end condition; Three-directional coupling for welded-end condition; Point contact between adjacent layer wires in spiral strands; Line contact between same-layer wires; Coulomb friction with μ=0.5; Contact compression calculated from X,Y spring forces

• Simulation Type: Nonlinear static analysis with displacement-controlled loading; 3D analysis capturing out-of-plane deformation; Multi-step simulation with iterative friction resistance determination; Bilinear elastic-plastic like response modeling; Incremental bending deflection application (Δ, 2Δ, 3Δ...); Trilinear force-elongation relation for Z springs during bending progression
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2016_05_004.key_3:
• Physics Solved: Cable bending behavior with wire sliding mechanisms; contact extrusion and friction between adjacent helical wires; axial tension effects on bending stiffness; unwinding trends in semi-parallel cables; torsional compensation in spiral strands; sheath pinch effect; helical wire clenching under tension

• Target Outputs (Metrics): Flexural force vs. bending deflection curves; wire force distribution at mid-span and quarter-span sections; out-of-plane (Y-direction) sinusoidal deformation; axial wire force gradients; contact extrusion forces (X,Y spring forces); friction resistance magnitude (Z spring forces); transition strength between elastic and plastic-like bending regions; effective bending stiffness (initial and stabilized tangent stiffness)

• Optimization Goal: Accurately predict the bilinear elastic-plastic like flexural strength-deflection response; capture the varying trend of flexural stiffness between fully stuck and fully slipped wire states (differing by up to two orders of magnitude); efficiently simulate long cables (820mm bending span) with large wire counts (up to 91 wires) while maintaining computational efficiency; model wire slip progression during bending through multi-step friction resistance determination
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2016_05_004.key_4:
• Geometric/Design Space: 1050mm total cable length; 820mm bending span between supporting pads; Wire diameter fixed at 5mm; Cable diameters ranging from Φ38 to Φ63; HDPE sheath thickness of 8-9.5mm; Section interval Δ must satisfy θ_i + θ_{i+1} = 360/(6i) for spiral strand contact pattern; Lay angle controlled within 10-15° for Galfan strand fabrication; Element length constrained to 15-20mm for FE model

• Performance/Physics Limits: Steel wires assumed to remain elastic throughout bending (plasticity development not considered); Coulomb friction coefficient fixed at μ=0.5; Z springs initially assigned with 10N/mm ultimate friction resistance; Axial traction limited to 100 MPa (1963.5 N point force) for validation; Pretension levels constrained to 5, 8, and 10 Ton; Bending deflection analyzed up to 5mm; HDPE sheath thermal expansion coefficient of 1.4×10⁻⁴ C⁻¹ with 24°C temperature difference during fabrication

• Process/Manufacturing: HDPE sheath applied through hot extrusion process with cold contraction effect; Semi-parallel wire cables have uniform winding direction while spiral strands have alternating winding directions between layers; Galfan strands use anti-corrosion coating instead of external HDPE sheath; Cable ends constrained to three conditions: free-end (X,Y displacement restrained), welded-end (all three displacements restrained), and prestressed end with steel blocks; FE models cannot determine HDPE sheath bending strength contribution, only simulating its compaction as centripetal forces; Real friction conditions simplified to Coulomb friction due to unclear actual friction mechanisms in fabricated strands

- **Geometric/Design Space:** 5 μm edge length cubic RVE domain; grain size range limited to 0.5-1.5 μm; WC volume fractions constrained to 5-20%; TiB₂ volume fractions constrained to 10-40%; porosity levels limited to 0-1 vol%; Al₂O₃ matrix fraction constrained to 50-80% based on reinforcement phase percentages
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Linear elastic material behavior assumption for modulus prediction; brittle material behavior with minimal plasticity before failure; displacement load rate fixed at 0.5 mm/min; maximum fracture toughness achieved at 0.75 μm grain size with inverse Hall-Petch relationship observed below critical size; fracture toughness decreases with excessive reinforcement phase addition (beyond 10% WC and 20% TiB₂)
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Sintering temperature range constrained to 1300-1450°C; holding time constrained to 3-9 minutes; sintering pressure fixed at 30 MPa; porosity inevitably present due to incomplete gas discharge during sintering; insufficient grain growth at 1300°C; grain overgrowth observed at 1450°C; optimal processing at 1400°C with 7-minute holding time; WC content beyond 10% causes predominantly through-crystal fracture; TiB₂ content beyond 20% causes increased porosity due to high melting point characteristics

10_1016_j_agwat_2020_106148.key_1:

- Application & Importance: Quantifying water loss to improve conveyance efficiency and address water scarcity in agricultural irrigation systems
- Geometry / Domain: Three channel cross-sections (trapezoidal, rectangular, triangular) with side slopes (z) of 0, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5; bed width (b) 0-8 m; water depth (y) 0.2-4 m; wetted perimeter p = b + 2y√(1+z²); computational mesh with element sizes averaging 0.2 m (19,450-51,674 elements); specified potential boundary conditions (Head=13 m or y=1.5 m) at channel bed and walls; impermeable boundaries with ∂q/∂x = 0 and ∂q/∂y = 0 conditions at domain edges
10_1016_j_agwat_2020_106148.key_2:

- Boundary conditions: Zero flux (impermeable) boundaries with ∂q/∂x = 0 at left and right sides, ∂q/∂y = 0 at bottom
- Boundary conditions: Total flux = 0.0 specified at model walls and bottom
- Hydraulic head: Water depth (y) ranging from 0.2 to 4 m
- Soil properties: Hydraulic conductivity (k) values of 2×10⁻⁴, 2×10⁻⁵, and 2×10⁻⁶ m/s
- Channel geometry: Side slopes (z) of 0, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5; bed width (b) from 0 to 8 m
- Simulation type: Steady-state 2D finite element method (FEM)
- Computational domain: Mesh with 19,450 to 51,674 elements, average element size of 0.2 m

10_1016_j_agwat_2020_106148.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Seepage flow through porous media (soil) from unlined earthen irrigation channels governed by Darcy's law and Poisson equation
- Target Outputs: Dimensionless seepage rate (q/ky), where q = seepage discharge (m³/s/m), k = soil hydraulic conductivity (m/s), y = water depth (m); wetted perimeter (p = b + 2y√(1+z²)); statistical metrics including R², relative error (RE), and root mean square error (RMSE)
- Optimization Goal: Develop accurate prediction methods for seepage discharge with minimum error; achieve highest R² and lowest RE compared to field measurements from Zayandeh-Rud irrigation channels; validate numerical model against empirical equations and field data
10_1016_j_agwat_2020_106148.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: Channel side slopes (z) limited to 0, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5; bed width (b) ranging from 0 to 8 m in specified increments; water depth (y) from 0.2 to 4 m; wetted perimeter (p = b + 2y√(1+z²)); analysis restricted to three cross-section types (trapezoidal, rectangular, triangular); y/p ratio constraint where z effect diminishes for y/p > 0.15
- Performance/Physics Limits: Hydraulic conductivity (k) values restricted to 2×10⁻⁴, 2×10⁻⁵, and 2×10⁻⁶ m/s; boundary conditions limited to specified potential (Head=13 m or y=1.5 m) at channel bed/walls and zero flux at domain boundaries; steady-state flow analysis only (ignoring time-dependent effects); isotropic soil assumption (Kx = Ky) despite acknowledging anisotropy would impact seepage
- Process/Manufacturing: Empirical relationships require site-specific coefficient calibration (C values vary widely by location); analysis limited to unlined earthen channels only; groundwater depth under channel bed not fully considered as a variable parameter; channel geometry restricted to ranges where empirical equations like Swamee et al. (2000) were previously validated (0.5 ≤ z ≤ 5 and 0.5 ≤ b/y ≤ 10)

10_1016_j_finel_2024_104151.key_1:
- **Subject of analysis**: Wedge splitting test (WST) geometry for fracture behavior simulation of magnesia spinel refractories
- **Material**: Magnesia spinel refractory (quasi-brittle material)
- **Material properties**: Young's modulus E = 20 GPa, Poisson's ratio ν = 0.2, tensile strength ft = 2.24 MPa, h = 10 (compressive/tensile strength ratio)
- **Geometry dimensions**: 100 mm × 100 mm overall, 24 mm wide notch, 22 mm notch height, 3 mm notch depth
- **Boundary conditions**: 0.38 mm horizontal displacement applied to upper lateral faces of notch
- **Analysis type**: Plane strain conditions with 75 mm domain thickness
- **Element types**: 8-noded elements for displacement (quadratic interpolation), 4-noded elements for non-local equivalent strain (linear interpolation)
- **Gradient parameters studied**: c = 1, 2, 5, 20, 100 mm² across different GED models
- **Softening laws**: Exponential law and modified power law
- **Heterogeneous distribution**: 10 element groups following Weibull distribution with proportions: E1=1.95%, E2=8.40%, E3=17%, E4=23%, E5=22.5%, E6=15.9%, E7=7.9%, E8=2.7%, E9=0.6%, E10=0.05%
- **Mesh characteristics**: Unstructured mesh for GED models; structured mesh with 0.75 mm edge length for heterogeneous studies
- **Damage threshold parameters**: κi values ranging from 0.000146 to 0.000171 for exponential law; κi = 0.00029 for modified power law
- **Critical damage threshold**: κc = 0.82 for modified power law
- **RMSE values**: Ranging from 30 to 117 across different model configurations
- **Notch width**: D = 3 mm (used as reference dimension in mesh convergence studies)
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104151.key_2:
- Horizontal displacement of 0.38 mm applied to upper lateral faces of the notch
- Triangular support at bottom center of specimen
- Neumann boundary conditions: σ · n = t* (prescribed boundary traction)
- Neumann boundary conditions: ∇ε̄eq · n = 0 for non-local equivalent strain
- Plane strain conditions with 75 mm domain thickness
- Quasi-static loading conditions
- Displacement applied incrementally and monotonically using Newton-Raphson iterative scheme
- Room temperature environment (as per experimental data reference)
- Quadratic interpolation for displacement field using 8-noded elements
- Linear interpolation for non-local equivalent strain field using 4-noded elements
- No-slip condition at support interface (inferred from the fixed support representation)
- Unstructured mesh for GED models with varying element sizes based on gradient parameter
- Structured mesh with 0.75 mm edge length for heterogeneous distribution studies
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104151.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Fracture behavior of quasi-brittle materials including damage evolution, fracture process zone formation, and crack propagation
- Target Outputs: Load-displacement curves, damage contour plots, non-local equivalent strain profiles, Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) values, fracture process zone width and shape, crack propagation path
- Optimization Goal: Minimize spurious damage spreading while accurately representing the fracture process zone; achieve mesh-independent results; replicate realistic crack patterns with tortuous paths and branching as observed in experiments; minimize RMSE between simulated and experimental load-displacement curves
- Primary comparison metrics: RMSE values (ranging from 30-117 across different model configurations), damage zone width, crack path tortuosity, and computational efficiency
- Critical evaluation criteria: Ability to limit unphysical damage distribution along the notch, accuracy in representing the narrow fracture process zone observed experimentally, and capability to produce mesh-objective results
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104151.key_4:
- Geometric constraint: Wedge splitting test geometry with 100 mm × 100 mm overall dimensions, 24 mm wide notch, 22 mm notch height, and 3 mm notch depth
- Domain thickness constraint: Fixed at 75 mm under plane strain conditions
- Displacement constraint: Horizontal displacement of exactly 0.38 mm applied to upper lateral faces of the notch
- Material property constraints: Young's modulus E = 20 GPa, Poisson's ratio ν = 0.2, tensile strength ft = 2.24 MPa, h = 10 (compressive/tensile strength ratio)
- Damage variable constraint: d ∈ [0,1] where d=0 represents no damage and d=1 represents complete fracture
- Meshing constraint: 8-noded elements required for displacement field (quadratic interpolation), 4-noded elements required for non-local equivalent strain field (linear interpolation) to prevent unphysical stress oscillations
- Gradient parameter constraint: Localizing GED model requires c ≥ 5 mm² for feasible element sizes; c = 100 mm² causes unphysical oscillations at onset of non-linearity
- Modified power law constraint: β parameter limited to maximum value of 1.35 to avoid convergence issues
- Numerical constraint: Localizing model requires very small coupling modulus h = E*10^-9 to avoid stress locking
- Load increment constraint: Modified power law requires smaller load increments in Newton-Raphson scheme to ensure convergence
- Heterogeneous model constraint: 10 element groups following Weibull distribution with specific proportions (E1=1.95%, E2=8.40%, E3=17%, E4=23%, E5=22.5%, E6=15.9%, E7=7.9%, E8=2.7%, E9=0.6%, E10=0.05%)
- Computational constraint: Localizing GED model requires finer mesh discretization for lower gradient parameters, increasing computational cost
- Damage threshold constraint: κi values must be carefully calibrated (ranging from 0.000146-0.000171 for exponential law; κi = 0.00029 for modified power law)
- Minimum damage bound: 0.95 used to delineate critical damage zone for fracture process zone characterization

10_1016_j_engfracmech_2025_111142.key_4:

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109636.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Spherical-based porous architectures for additive manufacturing, including uniform porous structures (UPSs) and graded porous structures (GPSs)
- **Material / Medium:** Flexible 80A V1 resin (elastomeric); elastic modulus 8.4 MPa; Poisson's ratio 0.49; water (density 998.2 kg/m³, viscosity 1.002×10⁻³ kg/(m·s)) for fluid flow simulations
- **Application & Importance:** Biomedical applications including tissue engineering scaffolds and soft bioreactor systems; mechanical validation for energy absorption capabilities; fluid flow assessment for bone tissue engineering applications
- **Geometry / Domain:** 10×10×7.5 mm³ structures; UPSs with uniform interconnected pore sizes (0.46, 0.56, 0.82, 1.10 mm); GPSs with average interconnected pore sizes (0.73, 0.79, 0.91, 1.01 mm) and interconnected pore size gradients (0.14, 0.17, 0.20, 0.23 mm); porosity range 65-90%; generated by subtracting networks of interconnected spheres from bulk prisms
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109636.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Uniaxial compression (uᵧ ≠ 0, uₓ = u_z = 0) at top surfaces; symmetry boundary conditions (uₓ = 0 and u_z = 0) on lateral surfaces at positive x and z coordinates; bottom surfaces set as either symmetry region (UPSs) or compression supports (GPSs) with uᵧ = 0 constraint; inlet velocity at fluid inlet; zero-gauge pressure (P_gauge = 0 = P_atm) at outlet; symmetry boundary conditions on lateral surfaces; no-slip boundary conditions on all other surfaces; inlet and outlet sections extended by 1 mm for well-developed flow

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109636.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Normalized compression stiffness (unitless); specific absorbed energy (10⁻³ J/cm³); elastic modulus (MPa); densification strain; permeability (m²); wall shear stress (mPa); stress-strain curves; fitted exponents of absorbed energy vs strain curves; percentage of scaffold surface promoting bone cell differentiation (0.1-30 mPa range)
- **Optimization Goal:** Maximize energy absorption capabilities while maintaining suitable mechanical properties for biomedical applications; achieve hydraulic permeability in range of 10⁻⁹–10⁻⁸ m² for bone tissue engineering; maintain wall shear stress between 0.1-30 mPa across >90% of scaffold surface; validate structural printability while optimizing pore size, porosity, and pore size gradients for tissue engineering scaffolds
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109636.key_4:

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Wall shear stress must be between 0.1-30 mPa for bone cell differentiation (WSS >60 mPa causes cell death); hydraulic permeability must be within 10⁻⁹–10⁻⁸ m² for bone tissue engineering applications; error threshold of 25% set for FE model validation (e = |E_exp - E_model|/E_exp × 100%); FE model only valid for porosity up to 80% due to manufacturing limitations
- **Process/Manufacturing:** 13% average shrinkage during post-printing curing process; high-porosity structures (above 80%) exhibit significant printing inaccuracies due to thin struts; structures with thin struts showed truncated sections due to minimum feature size limitations; overcuring or poor solvent bathing caused internal bulk sections in some samples; samples with broken struts during printing due to inability of interconnections to withstand structure weight; manufacturing process limited to porosity range where FE model MAPE <20% for reliable predictions; UV curing at 60°C caused thermal stress release leading to dimensional changes

10_1016_j_finel_2015_04_008.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Cohesive zone modeling in fracture mechanics using discontinuous Galerkin finite element method for small strain elasticity
- **Material / Medium:** Elastic material with E=10 MPa, ν=0.45; inclusions with Young's modulus 100× base material; maximum cohesive strength=1 MPa; maximum critical separation=0.02 mm; fracture energy=0.1 J/mm²

- **Geometry / Domain:** Rectangular specimen with W=1.00 mm, H=1.00 mm; hole diameter D=0.20 mm; hole center at (0.75,1.00) mm; two inclusions with D=0.20 mm at (0.75,1.00) mm and (0.45,1.10) mm; initial crack at (0.40,0.90) mm inclined 33° to horizontal; clamped bottom edge (ux=uy=0); top edge constrained horizontally (ux=0) with controlled vertical displacement (uy=Δ)
10_1016_j_finel_2015_04_008.key_2:

- **Loads / Excitations:** Vertical displacement control (Δ); maximum cohesive strength = 1 MPa; maximum critical separation = 0.02 mm; fracture energy = 0.1 J/mm²
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Cohesive zone modeled at all element boundaries; interface compliance K = K(〚u〛); Nitsche's method applied at element interfaces; traction-separation laws govern cohesive behavior; cracks propagate along element boundaries without dedicated cohesive elements
- **Simulation Type:** Small strain elasticity; 2D domain; linear elasticity with cohesive layer; discontinuous Galerkin method; nonlinear solution using secant method for cohesive laws
10_1016_j_finel_2015_04_008.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Fracture mechanics in small strain elasticity with cohesive zone modeling; crack initiation and propagation along element boundaries without dedicated cohesive elements
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Traction–separation curves (normal and tangential); energy release rates (Γ_I, Γ_II); fracture energy (0.1 J/mm²); crack path propagation patterns; secant compliance matrix; displacement fields
- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve seamless transition between discontinuous Galerkin method and cohesive zone modeling without threshold-based discretization switching; eliminate mesh dependency in crack path prediction; enable cohesive modeling between non-matching meshes without interface elements
10_1016_j_finel_2015_04_008.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Crack propagation constrained to element boundaries; hole diameter D=0.20mm; specimen width W=1.00mm, height H=1.00mm; inclusions diameter D=0.20mm; initial crack inclined at 33° to horizontal; hole center at (0.75,1.00) mm from lower left corner
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Maximum cohesive strength=1 MPa; maximum critical separation=0.02 mm; fracture energy=0.1 J/mm²; Lamé constants satisfying 0 < μ₁ < μ < μ₂ and 0 < λ < ∞; symmetric positive semi-definite flexibility matrix K; penalty parameter γ₀ must be sufficiently large for stability; compliance must be initially zero and gradually increase with load
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Mesh dependency as major issue (reduced with finer discretization); no dedicated cohesive elements required (cracks form along continuum element boundaries); method requires Nitsche's method for interface treatment; cohesive law implementation requires secant method for nonlinear solution

10_1016_j_compgeo_2024_106517.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Hydraulic fracture propagation in fractured porous rock media using combined finite-discrete element method (FDEM) with unified pore-fracture seepage model
- **Material / Medium:**

  - Fracture aperture: initial 1.0×10⁻⁵ to 7.0×10⁻⁵ m, minimum 1.0×10⁻⁵ m, maximum 3.0×10⁻³ m
  - Intrinsic permeability: 1.0×10⁻¹³ to 1.0×10⁻¹¹ m²
  - Biot modulus: 11-22 GPa, porosity: 0.1-0.2
- **Application & Importance:** 
  - Simulating hydraulic fracturing for unconventional energy exploitation (shale gas, tight oil)
  - Analyzing stress shadowing effects in multi-stage hydraulic fracturing
  - Improving computational efficiency of pore seepage simulation by ~120× for models with ~6000 elements
  - Capturing pore pressure discontinuity across fractures while maintaining continuous pore seepage in intact rock
- **Geometry / Domain:**
  - Square plates: 70.7 mm × 70.7 mm (single fracture), 10 m × 10 m (parallel fractures)
  - Rectangular plates: 1 m × 0.25 m (transient seepage), 2 m × 0.3 m (efficiency comparison), 1 m × 0.5 m (inclined fracture)
  - Hollow cylinder: inner radius 0.05 m, outer radius 0.5 m
  - Large-scale models: 100 m × 100 m with four injection points spaced 10 m apart
  - Borehole models: 2 m × 2 m with 0.1 m radius borehole
  - Pre-existing fractures: 15 mm (small scale), 3 m (parallel fractures), 20 m (large scale)
10_1016_j_compgeo_2024_106517.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Left boundary: constant pore pressure P_L (0 MPa, 9.5 MPa, or 15 MPa depending on model)
  - Right boundary: constant pore pressure P_R (1 MPa, 4.5 MPa, or 10 MPa depending on model)
  - Bottom and top boundaries: impermeable
  - Hollow cylinder inner boundary: fixed pressure P_i = 2 MPa
  - Hollow cylinder outer boundary: fixed pressure P_o = 1 MPa
  - Fracture seepage model left boundary: constant pressure P_0 = 5 MPa
  - Fracture seepage model right boundary: impermeable
  - Vertical displacement constrained on lower and upper edges
  - Horizontal displacement constrained on lateral edges
  - Boundary fluid pressure maintained at 0 MPa for single fracture propagation
  - In situ stresses increased gradually from 0 to 4 MPa (horizontal) and 2 MPa (vertical) over 3×10⁻⁴ s for borehole injection
  - In situ stresses increased gradually from 0 to 10 MPa (horizontal) and 15 MPa (vertical) over 0.6 s for multiple hydraulic fracturing
  - Pre-existing fracture length: 15 mm (small scale), 3 m (parallel fractures), 20 m (large scale)
  - Monitoring line established at center of models for pore pressure tracking

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Constant flow rate injection at pre-existing fractures (Q = 0.002 m²/s, 0.01 m²/s, 0.004 m²/s, or 0.2 m²/s depending on model)
  - Internal fluid pressure on fracture surfaces increased from 0 to 20 MPa over 1×10⁻³ s
  - Fluid viscosity values: μ_f = 2×10⁻³ Pa·s, 1×10⁻² Pa·s, and 5×10⁻² Pa·s for comparative analysis
  - Constant injection rate at multiple points (four injection points spaced 10 m apart)
  - Borehole injection at radius r_0 = 0.1 m

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Fluid exchange between fracture (P_f) and rock matrix (P_p⁺ and P_p⁻) with exchange coefficient h_c
  - Hydro-mechanical coupling between pore pressure and mechanical deformation
  - Pore pressure discontinuity across fractures while maintaining continuous pore seepage in intact rock
  - Fracture seepage modeled using cubic law
  - Pore seepage modeled using Darcy's law
  - Master-slave node binding scheme for pore seepage continuity in intact regions
  - Dynamic updating of master-slave lists when cohesive elements break

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 2D continuous-discontinuous unified pore-fracture seepage model
  - Transient and steady-state seepage analysis
  - Combined finite-discrete element method (FDEM)
  - Explicit time integration schemes
  - Quasi-static equilibrium cases with viscous damping
  - Hydro-mechanical coupling simulation
  - Computational efficiency comparison between proposed and original approaches (r_effi)
10_1016_j_compgeo_2024_106517.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Continuous pore seepage in intact rock matrix using Darcy's law
  - Discontinuous fracture seepage along fluid-filled fractures using cubic law
  - Hydro-mechanical coupling between fluid flow and rock deformation
  - Dynamic propagation of hydraulic fractures in porous media
  - Fluid-driven fracturing process with pore pressure discontinuity across fractures

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Pore pressure distribution in rock matrix (0-9.5 MPa range)
  - Fracture fluid pressure distribution (0-7.3 MPa range)
  - Fracture aperture evolution (0-10 mm)
  - Fracture propagation paths and patterns
  - Peak fluid pressure at injection points (15-28 MPa)
  - Computational efficiency ratio (r_effi up to 120×)
  - Open displacement along fractures
  - Fluid pressure evolution over time at monitoring points

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Eliminate fictitious fluid exchange coefficient between adjacent finite elements
  - Increase computational efficiency by ~120× for models with ~6000 elements
  - Achieve continuous pore seepage in intact rock while maintaining pressure discontinuity across fractures
  - Accurately simulate stress shadowing effects in multiple hydraulic fracturing
  - Validate against analytical solutions for both steady-state and transient seepage conditions
  - Demonstrate capability to capture fluid viscosity effects on fracture propagation patterns
10_1016_j_compgeo_2024_106517.key_4:

  - Minimum fracture aperture a_r = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ m to avoid zero-division errors
  - Maximum fracture aperture a_t = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ m to 3.0 × 10⁻³ m depending on model to maintain laminar flow assumption
  - Element size constraints: 0.284 mm (single fracture), 0.042 m (parallel fractures), 7.76 mm (borehole), 1.0 m (multiple hydraulic fracturing)
  - Model dimensions: 70.7 mm × 70.7 mm (single fracture), 10 m × 10 m (parallel fractures), 2 m × 2 m (borehole), 100 m × 100 m (multiple hydraulic fracturing)
  - Pre-existing fracture constraints: 15 mm length (small scale), 3 m length (parallel fractures), 20 m length (large scale)

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Pore seepage timestep constraint: Δt_fp ≤ V/(M_b∑ᵢ kᵢ/μ_f)
  - Fracture seepage timestep constraint: Δt_ff ≤ V/(K_w∑ᵢ aᵢ³/(12μ_f))
  - Fluid viscosity range: μ_f = 2×10⁻³ to 5×10⁻² Pa·s for multiple hydraulic fracturing analysis
  - Upper limit on fluid exchange coefficient: h_c ≤ min(V_p/(M_bΔt_fp L), V_f/(K_wΔt_ff L))
  - Viscous damping coefficient constrained by η = 2√(hEρ) for all numerical cases
  - Biot modulus range: 11-22 GPa across different simulations
  - Intrinsic permeability range: 1.0×10⁻¹³ to 1.0×10⁻¹¹ m² depending on model

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Unstructured Delaunay triangulation mesh scheme used for all simulations
  - Node binding scheme applied only to pore seepage, not to cohesive zone model
  - Fluid flow channel activation only occurs when cohesive elements are completely broken (not during damage process)
  - 2D limitation: 3D extension mentioned as future work
  - Assumption that cohesive tractions from peak strength to breakage point is relatively small compared to simulated time
  - Process assumes fluid flow along fracture is laminar with low Reynolds number
  - Initial node saturation set to unity in all numerical cases
  - Fracture seepage timestep is far smaller than pore seepage timestep due to cubic dependence on fracture aperture

- Interactions/interfaces: Gear and pinion assembly modeled in Pro/E software; six-tooth model created from single tooth mesh; VH adjustment determining pinion mounting position; contact-disengagement-contact characteristic of hypoid gear meshing

- Optimization goal: Minimize square of deviation between actual and target tooth flanks; match transmission error to preset parabolic curve with 9″/6″ mesh transition amplitudes; reduce vibration noise through tooth topology optimization; achieve concave-convex tooth deviation reduction of 52.7% and 70.15%; reduce maximum contact stress by 5.25% (pinion) and 4.58% (gear); decrease loaded transmission error amplitude by 30.35%

10_1016_j_cmpb_2025_108760.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Novel Pedicle Screw-Plate System (NPSPS) for thoracic spine internal fixation
- **Material / Medium:** NPSPS elastic modulus (NPSPS-E) varied from 3.6 GPa (PEEK) to 110 GPa (titanium alloy); cortical bone Young's modulus 8040 MPa (67% normal); cancellous bone Young's modulus 34 MPa (34% normal); posterior structure Young's modulus 2345 MPa (67% normal); endplate Young's modulus 670 MPa (67% normal); nucleus pulposus Young's modulus 1 MPa; annulus fibrosus Young's modulus 4.2 MPa; articular cartilage Neo-Hookean hyperelastic (C10=30, D1=0)
- **Application & Importance:** Analysis of biomechanical properties under osteoporotic conditions; evaluation of stress shielding effects; prevention of adjacent segment degeneration and bone resorption; optimization of fixation material elastic modulus for osteoporosis patients
- **Geometry / Domain:** T7-T11 thoracic spine FE model; NPSPS fixation at T8-T10 segments; screw length 40.0mm, diameter 6.0mm; plate length 60.0mm, thickness 5.7mm; endplate thickness 0.5mm; facet joint cartilaginous gap 0.5mm; frictional contact (μ=0.3) at plate-bone, screw-bone, screw-plate, and articular surfaces interfaces
- **Boundary Conditions:** T11 vertebra fully restrained in six directions; 390 N vertical compressive load on T7 superior surface; 7.5 N·m moment applied for four motions (flexion, extension, lateral bending, axial rotation)
- **Biomechanical Metrics:** Range of motion (ROM) of surgical segments; mean von Mises stresses of surgical vertebrae (T8-T10); mean von Mises stresses of adjacent intervertebral discs (T7/8, T10/11); stress shielding ratios; total stress ratios
- **Stress Shielding Ratio Formula:** η₁ = (1 - σ_fixed/σ_unfixed) × 100%
- **Total Stress Ratio Formula:** η₂ = σ_internal_fixation/σ_surgical_segments × 100%
- **NPSPS-E Effects:** ROM of T8-T10 segments decreased from 0.51°-4.06° to 0.24°-1.45° as NPSPS-E increased; mean von Mises stress in T8-T10 vertebrae declined from 1.36 MPa-2.03 MPa to 1.15 MPa-1.79 MPa; stress shielding ratios increased from 3.66%-48.07% to 10.70%-56.20%; total stress ratios increased from 13.96%-26.96% to 52.62%-64.40%
- **Mesh Convergence:** Mesh 2 (657,769 elements, 162,015 nodes) validated as achieving stress convergence with <5% difference from Mesh 3 in most structures
10_1016_j_cmpb_2025_108760.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** T11 vertebra fully restrained in six directions; facet joints modeled with 0.5 mm cartilaginous gaps; cortical bone thickness set to 1 mm; cartilaginous endplates set to 0.5 mm
- **Loads / Excitations:** 390 N vertical compressive load applied to superior surface of T7 vertebra; 7.5 N·m moment applied to simulate four physiological motions (flexion, extension, lateral bending, axial rotation)
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Frictional contact (μ=0.3) defined between plate-bone, screw-bone, screw-plate, and articular surfaces; Boolean calculations performed at screw-bone interface; articular cartilage modeled as Neo-Hookean hyperelastic material (C10=30, D1=0); seven major ligaments implemented as three-dimensional two-node truss units (T3D2) resisting axial tension only
- **Simulation Type:** 3D parametric finite element analysis; static biomechanical simulation; nonlinear analysis due to hyperelastic articular cartilage; NPSPS elastic modulus varied from 3.6 GPa to 110 GPa in 5 GPa increments (23 distinct values); power-law regression analysis performed on results; mesh convergence validated with three distinct mesh resolutions (Mesh 1: 320,546 elements; Mesh 2: 657,769 elements; Mesh 3: 1,303,918 elements)
10_1016_j_cmpb_2025_108760.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Static biomechanical behavior of spinal column with internal fixation; stress distribution and load transfer in osteoporotic spinal segments; range of motion analysis under physiological loading; von Mises stress calculations in spinal components and implant
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Range of motion (ROM) of surgical segments (T8-T10); mean von Mises stresses of surgical vertebrae (T8-T10); mean von Mises stresses of adjacent intervertebral discs (T7/8, T10/11); stress shielding ratios of NPSPS; total stress ratios of NPSPS; power-law regression coefficients between NPSPS elastic modulus and biomechanical properties

10_1007_s10704_024_00778_3.key_1:

- **Geometry / Domain:** 3D solid elements with aspect ratios ranging from 1:1 to 1:10; coupon specimens, open-hole specimens (100 mm × 30 mm × 2 mm with 5 mm hole), and 24-layer laminated plates (150 mm × 100 mm × 4.8 mm) with [45°, 0°, -45°, 90°]3s layup; elements discretized with hexahedral shapes projected onto fracture planes for characteristic length calculation

- **Loads / Excitations:** Tensile loads applied in transverse direction for coupon specimens; low-velocity impact with 1.325 kg impactor with 16 mm diameter hemispherical tip; 12 J and 35 J impact energy levels following ASTM D7136 standard; displacement-controlled loading for tensile tests
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Zero-thickness cohesive elements for ply interfaces to account for delamination failure; bi-linear traction-separation behavior with quadratic stress failure criterion for damage initiation; mixed model fracture energy law (Benzeggagh and Kenane 1996) for delamination propagation; rigid contact between impactor and specimen
- **Simulation Type:** Abaqus/Explicit 3D transient nonlinear finite element analysis; reduced integration elements (C3D8R) used throughout; implementation using VUMAT and VUCHARLENGTH subroutines; progressive damage modeling with strain-softening behavior
10_1007_s10704_024_00778_3.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Characteristic element length calculation for regularization in composite failure simulations; strain localization phenomena in finite element analysis of composites; progressive damage modeling including fiber fracture and inter-fiber fracture modes; fracture plane orientation determination; delamination propagation using cohesive elements
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Characteristic element length values for different fracture orientations; dimensionless fracture energy (Gmt/Gmt0); force-displacement curves; tensile and compression matrix damage area; delamination area; peak force (kN); maximum displacement (mm); dissipated energy (J); ultimate strength predictions; layer-by-layer matrix damage distribution; predicted strength (kN); stress-strain responses; element characteristic length ratios
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize mesh sensitivity across different element aspect ratios (1:1 to 1:10); achieve consistent strength predictions regardless of element geometry; improve accuracy in damage pattern prediction for high aspect ratio elements; reduce directional bias in failure propagation; maintain consistent error rates between numerical and experimental results across varying mesh configurations; provide failure mode-dependent characteristic element length calculations that account for material orientation and fracture plane orientation
10_1007_s10704_024_00778_3.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Element aspect ratios constrained to 1:1, 1:2.5, 1:5, 1:7.5, and 1:10; open-hole specimens with 5 mm central hole diameter (100 mm × 30 mm × 2 mm); 24-layer laminate specimens with [45°,0°,-45°,90°]3s layup (150 mm × 100 mm × 4.8 mm3); hexahedral elements used for all implementations; reduced integration elements (C3D8R) employed throughout; coupon specimens discretized with solid elements of 0.2 mm × 0.2 mm × 0.5 mm (1:2.5 aspect ratio)
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Volumetric method (VM) exhibits >400% error for 1:10 aspect ratio elements; consistent error rates must be maintained across aspect ratios (SPM achieves 7.6% error for 1:1 vs. 35.4% for 1:10 with VM); maximum error threshold of 12.3% for dissipated energy in low-velocity impact simulations; mesh sensitivity must be reduced for high aspect ratio elements while maintaining physical accuracy of damage patterns; fracture energy must remain consistent regardless of element geometry
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Computational time increases from 301 to 5060 minutes when changing aspect ratio from 1:5 to 1:1; maintaining 1:1 aspect ratio leads to computationally inefficient models with excessive CPU time; implementation restricted to Abaqus/Explicit using VUMAT and VUCHARLENGTH subroutines; the SPM algorithm requires transformation to local coordinate system with x'y' parallel to fracture plane; element projection requires calculation of 4, 5, and 6 nodes for tetrahedron, pentahedron, and hexahedron elements respectively; method limited to elements that form convex polygons when projected onto fracture plane

10_1016_j_finel_2016_02_001.key_1:
- **Subject of analysis**: Fracture process in plain concrete, transitioning from continuum (smeared micro-crack) representation to discrete macro-crack description using coupled continuum-discontinuum modeling
- **Material properties**: 
  - Plain concrete with Young's modulus E = 30-35 GPa
  - Poisson's ratio ν = 0.0-0.2 (0.0 in uniaxial tension tests to replicate 1D state)
  - Tensile strength f_t = 2.1-3.0 MPa across different simulations
  - Fracture energy G_f = 70-120 N/m in various test configurations
  - Characteristic length l = 1.5-10 mm depending on test type
  - Non-locality parameter m = 2 in most simulations
  - Softening parameters κ_u varying from 1.74×10^-3 to 6.0×10^-3
- **Application purpose**: Accurately simulate concrete fracture progression from initial micro-crack formation (fracture process zone) to distinct macro-crack development while maintaining physical realism and energy conservation
- **Geometries tested**:
  - Uniaxial tension specimen: 100×150 mm with 10 mm weak zone at mid-height
  - Three-point bending beams: un-notched with 150 mm height and notched beams with 80 mm height
  - Nooru-Mohamed test: 200×200 mm double edge notched specimen with 25×5 mm notches
  - Schlangen test: 440×100 mm single-edge notched beam with 20 mm deep notch
  - All simulations conducted under 2D plane stress conditions
10_1016_j_finel_2016_02_001.key_2:
- **Boundary constraints**:
  - Uniaxial tension: bottom nodes fixed vertically, bottom mid-node fixed horizontally, vertical displacement increment (Δu = 0.1 mm) applied to top edge nodes
  - Three-point bending: symmetry along vertical axis, bottom supports with fixed vertical displacement, vertical displacement control at top
  - Nooru-Mohamed test: horizontal shear force (P_s) applied to rigid steel frames, vertical tensile displacement prescribed after shear force reached, linear elastic behavior enforced at top-right and bottom-left corners to prevent unwanted cracking
  - Schlangen test: four-point anti-symmetric shear loading, supports at bottom of beam

- **Loading conditions**:
  - Uniaxial tension: vertical displacement increment (Δu = 0.1 mm)
  - Three-point bending: final vertical displacement u_fin = 0.4 mm
  - Nooru-Mohamed test: horizontal shear force P_s = 5 kN, 10 kN, or 27.5 kN followed by vertical tensile displacement
  - Schlangen test: crack mouth sliding displacement (CMSD) as driven variable using indirect displacement control

- **Model interactions**:
  - Coupled continuum-discontinuum transition at κ_cd threshold
  - Transfer of stresses/strains between continuum and XFEM regions
  - Crack activation checked in integration points at crack front and in circular section (radius l_crk, angle φ_crk)
  - Mixed zone length d_mix = 0-5 cm where continuum and discontinuum descriptions coexist

- **Simulation parameters**:
  - 2D plane stress conditions throughout
  - Quasi-static monotonic loading regime
  - Nonlinear analysis with softening behavior
  - Mesh types: T3 triangular and Q4 quadrilateral elements
  - Mesh densities: coarse (600 elements), medium (1,260 elements), fine (2,280 elements)
  - Convergence criteria: r_max ≤ 0.01q̃ and c_max ≤ 0.01Δu_max
10_1016_j_finel_2016_02_001.key_3:
- **Physics Solved**:
  - Fracture progression in concrete from diffuse micro-cracking to discrete macro-crack formation
  - Energy dissipation during transition from continuous damage to discrete crack representation
  - Strain localization and fracture process zone (FPZ) development
  - Mixed-mode crack propagation under shear-tension loading conditions

- **Target Outputs**:
  - Force-displacement curves with smooth transition between continuum and discontinuum regimes
  - Crack patterns and trajectories matching experimental observations
  - Crack height (h_c) measurements in Nooru-Mohamed test specimens
  - Crack mouth opening displacement (CMOD) evolution
  - Horizontal displacement (u_x) and strain (ε_xx) fields in fracture process zones
  - Number of global equilibrium iterations required for convergence
  - Softening parameter (κ) distribution and evolution

- **Optimization Goal**:
  - Achieve smooth transition between continuum and discontinuum descriptions without energy loss
  - Eliminate oscillations on load-displacement curves during crack representation transition
  - Develop mesh-independent results for fracture simulations
  - Properly capture localized zone width matching experimental DIC measurements
  - Accurately reproduce experimental crack patterns in both mode-I and mixed-mode conditions
  - Maintain correct energy dissipation balance during the continuous-discontinuous transition
  - Identify optimal transition point (κ_cd) based on experimental fracture process zone development
10_1016_j_finel_2016_02_001.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space Constraints**:
  - Maximum finite element size in localized zones ≤ 1.5mm (for characteristic length l = 2mm)
  - Mesh refinement requirements: 20, 40, and 80 elements along vertical symmetry axis for coarse, medium, and fine meshes respectively
  - Element size in fracture process zones < 0.5mm for notched beam simulations
  - Characteristic length l constrained by experimental DIC measurements (fracture process zone width 5-6mm)
  - Non-local averaging radius truncated at r_max = 3l (despite Gaussian function's unbounded support)

- **Performance/Physics Limits**:
  - Linear elastic behavior enforced at top-right and bottom-left corners to prevent unwanted cracking
  - Convergence criteria: r_max ≤ 0.01q̃ and c_max ≤ 0.01Δu_max (standard tolerance 0.01)
  - Shear stiffness T_s = 0 N/m³ by default (zero shear stiffness in most simulations)
  - Transition point κ_cd constrained to physical fracture progression (default 50% of tensile strength)
  - Maximum shear force P_s = 27.5 kN for Nooru-Mohamed test (path '4c')
  - Isotropic damage models cannot provide realistic crack patterns in tension-compression regimes

- **Process/Manufacturing Constraints**:
  - Mixed zone length d_mix = 0-5 cm (1 cm optimal for elasto-plastic models, 0 for damage models)
  - Crack activation criterion checked in circular section with φ_crk = 30° and l_crk = 5-6 mm
  - Averaging length l_av constrained to 6.0-7.5 mm depending on test configuration
  - Algorithm 'B1' required for stable convergence with mesh-independent results
  - Minimum 200 time increments required for numerical completion
  - Switch-off zone width for non-local softening = 6×l to embrace all integration points within active softening
  - Crack growth activation limited to elements with maximum size matching characteristic length requirements

10_1016_j_cad_2022_103267.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** 3D subsurface geological structural modeling; creation of conformable geological surfaces and layers from sparse sample points; implicit representation using scalar fields for horizons and faults.

- **Material / Medium:** Subsurface rock formations with geological interfaces; materials not specified by type but differentiated by geological age and structural properties.

- **Application & Importance:** Numerical representation of subsurface structures from borehole data and seismic image interpretation points; creating sealed structural models where geological layers do not intersect; handling discontinuities (faults) while minimizing curvature artifacts; enabling accurate interpolation from sparse data.

- **Geometry / Domain:** 3D tetrahedral mesh domain with internal boundaries at fault surfaces; mesh vertices duplicated across faults to introduce discontinuities; domain contains multiple non-intersecting horizons represented by level sets of scalar fields; regularization operators (ℛ₁, ℛ₃, ℛ₆) applied to minimize curvature of implicit functions; boundary-free discretization that does not assume vanishing Neumann boundary conditions.
10_1016_j_cad_2022_103267.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - No explicit boundary conditions required; method designed for cases where boundary conditions are unknown
  - Traditional finite element methods assume vanishing Neumann boundary conditions (∇ϕ(x)⋅n = 0 for x ∈ Ω_B), but this introduces artifacts
  - Mesh vertices on faults are duplicated to introduce discontinuities in the grid
  - Each discontinuity surface (fault) introduces an internal boundary within the computational domain
  - Boundary-free discretization that does not impose constraints on the implicit function ϕ(x) at boundary points

- **Loads / Excitations:** 
  - Sparse geological sample points from borehole data and seismic image interpretation
  - Horizon data points representing geological interfaces between different rock materials
  - Input consists of point sets from multiple horizons and fault surfaces (e.g., 8 horizons and 27 fault surfaces in Fig. 1)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** 
  - Geological discontinuities (faults) are represented by duplicated vertices in the mesh
  - Multiple conformable geological surfaces (horizons) represented by one single scalar field
  - Mesh is conformal to faults and generated to be discontinuous across fault surfaces
  - Data system D̄̄Φ̄ = f̄ assembled from geological interpretation data supplemented with regularization system R̄̄Φ̄ = 0̄

- **Simulation Type:** 
  - 3D static implicit geological structural modeling (not time-dependent)
  - Linear system of equations (data system and regularization system)
  - Finite element discretization on tetrahedral meshes
  - Applicable to both structured and unstructured grids
  - Mesh-based implicit modeling approach (not mesh-free)
10_1016_j_cad_2022_103267.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Implicit geological structural modeling using scalar fields
  - Interpolation of sparse geological data (horizon points and fault surfaces) through discretized Laplacian and Hessian regularization energies
  - Calculation of scalar field curvature on tetrahedral meshes

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Scalar field φ(x) representing geological structures
  - Conformable geological surfaces (horizons) as level sets of the scalar field
  - Sealed structural models with non-intersecting layers
  - Curvature of the implicit function at all points
  - Fault-horizon contact lines
  - Extracted geological surfaces and isolines

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Minimize the curvature of the implicit function φ(x) while interpolating sparse geological data
  - Find a scalar function that satisfies "dₖᵀH̄̄dₖ = 0 for all directional vectors dₖ" (zero curvature condition)
  - Eliminate boundary artifacts introduced by inappropriate boundary conditions
  - Achieve smooth interpolation of geological data without introducing artificial curvature concentrations
10_1016_j_cad_2022_103267.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Mesh must be conformal to faults and geological discontinuities
  - Vertices on faults must be duplicated to introduce discontinuities in the grid
  - Each discontinuity surface introduces internal boundaries within the computational domain
  - Mesh must accommodate multiple non-intersecting horizons represented by a single scalar field
  - Traditional mesh constraint requiring "each triangle of the mesh should have at least one internal vertex" is difficult to enforce in practice, especially with discontinuities

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Must not impose vanishing Neumann boundary conditions (∇ϕ(x)⋅n = 0 for x ∈ Ω_B), which causes boundary artifacts
  - Must handle sparse geological data without creating artificial curvature concentrations
  - Regularization operators must minimize curvature while preserving geological consistency
  - On tetrahedral meshes, minimizing ℛ₁ may not necessarily minimize the curvature of φ as defined by dₖᵀH̄̄dₖ = 0 for all directional vectors dₖ
  - ℛ₃ is identified as "the least effective of the three regularizations operators in terms of curvature minimization"
  - Must handle isolated fault blocks with insufficient constraining data (e.g., all data lying on a vertical plane)

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Boundary conditions are unknown in subsurface modeling applications
  - Mesh must be generated to be discontinuous across fault surfaces
  - Geological inconsistencies can occur (e.g., different layer thicknesses across faults, reversal of fault throw)
  - Method must work with both structured and unstructured grids
  - Must handle cases where constraining data is sparse or geometrically limited (e.g., all data in a fault block lying on a vertical plane)

10_1016_j_engfracmech_2023_109803.key_1:
- Subject: Thermal failure process simulation of quasi-brittle solids under thermo-mechanical loading
- Materials: LdB granite (Young's modulus 67 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.33, density 2650 kg/m³, thermal conductivity 3.5 W/m·°C, specific heat 1015 J/kg·°C, thermal expansion coefficient 3.5×10⁻⁶, tensile strength 6.55 MPa, fracture toughness 0.4 MPa√m); benchmark material (Young's modulus 340 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.22, density 2450 kg/m³, thermal conductivity 300 W/m·K, specific heat 0.775 J/kg·K, thermal expansion coefficient 8.0×10⁻⁶)
- Applications: Nuclear waste storage facilities, geothermal resource exploitation, and oil exploitation where thermal loads impact deformation and fracture of quasi-brittle solids
- Geometries: 1 m × 1 m square plates with 0.5 m initial edge crack for benchmark examples; 1 mm × 1 mm square plates with 0.5 mm edge flaw for tensile/shear tests; 220 mm high LdB granite specimen with 30 mm outer diameter and 3 mm inner diameter borehole
- Boundary conditions: Dirichlet (temperature), Neumann (heat flux), and Robin (convection) boundary conditions applied to edges; 300 K bottom temperature, 400 K initial temperature in benchmark examples; 20°C initial temperature with 160°C environment temperature for LdB granite specimen
- Failure criteria: Maximum principal tensile stress criterion for holes, Maximum tangential stress criterion (MTS) for cracks
- Thermal loading cases: Temperature variations from -75 K to +75 K in single edge flaw tests; convective heat transfer coefficient h = 1.0×10⁵ W/m²·K for LdB granite specimen
- Crack representation: Smeared crack method using field variable d with degradation function g(d) = (1-d)² + m (m = 10⁻⁶)
10_1016_j_engfracmech_2023_109803.key_2:
- Dirichlet boundary condition: Top edge temperature set to 300 K (benchmark 1), 375 K (tensile case 2), 350 K (tensile case 3), 250 K (tensile case 4), 225 K (tensile case 5), 350 K (shear case 2), 330 K (shear case 3), 270 K (shear case 4), 250 K (shear case 5); Bottom edge temperature fixed at 400 K (benchmark examples), 300 K (tensile/shear tests), 20°C (LdB granite)
- Neumann boundary condition: Top edge heat flux q̄_n = 5.0×10⁴ W/m² (benchmark 2); Right edge heat flux q̄_n = 5.0×10⁴ W/m² (benchmark 4)
- Robin boundary condition: Top edge convective heat transfer coefficient h = 1.0×10⁵ W/m²·K with environment temperature T₀ = 300 K (benchmark 3); Void edge convective heat transfer coefficient h = 1.0×10⁵ W/m²·K with T₀ = 300 K (benchmark 4); Inner hole boundary convective heat transfer coefficient h = 1.0×10⁵ W/m²·°C with environment temperature Tᵣ = 160°C (LdB granite)
- Mechanical boundary conditions: Fixed bottom edge; Horizontal displacement constrained on left and right edges; Vertical displacement applied to top edge (Δu = 0.5×10⁻⁵ mm or 0.5×10⁻⁶ mm in tensile test); Horizontal displacement applied to top edge (Δu = 1×10⁻⁵ mm or 1×10⁻⁶ mm in shear test)
- Adiabatic boundaries: Left and right edges (benchmark 1); Left edge (benchmark 4); Initial crack considered adiabatic in all thermo-mechanical tests
- Thermal loading rates: Temperature change rate ΔT = ±0.1 K per time step in tensile and shear tests
- Time integration: Backward difference method (θ = 1) for transient heat equation
- Time steps: Δt_Th = 1.0×10⁻³ s (benchmark examples); 0.5×10⁻⁹ s (tensile test); 1.0×10⁻⁹ s (shear test)
- Crack representation: Adiabatic crack interface with degraded thermal conductivity at crack location
- Coupling mechanism: Thermal strain calculated as ε^T = α(T-T_a)I where α = 8.0×10⁻⁶ (benchmark) or 3.5×10⁻⁶ (LdB granite)
- Simulation domain: 2D plane stress condition for all examples
- Analysis type: Transient coupled thermo-mechanical simulation with field-enriched finite element method (TM-FE-FEM)
10_1016_j_engfracmech_2023_109803.key_3:
- Physics solved: Coupled transient thermo-mechanical behavior including heat conduction, thermal deformation, and crack propagation in quasi-brittle solids
- Target outputs: Temperature distribution (K), displacement field (m), crack path coordinates, damage field (field variable d), maximum principal stress distribution (Pa), stress intensity factors, temperature jumps across cracks (K), comparison metrics with ABAQUS FEM results
- Validation objectives: Accurate representation of temperature discontinuities across adiabatic cracks, proper simulation of heat conduction under Dirichlet (prescribed temperature), Neumann (prescribed heat flux), and Robin (convective) boundary conditions, correct crack propagation direction under different thermal loading scenarios, reproduction of experimental thermal fracture patterns in LdB granite specimen
- Simulation metrics: Minimum/maximum temperature values, displacement profiles along AA' and BB' line segments, crack path deviations under thermal loading (±75 K, ±50 K, ±30 K cases), temperature jump magnitudes across cracks, stress concentration patterns around boreholes
- Method validation: Comparative analysis with ABAQUS FEM results for temperature and displacement fields, verification against laboratory experiments on LdB granite thermal fracture, demonstration of method capability for handling mixed boundary conditions and complex geometries with holes and cracks
10_1016_j_engfracmech_2023_109803.key_4:
- Geometric constraints: 1 m × 1 m square plate with 0.5 m initial horizontal edge crack at center of left boundary for benchmark examples; 1 mm × 1 mm square plate with 0.5 mm edge flaw for tensile/shear tests; 220 mm high LdB granite specimen with 30 mm outer diameter and 3 mm inner diameter borehole
- Time step limitations: Δt_Th = 1.0×10⁻³ s for thermal integration in benchmark examples; 0.5×10⁻⁹ s for tensile test; 1.0×10⁻⁹ s for shear test
- Field variable constraints: Exponential function parameters a = 6 and b = 2 for smeared crack representation; degradation function g(d) = (1-d)² + m with m = 10⁻⁶ to avoid singularity
- Crack representation: Adiabatic crack assumption where thermal conductivity and thermal stability degrade at crack location
- Material limits: LdB granite tensile strength = 6.55 MPa; LdB granite fracture toughness = 0.4 MPa√m; Young's modulus of LdB granite follows Weibull statistical model with homogeneity index m = 20
- Temperature constraints: Maximum temperature of 400 K in benchmark examples; 20°C initial temperature for LdB granite specimen with 160°C environment temperature at inner hole boundary

10_1016_j_finel_2015_08_002.key_2:
- Boundaries & Constraints: 100m straight horizontal wellbore with 8in diameter; drillpipe with 6in outer diameter and 5in inner diameter; wellbore trajectory defined by discretized well points forming reference coordinate system; spiralled section between 20m and 80m depth; elliptical wellbores defined by major axis (a), minor axis (b), and tilt (β); spiralled wellbores defined by period (P) and amplitude (A) with offset equations y(m) = A/2 sin(2πm/P) and z(m) = A/2 cos(2πm/P)
- Loads / Excitations: Weight of the pipe; applied loads; contact force calculated as f_c = k_c (d - c)+ where k_c = 10^7 N/m, d is total lateral displacement, c is clearance; contact force components f_cy = k_c (u_y/d)(d - c) and f_cz = k_c (u_z/d)(d - c)
- Interactions / Interfaces: Pipe-wellbore contact detected when total lateral displacement exceeds clearance; contact force direction aligned with pipe movement for circular holes but calculated from tangent to wellbore surface for noncircular holes; frictional contact applied when displacement exceeds clearance; clearance calculated as minimum distance between pipe and wellbore for given movement direction
- Simulation Type: Nonlinear static finite element analysis; 3D beam elements with Co-rotational formulation; Newton-Raphson iterative solution; large displacements and rotations with small strains; geometric nonlinearities handled through rigid body motion decomposition
10_1016_j_finel_2015_08_002.key_3:

10_1016_j_compstruct_2021_114711.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** 3D braided composite structures generated by 1×1 four-step braiding process, analyzed using multi-scale finite element method with three-cell model (interior, surface, corner cells)
- **Material / Medium:** T300 carbon fiber (E₁=220 GPa, E₂=13.8 GPa, G₁₂=9.0 GPa, ν₁₂=0.2, ν₂₃=0.25); TDE-85 resin matrix (E=4.5 GPa, G=0.34 GPa, ν=0.34)
- **Application & Importance:** Mechanical behavior analysis for aerospace applications (aircraft stiffened skin, propeller blades, fuselage frames, cabin window panels); prediction of effective elastic modulus and microscopic stress for damage/failure analysis
- **Geometry / Domain:** Three-cell model with interior cell (Wᵢ=2√2d, Tᵢ=2√2d, tanγ=4d/h), surface cell (Wₛ=2√2d, Tₛ=2√2d, tanθ=2d/h), and corner cell (Wc=√2d, Tc=√2d, tanβ=4d/3h); relationship tanγ=2tanθ=3tanβ; periodic unit cells with height h; 1×1 four-step braiding pattern with yarn carriers arranged in rows and columns
10_1016_j_compstruct_2021_114711.key_2:

- **Loads / Excitations:** Unit initial strain fields applied to solve characteristic displacement; Macroscopic uniaxial tensile load with fracture strain of 0.00891 for specimen 1; Nodal force corresponding to unit initial strain (f⁰); Nodal force corresponding to characteristic displacement (f*); Macroscopic displacement (u⁰) from macro-scale analysis
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Matrix-fiber interfaces in multiphase model; Common plane displacement continuity requirements between different cell types; Periodic boundaries between adjacent unit cells; Blended elements containing both fiber and matrix material at Gauss point level
- **Simulation Type:** Multi-scale (macro/meso/micro) linear elastic analysis; Asymptotic homogenization method; 3D four-step braiding process simulation; Static analysis; Periodic unit cell analysis; Multiphase finite element approach with regular cuboid elements; Steady-state mechanical analysis; δ = 10⁻⁹ (mesoscale y ~ nm, macroscale x ~ m)
10_1016_j_compstruct_2021_114711.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Equivalent engineering elastic modulus (E11, E22); Poisson's ratio (v12); microscopic stress (σ_z) distribution in interior, surface, and corner cells; fiber volume fraction (V_f); braiding angles (γ, θ, β); characteristic displacement field (χ); nodal forces corresponding to unit initial strain (f⁰) and characteristic displacement (f*)
- **Optimization Goal:** Accurate estimation of effective mechanical properties of braided preforms with different braiding parameters (braiding angle, pitch length, fiber volume fraction); prediction of microscopic stress for damage and failure behavior analysis; validation of calculated equivalent engineering elastic modulus against experimental measurements; optimization of mechanical performance through parameter variation (e.g., braiding angle effect on elastic modulus)
10_1016_j_compstruct_2021_114711.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Three-cell model with interior cell (Wᵢ=2√2d, Tᵢ=2√2d), surface cell (Wₛ=2√2d, Tₛ=2√2d), and corner cell (Wc=√2d, Tc=√2d); braiding angle relationship tanγ=2tanθ=3tanβ; preform volume defined as V=(2m+2)(2n+2)d²; braiding pitch length h=4d/tanγ; 1×1 four-step braiding pattern requiring identical distance traveled by all rows/columns in each step
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Fracture strength of specimen 1 is 665 MPa with fracture strain of 0.00891; maximum microscale stress in surface cell (4.91 GPa) exceeds macroscopic fracture stress; fiber volume fraction Vf=CiVi+CsVs+CcVc; yarn packing factor ε=Df²/kd² where Df=4λ/πρ; constituent material properties constrained to T300 carbon fiber (E₁=220 GPa, E₂=13.8 GPa) and TDE-85 resin (E=4.5 GPa)
- **Process/Manufacturing:** 3D four-step braiding process where yarns interweave at angle deviating from weaving direction; one braiding cycle requires four steps per yarn carrier; preform advances by pitch length after tightening; characteristic displacement field must be continuous on common planes between cell types; multiphase finite element method requires regular cuboid elements without separate fiber/matrix meshing; periodic boundary conditions must be applied to finite element model; mesh dependence exists but is weak (verified with different element numbers from 10×10×10 to 20×20×20)

10_1007_s40314_022_02144_2.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Swift-Hohenberg equation modeling phase field dynamics and pattern formation
- **Material / Medium:** Density field (u) with physical parameter 0 < ε < 1; applied to supercooled liquids for crystal growth studies
- **Application & Importance:** Studying thermal fluctuations in Rayleigh-Bénard instability, phase transitions, and nonequilibrium processing where analytical solutions are intractable
- **Geometry / Domain:** Convex polygonal domain Ω with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions; specific test domains include (-20,20)×(-20,20), (-30,30)×(-30,30), and circular domain centered at (90,90) with radius 90
10_1007_s40314_022_02144_2.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions ∂ₙu = ∂ₙω = ∂ₙμ = 0 on ∂Ω × (0, T]; Computational domains: (−20, 20) × (−20, 20), (−30, 30) × (−30, 30), circular domain with center (90, 90) and radius 90
- **Loads / Excitations:** Initial condition u(x, y, 0) = 0.2 + 0.02rand(x, y) (random perturbation); Initial condition u(x, y, 0) = 0.14 + αrand(x, y) with α = 1 for crystal nucleus at (90, 90) (diameter 4); Physical parameter values: ε = 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.45, 0.5; Analytical solution u(x, y, t) = e⁻ᵗ cos(πx) cos(2πx) for convergence testing
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Coupled variables with ω = u³ - εu + (1 + Δ)μ and μ = (1 + Δ)u; Mixed formulation with three variables (u, ω, μ) interacting through time evolution equation ∂ₜu = -ω
- **Simulation Type:** Transient time-dependent simulation; 2D spatial domain; Nonlinear fourth-order partial differential equation; Second-order finite element scheme; Time step sizes τ = 1, τ = 1/2, τ = 1×10⁻⁹; Spatial mesh sizes h = 1/4, h = 2, h = τ/2; Final times T = 10, T = 100, T = 2000
10_1007_s40314_022_02144_2.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Pattern formation dynamics in nonequilibrium systems; Phase transitions; Thermal fluctuations in Rayleigh-Bénard instability; Crystal growth in supercooled liquids
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** L² errors between numerical and analytical solutions; Convergence rates (spatial and temporal); Energy dissipation/evolution (E₂(u, μ)); Phase variable (u) evolution; Pattern formation characteristics (laminar structures, crystal growth)
- **Optimization Goal:** Unconditional energy stability of numerical scheme; Second-order temporal accuracy; Unconditional unique solvability (without time step restrictions); Boundedness of discrete phase variable for any time/space mesh sizes; Accurate representation of physical phenomena including pattern formation and crystal growth
10_1007_s40314_022_02144_2.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Convex polygonal domain Ω; Quasi-uniform, shape-regular, conforming triangulations; Specific test domains: (−20, 20) × (−20, 20), (−30, 30) × (−30, 30), circular domain centered at (90, 90) with radius 90; 2D spatial domain (d = 2); P₁ and P₂ finite element discretization spaces
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Physical parameter constraint 0 < ε < 1; Energy dissipation law d/dt E₂(u(t), μ(t)) = −‖ω‖² ≤ 0 must be preserved; Boundedness of discrete phase variable required for any time and space mesh sizes; Unconditional energy stability requirement (no time step restrictions for stability); Unconditional unique solvability requirement (no time step restrictions for uniqueness); Density field u must satisfy the fourth-order Swift-Hohenberg equation
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Second-order finite element scheme in mixed formulation; Diffusive Crank-Nicolson time stepping (replacing standard Crank-Nicolson); Spatial discretization with h = τ/2 for temporal convergence tests; Time step constraints avoided through modified scheme (standard Crank-Nicolson requires τ ≤ 2/ε but the proposed scheme removes this limitation); Proper discretization of nonlinear terms required to maintain energy stability

10_1016_j_cad_2019_04_006.key_2:

- Loads / Excitations: Magnetic field (B) and dB/dt from MD_DW_exp16ms_catIII event; worst instant (t_w) at 380 ms with highest ||dB/dt|| · ||B||; B field values: B_X = -0.09 T, B_Y = -0.242 T, B_Z = 0.332 T for specific IAM simulation; constant dB_w/dt during simulation; current equations derived from B and dB/dt parameters; force curve fitting to F = F_max(1 - e^(-t/τ))

- Simulation Type: Transient 3D finite element analysis; ANSYS Maxwell simulation with T-Omega formulation; reduced time window to ~95% of estimated maximum force (22 ms for OH-ORU, 24 ms for IAM); mesh sensitivity analyses performed with relative differences kept under 1.3% (OH-ORU) and 2.6% (IAM)

- Optimization Goal: Minimize simulation resources while maintaining results within ITER accuracy requirement of 5% deviation; achieve conservative force results compared to full transient simulation; reduce total simulated time to ~95% of estimated maximum force (22 ms for OH-ORU, 24 ms for IAM) instead of simulating to 99% (saving 27% and 20% computation time respectively); ensure intermediate accuracy of results (under 5% error) with local models while including necessary structural connections
