10_1016_j_cad_2023_103574.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Space-time finite element methods for constructing 2D surface meshes embedded in 3D space-time (2D+t) and 3D hypersurface meshes embedded in 4D space-time (3D+t)
- **Material / Medium:** Mathematical methodology for fluid-structure interaction (FSI) problems; applicable to moving boundaries with linear or non-linear dependence on boundary motion; works with elastic properties of structures and local Reynolds/Mach numbers of fluids
- **Application & Importance:** Enables accurate simulation of dynamic phenomena with moving boundaries; overcomes limitations of traditional finite element methods restricted to stationary 3D geometries; allows handling of arbitrary large-scale boundary motions where extrusion-based methods fail; provides boundary-conforming hypervolume meshes in 4D space-time
- **Geometry / Domain:** Space-time domains partitioned into time slabs (Q₀, Q₁, ..., Qₙ₋₁); each slab consists of initial plane/hyperplane Ω(tₙ), terminating plane/hyperplane Ω(tₙ₊₁), and intermediate surface Pₙ; test cases include: stationary/expanding circles (2D+t), rotating cross (2D+t), stationary/expanding spheres (3D+t), rotating ellipsoid (3D+t), and rotating tandem ellipsoids (3D+t); triangular prisms in 4D space subdivided into 10 or 14 tetrahedral elements for mesh construction
10_1016_j_cad_2023_103574.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Space-time domain partitioned into slabs with spatial hyperplanes Ω(t) at t₀ < t₁ < ... < tₙ < ... < tₙ
  - Each slab Qₙ defined by initial plane/hyperplane Ω(tₙ), terminating plane/hyperplane Ω(tₙ₊₁), and intermediate surface Pₙ
  - Complete spatial CAD geometry required at time t = tₙ and t = tₙ₊₁
  - Characteristic element sizes specified near boundaries: h_circle/h_square/h_time for 2D cases, h_sphere/h_cube/h_time for 3D cases
  - Boundary conditions maintain conformity between adjacent space-time slabs through synchronization of mesh indices
  - Final vertex locations projected to CAD surface Γ(tₙ₊₁) to correct time-integration errors

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Local velocity of space-time CAD surface used to compute vertex trajectories via vₜ = dxₜ/dt
  - Time interval dt = tₙ₊₁ - tₙ subdivided into M subintervals for trajectory calculation
  - Forward Euler time-stepping method applied to solve ordinary differential equation for vertex trajectories
  - Angular velocity (0, 0, 0.1π) rads/s for rotating cross test case
  - Radial expansion speed m = 0.25 for expanding circle/sphere test cases
  - Rotational angular velocity ω = π/2 rads/s for rotating ellipsoid test case

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Initial plane mesh identical to terminating plane mesh from previous space-time slab to maintain volume mesh conformity
  - Vertices on initial and terminating planes connected to form quadrilaterals (2D+t) or triangular prisms (3D+t)
  - Intermediate surface Pₙ formed by connecting boundary edges/faces between initial and terminating planes
  - Mesh synchronization through rigorous bookkeeping with consecutive index numbering across initial, intermediate, and terminating surfaces
  - Triangular prisms in 3D+t subdivided into tetrahedral elements (10 or 14 elements per prism)

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Transient space-time finite element simulations in 2D+t and 3D+t domains
  - Space-time slabs generated sequentially "on an as-needed basis" starting from earliest times
  - Fully-unstructured meshing approach for boundary-conforming surface/hypersurface meshes
  - Second-order convergence rate demonstrated for all numerical experiments
  - Time intervals: [0,1] for stationary/expanding sphere/circle tests, [0,20] for rotating cross test
  - 2D+t surface meshing with triangular elements, 3D+t hypersurface meshing with tetrahedral elements
10_1016_j_cad_2023_103574.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Fluid-structure interaction (FSI) problems with moving boundaries; dynamic phenomena exhibiting linear/non-linear dependence on boundary motion with coupled relationships between structural elastic properties and local fluid Reynolds/Mach numbers

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - Surface area error for 2D+t space-time surface meshes
  - Hypersurface volume error for 3D+t space-time hypersurface meshes
  - Convergence rates of numerical errors with increasing mesh resolution
  - Approximate surface areas calculated via summation of triangular element areas using Heron's formula
  - Approximate hypersurface volumes calculated via summation of tetrahedral element volumes
  - Comparison against analytically-determined exact values for stationary/expanding circles/spheres and rotating objects
  - Element counts and vertex counts across mesh refinement sequences

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Achieve second-order convergence in surface area/hypersurface volume errors as mesh resolution increases
  - Generate boundary-conforming hypersurface meshes in 4D space-time with minimal required CAD information (only spatial geometry at tₙ and tₙ₊₁ plus surface velocity)
  - Enable simulation of arbitrary large-scale boundary motions where traditional extrusion-based methods fail
  - Maintain mesh conformity between adjacent space-time slabs while accommodating complex boundary motions
10_1016_j_cad_2023_103574.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Cannot handle destructive or non-affine changes to geometry (e.g., two objects colliding or single object splitting)
  - Cannot accommodate perforation or significant folding of the body's surface
  - Requires initial surface/hypersurface mesh connectivity to be maintained throughout simulation
  - Space-time domain must be partitionable into sequential slabs with known geometry at boundaries
  - Complete spatial CAD geometry (or prediction) required at start and end of each time interval (tₙ and tₙ₊₁)
  - Boundary motion must not cause topological changes to the geometry
  - Space-time slabs must be formed sequentially "on an as-needed basis" starting from earliest times

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Surface velocity must be known or predictable for time interval (tₙ, tₙ₊₁)
  - Connectivity of edge vertices must remain unchanged during simulation
  - Requires predictor-corrector approach when space-time domain geometry is not known a priori
  - Mesh conformity must be preserved between adjacent space-time slabs
  - Quadrilateral face splittings of triangular prisms must be identical under reflections/rotations of the prism
  - Method is limited to problems where boundary motion has linear or (sometimes) non-linear dependence on boundary motion

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Computationally more expensive than extrusion-based methods (generates new meshes for each space-time slab)
  - Time interval dt = tₙ₊₁ - tₙ must be subdivided into M subintervals for trajectory calculation
  - Requires forward Euler time-stepping method for solving vertex trajectory ODEs
  - Final vertex locations must be projected to CAD surface to correct time-integration errors
  - Implementation requires surface mesh at initial time as input (or ghost slab construction)
  - Mesh refinement requires characteristic element sizes to be decreased by factor of 1.25-2.0 between successive meshes
  - Implementation is based on the JENRE® Multiphysics Framework (as stated in numerical experiments)

- Fiber path functions: linear θ(x) = 2(T₀ - T₁)/a ||x + T₀; nonlinear θ(x) = A||x² + 2(T₁ - T₀)/a - (a²/A)x + T₀ where T₀ is fiber angle at x=0, T₁ at x=±a/2, T₂ at x=±a/4
- Mesh density of 100×100 elements for sufficient accuracy with buckling load errors less than 0.05%
10_1016_j_cja_2025_103457.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - SSSS-Uni: w = 0 at x = ±a/2 or y = ±a/2; v = 0 at (-a/2, -a/2); u = 0, v = 0 at (a/2, -a/2)
  - SSCC: w = 0, αx = αy = 0 at x = ±a/2; v = 0 at (-a/2, -a/2); u = 0, v = 0 at (a/2, -a/2)
  - SSSS-Bi: w = 0 at x = ±a/2 or y = ±a/2; v = 0 at (-a/2, -a/2); u = 0, v = 0 at (a/2, -a/2)
  - Where u, v, w are displacements in x-, y-, and z-directions; αx and αy are rotation angles around x- and y-axis

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Unidirectional compression applied evenly on two parallel sides for SSSS-Uni and SSCC cases
  - Bidirectional compression applied uniformly on all four sides for SSSS-Bi case
  - Static load of Ny = 1 N/mm used for prebuckling stress analysis
  - Nondimensional critical buckling load factor defined as Ncr = Ncr,av·a²/(E₁·h³) where Ncr,av = (1/a)∫[-a/2 to a/2] Nx(-a/2, y) dy

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Fiber paths generated using shifted fiber method with constant thickness maintained by setting displacement equal to fiber bundle width
  - VS plates defined as [±〈T₀|T₁〉]₄s for linear variation and [±〈T₀|T₁|T₂〉]₄s for nonlinear variation with 16 balanced symmetric lay-ups
  - Fiber angles within discrete elements assumed constant, calculated using centroid coordinates

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Linear buckling analysis (eigenvalue analysis)
  - 2D analysis of square composite plate with side length 1,000 mm
  - FEA using S4R shell elements (four nodes with simplified integration, five degrees of freedom per node)
  - Mesh density of 100×100 elements for sufficient accuracy (buckling load errors < 0.05%)
  - Prebuckling stress analysis for static load conditions
  - Fiber paths varied along x-axis with shifted fiber paths along y-direction
10_1016_j_cja_2025_103457.key_3:
- Buckling analysis of variable stiffness composite plates under compression loads
- Nondimensional critical buckling load factor (Ncr) calculated as Ncr = Ncr,av·a²/(E₁·h³)
- Buckling load values for linear variable angle plates (LVAP) and nonlinear variable angle plates (NVAP)
- In-plane stress distributions in x- and y-directions for prebuckling analysis
- Displacement distributions under various boundary conditions
- First buckling modes of optimized composite plates
- Complex correlation coefficient (R²) for surrogate model accuracy assessment
- Error percentages between predicted and actual values in optimization process
- Maximize buckling load (buckling resistance) of variable stiffness composite plates through fiber path optimization
- Achieve 8.8%, 11.8%, and 13.7% buckling load improvement for NVAP compared to LVAP under SSSS-Uni, SSCC, and SSSS-Bi boundary conditions respectively
10_1016_j_cja_2025_103457.key_4:
- Fiber angle constraints: 0° ≤ T₀, T₁, T₂ ≤ 90° for all optimization cases
- Square plate geometry with fixed side length of 1,000 mm
- 16 balanced symmetric lay-ups with stacking sequence [±〈T₀|T₁〉]₄s for linear variable angle plates (LVAP) and [±〈T₀|T₁|T₂〉]₄s for nonlinear variable angle plates (NVAP)
- Fiber path variations defined along x-axis only, with shifted fiber paths along y-direction
- Nonlinear fiber path defined with T₂ at x = ±a/4 position
- Mesh density requirement of 100×100 elements to achieve buckling load errors less than 0.05%
- Surrogate model accuracy requirement of R² > 0.9 for optimization termination
- Linear buckling analysis (eigenvalue) approach used for all simulations
- Constant thickness requirement maintained by setting displacement equal to fiber bundle width
- Wrinkling limitations in fiber placement: "excessive wrinkles can significantly reduce the performance of the composite"
- Parallel fiber method not widely used in practical engineering due to significant deviation from reference path
- Gaps and overlaps between fiber bundles must be avoided during manufacturing
- Fiber angle variation constrained to mitigate stress concentration and interlaminar spalling
- Boundary condition constraints specific to each case: SSSS-Uni, SSCC, and SSSS-Bi with defined displacement and rotation constraints at edges

10_1007_s12206_017_0418_4.key_1:
• Subject is finite element structural analysis for nodal force distribution during mesh refinement in mechanical components
• Primary test geometry is rectangular plate with central circular hole (2 m width, 4 m height, 0.2 m thickness, 0.3 m hole radius)
• Boundary conditions: all degrees of freedom fixed on bottom plane
• Loading: constant body force of 1 kN/m³ applied in y-direction
• Application to Test Blanket Modules (TBM) in International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) project
• Mesh types include 8-node hexahedral, 20-node hexahedral, and 10-node tetrahedral elements
• Model A (coarse mesh) contains 1744 nodes and 1152 elements for problem 1
• Model B (refined mesh) contains 13328 nodes and 10752 elements for problem 1
• Problem 2 refined model contains 103040 nodes and 86400 8-node hexahedral elements
• Problem 3 coarse model has 4640 nodes and 768 20-node hexahedral elements
• Problem 3 refined model has 20640 nodes and 6144 20-node hexahedral elements
• Problem 4 coarse model has 6937 nodes and 3652 10-node tetrahedral elements
• Problem 4 refined model has 49239 nodes and 31197 10-node tetrahedral elements
• Target stress field obtained when body force directly applied to refined mesh
• Maximum y-direction stress error ranges from 0.0% to 5.62% depending on element type and method
• Nodal force distribution methods tested with and without reference equivalent nodal forces (NOPTF = 0 or 1)
10_1007_s12206_017_0418_4.key_2:
• All degrees of freedom fixed on bottom plane
• Constant body force of 1 kN/m³ applied in y-direction
• 3D static structural analysis
• Linear elastic regime
• Nodal force distribution between coarse and refined meshes
• Analysis performed using 8-node hexahedral, 20-node hexahedral, and 10-node tetrahedral elements
• Target stress field obtained by direct application of body force to refined mesh
• Distributed nodal forces applied to refined mesh as boundary conditions for stress analysis
10_1007_s12206_017_0418_4.key_3:
• Stress distribution in finite element structural analysis during mesh refinement
• Maximum σx, σy, and |τxy| stress values near the hole
• Error percentage in maximum y-direction stress compared to target value
• Execution time for nodal force distribution calculation (2.2 s to 12.3 s depending on model size)
• Minimize error between distributed nodal force results and target stress field
• Achieve stress field accuracy with error <6% for 8-node hexahedral elements
• Achieve stress field accuracy with error <1% for 20-node hexahedral and 10-node tetrahedral elements
10_1007_s12206_017_0418_4.key_4:
• Plate geometry constrained to 2 m width, 4 m height, 0.2 m thickness with 0.3 m radius circular hole
• Analysis limited to 8-node hexahedral, 20-node hexahedral, and 10-node tetrahedral element types
• Nodal force distribution requires similar x, y and z coordinate ranges between model A and B
• Maximum stress error constraint: <6% for 8-node hexahedral elements
• Maximum stress error constraint: <1% for 20-node hexahedral and 10-node tetrahedral elements
• All degrees of freedom must be fixed on bottom plane as boundary condition
• Body force constrained to 1 kN/m³ in y-direction
• Geometric discrepancy constraint: some nodes of model A can be located outside model B and vice versa
• Method constrained to cases where field variable data are not available for direct numerical integration
• Large models require sectioning with overlap regions (2w width) to reduce memory requirements
• Elements with middle nodes require nodal forces to be moved to corner nodes before distribution

10_1007_s12541_024_01191_5.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Topology optimization of structural designs using Disp2Topo deep learning framework
- **Material / Medium:** Relative density values (0-1) in SIMP method; Young's modulus of actual material referenced but not specified
- **Application & Importance:** Designing lightweight structures with reduced computational cost; achieves results comparable to SIMP method while reducing computation time to 0.2% of traditional approach
- **Geometry / Domain:** 128×128 square structures with random empty domains (25×25, 50×50, 75×75); six degrees of freedom constraints on left side; varying X, Y, Z directional loads on right; fixed points and design domains incorporated; 128×128 matrix encoding for structural shapes; 4-dimensional tensor (boundary conditions + X/Y/Z deformations) for deformation results
10_1007_s12541_024_01191_5.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Six degrees of freedom constraints on the left side of structures; fixed degrees of freedom encoded as 1 in boundary condition tensor; design domain encoded as 0; empty domains encoded as -1
- **Loads / Excitations:** Varying X, Y, and Z directional loads applied on the right side; force applied at the bottom right corner of structures; random forces in X, Y, Z directions on right side; X-direction load, Y-direction load, and Z-direction load matrices with numerical values
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Linear static analysis performed to derive deformation results; topology optimization using SIMP method to generate relative density distributions; paired input data combining boundary conditions and deformation results
- **Simulation Type:** Linear static analysis; 2D structures (128×128) with 3D deformation considerations (X, Y, Z directions); topology optimization with 40% volume fraction constraint; mesh size of 1 mm; plate structure dimensions of 128 mm width and height
10_1007_s12541_024_01191_5.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Linear static structural analysis; deformation calculation under applied loads; topology optimization using SIMP method; relative density distribution modeling
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Relative density values (0-1) for each element; compliance (strain energy); structure weight; X/Y/Z directional deformations; volume fraction; Frechet Inception Distance (FID) score; Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR); Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM)
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize compliance (strain energy) to maximize structural stiffness; minimize structure weight; maintain volume fraction constraint of 40%; achieve topology-optimized structures with 90% similarity to traditional SIMP method results while reducing computation time to 0.2% of conventional approach
10_1007_s12541_024_01191_5.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** 128×128 grid structure as base template; empty domains of specific sizes (25×25, 50×50, 75×75); fixed boundary conditions on left side; varying X/Y/Z directional loads applied on right side; minimum structural element represented by square units
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Volume fraction constraint of 40% (Vc); relative density values constrained between 0 and 1 (0 ≤ ρi ≤ 1); Young's modulus calculated as Ei = ρi^n · E0; minimization of compliance (strain energy) as primary objective; structure weight minimization as secondary objective
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Mesh size fixed at 1 mm for linear static analysis; 128 mm width and height maintained for plate structures; sensitivity filtering required in post-processing to mitigate numerical instabilities like checkerboarding and branching; 128×128 matrix encoding for structural representation; 4-dimensional tensor requirement for deformation data (boundary conditions + X/Y/Z deformations)

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106276.key_1:
- Material Extrusion (MEX) wave infill thin-walled structures (TWS)
- Nylon-12 thermoplastic material with E₁ = 1276 MPa, E₃ = 1138 MPa, G₃₁ = 800 MPa, ν₃₁ = 0.3
- Wave infill geometry defined by beadwidth (W), thickness (T), period (P), and overlap (O)
- Core thickness T_C = T - 2W
- Amplitude H = T/2 - (W/2 + O)
- Wave infill TWS modeled as 3-ply composite: outer facing lamina, core lamina, inner facing lamina
- Principal axes: 1-axis aligned along wave direction, 2-axis perpendicular to wave, 3-axis along layers
- Four-point bending test setup: specimen length l = 120 mm, support pin spacing L_s = 80 mm, loading pin spacing a = 30 mm, pin radius = 5 mm
- Cantilever TWS dimensions: width w_c = 20 cm, height h_c = 40 cm, thickness T = 7.0 mm, overlap O = 0.1 mm
- Case 1 cantilever: W_f = W_c = 0.5 mm
- Case 2 cantilever: W_f = 1.0 mm, W_c = 0.5 mm
- Case 3 cantilever: section height dz = 20 mm
- Semi-cylindrical TWS: width w_s = 200 mm, height h_s = 400 mm, traction load ψ = 0.01 N/mm²
- Stiffness-to-mass ratio minimum occurs at period P ≈ 2.0 mm
- Infill density range: 45% to 95% corresponding to period range of 1.0-3.0 mm
- Effective core layer-to-layer modulus E₃^c = α(I₁₁^w/I₁₁^eff)E₃ where I₁₁^eff = (1/12)T_C³P
- Effective core shear modulus G₂₃^c = (4T_C W)/(P L_wave) G₃₁
- Effective core shear modulus G₂₁^c = E₁A₁(T_C/(P/2 b)) × det[C₁₁ C₁₂; C₁₂ C₂₂]/det[C₁₁ C₁₂ C₁₃; C₁₂ C₂₂ C₂₃; C₁₃ C₂₃ C₃₃]
- Correction factor α = 0.8 for wave infill overlap accounting
- 3-ply composite shell meshed with 4-node quadrilateral shell elements (S4R)
- Applied distributed edge load magnitude ψ per unit length
- Beam stiffness K = ψw_c/δ where δ is maximum deflection at top of cantilever
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106276.key_2:
- Support pin spacing L_s = 80 mm, loading pin spacing a = 30 mm, pin radius = 5 mm
- Y-direction motion U_Y = -4 mm applied to center of support and loading pins
- Symmetry boundary conditions: 2-3 plane (U_X = R_Y = R_Z = 0) and 1-2 plane (U_Z = R_X = R_Y = 0)
- Fixed boundary conditions at base edge of cantilever and semi-cylinder
- Straining rate of 0.10 mm/min for four-point bending test specimens
- Distributed edge load magnitude ψ per unit length applied about TWS's 1-axis for cantilevers
- Traction load magnitude ψ = 0.01 N/mm² applied along X-direction for semi-cylindrical TWS
- Normal contact with frictional coefficient μ = 0.15 between pins and specimen
- Wave infill TWS modeled as composite stack with homogeneous laminae
- Transverse orthotropy in in-plane and layer-to-layer material symmetry directions
- Anisotropic and linear elastic constitutive model with no temperature dependence
- 3D simulation with quarter symmetry for validation experiments
- 4-node quadrilateral shell elements with reduced integration (S4R)
- Large-strain formulation used in Abaqus®
- Mesh element size of 1 mm for validation experiments
- Mesh element dimensions of 20 mm x 4 mm x T for cantilever analysis
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106276.key_3:
- Structural mechanics of thin-walled structures with material extrusion wave infill
- Bending stiffness (K)
- Mass (M)
- Stiffness-to-mass ratio (K/M)
- Deflection (δ)
- Effective core material properties (E₃^c, G₂₁^c, G₂₃^c)
- Infill density
- Maximum deflection at top of cantilever
- Minimize mass while achieving desired structural stiffness
- Maximize stiffness-to-mass ratio (K/M)
- Achieve non-uniform wave infill for optimized structural performance
- Maintain infill density between 45% and 95% (period between 1.0-3.0 mm) to avoid underfilling and overfilling
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106276.key_4:
- Period of wave infill constrained between 1.0 mm and 3.0 mm
- Infill density constrained between 45% and 95% to avoid underfilling and overfilling
- Minimum stiffness-to-mass ratio occurs at period P ≈ 2.0 mm
- E₁^c and G₁₃^c are negligible according to analytical models
- For in-plane specimens, G₂₃^c and E₃^c have no effect on stiffness
- For layer-to-layer specimens, G₂₁^c and E₁^c have no effect on stiffness
- MEX facings assumed rigid during shear deformation of core
- Wave infill overlaps into inner and outer facings beyond core thickness T_C
- Correction factor α = 0.8 applied to account for overprediction of 3-direction stiffness
- Infill densities above 95% cause overfilling of wave infill
- Infill densities below 45% cause underfilling of wave infill

10_1007_s12541_018_0095_y.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Strain gauge pressure transducer designed for high-pressure hydraulic applications up to 500 MPa
- **Material / Medium:** Sensing element made of Stainless Steel 410 (SS410) with yield strength 620 MPa, Young's modulus 200 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.3; foil strain gauges (5 mm size, 350 Ω resistance, gain factor 2.1); pressure transmitting fluid: di (2-ethylhexyl) Sebacate oil
- **Application & Importance:** Measurement of high hydraulic pressures (0-500 MPa) with cost-effective design; provides leak-proof metal-to-metal contact coupling; essential for pressure metrology where piezoelectric transducers are limited to lower pressure ranges (≤280 MPa)
- **Geometry / Domain:** Cylindrical sensing element with internal radius 1.5 mm; closed-end design with strain gauges bonded near blind end; two strain gauges in longitudinal direction and two in hoop direction forming full Wheatstone bridge; transducer casing with hexagonal top; optimum autofrettage radius of 3.35 mm for 500 MPa operating pressure
10_1007_s12541_018_0095_y.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Closed-end cylindrical sensing element with internal radius of 1.5 mm; metal-to-metal contact at coupling point; 11 equally spaced pressure points (0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500 MPa) for testing; contacts not over-constrained as verified by Fig. 4(b)
- **Loads / Excitations:** Operating pressure range of 0-500 MPa; excitation voltage of 9 V; autofrettage pressures of 712 MPa, 800 MPa, 900 MPa, and 1000 MPa tested; di (2-ethylhexyl) Sebacate oil as pressure transmitting fluid
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Four foil strain gauges (5 mm size, 350 Ω resistance) bonded to sensing element (two in longitudinal direction, two in hoop direction); full Wheatstone bridge configuration; metal-to-metal contact at coupling point; contact pressure maximum of 55.927 MPa as shown in Fig. 4(a)
- **Simulation Type:** 3D finite element analysis using Ansys Workbench; multi-zone hexahedral mesh; static structural analysis; equivalent (von-Mises) stress calculation; stress analysis performed for both autofrettage and non-autofrettage cases at seven different operating pressures
10_1007_s12541_018_0095_y.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Equivalent (von-Mises) stress distribution in cylindrical pressure transducer sensing element; strain distribution (hoop and longitudinal); autofrettage-induced residual stresses; contact pressure at coupling points; hysteresis behavior; linearity of output response
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Maximum equivalent stress values (e.g., 455.78 MPa at 900 MPa autofrettage pressure); stress distribution across wall thickness; coefficient of determination (R² = 0.999); hysteresis error (0.18% of full scale); short term repeatability (0.32% of full scale); sensitivity (0.86 mV increase over 0-500 MPa range); optimum autofrettage pressure (900 MPa); pressure bearing capacity limits (712 MPa for elastic limit, 3915 MPa for full wall yielding)
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize maximum equivalent stress in sensing element through optimum autofrettage pressure (900 MPa found to be ideal); achieve uniform stress distribution across thickness; maximize pressure bearing capacity while maintaining factor of safety (1.4 at 500 MPa operating pressure); minimize hysteresis and improve linearity; maintain cost-effective design while operating in 500 MPa pressure range
10_1007_s12541_018_0095_y.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Internal radius fixed at 1.5 mm; optimum autofrettage radius of 3.35 mm for 500 MPa operation; saturation thickness limit beyond which increased thickness provides no additional strength; cylindrical sensing element with closed end design; strain gauges (5 mm size) bonded near blind end; multi-zone hexahedral mesh used for finite element analysis
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Operating pressure range of 0-500 MPa; plastic yielding begins at 712 MPa internal pressure; full wall thickness yielding at 3915 MPa; minimum factor of safety of 1.4 required at 500 MPa operating pressure; hysteresis error must be within 0.1% in 50-500 MPa range; maximum acceptable hysteresis error of 0.18% of full scale; short term repeatability must be ≤ 0.32% of full scale; linearity requirement with R² ≥ 0.999; maximum contact pressure of 55.927 MPa at coupling point; maximum equivalent stress of 455.78 MPa at optimum autofrettage conditions
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Cost-effectiveness constraint limiting use of high-strength materials like Maraging steel; leak-proof requirement necessitating metal-to-metal contact; local availability of components (strain gauges from local market); strain gauge bonding process limitations (adhesive damping effects); saturation thickness constraint limiting design options; tradeoff between autofrettage pressure and factor of safety (1000 MPa autofrettage gives better sensitivity but only 1.1 factor of safety); need to operate within elastic region to prevent permanent deformation

10_1016_j_finel_2015_12_008.key_1:
- Smart structures with integrated actuation capabilities, including adaptive beams, cylinders with bead patterns, and Flectofin® facade shading elements
- GFRP (wing: E₁=10 GPa, E₂=5 GPa, E₃=5 GPa, G₁₂=5 GPa, G₁₃=2.5 GPa, G₂₃=2.5 GPa, ν₁₂=0.2, ν₁₃=0.25, ν₂₃=0.25; backbone: E=24 GPa, ν=0.2; edge beam: E=37.6 GPa, ν=0.2), steel cramps (E=210 GPa, ν=0.3)
- To generate structures providing maximum response to actuator input with minimum actuation effort, combining structural optimization and actuator placement for efficient smart structure design
- Adaptive beam: length 10, circular curvature with rise 0.5, fixed supports on left, roller supports on right; Cylinder: length 30,000, diameter 10,000, 45° cut at one end; Flectofin®: 2m length, 25cm height, GFRP wing eccentrically attached to pre-bent GFRP backbone with steel cramp supports
10_1016_j_finel_2015_12_008.key_2:
- Fixed supports on left edge, roller supports on right edge (adaptive beam)
- All translatoric degrees of freedom fixed at 45° cut edge (cylinder)
- Metal cramps supported at bottom line (Flectofin)
- uₓ = uᵧ = u_z = 0 at fixed supports
- uₓ = 7mm horizontal displacement applied at backbone connection (Flectofin)
- 2cm height cuboid constraint for backbone shape adaptation (Flectofin)
- Pressure load acting on adaptive beam structure
- Vertical load uniformly distributed over entire cylinder body
- Vertical load at cylinder edge in upward or downward direction
- Element-wise pressure load scaling for actuator optimization
- Target displacements: 12cm in y-direction and 20cm in z-direction at five edge beam points (Flectofin)
- Geometrically nonlinear analysis
- Dynamic analysis using Newmark-Beta integration (density ρ = 7.5·10⁻⁷)
- Stiffness proportional Rayleigh damping
- Buckling constraint (smallest eigenvalue of tangential stiffness matrix > 0)
10_1016_j_finel_2015_12_008.key_3:
- Structural mechanics with geometric nonlinearity, large deformations, and actuator-structure interaction
- Horizontal displacement of roller support (adaptive beam), vertical deflection of un-cut edge (cylinder), vertical deflection of wing's free edge (Flectofin), load-displacement curves, displacement components at evaluation points, actuation benefit, actuation cost, efficiency function values
- Maximize displacement response per actuation effort (minimize efficiency function E = C(a)/B(a,s)), maximize vertical deflection for given actuator input, minimize deviations from target displacement values (12cm y-displacement and 20cm z-displacement), maximize actuation benefit while minimizing actuation cost
10_1016_j_finel_2015_12_008.key_4:
- Maximum allowable increase of structure's weight to 50% (m - 1.5·m₀ ≤ 0)
- Each node allowed to move ±250 in out-of-plane direction for bead pattern optimization
- 2cm height cuboid constraint for backbone shape adaptation in Flectofin optimization
- Ply thickness constrained between 0.3mm and 0.7mm (initial thickness 0.5mm)
- Smallest eigenvalue of tangential stiffness matrix constrained to remain strictly positive (buckling constraint)
- Target displacements constrained to 12cm in y-direction and 20cm in z-direction at five edge beam points (Flectofin)
- Filter radius parameter (R) used as design tool to control wave length of features (e.g., R=0.1m, R=0.2m for backbone optimization)
- Displacement evaluation restricted to five nodes distributed along the edge beam
- Thickness averaging performed on nodal level to avoid thickness jumps (classical Kirchhoff-Love shell theory limitation)
- Actuation cost computed as sum of absolute actuator variables (C = ∑|aᵢ|)

10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_118986.key_1:
- Hybrid bolted connection of steel box girders in non-axial force connections for earth-anchored cable-stayed bridges
- Steel (top/bottom flanges 12 mm: E=208.3 GPa, f_y=499.6 MPa, f_u=605.0 MPa; webs/stiffeners/diaphragms 20 mm: E=207.4 GPa, f_y=470.5 MPa, f_u=612.3 MPa; connection plates 14 mm: E=214.4 GPa, f_y=465.2 MPa, f_u=615.1 MPa) and M12 high-strength bolts (Grade 10.9: E=206.8 GPa, f_y=1085.92 MPa, f_u=1131.50 MPa)
- To enable longitudinal sliding of steel box girders to release deformation and secondary stress from temperature and seismic effects at mid-span of earth-anchored cable-stayed bridges while maintaining structural integrity under bending moments
- 1/3 downscaled specimens with 4660 mm length, 440 mm width, 620 mm height; inner flange connection with 140 bolt holes (Φ14 mm); three single-lap connection types (Type 1: 322×434 mm, Type 2: 398×84 mm, Type 3: 398×168 mm); bolt hole spacing of 42 mm with 21 mm edge distance; 5-layer thickness meshing for steel girder with mesh size transitioning from 6 mm to 35 mm
10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_118986.key_2:
- Fixed support constraints: Ux=Uy=0, Rotx=Rotz=0 at top support elements; Ux=Uy=Uz=0, Rotx=Rotz=0 at bottom support elements
- Line-load support with vertical displacement applied while constraining 4 other degrees of freedom; line-support constraining all degrees of freedom except Roty
- Surface-to-surface contact with "Hard" behavior in normal direction between all components
- Friction coefficient of 0.5 for contacts between steel girder and single-lap connections
- Friction coefficient of 0.2 for all other surface-to-surface contacts
- Vertical loading velocity of 60 kN/min during pre-loading stage until reaching 10% of capacity prediction
- Displacement-controlled loading at 0.5 mm/min vertical loading velocity after pre-loading
- Target time increment of 0.0003 s and total loading time of 200 s for explicit analysis
- Welding residual stress model per AASHTO LRFD standard with residual tensile stress equal to yield strength and residual compressive stress equal to 0.3 times yield strength
- Pretension force of 55 kN applied to high-strength bolts
- Regional cooling method used to simulate pretension with expansion coefficient of 0.00012
- ABAQUS/explicit solver with eight-node hexahedral solid elements with reduced integration (C3D8R)
- Quasi-static analysis regime
- Nonlinear analysis incorporating ductile fracture criterion
- 3D modeling approach with mesh size transitioning from 6 mm to 35 mm for steel girder, 8 mm for connection plates, and 2-5 mm for high-strength bolts
- Modified Bao-Wierzbicki ductile fracture criterion for steel and high-strength bolt materials
10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_118986.key_3:
- Bending behavior of hybrid bolted connections in steel box girders under in-plane and out-plane moments, including moment-transferring mechanisms, ductile fracture behavior, and bolt-slippage phenomena
- Load-displacement curves with elastic capacity (887 kN for S1, 775 kN for S2), yield capacity (3581 kN for S1, 2849 kN for S2), ultimate capacity (4379 kN for S1, 3568 kN for S2), and fracture capacity (3529 kN for S1, 3553 kN for S2); moment-curvature relationships; moment distribution ratios (M_g/M, M_f/M, M_c/M); stress distribution in high-strength bolts; fracture equivalent plastic strain; contact and internal forces; bolt-slippage displacement; ductile fracture initiation
- Understanding the three-stage bending mechanism to improve connection design by achieving uniform stress distribution in high-strength bolts to increase bending moment resistance and deformation capacity, while maintaining longitudinal sliding performance for temperature and seismic deformation release
10_1016_j_engstruct_2024_118986.key_4:
- 1/3 downscale ratio for specimens (4660 mm length, 440 mm width, 620 mm height)
- Bolt hole diameter constraint of 14 mm with 2 mm radial clearance
- End distance (37 mm) and edge distance (30 mm) for inner flange connection; 21 mm for single-lap connections
- Bolt-hole spacing of 33 mm for inner flange connection and 42 mm for single-lap connections

10_1016_j_est_2025_117239.key_1:
- **Subject of analysis:** Lithium-ion pouch cell battery under mechanical loading conditions  
- **Components:** Anode, cathode, separator, and shell  
- **Anode composition:** Graphite coated on copper foil with lithium carbide; NMC (nickel manganese cobalt) active material  
- **Cathode composition:** Aluminum foil coated with NMC material  
- **Separator composition:** Wet-type polypropylene (C₃H₃)₁₅  
- **Shell composition:** Multilayer structure containing biaxially oriented nylon (outer), aluminum barrier layer, adhesive layer, and cast polypropylene/polypropylene sealant layer (inner)  
- **Battery dimensions:** 142 × 190 × 8.3 mm³; 8 Ah nominal capacity; 204 g weight; 3.7 V nominal voltage  
- **Component thicknesses:** Cathode (0.210 mm), anode (0.140 mm), separator (0.041 mm), shell (0.17 mm)  
- **Tensile test directions:** Machine direction (MD), transverse direction (TD), diagonal direction (DD)  
- **Testing methods:** Tensile tests, indentation tests with hemispherical indenter, XRD, FTIR, SEM, and EDS analyses  
- **Material properties characterized:** Young's modulus, yield stress, ultimate tensile stress, fracture strain, anisotropic behavior  
- **Failure analysis focus:** Internal short circuits, thermal runaway, and mechanical failure under crash conditions  
- **Key anisotropic findings:** Direction-dependent mechanical responses in all components, with MD generally showing higher strength than TD and DD  
- **Voltage monitoring:** Performed during indentation to detect internal short circuits; maintained at ~3.5 V up to 5 mm indentation depth  
- **Indentation test configuration:** Two-cell stack with custom fixture to eliminate bottom platen interference  
- **Failure strain values:** Cathode (0.004), anode (0.018), separator (0.131), shell (0.05)
10_1016_j_est_2025_117239.key_2:
- **Boundary conditions:** Fixed support at cell bottom; vertical displacement allowed for indenter; surface-to-surface contact with finite sliding between layers; friction coefficient of 0.2 between layers; custom fixture used to prevent wrinkling and eliminate bottom platen influence  
- **Tensile test constraints:** Dogbone samples (gauge length 3.64 mm, width 3.64 mm, grip width 10 mm, fillet radius 3.18 mm) for cathode/anode/shell; strip samples (total length 40 mm, gauge length 24 mm, width 10 mm) for separator following ASTM D882  
- **Loading rates:** Quasi-static tensile tests at strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; constant displacement rate of 0.25 mm/min for tensile tests  
- **Indentation configuration:** Hemispherical indenter; two-cell stack configuration; indenter modeled as deformable body with 977 C3D8R elements  
- **Contact definition:** Surface-to-surface contact with penalty method between all layers; mesh refined in indentation region  
- **Model geometry:** 3D layered structure incorporating cathode, anode, separator, and shell components; two pouch cells in stack for indentation simulation  
- **Simulation environment:** ABAQUS/Standard solver; linear hexahedral (C3D8R) and wedge (C3D6) elements; Hill48 anisotropic plasticity model with damage  
- **Operating conditions:** NMC pouch cells maintained at 72% state of charge (SOC); voltage monitored in situ using Agilent 34410 A Digital Multimeter  
- **Damage criteria:** Maximum principal strain criterion for damage initiation; linear degradation law for stiffness reduction post-initiation  
- **Mesh configuration:** 1170 hexahedral elements and 14 wedge elements per component in refined regions; mesh convergence study performed for accuracy
10_1016_j_est_2025_117239.key_3:
- **Physics solved:** Anisotropic mechanical behavior of layered lithium-ion pouch cell components under quasi-static mechanical loading; damage evolution and failure mechanisms in multilayer structures; contact mechanics between component layers; force-displacement response under tensile and indentation loading  
- **Target outputs:** Force-displacement curves for tensile tests (cathode, anode, separator, shell) and indentation tests; engineering stress-strain curves in machine (MD), transverse (TD), and diagonal (DD) directions; damage initiation strain values; component-level deformation patterns; voltage response during indentation to detect internal short circuits; Hill48 anisotropic plasticity parameters (R₁₁, R₂₂, R₃₃, R₁₂, R₃₁, R₃₂); failure strain and damage evolution parameters for each component  
- **Model validation metrics:** Correlation between experimental force-displacement data and finite element model predictions for tensile tests (with/without damage); agreement between experimental indentation results and FE model; voltage stability during indentation (no drop observed up to 5 mm penetration)  
- **Primary objective:** Accurate prediction of mechanical response and failure mechanisms in lithium-ion pouch cells under mechanical abuse conditions to identify structural failure thresholds and prevent internal short circuits leading to thermal runaway  
- **Critical safety parameters:** Maximum deformation limits before component failure; directional mechanical properties for safety design; damage initiation criteria for each component layer; voltage response correlation with mechanical deformation
10_1016_j_est_2025_117239.key_4:
- **Geometric constraints:** Pouch cell dimensions fixed at 142 × 190 × 8.3 mm³; component thicknesses fixed (cathode 0.210 mm, anode 0.140 mm, separator 0.041 mm, shell 0.17 mm); dogbone tensile specimens with gauge length 3.64 mm × width 3.64 mm (grip width 10 mm, fillet radius 3.18 mm); strip separator specimens with gauge length 24 mm × width 10 mm (total length 40 mm); two-cell stack configuration for indentation tests  
- **Material processing constraints:** Aluminum and copper foils undergo multiple rolling operations imparting plastic anisotropy; wet-type separators used to match real-world operating conditions (in contact with electrolyte); XRD analysis range limited to 5°-120° for cathode/anode/shell and 10°-40° for separator  
- **Testing constraints:** Tensile tests limited to three directions (MD, TD, DD); quasi-static strain rate fixed at 10⁻³ s⁻¹; constant displacement rate of 0.25 mm/min for tensile tests; hemispherical indenter used for indentation tests  
- **Performance limits:** State of charge maintained at 72% during testing; voltage monitored to detect internal short circuits (no drop observed up to 5 mm indentation depth); component-specific failure strain limits (cathode 0.004, anode 0.018, separator 0.131, shell 0.05)  
- **Modeling constraints:** Anode and cathode modeled as homogenized layers due to inability to isolate coating behavior; surface-to-surface contact with friction coefficient fixed at 0.2 between layers; damage initiation based on maximum principal strain criterion; linear degradation law for stiffness reduction post-initiation  
- **Measurement limitations:** Conventional strain measurement techniques only capture true stress-strain curve up to uniform elongation; diffuse necking creates non-uniform stress/strain distributions beyond yield point; previous homogeneous models incapable of predicting individual component damage during indentation  
- **Scope limitations:** Study focused on quasi-static loading rather than dynamic crash scenarios; model validated for mechanical response but not thermal runaway consequences; anisotropic characterization limited to three primary directions

10_1016_j_finel_2019_103344.key_3:

- Initiation crack length (l_c)
- Applied critical displacement (U_c)
- Critical stress intensity factor (k_c)
- Material characteristic length (L_mat = E·G_c/σ_c²)
- Incremental energy release rate (G_inc)
- Coefficient B (geometrical coefficient depending on V-notch opening angle)
- Dimensionless functions ξ and A for stress and energy conditions
- Crack initiation angle (γ_c) in mixed mode loading
- Simultaneous fulfillment of stress condition (σ(s) ≥ σ_c over crack path) and energy condition (G_inc(l) ≥ G_c) to determine initiation configuration
10_1016_j_finel_2019_103344.key_4:
- Inner domain radius must be at least 200 times larger than the largest characteristic length (R/l ≥ 200)
- Minimum mesh size at crack tip must be ≤ 1% of crack length (m_MA/l ≤ 0.01)
- Material characteristic length must be ≤ 1/5 of substrate thickness for MA validity (L_mat ≤ h/5)
- Initiation length must be ≤ 1/10 of notch length (l_c ≤ h/10 = 30 μm)
- Minimum mesh size for FFE approach must satisfy m_FFE ≤ L_mat/12π

- Crack length upper bound: l_c ≤ L_mat/2 for small notch defects under traction
- Crack length lower bound: l_c ≥ L_mat/2π for small opening angles

- Analysis limited to linear elasticity and small deformations assumptions
- Plane strain conditions applied throughout the analysis

- **Loads / Excitations:** Uniaxial compression with prescribed macroscopic true strain rate; strain rates of 1×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, 2.15×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, 4.64×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, and 1×10⁻³ s⁻¹; compression up to strain of 0.3 in most simulations (some configurations tested up to strain 1); strain rate range studied from 3×10⁻⁶ to 1 s⁻¹ for calibration purposes
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Pairwise particle interactions with piecewise linear normal forces (F_A→B = -F_B→A); mesh-particle interactions computed with similar contact law as particle-particle contacts; repulsive stiffness k_rep and attractive stiffness k_att with ratio k_rep/k_att = 10; interface parameters set to average of phase A and B parameters; attractive force activated only during tensile motion (ḣ > 0), canceled during compressive motion (ḣ ≤ 0)
- **Simulation Type:** Quasi-static simulations; transient time-dependent analysis; 3D discrete element modeling; uniaxial compression tests; Velocity Verlet explicit integration scheme; DEM computations using LIGGGHTS solver; single material and bi-material configurations (parallel, series, spherical inclusion)

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Engineering stress (MPa); true stress (MPa); flow stress at strain 0.3; strain rate sensitivity (M); stress level (K); volume relative error (%); shape factor (H/D) of inclusions; macroscopic equilibrium relative error (%); relative error on flow stress compared to FEM; natural period (t₀); normalized true flow stress
- **Optimization Goal:** Calibrate DEM parameters to match Norton viscoplastic law (σ = Kε̇^M); minimize relative error on flow stress (target < 10% in bi-material configurations); achieve volume conservation (minimize volume variation to ~5-10%); maintain macroscopic equilibrium (error < 0.1%); reproduce FEM results for elementary bi-material geometries; optimize particle discretization to achieve target precision on shape factor (error < 10% requires >200 particles per inclusion)
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2017_12_044.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** R_crown/R_seed ratio fixed at 1.5 to prevent catching second neighbors; minimum of 200 particles required to discretize inclusions for shape factor error <10%; particle count must exceed 5×10⁴ for relative error <2% in single material simulations; time step fixed at Δt = 5×10⁻⁴ s; repulsive seed radius fixed at R_seed = 0.5 mm; attractive crown radius fixed at R_crown = 0.75 mm; spherical inclusion configurations limited to 20% volume fraction of phase B
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Strain rate sensitivity limited to maximum value of 0.6; collapse regime occurs when ε̇·t₀² > 3×10⁻³ s (macroscopic equilibrium lost); plastic regime defined when ε̇·t₀² < 1×10⁻⁷ s (M < 4×10⁻³); volume conservation limited to 5% decrease for phase A and 10% for phase B; transient regime observed in first 0.15-0.2 strain before stable flow regime; strain rate validity range is narrow for higher sensitivities; cannot model arbitrary strain rates with fixed parameters; flow stress overestimated by ~10% in spherical inclusion configuration; macroscopic equilibrium error must remain <0.1% to maintain validity
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Model limited to compressive loading (not validated for tension); requires separate calibration for each material phase; no local adaptivity mechanism for discretization roughness; computing time scales linearly with particle count and time steps (3×10⁻⁶ cpu second per particle per time step); model only validated for quasi-static phenomena; FEM interface prohibits relative motion while DEM allows more permissive contact conditions; natural period must be 20-2000 times larger than time step for valid results

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106726.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Low symmetry piezoelectric shell structures for shear sensor design, specifically analyzing three configurations: torsional sensor (36 mode), transverse shear sensor (35 mode), and flexural sensor (31 mode)

- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Piezoelectric materials: Rochelle Salt (orthorhombic 222 symmetry, d36≠0) for torsional sensors, PZT with poling direction along α1 (d35≠0) for transverse shear sensors, PFRC (uniaxial symmetry) for flexural sensors
  - Passive substrate: Graphite/epoxy composite
  - Material properties include Young's moduli (Y11/Y22=25, Y33/Y22=1), shear moduli (G23=0.2Y22, G12=G13=0.5Y22), Poisson's ratios (v12=v13=v23=0.25), Y22=6.9 GPa

- **Application & Importance:** Designing simplified patch sensors for shear load measurement; traditional piezoelectric materials lack significant in-plane shear-electric field coupling (d36=0), requiring complex geometries; low symmetry materials enable simpler sensor geometries with direct shear-electric field coupling

- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Cylindrical shell structures with principal radii of curvature R1 and R2
  - Flexural sensor: piezoelectric layer (PFRC) at top, passive composite substrate at bottom
  - Torsional sensor: Rochelle Salt piezoelectric layer at top, composite substrate at bottom
  - Transverse shear sensor: three-layered structure with PZT core (poling direction along α1), substrate layers at top and bottom
  - Boundary conditions: SSSS (simply supported all edges), SCSS (clamped at α1=a), SSSC (clamped at α1=0), SCSC (clamped at α1=0,a), CCCC (fully clamped)
  - Geometric parameters: span-to-thickness ratio (a/h), depth-to-radius ratio (a/R), piezoelectric layer thickness ratio (hp/h)
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106726.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Mechanical boundary conditions:
    - Clamped (C): u₀ = v₀ = w₀ = Ψ₁ = Ψ₂ = φ₁ = φ₂ = 0
    - Simply Supported (S): u₀ = w₀ = Ψ₁ = φ₁ = 0 for edges α₂ = 0, b; v₀ = w₀ = Ψ₂ = φ₂ = 0 for edges α₁ = 0, a
    - Boundary condition combinations: SSSS (all edges simply supported), SCSS (clamped at α₁=a), SSSC (clamped at α₁=0), SCSC (clamped at α₁=0,a), CCCC (all edges clamped)
  - Electrical boundary conditions:

- **Optimization Goal:** Improve prediction accuracy of permanent elongation at load levels below nominal yield strength; rationalize inelastic elongation observations through residual stress modeling; enhance short and long term conductor sag prediction; determine required axial force for overhead line retightening; optimize manufacturing process to reduce permanent elongation and potentially increase conductor lifetime

10_1016_j_finel_2025_104314.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Periodic structures including phononic crystals (PCs), elastic metamaterials (EMs), and mechanical metamaterials for wave propagation analysis using Wave-based Finite Element Method (WFEM) combined with Generalized Bloch Mode Synthesis (GBMS)
- **Material / Medium:** 
  - Polylactic acid (PLA): Elastic modulus 3.5 GPa, density 1250 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio 0.35, hysteretic damping η=1%
  - Steel: Elastic modulus 200 GPa, density 7850 kg/m³, Poisson's ratio 0.3, hysteretic damping η=1%
- **Application & Importance:** Computation of harmonic forced responses and wave propagation characteristics; analysis of bandgaps (frequency bands where wave propagation is forbidden or attenuated); structural dynamics analysis and passive vibration reduction in periodic structures
- **Geometry / Domain:** 
  - Three example geometries with N=10 unit cells each: (1) PC with inertial amplification mechanism (unit cell length Δ=112 mm, plane stress model, 32,148 nodes), (2) EM with rectangular spiral resonators (Δ=120 mm, 5 mm spiral width, 9,845 nodes), (3) PC with arbitrary internal void (20 mm thickness, 34,440 nodes)
  - Unit cells modeled with varying mesh densities (0.25-1.5 mm element sizes) and different element types (4/3-noded plane elements, Reissner-Mindlin plate elements, solid elements)
10_1016_j_finel_2025_104314.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:**
  - Free-free boundary conditions with F_L(1) = 0 and F_L(N+1) = 0
  - Bloch-Floquet periodicity conditions applied to unit cell boundaries
  - DoFs' compatibility between adjacent unit cells: q_R^(n) = q_L^(n+1)
  - Load equilibrium between adjacent unit cells: F_R^(n) = -F_L^(n+1) + F_B^(n)
  - Fixed interface modes with constrained boundary DoFs for CB MOR method

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Harmonic force excitation applied at specific locations
  - Transfer FRFs calculated in frequency range 0-5000 Hz with 5 Hz increments
  - Input location for IAM-based PC: central node of rightmost edge (y-direction)
  - Output location for IAM-based PC: central node of leftmost edge (y-direction)
  - Input location for EM with rectangular spiral resonators: rightmost node of 10th unit cell at center (z-direction)
  - Output location for EM with rectangular spiral resonators: leftmost node at midpoint (z-direction)
  - Input location for PC with internal void: rightmost node at bottom corner (z-direction)
  - Output location for PC with internal void: leftmost node on top (z-direction)

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Spatial partitioning of DoFs into boundary (B) and interior (I) sets
  - Interface modes calculated for boundary DoF reduction
  - Constraint modes (Γ) and fixed interface modes (Ξ) used in CB MOR
  - Compatible modes required for boundary reduction to satisfy Bloch-Floquet conditions

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Frequency-domain harmonic analysis
  - One-dimensional wave propagation in periodic structures
  - Mid- to high-frequency band analysis (0-5000 Hz)
  - Transfer FRF calculations with specified input/output degrees of freedom
  - Free-free boundary condition implementation
  - Wave-based Finite Element Method (WFEM) with reduced-order unit cell models
10_1016_j_finel_2025_104314.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Elastic wave propagation in periodic structures; harmonic forced responses; dispersion characteristics (wavenumber-frequency relationships); bandgap analysis (frequencies where wave propagation is forbidden or attenuated)

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Frequency Response Functions (FRFs) in 0-5000 Hz range with 5 Hz increments
  - Resonance frequencies and relative errors between FEM and reduced-order models (RE_fj = (f_WFEM+GBMS_j - f_FEM_j)/f_FEM_j)
  - Cross Signature Scale Factor (CSF) for amplitude correlation between FRFs
  - Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) for mode shape correlation (0-1 scale)
  - Dispersion curves (wavenumbers vs. frequency)
  - Number of boundary and interior degrees of freedom in reduced models
  - Computational time for different modeling approaches
  - Singular value distributions for model reduction

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Maximize computational efficiency while maintaining accuracy in forced response calculations
  - Reduce unit cell model size (achieved 0.11-0.29% of original equations for different examples)
  - Mitigate numerical instabilities in wave mode calculations
  - Avoid computation of high-order evanescent modes that cause numerical issues
  - Achieve 72-760x speedup in computation time compared to traditional FEM while maintaining minimal errors (max relative error <1.2% for resonance frequencies, CSF >0.9 for amplitudes)
10_1016_j_finel_2025_104314.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Unit cell length fixed for IAM-based PC (112 mm) and cannot be modified without disturbing overall geometry
  - Mesh element size constraints: 0.25 mm for IAM-based PC, 1 mm for EM with spiral resonators, 1.5 mm for PC with internal void
  - Three specific unit cell geometries analyzed: IAM-based PC, rectangular spiral resonators EM, and PC with arbitrary internal void
  - Void shape in third example generated using splines passing through 33 control points
  - Unit cell thickness constraints: 30 mm for IAM-based PC (plane stress), 30 mm for spiral resonators (z-direction), 20 mm for PC with void

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Frequency range limited to 0-5000 Hz with 5 Hz increments
  - Mesh convergence criterion: relative error between successive refinements < 1% for largest natural frequency
  - Material property limits: PLA (3.5 GPa elastic modulus, 1250 kg/m³ density), Steel (200 GPa elastic modulus, 7850 kg/m³ density)
  - Threshold for MAC index: TV_MAC = 0.6-0.8 required for optimal accuracy
  - Frequency-based truncation criteria: n̂ = 5 for CB MOR and n̄ = 1.2 for L-CC MOR
  - Maximum relative error between resonance frequencies < 1.2% (worst case)
  - CSF values must exceed 0.9 for acceptable amplitude correlation
  - Unit cell model reduction must preserve boundary compatibility for Bloch-Floquet conditions
  - Computational feasibility constraint: full-order unit cell models make WFEM analysis infeasible

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Reference FRFs calculated using direct method (DM) rather than modal superposition due to defect modes
  - Mesh convergence requirement: "the unit cell mesh was considered converged when the relative error between successive mesh refinements in the larger natural frequency of the cell, was less than 1%"
  - The (N,L) eigenproblem method only applicable to symmetric unit cells (not suitable for spiral resonators or arbitrary void examples)
  - CB and L-CC MOR methods required prior to WFEM to ensure numerical stability
  - Condition numbers of matrices must remain manageable during solution of global eigenvalue problem (Eq. 14)
  - The paper notes that for "the cases one studied" no ill-conditioning issues were noted during solution of Eq. (14), but this "deserves attention when applying the proposed method"

10_1016_j_ast_2024_109728.key_1:

- **Geometry / Domain:** Circular cross-section tubes with longitudinal corrugations; nominal dimensions: wall thickness t=1 mm, diameter D=37 mm, length L=100 mm; geometric parameters: amplitude of corrugations A (0.4-1.6 mm), number of folds N (3-30), wavelength 2λ; corrugation profile defined by X = D/2 - A·cos(πZ/λ) where X is radius at height Z

10_1016_j_ast_2024_109728.key_3:

10_1016_j_ast_2024_109728.key_4:

10_1007_s00211_022_01310_2.key_1:

- Fluid viscosity μ = 10^-6 kPa·s, Biot-Willis constant αp = 1, Lamé parameters λp = 5/18 × 10^7 kPa and μp = 5/12 × 10^7 kPa
- Storativity coefficient s0 = 6.89 × 10^-2 kPa^-1, permeability K = 10^-8 × I m^2, Beavers-Joseph-Saffman friction coefficient αBJS = 1
- Applications include gas/oil extraction from fractured reservoirs, arterial flow modeling, and industrial filter design
- Domain consists of fluid region Ωf and poroelastic region Ωp separated by interface Γfp = ∂Ωf ∩ ∂Ωp
- Example geometries include rectangular domains with horizontal interface (Ωf = (0,1)×(0,1), Ωp = (0,1)×(-1,0)) and domains with irregularly shaped fluid-filled cavities
- Interface conditions include mass conservation, balance of stresses, and Beavers-Joseph-Saffman slip with friction condition
- Model handles poroelastic locking regimes with small permeability and storativity, large Lamé parameters

- Boundary segments ΓDf, ΓDp, and Γ̃Dp must maintain minimum distance s > 0 from interface Γfp (dist(ΓDf, Γfp) ≥ s, dist(ΓDp, Γfp) ≥ s, dist(Γ̃Dp, Γfp) ≥ s)

- Storativity coefficient must be s0 > 0
- Permeability tensor K must be symmetric and uniformly positive definite with 0 < kmin ≤ kmax
- Initial pressure condition must satisfy pp,0 ∈ Hp = {wp ∈ H1(Ωp) : K∇wp ∈ H1(Ωp), K∇wp · np = 0 on ΓNp, wp = 0 on ΓDp}
- Method requires shape-regular and quasi-uniform affine finite element partitions for both regions (may be non-matching across interface)

10_1016_j_dt_2024_08_007.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Polymer-Bonded Explosive (PBX) energetic composite with focus on crystal-binder interface characteristics
- **Material / Medium:** HMX explosive crystals, Estane binder; interface bonding energy 0.077 N/mm; critical hot spot density 0.68 mm⁻²; critical ignition pressure 3.0 GPa; minimum required compressive strength 16 MPa; friction coefficient range 0.01-0.3
- **Application & Importance:** Optimization of mechanical properties (compressive strength) and safety (impact ignition sensitivity) in weapon systems where both structural integrity and reduced accidental ignition risk are critical performance requirements
- **Geometry / Domain:** 2D mesostructure model (5.86 mm × 3.73 mm) with crystal-binder interface; 3% porosity; triangular mesh size 0.01 mm; includes voids, explosive particles, and polymer binder with varying surface roughness characterized by friction coefficient μ

- **Loads / Excitations:** Flyer impact velocity of 500 m/s; impact pressures of 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, and 4.0 GPa; strain rates of 800 s⁻¹, 1500 s⁻¹, and 1800 s⁻¹; friction coefficients μ = 0.01, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3; thermal decomposition parameters (Q = 2100 J/g, Z = 5×10¹⁹ s⁻¹, E = 2.0×10⁵ J/mol)

10_1016_j_dt_2024_08_007.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Hot spot count and density (mm⁻²); compressive strength (MPa); temperature distribution (K); pressure distribution (GPa); stress-strain response; hot spot formation time (μs); critical ignition density (0.68 mm⁻²); critical ignition pressure (3.0 GPa); interface friction coefficient (μ) effects on mechanical properties and safety
- **Optimization Goal:** Determine optimal crystal surface roughness (friction coefficient 0.06-0.12) that simultaneously achieves minimum compressive strength of 16 MPa while maintaining hot spot density below critical ignition threshold of 0.68 mm⁻², balancing mechanical integrity with impact ignition safety in PBX formulations
10_1016_j_dt_2024_08_007.key_4:

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Minimum required compressive strength of 16 MPa; critical hot spot density threshold of 0.68 mm⁻² for ignition; critical ignition pressure of 3.0 GPa; hot spot formation criteria requiring temperature > 780 K and pressure > 5.0 GPa; crystal surface friction coefficient range limited to 0.01-0.3; flyer impact velocity fixed at 500 m/s
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Surface roughness controlled through dopamine polymerization coating technique; PDA layer morphology and thickness regulated by reaction time, pH, and temperature; 5% grafting content required to form effective roughness shells; optimal friction coefficient range of 0.06-0.12 constrained by practical processing capabilities in explosive formulation manufacturing

10_1016_j_apacoust_2025_110767.key_1:

- ABH parameters: residual thickness h₀ = 0.3 mm, uniform partial thickness h_uni = 1.25 mm, residual length l₀ = 3 mm, variable thickness part length l_uni = 13 mm, power index m = 3

10_1007_s12206_018_0131_3.key_1:

- Material / Medium: Q690 steel frame material; SLD70 weld wire; thermo-mechanical properties of Q690 change with temperature
- Application & Importance: Rated load of 400 tons mine electric drive dump truck; zero failure time as important performance indicator; high-stress areas at connection position of left-right longitudinal beam and rear torsion tube; weld toe geometry affects structural strength and fatigue life
- Geometry / Domain: Frame composed of left-right longitudinal beam, portal-type girder assembly, bumper assembly, lifting cylinder support, central torsion tube, and rear torsion tube; fillet weld joint with 20 mm weld height; 15 mm weld toe in actual manufacture; 20 mm weld toe in optimization scheme; coordinate system defined with X, Y, Z axes
- Dimensions: Horizontal plate 200 mm × 100 mm × 30 mm; vertical plate 100 mm × 100 mm × 20 mm; groove angle 60 degrees; blunt edge length 3 mm
- Stress values: Peak stress 453.8 MPa before weld toe optimization; peak stress 340.6 MPa after optimization; stress concentration reduced at weld toe position
- Performance metrics: Frame failure time increases by more than 5000 hours with optimization; no fatigue failure observed in testing
- Loading conditions: Full ramp condition including turning and braking; centrifugal force FR = mv²/r; ground friction Ff = Gf; inertial force Fa = Ff; rated capacity twice gravity; friction coefficient f = 0.6
- Finite element model: 2801144 elements; 1425903 nodes; hexahedral and shell element combination; minimum grid size 1 mm for weld area; total grid units 43282 with 46838 nodes for weld model
- Optimization results: Weld height and toe of 20 mm produces smaller stress peak; welding seam surface forms concave arc after repair welding; stress peak reduced from 453.8 MPa to 340.6 MPa
10_1007_s12206_018_0131_3.key_2:
- Boundaries & Constraints: Full constraints under symmetrical part of portal-type girder and bumper assemblies; Center point constraints in holes of lifting cylinder support, central torsion, and rear torsion tubes; Rigid unit linking center point and hole-shaft (simplified as point constraint); Displacement constraints restricting X direction in middle section; Displacement constraints restricting Z direction in back of weld seam; Spring constraints restricting Y direction on weld center
- Loads / Excitations: Static loads from rated capacity and frame/ accessory weight; Dynamic loads from traction, full ramp, turning, braking, and lifting; Centrifugal force FR = mv²/r; Ground friction Ff = Gf where G = rated capacity × 2 and f = 0.6; Inertial force Fa = Ff; Loads applied along X direction on portal-type girder assembly and rear torsion tube; Rated capacity × 2 applied on up-surface of left-right longitudinal beam and hole of rear torsion tube; Arc voltage 20-22V; Arc current 200-220A; Welding speed 6 mm/s; Double ellipsoid heat source model
- Interactions / Interfaces: Coupled relationship between weld toe structure and frame stiffness; Rigid connection between center point and hole-shaft; Fillet weld joint interface; Isotropic material assumption; Constant ambient temperature; No weld pool flow considered; Effects of transformation and work hardening considered
- Simulation Type: 3D simulation; Thermo-elastic/plastic finite element analysis; Elastic-plastic finite element method; Von Mises stress evaluation (fourth strength theory); Transition grid approach; Minimum grid size of 1 mm in weld area; Total grid units: 43282 for weld model, 46838 nodes for weld model; Full frame model: 2801144 elements, 1425903 nodes (hexahedral and shell elements); Nonlinear analysis; Transient analysis for weld thermal process
10_1007_s12206_018_0131_3.key_3:

- Target Outputs (Metrics): Peak stress values (453.8 MPa before optimization, 340.6 MPa after); Stress distribution patterns across frame; Residual stress distributions at different weld bead geometries; Effective stress (MPa) in weld toe regions; Frame failure time; Stress concentration coefficient; Weld morphology
- Optimization Goal: Reduce stress peak value from 453.8 MPa to 340.6 MPa; Reduce stress concentration at connection position of left-right longitudinal beam and rear torsion tube; Create concave arc welding seam surface; Increase frame failure time by more than 5000 hours; Eliminate fatigue failure in frame structure; Optimize weld toe geometry to match weld height (20 mm)
10_1007_s12206_018_0131_3.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: Horizontal plate dimensions 200 mm × 100 mm × 30 mm; Vertical plate dimensions 100 mm × 100 mm × 20 mm; Groove angle 60 degrees; Blunt edge length 3 mm; Weld height 20 mm in actual manufacture; Weld toe 15 mm in actual manufacture; Optimized weld height and toe both 20 mm; Minimum grid size 1 mm in weld area and heat-affected zone; Frame geometry includes left-right longitudinal beam, portal-type girder assembly, bumper assembly, lifting cylinder support, central torsion tube, and rear torsion tube
- Performance/Physics Limits: Q690 steel material with temperature-dependent thermal, physical, and mechanical parameters; Plastic yield as failure form; Von Mises stress evaluation using fourth strength theory; Stress peak value limit of 453.8 MPa before optimization; Stress peak value target of 340.6 MPa after optimization; Frame failure time must increase by more than 5000 hours without fatigue failure
- Process/Manufacturing: Arc voltage 20-22V; Arc current 200-220A; Welding speed 6 mm/s; SLD70 weld wire; Weld height and toe not equivalent in general production; "Ship" weld seam difficult to implement and causes undercut defects; Repair welding required to achieve 20 mm height and 20 mm weld toe optimization; Welding seam surface must form concave arc after repair welding; Frame must be lifted to be coincident with center line of weld seam (challenging in actual production)

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109260.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Integral nonlocal elasticity problems using Eringen's strain-driven nonlocal elasticity theory, solved via multimesh finite element method (M²-FEM)
- **Material / Medium:** Nonlocal elastic materials with Lamé parameters μ = 1 Pa and λ = 1 Pa; applicable to metamaterials, porous solids, functionally-graded solids, lattice structures, composites, fluid-saturated porous media, and carbon nanotubes
- **Application & Importance:** To overcome limitations in existing nonlocal finite element solvers by enabling accurate simulation of nonlocal effects that classical continuum mechanics fails to capture; addresses long-range interactions at microstructural scales in complex materials
- **Geometry / Domain:** Square-shaped 2D domain (1m × 1m); nonlocal annulus (inner radius 0.3m, outer radius 0.5m); square domain with circular nonlocal horizon (radius 0.2m); local plane strain domain (1m × 1m) with nonlocal circular inclusion (radius 0.15m); nonlocal horizon defined as H(x,y) = [min(x-l_nl,0), max(x+l_nl,L)] × [min(y-l_nl,0), max(y+l_nl,L)]
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109260.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Fixed boundary conditions (u_x = u_y = 0) on all boundaries for square domain; fixed boundary conditions on left/right boundaries for plane strain problem; displacement boundary conditions u(x,y) = {-x^2 + x, 0} on top/bottom boundaries; fixed boundary condition on left boundary for inclusion problem; displacement boundary conditions u(x,y) = {x, 0} on remaining boundaries; fixed boundary condition on inner loop of annulus; traction boundary condition with |t_out| = 0.1 Pa on outer loop of annulus
- **Loads / Excitations:** Body forces f(x,y) = {-2(μ + λ), 0} applied within plane strain domain; external traction loads applied at boundaries; normal tractions of magnitude |t_out| = 0.1 Pa on annulus outer boundary; spatially-varying body forces for validation studies
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Nonlocal integral relation σ(x) = C : ∫_H(x) K(x,x')ϵ(x')dx'; mesh-decoupling between parent domain (material domain) and child domain (nonlocal horizon); scale-bridging algorithm mapping child Gauss points to parent elements; nonlocal interface between inclusion and matrix
- **Simulation Type:** Static (elasto-static) integral nonlocal problems; 2D plane strain; linear elasticity with Lamé parameters μ = 1 Pa and λ = 1 Pa; nonlocal elasticity using Eringen's strain-driven approach
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109260.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Integral nonlocal elasticity using Eringen's strain-driven approach; captures long-range interactions at microstructural scales through nonlocal integral relations; models nonlocal effects in complex materials including metamaterials, porous solids, and composites
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Displacement fields (u_x, u_y); maximum displacement values (e.g., ū_x_ref = 0.0625 m); relative error in displacement (e.g., Tables 1-4); computational time (e.g., Fig. 8a); convergence behavior (e.g., Tables 3-4); nonlocal softening/stiffening behavior; stress distributions; nonlocal discontinuity at interfaces
- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve simultaneous high accuracy and high computational efficiency through mesh-decoupling; enable simulation of irregular geometries with non-rectangular domains; accurately capture behavior with both non-singular (two-phase bi-exponential) and singular (power-law) nonlocal kernel functions; overcome the trade-off between accuracy and computational cost inherent in mesh-coupled methods
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2024_109260.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Nonlocal horizon must satisfy H(x) ⊆ Ω for all x ∈ Ω; parent domain size fixed at 1m × 1m for validation studies; nonlocal annulus with inner radius 0.3m and outer radius 0.5m; inclusion problem with 1m × 1m matrix and 0.15m inclusion radius; nonlocal horizon size l_nl = 0.2m for annulus example; parent and child domains must maintain compatibility through scale-bridging algorithm
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Nonlocal kernel must be positive-definite and symmetric for well-posedness; fractional-order parameter α ∈ (0,1) for weakly-singular power-law kernels; convergence criterion threshold of Δ = 2% relative difference; relative resolution r_p-c must avoid extremes (r_p-c ≪ 1 causes instabilities, r_p-c ≫ 1 causes poor efficiency); nonlocal horizon must be sufficiently large to capture majority of nonlocal interactions
- **Process/Manufacturing:** For weakly-singular kernels, singular points must be positioned on child element boundaries; child mesh must be structured to accommodate kernel function characteristics; minimum child domain resolution of 5×5 elements for power-law kernel and 6×6 for exponential kernel to achieve convergence; parent mesh number M_p and relative resolution r_p-c must be tuned independently to balance accuracy and computational cost; current implementation limited to static (elasto-static) problems and 2D plane strain analysis

10_1016_j_elstat_2025_104065.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Capacitors, including ideal theoretical configurations (1D, 2D, 3D) and real-world devices (coaxial, parallel wire, ring, semicircular disc). Analyzed using Algebraic Topological Method (ATM) for stored electrostatic energy and 3D Maxwellian capacitance evaluation.

  - jρ₀ω∇p ⋅ n = v̄ₙ on ∂Ω for Helmholtz problems, where v̄ₙ is the normal velocity

- **Geometric/Design Space:**  
  - Must use Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces as boundary representation  
  - Surface must be a single watertight manifold with G⁰ continuity  
  - FEM mesh size h(x) must be smaller than control net size H(x)  
  - Limit positions of extraordinary vertices (EVs) must be nodes in the initial mesh  
  - Surfaces are only tangent-plane continuous (G¹) at EV limit positions, not curvature-continuous (G²)  
  - Only finite number of virtual subdivisions can be applied for practical implementation (not infinite)  

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**  
  - Total boundary elements proportional to h⁻² while total elements proportional to h⁻³  
  - Linear elements used in implementation (though p-refinement is theoretically possible)  
  - 10th order Gauss quadrature rule typically required for machine precision with constant functions  
  - A coarser quadrature (2nd order rule on Λₐ) is sufficient for correct convergence behavior  
  - Number of elements with EV nodes is small compared to total elements (EV count is fixed feature of subdivision model)  
  - Geometrical error becomes limiting factor for higher-order polynomial approximations in spherical domains  

- **Process/Manufacturing:**

  - Control net must be refined during convergence analysis for spherical approximations  
  - Integration requires splitting parametric triangles into subtriangles when crossing patch boundaries  
  - Special quadrature strategy required for elements adjacent to extraordinary vertices
