10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2017_11_038.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Continuum modeling of auxetic materials at large strains using finite element analysis
- **Material / Medium:** Auxetic foams (specifically Scott foams from Choi-Lakes experiments); characterized by negative Poisson ratios (-0.7 for Lakes' polyurethane foam); highly compressible; transition from auxetic to conventional behavior during large deformations; specific parameters for Scott foam: μ₀ = 26.53 kPa, ν₀ = -0.53, λI = 1.33, f = 1
- **Application & Importance:** Enables efficient finite element analysis of auxetic structures without computationally expensive multiscale models; critical for applications requiring negative Poisson ratio behavior including enhanced pull-out resistance, improved indentation resistance (armored vehicles, bullet-proof vests), large shear-to-bulk stiffness ratio, improved fracture toughness, noise/vibration absorption, and biomedical implants
- **Geometry / Domain:** 32 mm × 16 mm plate with 4 mm radius centered hole under plane strain conditions; stretched longitudinally to double its length; analyzed using 9-node quadratic elements with 3×3 integration; also includes simple shear tests and uniaxial tension/compression tests
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2017_11_038.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Plane strain plate stretched longitudinally to double its length with displacements imposed via penalty formulation; larger sides of the plate left free; 9-node Lagrangean elements with 3×3 integration; global equilibrium equations solved using plain Newton procedure
- **Loads / Excitations:** Longitudinal stretching to double plate length; simple shear tests with "amount of shear" parameter γ; deformation gradient X = [(1+γ)^n, γ, 0; 0, (1+γ)^n, 0; 0, 0, 1] where n = 1/4, 1/2, or 3/4 for different test cases
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Stress-strain pair T-E and constitutive tensor converted to other work-conjugate pairs using mapping tensors; simulations performed with in-house finite element code Dulcinea
- **Simulation Type:** Large strain finite element analysis; plane strain condition; nonlinear static analysis; uniaxial tension-compression tests; simple shear tests
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2017_11_038.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Large strain hyperelastic behavior of auxetic materials; stress-strain relationships; transverse-to-longitudinal strain relationships (Poisson ratio evolution); deformation mechanics of auxetic foams; stress distributions during complex loading; energy-conservative isotropic material behavior
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Cauchy stress (kPa) vs. uniaxial stretch; transverse stretch vs. uniaxial stretch; Von Mises stress distributions (kPa); pressure distributions (kPa); longitudinal and transverse logarithmic strains; energy term derivatives (ω', U'); stress components (σ₁₁, σ₁₂, σ₂₂) vs. shear parameter; force and energy convergence residuals; Poisson ratio behavior during deformation
- **Optimization Goal:** Accurately capture experimental data from Choi and Lakes for auxetic Scott foams across all deformation ranges; validate continuum modeling approach for auxetic materials; demonstrate that J-WYPiWYG hyperelasticity can exactly replicate the Ciambella-Saccomandi model behavior in any loading condition; compare uncoupled (E-WYPiWYG) and coupled (J-WYPiWYG) hyperelasticity approaches for predicting auxetic material behavior at large strains
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2017_11_038.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Plate dimensions constrained to 32 mm length, 16 mm width with 4 mm radius centered hole; analysis limited to plane strain condition; use of 9-node Lagrangean elements with 3×3 integration; deformation gradient parameterized as X = [(1+γ)^n, γ, 0; 0, (1+γ)^n, 0; 0, 0, 1] with discrete n values (1/4, 1/2, 3/4); analysis limited to isotropic materials

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Theoretical Poisson ratio limits constrained to -1 < ν ≤ 0.5 for isotropic materials; Ciambella-Saccomandi model accuracy limited to strains below 50%; E-WYPiWYG based on Valanis-Landel decomposition not ideal for highly compressible auxetic foams; V-shaped energy terms require specific conditions on Poisson ratio evolution (νc < 1/2η(1+νt) - 1); J-WYPiWYG requires three experimental curves to determine all functions but only two are available for Scott foams (requiring assumption of Blatz-Ko relation W1' = fW', W2' = (1-f)W')

- **Process/Manufacturing:** J-WYPiWYG iterative procedure requires convergence criteria on function differences between iterations; noisy experimental data produces noisy computed functions (requiring data smoothing); computational implementation limited to in-house finite element code Dulcinea; analysis restricted to energy-conservative materials (no plasticity or viscoelasticity); requirement for discrete experimental data points to build spline functions; parameter f must be specified (f=1 or f=3/4 used in examples) due to limited experimental data

• Loads / Excitations: 200 MPa and 300 MPa load levels applied during tensile testing; bolt tightening load applied to industrial casting; constant cross-head displacement rate of 0.35 mm/min; stress levels reaching ultimate tensile strength of 347 MPa (experimental) and 340 MPa (simulated)

10_1016_j_jcde_2018_02_002.key_3:

• Optimization Goal: Accurate prediction of damage initiation and failure locations in heterogeneous cast structures; maximization of damage tolerance through controlled local microstructural refinement; reduction of local damage levels in critical regions using targeted solidification control (e.g., chills); optimization of local quality factor by minimizing porosity effects; enabling design of cast components with tailored material behavior and local damage tolerance
10_1016_j_jcde_2018_02_002.key_4:

• Process/Manufacturing: High Pressure Die Casting (HPDC) process with EN AC 46,000 alloy (AlSi9Cu3); iron content constrained to 0.6-1.1% to reduce sticking in permanent dies; initial melt temperature of 700°C for solidification; microstructural refinement controlled by local cooling rate; previous approaches limited to thin-walled structures where layered shell elements can be used; evolution of damage after initiation not studied in current work; difficulty isolating local variations in tensile toughness in component testing; simplistic relationship between porosity and quality factor (QLi = Qgen × (100 - porosityi)) used as preliminary model

10_1016_j_finel_2015_06_009.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Truck and bus radial (TBR) tire belt edge region; focus on cord-rubber composite structure at belt edge where cracks nucleate and propagate

- **Application & Importance:** Assess tire durability by accurately predicting belt edge strains; maximum shear strain occurs at belt edge where cracks nucleate and grow along belt-rubber interface; critical for preventing tire rupture accidents
- **Geometry / Domain:** Cords form helical shape twisted once every 16mm; global tire model with rebar elements in belt; local model representing 5° section of tire belt; coordinate system with x-axis (radial), z-axis (forward), y-axis (into page); wire cord geometry defined by parametric equations x = r·cos(a·t + θ), y = r·sin(a·t + θ), z = L·t (0 ≤ t ≤ 1)
10_1016_j_finel_2015_06_009.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Tensile test conducted with Instron 4301 machine; cord of 70mm length fixed to center of Teledyne Taber 150-D bending tester; penalty contact defined between wires in wire cord model to prevent penetration; displacements from global model applied as boundary conditions for local model in submodeling technique; one end of beam fixed with moment applied in bending analysis
- **Loads / Excitations:** Cord stretched until breakage in tensile test; disk rotated 15° in bending test to obtain reaction moment; tire rolling analysis conducted for 120° rotation; time-domain loading up to 2.0 seconds as shown in strain plots
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Wire-to-wire contact interaction in wire cord model; cord-rubber composite interface; global-local model interaction through submodeling technique; truss elements connected to solid elements in truss cord model; neutral axis location affected by tensile/compressive region interaction in bilinear model
- **Simulation Type:** Transient analysis (time-domain up to 2.0 seconds); 3D analysis with x-axis (radial), y-axis (into page), z-axis (forward) coordinate system; nonlinear material behavior with plastic deformation; global-local analysis using submodeling technique; bilinear cord model implemented via UMAT user material subroutine in ABAQUS
10_1016_j_finel_2015_06_009.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** zx shear strain at belt edge; strain components (xx, xy, xz, yy, yz, zz) as time-domain functions; stress-strain curves; reaction moment from bending analysis; tensile force-deflection relationships; comparative strain magnitudes between modeling approaches (74.5% higher for truss model, 87.2% for bilinear model, 108.7% for solid model vs. global rebar model)
- **Optimization Goal:** Reduce zx shear strain at belt edge to improve tire durability; accurately predict strain magnitudes at belt edge to prevent crack nucleation and growth that leads to tire rupture; develop equivalent cord models that capture both tensile and bending behaviors of actual cords for accurate strain prediction
10_1016_j_finel_2015_06_009.key_4:

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Tensile testing conducted until cord breakage; bending test with 15° disk rotation; wire cord Young's modulus of 164.8 GPa; bilinear model with tensile Young's modulus 164.8 GPa and compressive Young's modulus 9.78 GPa; linear Young's modulus variation defined between strain -0.0001 to 0.0; tire rolling analysis performed for 120° rotation; time-domain analysis up to 2.0 seconds; maximum zx shear strain at belt edge used as critical failure indicator
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Wire cord model requires ~20,000 elements per cord; whole tire belt requires ~1370 cords (total ~2 million elements for cords only); whole tire model requires ~50 million elements due to fine rubber meshing; truss cord model requires 630 elements per cord; bilinear cord model requires 1120 elements per cord; global-local analysis technique required due to computational limitations of modeling entire tire with detailed cord models; bilinear model required user material subroutine (UMAT) implementation in ABAQUS due to non-standard material behavior

10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106427.key_1:
- Hydrodynamic journal bearings in rotor systems
- Oil lubricant with dynamic viscosity μ in lubrication gap between shaft and shell
- Nonlinear bearing forces affect rotor stability; self-excited shaft oscillations cause component damage and noise emissions
- Cylindrical bearing geometry with unwound lubrication gap domain (0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, -0.5 ≤ Y ≤ 0.5)
- Radial clearance c, eccentricity q, eccentricity angle θex, slenderness ratio γ = lb/db
- Oil supply grooves with axial length ls, circumferential position θs, and width αs
- Solution domain discretized with circumferential node spacing Δθ and axial spacing ΔY
- Periodic boundary conditions at θ = 0 and θ = 2π
- Symmetric pressure distribution with respect to Y = 0 when ambient pressures are identical at both axial boundaries
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106427.key_2:
- Periodic boundary condition at circumferential boundaries: P(θ, Y) = P(θ + 2π, Y)
- Symmetric boundary condition at axial center: P,Y(Y = 0) = 0
- Ambient pressure boundary condition at axial ends: P(θ, ±0.5) = Pamb = 0 (in most simulations)
- Oil supply pressure boundary conditions at groove location: P(θs - αs/2 ≤ θ ≤ θs + αs/2, Y) = Ps = 0.02
- Circumferential groove position: θs = 3π/5 (in convergence study) or θs = π/4 (in FEM verification)
- Circumferential groove width: αs = 2π/15 (in convergence study) or αs = π/10 (in FEM verification)
- Axial groove length: ls = lb (long groove model) or ls < lb (realistic groove model with ΔYi = 0.25)
- Negative pressures set to zero after solution (Gümbel condition)
- Shaft rotational velocity: ω (appears in Reynolds equation and as time derivative parameter)
- Eccentricity: ε = {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9} (in convergence study)
- Eccentricity angle: θex = 0, π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4 (in various simulations)
- Time derivatives: ε̇ = 0 or ω/(5π), θ̇ex = 0 or ω/4 or ω/2
- Slenderness ratio: γ = 1, 1.5, or 2 (in efficiency study)
- Transient simulations with time integration of state space vector
- 2D domain in unwound lubrication gap (0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π, -0.5 ≤ Y ≤ 0.5)
- Nonlinear simulations due to nonlinear bearing force characteristics
- Pressure field integrated to obtain bearing forces for coupling with equation of motion
10_1016_j_ijmecsci_2021_106427.key_3:

- Computational time t_comp for solving the Reynolds equation

- Relative error δF of the resulting bearing forces compared to reference solutions

10_1007_s12008_023_01527_x.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Friction Stir Spot Welding (FSSW) process for joining dissimilar metals
- **Material / Medium:** AZ31B magnesium alloy (1.5 mm thick) and AA6061-T6 aluminum alloy (1.5 mm thick); AZ31B contains Zn (0.8%), Al (2.6%), Mn (0.15%), Cu (0.04%), Si (0.04%), Fe (0.002%), Ni (0.001%) with balance Mg; AA6061-T6 contains Zn (0.23%), Mn (0.12%), Cu (0.21%), Si (0.4-0.8%), Fe (0.6%), Ni (0.95%) with balance Al
- **Application & Importance:** Optimizing FSSW parameters to maximize tensile shear fracture load (TSFL) for automotive applications where lightweight, good mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance are required; dissimilar fusion welding is challenging due to intermetallic compound formation causing solidification cracking
- **Geometry / Domain:** Lap joint configuration with 75×25 mm tensile shear fracture test specimens; 1.5 mm thick sheets; spot weld location shown in specimen diagrams; FSSW process involves three stages (plunging, stirring, extraction) with tool rotational speed (600-1400 rpm), tool plunging rate (8-24 mm/min), dwell time (3-7 s), and tool diameter ratio (1.5-3.5) as key parameters
10_1007_s12008_023_01527_x.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - TRS range: 600-1400 rpm (lower limit <600 causes low heat generation and lack of filling material; upper limit >1400 causes high heat generation and keyhole defect)
  - TPR range: 8-24 mm/min (lower limit <8 causes insufficient joint due to less heat generation; upper limit >24 causes high heat generation and keyhole defect)
  - DT range: 3-7 s (lower limit <3 causes less flow of plasticized material and low filling; upper limit >7 causes keyhole defect)
  - TDR range: 1.5-3.5 (lower limit <1.5 causes insufficient heat supply and lack of material flow; upper limit >3.5 causes high heat input, high work hardening and keyhole)
  - Tensile shear fracture test specimens: 75 mm total length, 25 mm width, with spot weld positioned 25 mm from one end

- **Loads / Excitations:** 
  - Specimens loaded at 1.50 kN/min as per ASTM D1002 standard for shear testing
  - Tensile shear fracture load (TSFL) range: 1.8-3.61 kN
  - Tool rotational speed (TRS): 600-1400 rpm
  - Tool plunging rate (TPR): 8-24 mm/min
  - Dwell time (DT): 3-7 s
  - Tool diameter ratio (TDR): 1.5-3.5

- **Interactions / Interfaces:** 
  - Dissimilar interface between AZ31B magnesium alloy and AA6061-T6 aluminum alloy
  - FSSW process involves three distinct stages: plunging, stirring, and extraction
  - Formation of intermetallic compounds at the interface between dissimilar materials
  - Lap joint configuration for tensile shear testing

- **Simulation Type:** 
  - Second-order polynomial regression modeling
  - Response surface methodology (RSM) with central composite design
  - Four-factor, five-level experimental matrix (30 experimental runs)
  - Parametric mathematical model (PMM) for predicting tensile shear fracture load
  - 3D response surface graphs showing TSFL as function of paired parameters
10_1007_s12008_023_01527_x.key_3:

  - Tensile shear fracture load (TSFL) in kN (range: 1.8-3.61 kN)
  - Regression coefficients for second-order polynomial model
  - ANOVA results showing significance of parameters (F-value: 159.68, p<0.0001)

  - Achieve maximum TSFL of 3.617 kN at optimal parameters: TRS 1129.2 rpm, TPR 17.48 mm/min, DT 3.93 s, TDR 2.63
  - Experimental verification showing maximum TSFL of 3.60 kN at TRS 1000 rpm, TPR 16 mm/min, DT 5.0 s, TDR 2.5

10_1007_s12008_023_01527_x.key_4:

  - Tensile shear fracture test specimens: 75 mm total length, 25 mm width, with spot weld positioned 25 mm from one end

  - Tool diameter ratio (TDR) constrained between 1.5 and 3.5

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**

  - Tool plunging rate (TPR): 8-24 mm/min (<8 mm/min causes insufficient joint due to less heat generation; >24 mm/min causes keyhole defect)

10_1007_s40430_023_04116_x.key_1:

10_1007_s40430_023_04116_x.key_2:

10_1007_s40430_023_04116_x.key_4:

10_1016_j_apmt_2025_102722.key_1:

- Material / Medium: Hard phase (VeroCyan™ RGD841, E = 2651 MPa, ν = 0.4); Soft phase (Agilus30™ Clear FLX935, Ogden model N=1, μ₁ = 0.266 MPa, α₁ = 3.006, D₁ = 0.113)

- Validation: 4×4 unit cell lattices with 3 mm off-plane thickness; 8 µm³ voxel size for printing

10_1016_j_apmt_2025_102722.key_2:

10_1016_j_apmt_2025_102722.key_3:

- Target Outputs (Metrics): Elastic moduli (E₁₁, E₂₂); Poisson's ratios (ν₁₂, ν₂₁); Strain energy density distribution (normalized SED [%]); Ultimate tensile strength (σ_UTS); True stress-strain curves; First principal strain (εₚ); Toughness (area under stress-strain curve until rupture); Resilience (energy absorbed until maximum stress)
- Optimization Goal: Minimize local strain energy density concentrations; Achieve homogeneous SED distributions; Expand envelope of achievable elastic properties; Increase mechanical strength (up to 78% improvement over initial designs); Create stress-worthy metamaterials with unusual elastic properties (including auxetic behavior); Introduce intermediate length scale between unit cell and voxel dimensions; Maintain constant hard volume fraction (ρ) during remodeling process

10_1016_j_finel_2017_06_001.key_2:

10_1007_s00419_024_02718_y.key_1:
- Sandwich panels under in-plane compression with focus on wrinkling failure modes
- Face sheets: Glass fiber-reinforced polymer (GFRP) with Young's modulus Ef=13.23 GPa; Aluminum with Ef=69 GPa in test cases
- Core: Polyurethane foam with Young's modulus Ec=2.1 MPa, shear modulus Gc, Poisson's ratio νc=0.3; Foam with Ec=3.59 MPa and Gc=2.28 MPa; Foam with Ec=9.65 MPa and Gc=6.76 MPa
- Three wrinkling modes: symmetric (η=1), antisymmetric (η=-1), and one-sided (η=0)
- Geometric parameters: face sheet thickness f (2 mm, 0.4978 mm, 0.3048 mm), core thickness c (150 mm, 25.4 mm, 19.05 mm), total panel thickness 2f+c
- Panel dimensions: 620 mm×154 mm (L×(2f+c)) in FE model
- Wrinkling half-wavelength denoted as a
- Core discretized into n virtual plies (n=300 in verification, n=200 in FGM analysis)
- Functionally graded material (FGM) cores with relative density ρ* varying from 0.35 to 0.1 from surface to core center
- Plane stress state considered in analysis; plane strain requires modified moduli (Ef/(1-νf²), Ec/(1-νc²))
- Critical wrinkling stress σcr calculated as minimum value of σf under proper choices of half-wavelength a and decay coefficients ki
- Wrinkling stress formula: σcr = min(ki,a) [π²Ef f²/(12a²) + (a²/f(1+η²))Σ(Ec i(ki-ki-1)²/ti) + (1/f(1+η²))Σ(Gc i ti ki²)]
10_1007_s00419_024_02718_y.key_2:
- Simply supported boundary conditions on all four corners in FE model
- Axial compression applied to face sheets as longitudinal stress
- Longitudinal displacement negligible due to panel length assumption
- Boundary effects on wrinkling behavior ignored in analytical model
- Constraint k₁ = 1 at upper face sheet interface
- Constraint kₙ = η at lower face sheet interface (where η = 1 for antisymmetric, -1 for symmetric, 0 for one-sided wrinkling)
- Box constraints -1 ≤ kᵢ ≤ 1 for i = 2,..., n-1
- Plane stress state considered in analysis (plane strain requires modified moduli)
- FE analysis used quadrilateral four-node plane element (solid 182) with 381,920 elements
- Generalized eigenvalue problem solved using Block Lanczos method in FE analysis
- Structural optimization problem formulated to minimize wrinkling stress
- Iterative optimization procedure: Initialize guess kᵢ, Calculate a, Calculate σf, Perform sensitivity analysis, Update kᵢ, Check convergence
- Compression force fully applied to face sheets due to Ef >> Ec
- Relative density ρ* varying from 0.35 at surface to 0.1 at core center for FGM cores
- Core subdivided into n virtual plies (n=300 in verification, n=200 in FGM analysis)
- Material properties mapped between discrete FGM layers (I=1,...,N) and virtual plies (i=1,...,n)
10_1007_s00419_024_02718_y.key_3:

- Critical wrinkling stress (σcr) in MPa
- Wrinkling half-wavelength (a) in mm
- Vertical displacement decay coefficients (ki) across core thickness
- Wrinkling mode identification (symmetric, antisymmetric, one-sided)

- Convergence of wrinkling stress and half-wavelength values for functionally graded material (FGM) cores with increasing layer count N
10_1007_s00419_024_02718_y.key_4:

- Material properties must satisfy the cellular solids relationship for foam cores: Ec ≈ (ρ*)²Es, Gc ≈ 0.375(ρ*)²Es

10_1016_j_cad_2016_08_005.key_1:
- **Subject of analysis:** Strain gradient elasticity models (classical, first-order, second-order) implemented via isogeometric analysis within Abaqus
- **1D bar models:** Clamped bar under static tension (L=1 mm, A=1 mm², E=1 MPa, P=1 N, l_s1=l_s2=0.1L) and free vibrations (E=4 MPa, ρ=1 T/mm)
- **2D square plate:** Tangentially clamped plate (a=1 mm, E=1 MPa, ν=0.3, l_s1=l_s2=0.1a) under body forces; vibration analysis (a=10 mm, E=210 GPa, ρ=7850 kg/m³, l_s1=0.1a, l_s2=0.2a, l_d1=l_d2=0.05a)
- **2D annulus plate:** Quarter-annulus under compression (a=5 mm, b=10 mm, E=210 GPa, ν=0.3, l_s1=l_s2=0.2a, P=100 MPa)
- **Kraus problem:** Quarter-circular plate with central hole and four circumferential holes (R_0=200 mm, R_i/R_0=0.25, R/R_0=0.625, a/R_0=0.1, E=210 GPa, ν=0.3, l_s1/a=0.5, P=-100 MPa)
- **Micro-structural parameters:** l_s1 and l_s2 (length-scale parameters) for first/second strain gradient elasticity; l_d1 and l_d2 for micro-inertial effects
- **Continuity requirements:** C¹-continuous discretization for first strain gradient; C²-continuous for second strain gradient elasticity
- **Geometry representation:** NURBS-based isogeometric discretization with exact geometry representation
- **Stress concentration analysis:** Maximum von Mises stress 322 MPa (K_t=3.22) for classical model vs. 230 MPa (K_t=2.3) for first strain gradient model in Kraus problem
- **Basis functions:** NURBS of orders p=3,4,5 with C^(p-1) continuity; seventh-order B-splines (C⁶) for 1D static tension benchmark
- **Convergence properties:** Energy norm convergence O(h^(p)) for classical, O(h^(p-1)) for first strain gradient, O(h^(p-2)) for second strain gradient elasticity
10_1016_j_cad_2016_08_005.key_2:
- **1D static bar (clamped in tension):**
  - Fixed displacement: u(0) = 0, u'(0) = 0, u''(0) = 0 at x = 0
  - Applied force: P₁(L) = P = 1 N at x = L
  - Zero slope: u'(L) = 0 at x = L
  - Zero curvature: u''(L) = 0 at x = L
  - Zero body force: b = 0

- **1D vibration bar (clamped):**
  - Fixed displacement: u = 0 at x = 0 and x = L
  - Zero double traction: P₂ = 0 at x = 0 and x = L
  - Zero triple traction: P₃ = 0 at x = 0 and x = L
  - Zero body force: b = 0

- **2D static square plate (tangentially clamped):**
  - Tangential displacement constraint: u · s = 0 on ∂Ω
  - Zero normal traction: t₁ · n = 0 on ∂Ω
  - Zero double traction: t₂ = 0 on ∂Ω
  - Zero triple normal traction: t₃ · n = 0 on ∂Ω
  - Triple tangential traction: t₃ · s|y=0,a = 8μπ³l_s2⁴/a³
  - Triple tangential traction: t₃ · s|x=0,a = -8μπ³l_s2⁴/a³
  - Body forces: b_x(x,y) = 4μa⁶sin(2πy/a)(a⁴π² + 4l_s1²a²π⁴ + 16l_s2⁴π⁶), b_y(x,y) = 4μa⁶sin(2πx/a)(a⁴π² + 4l_s1²a²π⁴ + 16l_s2⁴π⁶)

- **2D static annulus plate (under compression):**
  - Clamped left edge: u = 0, t₂ = 0, t₃ = 0 at x = 0
  - Compressed bottom edge: t₁ · n = -P = -100 MPa, t₁ · s = 0, t₂ = 0, t₃ = 0 at y = 0

- **2D vibration square plate:**
  - Tangential displacement constraint: u · s = 0
  - Zero normal traction: t₁ · n = 0
  - Zero double traction: t₂ = 0
  - Zero triple traction: t₃ = 0

- **Kraus problem (circular plate with holes):**
  - Symmetry condition (classical): u · n = 0 on left and bottom edges
  - Symmetry condition (gradient): u · n = 0, ∂(u · s)/∂n = 0 on left and bottom edges
  - External tension: P = -100 MPa on outer surface
  - Single-patch domain with C⁴ continuity (except C¹ on red lines and C² on blue lines)

- **Simulation types:**
  - Static analysis for tension, compression, and square plate problems
  - Eigenvalue analysis for vibration problems
  - Plane strain state for square plate and annulus plate statics
  - Plane stress state for Kraus problem
  - 1D bar models and 2D plane stress/strain models
  - Convergence studies with NURBS orders p = 3, 4, 5 with C^(p-1) continuity
10_1016_j_cad_2016_08_005.key_3:

10_1016_j_cad_2016_08_005.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Kraus problem: R_0 = 200 mm, R_i/R_0 = 0.25, R/R_0 = 0.625, a/R_0 = 0.1

10_1016_j_finel_2019_01_011.key_1:

- Diffusion domain: 3×7 rectangular region with matrix (isotropic diffusion tensor = identity matrix) and nearly impermeable inclusions (diffusion tensor = 10⁻⁵ of matrix)

- Representative Volume Elements (RVEs) used for homogenization with boundary conditions: Taylor (TT), Linear (LC), Periodic (PC), and Minimally constrained (TC)
- Analysis compares VEM with traditional FEM and direct numerical simulation (DNS) for stress/flux prediction in composite materials
- Study demonstrates VEM advantages for complex RVE geometries with arbitrary polyhedral meshes requiring fewer elements than FEM
10_1016_j_finel_2019_01_011.key_2:

- Diffusion problem domain (3×7 rectangle): S8 has unitary incoming flux; S1, S2, S6, and S7 have homogeneous Neumann BCs; S3, S4, and S6 have homogeneous Dirichlet BCs (zero pressure)

- Diffusion analysis: Steady-state diffusion with matrix (isotropic diffusion tensor = identity matrix) and nearly impermeable inclusions (diffusion tensor = 10⁻⁵ of matrix)
- Simulation type: 2D linear elasticity and steady-state diffusion problems

10_1016_j_finel_2019_01_011.key_3:
- Linear elasticity and steady-state diffusion in heterogeneous media with inclusions
- Stress distributions (X and Y components), flux through boundary sides (bottom, right, top), homogenized constitutive tensor (C_hom), homogenized diffusion tensor (K_hom), total reaction forces (horizontal/vertical), pressure values, percentage of flux through boundaries
- Validation of VEM-based multiscale approach accuracy against direct numerical simulation (DNS), demonstration of VEM advantages for complex RVE geometries with fewer elements compared to FEM, evaluation of boundary condition effects (TT, LC, PC, TC) on homogenization results, assessment of interpolation order impact on solution accuracy
10_1016_j_finel_2019_01_011.key_4:
- Elasticity domain constrained to 200×200 square with hexagonal inclusions occupying ~22% area of each cell
- Diffusion domain constrained to 3×7 rectangle with 1×1 square for boundary condition application
- Inclusion aspect ratio fixed at 6:1 (length:height) in diffusion problem
- Inclusion sizes in diffusion problem limited to four groups: 1/10, 1/20, 1/50, and 1/100 of total volume

- Maximum element node count limited to 70 nodes (in RVE with 60° inclusions)

- Material properties fixed: diffusion matrix (isotropic diffusion tensor = identity) and inclusions (diffusion tensor = 10⁻⁵ of matrix)

10_1016_j_compstruct_2016_11_039.key_2:

- Rotating Domain: Rotation velocity at 72 RPM
- Opening and Outlet: Atmospheric pressure
- Blade surface: Smooth no-slip wall condition
- Aerodynamic forces due to pressure gradients and viscous flow

- Two opposite radial forces P = 2.5×10⁴ N for benchmark problem
- Prescribed operation conditions: 7 m/s wind velocity and 72 RPM rotational velocity
- Uniaxial fibers oriented parallel to blade longitudinal axis
- Biaxial fabrics woven at 0°/90° (0° parallel to blade axis)

- Two analyzed domains: rectangular domain (L × 2L) with Dirichlet boundary conditions on horizontal sides and Neumann on vertical sides; L-shaped domain (3 × L × L) with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions on entire boundary including re-entrant corner of angle 3π/2

- Boundary conditions enforced weakly using Nitsche's method with stabilization parameter α

- Dirichlet boundary conditions (u = 0) enforced weakly via Nitsche's method on specified boundaries
- Neumann boundary conditions on vertical sides of rectangular domain
- Homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions on entire boundary of L-shaped domain including re-entrant corner of angle 3π/2
- Stabilization parameter α with values referenced as α/C = 0.9, 1.052, 1.2, 2C, 10C (where C = 1/h)
- Critical stabilization threshold α > C required for coercivity
- Unstabilized condition α < C with indefinite constraint eigenvalues
- Conforming meshes of bilinear Lagrange elements with C = 1/h
- Non-uniform mesh configurations with perturbed structured mesh
- Reduced system formulation via Irons-Guyan elimination of boundary degrees of freedom
- Two-dimensional domain analysis (rectangular L × 2L and L-shaped 3 × L × L geometries)
- Eigenvalue problem for Laplacian operator Δu + λu = 0
- Physical domain with Dirichlet boundary conditions on top and bottom edges, Neumann on side edges (rectangular case)
10_1016_j_finel_2018_03_005.key_3:
- Eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian operator (Δu + λu = 0) with boundary conditions enforced via Nitsche's method
- Physical eigenvalues and constraint eigenvalues as distinct spectral components
- Boundary quotient (‖u‖_Γ²/‖u‖²) as measure to distinguish physical from constraint eigenpairs
- Eigenvalue veering behavior at specific stabilization parameter values
- Relative accuracy of physical eigenvalues compared to standard formulation
- Condition number dependence on stabilization parameter
- Critical time step for explicit dynamics (proportional to inverse of largest eigenvalue)
- Separation of physical eigenpairs from mesh-dependent constraint eigenpairs
- Development of reduced system approach to eliminate constraint eigenpairs while preserving accuracy
- Achievement of virtually constant physical eigenvalues in recommended stabilization range (α > C)
- Maintenance of conditioning comparable to standard formulation through reduced system approach
10_1016_j_finel_2018_03_005.key_4:
- α > C required for coercivity of the discrete operator (where C = 1/h is the discrete trace inequality constant)
- Constraint eigenvalues are indefinite for α < C (unstabilized case)
- Physical eigenvalues become virtually constant when α > 2C
- Constraint eigenvalues increase linearly with stabilization parameter at rate approximately 3/h for rectangular domain
- Six of seven constraint eigenvalues in L-shaped domain increase linearly at equal slope (≈3.4/h), one at smaller slope (≈2.4/h)
- Condition number grows linearly with stabilization parameter
- Mesh must be conforming for the presented spectral analysis (elements aligned with geometric features)
- Boundary degrees of freedom added by Nitsche formulation must be eliminated via Irons-Guyan reduction to obtain a system free of constraint eigenpairs
- Reduced system preserves symmetry and banded structure of original formulation
- Practical implementation requires stabilization parameter above critical threshold (α > C) to avoid singularities
- Non-conforming meshes require special measures to address potential ill-conditioning (not addressed in this study)
- The analysis is limited to Laplacian eigenvalue problems with Dirichlet boundary conditions
- Incompatible discretizations are rarely used for eigenvalue problems in engineering due to potential presence of mesh-dependent constraint eigenpairs

- Parameter values: ϵ = 0.01, h = 0.01 or 0.02 or 1/128, τ = 0.1, 0.5, 1.5, 2.0, κ = 0, 2, 3, 4
- Maximum bound values: β = 1 (AC and BBLM), β = 2√3/3 (RSLM)
- Initial conditions: Multiple circular/elliptical regions (bubbles), concave octahedron
- Simulation type: Transient, 2D and 3D, nonlinear, using mass-lumping finite element method with P1 and P2 discretization
- Time integration schemes: RK(2,2), RK(3,3), RK(4,4) with sIFRK, isIFRK1, isIFRK2 methods
- Conservative formulations: RSLM (λ(u,t) = (1/|Ω|)∫Ω f(u)dx), BBLM (λ(u,t) = λ₀(t)/4F(u))
10_1016_j_apnum_2023_03_002.key_3:
- Physics solved: Phase field modeling of interface dynamics, antiphase domain coarsening in binary alloys, and phase separation processes using the Allen-Cahn equation and its conservative formulations
- Target outputs: Maximum norm ||u||_∞, absolute mass error |M_h^n - M_h^0|, energy dissipation E(u), L^∞ error for convergence testing, time evolution of phase interfaces, and numerical stability characteristics
- Optimization goal: Develop unconditionally maximum-principle preserving schemes that maintain mass conservation and energy stability while achieving 2nd-4th order temporal accuracy with larger time steps (up to τ=2.0) without requiring post-processing or limiters
10_1016_j_apnum_2023_03_002.key_4:
- Maximum principle constraint: |u| ≤ β, where β = 1 for AC and BBLM, and β = 2√3/3 for RSLM
- Stabilization parameter constraints: κ ≥ max|ξ|≤β |f'(ξ)| for AC and RSLM, κ ≥ 4 for BBLM
- Spatial discretization constraint: Linear finite element method (r=1) is proven to satisfy maximum principle; higher-order spatial discretizations (r>1) are not theoretically proven but numerically demonstrated to work
- Time integration constraint: Classical RK(4,4) is the only fourth-order scheme satisfying maximum principle conditions; no explicit method higher than fourth order satisfies the first condition for unconditional maximum principle preservation
- Mass matrix constraint: Standard finite element method breaks maximum principle due to non-diagonal mass matrix; mass-lumping technique is required
- Computational domain constraint: Periodic or homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions required for contraction semigroup property
- Matrix property constraint: The linear operator L must be a generator of contraction semigroup (||e^(τL)||_∞ ≤ 1, ∀τ > 0) for maximum principle preservation
- Mesh constraint: Simplex mesh discretization with specialized P̃_r spaces (polynomials with bubble functions) needed for mass-lumping in 2D/3D
- Conservative formulations constraint: RSLM changes the maximum bound of classical AC equation due to non-locality, while BBLM preserves the maximum bound of β=1

10_1016_j_finel_2024_104179.key_1:
- Identity & Domain: Solid-shell elements for finite strain hyperelastic analysis of thin structures using stabilized stress-displacement finite element formulations
- Material / Medium: Compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelastic material with specified shear modulus (μ), Lamé coefficients (λ), Young's modulus (E), Poisson's ratio (ν), and density (ρ); examples include E = 2.1×10⁴ kN/mm², ν = 0 for slit annular plate; μ = 60 kN/mm², λ = 240 kN/mm² for hyperelastic cylinder; λ = 0.039375 kN/mm², μ = 0.02625 kN/mm² for hemispherical shell
- Application & Importance: Characterization of numerical locking effects in solid-shell elements and development of robust stabilized mixed formulations to overcome locking; providing locking-free approximation of thin structures undergoing finite deformations with enhanced stress field accuracy while maintaining displacement field accuracy
- Geometry / Domain: Multiple benchmark geometries including: slit annular plate (Ri=6 mm, Ro=10 mm, t=0.03 mm); hyperelastic cylinder (L=30 cm, R=9 cm, t=0.2 cm); hemispherical shell (R=10 mm, t=0.04 mm, 18° hole); twisting column (L=6 m, square cross-section a=1 m); manufactured solution (2D square domain Ω₀=(0,1)×(0,1)); shell mid-surface with normal extrusion to create 3D solid-shell domain with local basis vectors {g₁,g₂,g₃}
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104179.key_2:
- Boundaries & Constraints: Clamped boundary (bottom face in twisting column, one end in slit annular plate); Symmetry boundaries with ux=0 and uz=0 (hemispherical shell); Symmetry with uy=0 (hyperelastic cylinder); Fixed support (hyperelastic cylinder); Free boundaries (hemispherical shell); 18° hole at top (hemispherical shell)
- Loads / Excitations: Lifting line force q = 0.8 N/mm (slit annular plate); Line force q kN/m in closing direction (hyperelastic cylinder); Diametrical opposite forces P = 1 N along X and Y axes (hemispherical shell); Initial velocity field v₀(X,Y,Z) = ω sin(πZ/2L)[Y, -X, 0]^T with ω = 100 rad/s (twisting column); Radially slit annular plate with transverse lifting force
- Interactions / Interfaces: Solid-shell domain constructed through extrusion of 2D mid-surface with continuous normal vector field; No explicit fluid-structure or contact interfaces described
- Simulation Type: Finite strain solid dynamics; Total Lagrangian description; Nonlinear transient analysis; Three-dimensional; Backward Differentiation Formula (BDF) time integration (BDF1 and BDF2 schemes); Mixed stress-displacement formulation; Stabilized Variational Multiscale framework
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104179.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Finite strain hyperelastic solid dynamics; Numerical locking phenomena in solid-shell elements; Stress-displacement coupling in thin structures undergoing large deformations
- Target Outputs (Metrics): PK2 stress tensor field; Displacement fields; Load vs. displacement response curves; L² error norm for displacements and PK2 stress; Convergence rates with respect to element size and degrees of freedom; Relative displacement metrics at specific points (A, B, C); Stress magnitude time histories; Displacement magnitude time histories
- Optimization Goal: Achieve locking-free approximation of thin structures under finite deformations; Enhance stress field accuracy while maintaining displacement field accuracy; Overcome compatibility restrictions of interpolation spaces in mixed formulations; Enable equal-order interpolation of displacements and stresses without inf-sup condition constraints; Reduce computational cost by achieving comparable stress field accuracy with approximately 3.5% of the degrees of freedom required by quadratic irreducible formulations
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104179.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: Shell thickness constraints (t = 0.03 mm for slit annular plate; t = 0.2 cm for hyperelastic cylinder; t = 0.04 mm for hemispherical shell); inner radius Ri = 6 mm and outer radius Ro = 10 mm for annular plate; cylinder length L = 30 cm and radius R = 9 cm; hemispherical shell radius R = 10 mm with 18° hole; solid-shell domain constructed through extrusion of 2D mid-surface with continuous normal vector field
- Performance/Physics Limits: Limited to compressible materials (explicitly states "the present approach does not contemplate solving incompressible materials"); time step constraint δt = 0.002 s required to retain physical oscillations in twisting column simulation; BDF2 integration scheme can dissipate physical oscillations (though less than first-order schemes); stabilization parameters defined as τu = cu·hK²/(2μ), τS = cS; formulation designed specifically for finite strain regime

10_1007_s00211_022_01312_0.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Linear 3D elasticity problem with cracked domains; Stable Generalized Finite Element Method (SGFEM) for crack modeling; Planar and fully 3D planar crack problems in solid mechanics.
- **Material / Medium:** Linear elastic solid with Young's modulus E = 90, Poisson's ratio ν = 0.28; Lamé constants λ = 44.74431818 and μ = 35.15625; Material-independent BB enrichment functions: √r sin(θ/2), √r cos(θ/2), √r sin(θ/2)sin(θ), √r cos(θ/2)sin(θ).
- **Application & Importance:** Overcoming poor conditioning in conventional GFEM/XFEM for 3D crack problems; Achieving optimal convergence order O(h) in energy norm; Maintaining scaled condition number (SCN) of O(h⁻²) (same as standard FEM); Ensuring robustness when crack surface approaches element boundaries.
- **Geometry / Domain:** 3D domain Ω = (0, 1) × (0, 1) × (-1/6, 1/6); Traction-free crack surface Γₒ with straight crack front O parallel to z-axis; Essential boundary conditions on top/bottom surfaces (Γ_D); Natural boundary conditions on remaining boundaries (Γ_N = ∂Ω \ Γ_D); Crack orientation varies: passing through element middle, intersecting mesh lines at arbitrary angles, approaching element boundaries (y = 0.5).
10_1007_s00211_022_01312_0.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Essential boundary condition (Dirichlet) imposed on Γ_D (top and bottom surfaces marked with "///"); Natural boundary condition (Neumann) imposed on Γ_N = ∂Ω \ Γ_D; Traction-free condition (σ(u)n_O = 0) on crack surface Γ_O; For domain Ω = (0,1)×(0,1)×(-1/6,1/6), Γ_D = {0 ≤ x ≤ 1, y = 0, -1/6 ≤ z ≤ 1/6} ∪ {0 ≤ x ≤ 1, y = 1, -1/6 ≤ z ≤ 1/6}; Crack surface Γ_O varies: passing through element middle (y=0.5), intersecting mesh at arbitrary angles, approaching element boundaries (y=0.5+δ).
- **Loads / Excitations:** Body force f ∈ L²(Ω; R³); Natural boundary condition g ∈ L²(Γ_N; R³); For manufactured solutions, f = 0; Boundary conditions g and u_0 derived from exact solutions u_k; Linear Heaviside functions used as enrichments: H = {H, Hx, Hy, Hz}.
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Discontinuity across crack surface Γ_O handled by Heaviside enrichment; Singularity around crack front O handled by BB enrichment functions (√r sin(θ/2), √r cos(θ/2), √r sin(θ/2)sin(θ), √r cos(θ/2)sin(θ)); Traction-free condition on crack surface σ(u)n_O = 0.
- **Simulation Type:** Linear elastic fracture mechanics; 3D static (elastostatic); Steady-state; Planar crack problems (u_1 constant along z-direction) and fully 3D planar crack problems (u_2, u_3 involving r^(3/2) and r^(5/2) terms); Analysis performed for multiple crack orientations relative to mesh.
10_1007_s00211_022_01312_0.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Linear elastic fracture mechanics in 3D cracked domains; Displacement and stress fields with discontinuities at crack surfaces and singularities at crack fronts; Condition number behavior of stiffness matrices in enriched finite element methods.
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Scaled Condition Number (SCN) of stiffness matrices; H¹ error (energy norm error) measured as |u - uh|H¹(Ω;R³)/|u|H¹(Ω;R³); Convergence rates (O(h) vs O(√h)); Condition number behavior as mesh parameter h decreases; Robustness of conditioning with respect to crack position relative to element boundaries.
- **Optimization Goal:** Achieve optimal convergence order O(h) in energy norm; Maintain scaled condition number (SCN) of O(h⁻²) (same as standard FEM); Ensure robustness where conditioning does not worsen as crack surface approaches element boundaries; Eliminate the need for mesh matching to crack geometry while preserving solution accuracy.
10_1007_s00211_022_01312_0.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Domain Ω = (0, 1) × (0, 1) × (-1/6, 1/6) with thickness 2t where t < 1; Crack front O is straight line parallel to z-axis; Uniform n×n×n³ hexahedral mesh with h = 1/n; Crack surface Γ_O defined as {0 ≤ x ≤ 0.5, y = 0.5+δ, -1/6 ≤ z ≤ 1/6} with δ varying from 3×10⁻² to 5.72×10⁻⁸; Geometric enrichment radius R = 0.2; Crack orientation varies (passing through element middle, intersecting at arbitrary angles).
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Scaled condition number (SCN) must be O(h⁻²) (same as FEM); Must achieve optimal convergence order O(h) in energy norm; Material properties fixed: E = 90, ν = 0.28, λ = 44.74431818, μ = 35.15625; Traction-free condition (σ(u)n_O = 0) on crack surface; PU functions must satisfy ‖ψi‖L∞(Ω) ≤ C, ‖∇ψi‖L∞(Ω) ≤ Ch⁻¹; LPCA threshold λ = 10⁻¹⁰ for removing redundant enrichments.
- **Process/Manufacturing:** LPCA applied only to nodes in (IH \ IS) ∪ (IH ∩ IS) (O(h⁻²) nodes versus O(h⁻³) total nodes); Cubic polynomial PU (Q¹_i) used instead of standard FE hat-functions; Linear Heaviside enrichment functions H = {H, Hx, Hy, Hz}; BB enrichment functions: √r sin(θ/2), √r cos(θ/2), √r sin(θ/2)sin(θ), √r cos(θ/2)sin(θ); Quadrature rules: 12×12×12 Gauss for non-cut elements, 4-point Gauss for tetrahedrons; Geometric enrichment scheme used for optimal convergence.

10_1007_s12541_025_01234_5.key_1:

10_1007_s12541_025_01234_5.key_2:

  - Constant growth velocity of outer radius: 2.5 mm/s for 142 s

  - Circumferential velocity at entrance of MDZ: v₀y

  - Shear power at axial neutral surface (Ẇⁿₛ)
  - Contact arc length inside and outside ring approximately equal

10_1007_s12541_025_01234_5.key_3:

10_1007_s12541_025_01234_5.key_4:

  - Total height H1: 200-500 mm (default 350 mm)

  - Friction coefficient μ: 0.1-0.5 (default 0.3)
  - Circumferential velocity constraint: (1 - (b0-b1)/b0)vq ≤ v0y ≤ vq

10_1016_j_cep_2025_110221.key_1:

- Rectangular section width W_m = 75-135 μm
- Outer curvature radius r_2 = 150 μm (fixed)

- Element size limitations: maximum sizes of 2, 4, and 8 voxels in different cases, minimum size of 1 voxel (n=0)
- Bounding box constraints for octree decomposition defined by 2ⁿ×2ⁿ×2ⁿ image matrix
- Material properties constraints: Young's modulus E₀ = 1, Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3
- Polynomial material interpolation with fixed penalization power p = 3
- Convergence criteria: 0.01% tolerance for objective function variation over 5 iterations, minimum 10 successive iterations for convergence confirmation
- PCG solver constraints: tolerance ε = 1×10⁻⁹, maximum iterations = 200,000
- Maximum optimization iterations: 250 permitted
- Balanced octree mesh with strict 2:1 length ratio between adjacent cells
- Limited to 144 distinct octree cell patterns instead of 4096 possible configurations
- Face discretization limited to 6 distinct node configurations for octree cells

- Sensitivity filter radius: r_min = 4 voxels for cantilever beam and tower, r_min = 5 voxels for donut structure
- Evolutionary rate ratio: ER = 2% for cantilever beam, ER = 5% for donut and tower structures

- Single-core CPU processing limitation causing challenges for large-scale (high-dimensional) design domains
- Memory limitations for SBFE analysis of large-scale problems with millions of elements

10_1007_s00170_025_15048_2.key_1:
- Identity & Domain: Segmented thermal bed with resistive elements (HRE) for FDM 3D printers
- Material / Medium: Copper-clad phenolic resin PCB; ABS material for test specimens; both segmented and commercial beds fabricated using identical base material
- Application & Importance: Address non-uniform thermal distribution causing warping, dimensional inaccuracies, and compromised mechanical properties; enable precise temperature control, reduce energy consumption, and improve part quality
- Geometry / Domain: 200×200 mm PCB divided into 4×4 matrix of 16 resistive elements (49×49 mm each); zigzag resistive track pattern; 1 mm resistive track thickness; 3.5 mm line/column thickness; 1 mm space between tracks; 1847 mm track length
10_1007_s00170_025_15048_2.key_2:
- Boundaries & Constraints: 200×200 mm PCB with 4×4 matrix configuration; ambient temperature (22.0 ± 0.5) °C during thermographic tests; relative humidity 50% for thermographic measurements; emissivity coefficient 0.95; 1 mm space between resistive tracks; 3.5 mm line/column thickness; 1 mm resistive track thickness
- Loads / Excitations: AC voltage (25 ± 1) V for HRE bed; DC voltage (12 ± 1) V for commercial bed; target temperature (100 ± 2) °C for energy tests; bed temperature (110.0 ± 2.2) °C for printing; extrusion nozzle temperature (250 ± 5) °C; printing speed 50 mm/s; tensile test speed 50 mm/min
- Interactions / Interfaces: Closed-loop thermal control system with temperature sensors; matrix addressing (4 rows and 4 columns) for individual element control; copper layer functioning as conductive surface; direct printing base without additional surfaces; optional borosilicate glass attachment for enhanced adhesion
- Simulation Type: Transient energy consumption analysis; steady-state thermographic measurements; mechanical tensile testing at 50 mm/min; comparative analysis between commercial bed (MK2a) and HRE bed; time-based measurements for voltage, current, and energy consumption
10_1007_s00170_025_15048_2.key_3:
- Physics Solved: Thermal distribution across printing bed surface; energy consumption characteristics; mechanical properties of printed specimens; morphological layer characteristics
- Target Outputs (Metrics): Temperature distribution (°C) with central vs. edge measurements; heating time to reach (100 ± 2) °C; energy consumption (mWh); voltage and current measurements; tensile strength (MPa); elastic modulus; layer thickness uniformity; interlayer adhesion quality; temperature differentials (ΔT); energy savings percentage
- Optimization Goal: Achieve plateau-like thermal distribution (replacing convex profile); minimize temperature gradients to prevent warping; reduce energy consumption (20% for fully heated areas, 95% for single segment activation); improve mechanical properties (3% tensile strength increase); enhance layer thickness uniformity and interlayer adhesion
10_1007_s00170_025_15048_2.key_4:
- Geometric/Design Space: 200×200 mm PCB size; 4×4 matrix configuration with 16 elements (49×49 mm each); 1 mm resistive track thickness; 3.5 mm line/column thickness; 1 mm space between tracks; 1847 mm track length; designed for compatibility with Anet ET-4 3D printer
- Performance/Physics Limits: Commercial bed central temperature (97.1 ± 1.8) °C with edges at (78.4 ± 0.9) °C; HRE bed average temperature (89.4 ± 1.8) °C when fully energized; element A22 temperature range (100-105) °C; target temperature (100 ± 2) °C for energy testing; AC voltage (25 ± 1) V for HRE; DC voltage (12 ± 1) V for commercial bed; thermal stability dependent on control strategy rather than material properties
- Process/Manufacturing: Manual thermal control implementation requiring operator programming; copper-clad phenolic resin PCB material; limited sample size in mechanical testing; energy comparisons based on simplified extrapolations; thermal interactions between adjacent elements not fully accounted for in consumption calculations; control system uses STM32L053R8 microcontroller with DS18B20 sensors and SCR 40TPS16 drive; need for future automation of element selection and statistical validation of mechanical improvements

10_1016_j_cemconcomp_2025_106101.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Single-Cell Unit Rotation Rigid Body (SCRR) structures fabricated using 3D-printed Engineering Cementitious Composites (ECC)
- **Material / Medium:** Engineering Cementitious Composites (ECC) with 12 mm polyethylene fibers at 1.2% volume ratio; compressive strength >40 MPa; tensile strain capacity >4%; fracture toughness >2 MPa·m^(1/2); composed of Portland cement, quartz sand, fly ash, polyethylene fiber, water reducer, thickener, defoaming agent, and water
- **Application & Importance:** Evaluation of negative Poisson's ratio effect, energy absorption capacity, and mechanical performance; provides foundation for rigid rotational body applications in construction, enabling lightweight design and energy-absorption optimization for building systems
- **Geometry / Domain:** SCRR structures with rotation angle (α) of 30°, 45°, 60°, or 90°; node thickness (e) varying from 20.00 mm (α=30°) to 10.00 mm (α=90°); effective cross-sectional length (L) from 136.97 mm to 159.71 mm; thickness (t)=40 mm; side length (h)=60 mm; deformation occurs through three stages: elastic (Stage I, ending at ~3% strain), rotational (Stage II, ending at 11-19% strain), and densification (Stage III)
10_1016_j_cemconcomp_2025_106101.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Loading plates at top and bottom of specimen; lower plate fixed, upper plate with vertical displacement applied at reference point
  - Surface-to-surface penalty contact between loading plates and specimen; friction coefficient = 0.105
  - Specimen set as self-contact; self-contact friction coefficient = 0.95, shear stress limit = 0.5 MPa, elastic slip stiffness = 17 GPa
  - Normal contact stiffness = 22 GPa for cementitious material elements
  - Two LVDTs fixed on lateral faces with 10 mm range for tensile tests
  - Digital Image Correlation (DIC) with two CCD cameras for displacement monitoring

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Uniaxial compression tests with loading rate of 0.5 mm/min
  - Tensile tests with 20 kN capacity machine at 0.5 mm/min loading rate
  - Three-point bending tests with constant loading rate of 0.5 mm/min
  - Vertical force applied in X-direction (compression) as shown in Fig. 2

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Surface-to-surface contact between loading plates and specimen
  - Self-contact within the SCRR specimen during deformation
  - Frictional contact with specified coefficients (0.105 for plate-specimen, 0.95 for self-contact)
  - Digital Image Correlation (DIC) for non-contact displacement measurement
  - Two LVDTs for measuring deformation in middle 80 mm of dogbone specimens

- **Simulation Type:**
  - 2D explicit dynamic analysis using ABAQUS/Explicit
  - Geometric nonlinearity (Nlgeom) with Concrete Damage Plasticity (CDP) constitutive model
  - Modified six-node quadratic plane stress triangular elements (CPS6M) with 1 mm mesh size
  - Double precision analysis for accuracy
  - Two separate constitutive models for cast and printed specimens
  - Boundary conditions include vertical displacement on upper loading plate with fixed lower plate
10_1016_j_cemconcomp_2025_106101.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** 
  - Deformation mechanics of auxetic structures under uniaxial compression
  - Negative Poisson's ratio (NPR) behavior in rotating rigid body configurations
  - Three-stage compression response (elastic, rotational, densification) of SCRR structures
  - Fracture mechanics and crack propagation in ECC-based auxetic structures
  - Energy dissipation mechanisms through rotational deformation

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):**
  - First peak stress (σ₁max) and corresponding strain (ε₁max)
  - Second peak stress (σ₂max) and corresponding strain (ε₂max)
  - Negative Poisson's ratio (ν) as function of strain
  - Total absorbed energy (E), Specific Energy Absorption (SEA)
  - Average compressive stress (σm) and Compressive Force Efficiency (CFE)
  - Strain ranges for each deformation stage (Stage I ends at ~3% strain; Stage II ends at 11-19% strain depending on α)
  - Ultimate tensile strain (εtu) and strength (ftu)
  - Fracture toughness parameters (KICini, KICun)
  - Relationship between rotation angle (α), node thickness (e), and CFE

- **Optimization Goal:**
  - Maximize Specific Energy Absorption (SEA) while maintaining structural integrity
  - Identify optimal rotation angle (α) and node thickness (e) combination for auxetic behavior
  - Achieve balanced lightweight design with sufficient load-bearing capacity
  - Determine geometric parameters that extend Stage II (rotational stage) to maximize energy dissipation
  - Find α-e relationship that stabilizes compressive force efficiency (CFE) while enhancing SEA
  - Optimize for near -1 NPR effect with consistent deformation characteristics across loading stages
10_1016_j_cemconcomp_2025_106101.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Rotation angle (α) limited to discrete values (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°), with α=90° excluded from analysis due to elimination of rotational potential
  - Node thickness (e) constrained by geometric relationship with α (20.00 mm at α=30°, 14.14 mm at α=45°, 11.55 mm at α=60°, 10.00 mm at α=90°)
  - Effective cross-sectional length (L) constrained to 136.97-159.71 mm range based on α
  - Fixed thickness (t)=40 mm and side length (h)=60 mm for all SCRR specimens
  - Geometric relationship between α and e must maintain rotational capability while avoiding structural collapse

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Compressive strength must exceed 40 MPa (FC40 standard)
  - Tensile strain capacity must exceed 4% for ECC material
  - Fracture toughness must exceed 2 MPa·m^(1/2)
  - First peak stress (σ₁max) decreases with increasing α due to reduced node thickness
  - Maximum strain capacity constrained by Stage III densification (22-23% at α=60°)
  - Negative Poisson's ratio must remain below 0 and approach -1 for auxetic behavior
  - Compressive Force Efficiency (CFE) must remain above practical minimum for structural stability
  - Energy absorption capacity (SEA) increases with α but must be balanced with structural integrity

- **Process/Manufacturing:**
  - Fiber content constrained to 1.2% (1.5% causes printing failure, 0.9% results in poor buildability)
  - Fluidity must be maintained between 12-18 cm in flow table tests
  - Buildability requires ability to stack 5+ layers without collapse
  - Printing path must follow "one shot" principle to maintain fiber continuity at node joints
  - Printhead diameter limited to 12 mm with rotational speed of 1 r/s and nozzle traveling speed of 30 mm/s
  - Printed SCRR requires edge polishing to ensure uniform force application
  - ECC must be demolded after 24 hours of resting
  - Resinous printing mold requires 24 hours in silica gel solution before release
  - Interlayer weakness in printed specimens must be mitigated through optimized printing paths

10_1016_j_ast_2024_109582.key_1:
- Novel glass sponge inspired body-centered cubic (GSIBCC) lattice structure based on biomimetic design of deep-sea glass sponge (Euplectella aspergillum) skeletal system
- Fabricated using stainless steel 316L with elastic modulus of 180 GPa, Poisson's ratio of 0.3, and density of 9.8 g/cm³
- Unit cell length L = 7 mm with 6 × 6 × 6 unit cells along three orthogonal directions
- Relative densities studied: 0.078 and 0.124, with corresponding rod radii (e.g., GSIBCC: 0.267 mm at ρ̄=0.078, 0.345 mm at ρ̄=0.124)
- Deviation coefficient m (0 ≤ m ≤ 1/2) controls the double diagonal reinforcement geometry, with optimal performance at m = 1/4
- GSIBCC exhibits second stress reinforcement effect in strain range 0.4-0.6, unlike conventional BCC and OCT lattices
- Whole deformation type observed in GSIBCC (m=1/4) instead of local cell collapse seen in BCC and OCT lattices
- Maximum 145.06% improvement in specific energy absorption (SEA) with respect to BCC at relative density 0.124
- Maximum 117.4% improvement in SEA with respect to OCT at relative density 0.124
- Yield strength of GSIBCC is 3.02 MPa (minimum) to 10.90 MPa (maximum) across optimized designs
- Specific energy absorption of GSIBCC is 8.61 J/g (minimum) to 19.90 J/g (maximum) across optimized designs
- Element size of 0.6 mm used in finite element simulations for convergence
- Compression strain range studied: 0.0 to 0.8 with maximum displacement of 33.6 mm
- Kinetic energy maintained below 5% of internal energy to ensure quasi-static simulation conditions
- GSIBCC shows maximum -38.71% reduction in yield strength compared to OCT at relative density 0.124
- Second stress reinforcement effect is observed only when both double diagonal struts (0 < m < 1/2) and hybridization of unit cells are present

10_1016_j_engappai_2025_110906.key_1:

- **Application & Importance:** Structural optimization of modular construction to minimize compliance (maximize stiffness) while addressing computational complexity challenges; modular construction offers efficiency, scalability, and reusability but requires optimization to overcome perceived material inefficiency
- **Geometry / Domain:** Regular grid domains (6×6, 10×10, 20×20 module configurations); specific shapes include symmetrical cantilever beams (5×4 modules), simply supported beams, and L-shaped cantilevers; structures analyzed with boundary conditions applied at grid nodes; reduced-order modeling using Schur complement approach with condensed stiffness matrices at module interface nodes

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Vertical displacement (d) at specified load points; compliance matrix (C = K⁻¹); stiffness matrix (K); relative error of displacement predictions; normalized displacement (Jᵈ); penalty term (Jᶜ) for volume constraint violation; total objective function J = Jᵈ + Jᶜ
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize structural compliance (maximize stiffness) under given boundary conditions and loading, subject to global volume fraction constraint (ρ(x) ≤ 0.75); achieve displacement reduction of 24-34% compared to uniform module structures while maintaining structural integrity; find optimal module arrangements that minimize u(x)/u(x₂,₂) where x₂,₂ represents structure built from (2,2) modules
10_1016_j_engappai_2025_110906.key_4:

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Linear elastic material behavior with Poisson's ratio ν = 0.3; Young's modulus values restricted to E ∈ {0.0, 0.01, 1.0}; volume fraction constraint ρ(x) ≤ 0.75 for varied-density module sets; maximum relative total mass/volume constraint m(x) ≤ M; displacement must be minimized under static loading; all solutions require verification by full-scale simulations as model does not account for yielding, buckling, or fracture; two-dimensional plane strain conditions
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Modules must be mutually compatible to form an intact continuum; module interface nodes must reflect intended connections in real applications; modules discretized with 8×8 quadrilateral elements; manufacturing constraints limit module topology (not fully explored in paper); distributed loads must be substituted by equivalent concentrated forces at interface nodes; upper limit on number of different module types is difficult to predict; real-life design limited by manufacturing capabilities and connection types

10_1016_j_finel_2024_104167.key_1:

- **Material / Medium:** Solid material (C_S) and void material (C_V = 1e-7 × C_S); Poisson's ratio = 0.3; ersatz material approach used for elasticity matrices
- **Application & Importance:** Maximizing structural stiffness by minimizing strain energy; enabling design of complex multiscale structures compatible with additive manufacturing; achieving smooth boundaries in final topology
- **Geometry / Domain:** L-shaped beam (10×5 dimensions with 1 unit thickness), cantilever beam (10×4 dimensions), Michell-type structure (5×2 dimensions), quarter-ring structure; macrostructures divided into subdomains (4, 18, 50, or 450) with periodic microstructures; parameter space defined as unit square independent of physical geometry
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104167.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Fixed support on left edge for L-shaped beam; fixed support at bottom for quarter-ring structure; vertical load applied at bottom right corner for L-shaped beam; vertical load at top for quarter-ring structure; global volume constraint (V ≤ V_max); micro volume constraints (V_z^m ≤ V_z^max for z = 1,..., n_m); periodic boundary conditions for unit cells; uniform open knot vectors for microstructures; convergence criterion |J_i - J_k| < 0.005 for 5 sequential iterations
- **Loads / Excitations:** Vertical loads applied at specific points in multiple examples; three prestrain cases for homogenization (two tensile strains and one shear strain); strain energy minimization as objective function (J = 1/2 ∑_e=1^n_k^M (u_e^M)^T k_e^M u_e^M)
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Homogenization bridges macro and micro scales by deriving elasticity tensor from microstructure layout; macrostructure size assumed much larger than microstructures with periodic microstructure distribution; parameter space to physical space mapping for level set functions
- **Simulation Type:** 2D and 3D examples; isogeometric analysis framework; level set method with reaction-diffusion equation; linear elastic analysis; steady-state optimization; multiscale (macro and micro) topology optimization; NURBS degree = 2 in both directions; Poisson's ratio = 0.3; 400 control points in micro scale
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104167.key_3:

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Strain energy (J = 1/2 ∑_e=1^n_k^M (u_e^M)^T k_e^M u_e^M); global volume fraction; micro volume fractions for each subdomain; objective function value; convergence criteria (|J_i - J_k| < 0.005 for 5 sequential iterations); final topology at macro and micro scales
- **Optimization Goal:** Minimize strain energy (maximize structural stiffness); satisfy global volume constraint (V ≤ V_max); satisfy micro volume constraints (V_z^m ≤ V_z^max for z = 1,..., n_m); achieve smooth boundaries in final topology at both scales; reduce final objective function value with increased number of microstructures
10_1016_j_finel_2024_104167.key_4:

- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Elasticity matrix for void material is 1e-7 times solid material (C_V = 1e-7 × C_S); Poisson's ratio = 0.3; NURBS degree = 2 in both directions; augmented Lagrangian parameters (Δγ = 0.05, γ_max = 5, γ_0 = 0.4 for macro/0.3 for micro, μ = 4-6); relaxation iterations parameter nr (30-70 iterations); strain energy minimization as objective function

10_1016_j_finel_2018_10_002.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Ten-node tetrahedral Macro-Cosserat Point Element (MCPE) for structural finite element analysis; modeled as eight sub-elements with quadratic kinematics; evaluated for thin beams, rhombic plates, square plates, cylindrical tubes, Cook's membrane, and plane strain blocks.
- **Material / Medium:** Isotropic hyperelastic (neo-Hookean) with K = 1 GPa, μ = 0.6 GPa, ν = 0.25 (compressible); nearly incompressible with K = 1000 GPa, μ = 0.6 GPa, ν ≈ 0.4997; orthotropic hyperelastic with K_i = {10, 2700, 180, 90, 180, 270, 9000} MPa, n_01 = 1, n_02 = -1, n_03 = 0.
- **Application & Importance:** General-purpose element evaluation for meshing complex regions; comparison of accuracy/robustness with standard elements (CPE, F, M); assessment for large deformations, nearly incompressible materials, and distorted elements; verification against benchmark problems including Cook's membrane.
- **Geometry / Domain:** Cantilever beam (L1 = 0.2 m, L2 = L3 = 0.01 m); rhombic plate (L1 = L2 = 1.0 m, L3 = 0.01 m, θ = 0-60°); square plate (L1 = L2 = 1.0 m, L3 = 0.01 m); cylindrical tube (inner radius R, outer radius 2R, height R with R = 0.5 m); Cook's membrane (48 mm × 44 mm × 5 mm thickness); tetrahedral MCPE with 10 nodes (4 corners, 6 mid-edge).
10_1016_j_finel_2018_10_002.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** Fixed support at beam end (X₁ = 0); simply supported midlines on all plate edges (u(X₁,0,L₃/2) = 0, u(X₁,L₂,L₃/2) = 0, u(0,X₂,L₃/2) = 0, u(L₁,X₂,L₃/2) = 0); symmetry plane at X₃ = L₃/2 (half-beam modeled); vertical plane constraint at X₁ = 0 (free to slide); horizontal plane constraint at X₂ = 0 (slides freely); fixed bottom surface (X₃ = 0) for cylindrical tube; zero radial/circumferential displacements on tube inner surface; e₃ displacement component constrained to zero for Cook's membrane; clamped edges on rhombic plate (all nodes fixed).
- **Loads / Excitations:** Uniform shear stress τ in e₂ direction (1 kPa); follower shear stress τ (50.0 MPa, 20.0 kPa, 25 MPa) remaining tangent to deformed configuration; uniform pressure P normal to bottom surface (10.0 MPa); maximum shear stress τ = τ_f = 20.0 kPa on rhombic plate; follower shear stress τ = 25 MPa on Cook's membrane right edge.
- **Interactions / Interfaces:** Rigid plate perfectly bonded to half of block top surface; traction-free lateral surfaces; traction-free top/bottom surfaces on plates; outer surface traction-free on cylindrical tube; unclamped edges subjected to follower shear stress on rhombic plate; follower traction vector with no e₃ component for cantilever beam.
- **Simulation Type:** Large deformation nonlinear analysis; small deformation linear analysis; 3D isotropic hyperelastic (ν = 0.25) and nearly incompressible (ν ≈ 0.4997) materials; orthotropic hyperelastic with K_i = {10, 2700, 180, 90, 180, 270, 9000} MPa; structured brick meshes converted to tetrahedral elements; plane strain condition simulated via e₃ displacement constraint; follower load conditions maintaining direction relative to deformed configuration.
10_1016_j_finel_2018_10_002.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Nonlinear large deformation structural mechanics; isotropic and anisotropic hyperelastic material behavior; nearly incompressible material response; stress distribution in complex geometries under follower loads; buckling and instability phenomena in thin structures.
- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** Displacement components (u_A1/L₁, u_A2/L₂, u_A3/L₁) at critical points; force components (F₂, F₃); normalized stress (τ/τ_f, P/P_f); error E in displacement predictions; last points of convergence for different element types; von Mises stress σ_e and pressure p distributions; deformed shapes; eigenvalues of tangent stiffness matrix.
- **Optimization Goal:** Develop a general-purpose element with enhanced robustness for nearly incompressible materials and large deformations while maintaining versatility for complex geometries; achieve better convergence behavior than standard elements (F, M) for distorted meshes and combined compression-bending scenarios; eliminate checkerboard instability while preserving ability to model both isotropic and anisotropic hyperelastic materials.
10_1016_j_finel_2018_10_002.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:** Ten-node tetrahedral element geometry only; reference shapes limited to simple (straight edges) or non-simple (curved edges with α = 1/5); cylindrical tube with inner radius R, outer radius 2R, height R; Cook's membrane with 48 mm width, 44 mm height, 5 mm thickness; cantilever beam with L₁ = 0.2 m, L₂ = L₃ = 0.01 m; rhombic plate with L₁ = L₂ = 1.0 m, L₃ = 0.01 m; symmetry constraints (e.g., modeling one quarter of cylindrical tube).
- **Performance/Physics Limits:** Maximum Poisson's ratio ν ≈ 0.4997 for nearly incompressible materials; element M exhibits unphysical instabilities for follower loads and plane strain problems; MCPE shows moderate loss of accuracy (1-2% error) for small deformations of coarsely meshed thin structures; element F lacks robustness for nearly incompressible materials with contact; tangent stiffness matrix has 4 large eigenvalues for simple MCPE and 8 for non-simple MCPE under nearly incompressible conditions.
- **Process/Manufacturing:** Implementation in ABAQUS requires UEL subroutine; numerical approximation of tangent modulus used instead of analytical form; indentation problems require C3D10M as virtual element with zero stiffness; computational cost increased due to eight sub-elements per MCPE; general mesh generator used for tetrahedral elements with no specialized meshing requirements.

10_1007_s10338_025_00601_z.key_1:
- **Identity & Domain:** Inverse finite element method (iFEM) for large deformation reconstruction of plate and shell structures; specific structures analyzed include cantilever beam under shear load, slit annular plate under transverse shear force, and hemispherical shell subjected to alternating radial forces
- **Material / Medium:** Isotropic material for cantilever beam (E = 2 MPa, ν = 0.3); isotropic material for slit annular plate (E = 21 MPa, ν = 0); isotropic material for hemispherical shell (E = 20 MPa, ν = 0.3)
- **Application & Importance:** Structural health monitoring (SHM) through real-time processing of sensing system data; addressing limitations of linear inverse finite element methods for structures with large deformations; solving shear self-locking problems in shell element reconstruction
- **Geometry / Domain:** Cantilever beam (L = 10 m, B = 1 m, t = 10 mm); slit annular plate (Ri = 6 m, Re = 10 m, t = 0.05 m); hemispherical shell (R = 10 m) with thickness-to-radius ratio ranging from 1/100 to 1/1000
10_1007_s10338_025_00601_z.key_2:
- **Boundaries & Constraints:** 
  - Cantilever beam: Left side completely clamped
  - Slit annular plate: Clamped at one end, free at the other end with transverse shear force
  - Hemispherical shell: One-quarter modeled due to symmetry; Ux = θy = θz = 0 along BC; Uy = θx = θz = 0 along AC; Uz = 0 at point C
  - Strain rosettes positioned at the center of both sides of each inverse element for all structures
  - Thickness-to-radius ratio ranging from 1/100 to 1/1000 for hemispherical shell analysis
  - Reference solutions used: 250 uniform quadrilateral elements (1500 DOF) for cantilever beam; 816 uniform quadrilateral elements (4896 DOF) for slit annular plate

- **Loads / Excitations:**
  - Cantilever beam: Shear load of P = 10 N applied in negative y-direction at midpoint of free end
  - Slit annular plate: Shear force of P = 1 N applied at free end
  - Hemispherical shell: Two radial forces P with magnitude of 1 N along equator
  - Load application: Inverse load gradually applied from zero to maximum; P/Pmax ratio range [0,1]

- **Interactions / Interfaces:**
  - Experimental strain measurements from top and bottom surfaces used as input for inverse FEM
  - Strain data used to obtain experimental strain value at any thickness coordinate via εmea_i = (1+t)/2 ε+_i + (1-t)/2 ε-_i
  - Weighted least-squares function minimizes discrepancy between theoretical strain and measured strain
  - Mixed interpolation of tensorial components (MITC) method used to mitigate shear locking

- **Simulation Type:**
  - Geometric nonlinear analysis using incremental-iterative method
  - Newton-Raphson iteration method used in each increment step until |R| < 1% of |F|
  - Large deformation reconstruction with nonlinear Green-Lagrange strain relationship
  - Analysis conducted with varying mesh densities (N × 5N where N = 2, 4, 6 for slit annular plate; N = 10, 20, 30 for hemispherical shell)
10_1007_s10338_025_00601_z.key_3:
- **Physics Solved:** Large deformation reconstruction of plate and shell structures using inverse finite element method; nonlinear displacement-strain relationship; shear locking mitigation in thin shell structures; displacement and stress field reconstruction from experimental strain measurements

- **Target Outputs (Metrics):** 
  - Total displacement (Ut = √(Ux² + Uy² + Uz²))
  - Von Mises stress (σv = √[(σx - σy)² + (σy - σz)² + (σz - σx)²]/2)
  - Percentage difference (PD = (U^FEM_ti - U^iFEM_ti)/U^FEM_ti × 100)
  - Green-Lagrange strain tensor components
  - Displacement reconstruction accuracy at specific points (e.g., point A of hemispherical shell)
  - Shear strain distribution

- **Optimization Goal:** 
  - Achieve accurate large deformation reconstruction using nonlinear strain relationships
  - Mitigate shear locking in thin shell structures through MITC method
  - Maximize reconstruction accuracy compared to reference FEM solutions
  - Demonstrate superior performance over existing iQS4 element in both deformation and stress reconstruction
  - Validate effectiveness across varying thickness-to-radius ratios (1/100 to 1/1000)
10_1007_s10338_025_00601_z.key_4:
- **Geometric/Design Space:**
  - Cantilever beam dimensions constrained to L = 10 m, B = 1 m, thickness = 10 mm
  - Slit annular plate constrained to Ri = 6 m, Re = 10 m, thickness = 0.05 m
  - Hemispherical shell radius constrained to R = 10 m with thickness-to-radius ratio limited to range 1/100 to 1/1000
  - Only one-quarter of hemispherical shell modeled due to symmetry constraints (shaded region ABC)
  - Inverse element meshing constrained to specific configurations: 20 elements for cantilever beam; N × 5N (N = 2,4,6) for slit annular plate; N = 10,20,30 per edge for hemispherical shell

- **Performance/Physics Limits:**
  - Newton-Raphson iteration convergence criterion: |R| < 1% of |F| for equilibrium
  - Maximum load ratio P/Pmax constrained to [0,1] range for gradual load application
  - Linear inverse finite element methods inapplicable for structures with large deformations (explicitly stated limitation)
  - Shear self-locking becomes problematic as thickness-to-length ratio decreases (demonstrated in hemispherical shell analysis)
  - Discrete strain measurements from FEM analysis used as inputs for iMITC4 and iQS4

- **Process/Manufacturing:**

  - Reference FEM solutions constrained to specific mesh densities: 250 elements (1500 DOF) for cantilever beam; 816 elements (4896 DOF) for slit annular plate
  - Inverse load application constrained to incremental method where next increment applied after previous converges
  - Experimental strain measurements constrained to use of top and bottom surface data via εmea_i = (1+t)/2 ε+_i + (1-t)/2 ε-_i relationship

10_1007_s10439_017_1962_x.key_1:

- Material: CMHA-S hydrogel film (Marlow hyperelastic model, Prony-series viscoelastic), lower eyelid (linear-elastic, E=58.2 MPa, ν=0.49, ρ=1.05 g/cm³), globe (discrete rigid body, 22 mm diameter)
- Application: Improved retention in inferior fornix of eye for sustained drug delivery to ocular surface
- Geometry: Eight film geometries tested; globe (22 mm diameter spherical shell), lower eyelid (0.25 mm thick); target film volume of 30 μL for all geometries
- Immobilization requirement: μ_lid = 1.4 × μ_globe + 0.07 (R² = 0.9976)
- Minimum friction ratio: μ_lid must be at least 1.4 times greater than μ_globe for immobilization
- Immobilization threshold: displacement < 0.05 mm (center node displacement)
- Cylindrical geometries (1 and 4) dislodged at all tested friction values
- At μ_lid:μ_globe ≥ 2 (μ_globe = 0.05, μ_lid ≥ 0.1), all geometries remained in lower fornix
- Contact areas: 40–90 mm² on either side of hydrogel film
- Thickness-volume correlation: r = 0.659 (thickness), r = 0.738 (volume) at μ_lid = 0.175
- Geometry 7 showed least displacement across all tests (≤0.05 mm at μ_lid ≥ 0.1)
- Contact area correlations: r = 0.328 (total contact area), r = 0.340 (lid-to-globe contact area ratio) at μ_lid = 0.175
10_1007_s10439_017_1962_x.key_2:
- Boundary conditions: Posterior edge of eyelid fixed in translational degrees of freedom; globe fixed in all degrees of freedom; hydrogel film originated inside globe with eyelid lying flat in direct contact with globe
- Placement step: Hydrogel displaced out of globe by 2-4 mm (depending on geometry) to push eyelid away until hydrogel inner surface contacted globe outer surface; contact between globe and hydrogel muted during placement
- Rotation step: Globe rotated 60° around center axis to simulate upward eye movement (saccade); hydrogel displacement terminated and contact established between hydrogel and globe
- Contact interactions: Eyelid-globe contact defined as frictionless; hydrogel-globe contact defined with coefficient of friction (μ_globe); hydrogel-eyelid contact defined with coefficient of friction (μ_lid)
- Material constraints: Hydrogel modeled as hyper- and viscoelastic solid; lower eyelid modeled as isotropic linear-elastic solid (E=58.2 MPa); globe modeled as discrete rigid body
- Simulation type: Explicit solver; 3D finite element model; two-step simulation (hydrogel placement step followed by globe rotation step)
- Mesh specifications: Global seed sizes of 0.001 (globe), 0.0005 (eyelid), and 0.0003 (all film geometries)
- Material properties: Hydrogel density=1 g/cm³, Poisson's ratio=0.49; eyelid density=1.05 g/cm³, Poisson's ratio=0.49; globe diameter=22 mm, thickness=0.25 mm
- Friction parameters: μ_globe held constant at 0.05; μ_lid varied from 0.05-0.175; friction ratio (μ_lid:μ_globe) tested from 1 to 3.5
- Immobilization criterion: Center node displacement < 0.05 mm during rotation step
- Simulation time: 15 ms intervals measured from beginning of rotation step until simulation conclusion
10_1007_s10439_017_1962_x.key_3:
